passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: SERMON XXIV.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: ON PRAYER.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: “Behold a woman of Canaan, who came out of those coasts, saying: Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou Son of David! my daughter is grievously troubled by a devil.” MATT. xv.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: If ever the force and efficacy of prayer were discovered in a sensible and striking manner, was it not, Christians, in the example which this passage of the gospel exhibits? It discovers (says St. Ambrose) even a God surprised and struck with admiration. He confounds the powers of hell and darkness; works miracles and exerts his powers in behalf of a foreigner who hath recourse to him; and who, though an idolater, ought to serve us as a pattern, and teach us how to pray. Surprised he was, and struck with admiration: “O woman, great is thy faith!” Matt. xv. Thus, Christ explains himself. And do not her faith and the fervour of her prayer seem to give him surprise and unusual emotion? He confounds the powers of hell and darkness, and works miracles. For, what petition doth this woman make? That he would cure her daughter, who was cruelly worried by the evil spirit; and the Son of God, by one word speaking, not only restored the possessed daughter to her right mind, but sanctified the mother: “Be it unto thee as thou wilt.” Matt. xv.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: Nothing, therefore, is more efficacious with God than prayer. And yet, beloved hearers, how comes it that we find him, by daily experience, not inclined to hear our petitions? That although we pray, he hears us not? And that although we ask, we obtain nothing? This is what I now am about to examine, and this is to be the ground of the present discourse. It is a great subject, and of extreme consequence, and therefore deserving of particular reflection; for I mean to inculcate the most excellent of all sciences—that of using the most powerful means of salvation in a proper manner. I mean to let you know the inestimable method and divine art of obtaining admittance to the throne of God, and prevailing with him to send down upon us the most precious treasures of his holy grace. But in order to receive this gift of prayer, let us have recourse to prayer, and let us implore the divine aid in the usual form.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: There is nothing more solidly established in religion, and in Christian theology, than the infallibility of prayer. Such is the force of it, (says St. Chrysostom,) that it renders, it should seem, the word of man equally powerful in a manner with the word of God. Equally powerful: for as God, with a word created all things: “He said, and they were made;” (Ps. cxlviii.;) so man need but ask, and all is granted him: “Ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you.” John xv. Every day we hear Christians complain of the little advantage that accrues from prayer. Nor is it surprising. For how do we say that prayer is infallible? We suppose, to that purpose, a holy prayer: we suppose it performed with all the conditions that ought to attend it, and that God requires from us when he promises to grant whatever we shall ask. Now this is a common defect in our prayers. They are defective in regard to the matter and the form: in regard to the matter, which is the thing we pray for; and in regard to the form, which is the manner of praying. This, St. James told the faithful of his time: “Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss.” James iv. We ask not, in fact, for that for which God would have us ask; and this is a defect as to the matter of prayer. Neither do we ask in the manner in which he would have us ask; and this is a defect as to the form of prayer. But let us put up our prayers like the woman of Canaan. Nothing more proper than her prayer to Christ. She asks him to cast out the devil from her daughter. Nothing more engaging. In her prayer she puts all the virtue in practice which can gain upon our Saviour and move his heart. I say, let us pray like this woman, else our prayers are fruitless. Either because we ask not for the things for which we ought to ask: or, because we ask not for them in the manner in which we ought to ask for them.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: These are two lessons on which my duty obliges me to throw what light I can. Be attentive, Christians, and use your best endeavours to profit by them.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: PART I. It is on the nature of the things which we ask of God, that the very essence, and of course the merit, the efficacy, and the virtue of prayer depends; and St. Chrysostom tells us, that it is by this rule we must call ourselves to an account for the small value which God sets on all the prayers we offer, and the little effect they have in his sight. And this is the admirable instruction which the gospel affords us by the example of the woman of Canaan. For observe, if you please, (and may I be allowed to explain myself in this manner,) that whereas this woman, prostrate at the feet of our blessed Saviour, beseeches him to deliver her daughter from the power of the devil that possesses her; we, on the contrary, influenced by a spirit directly opposite, beg of God every day what preserves in our souls the dominion of the devil—nay of many devils, of which we are unwilling to be dispossessed. What more is necessaay [sic] to make you comprehend why the Saviour of the world gives ear to this foreigner, and works in her favour a miracle of his omnipotence; and why, on the contrary, God is deaf to our supplications and rejects our prayers for the greatest part? Apply your minds, beloved Christians, to the sublime doctrines which this subject will give me a favourable opportunity of displaying, as it includes the most important points concerning your predestination.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: I say we beg every day of God what preserves in our souls the dominion of Satan—because we beg of him things in our prayers, either prejudicial to salvation, or purely temporal and unprofitable for salvation; or even supernatural and divine graces, but which, seeing the manner in which we conceive them, and in which we desire them, far from sanctifying us, serve rather to seduce us and withhold and divert us from the way of salvation. These three positions I shall endeavour to explain with all the clearness and precision I am able.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: 1st. In our prayers to God we ask for things prejudical [sic] to salvation: the first obstacle which stops the course of the divine mercies. For we must not imagine, beloved hearers, that we are not, though Christians, addicted in practice to the irregularities of paganism. Now, if we may credit the pagans themselves, one of the irregularities of the pagans was to have recourse to their gods, and to ask of them that which they would not have asked of an honest man; which they would not have asked openly in the temple, or at the foot of the altar without a blush—as the death of a relation whose estate they longed for, or of a competitor at whose credit and merit they repined and envied—the ward’s inheritance which they meant to embezzle, and which they beheld with avaricious eyes. Such was the subject of their prayers. And, to give them more weight, they added the ceremonies of a superstitious worship, offerings, sacrifices, and corporal lustrations.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: To us, all this appears enormous and senseless. But, beloved Christians, in condemning them do we not pronounce sentence against ourselves? If we compare their prayers with our own, are we less culpable? What do I say? Are we not more culpable to a great degree? For, in short, they were pagans, and these pagans adored not only vain and false, but even vicious and dissolute deities, according to their own belief. Now what was more natural, than to ask of such deities that which favoured their vices, and the corruption of their morals? Was it not almost a necessary consequence of their infidelity? But, Christian brethren, the God whom we serve is as pure and holy as he is powerful and great; a God as essentially an enemy to injustice and to all sin, as he is God. And yet of this God, so pure, so holy, so equitable and just, what do we ask? The accomplishment of our wishes and sensual desires, and the success of our base and criminal undertakings. This is miscalled an irregular proceeding: it is, I am bold enough to say it, an impiety, a sacrilege.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: True it is, and I freely grant, that now a-days Christians have learned the method of giving their prayers a more specious appearance, and a better varnish, and of expressing them in terms not quite so invidious; for, modern dissimulation and artfulness are carried to the highest perfection. But, although we may impose upon our own weakness, we cannot deceive God Almighty who hears us, and sees us, and distinguishes between the malignity of our intentions and the simplicity of our expressions. To no purpose, therefore, doth the man of the world beg of God a subsistence suitable to his profession, and wherewithal to support him according to his rank: for as his rank, or rather the idea which he forms of his rank, is founded in the principles of an unbounded ambition, or rather an insatiable avarice, God’s infinite penetration discovers his designs, counteracts his schemes, and defeats his hopes. To no purpose doth the father of a family beg of God a settlement for his children in the world: for, as his views and schemes in their regard are profane and worldly, regulated neither by conscience nor by divine vocation, God Almighty overlooks the external appearance of an humble prayer, and knows its tendency; and, by a just judgment, far from raising this family to dignities, permits its ruin to all intents and purposes, letting it moulder away, or sink into obscurity. To no purpose doth the woman of the world beg of God health of body. For, whereas her health, considering the use to which she turns it, is productive only of sloth and idleness, of vicious delicacy, perhaps of libertinism and a disorderly life, God, who beholds it, instead of keeping back the weight of his arm, strikes the more severely, and deprives her in that habitual listlessness of what might feed her self-complacency, and flatter her vanity. To no purpose doth a man unjustly engaged in a law-suit, in which his whole fortune and dependence are at stake, beg of God to determine the cause in his favour: for as this law-suit is nothing, at bottom, but a covert injustice, maintained by chicanery, God Almighty, who knows it, in opposition to him espouses the cause of the widow and the orphan, and compels him to give up his pretensions with shame. Every means possible, however, are employed to move the will of God and procure his assistance. The very prayers, the very sacrifice of the church is interposed. But because this business, which is carried on so warmly, is nothing but the secret machinations of a junto, a wicked intrigue, which can succeed only to the detriment of their neighbour, God Almighty, the protector of the innocent and the poor, on this occasion rejects even the most holy prayers of the church, even the most adorable sacrament of the altar. These particulars, were I to set them forth in their full extent, would lead me too far. But were you, beloved hearers, to apply them to yourselves, you would soon perceive that hundreds of times your hearts have beguiled you in the same manner, and induced you to pervert the end of prayer, in order to obtain of God himself the gratification of your passions.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: But to return to that on which I was discoursing, and to depict this matter in the strongest colours of which it is susceptible, give me leave, Christians, to dwell a little longer on the morals of the pagans. I said they were enough to work conviction; but I said too little, and I add that in one sense, even in this place, they are more proper to put us to the blush than the doctrine of the fathers. Permit me, therefore, to make a profane author speak in this pulpit, and to impeach your conduct—either for your instruction, or for your confusion—as he did the manners of his own times in such spirited and energetic terms. Tell me, (says he,) deploring the abuses in ancient Rome, and upbraiding the false devotees of paganism, who importuned the gods with their unrighteous prayers; tell me your thoughts concerning Jupiter, and the place he holds in your estimation. Have you the same respect for the greatest of your gods as for the wisest of your magistrates. This question (continues he) surprises you. But I do not propose it without reason. For would you wait on this magistrate, whose virtue you revere, to offer him in his palace the infamous supplication which you make to Jupiter in the most awful of his temples? You, therefore, suppose Jupiter more liable to be corrupted, when you think him disposed to hearken to your prayers, and even ready to grant them a favourable hearing. Thus spoke a pagan upon this subject. In this sarcastic strain he reproached his fellow-subjects with the scandal of their religion, and perhaps was conducive to their reformation. Thus infidelity gives us wholesome lessons, and condemns the impropriety of our proceedings. Let us apply this to our own morals.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: And what must our notions be of our God, the God of holiness? Is he the promoter of our vices? The accomplice of our crimes. Is it possible he could, or would be such? From this source, however, flow all our actions, and our behaviour towards him. For when I pray—take with you in your minds this remark of St. Chrysostom—when I pray I expect, that God in his mercy and paternal condescension will conform to my wishes; that his divine will, efficacious and all-powerful, shall coincide with mine which is nothing but weakness; and that he will accomplish my desires, which without his aid would be to no purpose. Put then the case, that blinded by the spirit and maxims of the world, far from praying in a Christian manner, I pray with a view to satisfy my ambition, my pride, my resentment, my revengeful heart—what do I do? I ask God to agree with me upon these heads; that is, I wish he would be vain like myself, passionate like myself, violent like myself; and that for me, who am his creature, he would vouchsafe to do that which he cannot do without ceasing to be God. Now to address our prayers to him in this manner, would not be to pray to him as the God of heaven, but to dishonour in a high degree the most adorable of his attributes; it would be to make him, as far as on me depends, subservient to my iniquities, as he complains himself by the mouth of his prophet: “Thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast put me to pain with thy iniquities.” Isai. xliii. The expression is remarkable: “Thou hast put me to pain.” As who should say: your prayer hath given me uneasiness; for, on one hand, I would gladly have been propitious to it; and, on the other, I could not give it a favourable hearing; my heart was according in a kind of fluctuation, and, as it were, divided between my holiness and my goodness: my goodness which took part with you, and my holiness which was against you; my goodness which inclined me to compassionate your distress, and my holiness which obliged me to reject your supplication: “Thou hast put me to pain with thy iniquities.” And truly, Christians, if God in that case had made account of our prayers, would it not be a stumbling-block? Would it not make us call his providence in question?

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: I know that we have (as St. John informs us) the Son, a powerful advocate with the Father, and that we pray through the merits of this adorable Son. But to apply in particular to God made man what I said of God in a general way—would we make him the patron of our blind desires, by which we are swayed? And if this be not the sentiment by which we are impelled, why should we lay stress and dependence on his merits, in the prayers which our desires alone inspire?

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: Happy it is for you, that your gracious God, to obstruct your perdition, is inflexible to your prayers. In this seeming rigour you should acknowledge his mercy. What would become of you, were he more indulgent and more conformable to our inclinations? What hath been the ruin of, and what ruins daily, such numbers of families, but too vast and unlimited, nay, criminal wishes? What hath occasioned the eternal reprobation of so many Christians? Was it not the having obtained what God could not grant but in the excess of his wrath? And whence comes the loss of so many worldlings, who are damned amidst opulence, ease, and effeminacy, but from those supposed favours of God, who hears them and indulges the senseless desires of their heart, contrary to the designs of his amiable providence? You ask that of God which sooths your passion; and if he lends a favourable ear to your request, he who foresees that which will pervert you, that which will corrupt you, that which will plunge you into the mighty gulf, what more rigorous punishment can be inflicted? What more dreadful vengeance can be exerted? But to proceed:

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: 2ndly. If you do not ask always for things prejudicial, and with views directly contrary to salvation, you supplicate, at least, for things merely temporal and no way profitable to that end. I would not, however, be supposed to insinuate that the good things of this life are not the gifts of heaven, or that they are absolutely contrary to salvation. But when are they such—and on what account doth God refuse them? When we ask for them neither according to the order which himself hath established, nor relatively to the end which he hath pointed out to us.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: In the first place, regardless of spiritual favours, we ask only for temporal ones, as the advantages of fortune, prosperity, tranquillity, all which terminate in the necessaries of life. These we desire, and these we seek; and these are desired and sought by infidels, as well as by us: “For, all these things do the heathens seek.” Matt. vi. These are good things, I own: but they are perishable things—things of an order inferior to man, especially to a Christian man; dangerous things and liable to be perverted, though really good, into real evils. In regard to solid and incorruptible things, as purity of manners, a good conscience, humility, faith, the love of our neighbour, whatever may serve to sanctify the soul, and raise it to perfection, to our shame be it said, we supinely neglect and seldom revolve at the foot of the altar. Which of you hath ever had recourse to God with a view of becoming more moderate in his passions and more regular in his conduct? You visit the tombs of the martyrs, but why? To be cured of a distemper, not to be delivered from a temptation. You invoke the saints, but why? To be more happy and more opulent, not more humble and more an enemy to pleasures. Ah! cries Salvian, if we groan under the pressure of public calamities; if the land be threatened with famine or pestilence; if the people be swept away by a raging mortality, we run precipitately and in crowds to the temple of the living God, and our sighs, lamentations, and prayers are heard in every corner. But though unbridled libertinism dishonours Christianity, and brings grief to the church, we enjoy tranquillity and a peaceful mind. Instead of praying that heaven would put a stop to scandalous impieties, we suffer our days to pass in quietness and a dreadful indolence.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: Thus we pray like the wretched Antiochus, whose selfish prayer was unable to find grace in the presence of God: “This wicked man prayed unto the Lord, of whom he was not to find mercy.” Mach. ix. He prayed, neither can it be denied that he prayed with all possible ardour; he prayed, but he prayed in a worldly way; he prayed, but asked not for the spirit of penitence, or the gift of piety, or respect for the sacred things he hath profaned, but for health which he preferred to all the rest and of which he was fond to a great degree: “This wicked man prayed unto the Lord,” but the Lord shut the bowels of his mercy against him. We, too, pray in the same manner; but God never promised to warrant such prayers. Examine the gospel, and you will there find the reason of it.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: Christ says to his disciples: “If you shall ask the Father any thing in my name, he will give it you.” John xvi. But observe (says St. Augustin) these words, any thing, by which our Saviour lets us understand that what we ask in his name should be something, and something worthy of him, because it were improper, in the other supposition, that he should exert and manifest his power in our behalf. Now all the good things of the world together, considered disjunctively from eternal bliss, are as nothing in the presence of Almighty God. To ask, therefore, of God in this manner, is to ask for nothing; and although the promise of Christ is general, or should seem to be so, they are not by themselves comprised therein. In order to be convinced of it, hear what he adds, speaking to the apostles: “Hitherto ye have asked nothing in my name.” John xvi. And, indeed, to remain in his presence on Thabor was a delightful sensation of which St. Peter desired the continuance. To possess in his kingdom the chief places, was, according to the meaning of those two disciples, a vain honour which their ambition grasped at, because they beheld it through a false medium. But the zeal of souls, constancy in persecution, and self-denial, were the essential favours of which they stood in need, as no other favours could uphold and animate them, and raise them to perfection in their apostolic functions. For these, however, it never entered into their heads to petition their Master: “Hitherto ye have asked nothing.”

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: Now, of how many Christians might I not at this day make the same complaint? And of those who hear me, to how many might I not have just cause to say for the same reason: O man of the world, thou hast hitherto petitioned thy God for nothing, forasmuch as thou hast not, in thy sinful state, petitioned him for thy conversion, for an humble mind, for a contrite heart, for the grace to renounce thy evil habits, and to stifle and conquer thy vicious inclinations? This, however, was the signal grace, the grace of graces which thou oughtest to have asked for and sought with all diligence.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: Further: when the Saviour of the world assures us, in the gospel, that whatever we shall ask in his name shall be granted, he supposes we shall ask according to the rule which he hath himself laid down. For, as Tertullian well observes, it is he himself who regulates prayer, and quickens it with his Spirit, communicating to it the special power and privilege of penetrating into the highest heaven, and moving to compassion the heart of God, by laying before his all-seeing eyes the weaknesses and miseries of mankind. Now what is that rule, that divine rule by which Christ Jesus commands us to pray? Seek first, says he, the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and you shall want for nothing. Ask of my Father the sanctification of his name, the coming of his kingdom, the fulfilling of his will, not the material bread which serves for aliment, and then will I assist you. But if you run counter to this regulation, and, by an attachment to the world unbecoming your profession, you seek earthly bread before the kingdom of God, put your affiance no longer in my merits, however infinite, as your prayer how fervent soever it may be is not calculated according to the plan which I have sketched: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness.” Matt. vi. Not but we may ask for temporal blessings: the church herself is wont to do so. But let us ask for them like the church; let us ask for them after having first, and above all things, asked for spiritual favours; let us ask for the blessing conferred on Jacob and not on Esau. What a noble allegory doth the example of these two brothers exhibit! Mind the application I make of it to my subject. They had each to his share the dew af [sic] heaven and the fat of the earth. Where lies the difference; and by what special sign doth the scripture make appear the election of Jacob and reprobation of Esau? Ah! Christians, by this—that in the blessing conferred on Jacob, the dew of heaven is expressed antecedently to the fat of the earth: “God give thee of the dew of heaven and fatness of the earth;” whereas in the other, the fat of the earth is mentioned previously to the dew of heaven: “In the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above shall be thy blessing.” Gen. xxvii.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: This is what every day happens among us, and what discriminates prayers truly Christian from those which are not. A righteous man and a worldly-minded man put up their prayers in the same church, and before the same altar; but one prays righteously, and the other like a worldling. How? Doth one beg only the influence of grace, and the other nothing but earthly advantages? No: for it may so happen that the righteous man, with the influence of grace shall supplicate sometimes for an increase of fortune, as well as the worldly man; and that the worldly man shall ask with an increase of fortune the influence of grace, as well as the righteous man. But the worldly man, instigated by the spirit of the world, places an increase of fortune before the influence of grace, “the fatness of earth and the dew of heaven;” but the righteous man, prompted by the Spirit of God, prefers the influence of grace to an increase of fortune, “the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth.” He says to God: Lord, sanctify me; make me chaste, charitable, merciful, patient; give me the dew of heaven, and grant me forthwith the good things of this life, so far as they may conduce to my eternal welfare; give me the fatness of the earth. But the worldly man says: “Lord, make me rich, great, powerful; give me the fatness of the earth; neither refuse me the grace which is necessary to the leading of a virtuous life—give me the dew of heaven. An accursed prayer, which when we offer up, it is not to be wondered at, that God should reject it and hold it in execration.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: 3rdly. But let us proceed to the fountain-head; and, in order to discover on what rests the important doctrine I am expounding, take this sound principle of St. Cyprian with you: that your prayers have no virtue, but inasmuch as they are united with the intercession of Christ. For, it is only of Christ that we can say with St. Paul: “He was heard for his own reverence.” Heb. v. When the Almighty hears us, it is not in consideration either of what we are or of what we merit, as we are nothing of ourselves and can merit nothing; but in consideration of his only begotten Son, who prayed for us before we could pray for ourselves. Taking this for granted, how can those prayers, by which we petition for the things of this world in preference to heaven be acceptable to God, whereas, in that case they have no conformity or connexion with the prayers of the God-man who became our Mediator? What did he ask for us? You know it well. That we might be united by the bond of charity, “that we might be one;” (John xvii.;) that, without ostentation or dissimulation, we might be sanctified in truth; that, living in the midst and hurry of the world, according to our vocation and situation in life, we might have over ourselves a watchful eye, and be fortunate enough to keep clear of its iniquity: “I pray not,” says our Redeemer, “that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from evil.” John xvii. But what is our practice? We ask Almighty God for riches, honours, a vain reputation, an easy life; and without asking for them after salvation, or relatively to salvation, we ask for those riches, to wallow in plenty; for these honours, to make a figure in the world; for this reputation, to be known and distinguished; for this easy life, to enjoy the sweets of it; that is, we ask for those things for which our Saviour never meant to ask. And why did he not ask for them? Mind this reason. Because (says St. Cyprian) he could not but pray conformably to the end for which he was sent. Now he was sent as a Saviour, and his mission regarded the salvation only of mankind. It was, therefore, for the salvation only of mankind that he could labour, that he could suffer, that he could merit, and, by a necessary consequence, it was for the salvation only of mankind, and for whatever bore relation thereto, that he could pray.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: Wherefore, Christians, you ask but obtain not, because you ask not with Christ our Lord, and because, were your prayers, independently of this, capable to produce the intended consequence, you might say that favours were conferred on you without your being indebted to your Redeemer for them, which were blasphemy, according to the maxims of our religion. And on this basis it is that St. Augustin rests his argument, when he proves so solidly, that the things of this life are by no means the object of Christian hope. Let no one deceive himself, (says this holy doctor,) and vainly promise himself temporal felicity, because he appertains to Christ our Lord. Christ did not choose us for that end, nor call us to faith on that condition. Without failing in his word, he may leave us in poverty, debasement, and sufferings. True it is, he engaged his word to present our prayers before the throne of God; but he supposed we should pray, like Christians, for heaven where he placed our inheritance. And this excellent way of reasoning the same father made use of afterwards in opposition to the raillery of the pagans. You object to us, (says he,) that notwithstanding our prayers, we live in indigence and want of all things. But to wipe off thoroughly this reproach, and to justify our God, suffice it to say, that when we put up our prayers to heaven, we pray not precisely for the things appertaining to this life, but to eternity. If therefore, we are poor and needy in this world, the distressful situation in which we live, not only is no proof that our prayers are unprofitable, but gives us an assurance that the fruit of them is reserved for an immortal life.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: Such was the reply of the great St. Augustin, which he concludes with a reflection extremely affecting. In this (says he) we should admire the liberality of our God. He limits not his favours to the things of this world, because they are beneath us; because they are insufficient to satisfy our desires; because they are disproportionate to the nobleness of our being, and to the worth of our prayers. He would not put us in the category of children, who are pleased with trifles, and things of no moment; nor in that of idolaters, whose moral virtues he rewards in this life with apparent happiness. He will himself be our happiness—our reward. Ah! my brethren, let us therefore beware of mistaking in the choice of the things we ask. Let us place our confidence in the word of our God, who hath faithfully promised that he himself will be our reward; and as he hath promised, let us only petition that he would give himself to us. Many there are, St. Augustin tells us, who hope in God, but who hope for everything except God. Let us dread a separation so disadvantageous to us; and, as we hope for nothing but from the hand of God, let us hope for nothing but God, or things relating to God.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: 4thly. But I ask not for temporal favours of God; my prayers are offered up for supernatural grace—the grace of salvation; and yet I have it not. No, beloved hearers, you have it not I know; because even in that respect you are guilty of a third abuse in prayer, which perhaps you perceive not, but which I now shall make appear and lay before you.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: It is this; that instead of regarding prayer as the instrument which God hath put into our hands in order to procure the true grace of salvation, that is real and possible grace—grace regulated and proportionally adjusted to the divine appointment; we employ it for the imploring of chimerical grace, superfluous grace—grace adapted to our own taste and mistaken notions. My [m]eaning is this: we pray, and as we think with a true desire of obtaining salvation; but by a blind confidence, we rely on prayer, as though it were sufficient without good works; as though all depended on it; as though Christ Jesus in commanding us to pray, did not also command us to watch and do good; as though there were graces which might and should save us without our own co-operation. We pray, and ask the grace of a good death, persuaded that no more than to pray is required; and thus we remain without care or solicitude, or the trouble to merit it or to prepare for it by a good life. We pray, and ask the grace of penance and sanctification; but the grace we ask is for the future only; grace which should remove all difficulties and dangers, and leave no laborious endeavour to be made or obstacle to be surmounted; miraculous grace which should transport us like St. Paul, and not dispose us by little and little, and oblige us to proceed; grace which should accompany us wherever we went, which should be ready at hand on all occasions; which should allow us to expose ourselves to every kind of hazard, and not grace which it should import us to attend to watchfully, and make the best advantage of. That is, in short, we ask for grace that would change the whole order of divine providence, and annul the dispensation by which our eternal lot is ascertained.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: And now, Christians, let us close this first part with the prophet’s prayer: “One thing have I desired of the Lord, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the Lord.” Ps. xxvi. For (adds St. Augustin) I now perceive and thoroughly comprehend the reasons that induced you so often to reject the prayers of your servant. In order to answer the designs of your mercy I should have put up my prayers for things not common to me, and to pagans, and to impious men. You wanted that my prayers should distinguish me from the enemies of your holy name. Nevertheless I find that between their prayers and mine the difference was, that they for the most part obtained their request, and you generally refused me the things I petitioned for, either because they were contrary in themselves to salvation, or I asked not for them with a view to salvation. But in this, O Lord, I confess you favoured me; because those favours would have drawn me to perversion, whereas the paternal scourge of your justice hath been my amendment. By being happy in the world, I should have forgotten you the more easily; and if my wishes had been crowned with prosperity, I should have trodden in the footsteps of bad men. Accordingly, my God, far from complaining that you gave me the denial, I bless your holy name and reckon it as a favour that you heard me not according to the desires of my heart, but according to the order which your wisdom had established, and my salvation required. But henceforward, my God, you will hear my supplications, because they will only be offered up for things appertaining to eternity; because among the graces of salvation which I shall ask, I shall ask only for those which may be profitable to me—which may operate the most securely, and which may lead me the most directly to everlasting bliss. Thus, beloved Christians, the words of Jesus Christ will be fulfilled in our regard: we shall ask and shall receive. Whereas we receive not, either because we ask not for the things for which we ought to ask, as you have seen in the first part; or because we ask not for them in the manner in which we ought to ask for them, as I shall show you in the second.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: Part II. If God hears my prayers, it is on certain necessary and essential conditions. But, beloved hearers, in what manner soever he is pleased to deal by us, and in his providential wisdom to dispose and order things, it would be a gross error to suppose that the conditions required to the due performance of prayer were an obstacle to our wishes, and a motive which God used to refuse us his gifts. Ah! (cries St. Augustin) heaven forbid we should ever entertain or admit such notions, as nothing is more contrary to the goodness of God! He who does not stop (according to the scriptures) the course of his mercies, at the very time that we provoke him to anger: “Will he in his wrath keep in his mercies?” (Ps. lxxvi.) he who (according to the royal prophet) waits not for our prayers but beholds them, hearkening to mere desires: “Our Lord hath heard the desire of the poor;” (Ps. x.;) he who is so tender of us as to be affected with the very preparation of the heart: “The preparation of the heart thy ear hath heard;” (Ps. x.;) will he (if I may venture so to speak) be uncomplying when we invoke him with affection and sincerity? So far is he from availing himself of his greatness in the intercourse which he permits us to have with him by prayer, that we ought to confide that he will too indulgently and with too great condescension pass by our weaknesses, frailties, and imperfections. It cannot be denied that prayer, to be efficacious, should have certain qualities; but herein I maintain we cannot say that God withdraws his promises or withholds his graces. The reason is, that of these qualities there is not one which will not, on examination, be found easy in practice; not one of which the necessity is not justified by right reason; not one which is not required in a proportional degree between man and man; and (as I have already observed to you) not one of which the woman of Canaan hath not given us an example, and is not represented as a striking model. For, in short, (says St. Chrysostom, in the excellent homily which he composed on this subject,) what conditions doth God require for the infallibility of prayer? Humility, confidence, perseverance, attention of mind, and affection of heart. Now is there anything in all this, I do not say impracticable or impossible, but painful or burdensome?

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: 1st. Is anything more reasonable or even more natural, than to pray with the disposition of an humble mind? Is it possible to have a just idea of prayer, and forget this fundamental rule in our prayers? Do we otherwise offer our petitions to the princes and monarchs of the earth? Do we think it a hardship when we ask for favours, to pay homage and respect? And, if by this homage and this respect we compass our designs, do we murmur or complain as though our submission was ill bestowed? Do we say that they prize their favours too high, when they refuse them to the rash audacious man who demands them haughtily? And why should we make that objection to God, as it is much more reasonable, and consequently more easy to humble ourselves in his presence than in the presence of a man? Did the woman of Canaan make a difficulty to fall prostrate at the feet of Christ Jesus, and to pay him adoration? Was it a mighty effort to confess her unworthiness in that posture? And did she deem it a hardship to bear the repulse to which she was exposed? No, no, (says the Saviour of the world,) "it is not good to take the children's bread and cast it to dogs." Matt. xv. Could any comparison be more humiliating? But however humiliating it may be or seem to be, doth it seem to affect or afflict this woman? What do I say? Doth she not acknowledge the truth of those words by making the application of them to herself: "Yea, Lord?" Matt. xv.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: Such was this woman's way of praying: but which is ours? She was a pagan, and the pagan humbles herself: we are Christians, and bring with us to prayer a spirit of pride which we cherish in our breasts, at the same time that we are going to acknowledge our miseries and wants. And because this spirit hath dominion over us, we pray with presumption, as if God was obliged to consider us particularly, to treat us with distinction, and make account of our prayers. To say nothing of the ostentation which too frequently accompanies our offerings, and which instead of prevailing on God to hear us, induces him to punish us: to say nothing of the luxury we bear about us and display even in the house of God—of the grandeur and self-sufficiency we retain there; of the vain attitudes and artful negligence we affect there, directly contrary to the manner of a suppliant; all which (according to the sacred text) makes our prayers abominable in the sight of God, as he hates nothing more than "the poor man proud." Waving a detail of these matters, we ask favours of God—but we ask them as due; which if he graciously deign to grant we are puffed up and elated, but which if he refuse we murmur and complain. We ask them, and having received them, forget who it was that granted them. We employ them and use them without referring them to him. Can we then be surprised that he should have no bowels of compassion for us? Would it not be to dispense his favours and graces with a lavish hand—to bestow them indifferently on the proud and the humble?

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: 2ndly. Is anything more just than to pray with sentiments of a lively confidence? It is our sovereign Lord, our gracious God, who in his infinite mercy will be prayed to in that manner, and declares himself glorified by such confidence; who in a thousand places of the inspired writings attributes rather to it than to the divine mercy, (take not offence at this assertion, it is sound and orthodox,) when I say rather than to his very mercy the miraculous virtue and efficacy of prayer; not saying to those who have recourse to him and call upon him: it is my goodness and my power—but it is thy faith and thy confidence which hath been thy salvation: "Thy faith hath made thee whole." How could he have proposed a more advantageous condition? Did not the Canaanite, though an infidel, directly accept it? That openness of heart which she discovered to Christ by speaking to him in person: "Have mercy on me, O Lord;" (Matt. xv.;) that tender and affectionate motive which she used, with a view to move him, by calling him "Son of David;" those cries which she redoubled in proportion as the apostles reprimanded her importunity and commanded her to be silent: "Send her away, for she crieth after us;" (Matt. xv.;) that confidence with which she disclaimed all pretensions to the bread on the table, provided they furnished her with the crumbs that fell from it: that is, (according to St. Jerom's explanation,) to be resigned to, and content with the slightest efforts of our Saviour's power, convinced that it would be enough for the miraculous deed which she beseeched him to perform: "For the whelps partake of the crumbs which fall from their master's table." Matt. xv. Did not all this proceed from a soul that sincerely trusted in the God she invoked? What would she have done if, already a Christian, she had known Christ Jesus as perfectly as we do? If, instead of knowing him for the Son of David, she had known him for the Son of the living God? And yet is it not true that, notwithstanding all the ideas with which our religion furnisheth us of this God-man, scarce ever do we pray to him in that simple but heroical manner which the apostle hath marked out; I mean with faith, and without any doubt: "Let him ask in faith, nothing wavering." James i.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: Although Christ Jesus is so powerful to assist us, and although to overcome our incredulity and diffidence he engaged himself to us by the most solemn oath, swearing by himself; he who could not (as St. Paul testifies) have sworn by anything greater than himself; yet our diffidence and incredulity are more prevalent and carry it. We believe a man on his bare word, and we believe not the promise of God. We pray, but are inwardly at the same time disturbed; harbour vain disquietudes and carking agonies, and give ourselves up to a secret despondency. We have recourse to God, but always in extremity and when every other means of relief hath failed. We depend not so much on God as on ourselves, and place greater reliance on our prudence than our prayers. A strange infatuation, which St. Ambrose deplored, and which thoroughly manifests God's displeasure, when he withdraws his arm, and will not stretch it forth to our aid and relief.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: 3rdly. Is anything more expedient than to pray with perseverance? Is not God master of his own gifts? Who but himself hath power to dispose of them? Cannot he put them at what prices he pleases? And are not his graces sufficiently precious to be frequently asked and sought with perseverance? When Christ by his silence made trial of the woman I have mentioned from the gospel, "who answered not a word;" (Matt. xv.;) when he seemed by a severe and mortifying refusal inclined to neglect her and banish her from his presence; and when in her hearing he told the apostles that he was not sent for her: "I was not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel;" (Matt. xv.;) did she cease, on that account to pray, to solicit, to press with earnestness? No, Christians; the resistance of Christ increased her perseverance, and her perseverance outdid the resistance of Christ. The mystery was soon unfolded to her. She quickly comprehended the designs and inclinations of this God and Saviour; and seeing the necessity (as I may say) she was under of urging him, and even urging him by opposing real earnestness to seeming harshness, she broke through, in some measure, the laws of Providence; she deserved, though a foreigner, to be treated like an Israelite; she obtained a double miracle—the deliverance of her daughter from the evil spirit, and her own conversion to the true faith. O the charity of my bountiful God, (cries one of the fathers,) how adorable in your dissimulations and in the stratagems which you use to combat, in appearance, the very persons for whom in fact you combat. Wherefore, despair not, (adds he,) O Christian, who have begun to struggle with your God in prayer; for that kind of violence he loves to suffer, and it gives him pleasure to be disarmed by your hand. Neither must we imagine, (concludes he) my brethren, that this God of mercy can be invincible against us, who became, by a most astonishing prodigy, "weak, even unto death," upon our account.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: Such were the sentiments of the ancient fathers upon this head. But we, you well know, being influenced by an error directly opposite, hurried into the devious ways by frivolousness and volatility of mind, yield to God against his will. We yield to him, when he wishes, himself, to yield to us. We grow weary of telling him that we are poor, distressed, and in need of his assistance; and yet he is much pleased with our importunity. Assiduity of this kind is tiresome to us, provokes our patience, and causes disgust. We would have it be enough to present ourselves once. Delay appals us; and often on the point of obtaining our wishes, we lose all the merit and advantage of them. And tell me, at whose door ought the fault to be laid—at God's, or at our own?

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: 4thly. In fine, is anything more necessary and essential in our prayers to God, than attention of mind and affection of heart? I shall conclude with this point, which of all is much the most important. Attention of mind and affection of heart are what I call, with St. Thomas, the soul of prayer, without which it cannot any more subsist than a body without a soul, to quicken it and give it motion. For, what is prayer? Let us not here examine theological definitions, but the dictates of reason and good sense, and the common notions which mankind have of this holy exercise. What, then, is prayer? A conversation with God, in which the soul admitted and, if I may so express myself, introduced into the sanctuary, lays her wants before the Deity, represents her weaknesses, discovers her temptations, begs pardon for her unfaithfulness. And doth not all this suppose mental recollection, and inward sentiment? If, therefore, it so happen, that while I treat with God, my mind so wanders as absolutely and voluntarily to lose this internal attention and devotion, whatever else I may be said to do—I cannot be said to pray. Although I should sing laud and glory to the Lord; although I should spend whole days and nights at the foot of the altar; although, after the expression and example of David, I should be as it were fixed and glued to the ground—if I cease to be attentive, I cease to pray. And from hence, Christians, the angelical doctor made three deductions, to which I shall not make any addition, but which I earnestly beseech you to ponder for your edification. They will fully set forth the reasons why our prayers are disregarded and inefficacious in the presence of God.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: The first deduction. As it cannot be denied that attention is essentially requisite to prayer, we may say with great reason, but with still greater sorrow, that the exercise of it is, as it were, annihilated in the Christian world; because, if sometimes we seem to pray, it is without reflection. For, to what is all our piety reduced? To some prayers which we say with a dissipated and almost always absent mind. We move the lips, not like the godly mother of Samuel, on whom Heli, the high priest, passed so rash a judgment, but like the Jewish people, to whom God objected that their hearts were far from him while they praised him with their mouths. Thus our prayers are mostly hypocritical, and our blessed Saviour might well say to us what he said to the pharisees: "Ye hypocrites, well did Isaias prophecy of you, saying; this people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." Matt. xv. This disorder is not peculiar to the lower sort of people, whose intellectual coarseness is unhappily such, that day by day they say their prayers without praying, that is, without thinking either of what they say or of what they ask; nor to the devout sex, who, though addicted to prayer, make it their business to say a great deal without fixing the natural levity of their minds, or being at much pains to apply attentively. Men the most enlightened and the best instructed, men consecrated to God, the very ministers of God, by a deplorable perversion, from a habit of praying, pray not at all, and, instead of perfecting, corrupt and destroy so holy a practice.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: The second deduction. As prayer essentially includes attention, it follows that attention is, itself, of precept in those prayers which are strictly enjoined us. So that to pronounce the words is not then sufficient, but that a remarkable and voluntary evagation of mind should be looked upon as a grievous and deadly offence. Now this, my brethren, I say both on your account and my own, for that one of the principal engagements of your profession and mine consists therein, and for that vocal prayer is a kind of attribute which the church requires of us every day. And, indeed, it were strange that this action, in itself so holy—an action that naturally leads to holiness—should serve to condemn us, and that the origin of grace should be the source of reprobation. Nor let it be forgotten, that when we submitted to the obligation of reciting the Divine Office, we bound ourselves to perform an act of religion; that an act of religion is not a practice merely external; and that as the church, by enjoining confession enjoins contrition, so she enjoins attention by enjoining prayer. Whether this obligation arises from the precept of the church immediately, as some very able divines maintain, or from the precept naturally conjoined with that of the church, in virtue of which God commands us to perform holily and worthily the thing prescribed, as others imagine: however it be, the difference is only a scholastic question; and in either opinion we equally violate the laws of religion. Ah! my brethren, let us not draw down that curse upon us with which the prophet, in the excess of his zeal, threatened the sinner, when he said: "Let his prayer become sin." And is it not probable that this is applicable to numbers of those who attend at the altar? With far greater reason ought we to accuse ourselves than the great St. Augustin, who condemned himself for negligence in this behalf.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: The third and last deduction. God, therefore, with justice, rejects our prayers, as they resemble nothing so little as prayer—and as, far from honouring him, they are offensive to him and irritate him against us. For, what an injustice, beloved hearers! You expect that God will take heed of your prayers, when you chose to pray, and are heedless yourself of the words you utter. You say with the prophet: “O Lord, give ear unto my words, hearken to the voice of my prayer, (Ps. v.,) and suffer your mind at the same time to rove through various and useless objects. You desire him to speak to you, and you speak not to him; you desire him to hearken to you, and you hearken not to him: you hearken not to yourself, you wilfully distract yourself.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843
passages.text: Let us only reform, beloved Christians, in this one point, and a thorough reformation of life will ensue; for, according to St. Augustin, “he knows how to live well who knows how to pray well.” Why are we subject to so many lapses? Either because we pray not at all, or not as we should; and this, because we are unwilling to relinquish our inordinate ways, and fear to be led into the right path. Let us ask things of God worthy both of him and of ourselves, and in a manner worthy both of him and of ourselves. In a word, let us ask him as we ought to do, for graces and favours and we shall obtain them; but, above all, let us ask for the gift of prayer. Let us say like the apostle, Lord teach us to pray; our weakness is such that we cannot, without you, lay our wants before you, or implore your assistance in a proper manner. It is only yourself that can make us efficaciously feel our wants, that can bring us to the foot of your altar with a view to represent to you; that can inspire us with words and sentiments proper to move your heart. Give us, therefore, my God, yourself, that knowledge so necessary for us; and by a special grace in which are included, as in their origin, all the other graces, teach us to use prayer in order to procure the graces of conversion, of sanctification, of salvation, which may lead us to the mansions of eternal repose.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: This is an abridged historical counterpart of the French sermon, not an unabridged translation. Carroll's underlying French edition has not been identified here; the comparisons describe differences from the 1716 French edition used in this library without establishing the cause of each difference. His heading supplies no occasion. The French Thursday heading and the separate calendar browse mapping remain unchanged. Duplicate Latin/French quotations often become a single English quotation; the French edition's marginal references remain its own apparatus, available with the AI version or in Original only.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: The French explicitly concludes the introduction by asking heavenly aid through Mary's intercession and saying 'Ave, Maria.' Carroll replaces that invocation with 'in the usual form.'

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: The French adds a qualified claim that prayer makes man's word 'even more powerful' in a certain respect: God commands creatures, while through prayer God himself listens to man's voice. It supports this with the Joshua 10 quotation 'the Lord obeying the voice of a man.' Carroll omits that claim and explanation, retaining only the comparison of equal power.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: The French concludes this example with 'even the most adorable sacrifice, even the holiest prayers of his Church.' Carroll reverses the order and substitutes 'sacrament of the altar' for 'sacrifice.' Both editions' surrounding discussion concerns attempts to enlist the Church's prayer and sacrifice for unjust purposes; Carroll earlier retains 'the very sacrifice of the church.'

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: Carroll condenses the French's classical example, omitting the names Pompey and Caesar and the quotation about malign divinities. The warning that criminal wishes can destroy families remains.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: The French separately rebukes the worldly person for never asking detachment from and contempt for the world, then rebukes the sinner for never asking conversion and a contrite heart. Carroll combines the addresses and retains the conversion appeal, omitting the distinct request for detachment. The French identifies 'those two disciples' as the sons of Zebedee.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: The French says not to ask for material bread first. Its point is the order of petitions, not a prohibition of asking bodily necessities. Carroll drops 'first' from this clause, although the following sentences preserve that distinction and explicitly permit requests for temporal blessings.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: The French reads 'Excellente oraison' ('excellent prayer'); Carroll calls it 'this excellent way of reasoning.' This library retains the French reading without silently changing it to 'raison' ('reasoning'). The historical version's wording is a separate witness, not proof that the French should be emended.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: Printed page 174 has an ink-obscured initial letter in 'meaning'; 'eaning' is visible. The bracketed [m] is supplied from the immediate context, not claimed as a fully legible letter. Carroll's printed '4thly.' is followed by 'a third abuse'; both are retained.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: The French conclusion explicitly permits asking for other goods insofar as they are subordinate to eternal goods. Carroll compresses the conclusion and does not retain that clause here; his earlier discussion also permits properly ordered temporal requests.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: Carroll combines the Part II heading and two French paragraphs, retaining the listed conditions of prayer but condensing their introduction. Citations belong to their respective editions: the French margin prints Psal.6. here; Carroll prints Ps. x. Neither locator is silently harmonized.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: The French additionally asks whether God should hear the proud person's prayer at the cost of his own glory. Carroll compresses this part of the humility argument.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: The French opening refers to what Christ has done to help us; Carroll instead emphasizes Christ's power to assist. The French ends by saying this justifies God's conduct toward us, whereas Carroll writes that it 'manifests God's displeasure'. These are differences in historical wording, not changes made for this library.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: Carroll prints 'the woman I have mentioned from the gospel,' followed by 'who answered not a word'; this wording can ambiguously attach the silence to the woman. The French explicitly attributes the silence to Jesus Christ; the woman continues petitioning, as Carroll's surrounding paragraph also describes. His next paragraph condenses the French discussion of perseverance and omits its Sirach and Isaiah exhortations to wait.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: Where Carroll says they should consider 'what they say' while praying, the French asks them to consider to whom they are speaking. Both passages insist on attentive prayer and criticize deliberate distraction.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: Carroll prints 'vocal prayer is a kind of attribute'; the French calls vocal prayer a sacred tribute that the Church requires daily. 'Attribute' is retained as historical wording, not a correction to 'tribute.' The passage's qualifications concerning serious fault, voluntary and notable distraction, and the Divine Office remain in Carroll.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: Carroll shortens the French's sequence of Psalm invocations and prints an opening quotation before 'O Lord' without a closing mark, followed by '(Ps. v.,)'. The French says 'you do not understand yourself'; Carroll writes 'you wilfully distract yourself.' These historical readings and punctuation are retained.

passages.label: A. Carroll · 1843 editorial note
passages.text: Carroll prints 'Let us say like the apostle' (singular), 'with a view to represent to you' without an expressed object, and 'Give us, therefore, my God, yourself, that knowledge'. The French has the Apostles (plural), asks God to bring us to his altar to represent our miseries, and asks him himself to give this necessary knowledge. Carroll's awkward syntax is retained; his ending 'eternal repose' renders the French conclusion 'glory, &c.' without reproducing its abbreviation.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: In this Ash Wednesday sermon, Bourdaloue presents ashes as a reminder of mortality and a summons to penitence. Its two parts call for the humbling of pride and the mortification of the body. He addresses converts newly received into the Catholic Church.

passages.label: French original
passages.text: AUTRE SERMON POUR LE MERCREDI DES CENDRES.

passages.label: English
passages.text: ANOTHER SERMON FOR ASH WEDNESDAY

passages.label: French original
passages.text: Sur la Cérémonie des Cendres.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the Ceremony of Ashes

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Pulvis es, & in pulverem revertéris.

passages.label: English
passages.text: You are dust, and to dust you will return.

passages.label: French original
passages.text: Vous êtes poussiére, & vous retournerez en poussiére. Dans la Genese, chap. 3.

passages.label: English
passages.text: You are dust, and you will return to dust. In Genesis, chapter 3.

passages.label: French original
passages.text: CE sont les mémorables paroles, que Dieu dit au premier homme dans le moment de sa désobéissance: & ce sont celles que l'Eglise adresse en particulier à chacun de nous par la bouche de ses ministres dans la cérémonie de ce jour. Paroles de malédiction, dans le sens que Dieu les prononça; mais paroles de grâce & de salut, dans la fin que l'Eglise se propose, en nous les faisant entendre. Paroles terribles & foudroyantes pour l'homme pécheur, puisqu'elles lui signifiérent l'arrêt de sa condamnation; mais paroles douces & consolantes pour le pécheur pénitent, puisqu'elles lui enseignent la voie de sa conversion & de sa justification. Ainsi, remarque saint Chrysostome, Dieu en a-t-il souvent usé, & s'est-il servi du même moyen, tantôt pour imprimer aux hommes la terreur de ses jugemens, & tantôt pour leur faire éprouver l'efficace de ses miséricordes.

passages.label: English
passages.text: THESE are the memorable words God spoke to the first man at the moment of his disobedience; they are also the words the Church addresses to each of us personally, through the mouths of her ministers, in today's ceremony. They were words of malediction in the sense in which God pronounced them, but words of grace and salvation in the purpose the Church has in making us hear them. They were terrible, thunderous words for sinful man, announcing the sentence of his condemnation; but they are gentle, consoling words for the repentant sinner, teaching him the way to conversion and justification. As Saint John Chrysostom observes, God has often acted in this way, using the same means at one time to impress upon men the terror of his judgments, and at another to make them experience the power of his mercies.

passages.label: French original
passages.text: Je ne sçais, Chrétiens, si vous avez jamais fait réflexion à ce que nous lisons dans le livre de l'Exode. Ecoutez-le: l'application vous en paroîtra naturelle, & elle convient parfaitement à mon sujet. Quand Dieu voulut punir l'Egypte, il commanda à Moïse de prendre dans sa main une poignée de cendres; & en présence de Pharaon, de la répandre sur tout le peuple: Tollite manus plenas cineris, & spargat illum Moyses coram Pharaone. L'Ecriture ajoute que cette cendre ainsi dispersée, fut comme la matière, dont Dieu forma ces fléaux qui affligèrent toute l'Egypte, & qui y causérent une désolation si générale: Sitque pulvis super omnem terram AEgypti. A en juger par l'apparence, Dieu fait aujourd'hui le même commandement aux ministres de son Eglise. Il veut que les Prêtres de la loi de grâce, comme dispensateurs de ses mystéres, prennent la cendre de dessus l'autel, & qu'ils la répandent solemnellement sur tout le peuple Chrétien: Tollite manus plenas cineris. Mais dans l'intention de Dieu, l'effet de cette cérémonie est par rapport au Christianisme, bien différent de ce qu'elle opéra dans l'ancienne loi. Car au lieu que Moïse & Aaron ne répandirent la cendre sur les Egyptiens, que pour leur faire sentir le poids de la colère de Dieu; que pour marquer à Pharaon, qu'il étoit réprouvé de Dieu; que pour dompter l'impiété & l'endurcissement de ce Monarque livré dès-lors à la vengeance de Dieu: par une conduite toute opposée, les Prêtres de la loi nouvelle ne répandent aujourd'hui la cendre sur nos têtes, que pour nous attirer les grâces & les faveurs du même Dieu, que pour nous mettre en état & nous rendre capables d'en éprouver la bonté, que pour exciter dans nos coeurs les sentimens d'une véritable pénitence. C'est ce que j'entreprends de vous faire voir, & par où je commence à m'acquitter auprès de vous du ministére dont Dieu m'a chargé & que j'ai à remplir pendant tout ce saint tems du Carême.

passages.label: English
passages.text: Christians, I do not know whether you have ever reflected on what we read in Exodus. Listen: you will find the application natural and perfectly suited to my subject. When God wished to punish Egypt, he commanded Moses to take a handful of ashes and scatter it over all the people in Pharaoh's presence: ‘Take handfuls of ashes, and let Moses scatter them before Pharaoh.’ Scripture adds that the ashes thus dispersed became, as it were, the material from which God formed the plagues that afflicted all Egypt and caused such general devastation: ‘Let it become dust over the whole land of Egypt.’ Judging by appearances, God gives the same command today to the ministers of his Church. He wishes the priests of the law of grace, as stewards of his mysteries, to take ashes from the altar and solemnly scatter them over all the Christian people: ‘Take handfuls of ashes.’ But in God's intention the effect of this ceremony in Christianity is very different from what it accomplished under the old law. Moses and Aaron scattered ashes over the Egyptians only to make them feel the weight of God's anger, to show Pharaoh that God had rejected him, and to subdue the impiety and hardness of this monarch already handed over to God's vengeance. By an entirely opposite course, the priests of the new law scatter ashes on our heads today only to draw down upon us the graces and favours of that same God, to prepare us and make us capable of experiencing his goodness, and to awaken in our hearts the sentiments of true repentance. This is what I undertake to show you, and how I begin to fulfil among you the ministry God has entrusted to me throughout this holy season of Lent.

passages.label: French original
passages.text: Vous, mes Fréres, qui par la miséricorde du Seigneur, avez enfin renoncé au schisme pour vous réunir à l'Eglise. Vous, pour qui je suis particuliérement envoyé, que je regarde ici comme le premier objet de mon zéle, & plaise au ciel que je puisse vous appeller un jour ma couronne & ma joie, Gaudium meum & corona mea! Vous, dis-je, nouvelle conquête de la grâce de Jesus-Christ, apprenez à respecter une de ces cérémonies religieuses dont use l'Eglise Catholique, dans le sein de laquelle vous êtes rentrés. Il y en a de plus essentielles: mais sans parler des autres, ou pour juger des autres par celle-ci comment l'hérésie l'a-t-elle pû rejetter, puisque l'Auteur même de cette fatale division où vous fûtes malheureusement engagés, reconnoît que les cérémonies peuvent aider la piété des fidéles; qu'il est non-seulement bon, mais nécessaire d'en conserver quelques-unes; que pour n'être plus dans la loi de Moïse, il ne s'ensuit pas qu'il les faille toutes abolir; qu'il est juste que par des signes extérieurs l'on montre les sentimens de religion qu'on a dans le coeur, & que d'ôter tout ce qui s'appelle cérémonie, c'est mettre parmi le troupeau une confusion monstrueuse: Or entre les cérémonies, quelle autre a dû moins blesser l'Eglise Protestante que la cérémonie des cendres? Qu'a-t-elle de superstitieux? qu'a-t-elle qui ne soit autorisé par l'Ecriture? quel souvenir nous est plus utile que celui de notre foiblesse, de notre néant; & n'est-ce pas là ce qu'elle nous remet devant les yeux? Cependant cette cérémonie dont la simplicité & la sainteté devoient édifier, a été un scandale pour ces ministres que vous avez suivis. Ils l'ont réprouvée, & ils vous l'ont fait réprouver comme eux, parce qu'ils ne la connoissoient point assez, ou parce qu'ils ne vous la faisoient point assez connoître. Mais oublions le passé; & bénissons Dieu du présent. Bénissons-le même par avance de l'avenir, qui nous promet l'entier accomplissement de ce grand ouvrage que le Seigneur a commencé. Nous nous unirons tous; & tous de concert nous conspirerons à le soutenir, à le perfectionner, à le consommer. Qu'il me soit permis d'en faire ici le voeu solemnel & public; ce ne sera pas en vain. Oui, mon Dieu, votre oeuvre s'achèvera, votre nom sera glorifié, votre loi observée, votre Eglise reconnue: vous verserez sur mes Auditeurs vos grâces les plus abondantes; vous les verserez sur moi, & elles donneront de l'efficace à mes paroles. C'est pour cela même encore que je m'adresse à Marie, & que je lui dis, Ave, Maria.

passages.label: English
passages.text: You, my brethren, who by the Lord's mercy have at last renounced schism to be reunited with the Church; you for whom I have been especially sent, whom I regard here as the first object of my zeal—and may heaven grant that one day I may call you my crown and my joy, ‘my joy and my crown’! You, I say, newly won by the grace of Jesus Christ, learn to respect one of those religious ceremonies used by the Catholic Church, into whose bosom you have returned. There are more essential ceremonies; but without discussing the others—or, to judge the others by this one—how could heresy reject it? For the very author of that fatal division in which you were unhappily involved acknowledges that ceremonies can assist the piety of the faithful; that it is not only good but necessary to retain some of them; that no longer being under the law of Moses does not mean we must abolish them all; that it is right to show by outward signs the religious sentiments of the heart; and that removing everything called ceremony introduces monstrous confusion into the flock. Now among these ceremonies, which should have offended the Protestant Church less than the ceremony of ashes? What is superstitious about it? What does it contain that is not authorized by Scripture? What reminder is more useful than that of our weakness and our nothingness? And is that not what it sets before our eyes? Yet this ceremony, whose simplicity and holiness ought to have edified, became a stumbling block to those ministers you followed. They condemned it and made you condemn it with them, because they did not understand it sufficiently, or did not make it sufficiently understood by you. But let us forget the past and bless God for the present. Let us even bless him in advance for the future, which promises the full accomplishment of the great work the Lord has begun. We shall all unite and work together to sustain, perfect, and complete it. Allow me to make that solemn and public vow here; it will not be in vain. Yes, my God, your work will be completed, your name glorified, your law observed, your Church acknowledged. You will pour out your most abundant graces upon my hearers; you will pour them upon me, and they will give power to my words. For this same purpose I turn also to Mary and say to her: Hail Mary.

passages.label: French original
passages.text: IL ne suffit pas pour la foi de croire de coeur, si l'on ne confesse de bouche: c'est ce que saint Paul nous déclare en termes exprès; & à quoi j'ajoute, suivant la doctrine du même Apôtre, qu'il ne suffit pas pour la pénitence d'avoir un coeur contrit & humilié, si le pécheur au même tems n'offre à Dieu en forme d'hostie, une chair mortifiée & crucifiée avec ses désirs corrompus. Tel est, dit S. Grégoire Pape, le devoir de l'homme, qui se trouvant composé d'une ame & d'un corps, d'une ame spirituelle & toute céleste, d'un corps terrestre & tout matériel, doit selon l'un & l'autre honorer Dieu, s'il veut rendre à Dieu ce culte raisonnable, en quoi consiste l'intégrité de la religion.

passages.label: English
passages.text: FOR faith it is not enough to believe in the heart without confessing with the mouth: Saint Paul tells us this in express terms. Following that same Apostle's teaching, I add that for repentance it is not enough to have a contrite and humbled heart unless the sinner at the same time offers God, as a sacrificial victim, a flesh mortified and crucified with its corrupt desires. Such, says Pope Saint Gregory, is man's duty: composed of soul and body, a spiritual and wholly heavenly soul and an earthly and wholly material body, he must honour God in both if he wishes to offer God that reasonable worship in which the wholeness of religion consists.

passages.label: French original
passages.text: Excellent principe que je suppose d'abord & d'où je conclus que la pénitence Chrétienne prise dans toute son étendue, est donc un double sacrifice que Dieu exige de nous. Sacrifice de l'esprit, & sacrifice du corps: sacrifice de l'esprit, par l'humilité de la componction; & sacrifice du corps, par l'austérité même extérieure de la satisfaction: sacrifice de l'esprit, sans lequel, comme nous l'enseigne le maître des Gentils, le sacrifice du corps ne sert à rien ou presque à rien, ni ne peut jamais appaiser Dieu; & sacrifice du corps, sans quoi le sacrifice de l'esprit n'est souvent qu'une illusion & un phantôme devant Dieu. En sorte que l'union de ces deux sacrifices est absolument nécessaire pour rendre parfait l'holocauste dont je parle, & d'où dépend l'entiére réconciliation de l'homme pécheur avec Dieu.

passages.label: English
passages.text: This excellent principle is my starting point. From it I conclude that Christian penance, taken in its full extent, is a double sacrifice God requires of us: a sacrifice of the spirit and a sacrifice of the body. The spirit is sacrificed through humble compunction, and the body through the austerity, even outward austerity, of satisfaction. Without the sacrifice of the spirit, as the teacher of the Gentiles instructs us, bodily sacrifice is of no use or almost none, and can never appease God; without the sacrifice of the body, the sacrifice of the spirit is often only an illusion and a phantom before God. The union of these two sacrifices is therefore absolutely necessary to perfect the whole burnt offering of which I speak, upon which sinful man's complete reconciliation with God depends.

passages.label: French original
passages.text: Je m'attache à cette pensée qui me conduit naturellement à mon sujet: & parce que ces deux sacrifices que la pénitence doit faire à Dieu, trouvent en nous deux grands obstacles, dont le premier est l'esprit d'orgueil, & le second l'esprit de mollesse; l'esprit d'orgueil, incompatible avec l'humilité de la pénitence; l'esprit de mollesse essentiellement opposé à l'austérité de la pénitence: je veux pour ne vous rien dire aujourd'hui qui ne soit utile & pratique, vous apprendre à les surmonter par le souvenir de la mort que nous retrace l'Eglise dans la cérémonie des cendres. C'est tout le dessein de ce discours, que je réduits à deux propositions. Il faut par une pénitence solidement humble, anéantir devant Dieu l'orgueil de nos esprits; & c'est à quoi nous oblige la vue de ces cendres, qui sont pour nous les marques & comme les symboles de la mort: ce sera le premier point. Il faut par une pénitence généreusement austére, sacrifier à Dieu la mollesse & la délicatesse de nos corps; & c'est à quoi nous engage l'imposition de ces cendres, qui nous annoncent, ou plutôt qui nous font déjà sentir l'inévitable nécessité de la mort: ce sera le second point. Humiliation de l'esprit sous le joug de la pénitence, mortification de la chair dans l'exercice de la pénitence: deux fruits du saint usage que nous devons faire de ces cendres consacrées par la bénédiction des prêtres, & de la pensée de la mort que nous rappelle une cérémonie si touchante. Donnez-moi votre attention.

passages.label: English
passages.text: I hold to this thought, which leads naturally to my subject. These two sacrifices that penance must offer to God encounter two great obstacles in us: first, the spirit of pride; second, the spirit of self-indulgence. Pride is incompatible with the humility of penance, and self-indulgence essentially opposed to its austerity. Wishing to say nothing today that is not useful and practical, I shall teach you to overcome them through the remembrance of death that the Church sets before us in the ceremony of ashes. That is the whole purpose of this discourse, which I reduce to two propositions. Through truly humble penance we must bring the pride of our spirits to nothing before God; the sight of these ashes, marks and symbols of death for us, obliges us to do so: this will be the first point.
