C'est assez qu'un tel ait parlé de telle maniere, pour engager un tel à tenir un langage tout différent. C'est assez que celui-ci estime telle chose, pour porter celui-là à la condamner: comme si l'on n'avoit point d'autre règle, ou pour penser, ou pour agir, qu'une aveugle obstination à ne s'accommoder au gré de personne, & à ne convenir avec personne. Dans l'adorable Trinité point d'intérêts séparés: mais parmi nous mille intérêts qui nous divisent. On ne pense qu'à soi-même, on n'a égard qu'à soi-même, on rapporte tout à soi-même. Et comme cet intérêt propre à quoi l'on est résolu de ne rien refuser, ne peut souvent s'accorder avec l'intérêt du prochain, il n'y a point d'injustice & de violence à quoi l'on ne se porte, pour écarter ou pour détruire tout ce qui pourroit faire obstacle & arrêter les desseins qu'on a formés. De-là les mauvais tours, les trahisons, les faux rapports, les médisances, les calomnies, les chicanes, les procès, toutes les vexations qu'inspire la cupidité & qui ruinent la charité. C'est sur quoi l'Apôtre s'expliquoit encore avec tant d'éloquence & tant de zèle en parlant aux Corinthiens. Il avoit appris qu'ils s'appelloient les uns les autres devant les tribunaux de la justice pour terminer leurs différends, & là-dessus que leur disoit-il? Ah! mes Freres, que ne souffrez vous plutôt l'injure qu'on vous fait? Quare non magis injuriam accipitis? Que ne souffrez-vous plutôt le dommage que vous recevez? Quare non magis fraudem patimini? Mais bien loin, poursuivoit le saint Apôtre, d'être ainsi disposés à pardonner & à souffrir, vous vous outragez mutuellement & vous travaillez à vous entredétruire: Sed vos injuriam facitis & fraudatis. Ce qui le touchoit davantage, & ce qu'il leur reprochoit plus vivement, c'est que des freres, que des Chrétiens, se traitassent de la sorte: Et hoc fratribus. Comme s'il leur eût dit: Que des païens ayent ensemble des démêlés, je n'en suis point surpris; ils ont des Dieux qui leur en donnent l'exemple: mais nous, qui dans le Dieu que nous adorons, avons le modèle de la plus parfaite unité, d'une unité constante, d'une unité indivisible, d'une unité éternelle, qu'on nous voye former entre nous des partis, des intrigues, des cabales, que pour les moindres intérêts, & pour de viles prétentions dont nous ne voulons rien relâcher, on voye des fidèles s'élever contre des fidèles, parler contre des fidèles, agir contre des fidèles: Et hoc fratribus: c'est ce qui m'étonne, & ce que je n'accorde pas avec le caractère de leur religion.

passages.label: English
passages.text: But what do we see? The exact opposite, which we cannot deplore enough. No unity in Christianity, even among those whom nature's most inviolable and sacred laws should bind closely together. I mean, no unity among whom? Often among relatives; often among brothers and sisters; often among fathers and children. I say more: often no unity among ministers of Jesus Christ who, by their state and profession, ought nevertheless to be ministers of peace; often among persons consecrated to the God of peace by the most solemn vows, wearing the same habit and living under the same rule. This is what we see. Why? Because we do not know how—or rather, because we refuse—to form ourselves upon the great model faith places before our eyes. Take heed: in the adorable Trinity there are no opposed sentiments; what one divine person wills, the others will. Among us, however, there are endless contradictions. Whether through caprice of temper, malice of disposition, pride of mind or the false glory of never yielding, whatever the source of the evil, we have our private ideas and insist that they prevail over everything; we have our whims and insist that they be followed in everything. Because we do not always find people docile enough to submit to our whims and ideas, because on the contrary everyone claims to dominate, to be heard, to carry the day, there arise controversies and disputes, wars that begin in the mind and end in the heart, bitterness and a malicious determination always to set ourselves against one another. It is enough that one person has spoken in a particular way to induce another to speak quite differently. It is enough that this person esteems something to make that person condemn it, as though we had no other rule for thinking or acting than a blind obstinacy in accommodating no one and agreeing with no one. In the adorable Trinity there are no separate interests; among us there are a thousand interests that divide us. We think only of ourselves, consider only ourselves, refer everything to ourselves. Since this self-interest, to which we are resolved to refuse nothing, often cannot agree with our neighbour's interest, there is no injustice or violence we will not commit to remove or destroy everything that might obstruct and frustrate the designs we have formed. Hence come malicious tricks, betrayals, false reports, detraction, calumnies, quibbles, lawsuits, all the harassments that covetousness inspires and that ruin charity. This is what the Apostle also expressed with such eloquence and zeal when speaking to the Corinthians. He had learned that they summoned one another before courts of justice to settle their disputes. What did he say to them? Ah, my brothers, why do you not rather suffer the wrong done to you? Why do you not rather accept injury? Why do you not rather suffer the loss you receive? Why do you not rather endure fraud? But far from being thus disposed to forgive and suffer, the holy Apostle continued, you wrong one another and labour to destroy one another: But you yourselves do wrong and defraud. What moved him still more, and what he reproached them for more sharply, was that brothers, Christians, should treat one another in this way: And this to brothers. As if he had said to them: I am not surprised that pagans have disputes with one another; they have gods who set them the example. But we, who have in the God we adore the model of the most perfect unity, a constant, indivisible, eternal unity: that we should be seen forming parties, intrigues and factions among ourselves; that for the slightest interests and sordid claims of which we will yield nothing, the faithful should be seen rising against the faithful, speaking against the faithful, acting against the faithful—And this to brothers—this is what astonishes me, and what I cannot reconcile with the character of their religion.

passages.label: French original
passages.text: Appliquons-nous à nous-mêmes ces reproches, Chrétiens Auditeurs; car ils ne nous conviennent que trop: & en quels termes se fût exprimé saint Paul, s'il eût été témoin de notre conduite, je veux dire de nos animosités, de nos envies, de nos ressentimens, de nos vengeances, de tant d'éclats scandaleux qui font le sujet des entretiens du monde, & que le monde lui-même est le premier à condamner? C'est à vous, ô Dieu de la charité & de la paix, c'est à vous à maintenir parmi nous l'une & l'autre, ou plutôt à les y établir: car elles ne sont que trop altérées. Pere tout-puissant, vous avez formé nos cœurs, & vous êtes toujours maître de les tourner comme il vous plaît. Fils égal à votre Pere, & éternel comme lui, mais fait chair pour nous, vous nous avez rassemblés sous une même loi, & c'est une loi d'amour. Esprit Saint, vous êtes l'amour substantiel du Pere & du Fils, & c'est par vous que la charité est répandue dans les ames. Trinité souverainement adorable & aimable, c'est de votre sein que nous sommes tous sortis, & c'est dans votre sein que vous voulez tous nous rappeler. Unissez-nous sur la terre, comme nous devons l'être dans l'éternité bienheureuse, où nous conduise, &c.

passages.label: English
passages.text: Let us apply these reproaches to ourselves, Christian hearers, for they fit us only too well. In what terms would Saint Paul have expressed himself had he witnessed our conduct—I mean our animosities, envies, resentments, acts of revenge, all those scandalous outbursts that are the subject of the world's conversation and that the world itself is the first to condemn? It is for you, God of charity and peace, it is for you to maintain both among us, or rather to establish them here, for they are only too impaired. Almighty Father, you formed our hearts, and you always have the power to turn them as you please. Son, equal to your Father and eternal like him, yet made flesh for us, you have gathered us under one law, a law of love. Holy Spirit, you are the substantial love of the Father and the Son, and through you charity is poured into our souls. Trinity, supremely adorable and lovable, it is from your bosom that we have all come forth, and into your bosom that you will to call us all back. Unite us on earth as we are to be united in blessed eternity, to which may he lead us, &c.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: This first Advent sermon belongs to Guerric of Igny's medieval collection of sermons for the liturgical year, here read from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. Its individual date is unknown; the collection is associated approximately with his abbacy in 1138–1157. Guerric moves from the fulfilment of God's promises in Christ's first coming to patient hope for his return. The final prayer develops an image of remaining with Christ on the Cross. The source names Advent without assigning a particular Sunday.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De divinorum promissorum exspectatione.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On Waiting for God's Promises

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Salvatorem exspectamus (Tit. ii, 13). Vere exspectatio justorum laetitia, exspectantium beatam spem, et adventum gloriae magni Dei et salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi. Et nunc quae est exspectatio mea, inquit justus, nonne Dominus? (Psal. xxxviii, 8.) Et conversus ad Dominum: Scio, inquit, quia non confundes me ab exspectatione mea (Psal. cxviii, 116); quia jam substantia mea apud te est (Psal. xxxviii, 8), quia natura nostra de nobis sumpta, et pro nobis oblata, apud te glorificata est: spem nobis tribuens, quia ad te omnis caro veniet (Psal. lxiv, 3); caputque membra sequentur, ut holocaustum compleatur. Pleniore tamen fiducia, quia tutiore conscientia, Dominum exspectare potest, cui dicere datum est: Substantia possessiunculae meae, o Domine, apud te est; quia facultates meas, vel tibi erogando, vel pro te contemnendo, in coelis thesaurizavi, et ad pedes tuos omnia mea deposui, sciens quia potens es depositum meum non modo servare, sed etiam in centuplum restituere, et vitam aeternam adjicere. Quam beati vos, pauperes spiritu, quia juxta consilium admirabilis Consiliarii thesaurizastis vobis thesauros in coelo; ne si in terra thesauri vestri remanerent, corda vestra pariter putrescerent! Ubi enim, inquit, thesaurus tuus, ibi et cor tuum (Matth. vi, 21). Eant igitur, eant corda post thesauros suos; sursum affixa sit cogitatio, et ad Dominum suspensa exspectatio, ut et vobis competat dicere cum Apostolo: Nostra autem conversatio in coelis est, unde etiam Salvatorem exspectamus (Philipp. iii, 20). O exspectatio gentium! universi qui te exspectant non confundentur. Te expectaverunt patres nostri, omnes justi ab origine mundi in te speraverunt, et non sunt confusi (Psal. xxi, 5, 6). Jam enim suscepta misericordia tua in medio templi tui, chorus laetantium et laudantium concinit: Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini (Matth. xxi, 9). Exspectans exspectavi Dominum, et intendit mihi (Psal. xxxix, 2). Et in humilitate carnis agnoscentes majestatem divinitatis: Ecce, inquiunt, Dominus noster iste; exspectavimus eum, et salvabit nos: iste Dominus, sustinuimus eum; exsultabimus et laetabimur in salutari ejus (Isa. xxv, 9).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. We await the Saviour (Tit. ii, 13). Truly, the waiting of the righteous is joy, as they await the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. ‘And now, what am I waiting for,’ says the righteous person, ‘if not the Lord?’ (Psal. xxxviii, 8.) Turning to the Lord, he says: ‘I know that you will not disappoint my hope’ (Psal. cxviii, 116), ‘because my very being is already with you’ (Psal. xxxviii, 8): for our nature, taken from us and offered for us, has been glorified with you. This gives us hope that all flesh will come to you (Psal. lxiv, 3), and that the members will follow the Head, so that the whole burnt offering may be complete. Yet the person who has been granted these words can await the Lord with fuller confidence, because his conscience is more secure: ‘O Lord, the substance of my little property is with you. By spending my resources for you, or giving them up for your sake, I have stored them in heaven; I have laid all I possess at your feet, knowing that you can not only keep what I have entrusted to you, but return it a hundredfold and add eternal life.’ How blessed you are, poor in spirit! Following the advice of the wonderful Counsellor, you have stored up treasures for yourselves in heaven, lest your hearts decay along with treasures left on earth. ‘For where your treasure is,’ he says, ‘there is your heart also’ (Matth. vi, 21). Let our hearts go, then, let them follow their treasures. Let our thoughts be fixed above and our expectation hang upon the Lord, so that you too may say with the Apostle: ‘Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also await the Saviour’ (Philipp. iii, 20). O expectation of the nations! All who await you will not be put to shame. Our fathers awaited you; all the righteous from the beginning of the world hoped in you and were not put to shame (Psal. xxi, 5, 6). For now that your mercy has been received in the midst of your temple, the choir of those rejoicing and praising sings together: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’ (Matth. xxi, 9). ‘I waited and waited for the Lord, and he attended to me’ (Psal. xxxix, 2). And, recognizing the majesty of divinity in the lowliness of flesh, they say: ‘Look, this is our Lord; we have waited for him, and he will save us. This is the Lord; we have waited for him. We shall rejoice and be glad in his salvation’ (Isa. xxv, 9).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Sicut autem Ecclesia in antiquis justis exspectavit adventum primum; sic in novis reexspectat secundum: sicut in primo certa de pretio redemptionis; sic in secundo, de praemio remunerationis: atque hujus exspectatione spei suspensa a terrenis, tam feliciter quam ardenter inhiat aeternis. Cum igitur alii festinantes praesentibus beari, nec sustinentes consilium Domini, currunt ad diripiendam praedam hujus mundi; beatus vir cujus est nomen Domini spes ejus, et non respexit in vanitates et insanias falsas (Psal. xxxix, 5). Qui abstinet se a vitiis eorum, tanquam ab immunditiis, sciens melius esse humiliari cum mitibus, quam dividere spolia cum superbis (Prov. xvi, 19). Loquensque secum consolatur se, et ait: Pars mea Dominus, dixit anima mea: propterea exspectabo eum. Bonus est Dominus sperantibus in eum, animae quaerenti illum. Bonum est praestolari cum silentio salutare Dei (Thren. iii, 24–26). Defecit quidem anima mea in salutare tuum, o Domine, sed in verbum tuum supersperavi (Psal. cxviii, 81). Spes quidem quae differtur, scriptum est, affligit animam (Prov. xiii, 12): sed, licet lassa sit ex desiderii dilatione, secura est tamen ex promissione. In ipsum solum sperans, sed et supersperans adjiciam spem: sicut assidue adjicitur tribulatio super tribulationem, dilatio super dilationem. Certus sum enim quia apparebit in finem, et non mentietur. Ideoque, et si moram fecerit, exspectabo eum, quia veniens veniet, et non tardabit (Habac. ii, 3), ultra praestitutum tempus vel opportunum. Quod opportunum? Cum impletus fuerit numerus fratrum nostrorum, et consummatum fuerit tempus misericordiae ad poenitentiam indultum. Audi Isaiam ad superna saepius admissum consilia, quo videlicet consilio Dominus judicium differat. Propterea, inquit, Dominus exspectat ut misereatur vestri; et ideo exaltabitur parcens vobis, quia Deus judicii Dominus. Beati omnes qui exspectant eum (Isai. xxx, 18).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Just as the Church awaited the first coming in the righteous of old, so she awaits the second in the righteous of today: as sure of the price of redemption at the first as of the reward to be bestowed at the second. Lifted away from earthly things by this hopeful expectation, she longs for eternal things as happily as she does eagerly. While others hurry to find happiness in present things and, refusing to wait for the Lord's counsel, rush to seize this world's spoils, blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, who has not turned to vanities and lying follies (Psal. xxxix, 5). He keeps away from their vices as from filth, knowing that it is better to be humbled with the meek than to divide spoils with the proud (Prov. xvi, 19). Speaking within himself, he takes comfort and says: ‘The Lord is my portion, says my soul; therefore I shall wait for him. The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him. It is good to wait in silence for God's salvation’ (Thren. iii, 24–26). ‘My soul has indeed grown faint for your salvation, O Lord, but I have hoped all the more in your word’ (Psal. cxviii, 81). It is written that hope deferred afflicts the soul (Prov. xiii, 12); yet, though wearied by the postponement of its desire, it remains secure because of the promise. Hoping in him alone, and hoping beyond hope, I shall add hope, just as tribulation is continually added to tribulation and delay to delay. For I am certain that he will appear at the end and will not lie. Therefore, even if he delays, I shall wait for him, because he who is coming will come and will not be late (Habac. ii, 3), beyond the appointed or fitting time. What is the fitting time? When the number of our brethren has been completed, and the time mercifully granted for repentance has run its course. Listen to Isaiah, so often admitted to heavenly counsels, explaining why the Lord postpones judgment: ‘Therefore the Lord waits to have mercy on you; therefore he will be exalted in sparing you, because the Lord is a God of judgment. Blessed are all who await him’ (Isai. xxx, 18).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Propterea, si sapis, prospicies tibi quomodo dilationis hujus induciis utaris: utique si peccator es, ad poenitentiam, non ad negligentiam; si sanctus, ut proficias in sanctitate, non ut deficias a fide. Si autem dixerit malus servus ille in corde suo: Moram facit Dominus meus venire; et coeperit percutere conservos suos, manducet autem et bibat cum ebriosis: veniet Dominus servi illius in die qua non sperat, et hora qua ignorat, et dividet eum, partemque ejus ponet cum hypocritis: illic erit fletus et stridor dentium (Matth. xxiv, 48–51). Hujus servi nequam et infidelis videtur esse vox illa taedii et desperationis, quae apud Isaiam legitur: quia videlicet moram faciente Domino, frequentibus nuntiis ejus increduli et illusores insultare videntur: Manda, remanda, manda, remanda; exspecta, reexspecta; modicum ibi, modicum ibi. Sed quae poena sequatur miseros, propheta non tacuit, cum post pauca subintulit: Et erit eis, inquit, verbum Domini, quod videlicet subsannant, dicentes prophetis: Manda, remanda; manda, remanda; exspecta, reexspecta; modicum ibi, modicum ibi: ut vadant et cadant retrorsum, et conterantur, et illaqueentur, et capiantur (Isai. xxviii, 13). Vadunt retrorsum per apostasiam, cadunt in criminalia, illaqueantur mortifera delectatione, vel quadam inextricabili peccandi necessitate, ut nec velint, nec possint poenitere: capiuntur improvisa morte, conteruntur aeterna damnatione. Nescit enim finem suum homo: sed sicut pisces capiuntur hamo, et aves laqueo; sic homines, inquit Salomon, capiuntur tempore malo, cum eis extemplo supervenerit (Eccle. ix, 12). Propterea videlicet, ne pro dilatione spei fides nostra tepescat, aut aestuet patientia, et incipiamus esse de illis qui ad tempus credunt, et in tempore tentationis recedunt (Luc. viii, 13): clamat nobis de coelo qui fidem donat, donatam probat, probatam coronat, inquiens: Quis crediderit, non festinet (Isai. xxviii, 16), scilicet videre quod credit. Si enim quod non videmus, speramus: per patientiam exspectamus. Sponsae quoque suae, quam sibi desponsavit in fide, mandat Deus per Osee, dicens: Dies multos exspectabis me: non fornicaberis, et non eris viro (Osee iii, 3). Hoc nempe est Dominum veraciter exspectare, si fidem ei servemus: ut licet careamus consolatione praesentiae ejus, adulterum tamen non sequamur; sed pendeamus ad reditum ejus. Sic namque Dominus ait in eodem propheta: Pendebit populus meus ad reditum meum (Id. xi, 7). Pulchre omnino et proprie, pendebit, tanquam inter coelum et terram: licet adhuc apprehendere coelestia non valeat, non velit tamen tangere terrena. Et si aliquando tangit, nonnisi summis articulis, id est, extremis partibus animae; propter necessitatem scilicet corruptionis nostrae, cui cogimur servire, quamdiu creatura vanitati subjecta est, non volens (Rom. viii, 12). Vulgo dicitur: Male exspectat, qui pendet. Ego autem dico: Feliciter exspectat, qui sic pendet. Quamobrem elegit suspendium anima mea, et in ipso suspendio mortem ossa mea: ut perseveranter in cruce ista pendere merear, donec immoriar.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Therefore, if you are wise, consider how to use the respite of this delay: if you are a sinner, for repentance rather than negligence; if you are holy, to advance in holiness rather than fall away from faith. But if that wicked servant says in his heart, ‘My Lord is slow in coming,’ and begins to beat his fellow servants and eat and drink with drunkards, that servant's Lord will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him apart and assign him a place with the hypocrites: there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matth. xxiv, 48–51). The voice of weariness and despair that we read in Isaiah seems to be that of this wicked and faithless servant. Because the Lord delays, unbelievers and scoffers seem to jeer at his frequent messengers: ‘Command, command again, command, command again; wait, wait again; a little there, a little there.’ But the prophet did not keep silent about the punishment that would follow these wretched people, for a little later he added: ‘And the word of the Lord will be to them’—the word they mock when they say to the prophets, ‘Command, command again; command, command again; wait, wait again; a little there, a little there’—‘so that they may go and fall backward, and be broken, and ensnared, and captured’ (Isai. xxviii, 13). They go backward through apostasy, fall into grave sins, and are ensnared by deadly pleasure or by a kind of inescapable compulsion to sin, so that they neither wish nor are able to repent. They are captured by sudden death and broken by eternal condemnation. For man does not know his end: ‘As fish are caught by a hook and birds by a snare, so men,’ says Solomon, ‘are caught in an evil time when it suddenly falls upon them’ (Eccle. ix, 12). Therefore, lest the delay of hope make our faith grow lukewarm or our patience become agitated, and we begin to be among those ‘who believe for a time and fall away in the time of temptation’ (Luc. viii, 13), he who gives faith, tests the faith he has given, and crowns the faith he has tested, cries to us from heaven: ‘Let the one who believes not hurry’ (Isai. xxviii, 16)—that is, to see what he believes. For if we hope for what we do not see, we await it patiently. God also commands his bride, whom he has betrothed to himself in faith, through Hosea: ‘You will wait for me many days; you will not play the harlot or belong to a man’ (Osee iii, 3). This is truly waiting for the Lord: keeping faith with him, so that although we lack the comfort of his presence we do not follow an adulterer, but hang upon his return. For the Lord says in the same prophet: ‘My people will hang upon my return’ (Id. xi, 7). How beautifully and aptly he says ‘hang,’ as though between heaven and earth: though they cannot yet grasp heavenly things, they are unwilling to touch earthly things. And if they sometimes touch them, it is only with their fingertips, that is, the outermost parts of the soul, because of the necessities of our corruptible condition, which we are compelled to serve as long as creation is subjected to vanity against its will (Rom. viii, 12). People commonly say, ‘He who hangs waits badly.’ But I say, ‘He who hangs in this way waits happily.’ Therefore my soul has chosen hanging, and my bones death in that hanging, so that I may be found worthy to hang perseveringly upon this cross until I die upon it.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. O Domine Jesu, cum animam potestate positurus esses, et quo genere mortis id facere velles, tuo subesset arbitrio; suspendium elegit anima tua, ut exaltatus a terra, nos quoque ad te traheres, et a terrenis suspenderes. Sed nec ante mortem deponi passus es, et nos usque ad mortem in cruce perseveremus, et de ipsa tanquam de sublimi gradu facilior sit in coelum conscensus. Gratias tibi, Domine Jesu! ibi sumus, ibi te exspectamus, non Eliam, qui ad deponendum nos veniat; sed Eli, id est, Dominum nostrum, qui nos suscipiat. Modicum ibi, modicum ibi, si mandas atque remandas. Ego quidem mandatis tuis semel credidi; sed adjuva incredulitatem meam, ut immobilis ibi te exspectem, reexspectem, donec quod credo videam: credo enim videre bona Domini in terra viventium. Credis et tu: igitur exspecta Dominum, viriliter age, confortetur cor tuum, et sustine Dominum! (Psal. xxvi, 13, 14). Vae his qui perdiderunt sustinentiam, et diverterunt in vias pravas. Et quid facient, cum inspicere coeperit Dominus? Qui tamen longanimiter se mandat exspectari, alibi se cito venturum esse promittit: in altero nimirum sustinentiam informans; in altero pusillanimes confortans, imparatos terrens, et pigros excitans. Ecce, inquit, venio cito, et merces mea mecum est, reddere unicuique secundum opera sua (Apoc. xxii, 12): et ad Jerusalem: Cito veniet salus tua: quare moerore consumeris? (Mich. iv, 9). Et revera tempus breve est, maxime uniuscujusque nostrum; licet longum videatur aestuandi, seu prae labore, seu prae amore. Ideoque utrumque necesse est: ut timeamus Judicem qui prope est, et forsitan mihi, forsitan tibi in januis est; et longanimiter exspectemus, si moram fecerit. Veniens veniet ille Dominus, timor et desiderium nostrum, requies et merces laborantium, dulcedo et amplexus amantium, beatitudo omnium, salvator noster Jesus Christus, qui vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. O Lord Jesus, when you were about to lay down your life by your own power, and the kind of death you would choose lay within your own decision, your soul chose hanging, so that, lifted up from the earth, you might draw us too to yourself and suspend us above earthly things. You did not allow yourself to be taken down before death: may we too persevere upon the cross until death, and may ascent into heaven be easier from it, as from a lofty step. Thank you, Lord Jesus! There we are; there we await you—not Elijah, coming to take us down, but Eli, that is, our Lord, to receive us. ‘A little there, a little there,’ if you command and command again. I have indeed believed your commands once for all; but help my unbelief, so that I may remain there unmoved, waiting and waiting again for you, until I see what I believe: for I believe that I shall see the Lord's goodness in the land of the living. You believe too: then wait for the Lord; act courageously, let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord! (Psal. xxvi, 13, 14). Woe to those who have lost their endurance and turned aside into crooked ways. What will they do when the Lord begins his inspection? Yet he who commands us to await him with patience promises elsewhere that he will come quickly: in the one case teaching endurance, in the other comforting the fainthearted, terrifying the unprepared, and rousing the sluggish. ‘Look,’ he says, ‘I am coming quickly, and my reward is with me, to repay each according to his works’ (Apoc. xxii, 12); and to Jerusalem: ‘Your salvation will come quickly; why are you consumed by grief?’ (Mich. iv, 9). Truly the time is short, especially for each one of us, although it may seem long in our anguish, whether from toil or from love. Therefore both are necessary: to fear the Judge who is near, perhaps at my door, perhaps at yours, and to wait patiently if he delays. He who is coming will come: the Lord, our fear and our desire, the rest and reward of those who labour, the sweetness and embrace of those who love, the blessedness of all, our Saviour Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition prints Romans 8:12 beside words from Romans 8:20. The printed reference is retained.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The hanging/death language is Guerric's sustained image of perseverance on Christ's cross, with a Scriptural allusion to Job 7:15. The proverbial contrast and bodily imagery are retained rather than paraphrased away.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition cites Micah 4:9, although the whole sentence follows liturgical wording rather than that verse verbatim. Eli and Elias are Guerric’s wordplay on the Passion narratives.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition numbers both final paragraphs 4; that numbering is retained. In the first paragraph, the reading ne si (“lest”) corrects the printed ne se, and a missing opening parenthesis before Psalm 64:3 has been supplied.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: This second Advent sermon belongs to Guerric of Igny's medieval collection of sermons for the liturgical year, here read from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. Its individual date is unknown; the collection is associated approximately with his abbacy in 1138–1157. Guerric urges his hearers to run out with joy to meet the coming Christ, as the prophets and the just longed to see him. He then describes a hidden, spiritual coming between the first and the last, in which the soul is transformed into Christ's image. Until that is granted, faith and a pure conscience console the patient. The source names Advent without assigning a particular Sunday.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO II.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON II.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Quomodo Christo advenienti occurrendum

passages.label: English
passages.text: How to Go Out to Meet the Coming Christ

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Ecce venit Rex, occurramus obviam Salvatori nostro. Salomon pulchre ait: Aqua frigida animae sitienti, et nuntius bonus de terra longinqua (Prov. XXV, 25). Bonus itaque nuntius, qui adventum Salvatoris nuntiat, reconciliationem mundi, bona superventuri saeculi. Quam pulchri pedes annuntiantium pacem, annuntiantium bona! (Isa, LII, 7.) Multi siquidem, non unus. Multi inquam, sed in uno spiritu longa serie ab initio saeculi nobis supervenere nuntii, et omnium vox una, simul una sententia: Venit ecce venit (Ezech. XXXIX, 8). Et unde, inquis, isti venere nuntii? Ut scriptum est, de terra longinqua (Isa. XXXIX, 3); quia de terra viventium, quae magno interstitio separata est ab hac terra morientium: nam inter nos et illos adhuc chaos magnum firmatum est. Inde tamen prophetae nobis, sicut et angeli missi sunt; quia si corpore hic versabantur, spiritu illuc assumebantur, quando mittendi erant; ut illic audirent et viderent, quod hic nuntiarent. Hujusmodi nuntii aqua refrigerii, potusque sapientiae sunt salutaris animae Deum sitienti: cui nimirum qui nuntiat adventum vel alia mysteria Salvatoris, haurit ei, et propinat aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris, ut etiam nuntianti sibi, sive Isaiae, sive cuilibet ex prophetis, eadem anima respondere videatur verbis Elizabeth, quia eodem potata spiritu quo Elizabeth: Et unde mihi hoc, ut veniat Dominus meus ad me? (Luc. I, 34, 43.) Ecce enim, ut facta est vox annuntiationis tuae in auribus meis, exsultavit in gaudio spiritus in corde meo, gestiens occurrere Deo Salvatori suo.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Behold, the King is coming; let us go out to meet our Savior. Solomon says beautifully: “Cold water to a thirsty soul, and good news from a distant land” (Prov. XXV, 25). Good, then, is the messenger who announces the Savior’s coming, the reconciliation of the world, and the blessings of the age that is to come. “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things!” (Isa, LII, 7.) There are many of them, not just one. Many, I say, but in one spirit, in a long succession from the beginning of the world, messengers have come to us, and the voice of them all is one, their judgment together one: “Behold, he comes, yes, he comes” (Ezech. XXXIX, 8). And where, you ask, did these messengers come from? As it is written, “from a distant land” (Isa. XXXIX, 3); for they came from the land of the living, which is separated by a great interval from this land of the dying—for between us and them a great chasm is still fixed. Yet from there the prophets, like the angels, were sent to us; for although they were living here in body, in spirit they were taken there whenever they were to be sent, so that there they might hear and see what they were to announce here. Such messengers are water of refreshment and a drink of saving wisdom for the soul thirsting for God. Whoever announces to it the Savior’s coming or any of his other mysteries draws and offers it water with joy from the fountains of the Savior, so that the same soul seems to answer the one announcing it—whether Isaiah or any other of the prophets—with Elizabeth’s words, because it has been given to drink of the same Spirit as Elizabeth: “And how has this happened to me, that my Lord should come to me?” (Luc. I, 34, 43.) For behold, as the voice of your announcement sounded in my ears, the spirit in my heart leaped for joy, eager to go out to meet God its Savior.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Et revera, fratres, exsultatione spiritus Christo venienti occurrendum est. Et jam nunc a longe salutandus, vel certe resalutandus, qui mandat salutes Jacob. Amicum salutare non confundar (Eccli. XXII, 31), inquit Sapiens; quanto magis resalutare? O salutare vultus mei, et Deus meus! quanta dignatio fuit quod servos salutasti? sed quanto major, quod salvasti? Nec enim integra nobis salus esset, si salutes mandares, et non dares. Dedisti autem, non modo, quos salutaveras verbis pacificis, postmodum salutando in osculo pacis, videlicet per unionem carnis; sed etiam salutem operando per mortem crucis. Exsurgat igitur spiritus noster alacri gaudio, curratque obviam Salvatori suo, et jam a longe venientem adoret et salutet, acclamans ei et dicens: O Domine, salvum me fac; o Domine, bene prosperare! Benedictus qui venturus es in nomine Domini (Psal. CXVII, 25, 26). Salve, qui venis salvare nos; benedictus, qui venis benedicere nos. Igitur, o Domine, bene prosperare, qui tam prosper et salutaris advenis generi humano. Intende, prospere procede et regna. Prosperum iter faciet tibi Pater, Deus salutarium nostrorum. Prosperabitur, inquit Pater, in his ad quae misi illum (Isa. LV, 11): non pro votis carnalium, non pro voluntate Petri, qui abhorrebat illum pati. Et omnia quaecunque faciet prosperabuntur (Psal. I, 3): non ad praeproperam hominum voluntatem, sed ad veram eorum salutem. Vana quidem salus hominis (Psal. CVII, 13): sed Domini est salus (Psal. III, 9), qui operatus est salutem de sanguine suo, fundens illum in pretium, et propinans in potum. Veni ergo, o Domine, salvum me fac, et salvus ero (Jerem. XVII, 14). Veni et ostende faciem tuam, et salvi erimus (Psal. LXXIX. 4, 8, 20). Te enim exspectavimus: esto brachium nostrum, salus nostra in tempore tribulationis (Isai. XXXIII, 2). Sic Prophetae et justi desiderio et affectu tanto ante Christo venturo occurrebant, desiderantes, si fieri posset, oculis videre quod spiritu praevidebant. Unde Dominus discipulis dicebat: Beati oculi qui vident quae vos videtis. Dico enim vobis, quod multi prophetae, et reges voluerunt videre quae vos videtis, et non viderunt (Luc. X, 23, 24). Abraham quoque pater noster exsultavit, ut videret diem Christi: vidit, sed apud inferos, et gavisus est. In quo utique tepor et duritia cordis nostri suggillatur, si non videt eum gaudio spirituali.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. And truly, brothers, we must go out to meet the coming Christ with the rejoicing of the spirit. Even now, from afar, he must be greeted—or certainly greeted in return—he who sends greetings of salvation to Jacob. “I will not be ashamed to greet a friend,” says the Wise Man (Eccli. XXII, 31); how much more to greet him in return? O salvation of my face, and my God! How great was your condescension, that you greeted your servants; but how much greater was it that you saved them! For our salvation would not have been complete if you had sent greetings of salvation but had not given salvation. Yet you did give it—not only by greeting those whom you had greeted with words of peace, later greeting them with the kiss of peace, that is, through the union of flesh, but also by accomplishing salvation through the death of the cross. Let our spirit, then, rise up in joyful gladness, and run out to meet its Savior; let it already adore and greet him as he comes from afar, acclaiming him and saying: “O Lord, save me; O Lord, prosper!” “Blessed are you who are to come in the name of the Lord” (Psal. CXVII, 25, 26). Hail, you who come to save us; blessed are you who come to bless us. Therefore, O Lord, prosper, since you come to the human race so prosperously and as its Savior. Attend, proceed prosperously, and reign. The Father, the God of our salvation, will make your journey prosperous. “It shall prosper,” says the Father, “in the things for which I sent him” (Isa. LV, 11)—not according to the desires of the carnal, nor according to the will of Peter, who shrank from his suffering. “And all that he does shall prosper” (Psal. I, 3)—not according to the hasty will of human beings, but for their true salvation. “Vain indeed is the salvation of man” (Psal. CVII, 13); “but salvation belongs to the Lord” (Psal. III, 9), who accomplished salvation by his blood, pouring it out as the price and offering it as a drink. Come, then, O Lord, “save me, and I shall be saved” (Jerem. XVII, 14). “Come and show your face, and we shall be saved” (Psal. LXXIX. 4, 8, 20). For we have waited for you: “be our arm, our salvation in the time of tribulation” (Isai. XXXIII, 2). In this way the prophets and the righteous, with such great desire and longing, went out so long beforehand to meet the Christ who was to come, wishing, if it were possible, to see with their eyes what they foresaw in spirit. Hence the Lord said to his disciples: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you that many prophets and kings wished to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luc. X, 23, 24). Our father Abraham, too, rejoiced that he might see Christ’s day; he saw it, but in the netherworld, and rejoiced. In this, surely, the lukewarmness and hardness of our heart are reproved, if it does not see him with spiritual joy.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Christi nascentis diem anniversarium exspectamus; qui nobis in proximo videndus, Domino annuente, promittitur. Hoc sane gaudium nostrum tale videtur exigere Scriptura, ut spiritus noster levans se super se, Christo venienti quodammodo occurrere gestiat: et desiderio se extendens in anteriora, impatiensque morarum, jam videre contendat futura. Ego namque non solum ad secundum adventum, sed etiam ad primum arbitror pertinere, quod tot locis Scripturarum ei monemur occurrere. Quomodo, inquis? Quia videlicet sicut secundo adventui occurremus motu et exsultatione corporis: sic et primo occurrendum est affectu et exsultatione cordis. Scitis enim quia resumptis in resurrectione corporibus novis, secundum doctrinam Apostoli, rapiemur in nubibus obviam Christo in aera, et sic semper cum Domino erimus (I Thess. IV, 16). Sic nec modo desunt nubes, quae spiritus nostros, si nimis non fuerint pigri terraeque affixi, sublevabunt ad altiora; et sic cum Domino erimus, vel hora dimidia. Agnoscit, ni fallor, experientia vestra quod loquor, cum aliquando vocem dederunt nubes, id est, sonuerunt in Ecclesia prophetarum, vel apostolorum voces, ad quam sublimia sensus vestri, quasi vehiculo nubis, fuerint subvecti; et eo usque nonnunquam excesserint, ut gloriam Domini quantulumcunque mererentur speculari. Tunc, ni fallor, vobis innotuit veritas illius sermonis, quem Dominus de illa nube pluit, quam quotidie ponit ascensum vobis: Sacrificium laudis honorificabit me: et illic iter, quo ostendam illi salutare Dei (Psal. XLIX, 23). Ita ergo sit, ut ante adventum suum Dominus veniat ad vos, et antequam mundo generaliter adveniat, familiariter invisat vos. Non vos, inquit, relinquam orphanos: vado, et veniam ad vos (Joan. XIV, 18). Et quidem pro merito cujusque, vel studio, creber est ad unumquemque iste Domini adventus, hoc tempore medio inter adventum primum et novissimum, conformans nos adventui primo, et praeparans novissimo. Ad hoc nempe venit modo in nos, ne primo adventu frustra venerit ad nos, vel ne in novissimo veniat iratus adversus nos. Hoc siquidem adventu satagit reformare sensum superbiae nostrae, configuratum sensui humilitatis suae, quam primo veniens exhibuit; ut perinde reformet corpus humilitatis nostrae, configuratum corpori claritatis suae, quam denuo rediens exhibebit. Prorsus optandus omnibus votis, et expetendus studiis adventus iste familiaris, qui nobis gratiam impertiat adventus primi, et gloriam promittat novissimi. Quia enim misericordiam et veritatem diligit Deus, gratiam et gloriam dabit Dominus (Psal. LXXXIII, 12); per misericordiam praerogans gratiam, per veritatem reddens gloriam.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. We await the anniversary of Christ’s birth, which, with the Lord’s favor, is promised to us as something we shall soon see. Scripture certainly seems to require that our joy be such that our spirit, lifting itself above itself, eagerly desire in some way to go out to meet the coming Christ; stretching forward in its longing and impatient of delay, it strives already to see what is still to come. For I believe that it applies not only to the second coming but also to the first, that in so many places of Scripture we are urged to go out to meet him. “How so?” you ask. Because, just as we shall go out to meet his second coming through the movement and exultation of the body, so we must go out to meet his first through the affection and exultation of the heart. You know, in fact, that when our bodies have been taken up again in the resurrection, renewed, then, according to the Apostle’s teaching, “we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (I Thess. IV, 16). Even now, then, clouds are not lacking—clouds that will lift our spirits to higher things, if they are not too sluggish or fixed to the earth—and so we shall be with the Lord, even if only for half an hour. Your own experience, unless I am mistaken, recognizes what I am saying: sometimes the clouds have given voice—that is, the voices of prophets or apostles have sounded in the Church—and your understanding has been carried up to sublime heights, as though in a cloud’s chariot; sometimes it has risen so far that it merited, however slightly, to contemplate the glory of the Lord. Then, unless I am mistaken, you came to know the truth of that saying which the Lord rained down upon you from that cloud, which he sets before you every day as a means of ascent: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Psal. XLIX, 23). Let it be so, then: before his coming, may the Lord come to you, and before he comes to the world as a whole, may he visit you personally. “I will not leave you orphans,” he says; “I am going away, and I will come to you” (Joan. XIV, 18). And indeed, according to each person’s merit or devotion, this coming of the Lord to each one is frequent during this time between his first and final coming: it conforms us to the first coming and prepares us for the final one. For this is why he comes into us now: so that he may not have come to us in vain in his first coming, and so that at the last he may not come against us in anger. By this coming he earnestly strives to reform our proud mind, conforming it to the mind of his humility, which he displayed when he first came; and thereby to reform our body of humility, conforming it to the body of his glory, which he will display when he returns. This personal coming is wholly to be desired with every prayer and sought with every effort: it grants us the grace of his first coming and promises us the glory of the last. For because God loves mercy and truth, “the Lord will give grace and glory” (Psal. LXXXIII, 12), granting grace beforehand through mercy and repaying glory through truth.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Porro sicut dispositione temporis, sic etiam proportione similitudinis medius est adventus iste spiritualis inter adventum utrumque corporalem, et velut quidam mediator, participat cum utroque. Primus siquidem adventus, occultus et humilis; ultimus, manifestus et admirabilis: iste autem occultus quidem, sed mirabilis. Occultum sane dixerim, non quod ignoretur ab eo cui venit, sed quia secretus ei advenit. Unde glorians illa gloriosa anima secum cum dixit: Secretum meum mihi, secretum meum mihi (Isa. XXIV, 16). Sed nec ab ipso cui advenit, potest ante videri, quam teneri, juxta illud beati Job de se confitentis: Si venerit ad me, non videbo eum; si abierit, non intelligam (Job IX, 11). Nec veniens quippe videtur, nec recedens intelligitur, qui solummodo, dum praesens est, lumen est animae et intellectus, quo invisibilis videtur, et incogitabilis intelligitur. Caeterum quam admirabilis sit, licet occultus sit iste adventus Domini, quam suavi et felici stupore in admirationem sui suspendat et expendat animam contemplantis, quomodo omnia ossa interioris hominis acclament ei, Domine, quis similis tui (Psal. XXXIV, 10)? norunt quidem experti; sed utinam satis desiderent experiri non experti: ita duntaxat, ut non temeraria curiositas faciat scrutari majestatem opprimendos a gloria, sed pia charitas suspirare dilectum suscipiendos a gratia. Suscipiens enim mansuetos Dominus, humilians autem peccatores usque ad terram (Psal. CXLVI, 6), superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam (Jac. IV, 6). Cum igitur primus adventus sit gratiae; novissimus, gloriae: iste nimirum, gratiae pariter et gloriae; in quo videlicet per consolantem gratiam futuram nobis utcunque datur praelibare gloriam. Cum igitur in primo Deus majestatis visus sit contemptibilis, in novissimo autem videndus sit terribilis, in isto medio videtur mirabilis et amabilis: ut nec propter dignationem gratiae, qua se praebet amabilem, possit esse contemptui, sed admirationi; nec propter magnificentiam gloriae, qua mirabilis apparet, sit terrori, sed potius consolationi. De primo dicebat Videns: Vidimus eum, et non erat ei species, neque decor: unde nec reputavimus eum (Isa. LIII, 2, 3). De ultimo expavescit etiam justus, dicens: Et quis stabit ad videndum eum? (Malach. III, 2.) De isto autem dicit Apostolus: Gloriam Domini speculantes, in eamdem imaginem transformamur a gloria in gloriam, tanquam a Domini Spiritu (II Cor. III, 18). Mirabile prorsus, et amabile, cum Deus amor amantis sensibus illabitur: cum sponsam Sponsus in unitate Spiritus amplectitur, et in eamdem cum illa imaginem transformatur; per quam, velut per speculum, Domini gloriam speculatur. Quam beati, quorum ardens charitas hanc praerogativam jam meruit obtinere! sed et illi beati, quorum sancta simplicitas idem quandoque potest sperare! Et illi quidem jam de fructu amoris, sui capiunt solatium laboris: isti autem tanto fortasse majore merito, quanto interim minore solatio, portantes pondus diei et aestus, exspectant adventum remunerationis. Nos igitur, fratres, quos nondum consolatur tam sublimis experientia, ut patientes simus usque ad adventum Domini, consoletur interim certa fides et pura conscientia, quae tam feliciter quam fideliter cum Paulo dicat: Scio cui credidi, et certus sum quia potens est depositum meum servare in illum diem (II Tim. I, 12): in adventum scilicet gloriae magni Dei, et Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi, cui est gloria in saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Moreover, just as it is intermediate in the order of time, so also in the likeness it bears, this spiritual advent stands between the two bodily advents and, as a kind of mediator, shares in both. The first advent was hidden and humble; the last will be manifest and admirable; this one, however, is hidden yet wondrous. I call it hidden—not because it is unknown to the one to whom he comes, but because he comes to that person in secret. Hence that glorious soul, glorying within itself, said: “My secret is for me, my secret is for me” (Isa. XXIV, 16). Yet even by the one to whom he comes, he cannot be seen before he is possessed, in accordance with the blessed Job’s confession about himself: “If he comes to me, I shall not see him; if he goes away, I shall not understand” (Job IX, 11). For he is neither seen as he comes nor understood as he departs; only while he is present is he the light of the soul and of the intellect, by which the invisible is seen and the unthinkable is understood. But how wondrous this advent of the Lord is, even though hidden; how, with what sweet and joyful astonishment, it suspends and absorbs the soul that contemplates him in wonder at himself, so that all the bones of the inner person cry out to him, “Lord, who is like you?” (Psal. XXXIV, 10)—those who have experienced it know; but would that those who have not experienced it desired enough to experience it. Let it be only in such a way that reckless curiosity does not lead one to scrutinize the majesty and be overwhelmed by the glory, but devout love makes one sigh for the Beloved and be received by grace. For the Lord receives the meek, but humbles sinners to the ground (Psal. CXLVI, 6); he resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble (Jac. IV, 6). Since, then, the first advent is one of grace and the last one of glory, this advent is plainly of both grace and glory: in it, through the grace that consoles us, we are in some measure given a foretaste of the glory that is to come. Since, then, in the first advent the God of majesty appeared contemptible, while in the last he will be seen as terrifying, in this middle advent he is seen as wondrous and lovable: so that, because of the condescension of grace by which he makes himself lovable, he cannot be despised but rather admired; and because of the magnificence of the glory in which he appears wondrous, he is not a cause of terror but rather of consolation. Of the first advent the Seer said: “We saw him, and there was in him neither appearance nor beauty; therefore we did not regard him” (Isa. LIII, 2, 3). Of the last even the just man is afraid, saying: “And who will stand to see him?” (Malach. III, 2.) But of this advent the Apostle says: “Beholding the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (II Cor. III, 18). Truly wondrous and lovable it is when God, who is love, glides into the senses of the one who loves; when the Bridegroom embraces the bride in the unity of the Spirit and is transformed with her into the same image, through which, as through a mirror, the glory of the Lord is beheld. How blessed are those whose ardent love has already merited this privilege! Yet blessed also are those whose holy simplicity may one day hope for the same. The former already draw comfort from the fruit of love for their labor; the latter, perhaps with all the greater merit because meanwhile they have less consolation, bear the burden of the day and the heat while awaiting the advent of their reward. Therefore, brothers, we whom so sublime an experience does not yet console: that we may be patient until the coming of the Lord, may certain faith and a pure conscience console us meanwhile, saying with Paul, as happily as faithfully: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to guard my deposit until that day” (II Tim. I, 12)—that is, until the advent of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: This third Advent sermon belongs to Guerric of Igny's medieval collection of sermons for the liturgical year, here read from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. Its individual date is unknown; the collection is associated approximately with his abbacy in 1138–1157. Guerric begins from the uncertainty of the hour of Christ's coming and of one's own death: the only security is never to be secure. David is the model of a soul kept ready through persecution, and justice and judgment prepare a dwelling for the Lord. The source names Advent without assigning a particular Sunday.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO III.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON III.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Quod homo debeat semper esse paratus Domino advenienti.

passages.label: English
passages.text: That a man must always be ready for the coming Lord.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Paratus est Israel in occursum Domini, quoniam venit (Amos IV, 12). Et vos, fratres, estote parati; quia, qua hora non putatis, Filius hominis veniet (Luc. XII, 40). Nihil certius quam quod veniat, sed nihil incertius quam quando veniat. Usque adeo siquidem non est nostrum scire tempora, vel momenta, quae Pater posuit in sua potestate (Act. I, 7), ut nec angelis qui assistunt ei, de die illa vel hora scire datum sit. Dies quoque noster ultimus, certissimus nobis quod veniat: incertissimus est quando, vel ubi, vel unde nobis adveniat; nisi quod, ut ante nos dictum est, senibus est in januis, qui juvenibus est in insidiis. Et utinam vel illi se observarent, qui mortem tam paratam intrare, imo jam intrantem vident. An non ex parte jam intravit, quae aliquas partes corporis jam permortuas occupavit? In pluribus tamen semimortuis videre est adhuc viventem concupiscentiam mundi: frigescunt membra, et fervet avaritia: vita finitur, et ambitio protrahitur. Quandoquidem nobis quoque quibus fortassis aetas, aut salus aliquid longius promittere videtur, quanto minus mors in conspectu est, tanto magis utique, si sapimus, suspecta est: ne videlicet dies illa, sicut fur in nocte, incautos et imparatos nos comprehendat; quae in insidiis posita, quominus videri aut caveri potest, eo magis timenda est. Una igitur securitas est, nunquam esse securum: quatenus timor se observans reddat semper paratum; donec securitas succedat timori, non timor securitati. Observabo me, inquit sapiens, ab iniquitate mea (Psal. XVII, 24), quandoquidem non possum a morte mea; sciens quia justus, si morte praeoccupatus fuerit, in refrigerio erit (Sap. V, 7), imo in morte triumphat, cui non dominatur iniquitas in vita. Quam pulchrum, fratres, quam beatum, in morte non modo securum, sed et gloriosum triumphare; ex auctoritate conscientiae, spiritu et voce Martini cruentam bestiam, si astare praesumpserit, increpare; Judici venienti et pulsanti gratanter aperire! Tum vero videas, heu, similes mei trepidare, inducias petere, nec accipere: oleum conscientiae lamentis poenitentiae velle emere, nec tempus sufficere: larvales illas facies declinare velle, nec posse: a facie irae tonantis velle in corpore delitescere, et cogi exire! Exibit spiritus ejus, et revertetur peccator in terram suam, unde sumptus est. In illa die peribunt omnes cogitationes eorum. Scio quidem, quia conditionis humanae est, sub discrimine exitus conturbari, cum etiam perfecti nolunt exspoliari, sed supervestiri: et qui nihil sibi sunt conscii, quia tamen non in hoc sunt justificati, necesse habent judicium, quod ignorant, vereri. Sed, sive conditionis affectu, sive sanctitatis defectu, sive judicii metu conturbata fuerit anima mea, inquit justus: Tu, Domine, misericordiae memor eris, mittesque misericordiam tuam et veritatem tuam, et eripies animam meam de medio catulorum leonum (Psal. LVI, 4, 5): et qui prius conturbatus eram, postmodum in pace in idipsum dormiam et requiescam (Psal. IV, 9). Vocavit Deus terram, et audivit eum in tremore. Cum enim auditum fecit de coelo judicium, auditu solo terra tremuit, et terrore purgata quievit. Beati qui nunc eatenus excoquunt in se omnem scoriam peccati, ut tunc solo sufficiat timore purgari. Mecum siquidem servo inutili et negligenti bene agitur, si vel per ignem salvus fiam; si, crematis lignis, feno, stipula, quae mihi coarcervavi, vel semiustus evadam. Et quidem comparatione mali, bonum vel per ignem salvari; sed indubitanter longe melius, sola purgatione metus consummari: optimum autem et felicissimum, nec metu turbari.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "Israel is prepared to meet the Lord, for he comes" (Amos IV, 12). "And you, brothers, be ready; for the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect" (Luc. XII, 40). Nothing is more certain than that he will come, but nothing is more uncertain than when he will come. Indeed, it is so far beyond our power to know the times or seasons, which the Father has placed in his own power (Act. I, 7), that it has not even been granted to the angels who stand by him to know of that day or hour. Our last day too is most certain to us in that it will come, but it is most uncertain when, or where, or from what quarter it will come upon us — except that, as has been said before our time, it stands at the door for the old, while it lies in ambush for the young. And would that even those would watch themselves who see death so ready to enter — indeed already entering! For has it not in part already entered, seeing that it has already taken possession of some parts of the body already wholly dead? Yet in many who are half-dead one may still see the desire of the world alive: the limbs grow cold, yet avarice burns hot; life comes to its end, yet ambition is drawn out still further. Since even for us, to whom perhaps our age or our health seems to promise a somewhat longer life, the less death is in view, the more, certainly, if we are wise, it ought to be suspected: lest that day, like a thief in the night, seize us unwary and unprepared; for being set in ambush, the less it can be seen or guarded against, the more it is to be feared. There is therefore but one security: never to be secure — so that fear, keeping watch over itself, may render us always ready, until security succeed to fear, and not fear to security. "I will keep myself," says the wise man, "from my iniquity" (Psal. XVII, 24), since I cannot keep myself from my death; knowing that the just man, if he be overtaken by death, shall be in refreshment (Sap. V, 7) — indeed he triumphs in death, over whom iniquity has not had dominion in life. How beautiful, brothers, how blessed, to triumph in death not merely secure but even glorious; with the authority of conscience, in the spirit and voice of Martin, to rebuke the bloody beast should it presume to stand near; to open gladly to the Judge as he comes and knocks! Then indeed you would see, alas, those like me trembling, asking for a delay and not obtaining it; wishing to buy the oil of conscience with the laments of penitence, and time not sufficing; wishing to turn away from those ghastly faces, and not being able; wishing to hide in the body from the face of the thundering wrath, and being forced to go forth! "His spirit shall go forth, and the sinner shall return to his own earth, from which he was taken. In that day all their thoughts shall perish." I know indeed that it belongs to the human condition to be troubled at the crisis of one's departure, since even the perfect do not wish to be stripped, but rather to be clothed over; and those who are conscious of nothing against themselves — because they are not thereby justified — must still fear the judgment which they do not know. But whether my soul be troubled by the feeling natural to this condition, or by a lack of holiness, or by fear of judgment, says the just man: "You, Lord, will be mindful of your mercy, and you will send your mercy and your truth, and you will deliver my soul from the midst of the young lions" (Psal. LVI, 4, 5); and I, who was troubled before, will afterward sleep and rest in peace, in the very same (Psal. IV, 9). "God called the earth, and it heard him in trembling." For when he made judgment heard from heaven, the earth trembled at the mere hearing, and, purged by terror, grew quiet. Blessed are those who now so thoroughly burn away in themselves all the dross of sin, that then it may suffice for them to be purged by fear alone. For with me, a useless and negligent servant, it goes well if I am saved even by fire; if, when the wood, hay, and stubble which I have heaped up for myself are burned away, I escape even half-burned. And indeed, by comparison with evil, it is good to be saved even through fire; but without doubt it is far better to be made perfect by the purification of fear alone; but best and most blessed of all is not even to be troubled by fear.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Idcirco paratus esto, o verus Israel, in occursum Domini: non solum, ut cum venerit et pulsaverit, aperias ei; sed etiam adhuc illo longe agente, alacer et gratulabundus occurras ei; et tanquam fiduciam habens in die judicii, regnum ejus advenire pleno preceris affectu. Si ergo vis tunc paratus inveniri: Ante judicium para justitiam tibi (Eccli. XVIII, 19), juxta consilium Sapientis; paratus sis ad omne opus bonum faciendum; paratus sis nihilominus ad omne malum patiendum: ut sine reprehensione cordis cantet os tuum, Paratum cor meum, Deus, paratum cor meum. Paratum quidem, ut te cooperante faciam digna; paratum, ut patiar indigna. Et ideo paratum ad utrumque, quod cantabo et psallam in gloria mea: id est, laudabo et gloriabor pro utroque. Et statim in hoc ipsum se justus excitat, Exsurge, inquiens, psalterium et cithara (Psal. LVI, 8, 9); id est, cor meum et caro mea, ad exsultandum in Deum vivum: cor scilicet, propter speciales actiones; caro, propter suas passiones. Cor namque sapiens quae sursum sunt, psalterium est sonans de superiori: caro patiens quae deorsum sunt, cithara sonans ab inferiori. Sic et alibi devotionem suam David offerens Deo, Paratus sum, inquit, ut custodiam mandata tua: et tam paratus, quod non sum turbatus (Psal. CXVIII, 6), cum tentatio irrueret, et persecutio grassaretur. Cum persequeretur aemulus, malediceret servus, animam quaereret filius (II Reg. XV-XVIII); non sum tamen turbatus, quominus custodirem mandata perfectionis evangelicae: retribuentibus mala pro bonis, retribuens bona pro malis; sollicitus de persecutorum salute, moestus de morte; sustinens a servo exprobrari, non sustinens ab amico vindicari. Ecce ante Evangelium evangelica perfectio, charitas scilicet patiens et benigna, etiam erga malignos, quos tolerat. Quia igitur tam paratus erat, fiducialiter Domino nimirum occurrebat: Sine iniquitate, inquit, cucurri, et direxi distortos, quantum in me fuit. Tu exsurge igitur in occursum meum, occurrentis tibi: et quia nec sic pertingere possum ad celsitudinem tuam, nisi tu condescendens operi manuum tuarum porrigas dexteram: Exsurge in occursum meum (Psal. LVIII, 5, 6), et vide si via iniquitatis in me est: et si inveneris nescio quam viam iniquitatis, amove a me: et de lege tua misertus mei, deduc me in via aeterna (Psal. CXXXVIII, 24), id est, Christo, qui via est per quam itur, et aeternitas ad quam pervenitur; via immaculata, mansio beata.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Therefore be ready, O true Israel, to meet the Lord: not only that, when he comes and knocks, you may open to him; but also, while he is still far away, that you may run to meet him eagerly and with gladness; and, as one having confidence for the day of judgment, pray with full affection that his kingdom may come. If, then, you wish to be found ready at that time: Before judgment prepare justice for yourself (Eccli. XVIII, 19), according to the counsel of the Wise Man; be ready to do every good work; be ready likewise to suffer every evil: so that your mouth may sing, without reproach from your heart, My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready. Ready, indeed, that with you cooperating I may do worthy deeds; ready, that I may suffer unworthy things. And therefore ready for both, so that I shall sing and make melody in my glory: that is, I shall praise and glory for both. And immediately for this very purpose the just man rouses himself, saying, Awake, psaltery and harp (Psal. LVI, 8, 9); that is, my heart and my flesh, to exult in the living God: the heart, namely, for its special actions; the flesh, for its sufferings. For the heart, wise toward the things that are above, is a psaltery sounding from above; the flesh, suffering the things that are below, is a harp sounding from below. So also elsewhere David, offering his devotion to God, says: I am ready to keep your commandments; and so ready that I was not troubled (Psal. CXVIII, 6), when temptation rushed in and persecution raged. When a rival persecuted him, a servant cursed him, a son sought his life (II Reg. XV-XVIII); yet I was not troubled, so as to fail to keep the commandments of evangelical perfection: to those repaying evil for good, repaying good for evil; anxious for the salvation of his persecutors, sorrowful over the death; enduring reproach from a servant, not enduring vengeance taken by a friend. Behold, before the Gospel, evangelical perfection—namely, charity that is patient and kind, even toward the malicious, whom it bears with. Because, then, he was so ready, he indeed ran to meet the Lord with confidence: Without iniquity, he says, I have run, and I have set straight the crooked, as far as it was in me. Arise, therefore, to meet me as I run to meet you: and because even so I cannot attain to your height, unless you, condescending to the work of your hands, stretch forth your right hand: Arise to meet me (Psal. LVIII, 5, 6), and see whether there is a way of iniquity in me: and if you find some way of iniquity I know not of, remove it from me: and, having mercy on me according to your law, lead me in the way everlasting (Psal. CXXXVIII, 24), that is, in Christ, who is the way by which one travels, and the eternity to which one arrives; the way without stain, the blessed dwelling.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Puto tamen quia et ante mansionem illam beatam, si paraveris Domino viam immaculatam, ipse dignabitur saepius in via ponere gressus suos, dilatabitque subtus te gressus tuos, ut dilatato corde curras viam mandatorum; cujus angustum forte causabaris initium. Sapientia namque, ut ipsa perhibet, in viis justitiae ambulat (Prov. VIII, 20): et: Qui continens est justitiae apprehendet illam, et obviabit illi quasi mater honorificata. Dignos se ipsa circuit quaerens, et in viis suis ostendit se illis (Eccli. XV, 1, 2, et Sap. VI, 17). Si minus aut nunquam tibi eam occurrere conquereris, vide ne forte viam tuam corruperis. Sic enim scriptum habes: Insipientia viri corrumpit viam suam; Deus autem causabitur in corde suo. Ipse siquidem stat ad ostium et pulsat: ut si quis aperuerit ei, coenet cum eo coelestis mensae delicias. Loquitur sponsa: Vox dilecti mei pulsantis; Aperi mihi, soror mea sponsa (Cantic. V, 2). Aperi mihi cor tuum, et cibabo illud. Aperi mihi os tuum, et implebo illud. Os meum, inquit David, aperui, et attraxi spiritum (Psal. CXVIII, 131). Spiritus enim ante faciem nostram Christus Dominus, non modo invitandus, sed et attrahendus quadam violentia precis, vehementiaque fervoris in hospitium cordis: sicut de duobus discipulis in typum hujus rei historia refert Evangelii (Luc. XXIV, 28, 29). Et ipse siquidem non ob aliud, nisi ut probet devotionem charitatis tuae, aliquando se fingit longius ire: sicut et duo angeli, Loth adorante et obsecrante ut intrarent, dissimulabant tamen dicentes, Minime, sed manebimus in platea. Sed quid dicit Scriptura? Compulit illos oppido, ut diverterent ad eum (Gen. XIX, 2, 3). Pia violentia, qua regnum coeleste rapitur: laudabilis importunitas, quae Christum hospitem, aut angelos promeretur. Sed quid est, inquis, quod Jesus fingit se longius ire? Quid, nisi illud quod Ecclesiastes confitetur de se? Dixi, sapiens efficiar; et ipsa longius recessit a me (Eccle. VII, 24). Hoc autem sponsa manifestius exponit, nostram utique quotidianam exprimens querimoniam, ubi ait: Surrexi aperire dilecto meo: at ille declinaverat, atque transierat. Quaesivi illum, et non inveni (Cantic. V, 5, 6): vocavi, et non respondit mihi, sicut nec mulieri Chananeae. Spiritum sapientiae invocabas, spiritum gratiae quaerebas in oratione: si tibi videtur longius recedere, ne desperes, sed importunus insiste; donec respondeatur tibi, Magna est fides tua, fiat tibi sicut petisti (Matth. XV, 28).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. I think, however, that even before that blessed dwelling, if you prepare for the Lord an unstained way, he himself will deign often to set his steps upon the way, and will enlarge your steps beneath you, so that with enlarged heart you may run the way of the commandments, whose beginning you perhaps complained was narrow. For Wisdom, as she herself attests, walks in the ways of justice (Prov. VIII, 20): and: He who holds fast to justice shall lay hold of her, and she shall meet him like a mother held in honor. She goes about seeking out those worthy of herself, and shows herself to them in their ways (Eccli. XV, 1, 2, et Sap. VI, 17). If you complain that she meets you little or never, see whether perhaps you have corrupted your way. For thus it is written: The folly of a man corrupts his way, but he will accuse God in his own heart. For he himself stands at the door and knocks, so that if anyone opens to him, he may dine with him on the delights of the heavenly table. The bride speaks: The voice of my beloved knocking; Open to me, my sister, my spouse (Cantic. V, 2). Open to me your heart, and I will feed it. Open to me your mouth, and I will fill it. I opened my mouth, says David, and drew in the breath (Psal. CXVIII, 131). For the breath before our face is Christ the Lord, who is not only to be invited but also to be drawn in, by a certain violence of prayer and by the vehemence of fervor, into the lodging of the heart: just as the Gospel story relates of the two disciples, as a figure of this matter (Luc. XXIV, 28, 29). And he himself, indeed, for no other reason than to test the devotion of your charity, sometimes pretends to go farther: just as the two angels also, when Lot worshipped them and begged that they would come in, nevertheless feigned, saying, No, but we will stay in the street. But what does Scripture say? He pressed them greatly, so that they turned aside to him (Gen. XIX, 2, 3). A pious violence, by which the kingdom of heaven is seized; a praiseworthy importunity, which wins Christ as guest, or the angels. But what is it, you ask, that Jesus pretends to go farther? What, but that which Ecclesiastes confesses of himself? I said, I shall become wise; and she herself withdrew farther from me (Eccle. VII, 24). But the bride explains this more plainly, expressing indeed our daily complaint, where she says: I rose up to open to my beloved; but he had turned aside and passed on. I sought him, and I did not find him (Cantic. V, 5, 6): I called him, and he did not answer me, just as he did not answer the Canaanite woman either. You were calling upon the spirit of wisdom, you were seeking the spirit of grace in prayer: if he seems to you to withdraw farther off, do not despair, but press on importunately, until it is answered to you, Great is your faith; be it done to you as you have asked (Matth. XV, 28).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Cum tamen invitas Jesum, vide ne Deum majestatis ad sordidum et indignum invites hospitium; ubi nec te ipsum patiatur habitare quietum uxor litigiosa, seu fumus, aut stillicidium. Non enim nisi in pace fit locus ejus: nec aliud quam justitia et judicium praeparatio sedis ejus. Nunc autem me, inquit, de die in diem quaerunt, et scire vias meas volunt, quia gens quae justitiam fecerit, et judicium Dei sui non dereliquerit (Isa. LVIII, 2). Justitia, inquit, et judicium praeparatio sedis ejus (Psal. LXXXVIII, 15). Noli causari quasi sumptuosum [fort. praesumptuosum] sit, viresque tuae excedat paupertatis, tam magnifico, tamque potenti praeparare domum hospiti: habes ad manum unde id possis. Humanum dico propter infirmitatem carnis tuae, vel magis angustiam mentis tuae. Confitere perfecte de praeterito: bonam voluntatem habe de caetero; pax enim hominibus bonae voluntatis (Luc. II, 14), et hoc judicio et justitia sedem Altissimo praeparasti. Vis manifestius audire de confessione, quod eam oporteat fieri in praeparatione adventus Domini? Justus, ait Scriptura, in initio sermonis accusator est sui. Et quid sequitur? Venit amicus ejus (Prov. XVIII, 17), qui modo ante confessionem inimicus assistebat longius. Cum enim dixit, Confitebor adversum me injustitiam meam Domino (Psal. XXXI, 5); et ipse remisit: Venit, inquam, et investigabit eum. Prorsus investigabit, tanquam potio valida, scrutans corda et renes; pertingens usque ad divisionem animae et spiritus, exhauriens noxia de medullis animae, mentisque visceribus, purgans affectus ut fructum plus afferat: de cujus primitivo fructu confessionis jam gaudet pater agricola. Ipse tamen qui post confessionem nonnunquam et antequam invocetur, adest, nonnunquam exspectat ut tu prior eum invites: et ut meritum tibi augeat, saepe diutius dissimulat; ut tu attentius psallendo, instantius orando, dulciter violentus intrare compellas: alioquin planget propheta quod civitates austri clausae sint, nullo introeunte (Jerem. XIII, 19). Cum ergo dicere potueris, Paratum cor meum, Deus, quia vacuatum a malis; paratum cor meum, quia sanctis plenum desideriis: tunc sedulus fac quod sequitur, Cantabo et psalmum dicam (Psal. LXIV, 8). Et quicunque sit sonus cantantis vel psallentis, haec sit intentio mentis: Exsurge, gloria mea, exsurge in occursum mei; quia, quantum potui, occurri tibi. O benigne Jesu, quam alacer et promptus, quam laetus et festivus occurris hujusmodi devotioni! quam hilarem te ostendis in viis istis! Occurristi, inquit Isaias, laetanti et facienti justitiam: in viis tuis recordabuntur tui (Isa. LXVI, 5). Si enim psallas sapienter, in via immaculata veniet; veniet qui et illuminabit abscondita tua, ut quae nescis intelligas mysteria Scripturarum, eritque ut dicas: Psallam et intelligam in via immaculata, quando veniet ad me (Psal. C, 1, 2). Excita, Domine, potentiam tuam, quae excitet pigritiam nostram in occursum tui: et veni, ut salvos nos facias (Psal. LXXIX, 3), Salvator mundi; qui vivis et regnas per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Yet when you invite Jesus, see that you do not invite the God of majesty into a sordid and unworthy lodging—one in which not even you yourself could be permitted to dwell in peace, on account of a quarrelsome wife, or smoke, or a leaking roof. For his place is made only in peace, and the preparation of his throne is nothing other than justice and judgment. 'But now,' he says, 'they seek me day after day, and desire to know my ways, because they are a nation that has done righteousness and has not forsaken the judgment of its God' (Isa. LVIII, 2). 'Justice and judgment,' he says, 'are the preparation of his throne' (Psal. LXXXVIII, 15). Do not object, as though it were a costly thing [perhaps read: presumptuous], and beyond the strength of your poverty, to prepare a house for so magnificent and so powerful a guest: you have at hand the means by which you can do this. I speak in human terms, on account of the weakness of your flesh, or rather the narrowness of your mind. Make full confession concerning the past; have good will concerning what remains; for 'peace is to men of good will' (Luc. II, 14), and by this judgment and justice you will have prepared a seat for the Most High. Do you wish to hear more plainly about confession, that it must be made in preparing for the Lord's coming? 'The just man,' Scripture says, 'at the beginning of his speech is his own accuser. And what follows? His friend comes' (Prov. XVIII, 17)—he who, just before, before the confession, stood far off as an enemy. For when he said, 'I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord' (Psal. XXXI, 5), he himself forgave it; 'he comes,' I say, 'and will search him out.' He will indeed search him out thoroughly, like a strong medicine, examining hearts and loins, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, draining out the harmful matter from the marrow of the soul and the inward parts of the mind, purging the affections so that it may bear more fruit; and in the first-fruit of this confession the Father, the husbandman, already rejoices. Yet he himself, who after confession is sometimes present even before he is invoked, at other times waits for you to invite him first; and in order to increase your merit, he often pretends for a longer time not to notice, so that you, by singing more attentively, by praying more insistently, may compel him, sweetly violent, to enter—otherwise the prophet will lament that the cities of the south are shut up, with no one entering (Jerem. XIII, 19). Therefore, when you are able to say, 'My heart is ready, O God,' because it is emptied of evils; 'my heart is ready,' because it is filled with holy desires—then diligently do what follows: 'I will sing and recite a psalm' (Psal. LXIV, 8). And whatever be the sound of the one singing or playing, let this be the intention of the mind: 'Arise, my glory, arise to meet me; for, as much as I was able, I have come to meet you.' O kind Jesus, how eager and ready, how joyful and festive you come to meet such devotion! How cheerful you show yourself along these paths! 'You met,' says Isaiah, 'the one who rejoices and does justice: in your ways they will remember you' (Isa. LXVI, 5). For if you sing wisely, he will come in the undefiled way; he will come who will also illumine your hidden things, so that you may understand the mysteries of the Scriptures which you did not know, and it will come to be that you say: 'I will sing and understand in the undefiled way, when he comes to me' (Psal. C, 1, 2). Stir up, O Lord, your power, that it may stir up our sluggishness to meet you; and come, that you may save us (Psal. LXXIX, 3), O Savior of the world, who live and reign through all ages of ages. Amen.

sermons.title: Advent Sermon III: That One Should Always Be Ready for the Coming Lord

sermons.author: Guerric of Igny
metadata: Guerric of Igny, Sermones per annum, De adventu Domini, sermo IV, De vita solitaria, et de via Domino paranda, in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier frères, 1879), cols. 21-26.
