Advent; no particular Sunday is specified
sermons.occasion_detail: Advent; no particular Sunday is specified

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: This fourth Advent sermon belongs to Guerric of Igny's medieval collection of sermons for the liturgical year, here read from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. Its individual date is unknown; the collection is associated approximately with his abbacy in 1138–1157. Addressed to monks in the solitude of the desert, it reads John the Baptist's cry to prepare the way for the Lord as a call to correct one's life. Guerric commends the peaceful ways of wisdom, the spotless way of chastity, the baptism of penance and knowledge of God's law. The source names Advent without assigning a particular Sunday.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO IV.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON IV.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De vita solitaria, et de via Domino paranda.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the solitary life, and on preparing the way for the Lord.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Vox clamantis in deserto, Parate viam Domini (Isa. XL, 3). Primo omnium considerandam arbitror gratiam deserti, beatitudinem eremi; quae ab initio gratiae, quieti sanctorum meruit consecrari. Consecravit nobis plane habitationem deserti vox clamantis in deserto, Joannes praedicans et tribuens baptismum poenitentiae in deserto; quanquam et ante ipsum quibusque sanctissimis prophetarum, velut auditorium Spiritus, amica semper fuerit solitudo. Longe tamen excellentior atque divinior ipsi loco gratia sanctificationis accessit, cum Jesus Joanni successit: qui etiam, antequam praedicare poenitentibus inciperet, locum poenitentibus praeparandum putavit; atque per dies quadraginta, dum versatur in deserto, velut purificans locum, novumque novae vitae dedicans locum, tyrannum qui incubabat, omnemque malitiam et subtilitatem ejus, non tam sibi, quam illis qui accolae eremi futuri erant, superavit. Si ergo elongasti fugiens et manens in solitudine, ibi permane, ibi exspecta eum qui te salvum faciet a pusillanimitate spiritus, et tempestate. Quantalibet ingruat tibi tempestas bellorum, quantacunque patiaris in deserto, penuriam etiam victualium, noli pusillanimitate spiritus redire mente in Aegyptum. Felicius te pascet eremus manna, id est pane angelorum, quam Aegyptus ollis carnium. Ipse Jesus quidem in eremo jejunavit; sed multitudinem sequentium se in deserto, saepe et mirabiliter pavit. Saepius autem et mirabilius te satiabit, qui tanto gratiore merito, quanto sanctiore proposito secutus es eum in deserto. Cum enim diutius eum tui oblitum putaveris, ipse suae non immemor bonitatis, consolabitur te, et dicet tibi: Recordatus sum tui, miserans adolescentiam tuam, et charitatem desponsationis tuae, quando secuta es me in deserto (Jerem. II, 2). Tunc plane ponet desertum tuum quasi delicias paradisi: et ipse confiteberis quia gloria Libani data est ei, decor Carmeli et Saron (Isa. XXXV, 2). Sicut enim in multis hodie locis, etiam juxta litteram illud propheticum videmus impleri, Pinguescent speciosa deserti (Psal. LXIV, 13); et, Deserta in ubertatem versa advenae comedent (Isa. V, 17): sic quilibet Scripturae locus, qui ante tibi sterilis videbatur et aridus, repente ad benedictionem Dei mira replebitur ubertate, ac pinguedine spiritus; ut de saturitate mentis eructes hymnum laudis, Confiteantur, inquiens, Domino, misericordiae ejus, et mirabilia ejus filiis hominum: quia satiavit animam inanem, et animam esurientem satiavit bonis (Psal. CVI, 8, 9).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord (Isa. XL, 3). First of all, I think we must consider the grace of the desert, the blessedness of the wilderness; which from the very beginning of grace deserved to be consecrated to the rest of the saints. The voice crying in the desert clearly consecrated for us the dwelling-place of the desert—John, preaching and bestowing the baptism of repentance in the desert; although even before him solitude had always been a friend to the holiest of the prophets, as a hearing-chamber of the Spirit. Yet a far more excellent and more divine grace of sanctification came upon that very place when Jesus succeeded John, who, even before he began to preach to penitents, thought it right that the place be prepared for penitents; and for forty days, while he dwelt in the desert, as though purifying the place and dedicating this new place to a new life, he overcame the tyrant who lay brooding there, and all his malice and cunning—not so much for his own sake as for the sake of those who were to be future dwellers of the wilderness. If, then, you have fled far off and remain in solitude, stay there; wait there for him who will save you from faintness of spirit and from the storm. However great a storm of battles may rush upon you, whatever you may suffer in the desert, even a lack of provisions, do not, through faintness of spirit, turn back in your mind to Egypt. The wilderness will feed you more happily with manna, that is, with the bread of angels, than Egypt with its pots of meat. Jesus himself indeed fasted in the wilderness; but the multitude that followed him in the desert he often and wonderfully fed. But he will satisfy you still more often and still more wonderfully, since you have followed him into the desert with a purpose all the holier, and thus with a merit all the more pleasing. For when you have thought for a long time that he has forgotten you, he himself, not forgetful of his own goodness, will console you and say to you: I have remembered you, having pity on your youth and on the love of your betrothal, when you followed me into the desert (Jerem. II, 2). Then he will surely make your desert like the delights of paradise, and you yourself will confess that the glory of Lebanon has been given to it, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon (Isa. XXXV, 2). For just as today, in many places, we see that prophetic word fulfilled even according to the letter—The beautiful places of the desert shall grow fat (Psal. LXIV, 13); and, The deserts turned into abundance shall strangers eat (Isa. V, 17)—so too any passage of Scripture which before seemed to you barren and dry will suddenly, by God's blessing, be filled with wondrous abundance and with fatness of spirit, so that from the fullness of your mind you will belch forth a hymn of praise: Let them give praise to the Lord, he says, for his mercies, and his wonderful works to the children of men: for he has satisfied the empty soul, and filled the hungry soul with good things (Psal. CVI, 8, 9).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Illud sane mirabili gratia provisum est divinae dispensationis, ut in his desertis nostris quietem habeamus solitudinis, nec tamen consolatione careamus gratiae et sanctae societatis. Licet cuique sedere solitarium, et tacere, eo quod neminem patiatur interpellantem: nec tamen vae soli, eo quod non habeat confoventem: aut, si ceciderit, sublevantem (Eccle. IV, 10). In frequentia hominum sumus, et sine turba sumus; velut in urbe versamur, nullum tamen tumultum patimur, quominus vox clamantis in deserto a nobis audiatur: si modo interius, sicut exterius silentium habeamus. Verba namque sapientium, ait Salomon, audiuntur in silentio, plus quam clamor principis inter stultos (Eccle. IX, 17). Et nunc quoque si medium silentium teneant omnia interiora tua, omnipotens sermo tibi secretus illabetur de sede paterna. Felix igitur, qui sic elongavit fugiens tumultum mundi: qui tam procul recessit in secretum et solitudinem quietae mentis, ut non modo vocem Verbi, sed et Verbum ipsum; non Joannem, sed Jesum mereatur audire! Interim tamen quid vox Verbi nobis clamet audiamus, ut quandoque de voce ad Verbum proficiamus. Parate, inquit, viam Domino: rectas facite semitas ejus (Isa. XL, 3). Parat viam, qui corrigit vitam: rectam facit semitam, qui per arctiorem se dirigit viam. Plane vita correcta, via est recta, per quam Dominus veniat ad nos, qui in hoc ipsum praevenit nos. A Domino siquidem gressus hominis dirigentur, et viam sic ejus volet, ut gratanter per eam veniens ad hominem, cum eo jugiter ambulet. Nisi enim suum ad nos adventum ipse praeveniat, qui est via, veritas et vita (Joan. XIV, 6); non potest via nostra corrigi secundum regulam veritatis, ac per hoc nec dirigi ad vitam aeternitatis. In quo vero corrigit adolescentior viam suam, nisi in custodiendo sermones ejus, nisi in sequendo vestigia ejus, qui viam fecit se ipsum, qua veniamus ad ipsum? Utinam dirigantur viae meae, ad custodiendas, o Domine, vias tuas (Psal. CXVIII, 5); ut propter verba labiorum tuorum custodiam etiam vias duras: quae etsi durae videantur carni, quia infirma est, suaves et pulchrae videbuntur spiritui, si promptus est! Viae, inquit, ejus viae pulchrae, et omnes semitae ejus pacificae (Prov. III, 17). Non solum pacatae, sed et pacificae sunt viae sapientiae: quia, cum placuerint Domino viae hominis, etiam inimicos ejus convertet ad pacem (Id. XVI, 7). Israel, si in viis meis, inquit, ambulasset, pro nihilo forsitan inimicos eorum humiliassem, et super tribulantes eos misissem manum meam (Psal. LXXX, 14, 15). Quare enim contritio et infelicitas in viis eorum, nisi quia viam pacis non cognoverunt (Psal. XIII, 3)? Eapropter, si quando vidi hominem inquietum, contumacem, litigiosum, gravissima tentatione vexari, vel tribulatione flagellari, recordabar illius proverbii: Semper jurgia quaerit malus: angelus autem crudelis mittetur contra eum (Prov. XVII, 11), cui traditur forsitan in afflictionem carnis, ut spiritus salvus sit in die Domini. Si tamen aliquando prosperatur via impiorum, noli aemulari in eo qui prosperatur in via sua, in homine faciente injustitias (Psal. XXXVI, 7): quia haec via eorum scandalum ipsis; ut tanto liberius in mortem currant, quanto minus sepitur eis via qua ambulant. De istis Sapiens loquitur: Via peccantium complanata lapidibus: sed in fine illorum, inferi, tenebrae et poenae (Eccli. XXI, 11): et, Ducunt in bonis dies suos, et in puncto descendunt ad inferos (Job XXI, 13). Beati igitur immaculati in via, qui ambulant in via Domini! quia, etsi de torrente in via bibunt, propterea exaltabunt caput; quia caput suum, quod sequuntur per viam passionis, consequentur in fine mansionis.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. It was surely provided by a wonderful grace of divine dispensation that in these deserts of ours we should have the quiet of solitude, and yet not lack the consolation of grace and holy fellowship. Each one may sit solitary and be silent, in that he suffers no one interrupting him; and yet it is not "woe to him alone," in that he has no one to comfort him, or, if he should fall, to lift him up (Eccle. IV, 10). We are amid a throng of men, and yet we are without a crowd; we dwell as it were in a city, yet we suffer no tumult that would keep us from hearing the voice of one crying in the desert—provided only that we keep interior silence as we keep exterior silence. For, as Solomon says, the words of the wise are heard in silence more than the shouting of a prince among fools (Eccle. IX, 17). And even now, if all your inward parts keep deep silence, the omnipotent Word will steal into you secretly from the Father's throne. Happy, then, is he who has so withdrawn, fleeing the tumult of the world, who has retreated so far into the secrecy and solitude of a quiet mind, that he deserves to hear not only the voice of the Word, but the Word itself—not John, but Jesus! Meanwhile, however, let us listen to what the voice of the Word cries to us, so that one day we may advance from the voice to the Word. "Prepare," he says, "the way for the Lord; make straight his paths" (Isa. XL, 3). He prepares the way who corrects his life; he makes the path straight who directs himself along the narrower way. Clearly a corrected life is a straight way, by which the Lord may come to us—he who has gone before us for this very purpose. For indeed the steps of man are directed by the Lord, and he so wills his way that, gladly coming by it to man, he may walk continually with him. For unless he himself, who is the way, the truth, and the life (Joan. XIV, 6), should go before us in his own coming to us, our way cannot be corrected according to the rule of truth, and therefore cannot be directed toward the life of eternity. But in what does the young man correct his way, except in keeping his words, except in following the footsteps of him who made himself the way by which we come to him? "Would that my ways were directed, O Lord, to the keeping of your ways" (Psal. CXVIII, 5); that for the sake of the words of your lips I might keep even the hard ways—which, though they seem hard to the flesh, because it is weak, will seem sweet and beautiful to the spirit, if it is willing! "Her ways," it says, "are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceful" (Prov. III, 17). The ways of wisdom are not only peaceable but peace-making: because, when the ways of a man please the Lord, he will turn even his enemies to peace (Id. XVI, 7). "If Israel," he says, "had walked in my ways, I might perhaps have humbled their enemies with ease, and would have set my hand against those who troubled them" (Psal. LXXX, 14, 15). For why is there destruction and unhappiness in their ways, except that they have not known the way of peace (Psal. XIII, 3)? For this reason, whenever I have seen a restless, stubborn, quarrelsome man vexed by some very grave temptation or scourged by tribulation, I would recall that proverb: "The wicked man always seeks quarrels; but a cruel angel will be sent against him" (Prov. XVII, 11)—to whom perhaps he is handed over for the affliction of the flesh, that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord. Yet if sometimes the way of the impious prospers, do not envy the man who prospers in his way, the man who does unjust things (Psal. XXXVI, 7): for this very way of theirs is a snare to them; so that they run the more freely into death, the less their way is hedged in as they walk it. Of such the Wise Man speaks: "The way of sinners is made smooth with stones; but at their end are hell, darkness, and torments" (Eccli. XXI, 11); and, "They spend their days in good things, and in a moment they go down to hell" (Job XXI, 13). Blessed, then, are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the way of the Lord! For even if they drink of the torrent in the way, they shall therefore lift up the head; because the Head whom they follow through the way of suffering, they shall attain at the end of their dwelling.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Quidquid igitur occurrerit vobis in via Domini, laeto ac dilatato corde currite viam mandatorum Dei: quia etsi pusillanimis arcta videtur via, tamen recta; et si dura videtur, immaculata est. Plane beati immaculati in via! qui sic immaculato calle transeunt viam mundi, ut non inquinent vestimenta sua: aut certe, si inquinaverint, secundum beatitudinis non amittunt locum; sed lavant vestimenta sua baptismo poenitentiae, quo Joannes baptizat in eremo, viam parans Domino. Via utique immaculata, castitas; via grata, per quam Dominus gratiae dignanter veniat: cui propheta cantat, Deus meus, impolluta via ejus. Impolluta castitas Virginis, qua venit in uterum illius: impolluta necesse est sit castitas hominis, qua veniat in animam illius. Felix conscientia, cui convenit vox illa: Deus praecinxit me virtute continentiae, et posuit immaculatam viam meam (Psal. XVII, 31, 33)! Verumtamen, ne de castitate sine virtutibus aliis glorieris, quasi jam viam immaculatam Domino paraveris: scito quia nihilominus necesse est ut via haec etiam recta sit, plana sit, ut etiam tenebrosa vel lubrica non sit. Nam via impiorum tenebrae et lubricum; et angelus Domini persequens eos (Psal. XXXIV, 6). Et via impiorum tenebrosa: nesciunt ubi corruant (Prov. IV, 19). Putamusne, fratres, in aliquo nostrum inveniatur adhuc pravum aliquid in voluntatibus, asperum in moribus, tenebrosum per ignorantiam sensus, lubricum per inconstantiam actus? Quomodo autem scripturam de via paranda implebimus, nisi, sicut scriptum est, faciamus: Ut sint prava, in directa; et aspera, in vias planas (Isa. XL, 4, et Luc. III, 5)?

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Therefore, whatever may meet you on the way of the Lord, run the way of God's commandments with a joyful and enlarged heart: for even if the way seems narrow to the faint-hearted, it is nevertheless straight; and if it seems hard, it is spotless. Truly blessed are the spotless in the way! who so pass through the way of the world by a spotless path that they do not stain their garments: or if indeed they have stained them, they do not lose the second place of blessedness; but they wash their garments in the baptism of penance, with which John baptizes in the desert, preparing the way for the Lord. Surely the spotless way is chastity; the pleasing way, by which the Lord of grace may deign to come: to whom the prophet sings, 'My God, his way is undefiled.' Undefiled was the chastity of the Virgin, by which he came into her womb; undefiled must necessarily be the chastity of man, by which he comes into his soul. Happy is the conscience to which that voice applies: 'God has girded me with the strength of continence, and has made my way spotless' (Psal. XVII, 31, 33)! Yet, lest you boast of chastity apart from the other virtues, as though you had already prepared a spotless way for the Lord, know that it is likewise necessary that this way be also straight, be level, and also not be dark or slippery. For the way of the wicked is darkness and slipperiness; and the angel of the Lord pursues them (Psal. XXXIV, 6). And the way of the wicked is dark: they do not know where they will fall (Prov. IV, 19). Do we suppose, brothers, that there may still be found in any of us something crooked in our wills, something rough in our conduct, something darkened through ignorance of understanding, something slippery through inconstancy of action? But how shall we fulfill the Scripture about preparing the way, unless, as it is written, we do this: that the crooked places be made straight, and the rough ways be made smooth (Isa. XL, 4, et Luc. III, 5)?

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Primo itaque necesse est ut, si qua est in nobis prava et distorta voluntas, corrigatur, et ad regulam divinae voluntatis dirigatur. Aliter videbimur dicere, sicut impii dicunt: Non est recta via Domini. Sed statim refellit nos irrefragabilis veritas, et increpat terribilis severitas: Nunquid non viae meae rectae sunt, et non magis viae vestrae pravae sunt (Ezech. XVIII, 29)? Qui igitur viam Domino parare festinas primo omnium bona sit voluntas; quoniam in malevolam animam non introibit sapientia (Sap. I, 4). Cum autem hoc modo posueris prava in directa, scito quia non minus necesse est ut aspera sint in vias planas: ut scilicet omnem morum complanes asperitatem, et in quamdam vitae socialis sternas aequalitatem, ne mitis et suavis ille viator offensus asperitate viae resiliat. Quidni resiliret ille mitis et humilis corde, qui non nisi super mansuetum requiescit et humilem; cum etiam humanus omnis sensus refugiat et horreat hominem iracundum, et intractabilem? Sed, et si eatenus profecisti in via Domini, ut et propositum rectitudinis, et disciplinam mansuetudinis assecutus sis; profecisti quidem, sed non perfecisti, nisi lucerna sit pedibus tuis verbum Dei, et lumen semitis tuis. In via enim qua ambulabam, ait, absconderunt laqueum mihi (Psal. CXLI, 4). Et sunt viae quae videntur hominibus rectae, novissimum autem earum ducit in profundum inferni. Via enim impiorum tenebrosa, ut Salomon ait: nesciunt ubi corruant (Prov. IV, 19). Hoc et Dominus ait: Qui ambulat in tenebris, nescit quo vadat (Joan. XII, 35). At vero mandatum lucerna est, et lex lux, et via vitae increpatio disciplinae (Prov. VI, 23). Qui enim increpationes relinquit, errat. Si igitur sapis, in via qua nunquam ambulasti, non ipse tibi doctor aut ductor eris, sed aurem magistris inclinabis, et increpationibus eorum acquiesces, et consiliis; et operam scientiae et lectioni dabis, ne sero poenitens dicas: Cur detestatus sum disciplinam, et increpationibus non acquievit cor meum; nec audivi vocem docentium me, et magistris non inclinavi aurem meam? Pene fui in omni malo, in medio ecclesiae, et synagogae (Prov. V, 12-14). Quod enim scientia legis liberet a laqueis, audi confitentem David: Posuerunt peccatores laqueum mihi, sed de mandatis tuis non erravi. Quomodo id potuisti? Quia haereditate acquisivi testimonia tua. Et in via testimoniorum tuorum delectatus sum, sicut in omnibus divitiis. Me exspectaverunt peccatores ut perderent me: sed per hoc evasi, quia testimonia tua intellexi (Psal. CXVIII, 110, 111, 94, 95). Lex Dei, inquit, in corde justi, et per hoc non supplantabuntur gressus ejus (Psal. XXXVI, 31). Hinc et filius ejus Salomon ait: Simulator ore decipit amicum suum, justi autem liberabuntur scientia (Prov. XI, 9).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. First of all, then, it is necessary that, if there is in us any crooked and twisted will, it be corrected and directed to the rule of the divine will. Otherwise we shall seem to say, as the wicked say: 'The way of the Lord is not straight.' But immediately unanswerable truth refutes us, and terrible severity rebukes us: 'Are not my ways straight, and are not your ways rather crooked?' (Ezech. XVIII, 29). Therefore you who hasten to prepare the way for the Lord, let your will be good above all else; for wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul (Sap. I, 4). But when you have in this way made the crooked straight, know that it is no less necessary that the rough places be made into smooth ways: namely, that you smooth away every roughness of conduct, and spread a certain evenness in your life together with others, lest that gentle and sweet traveler, offended by the roughness of the way, draw back. And why would he not draw back—he who is gentle and humble of heart, who rests only upon the meek and the humble—since even every human sense flees and shudders at an angry and intractable man? But even if you have progressed thus far on the way of the Lord, so as to have attained both the purpose of rectitude and the discipline of gentleness, you have indeed made progress, but you have not reached perfection, unless the word of God is a lamp to your feet and a light to your paths. For 'in the way in which I walked,' he says, 'they hid a snare for me' (Psal. CXLI, 4). And there are ways that seem right to men, but their end leads into the depths of hell. For the way of the wicked is dark, as Solomon says: they do not know where they will fall (Prov. IV, 19). The Lord also says this: 'He who walks in darkness does not know where he goes' (Joan. XII, 35). But indeed the commandment is a lamp, and the law is light, and the way of life is the rebuke of discipline (Prov. VI, 23). For whoever abandons rebukes goes astray. If, then, you are wise, on a way you have never walked, you will not be your own teacher or guide, but you will incline your ear to teachers, and you will acquiesce to their rebukes and counsels; and you will give diligence to knowledge and to reading, lest, repenting too late, you say: 'Why have I hated discipline, and my heart did not consent to rebukes; and I did not hear the voice of those who taught me, nor did I incline my ear to my teachers? I was almost in every evil, in the midst of the church and the assembly' (Prov. V, 12-14). That knowledge of the law frees from snares, hear David confessing: 'Sinners have laid a snare for me: but I have not strayed from your commandments.' How were you able to do that? 'Because I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance. And in the way of your testimonies I have delighted, as in all riches. Sinners waited for me, to destroy me: but through this I escaped, because I understood your testimonies' (Psal. CXVIII, 110, 111, 94, 95). 'The law of God,' he says, 'is in the heart of the just, and therefore his steps shall not be overthrown' (Psal. XXXVI, 31). Hence also his son Solomon says: 'He who dissembles with his mouth deceives his friend, but the just shall be delivered by knowledge' (Prov. XI, 9).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Sed utinam haec via, qua salutem vel Salvatorem suscipere debemus, sicut jam non est tenebrosa per ignorantiam veri, sic nec lubrica sit per inconstantiam operis. Sed, sicut Balaam cadens apertos habebat oculos (Num. XXII, 27, 31), sic et nos: et videmus apertis oculis per scientiam, et cadimus per negligentiam. Volentes et scientes peccamus, et libentes lubricamus: nec tam lubricum viae causari possumus, quam propositum mentis, id est, pedem cui innitimur. Quis enim non ambulat in lubrico, dum in mundo, dum in corpore vivit luteo? Non igitur tam via quam pes in culpa est, qui in via Dei minus firmus est. Sed nunquid, qui cadit, non adjiciet ut resurgat? Septies cadit justus in die, et septies resurgit (Prov. XXIV, 16). Dominus enim erigit elisos, Dominus dirigit justos (Psal. CXLV, 8). Nam, si dicebam: Motus est pes meus; misericordia tua, Domine, adjuvabat me (Psal. XCIII, 18). Quando igitur aliter non potes cadens, surgens viam ambula, clamans tamen semper ei, quem sequi et consequi desideras, Perfice gressus meos in semitis tuis ut non moveantur vestigia mea (Psal. XVI, 5); et, si via iniquitatis in me est (ut est humana fragilitas), deduc me in via aeterna (Psal. CXXXVIII, 24); quatenus per te, qui es via et veritas, perveniam ad te, qui es veritas, et vita aeterna: tibi gloria per aeterna saecula. Amen

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. But would that this way, by which we must receive salvation or the Savior, just as it is now no longer dark through ignorance of the truth, so also might not be slippery through inconstancy of action. But, just as Balaam, when falling, had his eyes open (Num. XXII, 27, 31), so also do we: we see with open eyes through knowledge, and yet we fall through negligence. We sin willingly and knowingly, and we slip gladly: nor can we blame the slipperiness of the way so much as the disposition of the mind, that is, the foot on which we lean. For who does not walk on slippery ground, while living in the world, while living in a body of clay? It is not, then, so much the way that is at fault as the foot, which is less firm on the way of God. But shall he who falls not add to his falling a rising up again? The just man falls seven times in a day, and seven times rises again (Prov. XXIV, 16). For the Lord raises up those who are cast down, the Lord sets the just upright (Psal. CXLV, 8). For, if I said, 'My foot is moved'; your mercy, O Lord, helped me (Psal. XCIII, 18). Therefore, when you cannot do otherwise, walk the way falling and rising, yet always crying out to him whom you desire to follow and to attain: 'Perfect my steps in your paths, that my footsteps be not moved' (Psal. XVI, 5); and, 'if the way of iniquity be in me' (as is human frailty), 'lead me in the way everlasting' (Psal. CXXXVIII, 24); so that through you, who are the way and the truth, I may come to you, who are the truth and life everlasting: to you be glory through everlasting ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: This fifth Advent sermon belongs to Guerric of Igny's medieval collection of sermons for the liturgical year, here read from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. Its individual date is unknown; the collection is associated approximately with his abbacy in 1138–1157. The way for the Lord is prepared by walking it and has no end, so progress must always begin again. Fear of the Lord leads to penance, which goes before grace. Through Isaiah's holy way and the serpent shedding its skin in a narrow passage, Guerric keeps his monks on the royal road toward its promised end. The source names Advent without assigning a particular Sunday.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO V.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON V.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Quomodo proficiendum in paranda via Domino.

passages.label: English
passages.text: How to Make Progress in Preparing the Way for the Lord.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Parate viam Domino (Isa. XL, 3). Via Domini, fratres, quam parare jubemur, ambulando paratur, parando ambulatur. Et licet multum profeceritis in ea, semper tamen vobis restat paranda: ut de his in quae pervenistis, tendatis et extendatis vos in ulteriora; quatenus per singulos profectus Dominus, cujus adventui via paratur, quasi novus, ac seipso semper major occurrat. Ideo bene justus orat: Legem pone mihi, Domine, viam justificationum tuarum, et exquiram eam semper (Psal. CXVIII, 33). Ideo forsitan via aeterna dicta est; quia licet providentia semitam cujusque investigaverit, terminumque constituerit quousque proficiat; terminum tamen non habet illius, in quam proficitis, bonitatis natura. Itaque sapiens impigerque viator cum consummatus fuerit, tunc incipiet: ita scilicet obliviscens quae retro sunt, ut quotidie dicat sibi, Nunc coepi (Psal. LXXVI, 11). Exsultat ut gigas, quem nil terreat ad currendam viam mandatorum Dei: Idithumque factus, pigros qui in via resident, facile transilit in impetu cursus sui. Et licet novissima diei hora venerit, consummatus in brevi explet tempora multa; ut repente de novissimo primus, inter primos coronam accipiat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "Prepare the way for the Lord" (Isa. XL, 3). The way of the Lord, brothers, which we are commanded to prepare, is prepared by walking, and is walked by preparing. And however much progress you have made in it, it always remains for you to prepare further: so that from the point you have reached, you may stretch and extend yourselves into what lies beyond; so that through each advance the Lord, for whose coming the way is prepared, may meet you as it were new, and ever greater than himself. For this reason the just man rightly prays: "Set before me a law, O Lord, the way of your justifications, and I will always seek it" (Psal. CXVIII, 33). For this reason, perhaps, it is called the eternal way; because although providence has traced out the path for each person and set a limit up to which he may progress, the nature of that goodness toward which you are progressing has no limit. And so the wise and tireless traveler, when he has been made complete, then begins; forgetting, that is, the things that are behind, so that he may say to himself every day, "Now I have begun" (Psal. LXXVI, 11). He exults like a giant, whom nothing may frighten from running the way of God's commandments: having become like Idithun, he easily leaps over those slothful ones who sit by the roadside, in the very impetus of his course. And even though he comes at the last hour of the day, being made complete, he fulfills much time in a short span; so that from being last he suddenly becomes first, and receives the crown among the first.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Sed nos qui de profectu viae ejus loquimur, utinam vel initium ejus apprehenderimus! Meo namque sensu atque judicio non parum in ea proficit qui coepit; si tamen vere coepit, si viam civitatis habitaculi invenit. Quam pauci sunt, ait Veritas, qui inveniunt eam! (Matth. VII, 14.) Quam multi sunt qui in solitudine errant! prorsus omnes solitarii, id est omnes superbi, qui se solos reputant. Nullus eorum adhuc dicere potest: Nunc coepi, haec mutatio dexterae Excelsi (Psal. LXXVI, 11). Non enim est illis commutatio, ut desinant esse quod erant, quia non timuerunt Deum (Psal. LIV, 20), cum initium sapientiae sit timor Domini (Psal. CX, 10). Si initium sapientiae, nimirum et viae bonae. Ipse nempe timor Domini, ipse est qui statim illud sapiens consilium generat in corde viri, ut dicere possit: Cogitavi vias meas, et converti pedes meos in testimonia tua (Psal. CXVIII, 59). Ipse confessionem persuadet, quam Psalmista initium boni operis esse docet: Incipite, inquit, domino in confessione (Psal. CXLVI, 7). Ipse ad poenitentiam superbum inclinat, ut vocem clamantis in deserto viamque parari jubentis, et unde incipiendum sit ostendentis, audiat: Poenitentiam agite; appropinquabit enim regnum coelorum (Matth. III, 2). Huic sententia consonat Salomonis, qui manifesta definitione rudes instruit, dicens: Initium viae bonae, facere justa (Prov. XVI, 5). Quid est enim justa facere, nisi poenitentiam agere? nisi de nobisipsis quod Deo debemus exigere, et quod rapuimus exsolvere? Haec est justitia quae ante Dominum ambulat, viamque ei placitam parat, sicut scriptum est: Justitia ante eum ambulabit, et ponet in via gressus suos (Psal. LXXXIV, 14). Sicut enim Joannes Jesum, sic poenitentia gratiam praecedit; illam scilicet gratiam, qua post satisfactionem reconciliati, suscipimur in osculo pacis. In hac siquidem poenitentiae via, grato atque hilari occursu obviant sibi, seseque osculantur justitia et pax; justitia scilicet hominis se punientis, et pax Dei ignoscentis: laetumque ac jucundum celebrant in osculo sancto foedus reconciliationis. Denique ne parvi aestimetur meriti haec justitia hominis de semetipso facientis judicium et justitiam, neve oratiunculae, et vota pigrorum se laboribus poenitentium comparare praesumant; quid de ipsa Salomon sentiat; audiant: Initium, inquit, viae bonae, facere justa: accepta autem Deo magis, quam immolare hostias (Prov. XVI, 5). Si ergo videris hominem huic poenitentiae professum, regularibus ac sanctis laboribus, quorum debitor est, singulares oratiunculas praeferentem; ingere ei hanc Sapientis sententiam: Initium viae bonae, facere justa: accepta autem magis Deo quam immolare hostias. Similiter, si videris hominem, adversus quem frater suus aliquid habet, munus seu laudum, seu sacramentorum, ad altare offerentem; repete ei nihilominus eumdem sermonem: Initium viae bonae, facere justa, ut fratri reconcilieris: accepta autem Deo magis quam immolare hostias. Nam et illo etiam spectat haec sententia, ut daturus eleemosynam, prius, si quem defraudavit, vel simplum restituat. Sic et tu quoque voluntaria oris tui beneplacita nullatenus Deo esse credideris, illa scilicet quae in psalmis, vel in orationibus secretis ei obtuleris; si propterea canonem psalmorum ex Regula constitutum negligentius exsolveris. Nonne, si recte offeras, et non recte dividas peccasti? (Gen. III, sec. LXX.) Rectas, inquit, facite semitas ejus (Matth. III, 3, et Isa. XL, 3), vos qui paratis viam Domini.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. But we who speak of progress on this way—would that we had even grasped its beginning! For in my own sense and judgment, he who has begun makes no small progress on it; provided, however, that he has truly begun, if he has found the way to the city of habitation. "How few are they," says the Truth, "who find it!" (Matth. VII, 14.) How many are there who wander in solitude! Indeed, all the solitary—that is, all the proud, who consider themselves alone. None of them can yet say: "Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High" (Psal. LXXVI, 11). For there is no change for them, that they should cease to be what they were, because they have not feared God (Psal. LIV, 20), since the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Psal. CX, 10). If it is the beginning of wisdom, surely it is also the beginning of the good way. For it is indeed the fear of the Lord itself that immediately generates in a man's heart that wise counsel, so that he can say: "I have thought on my ways, and turned my feet unto your testimonies" (Psal. CXVIII, 59). It is this fear that persuades to confession, which the Psalmist teaches is the beginning of a good work: "Begin," he says, "to the Lord with confession" (Psal. CXLVI, 7). It is this fear that inclines the proud man to penance, so that he hears the voice of the one crying in the desert, commanding that the way be prepared, and showing where one must begin: "Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near" (Matth. III, 2). With this sentence agrees that of Solomon, who instructs the unlearned with a plain definition, saying: "The beginning of a good way is to do what is right" (Prov. XVI, 5). For what is it to do what is right, except to do penance? Except to exact from ourselves what we owe to God, and to repay what we have stolen? This is the righteousness that walks before the Lord, and prepares for him a way pleasing to him, as it is written: "Righteousness shall walk before him, and shall set her steps in the way" (Psal. LXXXIV, 14). For just as John preceded Jesus, so penance precedes grace; that grace, namely, by which, after making satisfaction, reconciled, we are received with the kiss of peace. In this way of penance, indeed, righteousness and peace meet one another with a welcome and joyful encounter, and kiss one another; namely, the righteousness of the man punishing himself, and the peace of God forgiving; and they celebrate, in a holy kiss, the glad and joyous covenant of reconciliation. Finally, lest this righteousness of a man passing judgment and doing justice upon himself be reckoned of little merit, and lest little prayers and the vows of the slothful presume to compare themselves to the labors of the penitent, let them hear what Solomon thinks of it: "The beginning," he says, "of a good way is to do what is right; but more acceptable to God than to offer sacrifices" (Prov. XVI, 5). If, therefore, you see a man professed to this penance, preferring his own private little prayers to the regular and holy labors of which he is a debtor, press upon him this sentence of the Wise Man: "The beginning of a good way is to do what is right; but it is more acceptable to God than to offer sacrifices." Likewise, if you see a man, against whom his brother has some grievance, offering a gift at the altar, whether of praises or of the sacraments, repeat to him nevertheless the same word: "The beginning of a good way is to do what is right, that you be reconciled to your brother; but it is more acceptable to God than to offer sacrifices." For this sentence also looks to this: that one who is about to give alms should first, if he has defrauded anyone, restore at least the simple amount. So also you yourself should by no means believe that the voluntary offerings of your mouth are pleasing to God—those, namely, which you offer him in psalms or in private prayers—if on that account you perform more negligently the canon of psalms established by the Rule. Have you not sinned, if you offer rightly but do not divide rightly? (Gen. III, sec. LXX.) "Make straight," he says, "his paths" (Matth. III, 3, et Isa. XL, 3), you who prepare the way of the Lord.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. O Domine, tu parasti directiones nobis, si modo nos recte ambulemus in illis. Tu legem posuisti nobis, viam justificationum tuarum, per illum scilicet, quem hujus sanctae institutionis Legislatorem dedisti: Haec via, inquiens, ambulate in ea, neque ad dexteram, neque ad sinistram (Isai. XXX, 21). Haec via plane, sicut propheta promiserat: Via directa nobis, ita ut stulti non errent per eam (Isa. XXXV, 8). Junior fui, etenim senui; et non vidi, si bene memini, stultum errantem per viam: cum vix aliquem sapientem viderim, qui rectitudinem ejus tenere potuerit. Vae, qui sapientes estis in oculis vestris, et coram vobismetipsis prudentes (Isa. V, 21)! quos sapientia vestra devios abducit a via salutis, nec sinit stultitiam sequi Salvatoris. Non ignorabat ille stultus propter Christum, quid haec sapientia terrena, animalis, diabolica mali faciat, qui dicebat: Si quis sapiens esse videtur in hoc saeculo, stultus fiat, ut sit sapiens apud Deum (I Cor. III, 18). Optabilis stultitia, quae divino judicio reputatur sapientia, quae hominem non sinit errare de via. Haec stultitia, nisi fallor, est illa desursum sapientia, pudica, pacifica, modesta, suadibilis, bonis consentiens (Jacob. III, 17): a quibus omnibus quam procul abhorreat sapiens in oculis suis, utinam nunquam experientia ipsa probasset in oculis nostris. Si contristat vos arrogantia, seu pervicacia hujusmodi sapientium, consolatur abundantius nostrorum pax atque modestia stultorum, qui quanto minus sibi credunt, tanto suadibiliores bonis consentiunt. Tales itaque stulti non errant facile de via Dei, sed juxta verbum prophetae semper audiunt vocem post tergum monentis: Haec via, ambulate in ea, neque ad dexteram, neque ad sinistram (Isai. XXX, 21): ne scilicet per fervorem excedentes modum, aut per teporem subsistentes citra modum, legem praescriptam, viamque deseratis regiam. Spiritus est ad dexteram, caro est ad sinistram; et haec sibi colluctantia semper sibi adversantur, ut non quaecunque vult, sive ista, sive ille, faciamus: ne, si plus justo sequimur impetum spiritus, declinemus ad dexteram; aut, si plus justo carni indulgemus, deviemus ad sinistram.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. O Lord, you have prepared straight paths for us, if only we walk rightly in them. You have set before us a law, the way of your righteous judgments, through him whom you gave as the Lawgiver of this holy institution, saying: 'This is the way, walk in it, neither to the right hand nor to the left' (Isai. XXX, 21). This is indeed the way, as the prophet had promised: 'A way made straight for us, so that fools should not err therein' (Isa. XXXV, 8). I have been young, and now am old; and I have not seen, if I remember rightly, a fool going astray in the way — though I have scarcely seen any wise man who was able to keep to its straight course. Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes, and prudent in your own sight (Isa. V, 21)! whom your wisdom leads astray from the way of salvation, and does not allow to follow the foolishness of the Savior. That man, a fool for Christ's sake, was not ignorant of what evil this earthly, animal, diabolical wisdom works, who said: 'If any man seem to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise with God' (I Cor. III, 18). Desirable is that folly, which by divine judgment is reckoned wisdom, which does not allow a man to stray from the way. This folly, unless I am mistaken, is that wisdom from above, chaste, peaceable, modest, easy to be persuaded, agreeing with the good (Jacob. III, 17): from all of which how far the man who is wise in his own eyes recoils, would that experience itself had never proved it before our eyes! If the arrogance or stubbornness of such wise men grieves you, the peace and modesty of our fools consoles you all the more abundantly, who, the less they trust themselves, the more readily they agree with what is good. Such fools, then, do not easily stray from the way of God, but, according to the word of the prophet, always hear behind them the voice warning: 'This is the way, walk in it, neither to the right hand nor to the left' (Isai. XXX, 21): that is, lest, by exceeding the measure through fervor, or by falling short of the measure through lukewarmness, you abandon the prescribed law and the royal road. The spirit is on the right, the flesh is on the left; and these, warring against each other, are always opposed to one another, so that we do not do whatever either the one or the other wills: lest, if we follow the impulse of the spirit more than is right, we turn aside to the right; or, if we indulge the flesh more than is right, we deviate to the left.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Hanc denique viam justificationum Domini, viam veritatis quam elegistis, quanta laude praedicet Isaias, delectat me cum charitate vestra recordari. Et erit, inquit, ibi, id est, in antiquis cubilibus draconum, in terra utique deserta et invia, semita et via, sicut hodie cernere est: quia in feris et incultis hominibus, qui sine lege vivebant, in ipsis invenitur ordo vitae, et disciplina. Et haec via, inquit, sancta vocabitur: quia nimirum sanctificatio est peccatorum, perditorumque salus. Quanta vero virtute ac reverentia sanctitatis praeemineat, inde probat propheta, quia non transibit, inquit, pollutus per eam (Isa. XXXV, 8). O mi Isaia, ibunt igitur qui polluti sunt per aliam viam? Imo potius huc omnes, huc veniant, hac incedant. Immundis enim praecipue Christus hanc viam stravit, qui venit quaerere et salvum facere quod perierat in viis saeculi. Quid igitur? transibit pollutus per viam sanctam? Absit! Veniat quantumlibet pollutus ad eam, non tamen transibit pollutus per eam: quia cum transierit, jam pollutus non erit. Admittit quidem via sancta pollutum, sed statim abluit admissum, quia diluit omne commissum, tanquam vere baptismus alter poenitentium. Hic plane, hic baptizat, non Joannes, sed Jesus baptismo poenitentiae: hic patet fons domus David in ablutionem peccatoris et menstruatae. Propterea namque via haec pollutum admittit, sed pollutum non transmittit: quia via arcta est, et quasi foramen illud angustum est, quo serpens innovandus cum exuviis suae vetustatis venire potest, sed cum ipsis transire non potest; sed novum suaque nuditate melius vestitum, transitus angustia trajicit, extricans omnem, quem attulerat, squalorem vetustatis. Bene ergo prudentiam serpentis imitari rogamur, qui nec aliter innovari possumus, nisi per angustum coarctemur.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Finally, it delights me to recall, together with your charity, with what great praise Isaiah proclaims this way of the Lord's righteous judgments, this way of truth which you have chosen. 'And it shall be there,' he says — that is, in the ancient lairs of dragons, in a land indeed desert and trackless — 'a path and a way,' as may be seen even today: because among wild and uncultivated men, who lived without law, there is found in them an order of life and discipline. 'And this way,' he says, 'shall be called holy': because it is, assuredly, the sanctification of sinners and the salvation of the lost. But how greatly it excels in the power and reverence of holiness, the prophet proves from this, that, he says, 'the unclean shall not pass through it' (Isa. XXXV, 8). O my Isaiah, shall those who are unclean, then, go by another way? Nay rather, let all come here, let them come here, let them walk by this road. For Christ laid this way especially for the unclean, he who came to seek and to save what had perished in the ways of the world. What then? Shall the unclean pass through the holy way? God forbid! Let him come to it however unclean he may be, yet he shall not pass through it unclean: because when he has passed through, he will no longer be unclean. The holy way indeed admits the unclean man, but immediately washes the one it has admitted, because it washes away every sin committed, being truly, as it were, a second baptism for penitents. Here plainly, here it is Jesus, not John, who baptizes with the baptism of penance: here the fountain of the house of David lies open for the washing of the sinner and of the menstruous woman. For this reason this way admits the unclean man, but does not let the unclean man pass through: because the way is narrow, and is like that narrow opening through which the serpent, needing to be renewed, can come with the worn skin of its old age, but cannot pass through still wearing it; rather, made new and better clothed in its own nakedness, it squeezes through the narrowness of the passage, freeing itself from all the squalor of the old age it had brought with it. Rightly, then, are we urged to imitate the prudence of the serpent, since we cannot be renewed in any other way unless we are compressed through a narrow strait.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Sane quod illius antiqui serpentis insidias evadamus, si per hanc arctam viam hujus novi serpentis exemplum sequamur, Isaias promittit, qui de eadem via subdit: Non erit ibi leo, et mala bestia non ascendet per eam, nec invenietur ibi (Isa. XXXV, 9). Securi ergo simus, si de via non exorbitamus. Potest leo ille, qui circuit quaerens quem devoret, juxta iter scandala ponere, laqueos abscondere, viatores rugitu terrere: sed persistentes in via laedere non potest; quippe cui via ipsa terror et supplicium est. Fortitudo nempe simplicis, via Domini, et pavor his qui operantur malum (Prov. X, 29). Si ergo in via es, hoc solum time, ne devies, ne Dominum offendas, qui te per viam ducit, ut dimittat te vagum in via cordis tui: praeter eum ne timeas alienum. Quod si nimis arctam viam causaris, prospice finem, quo te via ducit. Si enim omnis consummationis videris finem, continuo dices: Latum mandatum tuum nimis (Psal. CXVIII, 96). Si minus videre potes, crede videnti Isaiae, qui oculus tui corporis est. Ipse utcunque videbat, cum id quod sequitur dicebat: Et ecce ambulabunt hac via qui liberati fuerint, et redempti a Domino: et venient in Sion cum laude, et laetitia sempiterna super capita eorum Gaudium quoque et laetitiam obtinebunt, fugiet dolor et gemitus (Isai. XXXV, 9, 10). Qui satis hunc finem cogitat, puto quia non solum viam dilatat sibi; sed etiam pennas, ut jam non ambulet, sed volet, assumit sibi. Semper ergo, fratres, cogitate finem praemiorum, et cum omni facultate et alacritate curretis viam mandatorum. Per ipsam vos deducat et perducat ipse, qui est via currentium, et bravium pervenientium, Christus Jesus; cui honor et gloria per omnia saecula saeculorum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Isaiah promises that we shall indeed escape the snares of that ancient serpent, if along this narrow way we follow the example of this new serpent; for he adds concerning this same way: "There shall be no lion there, and the evil beast shall not go up by it, nor be found there" (Isa. XXXV, 9). Let us therefore be secure, if we do not stray from the way. That lion, who goes about seeking whom he may devour, can set stumbling blocks along the road, hide snares, and terrify travelers with his roaring; but he cannot harm those who remain on the way, since the way itself is his terror and his torment. For "the way of the Lord is strength to the simple, and fear to them that work evil" (Prov. X, 29). If, then, you are on the way, fear only this: that you may turn aside, that you may offend the Lord who leads you along the way, lest he abandon you to wander in the way of your own heart; apart from him, fear no other. But if you complain that the way is too narrow, look to the end to which the way leads you. For if you see the end of all perfection, you will at once say: "Your commandment is exceedingly broad" (Psal. CXVIII, 96). If you cannot see this well enough, believe Isaiah who sees it, for he is the eye of your body. He himself saw it, after a manner, when he said what follows: "And behold, they shall walk in this way who have been set free and redeemed by the Lord; and they shall come to Sion with praise, and everlasting joy shall be upon their heads. They shall obtain joy and gladness; sorrow and mourning shall flee away" (Isai. XXXV, 9, 10). He who meditates enough on this end, I think, not only widens the way for himself, but also takes to himself wings, so that he no longer walks but flies. Therefore, brethren, always think on the end of the rewards, and with all ease and eagerness you will run the way of the commandments. May he himself lead and bring you through it, who is the way of those who run and the prize of those who arrive, Christ Jesus; to whom be honor and glory for ever and ever.

sermons.title: Advent Sermon V: How to Make Progress in Preparing the Way for the Lord

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric reads the first Beatitude, "Blessed are the poor in spirit," as the opening of the Gospel and the first of eight steps that lead from renunciation of the world to the office of peacemaker and the merit of martyrdom. Those who possess God possess all things, while the miser is possessed by his money. Poverty of spirit lies more in humility than in want, and the poor already hold the kingdom, carrying God in their hearts. The sermon appears under the heading for the Solemnity of All Saints in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: IN SOLEMNITATE OMNIUM SANCTORUM,

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON THE SOLEMNITY OF ALL SAINTS,

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De pauperibus spiritu.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the poor in spirit.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Beati pauperes spiritu (Matth. V, 3). Agnosco notum illud ac nobile prognosticum, quod in testimonium sui, necdum natus in carne Dei Filius protulit; jam vero natus, sed nondum notus, sibi competere docuit: Spiritus, inquit, Domini super me, evangelizare pauperibus misit me (Isai. LXI, 1). Ecce pauperes evangelizantur, ecce pauperibus Evangelium regni nuntiatur: Beati, inquit, pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum coelorum (Matth. V, 3). Laetum prorsus ac novae plenum gratiae Novi Testamenti principium, etiam quantumlibet infidelem aut pigrum provocans ad audiendum, sed amplius ad faciendum, cum scilicet beatitudo miseris, exsulibus et egenis promittitur regnum coelorum. Gratum, inquam, et auspicatum novae legis initium, quando in ipso statim initio, tot beatitudinum benedictiones dat Legislator, quibus delectati eant de virtute in virtutem: per istos videlicet octo gradus ascensionis, quos in corde nostro disposuit structura Evangelii, secundum exemplar et imaginem coelestium, quod Ezechieli quoque ostensum est in monte visionum Dei. Est enim manifeste quidam ascensus cordium, et profectus meritorum iste per ordinem digestus octonarius virtutum, gradatim de imis ad summa perducens virum evangelicae perfectionis, donec ad videndum Deum deorum in Sion ingrediatur templum, de quo propheta dicit: Et in octo gradibus ascensus ejus (Ezech. XL, 37).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "Blessed are the poor in spirit" (Matth. V, 3). I recognize that well-known and noble sign which the Son of God, not yet born in the flesh, brought forth as testimony of himself; and indeed, now born, but not yet known, he taught that it applied to himself: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me," he says, "he has sent me to preach the gospel to the poor" (Isai. LXI, 1). Behold, the poor are evangelized; behold, to the poor the Gospel of the kingdom is announced: "Blessed," he says, "are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Matth. V, 3). A truly joyful beginning of the New Testament, full of new grace, which summons even the most unbelieving or slothful to listen, but still more to act — since blessedness is promised to the wretched, the exiles, and the needy, namely, the kingdom of heaven. A pleasing, I say, and auspicious beginning of the new law, since right at its very outset the Lawgiver gives so many blessings of beatitudes, by which men, delighted, may go from virtue to virtue: namely, through those eight steps of ascent which the structure of the Gospel has arranged in our heart, according to the pattern and image of heavenly things, which was also shown to Ezekiel on the mountain of the visions of God. For there is manifestly a certain ascent of hearts, and a progress of merits, this eightfold order of virtues arranged in sequence, leading step by step from the lowest things to the highest the man of evangelical perfection, until he enters to see the God of gods in Sion, into the temple of which the prophet says: "And by eight steps was its ascent" (Ezech. XL, 37).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Prima siquidem virtus inchoantium est renuntiatio saeculi, qua pauperes efficimur spiritu : secunda, mansuetudo, qua nos obedientiae subdimus, et assuescimus : deinde, luctus, quo peccata plorantur, vel virtutes implorantur. Ibi nimirum gustamus, unde amplius esuriamus, et sitiamus justitiam, tam in nobis quam in aliis, zeloque contra peccantes incipimus commoveri. Sed ne zelus immoderatior in vitium feratur, sequitur misericordia, qua temperetur. His ergo studiis, vel exercitiis, cum quis justus et misericors esse didicerit, idoneus erit fortassis contemplationi vacare, et mundando cordi, quo Deus videatur, operam dare. Exercitatus autem et probatus tam in actione, quam in contemplatione, tum demum dignus erit, qui nomen et officium Filii Dei gerens, pater et minister factus aliorum, tanquam mediator et sequester pacificet inter ipsos et Deum: pacificet ipsos ad invicem, vel etiam ad eos qui foris sunt, sicut scriptum est in laude sanctorum patrum, Pacificantes in domibus suis (Eccli. XLIV, 6). In hoc officio qui fidelis et constans fuerit, saepe virtutem et meritum sibi martyrii comparabit, persecutionem patiens propter justitiam; aliquando et ab his pro quibus pugnabit, ut sit ei dicere, Filii matris meae pugnaverunt contra me (Cantic. I, 5); et, Cum his qui oderunt pacem, eram pacificus; cum loquebar illis, impugnabant me gratis (Psal. CXIX, 7).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. For the first virtue of beginners is renunciation of the world, by which we are made poor in spirit; the second, meekness, by which we submit ourselves to obedience and grow accustomed to it; then, mourning, by which sins are wept over, or virtues are implored. There, surely, we taste that from which we may hunger and thirst all the more for justice, both in ourselves and in others, and we begin to be moved with zeal against sinners. But lest this zeal, growing too immoderate, turn into vice, mercy follows, by which it is tempered. By these pursuits, or exercises, when someone has learned to be just and merciful, he will perhaps be fit to devote himself to contemplation, and to give effort to the cleansing of the heart by which God may be seen. But one trained and proved both in action and in contemplation will then at last be worthy — bearing the name and office of the Son of God, having become a father and minister to others — to make peace, as a mediator and go-between, between them and God: to make peace among themselves, or even with those who are outside, as it is written in praise of the holy fathers, "Making peace in their own houses" (Eccli. XLIV, 6). Whoever is faithful and steadfast in this office will often win for himself the virtue and merit of martyrdom, suffering persecution for the sake of justice — sometimes even at the hands of those for whom he fights, so that he may say, "The sons of my mother have fought against me" (Cantic. I, 5); and, "With them that hated peace I was peaceable: when I spoke to them, they fought against me without cause" (Psal. CXIX, 7).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Quantae autem gloriae, quamque copiose mercedis in coelo sit culmen hujus perfectionis, inde utcumque licet aestimare, quod ipsa etiam abrenuntiantium saeculo primordia tantae Dominus praedicat felicitatis, ut dicat: Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum coelorum. Plane beati qui, projectis vilibus, sed gravibus sarcinulis hujus mundi, nolunt divites fieri, nisi de solo Creatore mundi, propter ipsum, tanquam nihil habentes, et per ipsum omnia possidentes. An non possident omnia qui possident continentem et disponentem omnia, quorum Deus portio est et haereditas; qui, ut nihil desit, timentibus eum, caetera prout expedire novit, dispensat ad utendum, et se ipsum servat ad fruendum? Cum haeres Dei, cohaeres autem Christi, adultus et emancipatus introducetur in plenariam possessionem exspectatae haereditatis, tunc profecto jus absolutum, ac liberum imperium habebit in creaturis: qui modo quanto tempore parvulus est, nihil differt a servo, cum sit Dominus omnium; sed sub tutoribus et actoribus est usque ad tempus praefinitum a Patre. Tunc mundus agnoscet justum ac legitimum haeredem Dominum suum, propter quem creatus est: agnoscet, inquam, quia jam non conformem sibi, sed reformatum in novitate sensus sui ad imaginem Dei, ad quam factus est. Sed et nunc quoque fideli homini totus mundus divitiarum est (Prov. XVII, sec. LXX) (12); non solum quia ad agnoscendum vel diligendum auctorem mundi, mundanis omnibus utitur tanquam ad hoc sibi datis; et in via testimoniorum Dei, quae videt facturam sicut et Scripturam perhibere factori, delectatur sicut in omnibus divitiis: sed etiam, quia ita sufficiens et gratus esse didicit, ut quasi totius mundi divitias computet illud prope nihil quod habet, sive hoc ipsum quod nihil habet. Ideo jure beatificat Ecclesiam sanctorum Salomon, quae pauper pro Christo, tam dives est in Christo. Multae, inquit, filiae congregaverunt divitias, tu supergressa es universas (Prov. XXXI, 29). Alii siquidem rapiunt non sua, et semper in egestate sunt: sancti dividunt propria, et ditiores fiunt. Divites enim eguerunt et esurierunt; inquirentes autem Dominum non minuentur omni bono (Psal. XXXIII, 11).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. How great a glory, however, and how abundant a reward in heaven belongs to the summit of this perfection may in some measure be estimated from this: that the Lord proclaims even the very beginnings of those who renounce the world to be of such great blessedness that he says, "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Truly blessed are they who, having cast off the cheap but heavy burdens of this world, refuse to become rich except from the Creator of the world alone, for his sake — as having nothing, and through him possessing all things. Do they not possess all things who possess him who contains and disposes all things, whose portion and inheritance is God himself; who, so that nothing may be lacking to those who fear him, dispenses the rest for their use as he knows to be fitting, and keeps himself for their enjoyment? When the heir of God and co-heir of Christ, having come of age and been emancipated, is brought into the full possession of the inheritance he has awaited, then indeed he will have absolute right and free dominion over creatures — he who, for as long as he is a little child, differs in nothing from a slave, though he is Lord of all, but is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by the Father. Then the world will acknowledge him as its Lord, the just and lawful heir for whose sake it was created; it will acknowledge him, I say, because he is now no longer conformed to the world, but reformed in the newness of his mind to the image of God, to which he was made. But even now, too, to the faithful man the whole world is a world of riches (Prov. XVII, sec. LXX) (12); not only because he uses all worldly things as given to him for this purpose — to know and love the author of the world — and in the way of the testimonies of God, which he sees creation, like Scripture also, bearing witness to its Maker, he delights as in all riches; but also because he has learned to be so content and grateful that he reckons as the riches of the whole world that almost nothing which he has, or even this very fact — that he has nothing. Therefore Solomon rightly calls blessed the Church of the saints, which, poor for Christ's sake, is so rich in Christ. "Many daughters," he says, "have gathered together riches; you have surpassed them all" (Prov. XXXI, 29). For others indeed seize what is not their own, and are always in want; the saints divide what is their own, and become richer. For "the rich have wanted and suffered hunger; but they that seek the Lord shall not be deprived of any good thing" (Psal. XXXIII, 11).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Avarus quo plura possidet, pluribus eget. Quanquam nil minus habeat, quam quod habere se putat; cum habeatur, non habeat, servus pecuniae, mancipium avaritiae, cultorque crumenae, idololatra detestandus, cui nummus est deus. Pulchre autem jam nunc quoque vindicat in peccatores justitia divina, res ipsas quas amant convertens eis in tormenta, et vitia faciens esse supplicia. Pecunia enim quae justum amplius justificat, et verius ditat dispensata, vel semel data; avarum cruciat servata, prodigum polluit profligata. Prorsus beati pauperes Christi, quorum fides sic elusit sapientiam mundi, ut sola, quis sit optimus divitiarum usus, invenerit: quod videlicet divitiae, quae pauperem faciunt et miserum, si diliguntur; tunc demum faciunt divitem et beatum, si pro Christo contemnuntur. Confiteor tibi, Pater, Domine coeli et terrae, quia abscondisti haec a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revelasti ea parvulis (Matth. XI, 25), id est, humilibus; qui utique non sunt alii quam pauperes spiritu, quorum hic beatitudo praedicatur.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. The miser, the more he possesses, the more he lacks. Yet nothing is less his than what he thinks he has; since he is possessed rather than possessing, he is the slave of money, the chattel of avarice, the worshiper of his purse, a detestable idolater, for whom a coin is god. And now too divine justice fittingly takes vengeance upon sinners, turning the very things they love into torments for them, and making their vices into their punishments. For money, which more fully justifies and more truly enriches the just man when it is distributed or given away, torments the miser when it is kept, and defiles the prodigal when it is squandered. Truly blessed are the poor of Christ, whose faith has so outwitted the wisdom of the world that it alone has discovered what is the best use of riches: namely, that riches, which make a man poor and wretched if they are loved, then at last make him rich and blessed if they are despised for Christ's sake. I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and have revealed them to little ones (Matth. XI, 25) — that is, to the humble, who are none other than the poor in spirit, whose blessedness is proclaimed here.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Hoc enim licet scientes tamen commonere vos velim, fratres, quod vera ac beata paupertas spiritus, plus est in humilitate cordis, quam in angustia rei familiaris: plus consistit in abdicatione superbiae, quam in contemptu substantiae. Substantia nonnunquam utiliter habetur; superbia nunquam nisi damnabiliter retinetur. Diabolus nihil in mundo possidet, aut possidere desiderat, quem sola, vel maxime superbia damnat. Parum igitur prodest renuntiare saeculi possessionibus, nisi renuntietur et moribus: imo stultum ac ridiculum est nudari divitiis, et divitum implicari vitiis; pauperem fieri rebus, nec ditari virtutibus; relinquere omnia, nec sequi Christum, sed magis forsitan in castris Christi juvare partes Antichristi. Plane Antichristi partes adjuvat, quisquis superbiae militat, nomenque sanctum, quod verbis vel habitu profitetur, moribus impugnat. Vexillum Christi humilitas; Antichristi, superbia, vel potius capitis ejus diaboli, qui super omnes filios superbiae regnat, et ab initio per superbiam peccat. Gloriemur igitur, fratres, quia pauperes sumus pro Christo; sed operam demus ut humiles simus cum Christo. Paupere superbo sicut nihil detestabilius, ita nihil miserabilius; cum eum et paupertas nunc affligat, et superbia in perpetuum abdicat. Pauper autem humilis, etsi uritur et purgatur in camino paupertatis, exsultat refrigerio conscientiae divitis: consolatur se promissione sanctae spei, sciens et sentiens quoniam ipsius est regnum Dei; quod jam intra se ipsum velut in semine vel radice gerit, primitias scilicet spiritus, et pignus aeternae haereditatis. Annon vestrum est, fratres, unde toties sicut vobis conscii estis, fructus suavissimos et beata gaudia decerpitis, quorum gustus amarescere vobis jam omnem fecit dulcedinem mundi? Gustastis enim, ni fallor, et vidistis quoniam bona est negotiatio vestra, qui pro re gratis contemnenda ac projicienda, summa comparastis bona. Denique non est regnum Dei esca et potus, sed justitia, et pax, et gaudium in Spiritu sancto (Rom. xiv, 17). Si haec ergo sentimus in nobis, cur non confidenter pronuntiemus intra nos esse regnum Dei? Quod autem intra nos est, illud vere nostrum est, quia nobis invitis eripi non potest.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. For though you know this, brothers, I would still like to remind you that true and blessed poverty of spirit consists more in humility of heart than in the straitness of one's household means; it consists more in the renunciation of pride than in the contempt of substance. Substance is sometimes held to good use; pride is never retained except to one's damnation. The devil possesses nothing in the world, nor desires to possess anything, and yet pride alone, or pride above all, condemns him. It profits little, then, to renounce the possessions of the world unless one also renounces its ways; indeed, it is foolish and ridiculous to be stripped of riches and yet entangled in the vices of the rich — to become poor in things but not enriched in virtues; to leave all things and yet not follow Christ, but rather, perhaps, while serving in the camp of Christ, to aid the cause of Antichrist. Clearly he aids the cause of Antichrist who serves in the army of pride, and who, while professing the holy name in words or in habit, fights against it by his conduct. The banner of Christ is humility; the banner of Antichrist is pride — or rather of his head, the devil, who reigns over all the sons of pride, and who from the beginning sins through pride. Let us glory, then, brothers, that we are poor for Christ's sake; but let us take care to be humble with Christ. As nothing is more detestable than a proud poor man, so nothing is more pitiable; for poverty afflicts him now, and pride casts him off forever. But the humble poor man, even though he is burned and purified in the furnace of poverty, exults in the refreshment of a rich conscience; he consoles himself with the promise of holy hope, knowing and feeling that the kingdom of God is his — which he already bears within himself as in a seed or a root, namely, the firstfruits of the Spirit, and the pledge of the eternal inheritance. Is it not yours, brothers, from which, as you yourselves are conscious, you so often pluck the sweetest fruits and blessed joys, the taste of which has already made all the sweetness of the world bitter to you? For you have tasted, unless I am mistaken, and have seen that your business dealing is good, you who for a thing to be freely despised and cast away have purchased the highest goods. For indeed the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom. xiv, 17). If, then, we feel these things within ourselves, why should we not confidently declare that the kingdom of God is within us? For what is within us is truly ours, because it cannot be snatched away from us against our will.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Recte itaque Dominus beatitudinem praedicans pauperum, non ait, ipsorum erit, sed, est regnum coelorum: non solum propter jus firmissimum, sed etiam propter pignus certissimum usumque felicissimum; non solum quia paratum est eis ab origine mundi, sed etiam quia jam in quamdam ipsius possessionem coeperunt introduci, jam habentes thesaurum coelestem in vasis fictilibus, jam portantes Deum in corporibus suis et cordibus. Quam beata gens, cujus est Dominus Deus ejus! quam vicini sunt Dei regno qui regem ipsum, cui servire regnare est, jam possident, et gestant in corde suo! Funes, inquit, ceciderunt mihi in praeclaris; etenim haereditas mea praeclara est mihi. Litigent alii de dividenda haereditate hujus mundi: Dominus pars haereditatis meae et calicis mei (Psal. xv, 6, 5). Pugnent inter se quis eorum fiat miserior, nihil omnium quae ambiunt, illis invideo: ego enim et anima mea delectabimur in Domino. O praeclara haereditas pauperum! o beata possessio nihil habentium! quoniam non solum omnem sufficientiam nobis subministras, sed etiam ad omnem gloriam abundas, ad omnem laetitiam redundas, tanquam in sinu reposita supereffluens mensura. Prorsus tecum sunt divitiae et gloria, opes superbae et justitia.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Rightly, then, did the Lord, in proclaiming the blessedness of the poor, not say, 'theirs shall be,' but 'theirs is the kingdom of heaven' — not only because of the most firm right, but also because of the most certain pledge and the most blessed enjoyment; not only because it has been prepared for them from the foundation of the world, but also because they have already begun to be brought into a certain possession of it, already having the heavenly treasure in earthen vessels, already carrying God in their bodies and hearts. How blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord! How near to the kingdom of God are those who already possess the King himself — whom to serve is to reign — and bear him in their own heart! 'The lines,' he says, 'have fallen for me among goodly places; yes, my inheritance is goodly to me.' Let others quarrel over the dividing of the inheritance of this world: 'The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup' (Psal. xv, 6, 5). Let them fight among themselves over which of them shall become more wretched; I envy them nothing of all they covet, for I and my soul shall take delight in the Lord. O goodly inheritance of the poor! O blessed possession of those who have nothing! For you not only supply us with every sufficiency, but you also overflow for every glory, and run over for every gladness, like an overflowing measure laid up in the lap. Truly with you are riches and glory, glorious riches and righteousness.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 7. Superbiat, o pauperes, superbiat, o humiles, anima vestra, glorians in humilitate sua, omnemque altitudinem hujus mundi longe sub pedibus suis jacentem despiciat; indignumque judicet gloriae suae, ad concupiscentiam vilis praedae suam ulterius majestatem inclinare. Quid? jam jam tollenda es in coelum, et nunc te demum mergeres in coenum? parata tibi sunt aeterna, et praeeligeres transitoria, somnoque similia? te praestolatur curia sanctorum, et praeponeres societatem daemoniorum? Quam miser homo, qui cum in honore esset, non intellexit, ac perinde comparatus est jumentis insipientibus, et similis factus est illis! (Psal. xlviii, 21.) Annon manifeste hoc illis contingit, quos cum beata paupertas fecisset honorabiles coelo, mirabiles mundo, et, ut nihil praeteritum sit, etiam formidabiles inferno: postea arbitrantes miseriam, caecato sensu, paupertatem, humilitatem, ignaviam; voluerunt divites fieri, et inciderunt in tentationes et laqueos diaboli; cumque essent domini universorum, vendiderunt se ipsos sine pretio propter ea quae nihil sunt. Vae his qui perdiderunt sustinentiam, et diverterunt in vias pravas! Et quid facient cum inspicere coeperit Dominus? Ipsi viderint quid facturi sint. Vos enim quibus amica est paupertas, et grata spiritus humilitas, securos fecit de possidendo regno coelorum incommutabilis Veritas: vestrum illud esse asserens, vobis illud repositum fideliter custodiens; si tamen et vos ipsi spem istam in sinu vestro repositam firmiter custodiatis usque in finem, cooperante Domino nostro Jesu Christo, cui est honor et gloria per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 7. Let your soul be proud, O poor; let it be proud, O humble, glorying in its own humility, and let it look down from far above upon all the loftiness of this world lying beneath its feet; let it judge it unworthy of its glory to bend its majesty any further toward the desire for vile prey. What? Are you now, even now, about to be lifted up into heaven, and would you at this very moment sink yourself into the mire? Eternal things are prepared for you, and would you choose instead transitory things, things like a passing dream? The court of the saints awaits you, and would you prefer the company of demons? How wretched is man, who, when he was in honor, did not understand, and so was compared to senseless beasts, and became like them! (Psal. xlviii, 21.) Does not this plainly happen to those whom blessed poverty had made honorable before heaven, admirable before the world, and—that nothing be left unsaid—even fearsome to hell: who afterward, their understanding blinded, judged poverty to be misery, and humility to be cowardice; who wished to become rich, and fell into the temptations and snares of the devil; and though they were lords of all things, sold themselves for no price for the sake of things that are nothing. Woe to those who have lost their endurance, and have turned aside into crooked ways! And what will they do when the Lord begins to examine them? Let them see for themselves what they are to do. But as for you, to whom poverty is a friend, and humility of spirit is dear, the unchangeable Truth has made you secure of possessing the kingdom of heaven: asserting that it is yours, faithfully keeping it stored up for you—if only you yourselves also firmly guard this hope stored up in your bosom even to the end, with the cooperation of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.
