passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric of Igny presents the Annunciation as spiritual joy within Lenten observance: the angel's promise to Mary announces pardon, redemption and life to those humbled by repentance. He contrasts the fullness of salvation with human ingratitude, then contemplates Mary's royal ancestry and Christ's body through the images of Wisdom's house and Solomon's ivory throne. Mary's virginal chastity leads him to urge chastity joined to humility in his hearers. The fragrance of myrrh and incense becomes an image of bodily continence and prayerful devotion, returning at the close to the Word's descent into Mary's womb. The individual sermon is undated; its collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157 and is read here from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The source names the Annunciation of the Lord.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: IN ANNUNTIATIONE DOMINICA.

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE LORD.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De gaudio hujus diei et de laudibus Virginis matris.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the joy of this day and the praises of the Virgin Mother.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Opportune nobis in his diebus Quadragesimalis observantiae solemnitas intervenit Dominicae Annuntiationis, ut qui fatigantur afflictione corporali, gaudio recreari valeant spirituali; et quos humiliavit poenitentiae luctus, annuntiatio illius qui tollit peccata mundi, consoletur. Sic quippe scriptum habes: Moeror in corde viri humiliabit eum; et sermone bono laetificabitur (Prov. xii, 25). Prorsus sermo bonus, sermo fidelis et omni acceptione dignus, Evangelium nostrae salutis; quod angelus missus a Deo, hodierna die Mariae evangelizavit, ac laetum de Incarnatione Verbi, dies diei, angelus Virgini verbum eructavit. Sermo ille, dum Filium promittit Virgini, veniam pollicetur reis, redemptionem captivis, adapertionem clausis, vitamque sepultis. Sermo ille, dum Filii regnum praedicat, justorum quoque gloriam annuntiat; terret inferos, laetificat coelos; et, sicut cognitione mysteriorum, sic etiam novitate gaudiorum perfectionem auxisse videtur Angelorum. Quem ergo non laetificet ille sermo bonus in afflictione sua, quem non consoletur verbum illud in humilitate sua? Memor esto, inquit David, verbi tui servo tuo, in quo mihi spem dedisti; haec enim me consolata est in humilitate mea (Psal. cxviii, 49, 50). Verbum tantum promissionis acceperat, sed nullo adhuc indicio sese effectus prodebat. Affligebat eum dilatio voti, sed consolabatur certitudo spei ex fide promittentis.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. The solemnity of the Lord's Annunciation comes at a fitting time for us in these days of Lenten observance, so that those wearied by bodily affliction may be refreshed by spiritual joy, and those whom the sorrow of repentance has humbled may be comforted by the announcement of him who takes away the sins of the world. For you find it written: Sorrow in a man's heart will humble him; and by a good word he will be gladdened (Prov. xii, 25). A good word indeed, a faithful word and worthy of all acceptance, is the Gospel of our salvation, which the angel sent by God proclaimed to Mary on this day; and, as day speaks to day, the angel poured forth to the Virgin a joyful word concerning the Incarnation of the Word. That word, in promising a Son to the Virgin, promises pardon to the guilty, redemption to captives, an opening to those shut in, and life to the buried. That word, in proclaiming the Son's kingdom, announces also the glory of the just; it terrifies the underworld and gladdens the heavens; and it seems to have increased the perfection of the Angels by new joys as well as by knowledge of mysteries. Whom, then, should that good word not gladden in his affliction? Whom should that word not comfort in his lowliness? Remember, says David, your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope; for this has comforted me in my lowliness (Psal. cxviii, 49, 50). He had received only a word of promise, and its fulfillment had not yet shown itself by any sign. The delay of his desire afflicted him, but the certainty of hope, arising from the faithfulness of the one who promised, comforted him.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Si ergo David sola spe salutis hujus, quae nobis servabatur, animum pascebat, quod gaudium quae deliciae, rei ipsius exhibitio nobis esse debuerat? O felicitas temporum istorum! o infelicitas temporum istorum! An non felicitas temporum in quibus tanta plenitudo gratiae et omnium bonorum? an non infelicitas temporum in quibus tanta ingratitudo redemptorum? Ecce enim venit plenitudo temporis, in quo mittit Deus Filium suum, ut fiat Filius hominis hominumque Salvator; et ecce magnitudo temporis, ut Salvatorem suum fastidiat homo peccator. Annuntiatur salus perditis, et contemnunt; promittitur vita desperatis, et negligunt; venit Deus ad homines, et non assurgunt. Assurgit, qui aliqua devotione se erigit ut det gloriam gratiae Dei; assurgit, qui saltem cum gaudio suscipit verbum propriae salutis. Scio autem, scio quis est qui laetificatur illo sermone bono. Ille procul dubio quem prius humiliavit pius moeror in corde suo: moeror de peregrinatione et exsilio, moeror de vinculis mortis et periculis inferni; qui moerens quotidie plangit, quod praeoccupaverint eum laquei mortis, et pericula inferni invenerint. Huic nimirum jucundus advenit hodiernus ille nuntius de coelo, hic gratulabundus excipit sermonem de Dei Filio; huic, inquam, lugenti et moerenti quod tantis sit malis praeventus et circumventus, non sine gaudio liberator annuntiatur; qui oleum gaudii daturus est pro luctu, pallium laudis pro spiritu moeroris; qui videlicet finem dabit miseriis, et sine fine beatitudinem dabit miseris. Beati ergo qui lugent, quoniam ipsi consolabuntur; beati duos humiliavit pius moeror in corde suo, quoniam laetificabuntur sermone bono. Bonus plane sermo et consolatorius omnipotens Sermo tuus, Domine, qui hodie a regalibus sedibus venit in uterum Virginis, ubi etiam sedem sibi regalem exstruxit; in qua cum etiam nunc sedeat, quasi Rex circumstante exercitu Angelorum in coelis, est tamen moerentium consolator in terris.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. If, then, David nourished his soul on the mere hope of this salvation, which was being kept for us, what joy, what delight should the manifestation of the thing itself have been to us! O happiness of these times! O unhappiness of these times! Are they not happy times in which there is such fullness of grace and of every good thing? Are they not unhappy times in which there is such ingratitude among the redeemed? For see, the fullness of time has come, in which God sends his Son to become the Son of man and the Savior of men; and see the enormity of the time, that sinful man should disdain his Savior. Salvation is announced to the lost, and they despise it; life is promised to the despairing, and they neglect it; God comes to men, and they do not rise to greet him. He rises who lifts himself up with some devotion to give glory to God's grace; he rises who at least receives with joy the word of his own salvation. But I know, I know who is gladdened by that good word. It is undoubtedly the man whom devout sorrow has first humbled in his heart: sorrow over his pilgrimage and exile, sorrow over the bonds of death and the perils of hell; the man who mourns and laments daily that the snares of death have overtaken him and the perils of hell have found him. To him that welcome messenger from heaven comes today; he welcomes with rejoicing the word concerning the Son of God. To him, I say, grieving and sorrowing that he has been overtaken and surrounded by such great evils, a deliverer is announced, bringing no little joy: one who will give the oil of gladness in place of mourning, a mantle of praise in place of a spirit of sorrow; one who will put an end to miseries and give the miserable blessedness without end. Blessed, then, are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted; blessed are those whom devout sorrow has humbled in their hearts, for they shall be gladdened by a good word. Truly good and comforting is your almighty Word, Lord, who today came from the royal throne into the Virgin's womb, where he also built himself a royal seat. Although even now he sits upon it as King in heaven, surrounded by the host of Angels, he is nevertheless the comforter of the sorrowful on earth.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Regali siquidem ex progenie Virgo electa est, generositatis quidem regiae nobilis proles, sed virtutis regiae nobilior indoles: ut aeterno Regi, Filio Regis, materna quoque nobilitas regium honorem deferret, et venientem a regali sede Patris, regalis etiam thronus in aula virginali Reginae susciperet Matris. In ipsa quippe et ex ipsa, Sapientia aedificavit sibi domum ((Prov. ix, 1), in ipsa et ex ipsa paravit sibi thronum, cum in ea et ex ea corpus aptavit sibi ita ad omnia perfectum et congruum, ut et domus ei sit ad quiescendum, et thronus ad judicandum, quod primo tabernaculum ei fuit ad pugnandum, et cathedra ad docendum. Vide autem ne forte ipsa sit sedes David patris ejus (Luc. i, 70), quam ei dandam promittit angelus; non quod David in ea sederit, sed quod ex semine David assumpta et fabricata sit. Et certe, si sedes David non est, tamen sedes tua, Deus, in saeculum saeculi ipsa est. Si solium David non est, certe solium excelsum et elevatum super omnem creaturam ipsa est. Si quis autem etiam thronum illum grandem, quem rex Salomon sibi fecit de ebore, corpus ipsum interpretetur, quod Pacificus noster hodie sumpsit ex Virgine, non multum a vero videbitur abhorrere; quandoquidem et illud quod sequitur, et vestivit eum auro fulvo nimis (III Reg. x, 18), eidem satis corpori congruit; quod jam Dominus decorem induit fulgoris intolerabilis. Vestivit, inquit, eum auro fulvo. Prorsus, si interroges oculos Apostolorum qui transfiguratum in monte viderunt (Matth. xvii, 1, 2), confitebuntur aurum nimis esse fulvum, id est, fulgorem corporis esse nimium, quem ferre nequiverunt, quamvis nimis pro Valde ponere consuetudinis sit Scripturarum. Caetera namque quae prosequitur Scriptura de illius throni magnificentia (III Reg. x, 18-20), accommodatius nisi fallor, si quis tractare voluerit, accipientur de corpore Christi, quod est Ecclesia.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. For the Virgin was chosen from royal stock, a noble offspring of royal birth, but nobler still in the character of her royal virtue, so that to the eternal King, the Son of the King, his mother's nobility too might render royal honor, and a royal throne in the virginal court of his Queen Mother might receive him as he came from the Father's royal seat. For in her and from her Wisdom built herself a house ((Prov. ix, 1); in her and from her he prepared himself a throne, when in her and from her he fitted himself with a body so perfect and suitable in every respect that it might be both a house for his rest and a throne for his judgment, having first been a tent for his warfare and a chair for his teaching. Consider, however, whether this may be the seat of David his father (Luc. i, 70), which the angel promises will be given to him: not because David sat upon it, but because it was taken and fashioned from David's seed. And certainly, if it is not David's seat, it is nevertheless your seat, O God, for ever and ever. If it is not David's throne, it is certainly a throne high and lifted up above every creature. But if anyone also interprets that great throne which King Solomon made for himself out of ivory as the very body which our Peacemaker took today from the Virgin, he will seem to be not far from the truth. For the words which follow, and he covered it with exceedingly bright gold (III Reg. x, 18), fit that body well, since the Lord has now clothed it in the beauty of unbearable radiance. He covered it, it says, with bright gold. Indeed, if you question the eyes of the Apostles who saw him transfigured on the mountain (Matth. xvii, 1, 2), they will confess that the gold is exceedingly bright, that is, that the body's radiance is excessive, which they could not endure; although Scripture customarily uses 'excessively' to mean 'very.' For the other things Scripture goes on to say about the magnificence of that throne (III Reg. x, 18-20) will, unless I am mistaken, be more fittingly understood of Christ's body which is the Church, should anyone wish to expound them.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Mihi sane magis mirari modo libet illud ebur tam pretiosum, imo et impretiabile, virginalis castimoniae, de quo scilicet sedem sibi facere delegit, qui sedet super Cherubim: Haec, inquiens, requies mea in saeculum saeculi; hic sedebo, quoniam elegi eam (Psal. cxxxi, 14). Quam nitidum ebur illud quod oculis tanti tamque divitis Regis placuit, in cujus diebus argentum nullius est pretii! quam frigidum, quod nec a conceptu incaluit, quam solidum, quod nec partus violavit! quam candidum simul et rubicundum, quod candor lucis aeternae ignisque Spiritus sancti, universa sui plenitudine replevit! Maria siquidem et ipsa candidior nive, rubicundior ebore antiquo; cui scilicet incomparabilem et castitas candorem, et charitas seu martyrium rutilantem prae antiquis electis noscitur contulisse ruborem. Nam et suam ipsius animam pertransivit gladius, ut mater summi Virginis et Martyris esset et virgo ipsa et martyr, candida et rubicunda, quemadmodum dilectus ejus candidus et rubicundus (Cantic. v, 10). Denique, sicut Salomon in omnibus thesauris suis et opibus tantis nihil habuit tam pretiosum, quod in opus illud, magnificum thronum scilicet gloriae suae judicaret ebori praeferendum, sic Maria singularem prae omnibus electis Angelorum et hominum invenit gratiam apud Deum, ut videlicet Dei conciperet et pareret Filium atque ex ebore corporis ejus thronum sibi virtus Altissimi sine manibus excideret gloriosum. Gloriosus prorsus ille thronus ac mirabilis, de quo Scriptura perhibet quia non est factum tale opus in universis regnis (III Reg. x, 20), quod facile testimoniis probaretur Angelorum, qui semper et insatiabiliter in gloriam et decorem Dominici corporis prospicere concupiscunt. Quia enim in universis regnis non est tale opus factum, quidquid factum est, flectat ei genu in omnibus regnis, coelestium, terrestrium, et infernorum. Quam beatus igitur ille venter eburneus, unde caro eburnea sumpta est Redemptoris, pretium animarum, miraculum Angelorum, solium summae majestatis, thronusque potestatis, cibus vitae immortalis, medicina peccati, restitutio sanitatis! Quotquot, inquit, tangebant eum, sanabantur a languoribus suis (Marc. vi, 56): nam virtus de illo exibat, et sanabat omnes (Luc. vi, 49).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. For my part, I would rather marvel now at that precious, indeed priceless, ivory of virginal chastity, from which he who sits above the Cherubim chose to make himself a seat, saying: This is my resting place for ever and ever; here I will sit, for I have chosen it (Psal. cxxxi, 14). How lustrous is that ivory which pleased the eyes of so great and wealthy a King, in whose days silver is of no value! How cool, since even conception did not heat it; how firm, since even childbirth did not violate it! How white and ruddy at once, filled with all the fullness of the brightness of eternal light and the fire of the Holy Spirit! For Mary herself is whiter than snow, ruddier than ancient ivory: chastity is known to have bestowed upon her an incomparable whiteness, and charity, or martyrdom, a glowing redness surpassing that of the elect of old. For a sword passed through her own soul too, so that the mother of the supreme Virgin and Martyr should herself be both virgin and martyr, white and ruddy, just as her beloved is white and ruddy (Cantic. v, 10). Finally, just as Solomon, among all his treasures and such great riches, had nothing so precious that he judged it preferable to ivory for that work, the magnificent throne of his glory, so Mary found singular grace before God above all the elect among Angels and men: namely, that she should conceive and bear the Son of God, and that the power of the Most High should carve for himself, without hands, a glorious throne from the ivory of her body. Glorious indeed and wonderful is that throne, of which Scripture declares that no such work was made in all the kingdoms (III Reg. x, 20). This could readily be proved by the testimony of the Angels, who always and insatiably long to look upon the glory and beauty of the Lord's body. For since no such work has been made in all the kingdoms, let everything that has been made bend the knee to him in all the kingdoms, in heaven, on earth and under the earth. How blessed, then, is that ivory womb, from which the Redeemer's ivory flesh was taken: the price of souls, the wonder of Angels, the seat of supreme majesty and throne of power, the food of immortal life, the medicine for sin, the restoration of health! As many as touched him, it says, were healed of their infirmities (Marc. vi, 56); for power went out from him and healed them all (Luc. vi, 49).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Beatus igitur venter, qui te, Domine Jesu, portavit! felix castitas uteri virginalis, quae huic operi materiam ministravit! Felix prorsus, fratres mei, nitor illius eboris, id est, candor castitatis: cui nec aurum mundanae sapientiae, nec argentum eloquentiae, nec gemmam alicujus excellentis gratiae, nostri praefert electio Salomonis; si modo tamen castitas humilitate commendetur, quia humilitatem ancillae suae respexit Dominus (Id. i, 48). Proinde namque Salomon, cum in carmine amoris castitatem praedicaret virginis, seu sponsae, videlicet seu sponsi (quia quorum spiritus unus et caro una, in plerisque etiam laus una), ut castitatem illius adornatam nostramque adornandam etiam aliis virtutibus doceret, ait Venter ejus eburneus distinctus sapphiris (Cantic. v, 14). Ut autem noveris quia castitas aliarum virtutum seu gratiarum sit receptaculum, apothecae aromaticae seu unguentariae nostri Salomonis non nisi domus eburneae sunt, sicut David in illo epithalamio cecinit, quod inscriptio tituli, Canticum pro dilecto, de Sponso Ecclesiae accipiendum ostendit. Myrrha, inquit, et gutta, et casia a vestimentis tuis, a domibus, eburneis ex quibus delectaverunt te filiae regum in honore tuo (Psal. xliv, 9, 10). Corpora siquidem eburnea sanctorum, domus Christi sunt, vestimentum Christi sunt: membra Christi sunt; templum Spiritus sancti sunt. Ab his vestimentis Christi, ab his domibus eburneis spirat ei omnis fragrantia virtutum et charismatum, ex quibus delectant et honorant Regem regum filiae Apostolorum et Prophetarum. Probastis et ipsi, fratres mei, ex quo coepistis possidere unusquisque vas suum in sanctificatione et honore, non passione desiderii, sicut et gentes quae ignorant Deum (I Thess. iv, 4, 5), quid unguentorum, quid odoramentorum divina largitate sit infusum; quo modo corpus, quod erat sentina sordium, nunc Spiritus sancti sit venerabile sacrarium; et quod erat vorago flagitiorum, nunc quaedam sit apotheca gratiarum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Blessed, then, is the womb that bore you, Lord Jesus! Happy the chastity of the virginal womb which supplied the material for this work! Happy indeed, my brothers, is the luster of that ivory, that is, the whiteness of chastity: our Solomon's choice prefers neither the gold of worldly wisdom nor the silver of eloquence nor the jewel of any excellent grace to it, provided, however, that chastity is commended by humility, for the Lord has looked upon the humility of his handmaid (Id. i, 48). Thus Solomon, when in the song of love he praised the chastity of the virgin, whether of the bride or of the bridegroom, since those who are one spirit and one flesh also share one praise in many things, wished to teach that the chastity of the one is adorned, and ours must be adorned, with other virtues too. He says: His belly is of ivory, set with sapphires (Cantic. v, 14). And so that you may know that chastity is a receptacle for other virtues or graces, our Solomon's storehouses of spices or ointments are nothing but houses of ivory. So David sang in that wedding song which the inscription of its title, A Song for the Beloved, showed was to be understood of the Bridegroom of the Church: Myrrh, he says, and stacte and cassia from your garments, from the ivory houses, from which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor (Psal. xliv, 9, 10). For the ivory bodies of the saints are Christ's houses, Christ's clothing, Christ's members and the temple of the Holy Spirit. From these garments of Christ, from these ivory houses, there breathes for him every fragrance of virtues and spiritual gifts, by which the daughters of Apostles and Prophets delight and honor the King of kings. You yourselves too have experienced, my brothers, since each of you began to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire like the nations who do not know God (I Thess. iv, 4, 5), what ointments and perfumes have been poured in by divine bounty; how the body which was a cesspool of filth is now a venerable sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, and what was an abyss of shameful deeds is now a kind of storehouse of graces.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Myrrha, inquit, et gutta, et casia a vestimentis tuis, a domibus eburneis. Inhabitamus quidem domos luteas, sed quae materiae qualitate sunt luteae, continentiae virtute fiunt eburneae; ex quibus si myrrha prima spirare coeperit per mortificationem voluptatum, consequentur et aliae species aromaticae, quae multiformem virtutum gratiam spirabunt. Spirabunt autem Christo delectabiliter, tanquam de vestimentis suis; spirabunt etiam longe lateque proximis, tanquam bonus odor Christi in omni loco. Horum vestimentorum Christi fragrantiam statim ut sensit Isaac: Ecce, inquit, odor filii mei sicut odor agri cui benedixit Dominus (Gen. xxvii, 27). Sed et Sponsus ad sponsam, quae etiam corpus et vestimentum ipsius est, loquitur dicens: Odor vestimentorum tuorum, sicut odor thuris (Cant. iv, 11). Quem nimirum odorem thuris Sponso gratissimum, pietas, o fratres, vestrorum spirabit cordium, si ita fragrans et devota fuerit ut dirigatur oratio vestra sicut incensum in conspectu Altissimi, et ascendat coram eo sicut virgula fumi ex aromatibus myrrhae et thuris (Id. iii, 6). Et quidem myrrha fragrat ei de corporibus vestris; fragrat utique et mihi: utinam ita et thus fragret de cordibus vestris, quatenus Sponsus probans vos sicut castos, sic etiam devotos, frequentius vos sua visitatione dignetur, et dicat: Ibo mihi ad montem myrrhae, et ad collem thuris (Id. iv, 6). Videtur tamen sermo iste, prophetia hujus esse diei, per Salomonem olim praedicta, per Jesum hodie impleta. Hodie namque venit in illum montem altissimum montium, montem non modo myrrhae et thuris, sed et omnium aromatum; dico autem Virginem virginum, omnium plenam gratiarum, inter quas tamen praecipue, nisi fallor, redolebat sponso myrrha castitatis, et thus pietatis. Odor, iste, fratres, mei, super omnia aromata; odor iste Dominum majestatis de excelsis attrahit et invitat, ut inclinet coelos et descendat, sicut probat dies haec, cum Altissimus, angelo misso de coelis, ipse quoque descendit in uterum Matris, qui semper manet in sinu Patris, cum quo vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Myrrh, it says, and stacte and cassia from your garments, from the ivory houses. We do indeed inhabit houses of clay, but those which are clay by the quality of their material become ivory through the virtue of continence. If myrrh first begins to breathe from them through the mortification of pleasures, other kinds of spices will follow, breathing forth the manifold grace of virtues. They will breathe pleasantly for Christ, as from his own garments; they will also breathe far and wide for their neighbors, as the good fragrance of Christ in every place. As soon as Isaac perceived the fragrance of these garments of Christ, he said: Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field which the Lord has blessed (Gen. xxvii, 27). The Bridegroom too speaks to the bride, who is also his body and his clothing, saying: The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense (Cant. iv, 11). That fragrance of incense, so pleasing to the Bridegroom, will surely be breathed forth, brothers, by the devotion of your hearts, if it is so fragrant and devout that your prayer is directed like incense before the Most High, and rises before him like a little column of smoke from spices of myrrh and incense (Id. iii, 6). Myrrh does indeed breathe forth for him from your bodies; its fragrance reaches me too. Would that incense might likewise breathe forth from your hearts, so that the Bridegroom, finding you devout as well as chaste, may more often deign to visit you and say: I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of incense (Id. iv, 6). Yet this saying seems to be a prophecy of this day, foretold long ago through Solomon and fulfilled today through Jesus. For today he came to that mountain, the highest of mountains, a mountain not only of myrrh and incense but of every spice: I mean the Virgin of virgins, full of every grace, among which, unless I am mistaken, the myrrh of chastity and the incense of devotion were especially fragrant to the Bridegroom. This fragrance, my brothers, surpasses every spice; this fragrance draws and invites the Lord of majesty from the heights to bow the heavens and descend, as this day proves, when the Most High, having sent an angel from heaven, himself also descended into his Mother's womb, he who always remains in the Father's bosom, with whom he lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The title and six numbered sections follow the printed edition. A second image of the same source resolves damage in the digitized pages.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition cites Luke 1:70 for the promise of David’s throne; the promise is in Luke 1:32. It also prints a doubled opening parenthesis before Proverbs 9:1. Both are retained.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition cites Luke 6:49 for “power went out from him and healed them all”; the saying is in Luke 6:19. The later Id. i, 48 means Luke 1:48.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: Historical III Regum corresponds to modern 1 Kings, and Psalm numbering follows the Latin edition. “Stacte” is the traditional name of an aromatic substance; no precise botanical identification is intended. The edition prints duos where the context calls for quos (“those whom”); the English follows that sense. The imagery of ivory, virginity and martyrdom, bodily chastity and fragrance belongs to Guerric’s argument. The repeated myrrh quotation has no new printed Psalm reference.

sermons.title: Annunciation Sermon I: The Joy of This Day and the Praises of the Virgin Mother

sermons.author: Guerric of Igny
sermons.calendar_label: The Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary
metadata: Guerric of Igny (collection attribution), Sermones per annum, SERMO II., De verbi incarnatione in Maria et in anima fideli., in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier frères, 1879), cols. 120-124.
Internet Archive, 2011; PIMS, University of Toronto; University of Toronto funding.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric considers the Incarnation in Mary and the formation of Christ in the faithful soul. He connects Mary's hearing and faith with love of God and neighbor, humility, chastity and care for the life of grace. The sermon appears under the Annunciation heading in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO II.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON II.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De verbi incarnatione in Maria et in anima fideli.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the incarnation of the Word in Mary and in the faithful soul.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Hodie Verbum caro factum est, et habitare coepit in nobis, secundum regulam scilicet sanae fidei, quam ecclesiasticorum dogmatum definitio tradidit nobis (7). Firmissime namque tenet, et nullatenus dubitat Ecclesia, carnem Christi non prius conceptam quam a Verbo susceptam; sed ipsum Verbum Dei carnis acceptione conceptum, carnemque Verbi incarnatione conceptam. Hodie itaque Sapientia aedificare coepit sibi domum corporis nostri in utero Virginis, et ad aedificandam unitatem Ecclesiae, angularem lapidem de monte sine manibus abscidit; dum sine opere humano de corpore virginali carnem sibi nostrae redemptionis separavit. Ab hoc ergo die Dominus virtutum nobiscum, susceptor noster Deus Jacob, quia hodie Domini est assumptio nostra, ut inhabitet gloria in terra nostra (Psal. LXXXIV, 10). Prorsus hodie benedixisti, Domine, terram tuam, illam benedictam in mulieribus. Hodie dedisti benignitatem Spiritus sancti, ut terra nostra daret benedictum fructum ventris sui, et rorantibus coelis desuper uterus virginalis Salvatorem germinaret. Maledicta terra in opere praevaricatoris, quae etiam exercitata spinas et tribulos germinat haeredibus maledictionis (Gen. III, 17, 18). At nunc benedicta terra in opere Redemptoris, quae remissionem peccatorum fructumque vitae parturit universis, et filiis Adae praejudicium originalis dissolvit maledicti. Prorsus benedicta illa terra, quae omnino intacta, nec fossa, nec seminata, de solo rore coeli Salvatorem germinat, et mortalibus panem Angelorum, alimoniam vitae aeternae ministrat. Haec itaque terra, quia inculta erat, videbatur esse deserta, sed erat opimo fructu referta; videbatur esse eremus solitudinis, sed erat paradisus beatitudinis. Plane hortus deliciarum Dei, eremus cujus campi germinaverunt germen odoris, plane desertum refertum, de quo Agnum dominatorem terrae Pater emisit. Emitte, inquit, Agnum, Domine, de petra deserti (Isai. XVI, 1), id est, abscinde Petram de Petra, Sanctum et inviolabilem sancta et inviolata proferat virginitas. Sane in hoc ipso satis decenter Christi occasus ortui, sepultura respondet conceptioni, dum videlicet emittitur Agnus de petra deserti, condendus in petra monumenti; et cujus corpori monumentum excidendum erat in petra, ipse ab initio conceptus sui, et corpus sibi excidit de petra, et corpori locum in petra; sic integritatem petrae, cum de ea emitteretur, non imminuens, sicut nec signatam sepulturae petram, cum de ea egrederetur, aperiens.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Today the Word was made flesh, and began to dwell in us, according, that is, to the rule of sound faith which the definition of the Church's teachings has handed down to us (7). For the Church holds most firmly, and in no way doubts, that the flesh of Christ was not conceived before it was taken up by the Word; but that the Word of God itself was conceived by the taking of flesh, and the flesh was conceived by the incarnation of the Word. Today, then, Wisdom began to build for herself the house of our body in the womb of the Virgin, and in order to build the unity of the Church, cut from the mountain the corner-stone without hands; while, without human labor, from the virginal body he separated for himself the flesh of our redemption. From this day, therefore, the Lord of hosts is with us, our protector, the God of Jacob, because today the assumption of our nature is the Lord's, so that glory may dwell in our land (Psal. LXXXIV, 10). Today, indeed, O Lord, you have blessed your land, that land blessed among women. Today you gave the kindness of the Holy Spirit, that our land might give forth the blessed fruit of its womb, and that, with the heavens raining down dew from above, the virginal womb might bring forth the Savior. Cursed was the earth in the deed of the transgressor, which even when tilled brings forth thorns and thistles for the heirs of the curse (Gen. III, 17, 18). But now the earth is blessed in the work of the Redeemer, which brings forth for all the remission of sins and the fruit of life, and dissolves for the sons of Adam the sentence of the original curse. Truly blessed is that land which, wholly untouched, neither dug nor sown, from the dew of heaven alone brings forth the Savior, and ministers to mortals the bread of angels, the nourishment of eternal life. This land, then, because it was untilled, seemed to be a desert, but it was filled with rich fruit; it seemed to be a wilderness of solitude, but it was a paradise of blessedness. Truly a garden of God's delights, a wilderness whose fields brought forth the bud of fragrance, truly a desert filled full, from which the Father sent forth the Lamb, ruler of the earth. "Send forth," he says, "O Lord, the Lamb from the rock of the desert" (Isai. XVI, 1), that is, cut off the Rock from the Rock; let holy and inviolate virginity bring forth the Holy and Inviolable One. Indeed, in this very thing it is quite fitting that Christ's setting should correspond to his rising, his burial to his conception, since the Lamb is sent forth from the rock of the desert, to be laid in the rock of the tomb; and he whose body was to have a tomb hewn for it in rock, himself from the beginning of his conception both hewed for himself a body from a rock, and a place for his body in a rock; thus not diminishing the integrity of the rock when he was sent forth from it, just as he did not open the sealed rock of the tomb when he came forth from it.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Si ergo petra Christus (I Cor. X, 4), ut ait Apostolus, non degenerat a Matre Filius, quando et ipsa petrae nomine censetur. An non recte vocatur petra, quae et in amorem integritatis proposito firma, affectu solida, sensu quoque ipso adversus illecebram peccati tota insensibilis erat et lapidea? an non recte petra virginalis integritas, quae et nihil parit per naturam sui; et cum parit, roris virtute divini, nec admittens conceptum, nec emittens partum, novit aperiri? Sed aperietur terra, inquit Isaias, aperiatur, et germinet Salvatorem (Isai. XLV, 8). O sancte Isaia, qui dicis aperiatur, quid ergo est quod Dominus ad Ezechielem testatur: Porta haec clausa erit, et non aperietur (Ezech. XLIV, 2)? An tibi reseratum fuit tantummodo consilium fecundandae Matris, et clausum tibi fuit mysterium clausae perenniter integritatis? Absit! inquit; nemo magis quam ego conscius hujus secreti. Quomodo enim me latuisset perpetuae virginitatis mysterium, qui tanto ante praedixi: Ecce virgo concipiet, et pariet filium (Isai. VII, 14)? Quaeris igitur quomodo dicamus, ego, aperiatur; ille, non aperietur? Non aperietur viro, aperietur Domino; sicut ibidem ad ipsum dicitur Ezechielem: Vir non transibit per eam, quoniam Dominus Deus Israel ingressus est per eam. Aperietur autem Domino non virginalis integritas corporis, quia, sicut Ezechiel post praedicta subdidit: Haec clausa erit ipsi etiam principi (Ezech. XLIV, 2, 3), sed aperietur auris et porta cordis; quia videlicet intravit per aurem Virginis Verbum incarnandum, et exivit per clausam portam corporis incarnatum. Omnipotens namque Verbum Dei, etsi infirmitatem nostram suscepit, nihil tamen de sua sibi omnipotentia minuit, quominus contra naturam carnis, et supra intelligentiam sensus nostri, corpus suum palpabile per clausa posset et integra trajicere, sicut etiam [ad] discipulos ingrediens januis clausis, oculis probavit, quod ratio non capit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. If then Christ is the Rock (I Cor. X, 4), as the Apostle says, the Son does not degenerate from his Mother, since she too is reckoned by the name of rock. Is she not rightly called rock, who was in the resolve of love for integrity firm, solid in affection, and even in sense itself wholly insensible and stony against the enticement of sin? Is not virginal integrity rightly called rock, which brings forth nothing by its own nature and, when it brings forth by the power of the divine dew, knows no opening either to receive conception or to bring forth the child? But Isaiah says, "The earth shall be opened; let it be opened and bud forth the Savior" (Isai. XLV, 8). O holy Isaiah, you who say "let it be opened," what then is it that the Lord testifies to Ezekiel: "This gate shall be shut, and shall not be opened" (Ezech. XLIV, 2)? Was the plan for making the Mother fruitful revealed to you alone, while the mystery of her perpetually closed integrity was hidden from you? "Far from it!" he says; "no one is more conscious of this secret than I. For how could the mystery of perpetual virginity have escaped me, who so long before foretold: 'Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son' (Isai. VII, 14)?" You ask, then, how we can say, I, "let it be opened"; he, "it shall not be opened"? It shall not be opened to man, it shall be opened to the Lord; just as it is said there to Ezekiel himself: "No man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it." But it is not the virginal integrity of the body that is opened to the Lord, because, as Ezekiel adds after the foregoing: "This shall be shut even to the prince himself" (Ezech. XLIV, 2, 3); rather, it is the ear and the gate of the heart that are opened; because, namely, the Word to be incarnated entered through the ear of the Virgin, and came forth incarnate through the closed gate of the body. For the almighty Word of God, although he took up our weakness, nevertheless diminished nothing of his omnipotence, so that, contrary to the nature of flesh and beyond the understanding of our sense, he could pass his palpable body through closed and intact things, just as also, entering [to] the disciples through closed doors, he proved by sight what reason cannot grasp.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Secura igitur, o Virgo intemerata, o porta sanctuarii perenniter clausa, secura aperi Domino Deo Israel, qui tibi jam dudum clamat: Aperi mihi, soror mea, amica mea (Cantic. V, 2). Non est quod timeas integritati tuae: Deus non novit integra violare, sed violata consolidare. Si Verbo Dei apta es, tum demum non modo clausa, sed et signata es. Pone me, inquit, ut signaculum super cor tuum, ut signaculum super brachium tuum (Id. VIII, 6). Jesus quippe impressus in corde, expressus in opere, sigillum plane et munimentum est inviolabile castitatis sponsae suae, et eo ipso quo se imprimit imitationis formam, imponit etiam incorruptionis custodiam. Sit ergo, o Virgo fidelis, auris tua aperta ad audiendum et mens tua ad credendum: aure percipe verbum angeli, et corde suscipe Verbum Altissimi, et corpore concipe Filium Dei. Dic et tu, o beata, tam humilis quam fidelis, dic Dominus aperuit mihi aurem; ego autem non contradico, retrorsum non abii (Isai. L, 5). Ecce ancilla Domini: praesto sum ejus voluntati; quinimo juvabo votis si possum, fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum (Luc. I, 38). Hoc dicere, sic suam devotionem offerre, istud plane est Domino pectus aperire, istud est etiam os aperire, et spiritum attrahere. Sic profecto aperiebatur terra, ut, quem rorabant coeli desuper, susciperet rorem, et germinaret Salvatorem. Nobile germen, germen justum, germen odoris, germen Domini, quod jam est in magnificentia et gloria, cum idem fructus terrae sub imis est super omnia, id est, exaltatus est super coelos Deus, et super omnem terram gloria ejus. Nihil enim interest sive germen, sive fructum aut florem dixeris, cum haec omnia, imo infinita alia unus Christus sit, res una, sed multiformis gratia, et virtutis unius operatio multifaria; cui si infinita nomina paupertas humani sensus et sermonis pro similitudine commodaverit, rei tamen implere significationem non poterit. Bene autem simul vocatur germen, et flos, et fructus, qui sine gradu profectus, ab initio conceptus sui omni virtute et gratia in se ipso exstitit perfectus. In nobis enim primum ipse germen est, cum fides in confessionem prorumpit vel opus manifestum: postmodum flos, cum super proficientem efflorescit sanctificatio Dei quodam spectabili decore virtutum; demum autem fructus, cum beatitudo satiat hominem consummatum. Pulcherrime sane ac vigilantissime non solum mysteria, sed et mysteriorum praesagia dispensatio praeordinavit divina, ut locus in quo terra germinavit Salvatorem germen justum, et flos de virga et radice Jesse ascendit, Nazareth, id est sanctitas, germen, flos, virgultum vocaretur; ut videlicet negotium loco, locusque negotio consona voce contestaretur, pariterque et nomen loci rem gerendam pronuntiaret, et res gesta causam nominis indicaret.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Therefore, without fear, O undefiled Virgin, O gate of the sanctuary closed forever, without fear open to the Lord God of Israel, who has long been crying out to you: 'Open to me, my sister, my love' (Cantic. V, 2). You have no reason to fear for your integrity: God does not know how to violate what is whole, but to make whole what is violated. If you are fitted to the Word of God, then you are not only closed, but also sealed. 'Set me,' he says, 'as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm' (Id. VIII, 6). For Jesus, impressed upon the heart, expressed in deed, is plainly the seal and the inviolable safeguard of the chastity of his bride; and by the very fact that he impresses himself as a pattern for imitation, he also imposes upon her the guardianship of incorruption. Let your ear, then, O faithful Virgin, be open to hear, and your mind to believe: with your ear perceive the word of the angel, with your heart receive the Word of the Most High, and in your body conceive the Son of God. Say, too, O blessed one, as humble as you are faithful, say: 'The Lord has opened my ear; but I do not contradict, I have not drawn back' (Isai. L, 5). 'Behold the handmaid of the Lord: I am ready for his will; indeed I will even assist his purposes if I can — be it done to me according to your word' (Luc. I, 38). To say this, to offer one's devotion in this way, is plainly to open one's breast to the Lord; it is also to open one's mouth and draw in the Spirit. Thus indeed was the earth opened, so that it might receive as dew him whom the heavens rained down from above, and bring forth the Savior as its sprout. A noble sprout, a righteous sprout, a sprout of fragrance, the sprout of the Lord, who is now in magnificence and glory, since that same fruit of the earth, though from the lowest depths, is above all things — that is, God has been exalted above the heavens, and his glory above all the earth. For it makes no difference whether you call him sprout, or fruit, or flower, since all these things — indeed, countless others besides — are one Christ, one reality, but grace of many forms, and the working of one power in many ways; and to him, even if the poverty of human understanding and speech lends countless names by way of likeness, it can never fulfill the full meaning of the reality. Rightly, however, is he called at once sprout, and flower, and fruit, who, without any gradual advance, existed perfect in himself in every virtue and grace from the very beginning of his conception. For in us, he is first a sprout, when faith breaks forth into confession or into a manifest work; afterward a flower, when the sanctification of God blossoms upon the one who is advancing, with a certain visible beauty of virtues; and finally a fruit, when beatitude satisfies the person brought to completion. Most beautifully indeed, and most watchfully, divine providence foreordained not only the mysteries themselves but also the foreshadowings of the mysteries, so that the place in which the earth brought forth the Savior, the righteous sprout, and where the flower arose from the rod and root of Jesse, should be called Nazareth — that is, 'holiness,' 'sprout,' 'flower,' 'shoot' — so that the event might bear witness to the place, and the place to the event, with a single harmonious voice, and that likewise the name of the place might proclaim the deed to be accomplished, and the deed accomplished might reveal the reason for the name.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Ignoscite mihi, fratres mei, quia, qui morum vestrorum servire debueram instructioni, plus forsitan quam necesse erat demoratus sum in illius ineffabilis admiratione et praeconio mysterii. Quid enim mirum si miror quod stupent Angeli, si praedicare gestio, quam coeli enarrant, gloriam Dei? quid mirum si me delectat quod beatos spiritus laetificat, quod peccatores justificat, justosque glorificat? Nescio tamen si ulla esse possit efficacior ac suavior morum aedificatio, quam hujus mysterii, id est Verbi incarnati, fidelis et pia consideratio. Quid enim sic hominem excitare potest ad amorem Dei, quam praeveniens hominem amor Dei tam vehemens ad hominem, ut homo propter hominem velit fieri? Quid autem ita nutrit amorem proximi, quam similitudo et natura proximi in humanitate Dei? Nam humilitatis exemplum nec cogitari posse majus aliquod existimo, quam exinanitionem Dei in formam servi, et servitutem plus quam servi. Castitatem porro quid aeque commendat, sicut quod ipsa castitas Salvatorem germinat? Aut fidei virtutem ac meritum quid evidentius ostendit, quam quod Virgo Deum fide concepit, fide omnia sibi promissa divinitus impleri promeruerit? Beata, inquit, quae credidit, quoniam perficientur quae dicta sunt ei a Domino (ibid. 45). Et ut plenius noveris conceptum Virginis non solum esse mysticum, sed et moralem; quod sacramentum est ad redemptionem, exemplum quoque tibi est ad imitationem; ut manifeste evacues in te gratiam sacramenti, si non imiteris virtutem exempli. Quae enim Deum fide concepit, si fidem habeas, idem tibi promittit, quod videlicet si verbum ex ore nuntii coelestis fideliter velis suscipere, Deum quem totus orbis non potest capere, possis et ipse concipere. Concipere autem corde, imo et corpore, licet non corporali opere aut specie, tamen plane corpore tuo; quandoquidem jubemur ab Apostolo glorificare et portare Deum in corpore nostro (I Cor. VI, 20). Attende itaque, ut scriptum est, diligenter auditui tuo, nam fides ex auditu, auditus autem per Verbum Dei (Rom. X, 17); quod tibi absque dubio evangelizat angelus Dei, cum de timore aut amore ejus tecum agit praedicator fidelis, quem angelum Domini exercituum dici et esse non est tibi fas ambigere (Malach. II, 16, 17). Quam beati qui dicere possunt: A timore tuo, Domine, concepimus et parturivimus spiritum salutis (Isa. XXVI, 17, 18)! qui nimirum non est alius quam spiritus Salvatoris, quam veritas Jesu Christi. Vide ineffabilem dignationem Dei, simulque virtutem incomprehensibilis mysterii: qui creavit te, creatur in te; et, quasi parum esset te ipsum habere patrem, vult etiam te sibi fieri matrem. Quicumque, inquit, fecerit voluntatem patris mei, ipse meus et frater, et soror, et mater est (Matth. XII, 50). O fidelis anima, expande sinus, dilata affectus; ne angustieris in visceribus tuis, concipe quem creatura non capit. Aperi Verbo Dei aurem audiendi: haec est ad uterum cordis via spiritus concipiendi, hac ratione compinguntur ossa Christi, id est, virtutes in ventre praegnantis.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Forgive me, my brothers, because I, who ought to have served the instruction of your morals, have perhaps lingered longer than was necessary in admiration and praise of that ineffable mystery. For what wonder is it if I marvel at what makes the Angels stand amazed, if I am eager to proclaim the glory of God which the heavens declare? What wonder is it if I am delighted by what gladdens the blessed spirits, what justifies sinners, and glorifies the just? Yet I do not know whether there can be any more effective or sweeter edification of morals than the faithful and pious consideration of this mystery, that is, of the Word incarnate. For what can so arouse man to the love of God as the love of God going before man, so vehement toward man that he willed to become man for man's sake? And what so nourishes love of neighbor as the likeness and nature of a neighbor found in the humanity of God? For I judge that no greater example of humility can even be conceived than the emptying of God into the form of a servant, and a servitude greater than that of a servant. Furthermore, what commends chastity so much as the fact that chastity itself brings forth the Savior as its offspring? Or what shows the power and merit of faith more clearly than that the Virgin conceived God by faith, and by faith merited that all things divinely promised to her should be fulfilled? Blessed, he says, is she who believed, for the things that were spoken to her by the Lord shall be fulfilled (ibid. 45). And that you may know more fully that the Virgin's conception is not only mystical but also moral — what is a sacrament for redemption is also an example for you to imitate — so that you plainly render void in yourself the grace of the sacrament, if you fail to imitate the virtue of the example. For she who conceived God by faith promises you the same thing, if you have faith: namely, that if you are willing to receive faithfully the word from the mouth of the heavenly messenger, you too can conceive the God whom the whole world cannot contain. And to conceive — in heart, indeed also in body, though not by bodily act or bodily form, yet truly in your body — since we are commanded by the Apostle to glorify and to carry God in our body (I Cor. VI, 20). Attend, therefore, as it is written, diligently to your hearing, for faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God (Rom. X, 17); which without doubt the angel of God announces to you as gospel, when a faithful preacher deals with you concerning fear or love of him — and you may not rightly doubt that he is rightly called, and truly is, the angel of the Lord of hosts (Malach. II, 16, 17). How blessed are they who can say: From fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived and brought forth the spirit of salvation (Isa. XXVI, 17, 18)! — which indeed is none other than the spirit of the Savior, the truth of Jesus Christ. Behold the ineffable condescension of God, and at the same time the power of this incomprehensible mystery: he who created you is created in you; and, as though it were not enough for him to have you yourself as a father, he wills also that you become a mother to him. Whoever, he says, does the will of my Father, he is my brother, and sister, and mother (Matth. XII, 50). O faithful soul, open wide your bosom, enlarge your affections; do not be straitened in your inmost being — conceive him whom no creature can contain. Open to the Word of God the ear of hearing: this is the way to the womb of the heart for conceiving the spirit; by this means the bones of Christ — that is, the virtues — are knit together in the womb of her who is pregnant.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Gratias tibi, sancte Spiritus, qui ubi vis spiras. Video munere tuo non unam, sed innumeras fidelium animas illo generoso germine gravidas; custodi opera tua, ne aliqua illarum abortiat, conceptumque divinae sobolis informem aut mortuum excutiat. Vos quoque, o matres beatae tam gloriosae prolis, attendite vobis ipsis, donec formetur Christus in vobis (Galat. IV, 19); attendite, ne qua foris offensa gravior fetum tenerum laedat, ne quid ingeratis ventri, id est menti, quod spiritum quem concepistis exstinguat. Parcite, si non vobis, certe Filio Dei in vobis; parcite, inquam, non solum ab operibus et sermonibus malis, sed etiam a cogitationibus noxiis et delectationibus mortiferis, quae plane suffocant semen Dei. Omni itaque custodia servate corda vestra, quia ex ipsis vita procedet, cum scilicet maturus se partus absolvet, et vita Christi, quae nunc abscondita est in cordibus vestris, manifestabitur in carne vestra mortali. Concepistis spiritum salutis, sed adhuc parturitis, nondum peperistis. Si labor in parturiendo, magna de spe partus consolatio. Mulier cum parit, tristitiam habet (Joan. XVI, 21) laboris; cum autem pepererit puerum, jam non memor erit pressurae propter gaudium, quia natus erit homo Christus in mundum exteriorem corporis nostri, quod et minor mundus solet appellari. Qui enim nunc conceptus est Deus in spiritibus nostris, configurans eos spiritui charitatis suae, tunc velut homo nascetur in corporibus, configurans ea corpori claritatis suae, in qua vivit et gloriatur Deus per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Thanks be to you, Holy Spirit, who breathe where you will. I see, by your gift, not one but countless souls of the faithful made heavy with that noble offspring; guard your works, lest any of them miscarry, and cast out the conceived offspring of divine progeny unformed or dead. You too, O blessed mothers of so glorious a child, attend to yourselves, until Christ be formed in you (Galat. IV, 19); take heed lest some graver offense from without injure the tender offspring, lest you introduce into the womb — that is, into the mind — anything that might extinguish the spirit you have conceived. Spare — if not yourselves, then certainly the Son of God within you; spare, I say, not only from evil deeds and words, but also from harmful thoughts and deadly pleasures, which utterly suffocate the seed of God. Keep your hearts, therefore, with all vigilance, for from them life shall proceed, when, that is, the mature birth is brought to completion, and the life of Christ, which is now hidden in your hearts, shall be made manifest in your mortal flesh. You have conceived the spirit of salvation, but you are still in labor; you have not yet given birth. If there is labor in giving birth, there is great consolation in the hope of the birth. A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow (Joan. XVI, 21) of her labor; but when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy, because the man Christ shall have been born into the outer world of our body, which is also commonly called the lesser world. For he who is now conceived as God in our spirits, conforming them to the spirit of his charity, shall then, as it were, be born as man in our bodies, conforming them to the body of his glory, in which God lives and is glorified through all ages of ages. Amen.
