passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric reads Isaiah's sign of the Virgin through the Incarnation, Passion and exaltation of Christ. His argument includes polemic against Jewish interpretations of the prophecy. He turns from Christ's hidden life in the womb to monastic silence, nourishment by the divine Word and patience within the Church. The sermon appears under the Annunciation heading in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO III.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON III.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De hujus mysterii signis.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the signs of this mystery.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Audite, domus David: ecce dabit Dominus ipse vobis signum. Ecce virgo concipiet (Isai. VII, 13, 14). Hodie impleta est haec prophetia in auribus vestris. Hodie namque illud ineffabile conceptus virginalis miraculum, sicut audieratis promissum, sic audistis impletum: Virgo hodie concepit. Et hoc signum, prioribus retro saeculis inauditum, nostris saeculis Dominus dedit. Et sicut Jeremias eodem spiritu et eodem sensu praedixit: Creabit Dominus novum super terram, quia femina circumdabit virum (Jerem. XXXI, 22). Quid est enim, creabit Dominus novum super terram, femina circumdabit virum, quod ait Jeremias, nisi quod ait Isaias: Dabit Dominus signum, Virgo concipiet filium (Isai. VII, 13, 14)? Hoc nempe est, circumdabit. Non de consortio virili suscipiet, sed de se sola intra semetipsam concipiet, et solius materni corporis involucro vestiet. Alioquin dicant, si possunt Judaei, quod signum Dominus in hoc dedit, si non virgo, sed adolescentula, ut ipsi falso interpretantur, concepit; aut quid novum Dominus creavit, si femina masculum de masculo susceptum circumdedit. Potest quidem mentiri iniquitas sibi; sed in multitudine virtutis tuae, o Domine, mentientur tibi inimici tui, ut virtutem tuam dum negat pravitas et paucitas Judaeorum, gloriosius et copiosius confiteatur fides omnium populorum. Confiteantur tibi populi, Deus, confiteantur tibi populi omnes, quia terra dedit fructum suum, Virgo germinavit Jesum (Psal. LXVI, 6). Velint, nolint Judaei, creavit Dominus novitatem hujus miraculi, in signum eorum incredulitatis; utique in signum cui contradicunt usque hodie, plus, nisi fallor, pertinacia odibili, quam ignorantia miserabili.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Hear, O house of David: behold, the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive (Isai. VII, 13, 14). Today this prophecy has been fulfilled in your hearing. For today that ineffable miracle of virginal conception, just as you had heard it promised, so you have heard it fulfilled: today a Virgin has conceived. And this sign, unheard of in former ages, the Lord has given to our age. And just as Jeremiah foretold in the same spirit and with the same meaning: The Lord will create something new upon the earth, for a woman shall encompass a man (Jerem. XXXI, 22). For what is it that Jeremiah says, "The Lord will create something new upon the earth, a woman shall encompass a man," except what Isaiah says: "The Lord will give a sign, a Virgin shall conceive a son" (Isai. VII, 13, 14)? This indeed is what "encompass" means: she will not conceive through union with a man, but will conceive within herself alone, from herself alone, and will clothe him solely in the wrapping of a maternal body. Otherwise, let the Jews say, if they can, what sign the Lord gave in this, if it was not a virgin but a young woman who conceived, as they falsely interpret it; or what new thing the Lord created, if a woman merely enclosed within herself a male conceived from a male. Iniquity can indeed lie to itself; but in the multitude of your power, O Lord, your enemies will lie to you, so that while the wickedness and the small number of the Jews deny your power, the faith of all peoples may confess it more gloriously and abundantly. Let the peoples confess to you, O God, let all the peoples confess to you, for the earth has given its fruit, the Virgin has brought forth Jesus (Psal. LXVI, 6). Whether the Jews wish it or not, the Lord has created the novelty of this miracle as a sign of their unbelief; indeed as a sign which they contradict even to this day, more, unless I am mistaken, out of hateful obstinacy than out of pitiable ignorance.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Non alienum tamen ab origine et consuetudine viperei germinis, si modo contradicunt huic signo, postquam factum est, qui ab initio in patre et rege suo impiissimo Achaz contradixerunt ne fieret. Locutus est enim Dominus ad Achaz, dicens: Pete tibi signum. Non petam, inquit, et non tentabo Dominum (Isai. VII, 10-12). O religio profana! o pietas exsecranda! o humilitas dolosa! Ne tentes, ut ais, Dominum, contemnis Dominum. Quomodo enim tentares, si fideliter obedires? Nunc autem quomodo non graviter tentas, quem manifesto contemptu irritas? Novimus utique, novimus dolum et invidiam Judaicae radicis, quae et antequam Christus nasceretur, invidere coepit gloriae illius. Nam et iste Achaz, quantum ex vita et moribus ipsius intelligi datur (nam cultor idolorum erat), non alia religione aut metu signum recusavit petere cum juberetur, nisi ideo scilicet ne Dominus glorificaretur. Sane mira et plane digna ira Dei et hominum, tam dira perversitas Judaeorum, qui, cum jubentur signa quaerere, renuunt, non, ut fingunt, ne tentent, sed ne glorificent Dominum (Matth. XVI, 4); cum non jubentur, tentant et quaerunt. Nam velut natura et usu Judaei signa quaerunt, et, si dantur, calumniantur et inficiari contendunt, ut manifeste confiteantur quia tentantes quaerebant, non ut crederent facienti, sed ut insultarent non facienti. O gens peccatrix; semen nequam, filii scelerati (Isai. I, 4)! ait Isaias, Numquid parum est vobis molestos esse hominibus, mihi et aliis prophetis, imo universo generi hominum, quia molesti estis et Deo meo? Propter hoc dabit Dominus ipse vobis signum (Isa. VII, 13, 14). Quia enim vos in perversum adversum eum inceditis, et ipse, ut ait, perversus incedet vobis. Non vultis signum dari, ne glorificetur auctor miraculi; et ipse propter hoc dabit, ut ipse glorificetur, et vos confundamini. Fac, Domine, fac mecum signum in bonum, ut videant qui me oderunt, et confundantur (Psal. LXXXV, 17), ait de Judaeis ad Patrem Filius.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Yet it is not foreign to the origin and custom of the viperous brood, if they now contradict this sign after it has been accomplished, seeing that from the beginning they contradicted in their father and most impious king Ahaz that it should ever come to pass. For the Lord spoke to Ahaz, saying: Ask for yourself a sign. I will not ask, he said, and I will not tempt the Lord (Isai. VII, 10-12). O profane religion! O execrable piety! O deceitful humility! When you say, "Lest I tempt the Lord," you are despising the Lord. For how would you be tempting him, if you obeyed faithfully? But now, how are you not gravely tempting him, whom you provoke by manifest contempt? We know indeed, we know the deceit and envy of the Jewish root, which even before Christ was born began to envy his glory. For this Ahaz too, as far as can be understood from his life and character (for he was a worshiper of idols), refused to ask for a sign when commanded, not out of any religious scruple or fear, but precisely so that the Lord might not be glorified. Truly wondrous, and plainly deserving the wrath of God and of men, is such dire perversity of the Jews, who, when commanded to seek signs, refuse — not, as they pretend, lest they tempt God, but lest they glorify the Lord (Matth. XVI, 4); and when not commanded, they tempt and seek. For as if by nature and custom the Jews seek signs, and, if given, they slander them and strive to deny them, so that they plainly confess that in tempting they sought not in order to believe in the one who performed the sign, but in order to insult the one who did not perform it. O sinful nation, wicked seed, corrupt children (Isai. I, 4)! says Isaiah. Is it too little for you to be troublesome to men — to me and to other prophets, indeed to the whole human race — that you are troublesome also to my God? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign (Isa. VII, 13, 14). For because you walk perversely against him, he too, as he says, will walk perversely toward you. You do not wish a sign to be given, lest the author of the miracle be glorified; and for this very reason he will give it, that he himself may be glorified, and you confounded. Work, O Lord, work with me a sign for good, that those who hate me may see it and be confounded (Psal. LXXXV, 17), says the Son to the Father concerning the Jews.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Primum autem signum quod Pater et Filius operati sunt in confusionem infidelium et gloriam fidelium, in testimonium suae virtutis et opus nostrae salutis, arbitror hodiernum esse Virginis conceptum. Nam de ipso cum praemissum esset, dabit Dominus signum, quasi quaerentibus quod signum, intulit contextus Prophetae, verbis tamen Evangelistae, Ecce virgo concipiet et pariet filium (Isai. VII, 14, et Luc. I, 31); ut plane aut consequentia vel veritate contextus careat, aut (quod est probabilius) mendacium Judaeorum latebram non habeat. Merito proinde cum jam generatio prava et adultera signum quaerit, signum non datur ei, nisi signum Jonae (Matth. XVI, 4); ut videlicet qui ob perversitatem mentis non aedificantur signo virtutis, scandalizentur signo infirmitatis, triduanae scilicet sepulturae et mortis. Nam verbum crucis et mortis Judaeis, qui pereunt, scandalum est; his autem qui salvi fiunt, id est, nobis, virtus Dei est (I Cor. I, 18); nec minor aut infirmior nobis est Filius hominis in corde terrae, quam in consessu paternae dexterae. Signum quippe quod illi recusaverunt, sive in profundum inferni, sive in excelsum supra, nos fide plena ac veneratione devota suscipimus, agnoscentes Filium quem concipit Virgo, in profundo inferni signum nobis esse liberationis et veniae; in excelsum supra, signum et spem exsultationis et gloriae. Qui enim primum descendit in inferiores partes terrae, ut in sanguine testamenti sui extraheret vinctos de lacu in quo non est aqua, ipse est et qui ascendit super omnes coelos, ut adimpleret omnia (Ephes. IV, 9, 10). Jam levavit Dominus signum primum in patibulo crucis, postmodum in throno regni, et exaltavit signum ad populos nationum, quia contradictum est ei a populo Judaeorum, et quotidie a quatuor ventis congregat dispersos veri Israel ad hoc signum. O Radix Jesse, qui stas in signum populorum, super quem jam continent reges os suum, obstruatur etiam os loquentium iniqua, id est, Judaeorum blasphemantium, qui adhuc signo immaculato conceptus tui contradicunt, et nec angelo Gabrieli credunt dicenti quia non est impossibile apud te omne verbum (Luc. I, 30, 31). Beata quae credidit, cui haec ratio satisfecit, et, cum quaesisset quomodo Filium susciperet, quae non cognosceret virum, tam de integritate quam de prole securam deinceps effecit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. The first sign which the Father and the Son worked for the confusion of unbelievers and the glory of the faithful, in testimony of their power and as the work of our salvation, I judge to be the Son's conception in the Virgin today. For concerning it, when it had been foretold, "The Lord shall give a sign," as though to those asking what that sign might be, the continuation of the Prophet added—though in the words of the Evangelist—"Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son" (Isai. VII, 14, et Luc. I, 31); so that plainly either the context lacks consequence or truth, or (which is more probable) the lie of the Jews finds no hiding place. Fittingly, then, since this crooked and adulterous generation now seeks a sign, no sign is given it except the sign of Jonah (Matth. XVI, 4); so that those who, on account of the perversity of their mind, are not built up by the sign of power, may be scandalized by the sign of weakness—namely, of the three-day burial and death. For the word of the cross and of death is to the Jews who perish a stumbling block; but to us who are being saved it is the power of God (I Cor. I, 18); nor is the Son of Man any less or weaker for us in the heart of the earth than seated at the Father's right hand. For the sign which they refused, whether in the depth of hell or on high above, we receive with full faith and devout veneration, acknowledging that the Son whom the Virgin conceives is, in the depth of hell, a sign to us of liberation and pardon; and on high above, a sign and hope of exultation and glory. For he who first descended into the lower parts of the earth, that in the blood of his testament he might draw out the bound from the pit in which there is no water, is also he who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things (Ephes. IV, 9, 10). The Lord has already raised up his first sign on the gibbet of the cross, afterward on the throne of the kingdom, and he has exalted the sign to the peoples of the nations, because it was contradicted by the people of the Jews, and daily he gathers from the four winds the scattered of the true Israel to this sign. O Root of Jesse, who stand as a sign of the peoples, before whom kings now keep their mouths shut, let the mouth of those who speak iniquity also be stopped—that is, of the Jews who blaspheme, who still contradict the immaculate sign of your conception, and do not even believe the angel Gabriel saying that with you no word is impossible (Luc. I, 30, 31). Blessed is she who believed, for whom this reasoning was satisfying, and who, when she had asked how she should receive a Son, she who knew not man, was thereafter made secure both as to her integrity and as to her offspring.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Quidquid ergo garriat impietas infidelium, nobis concipiat et pariat Virgo Filium; nos quippe signum habemus in bonum, etiam Matrem et Filium. Nobis plane Mater tota miraculum est, quae singulariter et sine exemplo mater est et virgo; nobis Filius totus miraculum, qui non solum singulariter, sed incomprehensibiliter Deus est et homo. Mater, virgo concipiens et pariens, signum nobis est quia Deus est homo iste qui concipitur et paritur; Filius, divina faciens, et humana patiens, signum nobis est quia in Deum transferet hominem, pro quo concipitur et paritur, etiam et patitur. Omnium tamen humanarum infirmitatum vel injuriarum quas pro nobis pertulit divina dignatio, sicut tempore primam, sic etiam humilitate fere maximam existimo, quod in utero concipi, in utero novem mensium tempore majestas illa incircumscripta passa est contineri. Ubi enim sic se exinanivit? aut quando ita penitus a semetipso defecisse visus fuit? Tanto tempore nihil illa sapientia loquitur, nihil illa virtus manifestum operatur, nullo signo visibili majestas, quae clausa latet, proditur. Non sic in cruce visus est infirmus, ubi quod infirmum ipsius fuit, statim apparuit fortius omnibus hominibus: quando et moriens glorificat latronem, et exspirans inspirat Centurionem; quando horarius dolor passionis ei non solum compati fecit elementa creaturarum, sed etiam contrarias fortitudines subigit aeternorum passioni dolorum. In utero autem sic est quasi non sit, sic omnipotens virtus vacat quasi nihil possit et Verbum aeternum sub silentio se premit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Whatever, then, the impiety of unbelievers may chatter, let the Virgin conceive and bear a Son for us; for we indeed have a sign for good, even the Mother and the Son. For us, the Mother is entirely a miracle, who singularly and without precedent is both mother and virgin; for us, the Son is entirely a miracle, who not only singularly but incomprehensibly is God and man. The Mother, a virgin conceiving and bearing, is a sign to us that this one who is conceived and born is God and man; the Son, doing divine things and suffering human things, is a sign to us that he will transfer into God the man for whom he is conceived and born, and also suffers. Yet of all the human infirmities or injuries which the divine condescension bore for us, I judge that, just as it was first in time, so also it was almost the greatest in humility, that his boundless majesty suffered to be conceived in the womb, and contained within the womb for the space of nine months. For where did he so empty himself? Or when did he seem so utterly to have ceased to be himself? For such a long time that wisdom speaks nothing, that power works nothing manifest, and majesty, lying hidden and enclosed, is betrayed by no visible sign. Not so did he appear weak on the cross, where what was weak in him immediately appeared stronger than all men: when, even while dying, he glorifies the thief, and, while breathing his last, he inspires the Centurion; when the brief pain of the Passion not only made the elements of creation suffer with him, but also subjects the opposing powers to the suffering of eternal pains. But in the womb he is as though he were not; thus the omnipotent power lies idle as though it could do nothing, and the eternal Word presses itself down into silence.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Vobis tamen, fratres, vobis illud silentium verbi loquitur, vobis clamat; vobis utique disciplinam silentii commendat. In silentio enim et spe erit fortitudo vestra (Isai. XXX, 15), sicut Isaias promittit, qui cultum justitiae silentium definivit (Id. XXXII, 17). Sicut namque puer ille conceptus in utero ad maturitatem partus sub alto et diuturno profecit silentio, sic et spiritum hominis disciplina silentii nutrit, format et roborat, et quanto occultius, tanto tutius et salubrius incrementum praestat. Nescit homo animalis, qui non percipit quae sunt spiritus Dei, quae sit via spiritus, et quomodo compingantur ossa in ventre praegnantis (Eccle. XI, 5); sed non occultatum os meum a te, ait sanctus Deo, quod fecisti mihi in occulto (Psal. CXXXVIII, 15) mentis, sub secreto silentii. Sed nec a vobis occultatum est hoc mysterium, fratres mei, quorum experientia et confessio testis mihi est quomodo quietus et modestus spiritus sub silentio roboretur, pinguescat et floreat; quomodo e contrario per verba, velut quadam paralysi, dissolvatur et defluat; quomodo macrescat, et marcescat, et aridus decidat. Denique si in silentio fortitudo non esset, Salomon nequaquam dixisset: Sicut urbs patens et absque murorum ambitu, ita vir qui non potest in loquendo cohibere spiritum suum (Prov. XXV, 28). Caeterum, si quaeris quo negotio sit occupanda mens in silentio, nihil tibi imponimus onerosum, comede panem tuum, sicut et ipse Dominus conceptus suo tibi commonstrat exemplo. Quid enim propheta de eo dixit, cum loqueretur de porta orientali semper clausa in domo Domini, quae tamen Deum Israel admisit et emisit? Princeps ipse, inquit, sedebit in ea, ut comedat panem coram Domino (Ezech. XLIV, 3). Sedebit, inquit, in ea, quoniam requiescet in ea, de qua et ipse loquitur: Haec requies mea (Psal. XXXI, 14); sedebit in ea tanquam in throno grandi, quem, sicut alias dixi, Salomon rex sibi de ebore fecit (III Reg. X, 18). Si attendas angustias uteri, locus prorsus angustus est, si latitudinem cordis, thronus grandis est, propter quam etiam uterus tantae majestatis capax factus est. In ea ergo princeps sedit et panem comedit; quia si quis, inquit, aperuerit mihi, intrabo ad eum, et coenabo cum eo, et ipse mecum (Apoc. III, 20).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Yet to you, brothers, to you that silence of the Word speaks, to you it cries out; to you indeed it commends the discipline of silence. For "in silence and hope shall your strength be" (Isai. XXX, 15), as Isaiah promises, who defined the practice of righteousness as silence (Id. XXXII, 17). For just as that child, conceived in the womb, advanced toward the maturity of birth under deep and prolonged silence, so too the discipline of silence nourishes, forms, and strengthens the spirit of man; and the more hidden it is, the safer and more wholesome growth it affords. The natural man, who does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, does not know what is the way of the spirit, and how the bones are joined together in the womb of her that is with child (Eccle. XI, 5); but "my bone is not hidden from thee," says the saint to God, "which thou hast made for me in secret" (Psal. CXXXVIII, 15) — in secret of mind, under the secrecy of silence. But neither is this mystery hidden from you, my brothers, whose experience and confession is witness to me how a quiet and modest spirit is strengthened, grows rich, and flourishes under silence; how, on the contrary, through words, as by a kind of paralysis, it is dissolved and wastes away; how it grows thin, and withers, and falls away dried up. Finally, if there were no strength in silence, Solomon would by no means have said: "As a city that lies open and without the enclosure of walls, so is the man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking" (Prov. XXV, 28). But if you ask with what business the mind ought to be occupied in silence, we impose on you nothing burdensome: eat your bread, as the Lord himself, conceived in the womb, shows you by his own example. For what did the prophet say of him, when he spoke of the eastern gate, always shut, in the house of the Lord, which nevertheless admitted and sent forth the God of Israel? "The prince himself," he says, "shall sit in it, to eat bread before the Lord" (Ezech. XLIV, 3). "He shall sit," he says, "in it," because he will rest in it, of which he himself also says: "This is my rest" (Psal. XXXI, 14); he shall sit in it as on a great throne, which, as I have said elsewhere, King Solomon made for himself of ivory (III Reg. X, 18). If you consider the narrowness of the womb, it is altogether a narrow place; if you consider the breadth of the heart, it is a great throne — on account of which the womb was made capable of so great a majesty. In it, therefore, the prince sat and ate bread; for "if any man," he says, "shall open to me, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me" (Apoc. III, 20).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Non est haec coena sine pane, quando et ipse qui coenat panis est vitae, panis qui hodie descendit de coelo et dat vitam mundo. Sed res mira, si idem est qui coenat, et quod coenatur; et qui comedit, ipse est panis qui ab eo comeditur. Revera res mira, sed res vera; quia Christus non alio pane quam se ipso pascitur. Ipse namque totus est panis, Verbum propter se, caro propter unionem Verbi. Alioquin caro non prodest quidquam, cum spiritus sit qui vivificat (Joan. VI, 64), nec in solo pane vivat homo, sed in omni verbo quod procedit de ore Dei (Matth. IV, 4). Omne verbum procedens de ore Dei unum et unigenitum est Verbum Patris, quod, cum simplex sit, in se tamen continet rationem et formam omnis verbi divini. Verbum itaque pascitur de Verbo, Filius vivit de se ipso; quia sicut Pater habet vitam in semetipso, sic dedit et Filio vitam habere in semetipso (Joan. V, 26). Alia tamen ratione, sed tamen ineffabili beatitudine, Verbo pascebatur anima illa, Verbo ipsi in persona conjuncta; et incomparabili felicitate princeps ille sedens in porta virginalis uteri, panem verbi coram Domino comedebat. Id igitur operis tu quoque, si sapis, in silentio tuo actitabis, ut panem verbi divini comedas coram Domino, conservans, sicut Maria, quae de Christo dicuntur, et conferens in corde tuo. Hunc panem tecum Christus manducare delectabitur; et qui te pascit, ipse in te pascetur (Luc. XXII, 15, 19); et panis ipse quo plus editur, plus abundabit edendus: quia gratia non minuitur usu, sed augetur.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. This supper is not without bread, since he himself who sups is the bread of life, the bread which today came down from heaven and gives life to the world. But it is a wondrous thing, if he who sups is the same as that which is supped upon; and he who eats is himself the bread which is eaten by him. Indeed it is a wondrous thing, but a true thing; for Christ is fed by no other bread than himself. For he himself is wholly bread: the Word on his own account, the flesh on account of its union with the Word. Otherwise the flesh profits nothing, since it is the spirit that gives life (Joan. VI, 64); nor does man live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God (Matth. IV, 4). Every word proceeding from the mouth of God is the one and only-begotten Word of the Father, which, although it is simple, nevertheless contains within itself the reason and form of every divine word. The Word, therefore, is fed from the Word; the Son lives from himself; for as the Father has life in himself, so has he given to the Son also to have life in himself (Joan. V, 26). Yet in another respect — though still by an ineffable blessedness — that soul was fed by the Word, being joined to the Word itself in person; and with incomparable felicity that prince, sitting in the gate of the virginal womb, ate the bread of the Word before the Lord. This work, therefore, you too, if you are wise, will carry on in your silence: that you may eat the bread of the divine Word before the Lord, keeping, as Mary did, the things that are said of Christ, and pondering them in your heart. Christ will delight to eat this bread with you; and he who feeds you will himself be fed in you (Luc. XXII, 15, 19); and this very bread, the more it is eaten, the more it will abound to be eaten: because grace is not diminished by use, but increased.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 7. In hoc propterea tibi sit exemplo Jesus conceptus et gestatus in utero, ut, sicut onus illud leve ac suave, etsi gravidavit, non tamen gravavit uterum Mariae, sic te non sentiat gravem aut molestum uterus Ecclesiae. Gravida est, o fratres, Ecclesia, non, sicut Maria, solo Jesu, sed, sicut Rebecca, Jacob et Esau, non solum scilicet bonis et modestis, sed etiam dyscolis et indisciplinatis; quos tamen et ipsos, propter nomen Jesu, vel forsitan aliquod initium substantiae ejus, Ecclesiae viscera suscipiunt et amplectuntur. Sed cum sese colliderent parvuli discordes in utero Rebeccae, quae prius oraverat ut conciperet, dolensque ventrem suum a tribulatione malorum et dolore, pene poenitebat quod concepisset: Si sic, inquit, futurum mihi erat, quid necesse erat concipere? (Gen. XXV, 22.). Si de aliquo nostrum, fratres, sic conqueri contigerit viscera matris nostrae, timeo ne melius fuisset si conceptus non fuisset homo ille; nisi quod nec de talibus sinit nos desperare, qui etiam de lapidibus suscitat filios Abrahae (Luc. III, 8). Ipse in eis, si qui tales sunt, emolliat cor lapideum, ne quatiant viscera matris; ipse viscera matris consoletur, ne fatigetur eos, qualescunque sint, portare, donec formetur in eis Christus, qui perfectus Deus, perfectus homo vivit et regnat, per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 7. Let Jesus, therefore, conceived and carried in the womb, be an example to you in this: that just as that burden, light and sweet, though it filled Mary's womb with pregnancy, did not weigh it down, so may the womb of the Church not feel you to be heavy or troublesome. The Church, O brothers, is pregnant — not, like Mary, with Jesus alone, but, like Rebecca, with Jacob and Esau — that is, not only with the good and well-behaved, but also with the unruly and undisciplined; yet even these, for the sake of the name of Jesus, or perhaps some small beginning of his substance in them, the womb of the Church receives and embraces. But when the quarreling little ones struggled against each other in the womb of Rebecca — she who had earlier prayed that she might conceive — grieving in her womb over the trouble and pain caused by these evil ones, she almost regretted that she had conceived, saying: 'If it was going to be like this for me, what need was there to conceive?' (Gen. XXV, 22.). If it should happen, brothers, that the womb of our mother thus complains concerning any one of us, I fear it would have been better if that man had not been conceived — except that he who raises up children of Abraham even from stones (Luc. III, 8) does not allow us to despair even over such as these. May he himself soften the stony heart in them, if any such there be, lest they shake the womb of their mother; may he himself console the womb of the mother, lest she grow weary of carrying them, whatever they may be, until Christ be formed in them — who, perfect God, perfect man, lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The words on the Lord choosing his resting place come from Psalm 131:14 in historical numbering; the edition prints Psal. XXXI, 14.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: Gabriel's words that no word is impossible with God come from Luke 1:37; the edition prints Luc. I, 30, 31.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The call for the peoples to praise God and the words on the earth yielding its fruit come from Psalm 66:6-7 in historical numbering; the edition prints Psal. LXVI, 6.

sermons.title: Annunciation Sermon III

sermons.author: Guerric of Igny
metadata: Guerric of Igny, Sermones per annum, In die ascensionis Domini, Sermo, De amore Christi in nos et de nostro in ipsum, in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier freres, 1879), cols. 153-156.
Internet Archive, 2011; PIMS, University of Toronto; University of Toronto funding.
Matthew 24:28 and Luke 17:37 (combined printed locator; closing parenthesis absent)

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric of Igny applies Christ's prayer before the Passion to the Ascension, reading his departure through the love shown to his disciples. The Eucharist offers a new manner of remaining with and in them, while the washing of their feet teaches humility and forgiveness. Christ's prayer promises protection from evil, sanctification in truth and glory with him, without excusing negligence. Guerric urges his brothers to practise the daily struggle against vice: like young eagles learning to fly, they must lift their hearts after the ascended Christ. The sermon ends with contemplation, love and the liturgical exchange Lift up your hearts / We have them lifted to the Lord, directing desire toward Christ as heavenly treasure. The individual sermon is undated; its collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138-1157 and is read here from the 1879 Patrologia Latina edition. The source names the day of the Lord’s Ascension.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: IN DIE ASCENSIONIS DOMINI.

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON THE DAY OF THE LORD'S ASCENSION.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De amore Christi in nos et de nostro in ipsum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On Christ's love for us and our love for him.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Pater, cum essem cum eis, ego servabam eos in nomine tuo (Joan. xvii, 11, 12). Haec oratio Domini habita est ante diem passionis. Non absurde tamen aptatur diei Ascensionis, quando scilicet supremo discessurus erat a filiolis suis, quos Patri commendabat. Qui enim in coelis creavit, docet et regit multitudinem Angelorum, in terris aggregaverat sibi pusillum gregem discipulorum sub praesentia suae carnis erudiendum, quoadusque grandiusculi sensus effecti, disciplinae Spiritus fierent idonei. Magnus itaque parvulos magna dilectione diligebat, quippe quos ab more mundi abstraxerat, et relicta omni spe saeculi, de se solo pendere videbat. Quandiu tamen cum eis corporaliter conversari voluit, non facile aut multum hunc suum eis affectum prodidit; maturiorem se eis, quam teneriorem exhibens, sicut magistrum decebat et patrem. Cum autem tempus quo ab eis recessurus erat instaret, tunc veluti vinci tenero eorum affectu visus est, ut magnam multitudinem dulcedinis suae, quam eis absconderat, dissimulare non posset. Hinc illud est, quod cum dilexisset suos qui erant in mundo, in finem dilexit eos (Id. xiii, 1). Tunc enim propemodum omnem vim amoris effudit amicis, antequam etiam ipse sicut aqua effunderetur pro inimicis. Tunc eis sacramentum Corporis et Sanguinis sui tradidit, et celebrandum instituit, nescio virtute an charitate mirabiliori, hoc novum genus mansionis adinveniens in consolationem recessus sui, ut si discederet ab eis specie corporis, maneret non solum cum eis, sed etiam in eis virtute Sacramenti. Tunc veluti prorsus suae oblitus majestatis, et velut injuriam faciens sibi, nisi quia gloria est charitatis humiliare se pro amicis, dignatione ineffabili Dominus, et talis Dominus, pedes servorum lavit: uno opere condens eis et humilitatis exemplum, et remissionis sacramentum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Father, when I was with them, I kept them in your name (Joan. xvii, 11, 12). This prayer of the Lord was offered before the day of his Passion. Yet it is fittingly applied to the day of the Ascension, when he was about to leave his little children for the last time and was commending them to the Father. For he who in heaven created, teaches and rules the multitude of Angels had gathered for himself on earth a little flock of disciples, to be instructed in the presence of his flesh until their understanding had grown somewhat and they became fit for the teaching of the Spirit. Thus the great one loved the little ones with great love: he had drawn them away from the ways of the world and saw them depending on him alone, having abandoned every worldly hope. Yet as long as he chose to live bodily among them, he did not readily or fully reveal this affection of his to them, showing himself more reserved than tender, as befitted a teacher and father. But when the time was drawing near for him to depart from them, he seemed overcome by tender affection for them, so that he could no longer conceal the great abundance of his sweetness that he had hidden from them. Hence the saying that, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end (Id. xiii, 1). For then he poured out almost the whole force of his love upon his friends, before he himself was also poured out like water for his enemies. Then he handed on to them the sacrament of his Body and Blood and instituted its celebration, devising this new manner of remaining to console them for his departure, with power or charity more wonderful, I know not which. Thus, though he departed from them in bodily appearance, he would remain not only with them but also in them through the power of the Sacrament. Then, as though utterly forgetful of his own majesty and as though doing himself an indignity, except that it is the glory of charity to humble oneself for friends, the Lord, and such a Lord, with ineffable condescension washed his servants' feet, establishing for them in a single act both an example of humility and a sacrament of forgiveness.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Tunc denique post exhortationem prolixioris sermonis Patri eos commendans, sublevatis in coelum oculis, inter caetera sic ait, Pater, cum essem cum eis, ego servabam eos in nomine tuo, et nemo ex his periit, nisi filius perditionis. Nunc autem ad te venio: serva eos in nomine tuo quos dedisti mihi. Non rogo ut tollas eos de mundo, sed ut serves eos a malo; et caetera, quae non est hujus temporis retexere, multo minus exponere. Summa tamen orationis, sicut indicat textus lectionis, est in his tribus, in quibus est et summa salutis, imo et perfectionis, ut nihil possit addi, scilicet, ut a malo serventur, ut in veritate sanctificentur, ut cum ipso glorificentur. Pater, inquit, quos dedisti mihi, volo ut ubi sum ego, et ipsi sint mecum, ut videant claritatem meam (Joan. xvii, 11-13, 15, 24). O felices, quorum advocatus ipse judex est; pro quibus orat qui pari honore cum eo quem orat adorandus est! Voluntate labiorum ejus non fraudabit eum Pater, cum quo est ei una voluntas et una potestas, quia unus Deus est. Omnino quod Christus orat, impleri necesse est: cujus sermo virtus est, et voluntas effectus; qui de omnibus quae sunt, dixit, et facta sunt, mandavit, et creata sunt (Psal. xxxii, 9). Volo, inquit, ut ubi ego sum, et ipsi sint mecum. O quanta securitas fidelium! quanta fiducia credentium! tantum non abjiciant gratiam quam acceperunt. Non enim solis Apostolis proposita est haec securitas, vel condiscipulis eorum, sed omnibus qui per eorum verbum credituri sunt in Dei verbum. Non pro eis, inquit, rogo tantum, sed pro eis qui credituri sunt per verbum eorum in me (Joan. xvii, 24, 20).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Then, finally, after the exhortation of a lengthy discourse, commending them to the Father and lifting his eyes to heaven, he said among other things: Father, when I was with them, I kept them in your name, and none of them perished except the son of perdition. But now I come to you: keep in your name those whom you have given me. I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from evil; and the rest, which this is not the time to repeat, much less explain. Yet the substance of the prayer, as the text of the reading shows, lies in these three things, in which also lies the fullness of salvation, indeed of perfection, so that nothing can be added: that they be kept from evil, that they be sanctified in truth, and that they be glorified with him. Father, he says, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they too may be with me, so that they may see my glory (Joan. xvii, 11-13, 15, 24). O happy people, whose advocate is himself their judge, for whom he prays who is to be adored with equal honor alongside him to whom he prays! The Father will not deny him the desire of his lips: with the Father he has one will and one power, because they are one God. What Christ prays for must assuredly be fulfilled: his word is power, and his will is accomplishment. Concerning all things that exist, he spoke and they were made; he commanded and they were created (Psal. xxxii, 9). I will, he says, that where I am, they too may be with me. O how great the security of the faithful! How great the confidence of believers! Only let them not cast away the grace they have received. For this security is offered not to the Apostles alone or to their fellow disciples, but to all who through their word will believe in the Word of God. I pray, he says, not for them alone, but for those who through their word will believe in me (Joan. xvii, 24, 20).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Vobis autem fratres, donatum est, ut ait Apostolus, non solum ut in eum credatis, sed etiam ut patiamini pro eo (Philipp. i, 29): quos scilicet fides promissionis Christi, non securitate negligentiores, sed alacritate faciens ferventiores, et quotidiano vitiorum conflictu, martyrio coronat assiduos: assiduo, sed facili; facili, sed sublimi. Facile est, ubi supra virtutem nihil imperatur; sublime, ubi de omni virtute illius fortis armati triumphatur. An non facile suave Christi jugum portare? an non sublime in regno ejus excellere? Quid facilius, rogo, quam portare pennas quae portent portantem se? quid sublimius, quam supra omnem coelorum altitudinem, quo Christus ascendit, evolare? Plane sancti, quorum sicut aquilae juventus renovabitur, assument pennas sicut aquilae, et volabunt. Quo volabunt? Ubicunque, inquit, fuerit corpus, illuc congregabuntur et aquilae (Matth. xxiv, 28, et Luc. xvii, 37.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. But to you, brothers, it has been granted, as the Apostle says, not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him (Philipp. i, 29). Faith in Christ's promise makes you more fervent through eagerness rather than more negligent through security, and crowns you, steadfast in the daily struggle against vices, with martyrdom: continual, yet easy; easy, yet sublime. It is easy where nothing beyond one's strength is commanded; sublime where the whole power of that strong armed one is overcome. Is it not easy to bear Christ's sweet yoke? Is it not sublime to excel in his kingdom? What is easier, I ask, than to carry wings that carry their bearer? What is more sublime than to fly above the whole height of the heavens, where Christ has ascended? Surely the saints, whose youth will be renewed like the eagle's, will take wings like eagles and fly. Where will they fly? Wherever the body is, he says, there the eagles too will gather (Matth. xxiv, 28, et Luc. xvii, 37.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Sed quid putamus, fratres, quomodo tunc repente de terris ad coelos evolare poterit, qui nunc exercitio et usu quotidiano volitare non didicerit? Si quaeris quo doctore, quo duce, nunquid non Christus sicut aquila, provocabat hodie ad volandum pullos suos, quando super eos volitabat, cum scilicet videntibus illis elevaretur, diuque sequerentur oculis euntem in coelum? Poterat utique repente in ictu oculi, ex oculis eorum rapi, et ubi vellet, constitui. Sed plane, sicut aquila provocans ad volandum pullos suos, et super eos volitans (Deut. xxxii, 14), et corda sursum levare post se nitebatur amore sui, et corpora similiter posse sublevari pollicebatur exemplo corporis sui: sicut Apostolus ait, aeterni conscius mysterii, quia et nos bajulis nubibus rapiemur obviam Christo (I Thess. iv, 16) redeunti. Ipse quidem ascendit super Cherubim, et volavit super pennas ventorum (Psal. xvii, 11), id est supergressus est virtutes Angelorum: tuae tamen condescendens infirmitati, expandet alas suas, et assumet te, atque portabit in humeris suis, si modo pullus degener non existas, ut a terra levari, et aura puriore perfrui non extimescas.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. But what do we think, brothers? How will someone suddenly be able then to fly from earth to heaven if he has not now learned to fly through daily practice and exercise? If you ask who is the teacher and who the guide, did not Christ, like an eagle, encourage his young to fly today when he flew above them, that is, when he was lifted up before their eyes and they followed him with their gaze for a long time as he went into heaven? He could certainly have been snatched from their sight suddenly, in the blink of an eye, and set wherever he wished. But indeed, like an eagle encouraging its young to fly and flying above them (Deut. xxxii, 14), he strove to lift their hearts up after him through love of himself and promised, by the example of his own body, that their bodies too could be lifted up. As the Apostle says, privy to the eternal mystery, we too, with clouds bearing us, shall be caught up to meet Christ (I Thess. iv, 16) as he returns. He himself indeed ascended upon Cherubim and flew upon the wings of the winds (Psal. xvii, 11), that is, he surpassed the powers of the Angels. Yet, stooping to your weakness, he will spread his wings, take you up and carry you on his shoulders, provided that you are not a degenerate fledgling, afraid to be lifted from the earth and enjoy a purer air.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Alii volant contemplando, tu saltem amando. Paulus mente excedit, et ad tertium usque pervolat coelum (II Cor. xii, 2); Joannes ad id quod id principio erat Verbum: tu saltem humi degenerem non trahas animum, nec patiaris obrutum inertia in terra putrescere cor tuum; sed clamanti, « Sursum corda, » Pontifici magno (qui hodie introivit in Sancta, aeterna redemptione inventa, ubi et assistit vultui Dei interpellans pro nobis) responde fideliter, « Habemus ad Dominum. » Sed et si aliquando quaesivisti non quae sursum sunt, sed quae super terram; jam te ipsum increpa, et dic Domino cum propheta: Quid enim mihi est in coelo? et a te quid volui super terram? (Psal. lxxii, 25) Heu, quam misere errabam! tam magnum est illud in coelo mihi repositum, quod contemnebam; tam nihil hoc super terram, quod tantopere expetebam! Christus itaque thesaurus tuus ascendit in coelum: ibi sit et cor tuum. Inde ducis originem, ibi habes Patrem et haereditatem, inde exspectas Salvatorem. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Others fly by contemplation; you, at least, by love. Paul passes beyond himself in mind and flies as far as the third heaven (II Cor. xii, 2); John to that Word who was in the beginning. You, at least, must not drag a debased spirit along the ground or let your heart, buried in sloth, rot in the earth. Rather, to the great High Priest crying, 'Lift up your hearts' (who today entered the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption, where he also stands before the face of God, interceding for us), answer faithfully, 'We have them lifted to the Lord.' And if at times you have sought not the things above but the things on earth, now rebuke yourself and say to the Lord with the prophet: For what have I in heaven? And apart from you, what have I desired upon earth? (Psal. lxxii, 25) Alas, how wretchedly I was mistaken! So great is that which was laid up for me in heaven and which I despised; so utterly nothing is this upon earth which I sought so eagerly! Christ, then, your treasure, has ascended into heaven: let your heart be there too. From there you draw your origin; there you have your Father and inheritance; from there you await the Savior. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition titles this simply “Sermon,” without a number. Its ending is “the Savior. Amen.”

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition’s Bible references and historical Psalm numbering are retained. The combined Matthew 24:28 / Luke 17:37 reference has no closing parenthesis in print.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The Latin prints id principio where the context calls for in principio (“in the beginning”). The translation follows that sense. “Lift up your hearts” and “We have them lifted to the Lord” are the liturgical call and response.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: “From the ways of the world” translates ab more mundi, not “from love of the world.” Christ’s bodily departure is contrasted with his continuing sacramental presence in the disciples. The daily martyrdom described here is spiritual combat against vice, not bodily execution.

Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary
sermons.occasion_detail: Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: This first sermon for the Assumption of Blessed Mary belongs to Guerric of Igny's medieval liturgical collection, associated approximately with his abbacy in 1138-1157 and read here from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The individual delivery year is unknown. Beginning with an invitation from the Office of Virgins, Guerric presents Mary as mother both of Christ and, through him, of Christians, contrasting her with Eve and relating her to the Church. He develops the image of Mary as God's throne and ends with a prayer for her intercession. The Assumption is the source’s historical occasion.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: IN ASSUMPTIONE B. MARIAE.

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON THE ASSUMPTION OF BLESSED MARY.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Quod Maria duplici titulo sit mater, quodque recte dicatur thronus Dei.

passages.label: English
passages.text: That Mary is mother by a double title, and is rightly called the throne of God.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Veni, electa mea, et ponam in te thronum meum (11). Multi vocati, pauci vero electi. Beati quos elegisti, Domine; habitabunt in atriis tuis (Psal. lxiv, 5) : imo tu in eis habitabis, tu in eis regnabis, thronumque regni tui in eis collocabis. Sane omnium beatorum beatissima est Maria, quae de numero omnium electorum singulariter est electa et praeelecta : quoniam elegit eam Dominus, elegit eam in habitationem sibi, dicens, Hic requies mea in saeculum saeculi : hic habitabo quoniam elegi eam (Psal cxxxi, 14). Habitavit in ea novem mensibus, habitavit cum ea et sub ea annis pluribus. Habitans in ea replebat eam singulari gratia charismatum : habitans cum ea pascebat eam incomparabili piorum suavitate morum, et divinorum desiderabili sapientia sermonum. Nunc autem in ea et cum ea, sicut interminabili aevo, sic incomprehensibili modo habitans, satiat eam beatificantium gloria visionum; foris quidem glorificatae carnis formam exhibens, intus autem formam Verbi glorificantis imprimens. O Maria, non vocaberis, ait Dominus, ultra derelicta, et terra tua non vocabitur ultra desolata, ut quia virgo, ideo sis infecunda : sed vocaberis Voluntas mea, id est, dilectus Filius meus in ea, quia complacuit Domino in te, et terra tua inhabitabitur. Habitabit enim juvenis in virgine, et habitabit in te Filius tuus; imo, si magis placet, ut non recedamus a verbis Scripturae, habitabunt in te filii tui (Isa. lxii, 4, 5).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Come, my chosen one, and I will set my throne in you (11). Many are called, but few are chosen. Blessed are those whom you have chosen, Lord; they will dwell in your courts (Psal. lxiv, 5) : rather, you will dwell in them, you will reign in them, and you will establish the throne of your kingdom in them. Certainly Mary is the most blessed of all the blessed, singled out and chosen before all among the whole number of the elect : for the Lord has chosen her, chosen her as a dwelling for himself, saying, This is my rest for ever and ever : here I will dwell, for I have chosen her (Psal cxxxi, 14). He dwelt in her for nine months; he dwelt with her and under her for many years. Dwelling in her, he filled her with a unique grace of spiritual gifts : dwelling with her, he nourished her with the incomparable sweetness of his holy ways and the desirable wisdom of his divine words. But now, dwelling in her and with her both for an endless age and in an incomprehensible manner, he satisfies her with the glory of visions that make her blessed; outwardly displaying the form of his glorified flesh, and inwardly impressing the form of the Word who glorifies her. O Mary, the Lord says, you will no longer be called forsaken, nor will your land any longer be called desolate, as though being a virgin meant that you must be barren : instead you will be called My Will, that is, my beloved Son is in her, because the Lord has taken pleasure in you, and your land will be inhabited. For the young man will dwell in the virgin, and your Son will dwell in you; or rather, if you prefer, so that we do not depart from the words of Scripture, your sons will dwell in you (Isa. lxii, 4, 5).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Quid, haeretice, caput erigis? quid mysterium pietatis ad occasionem perfidiae rapis? Unum quidem genuit : qui sicut unicus est Patri in coelis, ita unicus est Matri in terris. Neque enim sicut tu impie blasphemas, alios postea filios genuit; sed intemeratum manet, sicut signaculum perpetuae virginitatis in matre, ita sacramentum catholicae unitatis in prole. Ipsa tamen unica virgo Mater, quae se Patris Unicum genuisse gloriatur, eumdem unicum suum in omnibus membris ejus amplectitur, omniumque in quibus Christum suum formatum agnoscit, vel formari cognoscit, matrem se vocari non confunditur. Eva vetus illa, non tam mater quam noverca, quae filiis ante propinavit praejudicium mortis, quam initium lucis. Dicta est quidem mater cunctorum viventium : sed inventa est verius interfectrix viventium, seu genitrix morientium; cum suum generare nihil aliud sit, quam mortem ingenerare (Gen. iii). Et quia illa non potuit fideliter interpretari nomen suum, ista implevit mysterium : quae et ipsa, sicut Ecclesia, cujus forma est, mater est omnium ad vitam renascentium. Mater siquidem est Vitae qua vivunt universi; quam dum ex se genuit, nimirum omnes ex ea victuri sunt, quodammodo regeneravit. Unus generabatur, sed nos omnes generabamur : quia videlicet secundum rationem seminis, quo regeneratio fit, jam tunc in illo omnes eramus. Sicut enim in Adam fuimus ab initio propter semen carnalis generationis; sic in Christo ante initium, propter semen spiritualis regenerationis.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Why do you raise your head, heretic? Why do you seize the mystery of godliness as an occasion for unbelief? She bore one Son : who, just as he is the Father's only Son in heaven, is also his Mother's only Son on earth. For she did not afterwards bear other sons, as you impiously blaspheme; rather, just as the seal of perpetual virginity remains inviolate in the mother, so does the mystery of Catholic unity in her offspring. Yet this unique virgin Mother, who glories in having borne the Father's Only-begotten, embraces that same only Son of hers in all his members, and is not ashamed to be called the mother of all in whom she recognizes her Christ already formed or knows him to be taking form. That Eve of old was less a mother than a stepmother, who gave her children the sentence of death to drink before they first saw the light. She was indeed called the mother of all the living : but she proved more truly the slayer of the living, or the mother of the dying; for her giving birth means nothing other than bringing death into being (Gen. iii). And because she could not faithfully express the meaning of her name, this other mother fulfilled the mystery : she too, like the Church of which she is the figure, is mother of all who are born again to life. For she is the Mother of the Life by which all live; and in giving birth to that Life from herself, she in a certain manner gave rebirth to all who would live by it. One was being born, but we were all being born : for, in respect of the seed through which rebirth takes place, we were all already in him then. Just as we were in Adam from the beginning through the seed of bodily generation, so we were in Christ before the beginning through the seed of spiritual regeneration.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Porro beata Mater illa Christi, quia se matrem Christianorum cognoscit ratione mysterii; cura quoque se matrem eis praestat et affectu pietatis. Neque enim duratur ad filios, quasi non sint sui, cujus viscera semel quidem foeta, sed nunquam effoeta, nunquam desinunt fructum parturire pietatis. Benedictus siquidem fructus ventris tui, gravidam te, o pia Mater, inexhausta pietate reliquit; ex te quidem semel nascens, sed in te semper manens et affluens, et in horto concluso castitatis fontem signatum charitatis semper abundare faciens; qui licet signatus sit, foras tamen derivatur, et in plateis aquae ejus nobis dividuntur. Licet namque fons charitatis, proprius Ecclesiae, incommunicabilis sit alienis, beneficium tamen ejus impertire gaudet etiam inimicis. Denique si servus Christi filiolos suos iterum atque iterum parturit cura atque desiderio pietatis, donec formetur in eis Christus (Galat. iv, 19); quanto magis ipsa Mater Christi? Et Paulus quidem genuit eos, verbum veritatis quo regenerati sunt praedicando : Maria autem longe divinius atque sanctius, Verbum ipsum generando. Laudo quidem in Paulo praedicationis mysterium, sed plus miror ac veneror in Maria generationis mysterium.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Moreover, because that blessed Mother of Christ knows that she is the mother of Christians by reason of the mystery, she also shows herself their mother by her care and loving devotion. She does not harden herself toward her children as though they were not her own : her womb, fruitful once but never exhausted, never ceases to bring forth the fruit of loving devotion. For the blessed fruit of your womb left you, O loving Mother, pregnant with inexhaustible devotion; born from you once, yet always remaining and overflowing in you, he makes the sealed fountain of charity abound continually within the enclosed garden of chastity. Although sealed, it is nevertheless channeled outward, and its waters are shared with us in the streets. For although the fountain of charity belongs to the Church and cannot be shared with those outside her, it gladly shares its benefit even with enemies. Indeed, if the servant of Christ labors in birth for his little children again and again, with devoted care and longing, until Christ is formed in them (Galat. iv, 19); how much more does the Mother of Christ herself? Paul indeed begot them by preaching the word of truth through which they were born again : but Mary did so in a far more divine and holy manner, by giving birth to the Word himself. I praise in Paul the mystery of preaching, but I admire and venerate still more in Mary the mystery of giving birth.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Vide autem si non et filii Matrem videntur agnoscere, dictante utique ipsis veluti quadam naturali pietate fidei, ut ad invocationem nominis ejus, primo vel maxime refugiant in omnibus necessitatibus et periculis, tanquam parvuli ad sinum matris. Unde nimirum de his filiis puto non absurde intelligi, quod per prophetam promissum est ei. Habitabant in te filii tui (Isai. lxii, 5); salvo duntaxat intellectu, quo de Ecclesia haec prophetia principaliter accipitur. Et nunc siquidem habitamus in adjutorio Matris Altissimi, in protectione ipsius commoramur, tanquam sub umbra alarum ejus : et postmodum in consortio gloriae ipsius, tanquam in sinu ipsius confovebimur. Tunc erit vox una laetantium et aggratulantium Matri : Sicut laetantium omnium nostrum habitatio est in te (Psal. lxxxvi, 7), sancta Dei Genitrix. Nullatenus autem credideris majoris esse felicitatis et gloriae, habitare in sinu Abrahae, quam in sinu Mariae, cum thronum suum in ea posuerit Rex gloriae.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. See, too, whether the children do not seem to recognize their Mother, prompted, as it were, by a certain natural devotion of faith to flee first or above all to the invocation of her name in every need and danger, like little children to their mother's bosom. Hence I think it is reasonable to understand of these children what was promised to her through the prophet. Your sons dwelt in you (Isai. lxii, 5); always preserving the interpretation according to which this prophecy is understood principally of the Church. Even now we dwell in the help of the Mother of the Most High; we remain under her protection, as though beneath the shadow of her wings : and afterwards, sharing her glory, we shall be cherished as though in her bosom. Then there will be one voice of those rejoicing with their Mother and congratulating her : The dwelling of all of us who rejoice is in you (Psal. lxxxvi, 7), holy Mother of God. Never believe that dwelling in Abraham's bosom is a greater happiness and glory than dwelling in Mary's bosom, since the King of glory has established his throne in her.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Veni, inquit, electa mea, et ponam in te thronum meum. Non poterat signantius aut elegantius describi praerogativa gloriae ejus, quam ut thronus Dei regnantis esse diceretur. Nulli siquidem animae tanta plenitudine aut familiaritate copiam sui divina majestas videtur indulgere, sicut illi in qua specialiter prae caeteris residere delegerit. Discipulis quidem Dominus loquebatur, qui pauperes facti pauperem sequebantur : In regeneratione, cum sederit Filius hominis in sede majestatis suae, sedebitis et vos super sedes (Matth. xix, 28). Alibi quoque promittit idem Agonotheta noster, de coelo spectans et incitans decertantes : Qui vicerit, inquit, dabo ei sedere mecum in throno meo, sicut et ego vici et sedi in throno Patris mei (Apoc. iii, 21). Matri vero, cujus longe differens est meritum, nihilominus differens promittit praemium. Veni, inquit, electa mea, et ponam in te thronum meum. Parum est, inquit, ut judicanti consedeas, nisi et ipsa mihi sedes fias : ut majestatem regnantis eo felicius quo familiarius in te contineas, et specialius prae caeteris incomprehensibilem comprehendas. Continuisti parvulum in gremio : continebis immensum in animo. Fuisti diversorium peregrinantis; eris palatium regnantis. Fuisti tabernaculum pugnaturi in mundo; eris solium triumphantis in coelo. Fuisti thalamus Sponsi incarnati; eris thronus Regis coronati.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Come, he says, my chosen one, and I will set my throne in you. The prerogative of her glory could not be described more expressively or beautifully than by calling her the throne of God who reigns. For the divine majesty seems to grant no soul such full or intimate possession of himself as the soul in which he has chosen to dwell especially above all others. The Lord indeed spoke to the disciples who had become poor and followed him in his poverty : In the regeneration, when the Son of man sits on the seat of his majesty, you too will sit upon seats (Matth. xix, 28). Elsewhere our same Master of the contest, watching from heaven and urging on those who struggle, promises : To him who conquers, he says, I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I too conquered and sat on the throne of my Father (Apoc. iii, 21). But to his Mother, whose merit is far different, he promises a reward no less different. Come, he says, my chosen one, and I will set my throne in you. It is little, he says, for you to sit beside me as I judge, unless you yourself become my seat : so that you may contain within yourself the majesty of him who reigns, the more blessedly for being the more intimately, and may embrace the incomprehensible more particularly than all others. You held the little child in your lap : you will hold the boundless one in your soul. You were the lodging of the traveler; you will be the palace of him who reigns. You were the tent of him who was to fight in the world; you will be the throne of him who triumphs in heaven. You were the bridal chamber of the incarnate Bridegroom; you will be the throne of the crowned King.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. O Fili Dei, nihil tibi, nihil in illo tuo displicuit hospitio quod tam libenter repetit, tamque affluenter remunerat tua dignatio. Nihil utique in illo sordidum offendisti, quia nulla erat libido, sed purissima castitas : nihil ruinosum, quia nulla erat superbia, sed fundatissima humilitas : nihil obscurum, quia exclusa infidelitas : nihil angustum, quia diffusa erat charitas. Adornaverat thalamum Virgo prudentissima, te regem Christum non solum hospitem susceptura; sed et sponsum habitura. Adornaverat, inquam, multiplici decore virtutum et gloria, tanto fortasse locupletius, quanto interius totum erat. Hunc ornatum mirabatur qui dicebat, Omnis gloria ejus filiae regis ab intus, in fimbriis aureis, circumamicta varietate (Psal. xliv, 14, 15) : et alius, O quam pulchra est casta generatio cum charitate ! (Sap. iv, 1.) Domum tuam decet Domine, hujusmodi sanctitudo et decor. Is decor te invitavit ut intrares : illexit, ut redires. Intrans benedictionis gratiam multiplicasti : sed rediens cumulasti. Cum intrasti, homo natus es in ea : cum redisti, Deus glorificatus es in ea. Tunc tibi posuisti in ea sacrarium gratiae; nunc autem, thronum gloriae.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. O Son of God, nothing displeased you, nothing in that lodging of yours which your graciousness so gladly revisits and so abundantly rewards. Certainly you found nothing defiled there, for there was no lust, but the purest chastity : nothing ruinous, for there was no pride, but humility most firmly founded : nothing dark, for unbelief was excluded : nothing cramped, for charity was poured abroad. The most prudent Virgin had adorned the bridal chamber, ready to receive you, Christ the King, as her guest, and also to have you as her bridegroom. She had adorned it, I say, with the manifold beauty and glory of virtues, perhaps all the more richly because it was wholly inward. He admired this adornment who said, All the glory of her, the king's daughter, is within, in golden fringes, clothed about with variety (Psal. xliv, 14, 15) : and another said, O how beautiful is a chaste generation with charity ! (Sap. iv, 1.) Such holiness and beauty befit your house, Lord. That beauty invited you to enter : it drew you to return. By entering you multiplied the grace of blessing : but by returning you heaped it up. When you entered, you were born in her as man : when you returned, you were glorified in her as God. Then you established in her a sanctuary of grace for yourself; but now, a throne of glory.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 7. Dicuntur quidem et sunt alii throni, quidam scilicet spiritus divini, prae aliis, ut putamus, subjectis ordinibus, Dei praesidentis majestate pleni : quorum quae sit praerogativa, Scriptura non exprimit, licet innuat ex vocabulo quod nonnulla sit. Sed et anima cujuslibet justi dicitur sedes sapientiae. Quae autem nunc es sedes sapientiae, profecto tunc erit et gloriae. Sit igitur illud coeli palatium plenum sedibus et thronis, sedeatque Deus in omnibus, accommodans se et aptans cuique pro meritis. Non immerito tamen creditur, sine injuria vel invidia caeterarum sedium quoddam esse speciale Regis solium excelsum et elevatum super gloriam omnium : Mariam dico exaltatam super choros Angelorum, ut nihil contempletur supra se Mater nisi Filium solum; nihil miretur supra se Regina nisi Regem solum; nihil veneretur supra se Mediatrix nostra nisi Mediatorem solum : cui nos ipsa precibus suis conciliet, commendet, et repraesentet unico Filio suo Jesu Christo, cui est honor et gloria in saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 7. There are indeed others who are called thrones and truly are thrones : certain divine spirits, filled with the majesty of God who presides, beyond the other subordinate orders, as we suppose. Scripture does not express what their prerogative is, although their name suggests that they have some prerogative. The soul of every just person is also called a seat of wisdom. But you who are now a seat of wisdom will assuredly then be a seat of glory as well. Let that heavenly palace, then, be full of seats and thrones, and let God sit in all, accommodating and adapting himself to each according to their merits. Yet it is reasonably believed, without wrong or envy toward the other seats, that there is one particular royal throne, lofty and raised above the glory of them all : I mean Mary exalted above the choirs of Angels, so that the Mother contemplates above herself only the Son; the Queen admires above herself only the King; our Mediatress venerates above herself only the Mediator. May she by her prayers reconcile us to him, commend us to him, and present us to her only Son Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: (11) In Offic. de Virginibus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: (11) In the Office of Virgins.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The damaged source footnote number reads (11); it is retained.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The sermon follows historical Psalm numbering. In Isaiah 62:5 it first reads “your sons will dwell” and later “your sons dwelt”; both forms follow the edition. Genesis 3 is cited without a verse.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: Mary’s motherhood and throne, the contrast with Eve, and the distinction between Mediatress and Mediator are Guerric’s own imagery. “Mystery of Catholic unity” translates sacramentum catholicae unitatis without imposing a later sacramental classification. “Master of the contest” renders agonotheta. In section 2 the translation follows the sense of a grammatically irregular Latin clause. In section 7 a damaged final letter may be the t of est (“is”); the Latin retains the visible es, while the English gives the contextual sense. The phrase about those rejoicing means “one voice of those rejoicing.”
