Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary
sermons.occasion_detail: Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric reads the bride's words, "tell my beloved that I languish with love," as Mary's on her deathbed. Using a licence he credits to Jerome, he imagines the angels visiting her: she has languished with fear and with sorrow, and now with love. She declines Gabriel's attendance, content with the disciple Jesus loved, and asks for the kiss of her Son's mouth, trusting that his glory has not changed his gentleness. The sermon appears under the heading for the Assumption of Blessed Mary in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO II.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON II.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De mutuo amore Jesu et Mariae.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the mutual love of Jesus and Mary.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Filiae Jerusalem, nuntiate dilecto quia amore langueo (Cantic. V, 8). Verba ista quae a nobis hac nocte cantata sunt, qualiter ad Assumptionem beatae Mariae possint videri pertinere, volumus, si placet, cum vestra charitate tractare. Id autem eo genere sermonis faciendum videtur, quo non modo saecularium, sed etiam ecclesiasticarum auctores litterarum nonnunquam usi sunt, maxime in tractandis Canticis, unde haec sunt sumpta. Hoc namque genus sermonis, salva veritate, quadam ampliori utitur libertate, cum videlicet sumpto themate causae, ut beatus Hieronymus ait, non tam loquitur quae revera facta vel dicta sint, quam ejusmodi fuisse negotium ostendit, ut ea quae dicuntur, etsi facta vel dicta non fuerint, fieri tamen et dici potuisse, aut etiam in affectu facientis, vel dicentis fuisse non absurde credi possint. Maria igitur migratura corpore decumbebat, ut est humana infirmitas. Porro filiae Jerusalem quae sursum est, id est angelicae Virtutes, scientes nimirum quia obsequiis Matris captanda est gratia Filii, visitabant satis officiose Dominam suam, Matrem Domini sui. Et fortasse aliquid hujusmodi primo post salutationis officia locuti sunt ei Angeli; sicut speciem humano vultui, ita sermonem humano nimirum conformantes affectui vel usui:

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I languish with love" (Cantic. V, 8). We wish, if it please you, to treat with your charity how these words, which have been sung by us this night, may be seen to pertain to the Assumption of blessed Mary. This must be done, it seems, in that kind of discourse which not only the authors of secular letters but also of ecclesiastical letters have sometimes employed, especially in treating the Canticle, from which these words are taken. For this kind of discourse, while preserving the truth, makes use of a certain ampler liberty, since, having taken up the theme of the matter, as blessed Jerome says, it does not so much speak of what was actually done or said, as show that the business was of such a kind that the things which are said, even if they were not done or said, could nevertheless have been done and said, or could even, not absurdly, be believed to have been in the affection of the one doing or speaking. Mary, therefore, about to depart in body, lay abed, as is human weakness. Moreover the daughters of the Jerusalem that is above, that is, the angelic Virtues, knowing well that favor with the Son is to be sought through attentions paid to the Mother, were visiting their Lady, the Mother of their Lord, with due dutifulness. And perhaps the Angels said something of this sort to her first, after the courtesies of greeting; conforming their appearance to a human countenance, and so their speech to human affection or custom:

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Quid est, obsecro, mi Domina, quod sic aegra videris et languida? quid est quod praeter solitum tristis et pigra, ab heri et nudiustertius, sicut solebas, non sancta revisis loca, quorum contemplatione amorem tuum pascebas? Jam per aliquot dies non vidimus te, aut rupem Calvariae ascendentem, ut ibi locum crucis impleres lacrymis; aut ad sepulcrum Filii adorantem gloriam resurrectionis, aut in monte Oliveti deosculantem extrema vestigia ascendentis. --Ob hoc ipsum siquidem creditur in valle Josaphat commorata (ubi et sepulchrum ejus monstratur, ut ait Beatus Hieronymus, in ecclesia miro lapideo fabricata tabulatu), ne scilicet a sanctis locis longius recederet, sed saepius ea invisens, licet omnia memoria teneret, formam tamen gestorum, velut corporaliter in ipsis effigiatam locis, dulcius amplecteretur, ut vel sic suum aliquatenus amorem solaretur.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. "What is it, I beg, my Lady, that you seem thus sick and languishing? What is it that, contrary to your custom, you have been sad and sluggish since yesterday and the day before, and have not, as you were wont, revisited the holy places, by contemplation of which you used to nourish your love? For some days now we have not seen you either ascending the rock of Calvary, there to fill the place of the cross with your tears; or adoring the glory of the resurrection at the Son's tomb; or on the Mount of Olives kissing the last footprints of him who ascended." --For this very reason indeed she is believed to have dwelt in the valley of Josaphat (where also her tomb is shown, as blessed Jerome says, in a church wondrously built with a stone roof), namely so that she might not withdraw too far from the holy places, but by visiting them more often, although she held everything in memory, might the more sweetly embrace the form of the deeds, as it were bodily figured in those very places, so that even thus she might in some measure console her love.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Causam itaque percunctantibus illis, cur ab his modo vacaret, et ex toto decumberet: Langueo, inquit. Quare langues? Languor enim quem locum in corpore tuo reperit, in quo salus mundi tam diu habitavit? De corpore Filii tui virtus exibat et sanabat omnes, adeo ut etiam fimbria vestimenti haemorrhoissam sanaret (Matth. IX, 20-22; Marc V, 25-34 et Luc. VIII.43-48): et tu quae tamdiu ipsum in utero, in sinu, in gremio continuisti, ulli infirmitati, aut languori vel accessibilis esse potuisti? Non est, inquit, quod id miremini, si illud ipsum corpus Filii mei, quale aliquando fuerit recordemini. Et ipsum enim quam infirmum, quantisve defectibus subditum fuerit, voluntate tamen, ego novi quae ipsum in utero alui, uberibus lactavi, sinu fovi: nec solius infantiae, sed et sequentium defectus aetatum vidi, et eis, ut potui, ministravi: ad extremum non sine passione mea, ludibria et supplicia passionis et crucis aspexi, per singula discens quam vere de eo noster Isaias dixerit, Vere languores nostros ipse tulit, et dolores nostros ipse portavit (Isai. LIII, 4; Matth. VIII, 17). Cur ergo doleam non eum meo dedisse corpori, quod suo non dedit? Non sum ita delicata aut superba, ut quod ille dignatus est pati, ego quantulacunque ex parte pati non possim aut nolim. Et ille quidem misericordi voluntate, ego naturali necessitate. Sane aliud est sanitas, aliud est sanctitas. Sanctitatem dedit corpori meo, concepti sui corporis sacramento: sanitatem se daturum promisit, suscitati corporis exemplo. Denique, ut minus miremini languorem meum, amore langueo. Langueo plus impatientia amoris, quam passione doloris: plus vulnerata charitate, quam gravata infirmitate.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. When, therefore, they inquired the cause of why she was now free from these things, and lying abed altogether, she said: "I languish." "Why do you languish? For what place has languor found in your body, in which the salvation of the world dwelt for so long? Power went forth from the body of your Son and healed all, so much so that even the hem of his garment healed the woman with the flow of blood (Matth. IX, 20-22; Marc V, 25-34 et Luc. VIII.43-48): and you, who for so long held him in your womb, in your bosom, in your lap, could you be accessible to any infirmity or languor?" "There is no need," she said, "for you to marvel at this, if you remember what that body of my Son was once like. For how weak it was, and to how many defects it was subject, by his own will, I know, who nourished him in the womb, suckled him at my breasts, cherished him in my lap: and I saw the defects not of infancy alone but of the ages that followed, and I ministered to him as I was able: and at the last, not without my own suffering, I beheld the mockeries and torments of the passion and the cross, learning from each thing how truly our Isaiah said of him, 'Surely he has borne our languors, and carried our sorrows' (Isai. LIII, 4; Matth. VIII, 17). Why then should I grieve that he did not give to my body what he did not give to his own? I am not so delicate or proud that I cannot or will not suffer, to whatever small degree, what he deigned to suffer. He indeed suffered by merciful will, I by natural necessity. Yet health is one thing, holiness another. He gave holiness to my body, by the sacrament of his own body conceived; health he promised he would give, by the example of his body raised up. In short, that you may marvel less at my languor, I languish with love. I languish more from the impatience of love than from the suffering of pain: more wounded by charity than weighed down by infirmity."

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Heu! inquiunt illi, quam frequentes, imo continuae causae languoris! Bone Jesu, quomodo haec Mater tua postquam te genuit, nunquam fere nisi in languore fuit? Primo languit timore; postea, dolore; nunc, amore. Timore, a nativitate usque ad passionem, cum semper vitam Filii insidiis appeti videret: dolore, toto tempore passionis, donec redivivum reciperet: nunc amore et desiderio felicius, sed mirabilius cruciatur, quia sedentem in coelo non tenet. Quomodo, Jesu bone, qui summi fructus es gaudii, tam longi factus es illi causa martyrii, ut charissimam tibi ipsius animam, tot et tam acuti sine cessatione pertranseant gladii? Sed obsecramus te, Domina, quid vis faciamus tibi? Vis saltem ut resideat hic iste Gabriel symmystes tuus, ut assideat et ministret tibi, qui ab initio conscius et minister mysterii tui, custos quoque tui cubiculi meruit deputari? Non opus est, inquit Virgo. Sufficit mihi meus novus in carne angelus, discipulum dico quem diligebat Jesus, cujus me dilectionis haeredem reliquit, cum illum mihi, et me illi in cruce commendavit: cujus obsequio nihil mihi gratius, quia conversatione et affectu nihil castius, moribus nihil suavius, nihil sincerius fide, nihil sanctius sermone. Nos ergo, aiunt illi, in quo tibi esse poterimus officiosi? Filiae, inquit, Jerusalem, nuntiate dilecto quia amore langueo. Ipse novit quomodo meo medendum sit languori.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. "Alas," they say, "how frequent — nay, how continual — are the causes of your languishing! Good Jesus, how is it that this Mother of yours, after she bore you, has scarcely ever been free from languor? First she languished with fear; afterward, with sorrow; now, with love. With fear, from the nativity even to the passion, since she always saw the life of her Son beset by snares; with sorrow, throughout the whole time of the passion, until she received him alive again; now she is tormented more happily, but more wondrously, by love and longing, since she does not hold him as he sits in heaven. How is it, good Jesus, that you, who are the fruit of highest joy, became for her the cause of so long a martyrdom, that so many and so sharp swords should pass, without ceasing, through that soul of hers so dear to you?" "But we beseech you, Lady, what do you wish us to do for you? Do you wish at least that this Gabriel, your companion in the mystery, remain here, to sit by you and minister to you — he who from the beginning was made privy to, and minister of, your mystery, and deserved also to be appointed guardian of your chamber?" "There is no need," says the Virgin. "My new angel in the flesh suffices me — I mean the disciple whom Jesus loved, whose heir in love he left me to be, when on the cross he commended him to me, and me to him: nothing is more pleasing to me than his service, since in conversation and affection nothing is more chaste, in manner nothing more gentle, in faith nothing more sincere, in speech nothing more holy." "What, then," they say, "can we do to be of service to you?" "Daughters of Jerusalem," she says, "tell the beloved that I languish with love. He himself knows how my languor must be healed."

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. At nosti, inquiunt, quia cum sciat omnia, de multis quasi nescius interrogat. Si ergo quaesierit, quid illud sit quod tuo vulneri velis adhiberi, quid respondebimus ei? Sodales, inquit, estis sponsi, Gabriel iste meus paranymphus: non puto vobis esse celandum amoris mysterium. Dicam igitur: tantum ne judicer temeraria, quod majora me quaerere videar. Osculetur me osculo oris sui. Si quid mihi conscia essem, contenta essem cum Maria Magdalene osculo pedum, ubi indulgentia sumitur delictorum. Sed quia in omni vita mea non me reprehendit cor meum, non puto me arroganter flagitare de osculo oris, gratiam gaudiorum. Cur autem arrogans videar, si illud os mihi reposco, quod de me sibi formavit ipse conditus et conditor? Cum parvulum tenebam inter brachia, quoties osculari speciosum forma prae filiis hominum mihi libebat, satis licebat: nunquam faciem avertebat, nunquam matrem repellebat. Et si fortassis impatientia desiderii eram nimia; ipse tamen more suo, morem matri gerebat. Gaudebat eam replere gratia, quae diffusa erat in labiis ejus, et dulcedine qua totus erat plenus, totus concupiscentia et desiderium, castarum scilicet animarum. Unde sicut ipse de se confitetur, Qui edunt me adhuc esurient, et qui bibunt me adhuc sitient (Eccli. XXIV, 29, et Joan. VI, 35): quanto gratiam oris illius gustavi suavius, tanto nimirum repeto nunc ardentius. Crevit quidem gloria et majestate: sed nihil ab illa ingenita mutatus est mansuetudine et bonitate. Nihil ad illum illud superbiae saecularis elogium: “Honores mutant mores.” Sublimior est, sed non superbior; gloriosior, sed non dedignantior. Non fastidiet matrem quam elegit, nec aeternam electionem suam novo judicio reprobabit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. "But you know," they say, "that although he knows all things, he asks about many things as though ignorant. If, then, he should ask what it is you wish applied to your wound, what shall we answer him?" "You are companions of the bridegroom," she says, "and this Gabriel of mine is his paranymph: I do not think the mystery of love should be hidden from you. I will tell it, then — only let me not be judged presumptuous for seeming to seek things greater than myself. Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. If I were conscious of any guilt in myself, I would be content, like Mary Magdalene, with the kiss of the feet, where pardon of sins is received. But because, throughout my whole life, my heart does not reproach me, I do not think that in demanding the kiss of the mouth I am arrogantly asking for the grace of joys. But why should I seem arrogant, if I ask back for myself that mouth which he, both the one fashioned and the fashioner, formed for himself out of me? When I held him as a little one between my arms, as often as it pleased me to kiss him who was beautiful in form above the sons of men, it was granted me freely enough: he never turned away his face, never repelled his mother. And if perhaps I was too impatient in my longing, he nevertheless, after his own manner, indulged his mother's way. He rejoiced to fill her with the grace that was poured out upon his lips, and with the sweetness of which he was wholly full — wholly the desire and longing, namely, of chaste souls. Whence, as he himself confesses of himself, 'They who eat me shall still hunger, and they who drink me shall still thirst' (Eccli. XXIV, 29, et Joan. VI, 35): the more sweetly I have tasted the grace of his mouth, the more ardently, surely, do I now seek it again. He has indeed grown in glory and majesty; but he has in no way been changed from that innate gentleness and goodness. To him applies nothing of that maxim of worldly pride: 'Honors change manners.' He is more exalted, but not more proud; more glorious, but not more disdainful. He will not disdain the mother whom he chose, nor by some new judgment reject his eternal election."

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text:
6.

Ne timeas, Maria, ait Gabriel more suo: invenisti enim gratiam apud Deum. Etiam in caeteris qui longe jacent tuis sub vestigiis, probare consuevit improbitatem hujus affectus et precis; qui nihil nimium, aut injuriosum sibi deputat, quod in eum vera duntaxat charitas praesumat. Et conversus ad sociam multitudinem: Eamus, inquit, eamus ne ipsi Filio facere videamur injuriam, si gloriam Matris differamus. Cum ergo reversi nuntiassent haec Domino suo, quid putamus Jesum nisi tale aliquid locutum? Ego sum qui patrem et matrem filiis honorandos commendavi; ego ut facerem quod docui, et exemplo essem aliis, ut Patrem honorarem, in terram descendi: nihilominus, ut Matrem honorarem, in coelum reascendi. Ascendi et praeparavi ei locum, thronum gloriae; ut a dextris Regis Regina coronata consedeat in vestitu deaurato, circumdata varietate. Neque hoc dico, quod in parte thronus ei collocetur: quin potius ipsa erit thronus meus. Veni igitur, electa mea, et ponam in te thronum meum. In te mihi quamdam regni sedem constituam, de te judicia decernam, per te preces exaudiam. Nullus mihi plus ministravit in humilitate mea. Communicasti mihi praeter alia quod homo sum: communicabo tibi quod Deus sum. Flagitabas osculum oris, quinimo tota de toto osculaberis. Non imprimam labia labiis, sed spiritum spiritui osculo perpetuo et indissolubili: quia concupivi speciem tuam, etiam desiderantius quam tu meam; nec satis glorificatus videbor mihi, donec tu conglorificeris. Gloria tibi, Domine Jesu, subintulit chorus Angelorum. Gloria tibi, Domine Jesu, ingeminet coetus fidelium. Glorificatio Matris tibi proficiat ad gloriam, nobis ad veniam; te praestante cui est honor, et gloria, per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text:
6.

"Do not fear, Mary," says Gabriel, in his accustomed way, "for you have found grace with God." Even in others who lie far beneath your footsteps, he is accustomed to show that this boldness of affection and petition is no fault; for he counts nothing excessive or injurious to himself which true charity alone presumes to ask of him. And turning to the company gathered with him, he said, "Let us go, let us go, lest we ourselves seem to do injury to the Son, if we delay the Mother's glory." When, then, they had returned and reported these things to their Lord, what do we suppose Jesus said but something like this? "I am he who commended fathers and mothers to be honored by their children; I, in order to do what I taught, and to be an example to others, that I might honor my Father, descended to earth; nonetheless, that I might honor my Mother, I ascended again to heaven. I have ascended and prepared a place for her, a throne of glory, that at the right hand of the King the Queen, crowned, may sit in gilded raiment, surrounded with manifold adornment. Nor do I say this as though a throne were set apart for her in some portion: rather, she herself shall be my throne. Come, then, my chosen one, and I will set my throne in you. In you I will establish for myself a certain seat of my kingdom; from you I will decree judgments; through you I will grant hearing to prayers. No one has ministered more to me in my humility. You shared with me, besides other things, that I am man: I will share with you that I am God. You were begging for the kiss of the mouth; nay rather, you shall be kissed wholly, by the whole of me. I will not press lip to lip, but spirit to spirit, in a perpetual and indissoluble kiss; for I have desired your beauty, even more longingly than you have desired mine; nor shall I seem to myself sufficiently glorified, until you are glorified together with me." "Glory to you, Lord Jesus," the choir of Angels added. "Glory to you, Lord Jesus," let the assembly of the faithful repeat again and again. May the glorification of the Mother avail for your glory, and for our pardon; through you granting it, to whom is honor and glory, for all ages of ages. Amen.

Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Preaching on a feast that gives the brothers rest from the harvest, Guerric takes the words "In all things I sought rest" as the voice of Wisdom, of the Church and of Mary, who finds rest today. Christ still seeks rest among the humble and quiet, while the restless are driven like a wheel. Guerric urges quiet through humility and manual work, and recalls Paul's rebuke of those who walk unquietly. The sermon appears under the heading for the Assumption of Blessed Mary in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO III.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON III.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De quiete spirituali.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On spiritual rest.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text:
1.

In omnibus requiem quaesivi (Eccli. XXIV, 11). Grata quies fessis. Grate igitur et opportune vobis, qui fessi estis, dies iste quietis et feriationis intervenit, ut dum sanctae Dei Genitricis requiem celebramus, non solum corpora recreentur hac diurna quiete a labore messis, sed etiam corda respirent in recordationem et amorem illius aeternae quietis. Et tibi tamen, o fratres, ibi etiam metetis, sed requiem metetis qui nunc laborem hujus messis seminatis. Fructus hujus laboris, illa requies erit: requies a labore, merces pro labore, cujus etiam recordatio fideles vires reparat in labore. Umbra est aestuantibus, cibus esurientibus. Sic enim ait illa, quae memoriam abundantiae suavitatis ejus eructabat: Sub umbra illius quem desideraveram sedi, et fructus ejus dulcis gutturi meo (Cantic. II, 5). O qui laboratis, o qui portatis pondus diei et aestus! sub umbra alarum Jesu invenietis requiem animabus vestris, firmamentum, ut scriptum est, virtutis, tegimen ardoris, umbraculum meridiani (Eccli. XXXIV, 19); ut ex sententia cordis sit illa confessio oris: Domine, Domine, virtus salutis meae, obumbrasti super caput meum in die belli (Psal. CXXXIX, 8), in die aestus et laboris, certaminis et tentationis. Cum enim meditatio aeternae requiei capitibus laborantium obumbrat, non solum ab aestu tentationum refrigerat, sed etiam ad laborem animos innovat, juxta illud quod scriptum est de asino forti Issachar, Vidit requiem quod esset bona, et terram quod optima, et supposuit humerum ad portandum (Gen. XLIX, 15): id est, desiderio illius quietis et haereditatis sponte humiliavit se ad laborandum. Et iste ergo dicere potuit: In omnibus requiem quaesivi, et in haereditate Domini morabor.

passages.label: English
passages.text:
1.

"In all things I sought rest" (Eccli. XXIV, 11). Rest is pleasant to the weary. Pleasantly, then, and opportunely for you who are weary, this day of rest and holiday has come, so that while we celebrate the rest of the holy Mother of God, not only may our bodies be refreshed by this day's rest from the labor of harvest, but our hearts too may breathe again in remembrance and love of that eternal rest. And yet for you, O brothers, there too you shall reap — but you who now sow the labor of this harvest shall reap rest. The fruit of this labor will be that rest: rest from labor, wages for labor — the very remembrance of which restores the faithful's strength in labor. It is shade for those who are scorched, food for those who hunger. For thus she speaks, who poured forth the memory of his abundant sweetness: "Under the shadow of him whom I desired I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat" (Cantic. II, 5). O you who labor, O you who bear the burden of the day and the heat! Under the shadow of Jesus' wings you will find rest for your souls — a stronghold of strength, as it is written, a covering from the heat, a shade from the noonday sun (Eccli. XXXIV, 19); so that from the conviction of the heart may come that confession of the mouth: "Lord, Lord, the strength of my salvation, you have overshadowed my head in the day of battle" (Psal. CXXXIX, 8), in the day of heat and labor, of struggle and temptation. For when meditation on eternal rest overshadows the heads of those who labor, it not only cools them from the heat of temptations but also renews their minds for labor, according to what is written of the strong ass Issachar: "He saw rest, that it was good, and the land, that it was excellent, and he bowed his shoulder to bear burdens" (Gen. XLIX, 15): that is, out of desire for that rest and inheritance, he willingly humbled himself to labor. And so he too could say: In all things I sought rest, and I will abide in the inheritance of the Lord.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text:
2.

Felix qui in omnibus laboribus et viis suis requiem quaerit beatam: semper festinans ingredi, ut Apostolus monet, in illam requiem (Hebr. IV, 3), ejus desiderio corpus affligens, animum autem jam illi requiei parans et componens: cum omnibus hominibus, quod ex ipso est, pacem habens; requiem et otium Mariae voluntate praeeligens, laborem autem et negotium Marthae necessitate quidem suscipiens; sed quanta praevalet pace et quiete spiritus adimplens, et semper ad illud unum necessarium de illa multiplici distractione sese recolligens. Homo hujusmodi etiam cum laborat, quiescit: sicut e diverso impius etiam cum quiescit, laborat. Quomodo enim quiescerent, quibus Deus immittit rotam malorum: quibus juravit in ira sua, Si introibunt in requiem meam? (Psal. XCIV, 12.) Extra illam non est nisi afflictio et miseria; et in circuitu ejus tempestas valida: sicut et in natura rerum fit, ut quidquid extra simplicitatem et unitatem puncti fuerit, in motu et agitatione sit; tantoque concitatiore quilibet circulus impetu rotetur, quanto ab immobilitate principii sui, id est, a medietate centri recesserit longius. Sane in circuitu impii ambulant (Psal. XI, 9), quibus Deus immittit rotam malorum: ideoque in illam internam et aeternam requiem intrare non possunt. Ideo contritio et infelicitas in viis eorum, quia viam pacis non cognoverunt (Psal. XIII, 3): quia nec quaesierunt, ut dicere possint: In omnibus requiem quaesivi; ut videlicet in multiplicitate actuum suorum, quibus turbantur, et turbant, unum quod est necessarium, cogitent aut requirant. Justorum potius est vox illa, qui et dicere possunt, Unam petii a Domino, hanc requiram. Vultum tuum, Domine, quaesivi, vultum tuum requiram (Psal. XXVI, 4, 8): qui nonnisi quietis illius amore laborant, qui omnino praeoptant ingredi putredinem in ossibus suis, ut requiescant in die tribulationis, quam in bonis ducere dies suos, et in puncto ad infernum descendere.

passages.label: English
passages.text:
2.

Happy is he who in all his labors and ways seeks blessed rest: always hastening, as the Apostle counsels, to enter into that rest (Hebr. IV, 3), afflicting his body with desire for it, yet already preparing and composing his mind for that rest; having peace with all men, so far as it depends on him; preferring by choice the rest and leisure of Mary, yet undertaking, by necessity indeed, the labor and business of Martha — but carrying it out with as much peace and quiet of spirit as he can, and always gathering himself back, out of that manifold distraction, to that one thing which is necessary. Such a man, even when he labors, rests; just as, on the contrary, the wicked man, even when he rests, labors. For how could they rest, upon whom God sends the wheel of evils, to whom he swore in his wrath, "If they shall enter into my rest" (Psal. XCIV, 12.)? Outside that rest there is nothing but affliction and misery; and round about it a violent storm — just as happens also in the nature of things, that whatever is outside the simplicity and unity of the point is in motion and agitation; and the farther any circle recedes from the immobility of its origin, that is, from the center-point, the more violent is the impetus with which it is driven round. Indeed, the wicked walk round about (Psal. XI, 9), upon whom God sends the wheel of evils: and therefore they cannot enter into that inward and eternal rest. Therefore ruin and unhappiness are in their ways, because they have not known the way of peace (Psal. XIII, 3): because they have not even sought it, so that they might say, In all things I sought rest — that is, so that amid the multiplicity of their actions, by which they are disturbed and by which they disturb others, they might think of or seek that one thing which is necessary. Rather that voice belongs to the just, who can also say, "One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek. Your face, Lord, have I sought; your face will I seek" (Psal. XXVI, 4, 8): who labor only out of love of that rest — who altogether prefer that rottenness enter into their bones, that they may rest in the day of tribulation, rather than spend their days in good things and in a moment go down to hell.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Si quis tamen curiosius inquirere velit, cujus potissimum vox illa sit, In omnibus requiem quaesivi: vox est utique Sapientiae, vox est Ecclesiae, vox est Mariae, vox est cujuslibet sapientis animae. Sapientia in omnibus requiem quaesivit, sed in solis humilibus invenit. Ecclesia in omnibus mundi nationibus requiem quaesivit, sed in solis credentibus invenit. Maria, sicut et quaelibet fidelis anima, in omnibus actionibus suis requiem quaesivit; sed hodie demum invenit, cum post persecutionem Herodis, et fugam Aegypti, post tot insidias et atrocitates Judaicae impietatis, post tot passiones suas, de passione et morte Filii; postquam tot et tam acerbi ipsius animam pertransierunt gladii, tandem hodie dicere datum est ei: Convertere, anima, in requiem tuam, quia Dominus benefecit tibi (Psal. CXIV, 7). Qui creavit me, creatus ex me, requievit in tabernaculo corporis mei, negare non poterit mihi requiem coeli sui. Qui enim gratiam ultro cumulat aliis, par pari quomodo non referet matri? Perge, Maria, perge secura in bonis Filii tui; fiducialiter age tanquam regina, mater Regis et sponsa. Requiem quaerebas, sed amplioris gloriae est, quod tibi debetur, regnum et potestas. Indivisum habere tecum cupit imperium, cui tecum in carne una, et uno spiritu indivisum fuit pietatis et unitatis mysterium: dum scilicet salvo honore naturae, geminato munere gratiae, juncta est mater in matrimonium. Requiesce igitur, o felix, inter brachia Sponsi. Replicabit tibi, ni fallor, inter amplexus et oscula, quam suaviter requieverit in tabernaculo corporis tui, quam suavis in cubiculo cordis tui. Non est injustus Deus, o fratres, ut obliviscatur operis boni: vivit semper apud eum memoria beneficii semel accepti. Beatus, apud quem Deus vel semel requiem invenerit, in cujus tabernaculo vel hora una requieverit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Yet if anyone wishes to inquire more carefully whose voice above all this is, "In all things I sought rest": it is indeed the voice of Wisdom, the voice of the Church, the voice of Mary, the voice of any wise soul. Wisdom sought rest in all things, but found it only in the humble. The Church sought rest among all the nations of the world, but found it only among believers. Mary, like any faithful soul, sought rest in all her actions; but only today has she finally found it, when, after the persecution of Herod, and the flight into Egypt, after so many plots and atrocities of Jewish impiety, after so many sufferings of her own concerning the passion and death of her Son—after so many bitter swords had pierced her soul—it was at last granted to her today to say: "Return, O my soul, into thy rest, for the Lord hath been bountiful to thee" (Psal. CXIV, 7). He who created me, having been created from me, rested in the tabernacle of my body; he cannot deny me the rest of his heaven. For he who freely heaps grace upon others—how will he not repay his mother in like measure? Go forward, Mary, go forward secure in the goods of your Son; act with confidence as a queen, mother of the King and his spouse. You were seeking rest, but what is owed to you is of a greater glory—kingdom and power. He desires to have undivided rule with you, he with whom you had, in one flesh and one spirit, an undivided mystery of devotion and unity: since, with the honor of nature preserved, and the gift of grace doubled, the mother was joined to him in marriage. Rest, then, O blessed one, between the arms of the Bridegroom. He will tell you, unless I am mistaken, amid embraces and kisses, how sweetly he rested in the tabernacle of your body, how sweet he was in the chamber of your heart. God is not unjust, O brothers, that he should forget a good work: the memory of a benefit once received lives always with him. Blessed is he with whom God has found rest even once, in whose tabernacle he has rested even for a single hour.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Ecce nunc quoque Sapientia clamitat in plateis: in omnibus requiem quaesivi. Pulsavi, nec fuit qui aperiret: vocavi, nec fuit qui responderet. Filius hominis, factus, secundum prophetam, velut vir vagus, et quasi viator declinans ad manendum (Jerem. XIV, 9, 8), non habet ubi reclinet caput suum: foris stat plenus caput rore, et cincinnos guttis noctium. Quis ille in nobis tam humanus atque hospitalis, ut surgat et aperiat ei, et inducat in cubiculum suum; aut certe ostendat ei coenaculum grande stratum, ubi cum discipulis pascha manducet novum? Hoc enim dico, fratres, nisi requiem quam quaerit, invenerit apud nos, nec nos optatam requiem inveniemus in illo. Ait quidem Dominus per prophetam: Haec est requies mea, reficite lassum, et hoc est meum refrigerium (Isa. XXVIII, 12). Beatus qui intelligit super egenum et pauperem: in die mala (Psal. XL, 2) parabit ei Dominus vicissitudine debita requiem et refrigerium. Si ergo humanitatem membris suis exhibitam Deus imputat sibi: quanto magis quod ipsius fit spiritui, cum gratiarum actione recolet, Hospes, inquiens, fui et suscepistis me? (Matth. XXV, 35.) Nunquid enim multorum paupertas sanctorum, quae vagos colligere, esurientes pascere non sufficit, Domino qui magis apud pauperes hospitari consuevit, inhumana et inhospitalis erit? Super quem autem requiescam, inquit, nisi super humilem et quietum, et trementem verba mea? (Isai. LXVI, 2.) O humilitas angusta tibi, ampla divinitati; pauper et insufficiens tibi, sufficiens ei quem non capit orbis: copiose ac deliciose reficiens illum, qui et Angelos pascit. Super quem, inquit, requiescam nisi super humilem? In omnibus requiem quaesivi: sed apud humilem ancillam inveni. Non est inventa similis illi in gratia humilitatis: ideo in plenitudine humilitatis requievit etiam corporaliter omnis plenitudo divinitatis. Quanquam aliter requieverit in Filio: quia etsi Mater humillima, longe tamen Filius humilior. Idcirco Spiritus septiformis non solum super ipsum requievit, sed etiam omnibus qui mites et humiles ab eo esse didicerunt, diversas in eo felicissimae quietis mansiones praeparavit; imo totum ipsum quoddam aureum fecit reclinatorium ad quiescendum. Hujus nimirum reclinatorii beatissimam requiem visus est quadam specie praelibasse, qui supra pectus ejus meruit in coena recumbere.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Behold, even now Wisdom cries aloud in the streets: "In all things I sought rest." I knocked, and there was none to open; I called, and there was none to answer. The Son of man, made, according to the prophet, like a wandering man, and like a traveler turning aside to lodge (Jerem. XIV, 9, 8), has nowhere to lay his head: he stands outside, his head full of dew, and his locks with the drops of the night. Who among us is so humane and hospitable as to rise and open to him, and bring him into his chamber; or at least show him a large furnished upper room, where he may eat the new Passover with his disciples? For I say this, brothers: unless he finds among us the rest he seeks, neither shall we find in him the rest we desire. The Lord indeed says through the prophet: "This is my rest, refresh the weary, and this is my refreshment" (Isa. XXVIII, 12). Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor: in the evil day (Psal. XL, 2) the Lord will prepare for him, in due return, rest and refreshment. If then God counts as done to himself the kindness shown to his members: how much more will he, giving thanks, recall what was done to his own spirit, saying, "I was a stranger, and you took me in" (Matth. XXV, 35.)? For shall the poverty of many saints, which does not suffice to gather in the wandering or feed the hungry, be inhospitable and inhumane to the Lord, who is accustomed rather to lodge among the poor? "But upon whom shall I rest," he says, "but upon him that is humble and quiet, and trembleth at my words?" (Isai. LXVI, 2.) O humility, narrow to yourself, but spacious to divinity; poor and insufficient in yourself, yet sufficient for him whom the world cannot contain: abundantly and delightfully refreshing him who feeds even the Angels. "Upon whom," he says, "shall I rest but upon the humble?" "In all things I sought rest": but I found it with a humble handmaid. None was found like her in the grace of humility: therefore in the fullness of her humility the whole fullness of divinity rested even bodily. Though it rested differently in the Son: for although the Mother was most humble, the Son was far more humble still. For this reason the sevenfold Spirit not only rested upon him, but also prepared various dwellings of most blessed rest in him for all who learned from him to be meek and humble; indeed, he made him wholly a kind of golden resting-place for repose. The most blessed rest of this resting-place he who deserved to recline upon his breast at the supper seemed, in some fashion, to have tasted beforehand.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Sed adhuc libet intueri, quam plenum rationis et congruentiae sit quod ait: Super quem requiescam nisi super humilem et quietum? Quomodo namque super inquietum aliquid quiesceret? quomodo super basem, quae nutaret aut vacillaret, columna immobilis staret? Quis autem, nisi humilis, quietus esse potest? quis, nisi humilis in pace quieti et modesti spiritus, seipsum possidere potest? Impium projicit ventus a facie terrae (Psal. I, 4), circumferturque omni vento doctrinae. Impius, inquit propheta, quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest (Isai. LVII, 20). Fervet ira, aestuat avaritia, intumescit superbia, se ipsum jugiter pugna quatit intestina, ac seditione collidit domestica. Ut ergo requiescat in vobis, o fratres mei, amator ille largitorque quietis, date operam, juxta consilium Apostoli, ut quieti sitis. Quonam modo istud erit? Dico, inquit, vobis: Ut vestrum negotium agatis, et operemini manibus vestris (I Thess. IV, 11). Opus est onus, quo veluti pondus navibus, ita quies et gravitas inquietis additur cordibus, sed exterioris hominis fundatur atque componitur status. Magnorum initium malorum est, sicut legistis, mulier vaga, quietis impatiens, nec valens consistere in domo pedibus suis: nunc foris, nunc in plateis, nunc juxta angulos insidians (Prov. VII, 10-12). Nec sine causa est quod Magister gentium hoc inquietudinis malum sic habet suspectum, ut non solum correptione, sed etiam separatione censeat illud persequendum. Rogamus, inquit, vos, fratres, corripite inquietos (I Thess. V, 14). Et item in secunda ad eosdem Thessalonicenses, inter alia quae super inquietos velut e coelis tonabat: Audivimus, inquit, inter vos quosdam ambulantes inquiete, nihil operantes, sed curiose agentes. Hic qui ejusmodi sunt denuntiamus, ut cum silentio operantes, suum panem manducent. Quod si quis non obedit verbo nostro per epistolam, hunc notate: et ne commisceamini cum illo, ut confundatur (II Thess. III, 11, 12, 14).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. But it is still worth considering how full of reason and fittingness is what he says: Upon whom shall I rest, but upon him that is humble and quiet? For how could he rest upon something unquiet? How could an immovable column stand upon a base that trembled or wobbled? Who, indeed, except the humble, can be quiet? Who, except the humble man at peace, of a quiet and modest spirit, can possess himself? The wind casts away the wicked from the face of the earth (Psal. I, 4), and he is carried about by every wind of doctrine. The wicked man, says the prophet, is like the raging sea, which cannot rest (Isai. LVII, 20). He burns with anger, seethes with avarice, swells with pride, perpetually shakes himself with inward battle, and collides in domestic sedition. Therefore, my brothers, that he who loves and bestows rest may rest in you, strive, according to the counsel of the Apostle, to be quiet. How shall this be? I say to you, he says: that you do your own business, and work with your own hands (I Thess. IV, 11). Work is a burden, by which, just as weight is added to ships, so quiet and gravity are added to unquiet hearts, and the condition of the outer man is founded and composed. The beginning of great evils is, as you have read, a wandering woman, impatient of rest, unable to abide with her feet in her own house: now abroad, now in the streets, now lying in wait near the corners (Prov. VII, 10-12). It is not without cause that the Teacher of the Gentiles holds this evil of restlessness in such suspicion that he thinks it should be pursued not only by rebuke but even by separation. We beseech you, brothers, he says, rebuke the unquiet (I Thess. V, 14). And again in the second epistle to the same Thessalonians, among other things which he thundered down as from heaven against the unquiet: We have heard, he says, that there are some among you who walk unquietly, doing no work, but being busy about other men's business. Now them that are such, we charge, that working with silence, they eat their own bread. And if any man obey not our word by this epistle, note that man: and do not keep company with him, that he may be ashamed (II Thess. III, 11, 12, 14).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Si quis forte (quod absit!) ejusmodi invenitur inter vos, pulchrius et honestius, antequam tam graviter et publice notetur, ultro confundetur, inde scilicet, quia notabilis est, et dissimulatur; reprehensibilis, et toleratur. Sic autem confundatur, ut confusione corrigatur, correptione laetetur, laetificetque non modo nos, sed Spiritum Dei: qui cum dicat, In omnibus requiem quaesivi, non invenit eam nisi in quietis, nec praestat nisi quietis. Unde et inquietos per prophetam revocat et compescit: Si revertamini, et quiescatis, salvi eritis (Isai. XXX, 15). Omnes ergo pariter sic operam demus, ut quieti simus, ut in quiete nostra semper in meditatione aeternae quietis occupemur, ac desiderio illius ad omnem parati laborem inveniamur. Hoc nobis impetret beata Dei Genitrix, cujus requiem celebramus, ab eo qui requievit in tabernaculo corporis et cordis ejus. Ipse est requies aeterna Christus Jesus; cui est honor, et gloria per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. If perhaps (which God forbid!) someone of this sort is found among you, it would be fairer and more decent that, before he is so gravely and publicly noted, he should be shamed of his own accord beforehand—precisely because he is notable, and yet is overlooked; reprehensible, and yet is tolerated. But let him be so shamed that by shame he may be corrected, that he may rejoice in correction, and may give joy not only to us but to the Spirit of God: who, since he says, In all things I sought rest, finds it only in the quiet, and grants it only to the quiet. Hence through the prophet he recalls and restrains the unquiet: If you return and be quiet, you shall be saved (Isai. XXX, 15). Let us all, then, equally take care to be quiet, so that in our quiet we may always be occupied in meditation on eternal rest, and may be found ready, by desire of that rest, for every labor. May the blessed Mother of God, whose rest we celebrate, obtain this for us from him who rested in the tabernacle of her body and heart. He himself is eternal rest, Christ Jesus; to whom be honor and glory for all ages of ages. Amen.

Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary
sermons.occasion_detail: Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric applies "Mary has chosen the best part" to the Mother of the Lord, who served Christ as Martha did and listened as her sister did. He explains why Christ seemed to set his mother aside, and why he entrusted her to the virgin disciple John. Contemplation is the reward of faithful labor, as Leah came before Rachel, and Mary now reaps what she sowed. The sermon appears under the heading for the Assumption of Blessed Mary in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO IV

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON IV

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Quod beata Virgo Mariae et Marthae officia implevit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: That the Blessed Virgin fulfilled the offices of Mary and of Martha.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Maria optimam partem elegit (Luc. X, 42). Hoc de Maria sorore Marthae scriptum est: sed in Maria matre Domini plenius et sanctius impletum est. Hodie namque beata virgo Maria optimam partem elegit, imo quam dudum elegerat, hodie perpetuo possidendam accepit: ut scilicet inseparabiliter adhaereat Domino, perenniter fruatur Dei Verbo. Nec alienum aut incongruum, si quod de illa Maria dictum est, in istam transumatur; cum ad convenientiam transformationis, similitudo non solum nominis, sed etiam operis suffragetur. Illa siquidem Dominum hospitio tecti, haec thalamo suscepit uteri. Et qui creavit me, inquit, requievit in tabernaculo meo (Eccli. XXIV, 12). Illa sedens secus pedes Domini audiebat verbum illius (Luc. X, 39): haec sedula circa curam humanitatis ejus, conservabat omnia verba quae de illo erant, conferens in corde suo (Eccli. II, 19, 51). Sed et cum evangelizans circumiret Jesus civitates et castella, Maria comes individua vestigiis ejus adhaerebat, pendebatque ex ore docentis: adeo, ut nec procella persecutionis, nec horrore supplicii a consectatu Filii et Magistri potuerit absterreri, Stabat, inquit, juxta crucem Jesu Maria mater ejus (Joan. XIX, 25). Plane Mater, quae nec in terrore mortis filium deserebat. Quomodo enim morte terreri poterat, cujus charitas fortis ut mors, imo fortior quam mors erat? Plane juxta crucem Jesu stabat, cujus mentem dolor crucis simul cruci figebat, suamque ipsius animam tam multiplex pertransibat gladius, quantis confossum corpus Filii cernebat vulneribus. Merito igitur ibi mater agnita est, et cura ipsius idoneo tutori delegata est, ubi maxime probata est et Matris ad Filium sincera charitas, et Filii de Matre vera humanitas. Nam alias velut dissimulasse Matrem visus est: sive cum in nuptiis flagitanti miraculum ait, Quid mihi et tibi, mulier? (Joan. II, 4.) sive cum in mediis sermonibus Evangelii dicenti cuidam, Ecce mater tua et fratres tui stant quaerentes te: Quae est, inquit, mater mea? (Matth. XII, 47, 48.) Sed et Matri, cum miraculum posceret, sic respondendum erat, ut aliunde quam a Matre se miracula habere significaret: et illi qui sermonem Evangelii parentes annuntiando interrumpebat, melius respondere non poterat, ut videlicet spiritualia carnalibus praeferenda monstraret. Ac si more suo diceret parentibus, occupatum in negotio Evangelii quaerentibus: Quid est quod me quaeritis? Nescitis quia in his quae Patris mei sunt oportet me esse? (Luc. II, 49.)

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Mary has chosen the best part (Luc. X, 42). This was written of Mary the sister of Martha; but it was fulfilled more fully and more holily in Mary the Mother of the Lord. For today the blessed Virgin Mary has chosen the best part—or rather, the part which she had long ago chosen, she today received to possess forever: namely, that she might cling inseparably to the Lord, and enjoy the Word of God perpetually. Nor is it foreign or unfitting that what was said of that other Mary should be transferred to this one; since, for the fittingness of the transfer, the likeness supports it not only in name but also in deed. For the one received the Lord under the hospitality of a roof; this one, in the bridal chamber of her womb. And 'He who created me,' she says, 'rested in my tabernacle' (Eccli. XXIV, 12). The one, sitting beside the Lord's feet, was listening to his word (Luc. X, 39); this one, diligently occupied with the care of his humanity, kept all the words concerning him, pondering them in her heart (Eccli. II, 19, 51). But also, when Jesus went about preaching the gospel through the cities and towns, Mary, an inseparable companion, clung to his footsteps, and hung upon the mouth of the teacher: so much so that neither the storm of persecution nor the horror of the punishment could frighten her away from following her Son and Master. 'There stood,' it says, 'by the cross of Jesus, Mary his mother' (Joan. XIX, 25). Truly a Mother, who did not abandon her son even in the terror of death. For how could she be terrified by death, whose love was strong as death—indeed, stronger than death? Truly she stood beside the cross of Jesus, whose mind the sorrow of the cross fixed to the cross at the same time, and through her own soul there passed a sword as manifold as the wounds with which she saw the body of her Son pierced. Deservedly, then, she was there acknowledged as mother, and the care of her was entrusted to a fitting guardian, at the very place where both the Mother's sincere love for her Son and the Son's true humanity toward his Mother were most fully proven. For elsewhere he seemed, as it were, to disregard his Mother: whether when, at the wedding, as she urged him to a miracle, he said, 'Woman, what is that to me and to you?' (Joan. II, 4.); or when, in the midst of the discourses of the Gospel, to one who said, 'Behold, your mother and your brothers stand seeking you,' he said, 'Who is my mother?' (Matth. XII, 47, 48.). But to his Mother, when she was asking for a miracle, he had to answer in such a way as to show that he had his miracles from some source other than his Mother; and to the one who was interrupting the discourse of the Gospel by announcing his kinsfolk, he could not have answered better, in order to show that spiritual things are to be preferred to carnal ones. As if, according to his custom, he were saying to his parents, who sought him while he was occupied in the business of the Gospel: 'Why is it that you seek me? Did you not know that I must be about those things which are my Father's?' (Luc. II, 49.).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Absit enim ut Matrem aspernatus sit, qui tanta cura de parentibus honorandis legem dedit! Absit, inquam, ut in terra fastidierit Matrem, cujus e coelo concupivit decorem! Imo potius ordinabat in nobis charitatem, tam verbis quam exemplis nobiscum agens, ut carnalium affectibus necessitudinum, non solum Dei praeponamus dilectionem, sed etiam eorum qui Dei faciunt voluntatem. Ille siquidem affectus de cordibus exigitur omnium nostrum, quos summi Patris adoptavit dignatio, quo fideliter dicamus cum ipsius Unigenito: Quicunque fecerit voluntatem Patris mei qui in coelis est, ipse meus frater, et soror, et mater est (Matth. XII, 49). Prorsus filiis Dei competit vox ista, nec ullum fidelius testimonium reddit ipse Spiritus spiritui nostro quod simus filii Dei, quam ut sonet de cordibus nostris haec vox Unigeniti Dei. Itaque Mariam, quae secundum carnem mater erat, alia quoque ratione matrem sibi Jesus probat: quandoquidem et ipsa voluntatem Patris in tantum faciebat, ut de ipsa praediceret Pater, Vocaberis voluntas mea in ea (Isai. LXII, 4). Igitur ubi eam visus est ignorasse Filius, ibi amplius honorasse invenitur: cum ei scilicet materni nominis honor duplicatur, pro eo quod eumdem Filium, quem alvo gestaverat incarnatum, etiam nunc animo gestabat inspiratum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Far be it that he should have scorned his Mother, he who gave the law with such care concerning the honoring of parents! Far be it, I say, that he should have disdained on earth the Mother whose beauty he had desired from heaven! Rather, he was ordering love within us, acting with us both by words and by examples, so that we might set the love of God—and also the love of those who do the will of God—above the affections of carnal ties. For that affection is demanded of the hearts of all of us whom the condescension of the most high Father has adopted, so that we may faithfully say with his Only-Begotten: 'Whoever shall do the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother' (Matth. XII, 49). This utterance indeed belongs to the children of God, nor does the Spirit himself give any more faithful testimony to our spirit that we are children of God, than when this utterance of the Only-Begotten of God resounds from our hearts. And so Jesus proves Mary, who was his mother according to the flesh, to be his mother also by another title: since she herself did the will of the Father to such a degree that the Father foretold concerning her, 'You shall be called my will in her' (Isai. LXII, 4). Therefore, where the Son seemed to have disregarded her, there he is found to have honored her the more: since for her the honor of the maternal name is doubled, in that the same Son whom she had carried incarnate in her womb, she even now carried in her soul by inspiration.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Caeterum cum dilexisset eam Jesus, in finem dilexit eam, ut non solum propter ipsam finem vivendi, verum et in ipsam finem pene faceret loquendi: dum velut inter ultima verba testamenti, curam Matris, cujus debitorem se cognoscebat, charissimo transcribit haeredi. Sic quippe inter Petrum qui plus diligebat, et Joannem qui plus diligebatur, haereditatem suam Christus divisit, ut Petrus sortiretur Ecclesiam, Joannes Mariam. Huic plane competebat haec portio non solum jure propinquitatis, sed etiam amoris privilegio testimonioque pudoris. Decebat namque ut nonnisi virgo virgini deserviret, quatenus et Virgo beata, divino languens prae amore, floribus fulciretur castitatis, et virginitas adolescentis id interim perciperet remunerationis, ut de contubernio proficeret tantae sanctitatis. Qui etiam, quia fidelis probatus est in obsequio incorruptae matris; mysteria quoque divinitatis, et arcana Verbi incorruptibilis sibi credi promeruit. Decebat, inquam, ut Matri Domini non alius obsequeretur quam dilectus Filii: quatenus et Mater semper suspirans Filium in dilectum Filii suavius respiraret, et discipulus Magistrum sibi conquerens nimis cito subtractum, Magistram totius veritatis se reperisse gauderet. Idque satis commode provisum, ut scripturus Evangelium familiarius de singulis conferret cum ea, quae conscia erat omnium; quippe quae ab initio omnia Filii sui diligentius observaverat, conservans omnia verba quae de illo erant, conferens in corde suo (Luc. II, 19, 51). Sic nempe se Martham exhibuit in cura pueri nutriendi; ut nihilominus Mariae partes exsecuta credatur in studio verbi cognoscendi. Maxime tamen postquam idem Filius ascendit ubi erat prius, Mater absoluta omni sollicitudine temporali, sanctoque Spiritu, quem praeter singulares illas conceptus sui primitias communiter cum Apostolis acceperat, plenius illuminata, gaudebat nimirum vacare, et videre quoniam Jesus est Deus. Visio prorsus ineffabilis gaudii, summaeque delectationis omnibus qui diligunt Jesum; sed prae omnibus illi quae genuit Jesum: cui sicut singulariter excepta est gratia Deum generandi; sic et praerogativa gloriandi in eo quem genuit. Omnino singularis atque incomparabilis gloria Virginis matris, videre Deum regem omnium in diademate carnis quo coronavit eum; ut et Deum agnoscat et adoret in corpore proprio, et corpus proprium glorificatum videat in Deo. His interim, ut opinor, contemplationibus pascebatur Maria, hanc optimam partem elegerat: quae non ablata, sed perfecta est hodie in ea. Quia enim negligens aut segnis non exstitit in opere Marthae, nequaquam vacua derelicta est a fructu Mariae. Labor in actione, fructus seu merces in contemplatione. Propterea, inquit, quod laboravit anima ejus, videbit et saturabitur (Isa. LIII, 11).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Moreover, when Jesus had loved her, he loved her unto the end, so that for her sake he not only made an end of living, but in her regard almost made an end of speaking as well: since, as it were among the last words of his testament, he transferred the care of his Mother—whose debtor he knew himself to be—to his most beloved heir. For thus Christ divided his inheritance between Peter, who loved more, and John, who was loved more: so that Peter obtained the Church as his lot, and John, Mary. This portion plainly belonged to John not only by right of kinship, but also by the privilege of love and the testimony of chastity. For it was fitting that none but a virgin should serve a virgin: so that the Blessed Virgin, languishing for divine love, might be propped up by the flowers of chastity, and that the virginity of the young man might meanwhile receive this as its reward, that he might profit from the companionship of such great holiness. He also, because he was proved faithful in the service of the incorrupt Mother, deserved that the mysteries of the Godhead and the secrets of the incorruptible Word should be entrusted to him. It was fitting, I say, that none other than the beloved of the Son should serve the Mother of the Lord: so that the Mother, ever sighing for her Son, might breathe more sweetly in the beloved of the Son, and the disciple, lamenting that his Master had been taken from him too soon, might rejoice that he had found a Mistress of all truth. And this was quite fittingly provided, that he who was to write the Gospel might confer more intimately about particular matters with her who was privy to all things; since from the beginning she had more diligently observed all things concerning her Son, keeping all the words that were about him, and pondering them in her heart (Luc. II, 19, 51). Thus indeed she showed herself a Martha in the care of nursing the child; yet is nonetheless believed to have carried out the part of Mary in the pursuit of knowing the Word. But most of all, after that same Son ascended to where he was before, the Mother, freed from all temporal care, and more fully illumined by the Holy Spirit—whom, besides those singular first-fruits of her conceiving, she had received in common with the Apostles—rejoiced indeed to be at leisure, and to see that Jesus is God. A vision truly of ineffable joy and of the highest delight to all who love Jesus; but above all to her who bore Jesus: to whom, just as the grace of begetting God was singularly granted, so too was the prerogative of glorying in him whom she bore. Altogether singular and incomparable is the glory of the Virgin Mother, to see God, the King of all, in the diadem of flesh with which she crowned him; so that she both recognizes and adores God in her own body, and sees her own body glorified in God. With such contemplations, I suppose, Mary was being fed meanwhile; this best part she had chosen, which is not taken away but today is perfected in her. For because she was not negligent or slothful in the work of Martha, she was by no means left empty of the fruit of Mary. The labor is in action; the fruit, or reward, is in contemplation. Therefore, he says, because her soul labored, she shall see and be satisfied (Isa. LIII, 11).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Vobis haec dicimus, fratres, ut si quis desiderio tangitur illius optimae partis quae in Maria laudatur, sciat quia haec praemium est illius quae in Martha non improbatur: nec aequum est ut praemium ante meritum requiratur. Jacob prius oportet jungi Liae, quam fruatur amplexibus Rachel (Gen. XXIX): sed et ipsum prius vocari et esse Jacob, quam Israel. Rectorem, inquit, te posuerunt? curam illorum habe, et sic considera, et omni cura tua explicita recumbe, ut laeteris propter illos, et ornamentum gratiae accipias coronam (Eccli. XXXII, 1-3). Labor siquidem operis, seu sollicitudo administrationis, semina sunt justitiae: pro quibus gaudia metenda sunt ex ore consolantis misericordiae. Sic enim ait propheta: Seminate vobis in justitia, metite in ore misericordiae (Osee X, 12). At enim qui parce seminat, parce et metet: et qui seminat in benedictione, de benedictionibus et metet (II Cor. IX, 6). Nullus sane tam profusa benedictione seminavit, sicut illa benedicta in mulieribus; quae benedictum semen de ventre profudit. Sed semen dicam, an fructum? Melius utrumque. Qui enim semen est operantibus justitiam, fructus erit metentibus gloriam. Semen, in passione: fructus, in resurrectione. Potens in terra semen istud, quod cadens in terram mox excitavit potentiam suam, ut multum fructum afferret, et in semine illo benedicerentur omnes gentes. Unde et ibi sequitur: Generatio rectorum benedicetur (Psal. CXI, 2).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. We say these things to you, brethren, so that if anyone is touched by desire for that best part which is praised in Mary, he may know that this is the reward of that part which is not disapproved in Martha: nor is it right that the reward be sought before the merit. Jacob must first be joined to Leah, before he enjoys the embraces of Rachel (Gen. XXIX): and he himself must first be called and be Jacob, before he is Israel. Have they made you a ruler? he says; take care of them, and so consider, and when all your care has been discharged, take your rest, that you may rejoice because of them, and receive the crown as the ornament of grace (Eccli. XXXII, 1-3). For the labor of work, or the solicitude of administration, are the seeds of righteousness: for which joys are to be reaped from the mouth of consoling mercy. For thus says the prophet: Sow for yourselves in righteousness, reap in the mouth of mercy (Osee X, 12). But indeed he who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly; and he who sows in blessing shall also reap of blessings (II Cor. IX, 6). No one indeed has sown with so abundant a blessing as she who is blessed among women, who poured forth the blessed seed from her womb. But shall I call it seed, or fruit? Better to call it both. For he who is seed to those laboring in righteousness will be fruit to those reaping glory. Seed, in the Passion; fruit, in the Resurrection. Mighty on earth was that seed, which, falling into the earth, soon roused its power, so that it might bring forth much fruit, and in that seed all nations might be blessed. Whence it follows there also: The generation of the upright shall be blessed (Psal. CXI, 2).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. De benedictionibus suis itaque Maria metat: et quae benedictionem omnium gentium seminavit, benedictionem omnium gentium singulariter accipiat. Beatam me dicent, inquit, omnes generationes (Luc. I, 48). Parum est hoc. Beatam te dicent omnes beatorum spirituum ordines. Viderunt hodie ascendentem filiae Sion coelestis et beatam dixerunt, et reginae laudaverunt eam (Cantic. VI, 8). Prorsus de benedictionibus suis hodie Maria metit, quia refusa est spiritualiter in eam omnimoda benedictio illa quam de se profudit. Date ei, inquit Spiritus sanctus, de fructu ventris sui; et saturetur illo quem genuit. O Mater misericordiae, saturare gloria Filii tui; et dimitte reliquias tuas parvulis tuis. Tu jam ad mensam, Domina; nos sub mensa catelli. Sicut oculi ancillae in manibus dominae suae, ita familia haec famelica de te praestolatur alimoniam vitae. Per te fructum vitae communicavimus, in mensa praesentium sacramentorum: per te eumdem fructum vitae communicemus in mensa perennium gaudiorum, Jesum benedictum fructum ventris tui; cui est honor et gloria, per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. So let Mary reap from her own blessings: and let her who sowed the blessing of all nations receive singularly the blessing of all nations. "All generations shall call me blessed," she says (Luc. I, 48). This is too little. All the ranks of the blessed spirits shall call you blessed. Today the daughters of heavenly Sion saw her ascending, and called her blessed; and queens praised her (Cantic. VI, 8). Indeed, today Mary reaps from her own blessings, because that whole blessing which she poured forth from herself has been poured back upon her spiritually. "Give her," says the Holy Spirit, "of the fruit of her womb; and let her be satisfied with him whom she bore." O Mother of mercy, be satisfied with the glory of your Son; and leave your leftovers to your little ones. You are now at the table, O Lady; we are the little dogs beneath the table. As the eyes of the handmaid are on the hands of her mistress, so this famished household awaits from you the nourishment of life. Through you we have shared the fruit of life at the table of the sacraments now present: through you may we share that same fruit of life at the table of everlasting joys—Jesus, the blessed fruit of your womb; to whom be honor and glory, forever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: Mary keeping all these words in her heart is Luke 2:19 and 2:51. The edition prints Eccli. ii, 19, 51 here and Luc. ii, 19, 51 in paragraph 3.
