passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric considers perseverance in wisdom through monastic stability, prayer, Scripture, work and silence. He connects obedience under difficult teaching with sacramental nourishment and the fear of God. The sermon appears in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina under the feast of Saint Benedict. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: IN FESTO SANCTI BENEDICTI.

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON THE FEAST OF SAINT BENEDICT.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De mansione in sapientia.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On abiding in wisdom.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Beatus vir qui in sapientia morabitur, et qui in justitia meditabitur, et in sensu cogitabit circumspectionem Dei! (Eccli. XIV, 22.) Quam congrue verba haec in laudem beati Benedicti cantata sint, facile quivis vestrum intelligit, cui tamen vita et doctrina ipsius non ignota sit. Quam commode vero ad vitae nostrae doctrinam trahi possint, ipsa per se verborum facies ostendit, quae scilicet illa quibus nihil est utilius in vita, sapientiam, justitiam, timorem Dei, cum praemio etiam beatitudinis commendat. Beatus, inquit, vir qui in sapientia morabitur. Prorsus haec est beatitudo, haec sapientia, si moreris in sapientia, ut perseveranter eam teneas: non enim statim qui invenerit, sed qui tenuerit eam, beatus. Dicit quidem Scriptura: Beatus qui invenit sapientiam. Sed non ibi quievit, imo addidit, et qui affluit sapientia (Prov. III, 13); ne videlicet solum invenisse statim putaretur ad beatitudinem sufficere, nisi, cum inveneris, cum ea et in ea demoreris, et contubernio atque convictu ipsius delecteris; nec discedas a magisterio ejus, donec meditando justitiam, cogitando circumspectionem Dei, affluere prudentia possit. Nam et Salomon sapientiam invenit; sed, quia prudentia minus affluxit, nec satis prudenter sibi circumspexit, dum videlicet non caute sibi providit a mulieribus alienis, non modo sapientiam perdidit, sed usque ad ultimam idololatriae insipientiam proruit (III Reg. XI). Sapientes quoque hujus mundi, qui invisibilia Dei, a creatura mundi per ea quae facta sunt, intellecta conspexerunt, sapientiam invenisse visi sunt; sed, quia nec ipsi prudentia affluxerunt, et, cum cognovissent Deum, non sicut Deum glorificaverunt, stulti et ipsi facti sunt, et obscuratum est insipiens cor eorum usque ad reprobum sensum, et ignominiam turpitudinum (Rom. I, 21-32).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "Blessed is the man who shall abide in wisdom, and who shall meditate in justice, and in understanding shall think upon the circumspection of God!" (Eccli. XIV, 22.) How fittingly these words are sung in praise of blessed Benedict, anyone of you to whom his life and teaching are not unknown easily understands. But how conveniently they can be drawn into instruction for our own life, the very face of the words themselves shows, since they commend those things than which nothing is more useful in life—wisdom, justice, the fear of God—together with the reward of blessedness as well. Blessed, he says, is the man who shall abide in wisdom. This indeed is blessedness, this is wisdom: if you abide in wisdom, so that you hold it perseveringly; for blessed is not at once the one who has found it, but the one who has held fast to it. Scripture indeed says: "Blessed is he who finds wisdom." But it did not stop there; rather it added, "and who overflows with wisdom" (Prov. III, 13); lest, namely, one should think that merely having found it suffices at once for blessedness, unless, when you have found it, you remain with it and in it, and delight in its company and converse; nor do you depart from its teaching, until, by meditating on justice, by thinking on the circumspection of God, you can overflow with prudence. For Solomon too found wisdom; but because he overflowed less with prudence, and did not look about himself prudently enough—since, namely, he did not warily provide for himself against strange women—he not only lost wisdom, but rushed forward even to the final folly of idolatry (III Reg. XI). The wise men of this world too, who gazed upon the invisible things of God, understood from the creation of the world through the things that were made, seemed to have found wisdom; but because they too did not overflow with prudence, and, when they had known God, did not glorify Him as God, they themselves also became fools, and their foolish heart was darkened even unto a reprobate sense, and the disgrace of base things (Rom. I, 21-32).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Alios itaque, sicut istorum exemplo liquet, repellit a sapientia quam invenerant, superbia cordis; alios, sicut in Salomone patet, abstrahit illecebra carnis; alii autem levitate et inconstantia mentis, levi perturbatione offensi eam relinquunt, qui scilicet ad tempus credunt, et in tempore tentationis recedunt. Quare autem recedunt? Quia radices non habent, quibus teneantur? (Luc. VIII, 13, 14.) Quomodo autem radicari poterunt, nisi morentur? Quae unquam planta radicatur, nisi loco cui affixa fuerit immoretur? Sic justus plantatus in domo Domini, nec radicari nec fundari in charitate poterit, nisi mora et stabilitate loci. Si autem radicatus non fuerit, nec florere, nec fructum qui maneat, afferre poterit; et, si florere visus fuerit alicujus spei initio, dicetur de illo: Ante messem totus floruit, et immatura perfectio germinavit (Isai. XVIII, 5); et secundum alium prophetam: Si fecerit fructum, alieni comedent eum (Osee, VIII, 7). Vis autem scire quam sit necessaria stabilitas loci ut in sapientia moreris, ut radicari et fructificare possis mora temporis? Interroga Patrem tuum Benedictum, et annuntiabit tibi quia claustrum monasterii, et stabilitas in congregatione, locus idoneus sit ad ferendum omnium fere fructus virtutum, quarum longum ibidem texit catalogum (Reg. S. Bened. cap. 4). Quid enim de instabili Salomon ait? Sicut avis transmigrans de nido suo, sic vir qui relinquit locum suum (Prov. XXVII, 8). Invenerat turtur nidum ubi poneret pullos suos, coeperat eum calefacere et ab eo calefieri, venerant usque ad partum pulli, et ecce avolat, opusque coeptum imperfectum relinquit. Quare, unde, vel quo avolet, ipse viderit, vel quando tot dispendia, quae interim patitur, compensabit, vel qua ratione primam fidem irritam factam excusabit. Ego enim non putarem esse consilii, pro spe incerta, certa subire dispendia; etsi profectus quorumdam me jubeat interim a praecipitatione cohibere sententiam.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Therefore, as is clear from the example of these men, pride of heart drives some away from the wisdom they had found; others, as is plain in the case of Solomon, the allurement of the flesh drags away; while others still, by lightness and inconstancy of mind, offended by some slight disturbance, abandon it—namely, those who believe for a time, and in the time of temptation fall away. But why do they fall away? Is it not because they have no roots by which they might be held fast? (Luc. VIII, 13, 14.) But how will they be able to be rooted, unless they abide? What plant was ever rooted, unless it remained in the place to which it had been fixed? So the just man, planted in the house of the Lord, will not be able to be rooted or founded in charity, except through continued residence and stability of place. But if he has not been rooted, he will not be able either to flower, or to bring forth fruit that remains; and if he has seemed to flower with some beginning of hope, it will be said of him: "Before the harvest it flowered entirely, and an unripe perfection sprouted" (Isai. XVIII, 5); and according to another prophet: "If it bears fruit, strangers shall eat it" (Osee, VIII, 7). But do you wish to know how necessary stability of place is, so that you may abide in wisdom, so that you may be able to be rooted and to bear fruit through length of time? Ask your Father Benedict, and he will declare to you that the cloister of the monastery, and stability in the community, is a place fit for bearing almost all the fruits of the virtues, of which he weaves a long catalogue in that very place (Rule of St. Benedict, ch. 4). For what does Solomon say of the unstable man? "As a bird that wanders from her nest, so is the man who abandons his place" (Prov. XXVII, 8). The turtledove had found a nest where she might lay her young; she had begun to warm it and to be warmed by it; the young had come even to the point of birth, and behold, she flies away, and leaves the work she had begun unfinished. Why, whence, or whither she flies away, let her see to it herself; or when she will make up for the many losses which she meanwhile suffers; or by what reasoning she will excuse her broken first fidelity. For I would not think it a matter of good counsel, for an uncertain hope, to undergo certain losses; although the progress of certain persons bids me meanwhile restrain my judgment from precipitate haste.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Enimvero multum dissimilis est causa eorum qui amore sapientiae inquieti fiunt, et eorum de quibus loqui coeperam, qui levi et frivola permoti causa a sapientia resiliunt. Sicut enim per patientiam disciplinis sapientiae quis immoratur, ut discat sapientiam; sic qui facile perdunt sustinentiam, non demorabuntur, ut scriptum est, projicere illam. Quid autem eos offendat, praemisit Scriptura, cum ait: Quasi lapidis virtus, probatio erit in illis (Eccli. VI, 22). Offenderunt in lapidem offensionis et petram scandali, cujus probata virtus corripiebat et erudiebat insipientes, probabatque mentes; cum ipsi virtutem sapientiae duritiam lapidis interpretarentur, duraque omnia, disciplinam, vultum, sermonem causarentur. Durus est, inquiunt, hic sermo (Joan. VI, 61). Esto, sermo durus est; numquid non verus est? Lapis durus est; nunquid non pretiosus est? Quare autem veritas dura est tibi, nisi propter duritiam cordis tui? si cor tibi pietate mollesceret, plus tibi soliditas veritatis quam vanitas mendacii vel oleum adulationis placeret. Durus est, aiebant, hic sermo, quia quasi lapidis virtus erat illis probatio sapientiae; ideoque non sunt demorati eam projicere, et retro abire. Nec ob aliud pretiosum et electum a Deo lapidem reprobaverunt, nisi quia durum putaverunt. Et erat quidem petra Christus, sed virtute, non duritia. Erat petra, sed quae converti posset, imo et conversa est in stagna vel fontes aquarum, ubi mollia et humilia, quibus influeret, invenit corda fidelium. Nam et isti, qui tam cito offensi quadam specie duritiae retro abierunt, si permansissent cum Apostolis, bibissent forsitan et ipsi cum eis de consequenti eos Petra, bibissent flumina aquae vivae de petra percussa in cruce fluentis largissime, ita ut hodieque bibat populus et jumenta; imo suxissent etiam mel de petra, oleumque de saxo durissimo.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Indeed, the case of those who become restless out of love of wisdom is very different from that of those I had begun to speak of, who, moved by some light and frivolous cause, spring back from wisdom. For just as a man dwells patiently under the discipline of wisdom in order to learn wisdom, so those who quickly lose their endurance will not delay, as it is written, to cast it away. And Scripture has already told us what offends them, saying: "As the virtue of a stone, so shall the trial be in them" (Eccli. VI, 22). They stumbled against the stone of stumbling and the rock of scandal, whose proven virtue was correcting and instructing the foolish, and testing minds; while they themselves interpreted the virtue of wisdom as the hardness of a stone, and complained that everything—the discipline, the countenance, the word—was hard. "This is a hard saying," they said (Joan. VI, 61). Granted, the word is hard; but is it not true? A stone is hard; but is it not precious? Why then is the truth hard to you, unless because of the hardness of your heart? If your heart were softened by devotion, the solidity of truth would please you more than the vanity of falsehood or the oil of flattery. "This is a hard saying," they said, because the trial of wisdom was to them as it were the virtue of a stone; and therefore they did not delay to cast it away and turn back. Nor for any other reason did they reject the precious and chosen stone of God, except that they thought it hard. And indeed Christ was the Rock—but by virtue, not by hardness. He was a Rock, but one that could be turned—indeed, was turned—into pools or fountains of water, where it found the soft and humble hearts of the faithful into which it could flow. For these men too, who so quickly took offense at a certain appearance of hardness and turned back, if they had remained with the Apostles, would perhaps have drunk themselves, with them, of the Rock that followed them; they would have drunk most abundantly of the rivers of living water flowing from the Rock struck upon the Cross, so that even today the people and the cattle drink of it; indeed, they would even have sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Prorsus tu beatus es, Simon Bar-Jona, tibi jam revelabat Pater pietatem mysterii, latentem, ut videbatur, sub duritia sermonis, qui, interrogatis duodecim, an et ipsi vellent abire, constanter respondisti: Domine, verba vitae aeternae habes; ad quem ibimus? (Joan. VI, 69.) Plane beatus, qui cum sapientia morari, et cum domesticis ejus ad mensam ipsius pane interim Sacramenti nutriri delegisti; donec de fide proficientem ad intellectum pane vitae et intellectus te cibaret, et aqua sapientiae salutaris potaret. Beati et vos, fratres mei, qui in disciplinam sapientiae, et christianae scholam philosophiae nomina dedistis, sed, si perseveranter in sapientia moremini; ut cum durior sermo ipsius visus fuerit, duriora scilicet praecipientis aut durius corripientis, non sit in aliquo vestrum cor malum incredulitatis discedendi a Deo vivo, sed constanter dicatis cum Apostolo: Verba vitae aeternae habes; ad quem ibimus? Fingis quidem laborem in praecepto (Psal. XCIII, 20), duritiam in sermone; sed scimus quia magna est multitudo dulcedinis tuae, Domine, quam abscondisti timentibus te (Psal. XXX, 20), perficies sperantibus in te. Ego autem semper sperabo, etiamsi occideris me. Imo tunc amplius sperabo, cum flagellaveris, secueris, usseris, occideris quidquid vivebat in me; ut non ego, sed Christus vivat in me. Omnino non discedimus a te, quia vivificabis nos etiam occidens, sanabis percutiens. Vere beatus qui cum sapientia moratur, ac constantia et fide longanimiter patiens et fideliter obediens usque ad mortem, nec deserens locum suum, quotiescunque spiritus potestatem habentis ascenderit super eum, sciens quia curatio disciplinae faciet cessare maxima peccata (Eccle. X, 4).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Truly you are blessed, Simon Bar-Jona; to you already the Father was revealing the graciousness of the mystery hidden, as it seemed, beneath the hardness of the word—you who, when the twelve were asked whether they too wished to go away, answered steadfastly: "Lord, thou hast the words of eternal life; to whom shall we go?" (Joan. VI, 69.). Truly blessed are you, who chose to dwell with wisdom, and to be nourished for a time at her table among her household with the bread of the Sacrament; until, as you advanced from faith to understanding, she fed you with the bread of life and understanding, and gave you to drink the water of saving wisdom. Blessed also are you, my brothers, who have given your names to the discipline of wisdom and to the Christian school of philosophy—but only if you dwell perseveringly in wisdom; so that when her word seems harder—that is, when her precepts are harder, or her correction more severe—there may not be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, departing from the living God, but that you may say steadfastly with the Apostle: "Thou hast the words of eternal life; to whom shall we go?" You indeed fashion labor in your precept (Psal. XCIII, 20), hardness in your word; but we know that great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you (Psal. XXX, 20), and which you will perfect for those who hope in you. And I will always hope, even if you should slay me. Indeed, I will hope the more when you have scourged, cut, burned, and slain whatever was living in me; so that it is not I, but Christ who lives in me. We will in no way depart from you, for you will give us life even by killing us, and heal us even by striking us. Truly blessed is the one who dwells with wisdom, and who, with constancy and faith, patiently enduring and faithfully obeying even unto death, does not desert his place, as often as the spirit of the one having power rises up against him, knowing that "the remedy of discipline shall make the greatest sins to cease" (Eccle. X, 4).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Sane ad hanc sapientiam morandi in sapientia, illud praecipue pertinere arbitror, ut inquietudo vel quaelibet levis molestia non facile quodcunque opus sapientiae nobis excutiat, verbi gratia, solemnem psalmodiam, orationem, lectionem divinam, pensum operis diurni, aut silentii disciplinam. Quia enim sapientia in exitu canitur: Gaudebunt, ait sanctus, labia mea, cum cantavero tibi Psal LXX, 23), dum etiam ad litteram, exitus matutini et vespere delectabis (Psal. LXIV, 9.) De oratione quoque certum et ipsi quotidie capitis experimentum, quod melior est finis orationis quam principium; ut fidele probetis dominicum illud toties inculcatum, tot exemplis commendatum de orationis perseverantia consilium. Jam legere et negligere, vel, antequam ceperis librum, de manibus projicere, quem fructum, putas, tibi poterit parere? Si Scripturae immoratus non fueris, ut assiduitate studii ei fias familiaris, quando, putas, se tibi revelabit? Qui habet, inquit, amorem verbi, dabitur ei intellectus, et abundabit; qui vero non habet, et quod habet per naturam, auferetur ab eo (Matth. XIII, 12; XXV, 29) propter negligentiam. De opere autem manuum, nonne et de isto satis comperistis quia sicut denarius operariis, sic consolatio saepius servatur in fine operis? De silentio quippe nota est promissio prophetica, quia in silentio et spe erit, inquit, fortitudo vestra (Isai. XXX, 15). Si enim colas justitiam in silentio, et, sicut Jeremias bonum esse ait, praestoleris cum silentio salutare Domini; in medio silentio secretus tibi illabetur a regalibus sedibus omnipotens sermo, et aquae Siloe, quae vadunt cum silentio, convallem quieti ac placidi pectoris grato rigabunt profluvio. Hoc non semel, sed saepius experieris, si modo silentium tuum cultus justitiae sit (Isai. XXXII, 17), id est, si in justitia mediteris, ut perseveres in Scriptura quam proposui, et in sensu cogites circumspectionem Dei.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Indeed, I think this belongs especially to that wisdom of abiding in wisdom: that restlessness, or any slight annoyance, should not easily shake us loose from whatever work of wisdom we are engaged in—for example, the solemn chanting of the psalms, prayer, divine reading, the task of the day's work, or the discipline of silence. For wisdom is sung at its conclusion: 'My lips shall rejoice,' says the saint, 'when I shall sing to thee' Psal LXX, 23); as also, according to the letter, 'thou shalt make the outgoings of the morning and the evening to be joyful' (Psal. LXIV, 9.). Concerning prayer also, you yourselves receive daily a sure proof that the end of prayer is better than its beginning; so that you may prove faithful that counsel of the Lord, so often urged, commended by so many examples, concerning perseverance in prayer. Now what fruit, do you think, can it bear you, to read and then neglect what you have read, or to throw the book out of your hands almost before you have taken it up? If you do not linger over Scripture, so that by diligent study you become familiar with it, when, do you suppose, will it reveal itself to you? 'He who has,' it says, 'love of the word, to him shall understanding be given, and he shall have abundance; but he who has not, even what he has by nature shall be taken away from him' (Matth. XIII, 12; XXV, 29), on account of negligence. As for the work of the hands, have you not also learned well enough from this, that just as the wage is kept for the laborers, so consolation is more often reserved for the end of the work? Concerning silence, indeed, the prophetic promise is well known: 'In silence and in hope shall your strength be,' he says (Isai. XXX, 15). For if you cultivate justice in silence, and, as Jeremiah says it is good, wait with silence for the salvation of the Lord, then in the midst of silence the almighty Word will come down secretly to you from the royal throne, and the waters of Siloam, which flow with silence, will water the valley of a quiet and peaceful breast with their pleasant stream. This you will experience not once but often, provided only that your silence be the cultivation of justice (Isai. XXXII, 17); that is, if you meditate in justice, so that you persevere in the Scripture I have set before you, and in your understanding think upon the circumspection of God.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Haec meditare, in his esto, ut profectus tuus manifestus fiat. Si enim iniquitatem mediteris in cubili tuo, malitias scilicet quas malignus immittit, aut phantasias quas cor tuum parturit, aut inanes philosophias, seu fallaces theorias, quae sunt velut aegri somnia; nonne magis injustitiae quam justitiae cultus erit silentium tuum? Si ergo vis in sapientia morari, stude in justitia meditari. Concupisti, inquit, sapientiam? conserva justitiam, et Dominus praebebit illam tibi (Eccli. I, 33). Si autem quasi violente irruunt cogitationes noxiae, pone tibi virilem et fidelem custodiam, quae omni custodia servet cor tuum. Dico autem timorem Dei, qui nihil negligit, qui nullum indiscussum intrare permittit, saepius interrogans etiam angelum lucis: Noster es, an adversariorum? (Josue V, 13.) Undique enim sibi circumspicit, tanquam omni hora cogitans circumspectionem Dei, quem sine intermissione intueri ac judicare corda filiorum hominum attendit. Pulchre autem dictum est: In sensu cogitabit (Eccli. XIV, 22); quia prorsus sine sensu est et a corde excessit qui timorem Dei cogitare negligit, qui pondus tantae majestatis ac judicii sibi incumbentis non sentit. Signanter quoque circumspicere Deus dicitur, quia omnia tam praeterita quam futura habet praesentia, ut nec ista respiciat, nec illa prospiciat, sed similiter, quia simpliciter, cuncta circumspiciat; sitque illa aeternitas velut punctum, omnium media temporalium, cujus immobili simplicitati semper aequaliter praesens est circuitus et rota temporum. Hunc oculum aeternum, sine intermissione videntem et judicantem omnia, semper cogitat, suaque se cogitatione sollicitat timor Domini, qui revocat a malis non solum operibus, sed et cogitationibus; erudiens nos, ut justitiam potius meditemur; continens, ut cum sapientia moremur. Ita enim sensim fit ut qui primo coercetur timore judicii et poenae, postea pascatur amore ac meditatione justitiae, demumque requiescat ac delectetur in convictu et amplexu sapientiae. Haec non modo foras mittit timorem, diffundendo charitatem; sed etiam pellit ab animo taedium et langorem, infundendo suavitatem, sicut quidam, contubernium habens ipsius, de ea loquebatur: Intrans in domum meam conquiescam cum illa; non enim habet amaritudinem conversatio illius, nec taedium convictus illius, sed laetitiam et gaudium (Sap. VIII, 16). Horum participes nos faciat, qui particeps nostri fieri dignatus est Dei sapientia Christus Jesus, qui vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Meditate on these things, be occupied in them, that your progress may be manifest. For if you meditate on iniquity in your bed—that is, the malicious thoughts which the evil one injects, or the fancies which your own heart brings forth, or empty philosophies, or deceptive speculations, which are like the dreams of a sick man—will not your silence then be the cultivation of injustice rather than of justice? If, therefore, you wish to abide in wisdom, strive to meditate in justice. 'Have you desired wisdom?' it says. 'Keep justice, and the Lord will give it to you' (Eccli. I, 33). But if harmful thoughts rush upon you as though by force, set for yourself a manly and faithful guard, which may keep your heart with all watchfulness. I mean the fear of God, which neglects nothing, which allows nothing to enter unexamined, often questioning even an angel of light: 'Art thou one of ours, or of the adversaries?' (Josue V, 13.). For it looks about on every side, as though at every hour thinking upon the circumspection of God, whom it attends as beholding without ceasing and judging the hearts of the children of men. It is beautifully said: 'He shall think with understanding' (Eccli. XIV, 22); for he is utterly without sense, and has gone out of his heart, who neglects to think upon the fear of God, who does not feel the weight of so great a majesty and of the judgment pressing upon him. God is also fittingly said to 'look around,' because he holds all things, past as well as future, as present to him, so that he neither looks back upon the one nor looks forward to the other, but looks around upon all things equally, because simply; and that eternity of his is, as it were, a point in the midst of all temporal things, to whose unmoving simplicity the circling wheel of the ages is ever equally present. Upon this eternal eye, seeing and judging all things without ceasing, the fear of the Lord continually thinks, and by its own thought disquiets itself—that fear which calls us back from evils not only in deeds but also in thoughts; teaching us rather to meditate on justice, restraining us, that we may abide with wisdom. For thus it comes about by degrees that he who is first held in check by fear of judgment and punishment is afterward fed by love and meditation of justice, and at last rests and delights in the companionship and embrace of wisdom. This wisdom not only casts out fear, by pouring forth charity, but also drives weariness and listlessness from the soul, by infusing sweetness—just as a certain man, who had companionship with her, spoke of her: 'Entering into my house, I will take my repose with her; for her company has no bitterness, nor her companionship any tediousness, but joy and gladness' (Sap. VIII, 16). May he make us partakers of these things, who deigned to become a partaker of us—the Wisdom of God, Christ Jesus, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.text: The edition prints violente in its description of harmful thoughts forcing their way in.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Trust in God gives steadiness amid tribulation and the loss of spiritual consolation. Guerric develops the image of a tree rooted in living water through Scripture, compunction and the sacraments. The sermon appears in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina under the feast of Saint Benedict. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO II.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON II.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De fiducia in Deum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On Trust in God.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Benedictus vir qui confidit in Domino (Jerem. XVII, 7). Sanctus Pater noster gratia Benedictus et nomine, cujus memoria in benedictione est, ipse profecto fuit benedictus vir qui confisus est in Domino. Quem enim Dominus praevenit in benedictionibus dulcedinis, ut in Domino confideret, jam benedixit omni benedictione spirituali in coelestibus in Christo, quia in Domino confisus est. Nec solum in coelestibus benedictionem omnium angelorum, sed etiam in terrestribus benedictionem omnium gentium dedit illi Dominus. Ubi enim gentium non benedicetur hodie benedictus Domini Benedictus? Plane benedictio Domini super caput justi (Prov. X, 6), quem tot benedictionibus coeli et terrae gratia Dei cumulavit. Non tamen, sicut Esau, in pinguedine terrae et in rore coeli benedictio ejus (Gen. XXVII, 28); sed in pinguedine spiritus et in rore coeli, qui per prophetam loquitur: Ero quasi ros (Osee XIV, 6), et cui dicitur: Ros lucis, ros tuus (Isai. XXVI, 19). In Christo utique benedictio Patris, cui Pater imprecatus est: Qui benedixerit tibi, benedictionibus repleatur (Gen. XXVII, 29). Merito proinde benedictus in Domino vir qui confidit in Domino, quia qui in Domino fidit, in eo se ipsum figit. Ubi autem arbor radicem figit, inde succum vitae atque humorem pinguedinis bibit. Plane ad humorem radices misit, qui, ut verbis utar Benedicti magistri, spem suam Deo commisit, ac de ipso fonte summi boni aquas vitae totius benedictionis et gratiae bibit (Reg. S. Bened. cap. 4).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord (Jerem. XVII, 7). Our holy Father, Benedict both in grace and in name, whose memory is in benediction, was indeed himself a blessed man who trusted in the Lord. For him whom the Lord went before with the blessings of sweetness, so that he might trust in the Lord, the Lord had already blessed with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, because he trusted in the Lord. And the Lord gave him not only, in heavenly things, the blessing of all the angels, but also, in earthly things, the blessing of all nations. For in what nation today is Benedict, the Lord's blessed one, not blessed? Truly the blessing of the Lord is upon the head of the just man (Prov. X, 6), whom the grace of God has heaped with so many blessings of heaven and earth. Yet his blessing was not, like Esau's, in the fatness of the earth and the dew of heaven (Gen. XXVII, 28); but in the fatness of the spirit and the dew of heaven, who speaks through the prophet: I will be as the dew (Osee XIV, 6), and to whom it is said: The dew of light is your dew (Isai. XXVI, 19). In Christ indeed is the blessing of the Father, for whom the Father invoked this blessing: May he who blesses you be filled with blessings (Gen. XXVII, 29). Rightly, then, is the man blessed in the Lord who trusts in the Lord, because he who trusts in the Lord fixes himself in him. Now where a tree fixes its root, from there it drinks the sap of life and the moisture of richness. Clearly he sent his roots toward that moisture who, to use the words of our master Benedict, 'committed his hope to God,' and drank from that very fount of the highest good the waters of life of all blessing and grace (Rule of St. Benedict, ch. 4).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Per hanc nempe piam et fidelem fiduciam remittuntur peccata; sanitatum corporalium, sed magis spiritualium, obtinentur remedia; propulsantur pericula; terrores contemnuntur; vincitur mundus; omnia denique possibilia credenti redduntur. Illi quippe qui in peccatis erat: Confide, ait, fili, remittuntur tibi peccata tua. Illis quibus donabatur sanitas corporum vel animarum: Secundum fidem tuam fiat tibi; et: Fides tua te salvum fecit (Matth. IX, 2, 29, 22). Illis, qui periculo terrebantur naufragandi: Habete, inquit, fidem Dei (Marc. XI, 22); et: Quid timidi estis, modicae fidei? (Matth. VIII, 26.) Illis quos armabat adversus saevitiam mundi furoresque diaboli: Confidite, ait; ego vici mundum (Joan. XVI, 33). Et utique haec est victoria quae vincit mundum, fides nostra (I Joan. V, 4), si modo non sit tepida, non trepida; sed sit fiducia, id est fides non ficta, seu spes non infirma. Non solum autem mundus per eam vincitur, sed et coelum possidetur, super aeternitatem homo stabilitur, et in Deo ipso per charitatem radicatur et fundatur. Qui enim confidit in Domino, est sicut mons Sion; non commovebitur in aeternum, qui fundatus est super Aeternum (Psal. CXXIV, 1). Tam enim perire non potest, quam nec ille cui adhaerens unus cum ipso spiritus est. Quis enim speravit in Domino, et confusus est, permansit in mandatis illius, et derelictus est? (Eccli. II, 11, 12.) Si dixerit infidelis, Ille derelictus erat qui in cruce clamabat: Deus, Deus meus, utquid me dereliquisti? (Matth. XXVII, 46.) puto quia non usquequaque dereliquit, in quo erat mundum reconcilians sibi. O quanta consolatio, sic desolari; quanta dilectio, sic derelinqui, ut Unico Patris unice dilecto merearis vel in passionibus consociari!

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. By this devout and faithful trust, indeed, sins are forgiven; remedies are obtained for bodily health, but even more for spiritual health; dangers are driven off; terrors are held in contempt; the world is overcome; and finally, all things become possible to the one who believes. For to the one who was in sins, he said: Have confidence, son, your sins are forgiven you. To those to whom health of body or soul was granted: According to your faith be it done to you; and: Your faith has made you whole (Matth. IX, 2, 29, 22). To those who were terrified by the danger of shipwreck, he said: Have the faith of God (Marc. XI, 22); and: Why are you fearful, O you of little faith? (Matth. VIII, 26.) To those whom he armed against the savagery of the world and the ragings of the devil, he said: Have confidence; I have overcome the world (Joan. XVI, 33). And indeed this is the victory that overcomes the world, our faith (I Joan. V, 4), provided only that it be not lukewarm, not fearful; but be trust—that is, faith not feigned, or hope not weak. Not only is the world overcome through it, but heaven is also possessed, man is made stable upon eternity, and he is rooted and grounded in God himself through charity. For he who trusts in the Lord is like Mount Sion; he shall not be moved forever, who is founded upon the Eternal One (Psal. CXXIV, 1). For he can no more perish than can the one to whom, clinging to him, he is made one spirit with him. For who has hoped in the Lord, and been confounded? Who has remained in his commandments, and been forsaken? (Eccli. II, 11, 12.) Should the unbeliever say: He was forsaken who cried out on the cross: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matth. XXVII, 46.) — I think that he did not altogether forsake him, in whom he was reconciling the world to himself. O how great a consolation, thus to be desolated; how great a love, thus to be forsaken, that you might merit to be associated even in his sufferings with the Only-begotten of the Father, the uniquely beloved!

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Aperi, Domine, oculos hujus pueri, rudem loquor et novitium, cui, cum tribulatur, putat se derelictum. Novum hoc omnino et insolitum, si justum quempiam viderem derelictum, cum Ecclesia dicat: Junior fui, etenim senui, et non vidi justum derelictum (Psal. XXXVI, 25). Aperi, inquam, o Domine, oculos pueri tui, ut videat quia plures nobiscum sunt quam cum adversariis. Siquidem Dominus virtutum nobiscum, et cum eo omnis virtus et militia coeli, imo favor omnis creaturae, servientis nutui et arbitrio Creatoris sui. Si enim Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? (Rom. VIII, 31.) et quis est qui nobis noceat, si boni aemulatores fuerimus? (I Petr. III, 13.) Poterit invidus ille saevire; sed hoc erit servire. Poterit urere; tundere, dissecare; sed hoc erit coronas fabricare. Diligam te, Domine, fortitudo mea, per quem mihi vermiculo succumbit omnis fortitudo contraria, et illuditur ab angelis tuis, in ministerium nostrum missis, antiqui draconis astutia, ut, volens nocere, prosit. Diligam te, Domine, propugnator potens, gubernator prudens, consolator clemens, remunerator affluens. Securus in eum projicio omnem sollicitudinem meam, cujus nec potentia vinci, nec sapientia falli, nec benevolentia potest fatigari quominus expleat omnem indigentiam meam. Quam satius, quam securius est ipsum esse sollicitum, quam me ipsum pro me! quam bonum est confidere in Domino, quam in homine! quam jure maledictus qui confidit in homine, carnem ponit brachium suum, et recedit a Domino cor ejus! (Jerem. XVII, 5.) et quidem egenus et pauper ego sum; sed si Dominus sollicitus est mei, dives sum, beatus sum; cui nimirum omnia cooperantur in bonum. Sperent igitur in te qui noverunt nomen tuum, quoniam non derelinquis sperantes in te, Domine (Psal. IX, 11); sedeatque populus tuus, sicut scriptum est, in pulchritudine pacis, in tabernaculis fiduciae, in requie opulenta, in securitate sempiterna (Isai. XXXII, 18, 17). Omnino pulchra pax et securitas sempiterna, habitare in adjutorio Altissimi, in protectione Dei coeli commorari. Prorsus requies opulenta, sedere feriatum sub vite vera, ficu et oliva; et post saturitatem variorum fructuum, se ipsum mulcere carmine amatorio, ac dicere: Sub umbra illius quam desiderabam [Vulg. quem desideraveram] sedi, et fructus illius dulcis gutturi meo? (Cant. II, 5.) Plane dulcis gutturi fructus de cujus gustu tam dulcis erumpit ructus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Open, Lord, the eyes of this child—I speak of one unformed and a novice—who, when he is afflicted, thinks himself abandoned. This would be altogether new and unheard of, were I to see any just man abandoned, since the Church says: "I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the just man abandoned" (Psal. XXXVI, 25). Open, I say, O Lord, the eyes of your servant, that he may see that there are more with us than with our adversaries. For the Lord of hosts is with us, and with him every power and the army of heaven, indeed the favor of every creature, serving the nod and will of its Creator. For if God is for us, who is against us? (Rom. VIII, 31.) And who is there to harm us, if we are zealous for what is good? (I Petr. III, 13.) That envious one may rage; but this will be to serve us. He may burn, beat, cut apart; but this will be to fashion crowns. I will love you, Lord, my strength, through whom every opposing strength yields to me, a mere worm, and the cunning of the ancient dragon is mocked by your angels, sent for our service, so that, wishing to do harm, it profits us. I will love you, Lord, mighty defender, prudent governor, gentle comforter, abundant rewarder. Secure, I cast all my anxiety upon him, whose power cannot be conquered, whose wisdom cannot be deceived, whose benevolence cannot be wearied from supplying all my need. How much better, how much more secure it is that he himself be anxious for me, than that I should be anxious for myself! How good it is to trust in the Lord, rather than in man! How justly cursed is he who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart withdraws from the Lord! (Jerem. XVII, 5.) And indeed I am needy and poor; but if the Lord is anxious for me, I am rich, I am blessed; for to such a one, surely, all things work together for good. Let those, then, hope in you who know your name, for you do not abandon those who hope in you, O Lord (Psal. IX, 11); and let your people sit, as it is written, in the beauty of peace, in the tabernacles of confidence, in opulent rest, in everlasting security (Isai. XXXII, 18, 17). Truly it is a beautiful peace and an everlasting security, to dwell in the help of the Most High, to abide under the protection of the God of heaven. Truly it is an opulent rest, to sit at leisure beneath the true vine, the fig tree, and the olive; and, after being filled with manifold fruits, to soothe oneself with a love-song, and to say: "Under his shadow, which I desired [Vulg.: whom I had desired], I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat" (Cant. II, 5.). Truly sweet to the throat is that fruit, from the tasting of which so sweet an eructation breaks forth.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Haec sunt ergo tabernacula fiduciae, in quibus verus Israel habitat confidenter, pascit et cubat, et non est qui exterreat; et, sicut Sapientia promittit, Requiescet absque terrore, abundantia perfruetur, malorum timore sublato (Prov. I, 33). Et bene timore malorum sublato, non timore Domini; ne fiducia ista et securitate, quam commendamus, negligentiam putes generari, cum non in alio quam in timore Domini sit fiducia fortitudinis. Timor quippe, dum cavet offensam, custodit gratiam; locumque servat fiduciae, quandiu tibi conscius non es Dominum offendisse. Inde fit ut nonnisi caste timeas eum; praeter eum nullatenus timeas alienum. Sola ergo conscientia bona fiduciam istam praesumit, suadet corda nostra esse in conspectu Judicis aeterni. Quis enim bene sibi de illo promittat, a quo se minime diligi intelligat? Qui autem diligit, nunquam diffidit, sciens quia is quem corda non fallunt, diligentes se diligit, etiam cum arguit et corripit. Siquidem eruditis corde in sapientia non aufert, sed auget fiduciam Patris disciplina, scientes scriptum, Beatus qui corripitur a Domino (Job V, 17), et: Ego quos amo arguo et castigo (Apoc. III, 19; Prov. III, 12). Cum igitur exarserit in brevi ira ejus, beati omnes qui confidunt in eo (Psal. II, 13), quos scilicet amoris proprii conscientia consolatur, quia, cum iratus fuerit, misericordiae recordabitur; et, cum dixerint: Confitebor tibi, Domine, quoniam iratus es mihi, statim subsequentur: Conversus est furor tuus, et consolatus es me (Isa. XII, 1), eo quod nonnisi in brevi exarserit ira ejus, quam tam cito placaverit confessio reatus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. These, then, are the tabernacles of confidence, in which the true Israel dwells securely, feeds and lies down, and there is none to terrify him; and, as Wisdom promises, "He shall rest without terror, and shall enjoy abundance, the fear of evils being removed" (Prov. I, 33). And rightly is it "the fear of evils" that is removed, not the fear of the Lord; lest you should think that this confidence and security which we commend breeds negligence, since the confidence of strength lies in nothing other than the fear of the Lord. For fear, while it guards against giving offense, preserves grace, and keeps a place open for confidence, so long as you are not conscious of having offended the Lord. Hence it follows that you should fear him alone chastely; and besides him you should in no way fear any other. It is a good conscience alone, then, that lays claim to this confidence, persuading our hearts that they stand in the sight of the eternal Judge. For who could rightly promise himself good from one by whom he understands himself to be in no way loved? But he who loves never distrusts, knowing that he whom hearts cannot deceive loves those who love him, even when he rebukes and corrects them. Indeed, for those whose hearts are instructed in wisdom, the Father's discipline does not take away but increases confidence, since they know it is written: "Blessed is the man whom the Lord corrects" (Job V, 17), and: "Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise" (Apoc. III, 19; Prov. III, 12). When, therefore, his anger has been kindled but for a short while, blessed are all they who trust in him (Psal. II, 13), namely those whom the awareness of their own love consoles, because, when he has been angry, he will remember mercy; and when they shall have said: "I will give thanks to you, O Lord, for you were angry with me," there shall at once follow: "Your wrath is turned away, and you have comforted me" (Isa. XII, 1), because his anger was kindled only for a short while, which the confession of guilt so quickly appeased.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Merito igitur benedictum virum qui confidit in Domino ligno comparat Jeremias quod transplantatur super aquas: quod quia ad humorem amoris mittit radices cordis, non timebit cum venerit aestus irae et tribulationis; sed et in tempore siccitatis, cum multo tempore coelum clausum fuerit, nec ros nec pluvia gratiae super eum descenderit, non erit tamen sollicitum, quasi Deus eum projecerit (Jerem. XVII, 7, 8). Sentit quippe se plantatum fide, radicatum charitate super aquas vitae, quae, secundum Ezechielem, de sanctuario egredientes vivificant omnia, et habent in utraque ripa omne lignum pomiferum, cujus folium non defluit, nec fructus deficit (Ezech. XLVII, 3-12). Cur igitur lignum illud benedictum aut timeret aestum, aut de siccitate esset sollicitum, cui aqua viva, id est Spiritus sancti gratia, vitalem in occulto succum spei et charitatis subministrare non desinit; unde et folium sit viride, id est Verbum plenum gratiae et veritatis; et ipsum non desinat aliquando facere fructum quodcunque opus pietatis? Et grata quidem illa verna temperies, pacis et laetitiae; desiderabilis illa pluvia voluntaria, quam segregavit Deus haereditati suae; sed, si ita necesse est, adurat omnia aestus tribulationis, veniant iterum quaecunque prophetavit Jeremias de sermonibus siccitatis spiritualis; non tamen timebit, quem fiducia Domini radicavit super aquam refectionis (Jerem. XVII, 6, 8), id est gratiam Spiritus sancti; quae etsi manifeste non pluat, ut sensibiliter influat, occulte tamen interius vivificat et fecundat; quandiu videlicet fidem propositi conservat, ad perseverandum confortat, verbumque irreprehensible et opus stabile subministrat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Rightly, then, does Jeremiah compare the blessed man who trusts in the Lord to a tree that is transplanted beside the waters: because it sends the roots of its heart into the moisture of love, it will not fear when the heat of wrath and tribulation comes; but even in time of drought, when the sky has long been shut up, and neither dew nor rain of grace has descended upon it, it will nevertheless not be anxious, as though God had cast it off (Jerem. XVII, 7, 8). For it feels itself planted by faith, rooted by charity, upon the waters of life, which, according to Ezekiel, going forth from the sanctuary, give life to all things, and have on either bank every fruit-bearing tree, whose leaf does not fall nor its fruit fail (Ezech. XLVII, 3-12). Why, then, should that blessed tree either fear the heat, or be anxious about drought, since the living water—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit—does not cease to supply it, in secret, with the vital sap of hope and charity; whence its leaf also is green, that is, the Word full of grace and truth; and it itself never at any time ceases to bear fruit, whatever work of piety it may be? Pleasant indeed is that springtime mildness of peace and joy; desirable is that bountiful rain which God has set apart for his inheritance; but if it must needs be so, let the heat of tribulation scorch everything, let there come again whatever Jeremiah prophesied concerning words of spiritual drought; still he will not fear, whom trust in the Lord has rooted upon the water of refreshment (Jerem. XVII, 6, 8), that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit; which, even if it does not rain down openly so as to flow in perceptibly, nevertheless secretly gives life and fruitfulness within—so long, that is, as it preserves the faith of one's purpose, strengthens him to persevere, and supplies a blameless word and a stable work.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. In hujusmodi vestra, fratres, sit consolatio, quoties alias consolationes non modo carnales, sed et spirituales subtraxerit vobis non negligentia vestra, sed dispensatio divina. Et fortasse quidem illa, quam diximus, occulta gratia Spiritus irriguum est inferius, quo nimirum Axa non vult esse contenta, nisi adjiciatur ei et irriguum superius (Josue XV, 19); ut scilicet de excelso effundatur Spiritus, rorent coeli desuper, et nubes angelicae pluant justum, justificans Dei verbum, loquens ad cor Jerusalem. Et bene illud irriguum inferius, quod quasi ad radices fluens nutrit humilitatem; hoc autem superius, quod sese desuper effundens, spe et exsultatione attollit mentem. Si ergo et vos, fratres, ad illud suspiratis superius irriguum, laudabile quidem desiderium; si tamen nondum attingitis, mittite radices interim ad humorem, salubre remedium. Qui igitur non praevalet capere laetitiam contemplativae, meditetur justitiam vitae activae. Inde radices affectionum impinguet, dulcoret mores, omnemque vitae statum informet, quatenus in ipso nec marcescat aut defluat folium, id est verbum leviter aut inutiliter prolatum, nec aliquando vita desinat facere fructum. Benedictum lignum, cujus folium ad medicinam, fructus ad vitam; id est, cujus sermo gratiam parit audienti, et opus vitam facienti.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Let your consolation, brothers, be of this kind, whenever other consolations—not only carnal but also spiritual—are withdrawn from you, not through your own negligence, but by divine dispensation. And perhaps indeed that hidden grace of the Spirit of which we spoke is the lower watering, with which Axa surely does not wish to be content, unless the upper watering also be added to her (Josue XV, 19); so that, namely, the Spirit may be poured out from on high, the heavens may drop dew from above, and the clouds of angels may rain down the Just One, the justifying Word of God, speaking to the heart of Jerusalem. And rightly is that called the lower watering, which, flowing as it were to the roots, nourishes humility; but this the upper watering, which, pouring itself out from above, lifts up the mind with hope and exultation. If, then, you too, brothers, sigh after that upper watering, it is indeed a praiseworthy desire; yet if you do not yet attain it, in the meantime send your roots down to the moisture—a wholesome remedy. Let him, then, who cannot grasp the joy of the contemplative life, meditate upon the righteousness of the active life. From this let him fatten the roots of his affections, sweeten his habits, and shape his whole manner of life, so that in him the leaf may neither wither nor fall away—that is, no word spoken lightly or uselessly—nor may his life ever cease to bear fruit. Blessed is the tree whose leaf is for healing and whose fruit is for life; that is, whose speech brings forth grace for the hearer, and whose work brings forth life for the one who does it.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 7. Ad hoc profecto vos, fratres mei, quos carnalis generatio vel consuetudo saecularis plantaverat in terra inaquosa, in terra salsuginis, divina generatio vel mutatio dexterae Excelsi transplantavit super aquas refectionis; ut quibus prius propter sterilitatem parabatur securis et ignis, nunc plantati in domo Domini, in atriis domus Dei nostri, floreatis, et fructum faciatis, et fructus vester maneat. An non aquae refectionis Scripturae Spiritus sancti, in quibus meditamur die ac nocte? an non aquae refectionis, lacrymae compunctionis, quae nobis factae sunt panes die ac nocte? an non aquae refectionis, Sacramenta et subsidia nostrae salutis, quibus pascimur et potamur in altari? In his siquidem omnibus, quasi quibusdam rivulis, fons sapientiae qui oritur in medio paradisi, derivatur foris, et in plateis aquas suas dividit. Ego, inquit Sapientia, quasi aquaeductus exivi de paradiso. Dixi: Rigabo hortum meum plantationum, inebriabo partus mei fructum (Eccli. XXIV, 41, 42). Ecce, ut colligere potestis ex ipsius ore Sapientiae parientis et plantantis, hortus plantationum est congregatio filiorum. Numquid enim ego, qui alios parere facio, ipse non pariam, dicit Dominus? (Isai. LXVI, 9.) Ipse parit, cum ingenerat voluntatem bonam; plantat, cum instituit vitam; rigat, cum sensibus infundit gratiam; colit, cum moribus adhibet disciplinam. Audite me, divini fructus, et quasi rosa plantata super rivos aquarum fructificate (Eccli. XXXIX, 17). Mittite radices ad humorem vitae, id est ad amorem terrae viventium, non hujus in qua omnia senescunt et putrescunt. Non potest arbor facere fructum qui permaneat, nisi sursum in coelestibus radicem figat, ut quae sursum sunt, non quae super terram, quaerat et sapiat. Quod enim physici dicunt hominem esse arborem inversam, eo quod nervi corporis radicem et initium in vertice habeant, ego illo potius sensu interpretor, quod radicem amoris et desiderii figere debeat in coelo, in summo vertice rerum capite nostro Jesu Christo. Qui illuc radices miserit, et de illo fonte aeterno succum vitae et gratiae jugiter biberit, non timebit cum venerit aestus judicii; sed afferens et offerens fructum quem fecit plurimum, id remunerationis accipiet ut floreat in aeternum ante Dominum, cui est honor et gloria per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 7. For this very purpose, my brothers, you whom carnal generation or worldly custom had planted in a waterless land, in a land of saltiness, the divine generation or the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High has transplanted upon the waters of refreshment; so that you, for whom formerly, because of barrenness, the axe and the fire were being prepared, now, planted in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God, may flourish, and bear fruit, and your fruit may remain. Are not the waters of refreshment the Scriptures of the Holy Spirit, on which we meditate day and night? Are not the waters of refreshment the tears of compunction, which have become bread for us day and night? Are not the waters of refreshment the Sacraments and supports of our salvation, by which we are fed and given drink at the altar? In all these, as it were through certain little streams, the fountain of wisdom which rises in the midst of paradise is channeled abroad, and divides its waters in the streets. 'I,' says Wisdom, 'came forth from paradise like a watercourse. I said: I will water my garden of plantings, I will make drunk the fruit of my offspring' (Eccli. XXIV, 41, 42). See, as you can gather from the very mouth of Wisdom bringing forth and planting, the garden of plantings is the congregation of her sons. 'For shall not I, who make others to bring forth, myself also bring forth?' says the Lord (Isai. LXVI, 9.). He himself brings forth, when he begets a good will; he plants, when he establishes a life; he waters, when he pours grace into the senses; he cultivates, when he applies discipline to conduct. 'Hear me, divine fruits, and bear fruit like the rose planted beside streams of water' (Eccli. XXXIX, 17). Send down your roots to the moisture of life, that is, to the love of the land of the living, not of this land in which all things grow old and rot. A tree cannot bear fruit that will endure unless it fixes its root above, in the heavenly places, so that it may seek and savor the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth. For as the natural philosophers say that man is an inverted tree, because the nerves of the body have their root and beginning in the crown of the head, I interpret this rather in this sense: that he ought to fix the root of love and desire in heaven, in the highest crown of all things, our head, Jesus Christ. Whoever sends his roots there, and continually drinks from that eternal fountain the sap of life and grace, will not fear when the heat of judgment comes; but bringing and offering the fruit that he has produced in abundance, he will receive this as his reward: that he may flourish forever before the Lord, to whom be honor and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The quotation on sitting under the beloved's shadow and tasting his fruit comes from Song of Songs 2:3; the edition prints Cant. II, 5.
