passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric places friendship with God before human favor. He considers humility, charity, reputation and fraternal correction, including the hostility that truthful correction can provoke. The sermon appears in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina under the feast of Saint Benedict. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO III.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON III.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De amicitia Dei prae omnibus quaerenda.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On seeking the friendship of God above all things.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Dilectus a Deo et hominibus (Eccli. XLV, 1). Paucis expressit bonum ac beatum virum, qualem nimirum constat dilectum Domini fuisse Benedictum. Paucis, inquam, comprehendit summam perfectionis, plenitudinem gratiae et virtutis, simulque beatitudinem vitae perennis, et consolationem praesentis. Quid enim deesse potest ad aeternam felicitatem illi qui a Deo diligitur? quid ad praesentem consolationem, illi qui ab hominibus diligitur? Illi nempe qui a Deo diligitur, etsi aliquid deesse videtur, non ob aliud deest, nisi ut nihil ei desit, et suo, ut putatur, defectu perfectior sit. Nam virtus in infirmitate perficitur. Paule, ait Dominus, sufficit tibi gratia mea (II Cor. XII, 9). Cui gratia Dei sufficit, sine damno gravi, imo cum lucro non mediocri aliquid gratiae deficit, quandoquidem ipse defectus et infirmitas virtutem perficit; et imminutio cujusdam gratiae, summam omnium gratiam Dei ampliorem ei et stabiliorem efficit. Longe fac, Domine, a servis tuis gratiam illam, quaecunque sit, quae adimere aut imminuere gratiam tui possit; unde videlicet aliquis, gloriosior in oculis suis, odiosior fiat in oculis tuis. Non est illa gratia, sed ira, illis plane quibus iratus es dari digna; quibus propter dolos posuisti talia, dejiciens eos dum allevantur, et elidens valide, dum super ventum ponuntur. Ut igitur illa sola gratia, sine qua nullus a te diligitur, salva nobis maneat, omnem aliam gratiam tua nobis gratia subtrahat, aut certe gratiam utendi simul conferat; quatenus habentes gratiam, per quam serviamus placentes cum metu et reverentia, de gratia muneris gratiam promereamur remuneratoris; et quanto quis fuerit gratiosior, tanto tibi fiat gratior.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "Beloved of God and men" (Eccli. XLV, 1). In few words he has expressed the good and blessed man, such as Benedict is known indeed to have been, the beloved of the Lord. In few words, I say, he has comprehended the sum of perfection, the fullness of grace and virtue, and at the same time the blessedness of life everlasting and the consolation of the present life. For what can be lacking to eternal felicity in him who is loved by God? What can be lacking to present consolation in him who is loved by men? Indeed, for him who is loved by God, even if something seems to be lacking, it is lacking for no other reason than that nothing may be lacking to him, and that by his seeming defect he may be made more perfect. For virtue is perfected in weakness. "Paul," says the Lord, "My grace is sufficient for thee" (II Cor. XII, 9). To him for whom the grace of God suffices, some grace is lacking without grave loss—indeed with no small gain—since the very defect and weakness perfects virtue; and the diminishing of a certain grace makes God's grace, the highest of all graces, fuller and more stable for him. Keep far, O Lord, from Thy servants that grace, whatever it be, which could take away or diminish Thy grace; whereby, namely, someone, more glorious in his own eyes, becomes more hateful in Thine eyes. That is not grace but wrath, truly worthy to be given to those with whom Thou art angry; to whom, on account of deceits, Thou hast appointed such things, casting them down while they are being raised up, and dashing them violently while they are set upon the wind. Therefore, that that grace alone, without which none is loved by Thee, may remain safe to us, let Thy grace withdraw from us every other grace, or at least grant together with it the grace of using it rightly; so that, having the grace by which we may serve, pleasing with fear and reverence, we may merit from the grace of the gift the grace of the Rewarder; and the more gracious anyone is, the more may he become pleasing to Thee.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Sane mirabili arte, sed mirabiliori charitate, prudens clementia clemensque prudentia Dei, saluti consuluit humanae, ut, cum cunctos diligat, non tamen facile de dilectione sua certos aut securos esse sinat; nec ob aliud magnam multitudinem dulcedinis suae timentibus se abscondat, nisi ut, dum semper custodit humiles, semper habeat amabiles. Sunt enim justi et sapientes, et opera eorum in manu Dei, et tamen nescit homo utrum amore an odio dignus sit; sed omnia in futurum servantur incerta (Eccli. IX, 1, 2) Moderator nempe omnium sic eis dispensat gratiam munerum et operum, ut ex quibusdam quae concedit, consolationem quod digni sint amore tribuat; ex quibusdam quae subtrahit, suspicionem ac metum quod odio digni sint injiciat. Consolatur, cum diluculo visitat; terret, cum subito probat. Nunc mortificat, nunc vivificat; nunc deducit ad inferos, nunc reducit. Nunc pauperem facit et ditat, nunc humiliat et sublevat (I Reg. II, 6, 7). Et in tanta vicissitudinum varietate tanto certius salutem nostram operatur, quanto nos incertiores de ea, cum majore metu ac tremore ei cooperamur. Ait quidem Paulus: Certus sum quia nihil me separabit a charitate Dei (Rom. VIII, 38, 39). Sed vere Paulus hic erat, non ego aut tu, quibus omnia in futurum servari expedit incerta. Paulus, inquam, hic erat qui hoc dicebat, cui nimirum et illud dicere competebat: Vivo jam non ego, vivit vero in me Christus (Galat. II, 20), qui scilicet ita totus in quemdam divinum conversus erat affectum, ut adhaerens Domino unus cum ipso esset spiritus. Vide tamen hunc ipsum Paulum, qui ita modo certus erat, alias trepidum ac sollicitum, et castigantem corpus suum, ne forte, cum aliis praedicaverit, ipse reprobus efficiatur (I Cor. IX, 27): vide etiam colaphizari a Satana (II Cor. XII, 7), ne forte extollatur. In ipso itaque Paulo jam tibi est videre quomodo omnis certitudo quae ad horam confortatur et convalescit de spiritus consolatione, item infirmatur et evanescit superveniente tentatione. Ego igitur miser et ipsa indignus vita, qua consolatione, qua fiducia me dignum esse amore praesumam, cui omnia et interiora et exteriora manifestum odium denuntiant; cujus vita, non tentatio, non militia est adversus peccatum, sed ultronea servitus peccati; qui tam mente quam carne servio legi peccati; qui cum prudentia carnis et amicitia mundi, quae ambae inimicae sunt Deo, foedus miserum pepigisse videor, plane foedus cum morte, pactum cum inferno? Scio tamen, scio qui dixit: Delebitur foedus vestrum cum morte, et pactum cum inferno non stabit (Isai. XXVIII, 18); quia nimirum inimicis Dei nil amicum esse poterit, et non mortem aut infernum, sed omnem quoque creaturam ad ultionem inimicorum zelus armabit. Quam beatus in die illo quicunque erit ille dilectus a Deo! quam laudabiles quibus tunc laus erit a Deo, quibus dicet evidenti rerum argumento: Vos amici mei estis, eo quod feceritis quae praecepi vobis! (Joan. XV, 14). Et haec quidem prima virtus, istud optimum gratiae munus, praecipuus vitae fructus: quia beatitudinis certissimum pignus, Dei scilicet amicitia promereri; quo propitio poterit homini aliquis inimicari, sed nihil proficiet inimicus in eo, et filius iniquitatis non apponet nocere ei (Psal. LXXXVIII, 23).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Indeed, by a wonderful art, but by a more wonderful charity, the prudent clemency and the clement prudence of God has taken counsel for human salvation, so that, although He loves all, He does not easily allow them to be certain or secure of His love; nor does He, for any other reason, hide from those who fear Him the great abundance of His sweetness, except that, while He always keeps them humble, He may always have them lovable. For there are just and wise men, and their works are in the hand of God, and yet man does not know whether he is worthy of love or of hatred; but all things are kept uncertain for the future (Eccli. IX, 1, 2). The Ruler of all things indeed so dispenses to them the grace of gifts and works, that from certain things which He grants, He gives the consolation that they are worthy of love; from certain things which He withdraws, He instills the suspicion and fear that they are worthy of hatred. He consoles when He visits at daybreak; He terrifies when He suddenly puts to the test. Now He brings death, now He brings life; now He leads down to the underworld, now He brings back. Now He makes poor and makes rich, now He humbles and lifts up (I Reg. II, 6, 7). And in so great a variety of changes, He works our salvation all the more surely, the more uncertain we are about it, since we cooperate with Him with greater fear and trembling. Paul indeed says: "I am certain that nothing shall separate me from the charity of God" (Rom. VIII, 38, 39). But truly this was Paul speaking, not I or you, for whom it is expedient that all things be kept uncertain for the future. Paul, I say, was the one who said this, to whom indeed it was also fitting to say: "I live, now not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Galat. II, 20)—he who was so wholly turned into a certain divine affection that, clinging to the Lord, he was one spirit with Him. Yet see this very Paul, who was thus certain at one moment, at other times fearful and anxious, chastising his own body, lest perhaps, when he had preached to others, he himself should become reprobate (I Cor. IX, 27): see him also buffeted by Satan (II Cor. XII, 7), lest perhaps he be exalted. In Paul himself, then, you may now see how all certainty which is strengthened for an hour and grows strong from the consolation of the spirit, likewise grows weak and vanishes when temptation comes upon it. I, therefore, wretched and unworthy even of life itself—with what consolation, with what confidence shall I presume myself worthy of love, I to whom all things, both inward and outward, proclaim manifest hatred; whose life is not a temptation, not a warfare against sin, but a willing servitude to sin; who serve the law of sin as much in mind as in flesh; who seem to have struck a wretched covenant with the prudence of the flesh and the friendship of the world, both of which are enemies to God—plainly a covenant with death, a pact with hell? Yet I know, I know Him who said: "Your covenant with death shall be done away, and your pact with hell shall not stand" (Isai. XXVIII, 18); because surely nothing can be friendly to the enemies of God, and zeal will arm not only death and hell but every creature as well for the vengeance upon enemies. How blessed on that day will whoever is beloved of God be! How praiseworthy will those be to whom praise shall then come from God, to whom He will say, with manifest proof of the fact: "You are my friends, because you have done what I have commanded you!" (Joan. XV, 14). And this indeed is the first virtue, this the best gift of grace, the chief fruit of life: because it is the most certain pledge of blessedness, namely, to merit the friendship of God; with God favorable to him, someone may indeed be an enemy to a man, but the enemy will profit nothing against him, and the son of iniquity shall not have power to hurt him further (Psal. LXXXVIII, 23).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Jam vero si post hanc et per hanc summam omnium causamque bonorum, gratiam etiam illam promerearis, ut, dilectus a Deo, etiam dilectus sis ab hominibus, quae consolatio est illa in miseriis hujus vitae, quae requies, quod gaudium, quae deliciae; praesertim si didiceris favore gratiae humanae non evanescere, sed exardescere ad diligendum Deum amplius, propter quem diligaris ab hominibus? Alioquin nempe si aliunde oriatur, vel alio referatur, quid est favor humanus, nisi ventus urens, aura corrumpens vel pestilens, latrunculus spolians, homicida insidians, coluber in via, cerastes in semita, mordens ungulas equi, ut cadat ascensor ejus retro? Vir quippe vanus erigitur in superbiam, et vanitate sensus sui, velut equo praecipiti, fertur in ruinam. Hujusmodi nimirum serpens vulnerat et subvertit vestigia, dum, veluti blandiens capiti, tenera illius facit laudari primordia. Haud secus, nisi fallor, contingit homini qui, antequam diligere sciat, diligi nimie affectat, et, antequam vel sibi ipsi amicus esse didicerit, amicos sibi omnes conciliare quaerit; facit divitias non cum judicio, in medio dierum suorum derelinquet eas, et in novissimo suo erit insipiens, cum omnes amici ejus spreverint eum, pro quibus sprevit ipse Deum. Tunc fiet sermo qui scriptus est: Quoniam Deus dissipavit ossa eorum qui hominibus placent: confusi sunt, quoniam Deus sprevit eos (Psal. LII, 6).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Now if, after this and through this love, supreme above all and the cause of good things, you should also merit that grace, that, being loved by God, you might also be loved by men, what consolation is that in the miseries of this life, what rest, what joy, what delight—especially if you have learned not to grow vain through human favor, but rather to be kindled to love God the more, on whose account you are loved by men? Otherwise, indeed, if it arises from elsewhere, or is referred to something else, what is human favor but a scorching wind, a corrupting or pestilent breeze, a thieving brigand, a lurking murderer, a serpent in the way, a horned snake in the path, biting the horse's heels so that its rider falls backward? For the vain man is lifted up into pride, and by the vanity of his own mind, as if by a headlong horse, is carried to ruin. This kind of serpent indeed wounds and overturns the footsteps, while, as if flattering the head, it makes his tender beginnings to be praised. Not otherwise, unless I am mistaken, does it happen to a man who, before he knows how to love, excessively desires to be loved, and, before he has even learned to be a friend to himself, seeks to win all men as friends to himself; he gathers riches without judgment, in the midst of his days he will abandon them, and in his last end he will be a fool, when all his friends have despised him, for whose sake he himself despised God. Then will be fulfilled the saying that is written: 'For God has scattered the bones of those who please men: they are confounded, because God has despised them' (Psal. LII, 6).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Primo itaque omnium illa, quae prima et finis est omnium, quaerenda est dilectio Dei, cujus merito digni simus etiam ab hominibus diligi; et cujus studio docti simus, dilectione hominum qualiter nos oporteat uti. Cum autem rem in tuto locaveris; ita scilicet firmato affectu mentis, ut nonnisi in Deo et propter Deum diligi velis: tunc omnino volo ut dulcedo morum tuorum, humilitas obsequiorum, honestas studiorum, ad omnem te commendet conscientiam hominum, ut ultro rapias affectus omnium, testimonio praediceris omnium; quatenus ipsa religio, quae te commendat, justa vicissitudine per te commendabilis fiat. Sic in te quoque filio adoptivo, Unigeniti complebitur oratio: Pater, clarifica Filium tuum, ut Filius tuus clarificet te (Joan. XVII, 1); dum videntes claritatem operum tuorum glorificabunt Patrem tuum. Neque id dicimus, quod inter dilectionem Dei et dilectionem proximi sit aliquis ordo temporis, quamvis sit ordo affectionis. Statim quippe ab initio et illam oportet observare, et istam non negligere; quando nec Deus sine proximo, nec proximus sine Deo vere potest diligi; quamvis ordinata affectio ignorare non possit quae de duabus dilectionibus praeponderet alteri, quae debeat alteri formam et modum praescribere, finemque praefigere. Sed hoc dicimus, quod aliud est amari, aliud amari studere. Quod profecto studium sicut periculose assumitur ab illis qui plus vanitate quam charitate blandi sunt, sic periculose negligitur ab his qui plus superbia quam sapientia austeri sunt. Quam ob rem beatum dixerunt, qui inter utrumque vitium, illius scilicet vanae amicabilitatis, et superbae severitatis, mediam tenere potuit regalem viam veritatis; id est ut, vera charitate plenus, nec per vanitatem hoc studium sectetur, nec per tumorem dedignetur.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Therefore, before all things, that love of God must be sought which is the first and the end of all things, by whose merit we may be worthy to be loved by men as well; and by whose discipline we may be taught how we ought to make use of the love of men. But when you have placed the matter in a safe position—that is, when the affection of your mind has been so fixed that you wish to be loved only in God and for God's sake—then I wholly desire that the sweetness of your character, the humility of your service, the uprightness of your pursuits, should commend you to the conscience of all men, so that you may win the affections of all unsought, and be proclaimed by the testimony of all; so that religion itself, which commends you, may by a just reciprocity become commendable through you. Thus in you too, as an adopted son, the prayer of the Only-begotten will be fulfilled: 'Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you' (Joan. XVII, 1); while men, seeing the splendor of your works, will glorify your Father. Nor do we say this as though there were some order of time between the love of God and the love of neighbor, although there is an order of affection. For from the very beginning one must both observe the former and not neglect the latter, since neither can God truly be loved without neighbor, nor neighbor without God; although a well-ordered affection cannot fail to know which of the two loves outweighs the other, which ought to prescribe form and measure to the other, and set its end before it. But this we say: that it is one thing to be loved, another to strive to be loved. Which pursuit indeed is dangerously undertaken by those who are winsome more from vanity than from charity, and is just as dangerously neglected by those who are austere more from pride than from wisdom. For this reason they have been called blessed who, between both vices—namely that of vain amiability and that of proud severity—have been able to hold the middle royal road of truth; that is, so that, being full of true charity, they neither pursue this pursuit through vanity, nor disdain it through arrogance.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Illa tamen est vis et natura veri amoris, ut, etiam cum non affectat, tamen efficiat se reamari: quoniam veritas, etiam sine alieno, suffragio facile se ad omnem conscientiam commendat, nisi dira malignae mentis obsistat nequitia, quae parata est sinistre interpretari omnia. Ad hunc tamen sanctum amorem conciliandum quidam proprium donum habent ex Deo; qui exhilarans facies eorum in oleo, perfudit eos quodam placore ac nitore gratioso, omnia tam facta quam dicta ipsorum gratificans in oculis omnium; cum multi qui forsitan non minus, imo et amplius amant, non facile eamdem gratiam inveniant. Ad omnes autem pertinet ut, providentes bona non solum coram Deo sed etiam coram hominibus (Rom. XII, 17 et II Cor. VII, 21), nec conscientiam negligant amore famae, nec famam fiducia conscientiae. Nam et de ipsa conscientia quomodo tibi blandiri potes, nisi sine querela sis inter fratres; imo, nisi te fratrem inter fratres in omni conversatione tua demonstres? Putas enim satis esse, si non scandalizas? Imo scandalizas, si non aedificas; si non, testimonium habens bonum intus et foris, quantum ad gradum tuum attinet, Deum ubique glorificas. Sane malis, quibus non placet nisi malum, quibus justus gravis est etiam ad videndum, si illis placere te non sinit, non tua negligentia (cum omnes etiam inimicos diligas), sed ipsorum nequitia, qui retribuunt mala pro bonis, odium pro dilectione tua; consolatur te qui ait. Beati eritis cum vos oderint homines (Luc. VI, 22), et ille qui ait quia, talibus si placeret, Christi servus non esset (Galat. I, 10).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Yet it is the force and nature of true love that, even when it does not aim at it, it nevertheless brings it about that it is loved in return: because truth, even without another's support, easily commends itself to every conscience, unless the dire wickedness of a malignant mind stands in the way, which is ready to interpret everything in the worst sense. Yet for the winning of this holy love, some have a particular gift from God; who, gladdening their faces with oil, has suffused them with a certain graciousness and gracious brightness, making both their deeds and their words pleasing in the eyes of all; while many who perhaps love no less—indeed even more—do not easily find the same grace. But it belongs to all to take thought for what is good, not only before God but also before men (Rom. XII, 17 et II Cor. VII, 21), neither neglecting conscience out of love of reputation, nor neglecting reputation out of confidence in conscience. For how can you flatter yourself even about your conscience itself, unless you are without reproach among the brethren—indeed, unless you show yourself a brother among brothers in all your conduct? Do you think it enough if you do not give scandal? Nay, you do give scandal if you do not build up; if you do not, having good testimony both within and without, as far as pertains to your rank, glorify God everywhere. Indeed, as for the wicked, whom nothing pleases but evil, to whom the just man is grievous even to look upon—if they do not allow you to please them, it is not through your negligence (since you love even your enemies), but through their own wickedness, who repay evil for good, hatred for your love; he consoles you who says, 'Blessed shall you be when men hate you' (Luc. VI, 22), and he who says that if he pleased such men, he would not be a servant of Christ (Galat. I, 10).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Verum illud miserabile est malum, omnique lacrymarum flumine plangendum, quod quidem saepius experiuntur non modo praelati, sed etiam subditi, qui fratres suos aemulantur Dei aemulatione; quod scilicet et boni, licet non ex ea parte qua sunt boni, bonos inveniuntur odisse. Oderunt corripientem in porta (Amos V, 10), et inimici hominis domestici ejus (Mich. VII, 6), ita ut etiam Paulus ingemiscat quod filiis et amicis inimicus factus sit, vera dicens (Galat. IV, 16). Ergo et ipse expertus est quod comicus ait, « Veritas odium parit (6); » imo et illud quod sponsa memorat: Filii matris meae pugnaverunt contra me (Cantic. I, 5), cum ego pugnarem pro eorum salute. O victrix regina, o triumphatrix magnifica, pugna, ne cedas, ne discedas, aut lassescas. Noli vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum (Rom. XII, 21). Sapientia vincit malitiam (Sap. VII, 30); quanto magis infirmitatem aut imprudentiam? Neque contradictionem carnalium, malitiam interpretari potest charitas spiritualium; sed magis ignorantiam, aut infirmitatem qua praeventi sunt. Quanquam nec ipsis Apostolis contumelia visa sit quod mali a Domino sunt appellati. Quare autem haec ita loquor, fratres mei, dilecti Deo et mihi? Nunquid quia malum hujusmodi suspicer in aliquo vestrum, contra quod mihi vel fratribus meis sit pugnandum? Nunquid enim aliquis invenitur in vobis, non dico rebellis, sed vel durus et intractabilis? Loquor haec non quia ita in vobis sit, sed ne aliquando sit; ne forte aliquando cuipiam aliqua infirmitas subrepat, ut quamcunque correptionem charitatis, nisi cum charitate suscipiat. Sic fiet ut tam is qui corripit, quam ille qui corripitur, dilectus sit a Deo et hominibus, et memoria utriusque in benedictione sit; quod meritis beati Benedicti patris nostri praestare dignetur ille singulariter benedictus Dei Patris Jesus Christus, qui est Deus benedictus in saecula. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. But that is a wretched evil, to be mourned with every flood of tears, which indeed not only superiors but also subjects often experience, who are zealous for their brothers with a godly zeal; namely, that even good men—though not in that respect in which they are good—are found to hate good men. "They hate him who reproves in the gate" (Amos V, 10), and "a man's enemies are those of his own household" (Mich. VII, 6), so that even Paul groans that he has become an enemy to his sons and friends by telling them the truth (Galat. IV, 16). Therefore he too experienced what the comic poet says, "Truth begets hatred"; indeed, he experienced also that which the Bride recalls: "The sons of my mother have fought against me" (Cantic. I, 5), while I was fighting for their salvation. O victorious queen, O magnificent triumphant one, fight on; do not yield, do not withdraw, nor grow weary. "Be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good" (Rom. XII, 21). "Wisdom overcomes malice" (Sap. VII, 30); how much more, then, weakness or imprudence? Nor can the charity of spiritual men interpret the opposition of carnal men as malice; but rather as ignorance, or as a weakness by which they have been overtaken. Although it did not even seem an insult to the Apostles themselves that they were called evil by the Lord. But why do I speak this way, my brothers, beloved of God and of me? Is it because I suspect such an evil in any of you, against which I or my brothers must fight? Is anyone found among you who is—I do not say rebellious—but even hard and intractable? I say these things not because it is so among you, but lest it ever be so; lest perhaps at some time some weakness should creep upon someone, so that he would not receive any correction of charity except with charity. Thus it will come about that both he who corrects and he who is corrected will be loved by God and by men, and the memory of each will be in blessing; which may he who is singularly blessed of God the Father, Jesus Christ, who is God blessed forever, deign to grant through the merits of our blessed father Benedict. Amen.

sermons.title: Saint Benedict Sermon III

sermons.author: Guerric of Igny
metadata: Guerric of Igny (collection attribution), Sermones per annum, SERMO IV., De lenitate et fide., in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier frères, 1879), cols. 111-116.

Jeremiah, verse 3 (printed locator; quotation from Jeremiah 5:3)

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric compares Benedict with Moses through faith and gentleness. He distinguishes living faith from feigned belief and connects vigilance before God with hope of the promised reward. The sermon appears in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina under the feast of Saint Benedict. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO IV.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON IV.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De lenitate et fide.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On meekness and faith.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. In fide et lenitate ipsius sanctum fecit illum (Eccli. XLV, 4). Haec quidem de Moyse scripta sunt, sed hodie beato Benedicto non incongrue, quantum arbitror, aptata sunt. Qui, cum omnino plenus fuerit Spiritu sanctorum, multo magis de spiritu Moysi credendus est habuisse non minimum. Si enim Dominus de spiritu Moysi tulit, et posuit super omnem illam suffraganeam turbam seniorum, qui in partem ministerii sunt asciti (Num. XI, 24-27), quanto magis super istum qui plenitudinem totius ministerii tanto verius quanto spiritualius implevit? Ille dux fuit exeuntium de Aegypto; iste, renuntiantium saeculo: legislator ille, legislator et iste: ille tantum minister litterae occidentis; iste, spiritus vivificantis: ille ad duritiam cordis Judaeorum dedit eis justificationes non bonas, praeter pauca moralia; iste solam puritatem evangelicam simplicemque morum tradidit disciplinam: ille tam multa scribit intellectu difficilia, factu impossibilia, vel inutilia; iste rectissimam vitae scribit Regulam, sermone luculentam, discretione praecipuam. Denique dux ille filiorum Israel, quos de Aegypto eduxit, in requiem promissam non induxit; dux noster recta via, orientis tramite, tanquam signifer exercitus monachorum hodie praecessit nos in regnum coelorum. Itaque non erit absurdum si credatur illius adaequasse meritum, cujus invenitur etiam superasse ministerium. Nec incongrue videbitur ad ipsum esse translatum quod de illo scriptum legitur: In fide et lenitate ipsius sanctum illum Dominus; praesertim cum harum praecipue virtutum, fidei scilicet et lenitatis, nobis ipse magister sit, qui nequaquam aliter vixit quam docuit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "In his faith and meekness he made him holy" (Eccli. XLV, 4). These words indeed were written of Moses, but today, as far as I judge, they have not been unfittingly applied to blessed Benedict. For since he was altogether full of the Spirit of the saints, he is all the more to be believed to have had no small share of the spirit of Moses. For if the Lord took from the spirit of Moses and placed it upon that whole assisting crowd of elders who were taken into a part of his ministry (Num. XI, 24-27), how much more upon him who fulfilled the fullness of that whole ministry all the more truly as he fulfilled it more spiritually? That man was the leader of those going out of Egypt; this one, of those renouncing the world: that man was a lawgiver, and this one also a lawgiver: that man was only a minister of the letter that kills; this one, of the spirit that gives life: that man, on account of the hardness of the Jews' hearts, gave them statutes that were not good, apart from a few moral precepts; this one handed down only the purity of the Gospel and a simple discipline of morals: that man writes so many things difficult to understand, impossible or useless to do; this one writes a most upright Rule of life, brilliant in style, outstanding in discretion. Finally, that leader of the sons of Israel, whom he led out of Egypt, did not bring them into the promised rest; our leader, by the straight way, along the path of the rising sun, has today gone before us like a standard-bearer of an army of monks into the kingdom of heaven. Therefore it will not be absurd if it is believed that his merit equaled that of the one whose ministry he is even found to have surpassed. Nor will it seem unfitting that what is read as written of that man should be transferred to him: "The Lord made him holy in his faith and meekness"; especially since he himself is our master chiefly of these virtues, namely faith and meekness, he who never lived otherwise than he taught.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Quid enim praeclarius illius fide, qui in aetate puerili mundum sibi arridentem irridens, tam mundi quam corporis sui florem quasi jam aridum calcavit, magis appetens pro Deo mala mundi perpeti, quam in eo temporaliter prosperari? Quid similius illi fidei Moysi, quam Apostolus commendans ait: Fide Moyses grandis factus negavit se filium filiae Pharaonis, magis eligens affligi cum populo Dei, quam temporalis peccati habere jucunditatem (Hebr. XI, 24, 25)? Quid autem sanctius lenitate Patris nostri, qui nec malitia falsorum fratrum vitae ipsius insidiantium: et pro vino venenum propinantium, potuit exasperari? Moysen quidem Scriptura praedicat mittissimum fuisse super omnes homines qui morabantur in terra (Num. XII, 13); nunquid tamen exacerbatum spiritum ejus negat? nunquid non iratum et valde iratum adversus aemulos memorat (Id. XVI, 15)? Hujus autem magistri nostri mansuetudinem, non solum erga maledicos, sed etiam erga maleficos, mirabilem me legisse memini, iracundiam non memini. Quanquam nec in ipso, sicut nec in Moyse, praeconio sanctae lenitatis praejudicet, si justus zelo contra peccantes fervet, sine quo lenitas tepor aut timiditas est. Quomodo namque lenitas illa sanctum quempiam faceret, quae in Heli, qui alius sanctus erat, damnata est? (I Reg. II). Fratres, habete pacem inter vos, mandat ille Magister pacificus et lenis; prius tamen praemittit: habete salem in vobis (Marc. IX, 49); sciens nimirum pacis lenitatem vitiorum esse nutricem, nisi prius asperitas zeli mordacem eis insperserit salem; sicut et carnes vermescere facit clementia temporis, nisi desiccaverit eas fervor salis. Habete itaque pacem inter vos, sed quae sale condita sit sapientiae; sectamini lenitatem, sed quae ferveat fide.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. For what is more splendid than the faith of him who, in his boyhood, mocking the world that smiled upon him, trampled underfoot the flower both of the world and of his own body as though already withered, desiring rather to suffer the evils of the world for God's sake than to prosper temporally in it? What is more like that faith of Moses which the Apostle commends, saying: "By faith Moses, when he was grown a man, denied himself to be the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to have the pleasure of temporal sin" (Hebr. XI, 24, 25)? But what is holier than the meekness of our Father, who could not be provoked even by the malice of false brothers plotting against his very life, and offering him poison instead of wine? Scripture indeed proclaims that Moses was the meekest of all men who dwelt on the earth (Num. XII, 13); yet does it not also record his spirit as exasperated? Does it not relate him as angry, and very angry, against his rivals (Id. XVI, 15)? But I recall having read of the wonderful gentleness of this our master, not only toward those who spoke evil of him, but even toward those who did evil to him; I do not recall any anger in him. Although neither in him, nor in Moses, should this prejudice the praise of holy meekness, if a just man burns with zeal against sinners, without which meekness is mere lukewarmness or timidity. For how could that meekness which was condemned in Eli, who was otherwise a holy man, have made anyone holy? (I Reg. II). "Brothers, have peace among yourselves," that peaceful and gentle Master commands; yet he first says beforehand: "Have salt in yourselves" (Marc. IX, 49); knowing surely that the meekness of peace is a nurse of vices, unless the sharpness of zeal first sprinkles them with biting salt; just as the mildness of the weather causes flesh to breed worms, unless the heat of salt dries it out. Have peace, then, among yourselves, but peace seasoned with the salt of wisdom; pursue meekness, but meekness that burns with faith.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. In fide et lenitate vos quoque sancti eritis; nec jam lenitas suspecta erit, si fides praecesserit: tantum fides non ficta, sed vera sit; fides non mortua, sed viva et vivida sit. Non modo viva vel vivida, sed et constans et intrepida fides erat Moysi, de quo Paulus scribit: Fide reliquit Aegyptum, non veritus animositatem regis. Animosi sunt reges, sed animosior est fides, quippe quae potentiam eorum nullam esse videt, ac per hoc omnem persequentium insaniam secura, quasi superior, irridet; promptior et fortior ad perferendum, quam illorum furor ad persequendum. Duo sane commendare mihi videtur Apostolus in illa memorabili fide Moysi, cui occasione lectionis hodiernae comparandam diximus fidem sancti patris nostri Benedicti: scilicet quod idem Moyses, qui fidei exemplum factus est, hujus mundi contempsit prospera, nec timuit adversa. Prospera contempsit, majores divitias aestimans thesauris Aegyptiorum improperium Christi: adversa non timuit, non veritus scilicet animositatem regis. Ad utrumque vero causam Apostolus subjunxit, unde scilicet id potuerit, ut discamus unde fides nostra infirmetur in nobis. Majores divitias reputabat thesauris Aegyptiorum improperium Christi: aspiciebat enim, inquit, in remunerationem. Non est veritus animositatem regis: invisibilem enim, inquit, tanquam videns sustinuit (Hebr. XI, 27, 26). Nimirum inde fit ut nihil reputentur temporalia, si prae oculis habeantur aeterna; inde fit ut facile potestas contemnatur humana, si tanquam semper imminens potestas timeatur divina. Utrumque vero sola fides agit, cujus tam vividi, tam perspicaces sunt oculi, ut et in ea quae futura sunt prospectum vivaciter porrigat, et in ea quae, licet praesentia sint, occulta tamen, intuitum perspicaciter figat. Fidei siquidem, quam aeternus Spiritus illuminat, nec mora temporis, nec moles corporis praejudicare potest quin et tempus praecedat, praesumendo quod futurum est, et corpus excedat, intuendo quod spiritus est. Gemina siquidem est fidei virtus, contemplantis non ea quae videntur, sed quae non videntur; sicut gemina est ratio eorum quae non videntur. Aut enim ideo non videntur quia praesentia non sunt, aut ideo quia, etsi praesentia sunt, spiritualia sunt. Praesentia non sunt bona futura quae promittuntur; praesens est, sed occultus est, quia spiritus est, Deus ipse qui promittit vel minatur. Porro fides, quia est substantia sperandarum rerum, bona futura, quae sperat, quasi praesentia praesumit, et jam quasi subsistere in corde credentis facit. Item quia est argumentum non apparentium (Ibid. 1), Deum, etsi non appareat, praesentem tamen esse sibi coarguit, probat et convincit. Illi qui dicebat: Qui conresuscitavit et consedere fecit in coelestibus in Christo (Ephes. II, 6), fides erat substantia rerum sperandarum; illi qui invisibilem tanquam videns sustinebat (Hebr. XI, 27), argumentum erat non apparentium. Qui enim dicebat: Spe salvi facti sumus (Rom. VIII, 24), nonne quod sperabat et per patientiam exspectabat, jam per fidem in corde suo subsistere demonstrabat? Et qui proponebat Dominum in conspectu suo semper, nonne persuasum tenebat, argumento fidei, eum praesentem esse, qui non apparebat? (Psal. XV, 8).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. In faith and gentleness you too will be holy; and gentleness will no longer be suspect, if faith has gone before it—provided only that the faith be not feigned but true, not dead but living and vigorous. Not merely living or vigorous, but also steadfast and fearless was the faith of Moses, of whom Paul writes: "By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the fierceness of the king." Kings are fierce, but faith is fiercer, since it sees that their power is nothing, and therefore, secure as one who is superior, it laughs at all the madness of persecutors; it is more ready and stronger to endure than their fury is to persecute. Two things, surely, the Apostle seems to me to commend in that memorable faith of Moses, which, on the occasion of today's reading, we said should be compared to the faith of our holy father Benedict: namely, that this same Moses, who became an example of faith, both despised the prosperities of this world and did not fear its adversities. He despised prosperity, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of the Egyptians; he did not fear adversity, that is, he was not afraid of the fierceness of the king. For both the Apostle adds the cause, namely whence he was able to do this, so that we may learn whence our faith grows weak in us. He esteemed the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of the Egyptians: "for he looked," it says, "unto the reward." He did not fear the fierceness of the king: "for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible" (Hebr. XI, 27, 26). Surely it comes about from this that temporal things are reckoned as nothing, if eternal things are kept before the eyes; it comes about from this that human power is easily held in contempt, if divine power is feared as always imminent. But faith alone does both of these things, whose eyes are so lively, so keen-sighted, that it both stretches its gaze vividly toward things that are future, and fixes its sight keenly upon things which, although present, are nonetheless hidden. For to faith, which the eternal Spirit illumines, neither the delay of time nor the bulk of the body can be an obstacle, so that it both goes before time, presuming what is to come, and goes beyond the body, beholding what is spirit. The power of faith is indeed twofold, contemplating not those things which are seen, but those which are not seen; just as the reason of things not seen is also twofold. For either they are not seen because they are not present, or they are not seen because, although present, they are spiritual. The future goods that are promised are not present; but he who promises or threatens, God himself, is present, yet hidden, because he is spirit. Furthermore, faith, because it is the substance of things to be hoped for, presumes the future goods which it hopes for as if they were present, and makes them, as it were, already subsist in the heart of the believer. Likewise, because it is the evidence of things not appearing (ibid. 1), it proves, demonstrates, and convinces that God, even though he does not appear, is nevertheless present to it. To him who said: "Who raised us up together, and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ" (Ephes. II, 6), faith was the substance of things to be hoped for; to him who endured, as seeing him who is invisible (Hebr. XI, 27), faith was the evidence of things not appearing. For did not he who said, "We are saved by hope" (Rom. VIII, 24), show that what he hoped for and awaited through patience already subsisted in his heart through faith? And did not he who set the Lord always in his sight hold it firmly persuaded, by the evidence of faith, that he who did not appear was present? (Psal. XV, 8).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Huic fidei prorsus aptissime congruit quod Scriptura dicit: Justus ex fide vivit (Habac. II, 4, et Rom. I, 17). Haec enim justum facit, justumque custodit, et, ut vivat in aeternum, interim spei gaudio pascit. Quid enim sic hominem a peccato revocat et servat sicut fides, quae invisibilem tanquam videns sustinet et observat? quid ita spe gaudentem facit sicut fides, quae semper in remunerationem aspicit? Nos enim, fratres, quare negligentes sumus, nisi quia praesentiam Judicis nostri minus vigilanter intendimus? aut quare tristitia pene absorbemur, nisi quia remunerationem promissam minus fideliter cogitamus? Haec siquidem duo mala sunt, negligentia scilicet et tristitia, quibus miserabiliter infidelitas nostra laborat; quia videlicet aut negligimus mandata, aut, si necessitate timoris a negligentia coercemur, nequaquam hilariter operamur, nec, sicut fides postulat, spe remunerationis in labore consolamur. Credere, inquit, oportet accedentes ad Deum quia est, et inquirentibus se remunerator est (Hebr. XI, 6). Si non dissimulemus quia est, habemus custodiam timoris; si non dissimulemus quia inquirentibus se remunerator est, habemus consolationem spei. Ubi custodia timoris, nullus locus negligentiae; ubi consolatio spei, nullus locus tristitiae. Sicut autem de fide, qua Deus esse creditur, timor salutis nascitur, ita cum minime creditur, aut dissimulatur, omnibus malis frena laxantur. Quare enim corrupti et abominabiles facti sunt in iniquitatibus, nisi quia dixit ille generalis insipiens in corde suo: Non est Deus (Psal. LII, 2, 1)? aut certe si nescire Deum non permittitur, non est timor Dei ante oculos ejus, sed dolose agit in conspectu ejus, dissimulans quod novit invitus, ut inveniatur iniquitas ejus ad odium (Psal. XXXV, 2, 3). Merito prorsus dolosus ad odium, qui ignorantiam Dei non habet, sed odium. Quomodo enim non odit Deum, cujus declinat aspectum, contemnit imperium, vellet non esse judicium? Ignorans quidem ignorabitur, odiens autem et odietur. Ille reprobabitur veritate judicii, in istum vindicabitur severitate odii.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. To this faith what Scripture says applies most fittingly: "The just man lives by faith" (Habac. II, 4, et Rom. I, 17). For faith makes a man just, and keeps him just, and meanwhile, that he may live forever, feeds him with the joy of hope. For what so recalls a man from sin and keeps him from it as faith, which, as though seeing the Invisible One, endures and keeps watch? What so fills a man with the joy of hope as faith, which always looks toward the reward? For why, brothers, are we negligent, except because we attend less watchfully to the presence of our Judge? Or why are we almost swallowed up by sadness, except because we think less faithfully upon the promised reward? These indeed are two evils—negligence and sadness—under which our unfaithfulness miserably labors; for either we neglect the commandments, or, if we are restrained from negligence by the necessity of fear, we by no means work cheerfully, nor, as faith requires, do we console ourselves in our labor with the hope of reward. "It is necessary," he says, "that he who comes to God believe that he exists, and that he is a rewarder to those who seek him" (Hebr. XI, 6). If we do not pretend otherwise but believe that he exists, we have the guard of fear; if we do not pretend otherwise but believe that he is a rewarder to those who seek him, we have the consolation of hope. Where there is the guard of fear, there is no room for negligence; where there is the consolation of hope, there is no room for sadness. But just as from the faith by which God is believed to exist, a saving fear is born, so when he is not believed in at all, or is dissembled, the reins are loosed to every evil. For why are men become corrupt and abominable in their iniquities, except because that universal fool said in his heart, "There is no God" (Psal. LII, 2, 1)? Or certainly, if it is not permitted him not to know God, then "the fear of God is not before his eyes," but he deals deceitfully in his sight, dissembling what he unwillingly knows, "that his iniquity may be found unto hatred" (Psal. XXXV, 2, 3). Rightly indeed is he deceitful unto hatred, who has not ignorance of God, but hatred. For how does he not hate God, whose gaze he avoids, whose command he despises, whose judgment he would wish not to exist? He who is ignorant will indeed be ignored; but he who hates will also be hated. The former will be condemned by the truth of judgment; upon the latter vengeance will be taken by the severity of hatred.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Adeo, fratres, periculosior est fides ficta, fide dolosa, quae se ipsam dissimulat, quam fides nulla. Fides nulla, per insipientiam dicit in corde suo: Non est Deus; fides ficta per nequitiam dolose agit in conspectu ejus, et se scire Deum vel sciri a Deo dissimulat; dum sciens et prudens, imo imprudens et impudens sub oculis ejus peccat. Nescio tamen quomodo possit dici fides, quae fictos et dolosos potius facit quam fideles. Scio quidem quia confessione fidei plena est terra, sed tamen audio prophetam plangentem, quia periit fides de terra (Jerem. VII, 28). Putas enim, Filius hominis si nunc veniret, inveniret fidem super terram (Luc. XVIII, 8)? Nunquid fidem reputaret hanc fidem fictam negligentium et contemnentium, qua levius damnat caecitatem infidelium, qua meliorem judicat credulitatem daemonum? Daemones credunt et contremiscunt (Jacob. II, 19); homines credunt nec contremiscunt. Daemones quem credunt verentur; homines dum quem credunt, nec timent nec verentur, gravius de contemptu judicantur. Non fallamur ergo, fratres, generali nomine fidei, quasi quaecunque fides ad justitiam debeat reputari; sed meminerimus Doctor gentium in fide et veritate, qualem definierit fidem, qua Deo est placendum: Fides, inquiens, est substantia rerum sperandarum argumentum non apparentium. Haec est fides quae per dilectionem operatur; ut, suadente conscientia meritorum, de fide spes nascatur, fidesque supponatur velut subjectum et fundamentum, cui superaedificentur bona aeterna, quae speranda sunt. Sine ista fide impossibile est placere Deo (Hebr. XI, 1, 6), et cum ista impossibile est displicere Deo. Oculi tui Domine, respiciunt fidem (Jerem. 3 v.), dixit ille qui jugiter in conspectu tuo stabat per fidem. Omnino juste et merito. Prorsus debita vicissitudo, ut oculi tui, Domine, respiciant fidem, quia oculi mei semper ad Dominum fidelem.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. So much, brothers, is a feigned faith, a deceitful faith that dissembles itself, more dangerous than no faith at all. No faith at all, through folly, says in its heart, "There is no God"; feigned faith, through wickedness, deals deceitfully in his sight, and pretends either that it does not know God or that it is not known by God; while, knowingly and deliberately—nay, imprudently and shamelessly—it sins under his eyes. Yet I do not know how that can be called faith which makes men feigning and deceitful rather than faithful. I know indeed that the earth is full of the confession of faith, but yet I hear the prophet lamenting, because "faith has perished from the earth" (Jerem. VII, 28). Do you suppose that if the Son of Man came now, he would find faith upon the earth? (Luc. XVIII, 8). Would he reckon as faith this feigned faith of the negligent and the contemptuous, compared with which he condemns unbelievers' blindness more lightly and judges demons' belief better? "The demons believe and tremble" (Jacob. II, 19); men believe and do not tremble. The demons fear him whom they believe; men, while they believe him whom they fear not and do not revere, are more gravely judged for their contempt. Let us not, then, brothers, be deceived by the general name of faith, as though any faith whatsoever ought to be reckoned unto righteousness; but let us remember how the Doctor of the Gentiles defined, in faith and truth, the kind of faith by which God is to be pleased: "Faith," he says, "is the substance of things to be hoped for, the evidence of things not appearing." This is the faith that works through love; so that, with the consciousness of merits giving assurance, hope may be born from faith, and faith may be set beneath it as subject and foundation, upon which the eternal goods that are to be hoped for are built. "Without this faith it is impossible to please God" (Hebr. XI, 1, 6), and with it, it is impossible to displease God. "Your eyes, Lord, look upon faith" (Jerem. 3 v.), said he who stood continually in your sight through faith. Altogether justly and rightly. It is indeed a fitting exchange, that your eyes, Lord, should look upon faith, since my eyes are ever toward the faithful Lord.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Nos autem, fratres, si tanquam sine fide simus, Deum post dorsum nostrum ponimus, ut, dissimulantes timorem ejus, in vanitates potius respiciamus, quo merito nos respiciendos putamus? Imo respiciemur, sed quo vultu? Vultus Domini super facientes mala (Psal. XXXIII, 17); sed quam iratus, quam terribilis, quam importabilis, tunc demum scietur, quando fugient qui oderunt eum a facie ejus. Et a facie tua, Domine, quo fugient, nisi in tenebras exteriores, in illud chaos et abyssum ignis et caliginis? Tunc enim dicent montibus, Cadite super nos; et collibus, Operite nos (Luc. XXIII, 30), levius aestimantes absorberi voragine inferni, quam sustinere faciem Dei irati. Enim vero tunc stabunt justi in magna constantia; tunc fides, quae modo sollicita stat in conspectu Domini ad videndam voluntatem ipsius, secura stabit ad videndam gloriam ejus. Vigilate, fratres, state in fide (I Cor. XVI, 13). Quem fides timore sollicitat, non potest dormitare per negligentiam; quem fides in spe radicat, non potest titubare per diffidentiam. Omnia autem vestra in charitate fiant, ut fidei lenitas jungatur, quatenus de unoquoque vestrum dicatur, In fide et lenitate ipsius sanctum fecit illum Dominus (Eccli. XLV, 4); quod ipse praestet Sanctus sanctorum, qui vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. But we, brothers, if we are as though without faith, placing God behind our backs so that, disregarding fear of him, we look instead toward vanities—with what justice do we think we deserve to be looked upon? Indeed we shall be looked upon, but with what face? "The face of the Lord is against those who do evil" (Psal. XXXIII, 17); but how angry, how terrible, how unbearable that face will be, will only then be known, when those who hated him flee from before his face. And from your face, Lord, where will they flee, except into outer darkness, into that chaos and abyss of fire and gloom? For then they will say to the mountains, "Fall on us," and to the hills, "Cover us" (Luc. XXIII, 30), judging it lighter to be swallowed up in the chasm of hell than to endure the face of an angry God. But then indeed the just will stand in great steadfastness; then faith, which now stands anxiously in the sight of the Lord to see his will, will stand secure to see his glory. Watch, brothers, stand firm in faith (I Cor. XVI, 13). He whom faith troubles with fear cannot slumber through negligence; he whom faith roots in hope cannot waver through distrust. But let all your things be done in charity, so that gentleness may be joined to faith, so that it may be said of each one of you, "In his faith and gentleness the Lord made him holy" (Eccli. XLV, 4); which may he grant, the Holy One of holies, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition prints mittissimum, where mitissimum (most gentle) is expected.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The description of Moses as the meekest of men comes from Numbers 12:3; the edition prints Num. XII, 13.

passages.label: Editorial note

metadata:
Guerric of Igny (collection attribution), Sermones per annum, SERMO, In verba Cantici canticorum: « Quae habitas in hortis, amici auscultant, fac me audire vocem tuam. »
(Cant. VIII, 13.), in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier frères, 1879), cols. 210-214.
Internet Archive, 2011; PIMS, University of Toronto; University of Toronto funding.
Psalm 103:31 (historical numbering; printed locator; passage from verse 34)

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric takes the Bridegroom's words "You who dwell in the gardens, the friends are listening; let me hear your voice" and declines them for himself, as one who dwells among the tombs of the flesh. The brothers dwell in gardens when they meditate on Scripture, and Christ, the true gardener, plants and waters the Church. Paul walked in the gardens of paradise and sang of Christ to the friends who listened. The words call the devout to psalmody and prayer, with the angels listening, and the preacher to speak, with the faithful listening. The sermon follows the All Saints sermon in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina and carries no liturgical heading. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text:
In verba Cantici canticorum: « Quae habitas in hortis, amici auscultant, fac me audire vocem tuam. »
(Cant. VIII, 13.)

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the Words of the Song of Songs: "You who dwell in the gardens, the friends are listening; let me hear your voice." (Cant. VIII, 13.)

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. In conventu sodalium et amicorum, id est, Ecclesia sanctorum, cujus vocem deceat audiri, sponsus ipse sponsae loquens, innuit cum ait: Quae habitas in hortis, amici auscultant, fac me audire vocem tuam. Non sum ego cui hoc dictum debeat videri: non sum qui habitem in hortis; magis mihi videor esse de illis qui habitant in sepulcris. Corpora enim peccatorum, quid sunt nisi sepulcra mortuorum? Qui ergo dediti sunt corporibus suis, non in hortis habitant, sed in sepulcris: Deumque exasperant, donec qui educit vinctos in fortitudine, forti voce inclamet, Lazari, veni foras; suisque discipulis super eo praecipiat, Solvite eum et sinite abire (Joan. XI, 43, 44). Magna sane differentia est sepulcrorum et hortorum. Haec plena omni spurcitia et ossibus mortuorum; illi, omni suavitate et gratia florum, aut fructuum. Quid enim si aliquando sepulcra videntur in hortis? Nam et Dominus in horto sepultus fuit. Etsi enim sepulcra in hortis, nunquid tamen horti in sepulcris? Ita fortassis, sed in sepulcris justorum. Ibi plane vernabit gratissima quaedam amoenitas hortorum, verno scilicet illo tempore resurrectionis eorum, cum reflorebit caro eorum, et non solum ossa justi sicut herba germinabunt, sed et totus justus germinabit sicut lilium, et florebit in aeternum ante Dominum. Non sic impii, non sic, qui sepultura asini sepeliuntur (Jerem. XXII, 19), et sine omni spe melioris resurrectionis subditi corruptioni, hac praesenti futuram auspicantur. De sepulcris eorum dicere coeperam, quod quantum a spurcitia illorum abhorret florentium species hortorum, tantum, imo incomparabiliter amplius distat oblectatio spiritualium a voluptate gaudiorum carnalium.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. In the assembly of companions and friends, that is, the Church of the saints, whose voice it is fitting should be heard, the Bridegroom himself, speaking to the Bride, hints at this when he says: You who dwell in the gardens, the friends are listening; let me hear your voice. I am not one to whom this should seem to be said: I am not one who dwells in gardens; I seem to myself rather to be among those who dwell in tombs. For what are the bodies of sinners but tombs of the dead? Those, then, who are given over to their bodies do not dwell in gardens but in tombs, and they provoke God to anger, until he who leads forth the bound in strength cries out with a mighty voice, "Lazarus, come forth," and commands his disciples concerning him, "Loose him and let him go" (Joan. XI, 43, 44). There is indeed a great difference between tombs and gardens. The one is full of all filth and the bones of the dead; the other, of all the sweetness and grace of flowers or fruits. For what if tombs are sometimes seen in gardens? For even the Lord was buried in a garden. Though tombs may be in gardens, are gardens therefore in tombs? Perhaps so—but in the tombs of the just. There, surely, a most pleasing charm of gardens will bloom, namely in that springtime of their resurrection, when their flesh will flower again, and not only will the bones of the just sprout like grass, but the whole just person will sprout like a lily, and will flourish forever before the Lord. Not so the wicked, not so those who are buried with the burial of an ass (Jerem. XXII, 19), and who, subject to corruption without any hope of a better resurrection, in this present corruption begin the corruption to come. I had begun to speak of their tombs, to say that as much as the appearance of flourishing gardens recoils from their filth, so much—indeed incomparably more—does the delight of spiritual things differ from the pleasure of carnal joys.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Vos igitur, ni fallor, estis qui in hortis habitatis, qui scilicet in lege Domini meditamini die ac nocte, et quot libros legitis, tot hortos perambulatis; quot sententias eligitis, tot poma carpitis. Et beati quibus omnia poma nova et vetera servata sunt: id est, tam prophetarum, quam evangelistarum, vel apostolorum eloquia reposita sunt, ut et unicuique vestrum illud sponsae ad sponsum videatur dictum, Omnia poma, nova et vetera, dilecte mi, servavi tibi (Cantic. VII, 13). Scrutamini igitur Scripturas. Vos enim non falso vitam in ipsis putatis vos habere, qui nihil aliud in illis quaeritis quam Christum, cui testimonium perhibent Scripturae. Beati plane qui scrutantur testimonia ejus; in toto corde exquirunt eum. Mirabilia testimonia tua, Domine; ideo scrutata est ea anima mea (Psal. CXVIII, 2, 129). Scrutinio quidem opus est, non solum ut eruantur mystica, sed etiam ut sugantur moralia. Ideoque vos, qui perambulatis hortos Scripturarum, nolite negligenter et otiose transvolare; sed scrutantes singula, velut apes sedulae mel de floribus, spiritum de sermonibus colligite. Spiritus enim meus, inquit Jesus, super mel dulcis, et haereditas mea super mel et favum (Eccli. XXIV, 27). Ita probantes quid sapiat manna absconditum, eructabitis illud Davidicum: Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua! super mel et favum ori meo (Psal. CXVIII, 103).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. You, then, unless I am mistaken, are they who dwell in gardens, who meditate on the law of the Lord day and night, and for as many books as you read, so many gardens you walk through; for as many sentences as you choose, so many fruits you pluck. And blessed are those for whom all fruits, new and old, are kept in store: that is, the sayings of the prophets, as well as of the evangelists and apostles, are laid up, so that to each of you that word of the Bride to the Bridegroom may seem said: "All fruits, new and old, my beloved, I have kept for you" (Cantic. VII, 13). Search the Scriptures, then. For you do not falsely suppose that you have life in them, you who seek in them nothing other than Christ, to whom the Scriptures bear witness. Blessed indeed are they who search his testimonies; they seek him with their whole heart. "Wonderful are your testimonies, O Lord; therefore has my soul searched them" (Psal. CXVIII, 2, 129). There is indeed need for searching, not only that mystical meanings may be dug out, but also that moral lessons may be sucked out. Therefore you who walk through the gardens of the Scriptures, do not fly over them carelessly and idly; but searching out each thing, like busy bees gathering honey from flowers, gather spirit from the words. For "my spirit," says Jesus, "is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance above honey and the honeycomb" (Eccli. XXIV, 27). Thus, proving what the hidden manna tastes like, you will belch forth that word of David: "How sweet are your words to my palate! above honey and the honeycomb to my mouth" (Psal. CXVIII, 103).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Ab his hortis in alios, ubi requies secretior et voluptas beatior, et species mirabilior, sponsus, ni fallor, vos introducit, cum intentos laudibus suis in voce exsultationis et confessionis, rapit in locum tabernaculi admirabilis usque ad domum Dei, lucem scilicet inaccessibilem, ubi habitat, ubi pascit, ubi cubat in meridie. Si enim devotio psallentium et orantium habet aliquid de illa pia curiositate quaerentium, Rabbi, ubi habitas? puto quia merentur audire, Venite et videte. Venerunt, inquit, et viderunt, et apud eum manserunt die illo (Joan. I, 38, 39). Quandiu apud Patrem luminum sumus, apud quem non est transmutatio, nec vicissitudinis obumbratio; noctem nescimus, tantummodo die beato fruimur. Cum inde labimur, in noctem nostram recidimus. Heu mihi! quam cito defecerunt dies mei, quam cito sicut fenum arui, qui quandiu fui in horto cum illo, sicut paradisus Dei virui et florui! Cum illo hortus voluptatis: sine illo locus horroris et vastae solitudinis. Existimo enim qui in hortum illius intrat, quod et ipse hortus fiat; sitque anima illius velut hortus irriguus, ut et sponsus in laudem ejus dicat: Hortus conclusus, soror mea sponsa (Cant. IV, 12). An non sunt hortus, in quibus fit quod ipse hortulanus loquitur plantationi, quam plantavit Pater suus? Audite me, inquit, divini fructus, et quasi rosa plantata super rivos aquarum fructificate (Eccli. XXXIX, 17). Quasi Libanus, odorem suavitatis habete. Florete flores quasi lilium, date odorem, et frondete in gratiam.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. From these gardens into others, where the rest is more secret and the pleasure more blessed, and the beauty more wonderful, the Bridegroom, unless I am mistaken, leads you in, when, as you are intent upon his praises in a voice of exultation and confession, he snatches you away into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, that is, the inaccessible light, where he dwells, where he feeds, where he lies down at midday. For if the devotion of those singing psalms and praying has something of that holy curiosity of those who seek, "Rabbi, where do you dwell?" I think that they deserve to hear, "Come and see." "They came," it says, "and saw, and remained with him that day" (Joan. I, 38, 39). As long as we are with the Father of lights, with whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration, we know no night; we enjoy only the blessed day. When we slip away from there, we fall back into our own night. Woe to me! How quickly my days have failed, how quickly I have withered like grass—I, who, as long as I was in the garden with him, flourished and blossomed like the paradise of God! With him, the garden is a place of delight; without him, a place of horror and vast solitude. For I think that whoever enters into his garden becomes himself a garden; and that his soul becomes like a watered garden, so that the Bridegroom too may say in praise of it: "A garden enclosed, my sister, my spouse" (Cant. IV, 12). Are they not a garden, in whom happens what the Gardener himself speaks to the planting which his Father planted? "Listen to me," he says, "you divine fruits, and bear fruit like the rose planted beside the streams of water" (Eccli. XXXIX, 17). "Have a sweet fragrance like frankincense. Bloom like the lily, give forth fragrance, and put forth leaves in grace."

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. O Domine Jesu, vere hortulane, operare in nobis quod exigis a nobis; nam sine te nihil possumus facere. Tu enim verus es hortulanus, idem creator qui cultor vel custos horti tui, qui verbo plantas, spiritu rigas, virtute incrementum das. Errabas, Maria, quae eum existimabas hortulanum illius horti pauperis et exigui, in quo sepultus fuit. Hortulanus est totius mundi, hortulanus est coeli, hortulanus est Ecclesiae, quam hic plantat et rigat, donec incremento consummato transplantet eam in terram viventium, secus decursus aquarum viventium, ubi non timebit cum venerit aestus, sed erit folium ejus viride, nec aliquando desinet facere fructum. Beati qui habitant in illis hortis tuis, Domine! in saecula saeculorum laudabunt te. Paulus habitabat in illis, cujus conversatio erat in coelis: qui mente saepius excedens perambulabat paradisum beatae voluptatis, hortos deliciarum Dei, ubi et pertransiens rosas Martyrum, et lilia Virginum, desinens etiam mirari altitudinem cedrorum Dei delectabatur potius carpere de fructu ligni vitae, quod est in medio paradisi, in ipso nimirum gustans plenius et felicius quam suavis est Dominus. Ideoque cum inde redibat, amicis auscultantibus memoriam abundantiae suavitatis ejus profusius eructabat, et ex abundantia cordis os redundabat. Quia enim sicut adipe et pinguedine repleta erat anima ejus, ideo labiis exsultationis laudabat os ejus. Cor quippe sapientis erudiet os ejus, et labiis illius addet gratiam (Prov. XVI, 23). Eructabat itaque cor ejus verbum bonum, ac de bono thesauro bonus bona proferebat, sponsumque ipsum qui in amicis auscultabat, velut jucundo carmine oblectabat. Prorsus carmen jucundum, suavisque melodia, ubi tam canorum Spiritus sancti organum,, tanta morum et sermonum consonantia, tanta dulcedine amoris, tanta gratia oris Christum Jesum jubilum cordis sui personabat. Si enim lingua suavis vim carminis non haberet, scriptum non esset: Tibiae et psalterium faciunt suavem melodiam, et super utraque lingua suavis (Eccli. XL, 21). Si carmine hujusmodi Psalmista Deum oblectari nesciret, nequaquam diceret: Jucundum sit ei eloquium meum (Psal. CIII, 31). Sed nec ipse sponsus diceret: Fac me audire vocem tuam; sonet vox tua in auribus meis. Vox enim tua suavis (Cantic. VIII, 13, et II, 14), quia exaltationes Dei in faucibus tuis, tanquam habitantis in hortis, in deliciis paradisi. E contra vero, Non est speciosa laus in ore peccatoris (Eccli. XV, 9), qui habitat in sepulcris. Cujus enim vita Deum exasperat, lingua non delectat, sed terribiliter increpatur voce divina: Quare tu enarras justitias meas; (Psal. XLIX, 16.) Cantica lyrae tuae non audiam (Amos V, 25).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. O Lord Jesus, true gardener, work in us what you require of us; for without you we can do nothing. For you are the true gardener, being yourself the creator who is also the tiller and keeper of your garden, who plant by the word, water by the Spirit, and give increase by power. You were mistaken, Mary, when you thought him the gardener of that poor and small garden in which he had been buried. He is the gardener of the whole world, the gardener of heaven, the gardener of the Church, which he plants and waters here, until, the growth being completed, he transplants her into the land of the living, beside the courses of living waters, where she shall not fear when the heat comes, but her leaf shall be green, and she shall never cease to bear fruit. Blessed are they who dwell in those gardens of yours, Lord! They shall praise you forever and ever. Paul dwelt in them, whose citizenship was in heaven: who, often going out of himself in mind, walked through the paradise of blessed delight, the gardens of God's delights, where, passing by the roses of the Martyrs and the lilies of the Virgins, and ceasing even to marvel at the height of the cedars of God, he delighted rather to pluck from the fruit of the tree of life, which is in the midst of paradise, in it indeed tasting. And so, when he returned from there, with his friends listening, he poured forth more abundantly the memory of the abundance of its sweetness, and out of the abundance of the heart his mouth overflowed. For because his soul was filled, as it were, with fat and fatness, therefore his mouth praised with lips of exultation. For the heart of the wise shall instruct his mouth, and shall add grace to his lips (Prov. XVI, 23). And so his heart poured forth a good word, and as a good man out of a good treasure brought forth good things, and he delighted, as it were with a pleasant song, the very Bridegroom who was listening in his friends. Truly a pleasant song, and a sweet melody, where so tuneful an instrument of the Holy Spirit, so great a harmony of conduct and of words, with so much sweetness of love, with so much grace of mouth, sounded forth Christ Jesus, the jubilation of his heart. For if a sweet tongue did not have the power of song, it would not be written: 'The pipe and the psaltery make sweet melody, but a pleasant tongue surpasses them both' (Eccli. XL, 21). If the Psalmist did not know that God is delighted by a song of this kind, he would by no means say: 'Let my speech be pleasing to him' (Psal. CIII, 31). Nor would the Bridegroom himself say: 'Make me hear your voice; let your voice sound in my ears. For your voice is sweet' (Cantic. VIII, 13, et II, 14), because 'the exaltations of God are in your throat,' as of one dwelling in the gardens, in the delights of paradise. But on the contrary, 'Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner' (Eccli. XV, 9), who dwells among tombs. For whoever's life provokes God, his tongue does not delight him, but he is terribly rebuked by the divine voice: 'Why do you declare my justices?' (Psal. XLIX, 16.); 'I will not hear the songs of your lyre' (Amos V, 25).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Sed quoniam Scriptura quam assumpseram in excusationem sermonis, occasionem et materiam ministravit sermonis; si placet, finiamus quod de illa coeperamus. Dupliciter itaque potest intelligi, quod a sponso dicitur, Quae habitas in hortis, amici auscultant, fac me audire vocem tuam: vel quod devotum amatorem invitet ad psallendum vel orandum; vel quod sanctum praedicatorem excitet ad loquendum. Quod ut magis persuadeat, amicos auscultare memorat, angelos scilicet orantem vel psallentem; fideles praedicantem. Ubi primo intuemur, qua disciplina cordis et corporis nos oporteat in conspectu angelorum psallere vel orare, ne vacui dimissi vacuos nos dimittant, qui venerant ut vota deferrent, et dona referrent; imo recedant inimici qui venerant amici. Quinimo sponsus ipse, qui stat ad ostium et pulsat, si nulla ei digna devotio de intus respondens aperiat, recedet conquerens, et dicens: Attendi et auscultavi, nemo quod bonum est loquitur. Nullus est qui agat poenitentiam super peccato suo, dicens: Quid feci? omnes conversi sunt ad cursum suum, quasi equus impetu vadens in praelium (Jerem. VIII, 6). Si autem praedicatorem exhortatur, fiduciam ei loquendi tribuit de benevolentia et attentione auditorum, quia scilicet non increduli obloquuntur, aut litigant; non aemuli detrectant, aut subsannant; non tepidi dormitant, aut oscitant: sed amici attenti auscultant, quorum amor et meritum possit evangelizanti impetrare verbum et spiritum. Et bene amici auscultant. Est enim velut proprium amici, scilicet quod devotus audiat vocem sponsi, sicut Joannes ait: Amicus sponsi est qui stat, non vagans animo, aut prostratus somno, audit et gaudet gaudio propter vocem sponsi (Joan. III, 29), quam agnoscit etiam in servis. Et nos itaque inde probemus nos amicos, ut sive per os loquentis, sive legentis aut cantantis vox sponsi sonuerit, sic stemus ad audiendum, quatenus auditui nostro det gaudium et laetitiam; et non solum cum gaudio, suscipere verbum, sed et fructum afferre in patientia.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. But since the Scripture which I had taken up as an excuse for my sermon has furnished the occasion and material for the sermon, let us, if it please you, finish what we had begun concerning it. What is said by the Bridegroom—'You who dwell in the gardens, the friends are listening; make me hear your voice'—can therefore be understood in two ways: either as inviting the devout lover to sing psalms or to pray; or as rousing the holy preacher to speak. To make this more persuasive, he recalls that friends are listening—namely, the angels listening to one praying or singing psalms, and the faithful listening to one preaching. Here we first consider with what discipline of heart and body we ought to sing psalms or pray in the sight of the angels, lest, being sent away empty, they in turn send us away empty—they who had come to carry away our vows and bring back gifts; nay, lest those who had come as friends depart as enemies. Indeed, the Bridegroom himself, who stands at the door and knocks, if no devotion worthy of him answers from within and opens to him, will withdraw complaining, and say: 'I attended and listened; no one speaks what is good. There is none who does penance for his sin, saying, What have I done? They have all turned aside to their own course, like a horse rushing with impetuosity into battle' (Jerem. VIII, 6). But if he is exhorting the preacher, he grants him confidence to speak on account of the benevolence and attentiveness of his hearers—namely, that the unbelieving do not speak against him or quarrel; that rivals do not disparage or mock; that the lukewarm do not doze or yawn: but that attentive friends listen, whose love and merit can obtain for the one preaching the gospel both the word and the spirit. And rightly do friends listen. For it is, as it were, proper to a friend that the devout one should hear the voice of the Bridegroom, just as John says: 'He that stands is the friend of the bridegroom'—not wandering in mind, nor laid low in sleep—'he hears him, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom's voice' (Joan. III, 29), which he recognizes even in his servants. Let us, then, likewise prove ourselves to be friends, so that whether through the mouth of one speaking, or reading, or singing, the voice of the Bridegroom sounds forth, we may so stand ready to listen that it gives to our hearing joy and gladness; and that we may not only receive the word with joy, but also bring forth fruit in patience.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric's first Epiphany sermon asks what gifts Christ's poor can offer the newborn King. Seven numbered sections interpret myrrh as penitential sorrow and toil, incense as devotion, and gold as wisdom. The address to brothers whose clothing scarcely suffices in winter places the argument in its monastic setting. This reading follows the 1879 Patrologia Latina edition; the approximate 1138–1157 composition range is distinct from that printing date. Editorial notes explain retained quotation variants and anomalous Scripture locators. The source explicitly names Epiphany.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De donis Domino offerendis.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the gifts to be offered to the Lord.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Afferte Domino, filii Dei, afferte (Psal. xxviii, 1). Satius est ei afferre, quam sanguisugae, id est concupiscentiae, cujus duae filiae, voluptas et vanitas, non dant requiem die ac nocte, dicentes: Affer, affer (Prov. xxx, 15). Quid igitur afferemus Domino? Afferte Domino gloriam auri, et honorem thuris: afferte Domino gloriam nomini ejus, myrrham (Psal. xxviii, 1, 2) sepulturae ejus. Sed dicit mihi discipulus Christi, filius Petri: Argentum et aurum non est mihi (Act. iii, 6). Nec sacculi peregrinarum mercium myrrhae et thuris. Ergone vacuus apparebis in conspectu Domini, et cunabula novi Regis nullis honorabis xeniis? O dives paupertas, o locuples nuditas, si tamen Christiana et voluntaria! Quibus enim divitiis non abundas, non solum auri, sed etiam auri primi, auri igniti; non solum myrrhae et thuris, sed etiam universi pulveris pigmentarii? Imo qui sunt alii qui possint abundare divitiis hujusmodi, nisi pauperes Christi? In viis, inquit, justitiae ambulo, ut ditem diligentes me, et thesauros eorum repleam. Nec deest ei unde id possit: Mecum sunt, inquit, divitiae et gloria, opes superbae, et justitia (Prov. viii, 20, 21, 18). Bonae opes prorsus divitiae salutis, in quibus ita superbitur, ut justitia non deseratur. Fratres, superbia ista est gloria exsultantium in Domino, et insultantium mundo, quod nihil habeat tam pretiosum, ut paupertati valeat comparari sanctorum. O qui pusillo animo estis, cur non superbitis mecum in opibus istis? Superbiam istam non damnat, sed remunerat Magister humilitatis, si videlicet ita magnanimus sis in contemptu mundi, ut omnem gloriam ejus quasi de sublimi despicias, et nihili pendas prae amore et gloria tuae nuditatis. Omnino dives es, si in paupertate gloriaris, et de te quoque gratias aget congratulatio Apostoli: Gratias, inquit, ago Deo meo, quod in omnibus divites facti estis in illo, in omni verbo et sanctitate, ut nihil vobis desit in ulla gloria (I Cor. i, 4, 5, 7). Longe aliter illum alloquitur Dominus, qui sibi applaudebat de affluentia mundi hujus: Tu, inquit, dicis Quia dives sum, et nullius egeo; et tu miser es, et miserabilis, et pauper et caecus, et nudus (Apoc. iii, 17).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Bring to the Lord, children of God, bring (Psalm xxviii, 1). It is better to bring to him than to the leech, that is, concupiscence, whose two daughters, pleasure and vanity, give no rest day or night, saying: Bring, bring (Proverbs xxx, 15). What, then, shall we bring to the Lord? Bring to the Lord the glory of gold and the honour of incense; bring to the Lord the glory due to his name, myrrh (Psalm xxviii, 1, 2) for his burial. But a disciple of Christ, a son of Peter, says to me: Silver and gold I have none (Acts iii, 6). Nor have I bags of foreign wares, of myrrh and incense.
