Will you then appear empty-handed before the Lord, and honour the new King's cradle with no gifts? O rich poverty, O wealthy nakedness, provided that it is Christian and voluntary! For what riches do you not abound in: not only gold, but the finest gold, gold tried by fire; not only myrrh and incense, but every powder of the perfumer? Indeed, who else can abound in such riches except Christ's poor? I walk, he says, in the ways of justice, to enrich those who love me and fill their treasuries. Nor does he lack the means: With me, he says, are riches and glory, magnificent wealth and justice (Proverbs viii, 20, 21, 18). The riches of salvation are truly good wealth, in which one takes pride without abandoning justice. Brothers, this pride is the glory of those who exult in the Lord and mock the world because it has nothing so precious that it can compare with the poverty of the saints. O faint-hearted ones, why do you not take pride with me in these riches? The Master of humility does not condemn this pride but rewards it, provided that you are so great-hearted in despising the world that you look down, as from on high, upon all its glory and count it as nothing beside the love and glory of your nakedness. You are altogether rich if you glory in poverty, and the Apostle's rejoicing will give thanks for you too: I thank my God, he says, that in all things you have been made rich in him, in every word and in holiness, so that you lack nothing in any glory (1 Corinthians i, 4, 5, 7). Very differently does the Lord address the man who congratulated himself upon this world's abundance: You say, I am rich and need nothing; and you are wretched and miserable and poor and blind and naked (Apocalypse iii, 17).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Sane inter divitias hujusmodi, pro quibus Paulus congratulabatur discipulis, non dubitaverim aurum, thus, et myrrham posse reperiri, quae digne et grate Christo nato queant offerri. At ego, inquies, non sum mihi conscius tale quid accepisse, nec aliquid tam pretiosum, ut est aurum, thus et myrrha, penes me posse inveniri. Ego enim, videns paupertatem meam, vix mendicabo stipem quotidianam, pauperem exigens vitam. Putas, inquit, te nihil tale accepisse? vide magis ne acceptam a Patre substantiam dissipaveris vivendo luxuriose. Sed omitto istud; non enim improperandum est, ut Sapiens ait, homini avertenti se a peccato (Eccli. viii, 6). Vellem magis ut non pigeret te tentare et quaerere si forte vel minimum aliquid paternae substantiae resedisset apud te, unde initium recuperandi posses capere. Vellem foderes intra te; solent namque pretiosi latere thesauri in abditis terrae. In agro absconditus erat thesaurus ille qui desiderio sui compulit hominem omnia sua vendere (Matth. xiii, 44). In agro se dicebant thesauros absconditos habere decem viri Israelitae, et per hoc gladium evaserunt homicidae (Jerem. xli, 8). O quanti thesauri bonorum operum, quantae divitiae piorum fructuum absconditi latent in agro humani corporis, et quanto plures in abdito cordis, si modo sit qui exerceat et fodiat! Neque illud Platonicum dico, quod anima ante corpus artes didicerit, quae oblivione et mole corporis obrutae, disciplina et industria refodiendae sint: sed quod ratio hominis et ingenium, juvante gratia, omnium sit virtutum seminarium. Si ergo ad cor redeas, et corpus exerceas, non diffidas te inventurum thesauros desiderabiles; et si non auri statim in initio, aut thuris, certe vel myrrhae non inutilis. Inutilem aut vilem tu ne dixeris, quam Christus acceptat in munere, qua sui corporis sepultura non solum praesignari, cum ei offerretur, sed etiam consummari voluit, cum ex ea perungeretur.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Surely among those riches for which Paul congratulated his disciples, I would not doubt that gold, incense and myrrh can be found which may worthily and acceptably be offered to the newborn Christ. But I, you will say, am not aware of having received anything of the kind, nor can anything as precious as gold, incense and myrrh be found in my possession. Seeing my poverty, I can scarcely beg my daily pittance as I lead a poor life. Do you think, he says, that you have received nothing of the kind? Consider rather whether you have squandered the substance received from your Father by living in luxury. But I leave that aside; for, as the Wise Man says, one must not reproach a man who turns away from sin (Ecclesiasticus viii, 6). I would rather that you should not be reluctant to try and search whether perhaps some smallest part of your Father's substance remains with you, from which you might begin to recover. I would have you dig within yourself; for precious treasures often lie hidden in the secret places of the earth. Hidden in a field was that treasure which, through the desire for it, compelled a man to sell all he had (Matthew xiii, 44). Ten men of Israel said that they had treasures hidden in a field, and by this escaped the murderer's sword (Jeremiah xli, 8). O what treasures of good works, what riches of devout fruits lie concealed in the field of the human body, and how many more in the hidden heart, if only someone will cultivate and dig! I am not speaking of that Platonic notion that the soul learned the arts before entering the body, and that, buried by forgetfulness and the body's weight, they must be dug out again by instruction and effort; rather, that human reason and natural ability, with grace assisting, are a seedbed of all the virtues. If, then, you return to your heart and exercise your body, do not doubt that you will find desirable treasures; if not gold or incense immediately at the beginning, then certainly at least useful myrrh. Do not call useless or worthless what Christ accepts as a gift, by which he willed his body's burial not only to be foreshadowed when it was offered to him, but also to be accomplished when he was anointed with it.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Si ergo manifestius vis audire, myrrha in corde tuo dolor est, myrrha in corpore tuo labor est, si tamen iste vel ille poenitentialis est. Myrrham siquidem utrumque esse non solum probat etymologia nominis, aut qualitas saporis, sed etiam medicinalis operatio virtutis. Myrrha namque amarissimum gustum sui etiam nomine prodit, effectu autem, praeter alias sui utilitates, corruptioni resistit. Et quid gustu amarius, quid effectu salubrius, quam dolor quo peccator ad poenitentiam contristatur? Recogitat annos suos in amaritudine animae suae, dicens Deo, Noli me condemnare (Job. x, 2); sed omnis haec amaritudo nihil aliud quam myrrha est, vindicans a corruptione tam luxuriarum, in quibus computruit, quam vermium immortalium, quos meruit. Quid vero labor corporis? Non tam myrrha est, quam fasciculus myrrhae, si credere volumus his qui de saeculo nuper venere; quibus regula jejuniorum et vigiliarum, quotidianum opus manuum, asperitas vestium, et omnia pene amara, quia insolita, velut in unum colligata fasciculum, imposita sunt ad ferendum. Et quidem amarissime portarent hunc myrrhae fasciculum, nisi quia, etsi nondum gaudent communicare passionibus Dilecti, ut dicant, Fasciculus myrrhae dilectus meus mihi (Cantic. i, 12), dulce tamen nimium habent amaritudinem cordis amaritudine mitigare exteriori, tanquam choleram stomachi potu absinthii. Sicut enim stomachus, immoderato usu dulcium corruptus, potione purgatur amara, sic eorum qui suaviter vixerunt in amaricata conscientia, nunquam melius quam contrario, id est, vita et consuetudine curantur austera. Maxime autem, si saepius detur eis bibere vinum myrrhatum Dominicae passionis, id est potentur vino compunctionis, quod quanto amarius est ex recordatione peccati, tanto salubrius est peccatori. Ideo Jesus noluit bibere (Matth. xxvii, 48), quia peccatum non fecerat, quod ei crucifixor imputabat, qui de amaritudine vitis alienae ei propinabat qui de genimine vitis verae, vinum novum cum amicis in regno Patris habebat bibere.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. If, then, you wish to hear it more plainly, myrrh in your heart is sorrow; myrrh in your body is toil, provided that the one or the other is penitential. Both are myrrh, as is shown not only by the word's derivation or the nature of its taste, but also by the medicinal working of its power. For myrrh reveals its intensely bitter taste even by its name, while in its effects, besides its other uses, it resists corruption. And what is more bitter to taste, what more wholesome in its effect, than the sorrow by which a sinner is grieved into repentance? He recalls his years in the bitterness of his soul, saying to God: Do not condemn me (Job x, 2). Yet all this bitterness is nothing other than myrrh, rescuing him from the corruption both of the lusts in which he rotted and of the undying worms he has deserved. What, then, of bodily toil? It is not so much myrrh as a bundle of myrrh, if we believe those who have recently come from the world. The rule of fasts and vigils, daily manual work, rough clothing, and almost everything bitter because unfamiliar have been laid upon them to bear, as though bound into one bundle. They would indeed carry this bundle of myrrh with great bitterness, except that, even if they do not yet rejoice to share the sufferings of the Beloved and say, My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me (Song of Songs i, 12), they nevertheless find it exceedingly sweet to soothe the bitterness of the heart with outward bitterness, like the stomach's bile with a drink of wormwood. For just as a stomach spoiled by excessive consumption of sweets is purged by a bitter draught, so those who have lived pleasantly are never better cured in their embittered conscience than by the opposite, that is, an austere life and habit. Especially is this so if they are often given the myrrhed wine of the Lord's Passion to drink, that is, the wine of compunction: the more bitter it is from remembering sin, the more wholesome it is for the sinner. For this reason Jesus would not drink (Matthew xxvii, 48), because he had committed no sin, which his crucifier imputed to him by offering him the bitterness of a foreign vine, whereas he was to drink new wine from the fruit of the true vine with his friends in his Father's kingdom.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Caeterum quanquam perfectis, qualis Timotheus erat, exercitatio corporalis ad modicum utilis sit comparatione pietatis (I Tim. iv, 5); quantum tamen rudibus et imperfectis, quales nos sumus, utilis sit, vos ipsi, fratres, vobis testes estis; quomodo scilicet redimit de corruptione vitam nostram amaritudo parcimoniae et laboris. Ipsi etenim scitis quomodo vermescerent corda, quomodo vermescerent corpora, si non quotidie de manibus laborantium distillaret myrrha. An non vermis luxuria? Nescio si alter nocentior. Ingreditur blandiendo, mordet ridendo, transforat delectando, perimit consensu voluntario. An non vermis acedia et tristitia? Sicut tinea, inquit, vestimento, et vermis ligno, ita tristitia viri nocet cordi (Prov. xxv, 20). Quid omnia desideria mala? an non vermes et ipsa? At in desideriis est omnis otiosus, et desideria occidunt pigrum (Id. xxi, 26, 25). Beatus igitur cui ad mortificandos vermes hujuscemodi, manus propriae distillant myrrham per universum sui, jamque praevenit ungere corpus suum in sepulturam. Sed suum dicam, an Jesu? Imo et Jesu. Corpus enim illius, membrum est Jesu. Quisquis ille est qui sic unctus est, non est quod timeat vermem qui non moritur; quia jam mortuus est ei vermis unde illi moritur.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Yet although for the perfect, such as Timothy was, bodily exercise is useful for little in comparison with godliness (1 Timothy iv, 5), you yourselves, brothers, can testify how useful it is for beginners and the imperfect, such as we are: how the bitterness of frugality and toil redeems our life from corruption. For you yourselves know how hearts would breed worms, how bodies would breed worms, if myrrh did not drip daily from the hands of those who labour. Is lust not a worm? I do not know whether another is more harmful. It enters by flattering, bites with a laugh, pierces by giving pleasure, and kills through voluntary consent. Are sloth and sadness not a worm? As the moth, he says, harms clothing, and the worm wood, so a man's sadness harms his heart (Proverbs xxv, 20). What of all evil desires? Are they not worms too? But every idle man is among desires, and desires kill the sluggard (ibid. xxi, 26, 25). Blessed, then, is the man whose own hands drip myrrh over his whole being to mortify worms of this kind, and who thus anoints his body beforehand for burial. But should I say his body, or Jesus'? Indeed, Jesus' too. For his body is a member of Jesus. Whoever is thus anointed has no reason to fear the worm that does not die, because for him the worm through which he dies is already dead.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Myrrham itaque, et myrrham electam atque probatissimam Domino cum regibus rex et ipse obtulisti, si interim, cum non sufficit manus tua ad offerendum aurum sapientiae aut thus devotionis, saltem cor contritum corpusque afflictum cum amaritudine poenitentiae Domino sanctificasti. Existimo enim, sine praejudicio tamen melioris intellectus, myrrham esse primam oblationem incipientium, deinde thus proficientium, demumque aurum perfectorum; atque idcirco cum simul ab Evangelista nominata sunt, pretiosiora quaeque et digniora pro merito sui praelata esse in ordine nominum. Alias namque secundum ordinem profectuum myrrham thuri praepositam invenis, ut est illud, Sicut virgula fumi ex aromatibus myrrhae et thuris (Cantic. iii, 6). Et, Vadam ad montem myrrhae, et ad collem thuris (Id. iv, 6). Non parvus siquidem profectus est, cum de myrrha ad thus proficitur, cum de ista, quae ad usus est infirmitatis humanae, ad illud quod divinis et festivis deputatum est sacrificiis, pervenitur; ut qui sacrificium spiritus contribulati, corporisque humiliati offerebat non sine myrrha amaritudinis, jam sacrificium laudis offerat cum thure devotionis, et, juxta promissionem Domini, tanta consolatio immittatur lugentibus Sion, ut det eis coronam pro cinere, oleum gaudii pro luctu, pallium laudis pro spiritu moeroris (Isa. lxi, 3). Tunc cantat qui lugebat: Convertisti planctum meum in gaudium mihi, conscidisti saccum meum, spiritum moeroris; et circumdedisti me laetitia, pallio scilicet laudis, ut cantet tibi gloria mea, et non compungar (Psal. xxix, 12, 13). Gaudens enim gaudebo in Domino, et exsultabit anima mea in Deo meo, quia induit me vestimento salutis, et indumento laetitiae circumdedit me (Isa. lxi, 10).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. You too, then, have offered myrrh to the Lord with the kings, yourself a king, and myrrh choice and most excellent, if meanwhile, when your hand cannot supply the gold of wisdom or the incense of devotion, you have at least consecrated to the Lord a contrite heart and an afflicted body with the bitterness of penance. For I think, without prejudice to a better understanding, that myrrh is the first offering of beginners, then incense that of those making progress, and finally gold that of the perfect; and that, when the Evangelist named them together, each more precious and worthy gift was therefore placed earlier in the order of names according to its worth. Elsewhere you find myrrh placed before incense according to the order of progress, as in the saying, Like a slender column of smoke from the spices of myrrh and incense (Song of Songs iii, 6); and, I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of incense (ibid. iv, 6). Indeed, it is no small progress to advance from myrrh to incense, from what serves human infirmity to what is assigned to divine and festal sacrifices; so that he who offered the sacrifice of a troubled spirit and a humbled body, not without the myrrh of bitterness, may now offer a sacrifice of praise with the incense of devotion. And, according to the Lord's promise, such consolation is sent to those mourning in Sion that he gives them a crown for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, a mantle of praise for the spirit of sorrow (Isaiah lxi, 3). Then he who mourned sings: You have turned my lament into joy for me; you have torn my sackcloth, the spirit of sorrow; and surrounded me with gladness, that is, the mantle of praise, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with sorrow (Psalm xxix, 12, 13). For rejoicing I will rejoice in the Lord, and my soul will exult in my God, because he has clothed me in the garment of salvation and surrounded me with the robe of gladness (Isaiah lxi, 10).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. O fratres, quibus minus sufficiunt vestimenta vestrae paupertatis in hac asperitate hiemis, qui dicitis, Ante faciem frigoris hujus quis sustinebit? cur non induimini, quaeso, hoc vestimento laetitiae et salutis, hoc pallio laudis? Si Dominum laudatis, in Domino laudabitur anima vestra, et pallio laudis quo opertus est laudabilis nimis, vos quoque operiet et confovebit, quemadmodum gallina pullos suos sub alis, si modo velitis. Ah quoties voluit, et noluistis! Nunquid enim hoc pallium breve est, ut utrumque operire non possit? Non angustiamini, inquit, in nobis, angustiamini autem in visceribus vestris. Dilatamini et vos (II Cor. vi, 12, 13), et pallium dilatabit se usque ad vos. Non est abbreviata manus ejus, ut salvare nequeat: nec grande est ei ut consoletur nos, nisi pravitas nostra prohibeat. O qui algetis, pallium hoc calidum est; quia calor est, qui non modo interius, sed exterius calefacere potest. Nonne vestimenta tua calida sunt, cum terra tua perflata fuerit austro (Job xxxvii, 17); imo ignis missus in ossibus, ac vehementer accensus (Thren. i, 13)? Hoc igne thus illud adole, quod ubi cum regibus obtuleris, dirigatur oratio tua sicut incensum in conspectu Domini: et cum de sacrificio tuo odoratus fuerit odorem suavitatis, dicat tibi, Odor vestimentorum tuorum sicut odor thuris (Cantic. iv, 11).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. O brothers, whose poor clothing does not suffice in the harshness of this winter, who say, Who can endure before the face of this cold? Why, I ask, do you not put on this garment of gladness and salvation, this mantle of praise? If you praise the Lord, your soul will be praised in the Lord, and with the mantle of praise in which he who is exceedingly praiseworthy is clothed, he will cover and warm you too, as a hen her chicks beneath her wings, if only you will. Ah, how often he has willed it, and you have not! Is this mantle so short that it cannot cover both? You are not straitened in us, he says, but in your own affections. Be enlarged yourselves too (2 Corinthians vi, 12, 13), and the mantle will widen to reach you. His hand is not shortened so that he cannot save; nor is it difficult for him to console us, unless our wickedness prevents it. O you who are cold, this mantle is warm; for it is a warmth that can heat not only within but without. Are not your garments warm when the south wind has blown over your land (Job xxxvii, 17); indeed, is it not fire sent into the bones and fiercely kindled (Lamentations i, 13)? With this fire burn that incense; when you have offered it with the kings, let your prayer be directed like incense before the Lord. And when he has smelled a sweet fragrance from your sacrifice, may he say to you: The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense (Song of Songs iv, 11).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 7. Jam vero de auro sapientiae (quae oblatio, ut diximus, perfectorum est) loquatur vobis qui illud assecutus est, quia nec novit illud nisi qui accipit. Qui ergo sapientiam didicit, sapientiam loquatur inter perfectos; et de auro quod possidet, murenulas aureas auribus vestris fabricet. Ego enim non arbitror comprehendisse me; sequor autem si quo modo comprehendam (Philipp. iii, 13, 12). Magnus prorsus ac beatus qui invenit sapientiam, et affluit prudentia: sapientiam, in contemplatione aeternorum; prudentiam, in administratione temporalium: vel, ut moderatius sapientem definiam, qui novit se ipsum regere et alium. Pretiosus est hoc aurum cunctis opibus, etiam thure et myrrha; et omnia quae desiderantur in virtutibus vel gratiis, huic non valent comparari. Denique sapiens, tanquam vir virtutum, dives in omnibus, et si praevalet aurum offerre in sublimi contemplatione vel prudenti administratione, non tamen negligit offere thus in devotione divini operis, myrrham in mortificatione sui. Nos igitur, fratres, quod habemus offeramus in gloriam novi Regis: quod minus habemus, ab ipso petamus cui offerre cupimus. Si quis indiget sapientia, postulet a Deo, qui dat omnibus affluenter (Jac. i, 5). Munera mea, data mea, ait Pater luminum, a quo omne donum perfectum, et omne datum optimum; ipsi gloria in saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 7. Now let one who has attained it speak to you of the gold of wisdom, which, as we have said, is the offering of the perfect; for no one knows it except the one who receives it. Let him, then, who has learned wisdom speak wisdom among the perfect, and from the gold he possesses fashion little golden ornaments for your ears. For I do not consider that I have attained; but I press on, if somehow I may attain (Philippians iii, 13, 12). Truly great and blessed is the man who finds wisdom and abounds in prudence: wisdom in contemplating eternal things, prudence in administering temporal things; or, to define the wise man more modestly, one who knows how to govern himself and another. This gold is more precious than all wealth, even incense and myrrh; and all that is desired in virtues or graces cannot compare with it. Finally, the wise man, as a man of virtues, rich in all things, even when able to offer gold in lofty contemplation or prudent administration, nevertheless does not neglect to offer incense in devotion to the divine office, and myrrh in the mortification of himself. Let us, then, brothers, offer what we have to the glory of the new King; what we lack, let us ask from him to whom we desire to offer it. If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives abundantly to all (James i, 5). My gifts, my offerings, says the Father of lights, from whom comes every perfect gift and every bestowal that is best; to him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition’s quotation of 1 Corinthians 1:5, 7 reads “holiness” and “glory,” where the usual Vulgate reads “knowledge” and “grace.” The translation follows the sermon’s wording.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The Latin reads Pretiosus est hoc aurum, an irregular adjective agreement meaning “this gold is precious.” It also spells offerre as offere. Both forms are retained. The final phrase “My gifts, my offerings” has no printed Bible reference.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition cites Matthew 27:48 for the refusal of the drink, usually located at Matthew 27:34 (compare Mark 15:23). It cites 1 Timothy 4:5 for the bodily-exercise saying, usually located at 1 Timothy 4:8. The printed references are retained.

sermons.title: Epiphany Sermon I: Gifts to Offer the Lord

sermons.author: Guerric of Igny
metadata: Guerric of Igny, Sermones per annum, In Epiphania Domini, sermo II, De variis modis quibus nos Deus illuminat, in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier frères, 1879), cols. 51-54.
Internet Archive, 2011; PIMS, University of Toronto; University of Toronto funding.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: This second Epiphany sermon belongs to Guerric of Igny's medieval collection of sermons for the liturgical year, here read from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. Its individual date is unknown; the collection is associated approximately with his abbacy in 1138–1157. From Isaiah's "Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem", Guerric gathers the day's three manifestations: the star to the Magi, the Jordan baptism, and the water made wine. The Magi's faith, which saw only weakness and still adored, shows how faith begins and grows. He bids his hearers look up to the lights of heaven, the saints, before they can bear the Sun itself. An editorial note records a printer's error. The source explicitly names Epiphany.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO II

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON II

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De variis modis quibus nos Deus illuminat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the Various Ways in Which God Enlightens Us

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Surge, illuminare, Jerusalem, quia venit lumen tuum (Isa. LX, 1). Hodiernum diem luminum illuminavit nobis et consecravit lumen de lumine, quod hodie cum lateret incognitum, ad illuminationem omnium gentium sese dignatum est mundo revelare. Hodie namque se revelavit Chaldaeis novi sideris indicio, cum eorum primitiis omnium fidem gentium dedicavit. Hodie se revelavit Judaeis, non solum Joannis, sed et Patris et Spiritus sancti testimonio, ubi in Jordane baptizatus, baptisma omnium consecravit. Hodie manifestavit gloriam suam coram discipulis suis, quando mutatatione aquae in vinum, illud ineffabile praeostendit mysterium, in quo, verbo ipsius, substantiae mutantur rerum. His omnibus Dei apparitionibus praevidens Spiritus illuminandam Ecclesiae fidem, alloquitur eam sub typo et nomine Jerusalem, dicens: Surge, illuminare, Jerusalem, quia venit lumen tuum. Venerat quidem lumen; in mundo erat, et mundus per ipsum factus erat; sed mundus ipsum non cognoscebat. Erat natus, sed non erat notus, donec declarare eum coepit luminosa dies ista. Ait ergo propheta: O Jerusalem nova, civitas magna novi regis, mons Sion, latera aquilonis (Psal. XLVII, 3), id est, de utroque aedificanda pariete circumcisionis et praeputii; Surge, illuminare, quia venit lumen tuum. Surgite, qui sedetis in tenebris; intendite lumini, quod exortum est in tenebris, sed non comprehenditur a tenebris. Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini (Psal. XXXIII, 6), et in lumine ejus videbitis lumen, diceturque vobis, Fuistis aliquando tenebrae, nunc autem lux in Domino (Ephes. V, 8). Intendite lumini aeterno quod se vestris aspectibus temperavit, ut, qui lucem habitat inaccessibilem, infirmis quoque et lippientibus oculis posset accedi. Advertite lumen in lucerna testae, solem in nube, Deum in homine, in luteo vasculo carnis nostrae splendorem gloriae, candoremque lucis aeternae.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come" (Isa. LX, 1). The Light from Light has illumined and consecrated this day of lights for us: the Light which, though today it lay hidden and unknown, deigned to reveal itself to the world for the enlightenment of all nations. For today he revealed himself to the Chaldeans by the sign of a new star, when in their firstfruits he dedicated the faith of all the nations. Today he revealed himself to the Jews, not only by John's testimony, but by the testimony of the Father and the Holy Spirit, when, baptized in the Jordan, he consecrated the baptism of all. Today he manifested his glory before his disciples, when, by the changing of water into wine, he showed forth beforehand that ineffable mystery in which, by his own word, the substances of things are changed. Foreseeing that the faith of the Church would be enlightened by all these appearings of God, the Spirit addresses her under the type and name of Jerusalem, saying: Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come. Indeed the light had come; it was in the world, and the world was made through it; but the world did not know it. He had been born, but was not yet known, until this day of light began to declare him. The prophet therefore says: O new Jerusalem, great city of the new King, Mount Sion, on the sides of the north (Psal. XLVII, 3), that is, to be built up from both walls, of circumcision and of the uncircumcision; Arise, be enlightened, for your light has come. Arise, you who sit in darkness; attend to the light which has risen in the darkness, but is not comprehended by the darkness. Come to him, and be enlightened (Psal. XXXIII, 6), and in his light you will see light, and it will be said to you: You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord (Ephes. V, 8). Attend to the eternal light which has tempered itself to your sight, so that he who dwells in unapproachable light might also be approached even by weak and bleary eyes. Observe the light in the lamp of clay, the sun in the cloud, God in man, in the little earthen vessel of our flesh the splendor of glory and the brightness of eternal light.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Latet quidem majestas in humanitate, virtus in humilitate; sed signa virtutum erumpentia, unde haec prodeant, non sinunt ambigere. Opera, inquit, quae ego facio, testimonium perhibent de me (Joan. X, 25). Magnum quidem testimonium Joannis, qui venit ut testimonium perhiberet, lucerna de lumine; at enim multo majus illud testimonium coeleste, quod Pater et Spiritus sanctus Filio perhibuere (Luc. III, 16, 21, 22), Pater, in voce, Spiritus, in specie, cum in ore duorum testium stet omne verbum. Sed et hoc ipsum si minus accipitur: Opera, inquit, innumerabilia et irrefragabilia, quae ego facio, testimonium perhibent de me (Joan. X, 25). Plane incorruptus et irrevincibilis testis, cum creatura insensibilis sensum quemdam accipit in confessionem Creatoris, voluntatem ejus exaudiens, ac nutui incunctanter obediens. Quid enim divinius poterat exhiberi sensibus mortalium, quam hodiernae novitatis signum, quod etiam ante signorum suorum praemisit Jesus initium? Vagit puer novus in terris, et sidus novum creat in supernis, ut lumen testetur de lumine, stella de sole, et reges in splendore ortus sui, ad exortum quoque aeternum splendorem, ab oriente ad verum Orientem, id est, virum cui nomen Oriens (Zach. VI, 12), stella perducat; non quasi stella, sed quasi rationale animal in via praecedens, in fine viae consistens, ac velut digito ipsum qui quaerebatur ostendens. Sed esto, calumnietur infidelis hanc stellam non esse opus Christi, dummodo confiteatur opus esse Patris in testimonium Filii. Attamen obruet eum multitudo infinita ac magnitudo mirabilium plane divinorum, quae absque contradictione Jesus noster operatus est in carne, sed non ex carne.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Majesty indeed lies hidden in humanity, power in humility; but the signs of power breaking forth do not allow us to doubt whence they proceed. "The works," he says, "that I do bear witness of me" (Joan. X, 25). Great indeed is the testimony of John, who came to bear witness, a lamp testifying of the Light; but far greater is that heavenly testimony which the Father and the Holy Spirit bore to the Son (Luc. III, 16, 21, 22), the Father in the voice, the Spirit in the visible form, since every word stands firm in the mouth of two witnesses. But if even this be deemed insufficient: "the works," he says, "innumerable and irrefutable, which I do, bear witness of me" (Joan. X, 25). Clearly an incorruptible and unconquerable witness, when insensible creation receives, as it were, a certain sense in confessing the Creator, hearkening to his will and obeying his command without delay. For what more divine sign could be shown to mortal senses than the sign of today's newness, which Jesus sent forth even before the beginning of his own [other] signs? A new child cries on earth, and creates a new star in the heavens above, so that light might testify of Light, the star of the Sun, and lead kings, by the splendor of its rising, to the eternal Splendor, who likewise has arisen—from the east to the true East, that is, to the man whose name is the Orient (Zach. VI, 12)—the star leading them not as a mere star, but as a rational creature going before on the way, standing still at the end of the way, and pointing out, as it were with a finger, the very one who was being sought. But suppose the unbeliever should slander this, saying that the star is not the work of Christ—so long as he confesses it to be the work of the Father in testimony of the Son. Yet even so he will be overwhelmed by the infinite multitude and the magnitude of the plainly divine wonders which our Jesus worked in the flesh, but not from the flesh, without any possibility of contradiction.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Sed operiant tenebrae terram, et caligo populos, qui, cum lux venit in mundum, dilexerunt magis tenebras quam lucem (Joan. III, 19); dummodo tu illumineris, Jerusalem, civitas coelestis, quae in omni terra et populo, Deo paritura es filios lucis, quos de potestate tenebrarum transferet in regnum claritatis suae lumen verum. Gratias tibi, Pater luminum, qui de tenebris nos vocasti in admirabile lumen tuum (I Petr. II, 9). Gratias tibi, qui dixisti de tenebris lumen splendescere, et illuxisti in cordibus nostris ad illuminationem scientiae in facie Christi Jesu (II Cor. IV, 6). Haec siquidem est lux vera, imo vita aeterna, ut cognoscamus te unum Deum, et quem misisti Jesum Christum. Cognoscimus te, quia cognoscimus Jesum, quoniam Pater et Filius unum (Joan. XVII, 23, 11). Cognoscimus quidem per fidem, ipsam tenentes arrham fidelem, quia cognoscemus te per speciem. Interim tamen auge nobis fidem, deducens nos ex fide in fidem, a claritate in claritatem, tanquam a tuo Spiritu, ut de die in diem thesauros luminis profundius ingrediamur, quo fides amplior, scientia plenior, charitas ferventior fiat et diffusior, donec per fidem perducamur ad faciem, tanquam per stellam praeducem ad nostrum Bethlehemiticum ducem, qui egressus de Bethlehem regit Israelem, et regnat in Jerusalem; non ista quae occidit prophetas, ipsumque Dominum prophetarum, sed illa in qua coronat occisos idem Dominus, causa, virtus, et gloria martyrum

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. But let darkness cover the earth, and gloom the peoples, who, when the light came into the world, loved darkness rather than the light (Joan. III, 19); provided only that you be enlightened, O Jerusalem, heavenly city, who in every land and people are to bear sons of light for God—sons whom the true light will transfer from the power of darkness into the kingdom of its own brightness. Thanks be to you, Father of lights, who have called us out of darkness into your wonderful light (I Petr. II, 9). Thanks be to you, who said that light should shine out of darkness, and who have shone in our hearts for the illumination of the knowledge in the face of Christ Jesus (II Cor. IV, 6). For this indeed is the true light, nay rather eternal life, that we should know you the one God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ. We know you because we know Jesus, since the Father and the Son are one (Joan. XVII, 23, 11). We know you indeed through faith, holding fast that same faithful pledge, because we shall know you through vision. Meanwhile, however, increase our faith, leading us from faith to faith, from brightness to brightness, as it were by your own Spirit, so that from day to day we may enter more deeply into the treasures of light, whereby faith may become ampler, knowledge fuller, charity more ardent and more widely diffused, until through faith we be brought to the vision of your face, as it were through a guiding star to our Bethlehem-born Leader, who, having gone forth from Bethlehem, rules Israel, and reigns in Jerusalem—not that Jerusalem which killed the prophets, and the very Lord of the prophets, but that one in which the same Lord crowns those who were slain—he who is the cause, the strength, and the glory of the martyrs.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. O quanto gaudio ibi tripudiat fides Magorum, cernentium in illa Jerusalem regnantem, quem in Bethlehem adoraverunt vagientem! Hic visus est in diversorio pauperum, ibi in palatio videtur Angelorum; hic in pannis parvulorum, ibi in splendoribus sanctorum; hic in gremio Matris, ibi in solio Patris. Plane digna beatorum fides Magorum, ut tam felici visione remuneretur; quae cum in eo nihil nisi infirmum et contemptibile videret, non tamen scandalizari potuit, quominus Deum in homine, et hominem in Deo veneraretur. Procul dubio stella ex Jacob illuxerat in cordibus eorum; stella, inquam, matutina, lucifer qui nescit occasum, qui etiam foris stellam, matutini ortus sui indicem, accenderat cenderat in cordibus eorum. De his omnino convenienter intelligi potest quod apud Salomonem scriptum est: Justorum semita, quasi lux splendescens procedit, et crescit usque ad perfectum diem (Prov. IV, 18). Primo namque semitam justitiae ingressi sunt ad lucem splendentis sideris, cujus ductu profecerunt ad videndum novum ortum matutinae, lucis sicque demum pervenerunt ad contemplandam faciem meridiani Solis, in die virtutis suae rutilantis.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Oh, with what great joy does the faith of the Magi there leap for joy, beholding reigning in that Jerusalem the one whom they adored crying as an infant in Bethlehem! Here he was seen in the lodging-place of the poor, there he is seen in the palace of the Angels; here in the swaddling clothes of infants, there in the splendors of the saints; here in the lap of his Mother, there on the throne of the Father. Truly worthy was the faith of the blessed Magi, to be rewarded with so happy a vision—they who, though they saw in him nothing but what was weak and contemptible, could not be scandalized so as to be kept from venerating God in man, and man in God. Without doubt the star out of Jacob had shone in their hearts; the star, I say, the morning star, the light-bearer who knows no setting, who had kindled also outwardly the star, the sign of his own morning rising, within their hearts. Of these it can altogether fittingly be understood what is written in Solomon: The path of the just, as a shining light, goes forward, and increases even to perfect day (Prov. IV, 18). For first they entered the path of righteousness by the light of the shining star, under whose guidance they advanced to the seeing of the new rising of the morning light, and so at last they arrived at the contemplation of the face of the noonday Sun, in the day of his glowing power.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Pulchre igitur signanterque in his Gentium primitiis, in his nascentis Ecclesiae primordiis, praeostensus est fidei profectus in singulis: unde scilicet incipiat, quomodo proficiat, et quo demum perveniat; ut facile ipsorum qui patres sunt, in filiis agnoscantur vestigia. Sicut illi coeperunt a visione sideris, profecerunt ad visionem pueri, pervenerunt ad visionem Dei, sic in nobis fides nascitur supernorum praedicatione luminarium; roboratur visione quarumdam imaginum, per speculum et in aenigmate Deum velut incarnatum nobis exhibentium; consummabitur, cum praesens et nuda videbitur veritas rerum facie ad faciem contemplantibus quod vix tenuiter et raptim in aenigmate nunc attingitur; cum et ipsa fides transibit in cognitionem, spes in possessionem, desiderium in fruitionem. Lucent namque et nobis stellae, non una, sed multae; nisi quia multae una, quarum scilicet cor unum est, et anima una, fides eadem, praedicatio consona, similisque vita. Quae sint hae stellae, si dubitas, Danielem interroga: Qui ad justitiam, inquit, erudiunt multos, quasi stellae in perpetuas aeternitates (Dan. XII, 3). Paulus etiam luminaria vocat eos, qui lucent in medio nationis pravae et perversae (Philipp. II, 15), continentque verbum vitae, tanquam splendorem mutuatum ab aeterna luce, quo et noctem hujus mundi jussi sunt illuminare. Ideo Dominus fons et origo lucis, cum ordinaret lunam et stellas in potestatem noctis, dicebat illis, Vos estis lux mundi: et iterum, Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant opera vestra bona, et glorificent Patrem vestrum, qui in coelis est (Matth. V, 14, 16). Lucent itaque verbo, lucent exemplo, et utroque lucis radio ortum aeternae lucis annuntiant, dum coelestem, quem voce praedicant, etiam coelestis vitae similitudine commendant.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Beautifully then and significantly, in these firstfruits of the Gentiles, in these beginnings of the nascent Church, the progress of faith in each soul was shown beforehand: namely, whence it begins, how it advances, and to what at last it arrives; so that the footsteps of the fathers may easily be recognized in the children. Just as they began from the sight of the star, advanced to the sight of the child, and arrived at the sight of God, so in us faith is born from the preaching of the heavenly luminaries; it is strengthened by the vision of certain images, which, through a mirror and in a riddle, display God to us as it were incarnate; it will be consummated when the present and naked truth of things shall be seen, face to face, by those who contemplate it—that truth which is now attained but faintly and fleetingly, in a riddle—when faith itself shall pass into knowledge, hope into possession, desire into enjoyment. For stars shine for us too—not one, but many; except that many are one, namely those whose heart is one, and soul one, faith the same, preaching harmonious, and life alike. If you doubt what these stars are, ask Daniel: Those who instruct many unto righteousness, he says, shall shine as stars for all eternity (Dan. XII, 3). Paul too calls them luminaries, those who shine in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation (Philipp. II, 15), and who hold fast the word of life, as a brightness borrowed from the eternal light, by which they are also commanded to illumine the night of this world. Therefore the Lord, the fountain and origin of light, when he ordained the moon and the stars for dominion over the night, said to them, You are the light of the world; and again, Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matth. V, 14, 16). They shine therefore by word, they shine by example, and by both rays of light they announce the rising of the eternal light, while they commend, by the likeness of a heavenly life, that heavenly one whom they preach by voice.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Suspicite, fratres, in coelum; in coelo siquidem est conversatio eorum; suspicite, et intendite mentis oculos, si necdum potestis in rotam solis, saltem in fulgorem siderum; admiramini splendorem sanctorum, imitamini fidem, aemulamini sanctitatem. Stellae istae sicut flamma coruscant, et lumen luminum ortum demonstrant; ducunt ad cunabula novi Regis, ad cubiculum Virginis matris, quod est inviolabile fidei mysterium; imo perducent in templum Regis, in sanctuarium Dei Patris; quod est incogitabile fidei praemium. Interim autem, dum idonei non sumus, sapientiam Dei, quae in mysterio abscondita est, scrutari, vel majestatem quae in praemium reposita est, contemplari; contenti simus sanctorum claritatem mirari, sanctitatem imitari. Fili, inquit, concupisti sapientiam? serva mandata; et Dominus praebebit tibi illam (Eccli. I, 33). Altiora autem te ne quaesieris, et fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris: sed quae praecipit Dominus tibi, ipsa conserva semper (Eccli. III, 22). Praeceptum namque Domini lucidum, illuminans oculos (Psal. XVIII, 9), quibus postmodum ipsum corpus luminis valeas intueri, cum in luce radiorum, id est, in opere mandatorum, versari consueveris. Dulce quidem lumen, ut ait Salomon, et delectabile oculis videre solem (Eccle. XI, 7). Dulce prorsus et delectabile, sed illis quibus tolerabile. Sanos oculos fovet, infirmos torquet. Et quis est tam sano et acuto visu, ut in aspectu illius invisibilis Solis non caecutiat? quis ille scrutator majestatis, qui non opprimatur a gloria? Mirabilis facta est, o Domine, claritas tua, tum ex se, tum etiam ex me; quia confortata est adversum me, dum acies mea infirmata est in me, et jam non potero ad eam, sicut poteram in Adam. Potero forsitan ad claritatem siderum, qui non possum ad solem ipsum, et per hanc quandoque confortabor ad illum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Look up, brothers, to heaven; for their way of life is in heaven. Look up, and fix the eyes of your mind—if you cannot yet gaze upon the wheel of the sun, at least upon the brightness of the stars. Admire the splendor of the saints, imitate their faith, strive to equal their holiness. These stars flash like flame, and show forth the rising of the light of lights; they lead to the cradle of the new King, to the chamber of the Virgin Mother—which is the inviolable mystery of faith; indeed, they will lead us further, into the temple of the King, into the sanctuary of God the Father—which is the inconceivable reward of faith. Meanwhile, however, since we are not fit to search out the wisdom of God which lies hidden in mystery, or to contemplate the majesty laid up as reward, let us be content to admire the brightness of the saints and to imitate their holiness. Son, it says, have you desired wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will give it to you (Eccli. I, 33). But do not seek things higher than yourself, and do not search into things stronger than yourself; but keep always what the Lord commands you (Eccli. III, 22). For the commandment of the Lord is lightsome, enlightening the eyes (Psal. XVIII, 9), with which you may afterward be able to gaze upon the very body of light itself, once you have grown accustomed to dwell in the light of its rays—that is, in the doing of the commandments. Light is sweet indeed, as Solomon says, and it is delightful to the eyes to see the sun (Eccle. XI, 7). Sweet indeed and delightful, but only to those for whom it is bearable. It soothes sound eyes, it torments weak ones. And who has sight so sound and so keen that he would not be blinded at the sight of that invisible Sun? Who is that searcher of majesty who would not be overwhelmed by its glory? Wonderful, O Lord, has your brightness become, both in itself and also because of me; for it has grown strong against me, since my sight has grown weak within me, and now I can no longer attain to it as I could in Adam. Perhaps I shall be able to attain to the brightness of the stars, I who cannot attain to the sun itself, and through this I shall in time be strengthened toward that.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 7. Eia, surge, illuminare, anima mea, quae sedebas in tenebris suspice luminaria coeli, leva oculos tuos in montes unde veniet auxilium tibi, si veneris ad illum qui habitat in coelis, id est, in montibus ipsis. A montibus, inquam, veniet auxilium tibi, quia lux tibi inaccessibilis illuminat mirabiliter a montibus aeternis. Susceperunt montes lucem populo, a quibus ad valles camposque descendat subjectos. Hoc itaque, dico, fratres, optimum est, nostraeque infirmitati congruum illuminationis initium, si intendamus in eos qui illuminati sunt. Rectissima via est inveniendi Jesum, si praecedentium patrum sequamur lumen praevium. Semita justi recta est, rectus callis justi ad ambulandum (Isa. XXVI, 7). Qui justum sequitur, non ambulat in tenebris; non modo videbit, sed habebit lumen vitae. Videbit ad consolationem praesentis vitae: habebit in possessionem haereditatis aeternae. Pietas nempe promissionem habet vitae quae nunc est, et futurae. Exerceamur ad pietatem, et neutro nos fraudabit qui se ultro nobis fecit debitorem (I Tim. IV, 8, 7, 9). Exerceamur in operibus lucis, et qui abscondit lucem in manibus suis, annuntians de ea amico suo, quod possessio ejus sit, et ad eam possit ascendere (Job XXXVI, 32, 33), nunc aliquando in solatium operis eam nobis demonstrabit, et postmodum in praemium dabit, ipse lux nostra Jesus Christus qui vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 7. Come now, arise, be enlightened, my soul, you who were sitting in darkness; look up at the lights of heaven; lift up your eyes to the mountains, whence help will come to you, if you come to him who dwells in the heavens—that is, in those very mountains. From the mountains, I say, will help come to you, because the light inaccessible to you shines wonderfully from the eternal mountains. The mountains have received light for the people, that from them it may descend to the valleys and plains lying below. This, then, I say, brothers, is the best and most fitting beginning of enlightenment for our weakness: that we should fix our gaze upon those who have been enlightened. It is the most direct way of finding Jesus, if we follow the guiding light of the fathers who went before us. The path of the just is straight; the way of the just is straight for walking (Isa. XXVI, 7). He who follows the just man does not walk in darkness; he will not only see but will possess the light of life. He will see it for the consolation of the present life; he will possess it as an eternal inheritance. For godliness holds the promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come. Let us train ourselves unto godliness, and he who has of his own accord made himself our debtor will cheat us of neither (I Tim. IV, 8, 7, 9). Let us exercise ourselves in the works of light; and he who hides light in his hands, declaring to his friend concerning it that it is his possession and that he can ascend to it (Job XXXVI, 32, 33), will now at times show it to us for the comfort of our labor, and afterward will give it as our reward—he himself, our light, Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition prints mutatatione, evidently a printer's doubling of mutatione (the changing of water into wine). The printed form is kept.

sermons.title: Epiphany Sermon II: On the Various Ways God Enlightens Us

sermons.author: Guerric of Igny
metadata: Guerric of Igny, Sermones per annum, In Epiphania Domini, sermo III, Quibus gradibus ad sapientiae lumen perveniatur, in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier frères, 1879), cols. 54-59.
Internet Archive, 2011; PIMS, University of Toronto; University of Toronto funding.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: This third Epiphany sermon belongs to Guerric of Igny's medieval collection of sermons for the liturgical year, here read from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. Its individual date is unknown; the collection is associated approximately with his abbacy in 1138–1157. Guerric sets out the steps by which the soul comes to the light of wisdom: faith first, then righteousness, then knowledge, and at last wisdom, the taste of eternal things. Along the way he asks for the light to see one's own sins, and he draws on the healing of the blind man in two stages and on David's understanding gained from the commandments. The source explicitly names Epiphany.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO III.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON III.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Quibus gradibus ad sapientiae lumen perveniatur.

passages.label: English
passages.text: By What Steps One Comes to the Light of Wisdom

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Surge, illuminare, Jerusalem, quia venit lumen tuum (Isa. LX, 1). Benedictum lumen quod venit in nomine Domini, Deus Dominus, et illuxit nobis; de cujus munere etiam dies iste, dies sanctificatus de illuminatione Ecclesiae illuxit nobis. Gratias tibi, lux vera, quae illuminas omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum, quae ad hoc ipsum venisti homo in hunc mundum. Illuminata est Jerusalem mater nostra, mater omnium qui illuminari meruerunt: adeo ut jam luceat omnibus qui in mundo sunt. Gratias tibi, lux vera, quae lucerna es facta, ut Jerusalem illuminares, et lucerna pedibus meis Verbum Dei fieret. Gratias, inquam, tibi, quoniam ipsa Jerusalem illuminata facta est lucerna, ut luceat omnibus qui sunt in domo magni patris familias. Non solum enim illuminata est, sed exaltata, et super candelabrum illud totum aureum sita est; civitas super montem montium, illa quondam derelicta et odio habita, posita est in superbiam saeculorum, ut tam longe lateque fulgeat ejus Evangelium, quam longe lateque mundi vigebat imperium. Et si opertum est ejus Evangelium, in his qui pereunt opertum est (II Cor. IV, 3), in quibus Deus hujus saeculi excaecavit mentes infidelium, ut non fulgeat eis gloria Ecclesiae Christi. Quibus tamen non fulget ut videant, fulget ut invideant, et Ecclesiae torquentur gloria, qui ipsius illuminari nolunt gratia. Verum Ecclesia nec propter gloriam qua floret, superbiens, nec gratiam qua pollet, invidens, etiam illis quos molestos tolerat, lumen quod accepit implorat, dicens: Quoniam tu illuminas lucernam meam, Domine; Deus meus, illumina tenebras meas (Psal. XVII, 29). Mei forsitan sunt, quia praedestinati; sed adhuc tenebrae sunt, quia nondum vocati aut justificati. Voca et ipsos in admirabile lumen tuum, et praedicabunt mecum admirabile nomen tuum. Quanquam justus quisque ac sanctus in Ecclesia ita se illuminatum gaudeat, ut adhuc se non minima ex parte tenebrosum videat et doleat; et ideo necessario, cum illuminatus sit, adhuc se illuminari petat. Quanto namque amplius lucerna ejus illuminata fuerit, tanto verius ex lucerna ipsa tenebras suas deprehendit. Nec statim contrarium putaveris, quod in Evangelio Veritas ait: Lucerna corporis tui est oculus tuus. Si oculus tuus simplex fuerit, totum corpus tuum lucidum erit (Matth. VI, 22 et Luc. XI, 34). Non enim, quia ex oculo sincerae intentionis totum opus nostrum lucidum fit, ideo consequens est ut statim omnes tenebrae ignorantiarum nostrarum illuminatae sint. Is nempe modus est adhuc illuminationis nostrae, ut in lumen veritatis multum existimetur profecisse, qui defectum suum potuerit nosse, et scire quid desit sibi. Inde est quod et apud sapientes hujus mundi, qui magis sobrie disputaverunt de scientia, primus, numeratur gradus scientiae, scire quod nescias.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Arise, be enlightened, O Jerusalem, for thy light has come (Isa. LX, 1). Blessed is the light that comes in the name of the Lord — God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us; by whose gift this day too, a day made holy by the enlightenment of the Church, has shone upon us. Thanks be to thee, true light, who dost enlighten every man coming into this world, who for this very purpose didst come as man into this world. Jerusalem our mother has been enlightened, the mother of all who have deserved to be enlightened, so that now she shines for all who are in the world. Thanks be to thee, true light, who hast become a lamp, that thou mightest enlighten Jerusalem, and that the Word of God might become a lamp to my feet. Thanks, I say, to thee, because Jerusalem herself, once enlightened, has become a lamp, so that she might shine for all who are in the house of the great father of the family. For she was not only enlightened but exalted, and set upon that lampstand all of gold; a city upon the mountain of mountains — she who was once forsaken and held in hatred — has been set up as the pride of the ages, that her Gospel might shine as far and wide as the empire of the world once flourished far and wide. And if her Gospel is veiled, it is veiled in those who are perishing (II Cor. IV, 3), in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the glory of the Church of Christ may not shine upon them. Yet for them it does not shine so that they may see, but shines so that they may envy, and they are tormented by the glory of the Church, they who refuse to be enlightened by her grace. But the Church, neither growing proud on account of the glory in which she flourishes, nor begrudging the grace by which she is strong, even for those whom she patiently endures as troublesome, begs for the light she has received, saying: For thou wilt light my candle, O Lord; O my God, enlighten my darkness (Psal. XVII, 29). Perhaps they are mine, because predestined; but they are still darkness, because not yet called or justified. Call them too into thy wonderful light, and they will proclaim thy wonderful name together with me. Although every just and holy person in the Church rejoices that he has been enlightened, yet he sees and grieves that he is still, in no small part, dark; and so, necessarily, even though he has been enlightened, he still asks to be enlightened further. For the more his lamp has been enlightened, the more truly does he discover his own darkness by that very lamp. And you should not at once think this contrary to what the Truth says in the Gospel: The lamp of thy body is thine eye. If thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light (Matth. VI, 22 et Luc. XI, 34). For it is not the case that, because our whole work is made full of light from the eye of sincere intention, all the darkness of our ignorance is therefore at once illumined. For this indeed is still the measure of our enlightenment, that he is reckoned to have made great progress in the light of truth who has been able to know his own defect, and to know what he lacks. Hence it is that even among the wise men of this world, who have discussed knowledge more soberly, the first degree of knowledge is reckoned to be this: to know what you do not know.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Fratres, omnes vos filii lucis estis, et filii Dei. Non sumus noctis, neque tenebrarum. Nox enim praecessit, dies autem appropinquavit (Rom. XIII, 12). Et si fuimus aliquando tenebrae, nunc autem lux in Domino (Ephes. V, 8). Verumtamen si, quoniam non sumus tenebrae nec filii tenebrarum, dixerimus nos nihil pati tenebrarum, nos ipsos seducimus, et tenebras mortis, quae illuminari non mereantur, nobis inducimus. Quid enim, ait Lux mundi, quae in judicium venit in hunc mundum, ut qui non vident videant, et qui vident caeci fiant? Quia, inquit, dicitis, Videmus, peccatum vestrum manet (Joan. IX, 41). Video quantulumcunque, quoniam tu illuminas lucernam meam, o Domine, sed, quia parum est quod video, Deus meus, illumina tenebras meas (Psal. XVII, 29). Videmus ut multum per speculum et in aenigmate; sed multum longe est hoc ipsum a claritate vera claraque veritate, quae videbitur in facie. Ideo forsitan caecus, quem apud Marcum Dominus illuminare coeperat, homines quasi arbores ambulantes videbat (Marc. VIII, 22-24), quia videlicet non nisi per speculum et in aenigmate videbat; sed secundo imponens manum restituit eum, ita ut videret clare omnia; quod in nobis fiet, cum nos reficiet, et sanitatem perficiet impositione manuum secunda, quam coepit prima, restituens nos in claritate perfecta.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Brothers, you are all children of light, and children of God. We are not of the night, nor of darkness. For the night has passed, and the day is at hand (Rom. XIII, 12). And if we were once darkness, now we are light in the Lord (Ephes. V, 8). Yet if, because we are not darkness nor children of darkness, we should say that we suffer nothing of darkness, we deceive ourselves, and bring upon ourselves the darkness of death, which deserves not to be enlightened. For what does the Light of the world say, who came into this world for judgment, that those who do not see might see, and those who see might become blind? Because, he says, you say, We see: your sin remains (Joan. IX, 41). I see some little, however small, since thou, O Lord, dost light my candle; but because what I see is little, O my God, enlighten my darkness (Psal. XVII, 29). At most we see through a glass and in a dark manner; but this is very far indeed from the true clarity and clear truth which shall be seen face to face. Perhaps that is why the blind man, whom the Lord in Mark had begun to enlighten, saw men as though they were trees walking (Marc. VIII, 22-24), evidently because he saw only through a glass and in a dark manner; but by laying his hand on him a second time, he restored him so that he saw all things clearly — which shall happen in us, when he renews us and perfects our healing by a second laying on of hands, continuing what he began with the first, and restoring us to perfect clarity.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Sed hoc ipsum per speculum et in aenigmate, cui, aut quando, vel quandiu potest contingere? Quam misericorditer mecum ageretur, quam feliciter mihi viderer illuminatus, si peccata mea possem videre, cui quotidie necesse est plangere ac dicere: Circumdederunt me mala quorum non est numerus, et non potui ut viderem! (Psal. XXXIX, 13.) Nam delicta quis intelligit (Psal. XVIII, 13), quando etiam specie virtutis vitium decipiens interficit, quasi vere angelus tenebrarum transfigurans se in angelum lucis? Magnus utique, multumque illuminatus, qui delicta ad liquidum intelligere potuit et voluit; nam neque et dolosus potuit, et noluit intelligere, ut bene ageret (Psal. XXXV, 4). Deus illuminator omnium gentium, de te nobis cantabatur: Ecce veniet Dominus, et illuminabit oculos servorum suorum. Ecce venisti, o lumen meum, illumina oculos meos, ne unquam obdormiam in morte, ne peccatum ad mortem oculos nostros aliqua delectatione claudat, et ad consensum illiciat, aut, velut Isboseth, dormientem inveniens transfodiat (II Reg. IV, 7). Venisti, o lumen fidelium omnium, et ecce hodie de illuminatione verae fidei, id est, lucernae nostrae, dedisti nobis gaudere; da etiam de illuminatione tenebrarum nostrarum, quae residuae sunt, semper in Domino gaudere. Dedisti lumen verae fidei, da et lumen verae justitiae, da lumen divinae scientiae, da etiam et divinae sapientiae.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. But this very seeing "through a glass and in a dark manner" — to whom, or when, or for how long can it happen? How mercifully would it be dealt with me, how happily would I seem to myself illumined, if I could see my sins — I for whom it is necessary daily to lament and say: "Evils without number have surrounded me, and I was not able to see" (Psal. XXXIX, 13.)! For "who understands his faults" (Psal. XVIII, 13), when even vice, deceiving under the appearance of virtue, kills — as if truly an angel of darkness transforming himself into an angel of light? Great indeed, and much illumined, is he who was able and willing to understand his sins clearly; for the deceitful man could not and would not understand, that he might do well (Psal. XXXV, 4). O God, enlightener of all nations, of you it was sung to us: "Behold, the Lord will come, and he will enlighten the eyes of his servants." Behold, you have come, O my light; enlighten my eyes, lest I ever fall asleep in death, lest sin unto death close our eyes with some delight and entice us into consent, or, like Ishbosheth, find us sleeping and pierce us through (II Reg. IV, 7). You have come, O light of all the faithful, and behold, today you have given us to rejoice over the illumination of the true faith, that is, of our lamp; grant also that we may always rejoice in the Lord over the illumination of the darkness that still remains in us. You have given the light of true faith; give also the light of true righteousness, give the light of divine knowledge, give also the light of divine wisdom.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. His profecto gradibus proficiendum, hac via proficiscendum tibi esse puto, o anima fidelis, quo, fallacis mundi hujus tenebris exuta, pervenias ad patriam claritatis aeternae, ubi tenebrae tuae erunt sicut clara meridies, et nox sicut dies illuminabitur. Tunc prorsus, tunc videbis et afflues, et mirabitur, et dilatabitur cor tuum (Isa. LX, 5), quando replebitur divina majestate incircumscripti luminis omnis terra, et gloria ejus in te videbitur. Domus Jacob, venite, ambulemus in lumine Domini (Id. II, 3): ut veri filii lucis ambulemus de claritate in claritatem, tanquam praelucente Domini Spiritu, ut per singulos gradus virtutum regnum claritatis ulterius invadamus. Qui igitur jam per fidem sumus in lumine, ex ea et per eam in amplius et serenius lumen progrediamur, primo justitiae, dein scientiae, demumque sapientiae. Quod enim credimus per fidem, consequenter operandum vel promerendum est per justitiam, post intelligendum per scientiam, ac postremo contemplandum per sapientiam. Prima namque omnium accensa est lucerna fidei, ad quam operemur in nocte hujus saeculi. Inde scriptum est in laudem mulieris fortis, quae de nocte surrexit, et, de nocte ac die operans manibus suis, panem otiosa non comedit, Non exstinguetur, inquit, in nocte lucerna ejus (Prov. XXXI, 18), id est, non deficiet in tentatione fides ejus. Ad hanc lucernam non fiunt opera tenebrarum, sed exstinguitur cum fiunt. Qui enim male agit, odit lucem (Joan. III, 20). Ideoque exstinguit lucernam fidei, postponit memoriam Dei; non est timor Dei ante oculos ejus, et de tenebris quas sibi fecit, arbitrorumque absentia blanditur sibi, dicens: Quis me videt? Tenebrae circumdant me, et parietes cooperiunt me, et nemo circumspicit me. Quem vereor? Delictorum meorum non memorabitur Altissimus. Et non intelligit quoniam omnia videt oculus illius (Eccli. XXIII, 26, 27). Bona vero opera, etsi aliquando propter vanitatem declinandam in abscondito fiunt, ad lucem tamen internam et aeternam, id est sub judicio fidei et testimonio Dei fiunt, quia opera lucis sunt; lucernae utique ardentes in manibus operantium, et exspectantium adventum sponsi, qui educet quasi lumen justitiam tuam ad conspectum hominum et angelorum, et, sicut lux meridiana clara est, clarescere faciet opera tua, quia in Deo sunt facta, ut Deum in te, et te in Deo clarificent omnium judicia.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. By these steps indeed, I think, O faithful soul, you must advance; by this road you must set out, so that, stripped of the darkness of this deceitful world, you may arrive at the homeland of eternal brightness, where your darkness shall be as the clear noonday, and night shall be lit up as day. Then truly, then you shall see and overflow, and your heart shall wonder and be enlarged (Isa. LX, 5), when the whole earth shall be filled with the divine majesty of uncircumscribed light, and his glory shall be seen in you. "House of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord" (Id. II, 3): that as true children of light we may walk from brightness to brightness, as the Spirit of the Lord shines before us, so that through each degree of the virtues we may press on further into the kingdom of brightness. Therefore we who are already in the light through faith, from faith and through it let us advance into a fuller and more serene light — first of righteousness, then of knowledge, and finally of wisdom. For what we believe by faith must consequently be worked out, or earned, through righteousness; afterward it must be understood through knowledge; and finally it must be contemplated through wisdom. For of all lamps the first to be lit is the lamp of faith, by which we must work in the night of this present age. Hence it is written in praise of the valiant woman, who rose while it was yet night, and, working with her hands by night and by day, did not eat her bread in idleness: "Her lamp shall not be put out in the night" (Prov. XXXI, 18), that is, her faith shall not fail under temptation. By this lamp works of darkness are not done; rather, it is extinguished when such works are done. For "he who does evil hates the light" (Joan. III, 20). And so he extinguishes the lamp of faith, he puts away the memory of God; the fear of God is not before his eyes, and from the darkness he has made for himself, and the absence of witnesses, he flatters himself, saying: Who sees me? Darkness surrounds me, and walls cover me, and no one looks around at me. Whom do I fear? The Most High will not remember my sins. And he does not understand that the eye of the Most High sees all things (Eccli. XXIII, 26, 27). But good works, even when sometimes done in secret in order to avoid vanity, are nevertheless done before the inward and eternal light, that is, under the judgment of faith and the witness of God, because they are works of light — lamps indeed burning in the hands of those who work and who await the coming of the Bridegroom, who will bring forth your righteousness as light before the sight of men and angels, and, as the light of noonday is clear, he will make your works to shine clearly, because they were done in God, so that the judgment of all may glorify God in you, and you in God.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Quanta vero claritate justitia resplendeat etiam in praesenti, quanta luce laetificet conscientiam justi, familiarius et suavius conscientiae vestrae testimonium vos docebit. Saepe autem et fides radiat, et justitia coruscat, et adhuc tamen intellectus caligat, ut mysterium fidei, quod velut involutum tenens veneratur, explicare nesciat; signatus sit ei liber Scripturae, quasi litteras nesciat; sed nec ad discretionem boni et mali, veri et falsi sensus exercitatos habeat. Et tales quidem multi in Ecclesia, quorum fides multa, abundans justitia, scientia fere nulla. Quod tamen ad lumen justitiae accedere oporteat lumen scientiae, docet sermo prophetae, qui, cum praemisisset: Seminate vobis ad justitiam, ut ostenderet quas interim primitias colligamus de hoc semine, subjunxit: Illuminate vobis lumen scientiae (Osee. X, 12). Sic et Apostolus ait: Fructificantes in opere bono, et crescentes in scientia Dei (Coloss. I, 10). Tu quoque, David, sedens in cathedra sapientissimus princeps inter tres, quomodo super senes intellexisti? Quia mandata, inquit, quaesivi. A mandatis prorsus intellexi, quia intellectus bonus omnibus facientibus timorem Domini. Nam et unctio docens de omnibus, sciens nimirum quo ordine quidque apud eam discendum sit, prius docet bonitatem et disciplinam, et postmodum scientiam: si tamen qui docendus est, primo omnium crediderit, id est, elementa exordii sermonum justitiae didicerit. Ideo ille discipulus unctionis tam prudenter precem ordinabat, atque allegabat: Bonitatem, inquit, et disciplinam et scientiam doce me, quia mandatis tuis credidi (Psal. CXVIII, 100, 66). Ac si diceret: Didici prima elementa, id est, fidem non fictam; jam, quod sequitur, doce justitiam, id est bonitatem et disciplinam, ut sic demum provehat ad sanctorum scientiam. Vocasti ad gratiam fidei, jam justifica per bonitatem amoris, et disciplinam casti timoris, ut post magnifices munere scientiae spiritualis. Quos autem vocavit, hos et justificavit; et quos justificavit illos et magnificavit (Rom. VIII, 30).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. With how great a brightness righteousness shines even in the present life, with how great a light it gladdens the conscience of the just, the testimony of your own conscience will teach you more intimately and more sweetly. But often it happens that faith shines, and righteousness glitters, and yet understanding remains dark, so that one who holds and venerates the mystery of faith as though wrapped up cannot unfold it; the book of Scripture is sealed to him as if he did not know letters; nor does he have senses trained to discern good from evil, true from false. And indeed there are many such in the Church, in whom faith is great, righteousness abundant, but knowledge almost none. Yet that the light of knowledge ought to be added to the light of righteousness is taught by the word of the prophet, who, having first said: 'Sow for yourselves unto righteousness,' in order to show what first-fruits we are meanwhile to gather from this seed, added: 'Light for yourselves the light of knowledge' (Osee. X, 12). So too the Apostle says: 'Being fruitful in good work, and increasing in the knowledge of God' (Coloss. I, 10). You too, David, sitting in the chair, the wisest prince among the three—how did you understand above the elders? 'Because,' he says, 'I sought the commandments.' Entirely from the commandments I understood, for good understanding belongs to all who do the fear of the Lord. For the anointing which teaches concerning all things, knowing full well in what order each thing is to be learned from it, first teaches goodness and discipline, and afterward knowledge—provided, however, that the one to be taught has first of all believed, that is, has learned the elementary first principles of the words of righteousness. Therefore that disciple of the anointing so prudently ordered his prayer, and pleaded: 'Teach me goodness,' he says, 'and discipline and knowledge, for I have believed your commandments' (Psal. CXVIII, 100, 66). As if he were saying: I have learned the first elements, that is, unfeigned faith; now, what follows, teach me righteousness, that is, goodness and discipline, so that it may at last advance me to the knowledge of the saints. You have called to the grace of faith; now justify through the goodness of love and the discipline of chaste fear, so that afterward you may magnify with the gift of spiritual knowledge. 'Whom he called, these he also justified; and whom he justified, these he also magnified' (Rom. VIII, 30).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Sciendum sane quod, cum sit haec scientia sanctorum, non tamen omnes sancti docentur eam, sed illi duntaxat in quibus nec industria gratiam, nec gratia destituit industriam; sed utrumque mutuo sibi suffragio cooperatur, ut et docibilis sit homo discipulus, et spiritus adsit doctor sedulus. Cum autem varia charismata contineat haec scientia, Spiritus tamen moderator non in unum facile confert omnia, sed dividit singulis prout vult, alii notitiam mysteriorum, alii intellectum Scripturarum, alii interpretationem sermonum, alii discretionem spirituum, alii illam, quae pernecessaria est, velut in gustu dignoscentiam, atque dijudicationem virtutum ac vitiorum, ne fallant vitia specie virtutum. Non nocebunt, inquit, et non occident in universo sancto monte meo; quia repleta est terra scientia Domini (Isai. XI, 9).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. It should indeed be known that, although this is the knowledge of the saints, not all saints are taught it, but only those in whom neither does industry fail grace, nor grace fail industry; rather, each cooperates with the other by mutual support, so that the man is a teachable disciple, and the Spirit is present as a diligent teacher. But since this knowledge contains various charisms, the Spirit who governs does not readily confer all of them on one person, but divides them to each as he wills: to one, knowledge of the mysteries; to another, understanding of the Scriptures; to another, interpretation of discourses; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, that most necessary gift, as it were a tasting discernment, and a judging apart of virtues and vices, lest vices deceive under the appearance of virtues. 'They shall not hurt,' it says, 'nor shall they kill in all my holy mountain; for the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord' (Isai. XI, 9).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 7. Jam vero si quis post haec et per haec tria, fidem, justitiam atque scientiam, proficiat ad sapientiam, id est, saporem et gustum aeternorum, ut possit vacare et videre, videndoque gustare quam suavis Dominus; et quod oculus non vidit, et auris non audivit, et in cor hominis non ascendit, ei per Spiritum reveletur: hunc omnino dixerim illuminatum magnifice et gloriose, tanquam qui gloriam Domini revelata facie speculetur, et super quem gloria Domini saepius oriatur. Huic utique dicere habet non propheta, sed prophetarum Spiritus: Surge, illuminare, Jerusalem, quia venit lumen tuum, et gloria Domini super te orta est (Id. LX, 1). Fratres, non omnes capiunt hoc verbum, sed qui potest capere capiat. Non condemnatur qui non capit: sed qui non cupit, utique teporis arguitur. Qui autem cupit, noverit quia hoc lumen sapientiae fervens accendit oratio, sicut et lumen scientiae frequens lectio; si tamen cum legis, lucernam ardentem adhibueris, id est justitiam operum, piorumque experientiam sensuum. Tu autem, Domine, Pater luminum, qui lumen de te lumine unicum tuum, misisti sisti illuminare tenebras mortalium, da nobis per viam luminum pervenire ad lumen aeternum, ut placeamus coram te in lumine viventium, qui vivis et regnas per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 7. Now if anyone, after these and through these three—faith, righteousness, and knowledge—advances to wisdom, that is, to the savor and taste of eternal things, so that he may be free to see, and in seeing to taste how sweet the Lord is; and so that what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, may be revealed to him through the Spirit: this man I would call altogether magnificently and gloriously illumined, as one who beholds the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, and upon whom the glory of the Lord more often arises. To such a one, surely, it is not the prophet but the Spirit of the prophets who must say: 'Arise, be illumined, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has arisen upon you' (Id. LX, 1). Brothers, not all grasp this word, but let him who can grasp it, grasp it. He who does not grasp it is not condemned; but he who does not desire it is surely convicted of lukewarmness. But let him who desires it know that this light of wisdom is kindled by fervent prayer, just as the light of knowledge is kindled by frequent reading—provided, however, that when you read, you bring to it a burning lamp, that is, the righteousness of works and the experience of devout senses. But you, O Lord, Father of lights, who have sent your Only One, Light from your Light, to illumine the darkness of mortals, grant us to arrive by the way of lights at the eternal light, that we may be pleasing before you in the light of the living, you who live and reign through all ages of ages. Amen.

sermons.title: Epiphany Sermon III: By What Steps One Comes to the Light of Wisdom
