passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: This fourth Epiphany sermon belongs to Guerric of Igny's medieval collection of sermons for the liturgical year, here read from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. Its individual date is unknown; the collection is associated approximately with his abbacy in 1138–1157. Christ's baptism today brings a second birth for believers, but Guerric fears that monks keep the appearance of piety while denying its power. Naaman, washed seven times in the Jordan, becomes the figure of a sevenfold humility of Christ, in which those who lost the grace of their first Baptism may be cleansed again. The source explicitly names Epiphany.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO IV.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON IV.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De nova nostra nativitate et vita.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On Our New Birth and Life

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Secunda nobis hodie, fratres, nativitas celebratur, quae de illa prima nativitate, tanquam de causa effectus, consequenter nata videtur. Illa siquidem, quam usque hodie celebravimus, nativitas Christi est; ista, quam hodie celebramus, nativitas nostra est. In illa namque Christus natus est, in ista Christianitas nata est. Cum enim tria sint quae nos faciunt christianos, fides, Baptismus, et altaris participatio, hodierna dies fidem nobis initiavit, Baptisma consecravit, ac mensae coelestis miracula praeformavit. Quomodo sane prima gentium illuminatio fidem nobis initiaverit, quomodo Christus baptizatus Baptisma nostrum consecraverit, qualiter illa conversio aquae in vinum, mutationem rerum in convivio mensae Dominicae praeostenderit, nequaquam jam opus est ut doceamus: sed illud arbitror operae pretium, ut nosmetipsos commoneamus, ne fides in nobis a suis degeneret initiis, ne vacuetur in nobis gratia Baptismatis, ne cedat nobis in judicium participatio calicis Christi.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Today, brothers, we celebrate a second birth for ourselves, which seems to have been born as a consequence of that first birth, as an effect follows from its cause. For that birth which we have celebrated up until today is the birth of Christ; but this one, which we celebrate today, is our own birth. For in that birth Christ was born, but in this one Christianity was born. Since there are three things that make us Christians—faith, Baptism, and participation at the altar—today's feast has initiated faith in us, consecrated Baptism, and prefigured the miracles of the heavenly table. Indeed, there is no longer any need for us to teach how that first illumination of the Gentiles initiated faith for us, how Christ's being baptized consecrated our Baptism, how that turning of water into wine foreshadowed the change of things in the banquet of the Lord's table: but I think it worthwhile that we remind ourselves, lest faith in us should degenerate from its beginnings, lest the grace of Baptism be made void in us, lest our participation in the cup of Christ turn into judgment against us.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Et ipsa quidem fides, qualis ab illis Magis, primis videlicet auctoribus suis, nobis hodie tradita sit; qualiter maximum fidei sacramentum mysticis insinuaverint munerum figuris, satis abundeque disseruere patres nostri, ut ex ea parte nullus jam alius labor quam in labores eorum introire nobis resederit. Sed neque magnopere postulat status, imo ruina temporis hujus, ut de mysterio fidei disputetur sed ut magis id modis omnibus elaboretur ut, sicut Apostolus ait, in conscientia pura idem fidei mysterium habeatur (I Tim. III, 9). Ecce enim hodie si de mysterio fidei interrogas, omnes fere invenies christianissimos; si conscientias discutias, paucos admodum invenies vere christianos. Totus fere mundus confitetur verbis se nosse Deum, factis autem negat (Tit. I, 16); adeo ut et qui speciem pietatis videntur habere, virtutem ejus saepius inveniantur propemodum abnegare. Quid putatis autem, fratres mei, quos in hoc significare voluerim, quos scilicet dicam pietatis habere speciem, sed abnegare virtutem? Si illos qui spatiosam viam saeculi ambulant, intelligitis, quid illi vel de sola praeferunt pietatis specie, qui nomine solo christiani, atque in vacuum assumentes nomen sanctum Christi, tota ac libera professione sectantur quae huic inimica sunt nomini; qui omni specie conversationis et modo vitae, se protestantur inimicos crucis Christi? Haeccine est species pietatis quam in eis videmus, habitus et incessus meretricius, sermo scurrilis, oculus impudicus, venter qui pro Deo colitur, et omnis illa vitae contumelia, quae publice et gloriabunde, velut in faciem pietati irrogatur? Quae enim in occulto ab ipsis fiunt, turpe est et dicere (Ephes. V, 12). Fodiat parietem eorum qui ad ipsos missus est prophetare, ut adhuc majores abominationes videat, quas non erubescunt aut verentur coram illa tremenda majestate perpetrare. Quid enim mihi, qui monachus videor, de his qui extra hoc monasterium sunt judicare? Utinam nec de his ipsis qui hic intus sunt, mihi esset judicare. Ad me ipsum namque conturbata est anima mea, dum scilicet vereor ne haec ipsa species pietatis, quam utcunque vobiscum gero, gravius me incipiat accusare, si pietatem ipsa me convicerit abnegasse.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. As for faith itself—how it was handed down to us today by those Magi, who were indeed its first authors; how they expressed the greatest sacrament of faith through the mystical figures of their gifts—our fathers have discussed this fully and more than abundantly, so that in that regard no other labor remains for us than to enter into their labors. But neither does the condition of the times, or rather the ruin of this present age, greatly demand that we dispute about the mystery of faith, but rather that we strive by every means to hold, as the Apostle says, the same mystery of faith in a pure conscience (I Tim. III, 9). For behold, today, if you ask about the mystery of faith, you will find almost everyone most Christian; but if you examine consciences, you will find very few who are truly Christian. Almost the whole world confesses in words that it knows God, but denies it by its deeds (Tit. I, 16); so much so that even those who seem to have the appearance of piety are often found to deny its power almost entirely. But what do you suppose, my brothers, I meant to signify by this—whom indeed do I mean by those who have the appearance of piety, but deny its power? If you understand those who walk the broad way of the world, what mere appearance of piety do even they put forward, who are Christians in name only, and who, taking up the holy name of Christ in vain, pursue, by their whole and free profession, things that are hostile to this name; who, by every outward show and manner of life, declare themselves enemies of the cross of Christ? Is this the appearance of piety that we see in them—harlot-like bearing and gait, scurrilous speech, shameless eye, the belly that is worshiped in place of God, and all that reproach of life which is publicly and boastfully inflicted, as it were, upon the very face of piety? For the things that are done by them in secret are shameful even to mention (Ephes. V, 12). Let him who was sent to them to prophesy dig through their wall, that he may see even greater abominations, which they do not blush or fear to commit in the presence of that tremendous majesty. But what right have I, who only appear to be a monk, to judge those who are outside this monastery? Would that I had no need to judge even those who are within it. For within myself my soul is troubled, since indeed I fear lest this very appearance of piety, which I somehow bear among you, may begin to accuse me the more gravely, if that appearance itself should convict me of having denied piety.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Omnino, fratres, verendum est mihi, an vero et vobis ipsis, vos videritis, ne ad nos praecipue spectet ille sermo qui per Apostolum prophetatus est de temporibus novissimis; ubi, cum malitiam hominum describeret tunc futurorum, qualis nunc manifeste legi potest in vita et moribus eorum, longum tandem sic conclusit malorum catalogum: Habentes, inquit, speciem pietatis, virtutem autem ejus abnegantes (II Tim. III, 5). Quid enim ita speciem pietatis habet, sicut haec quam praetendimus, humilitas tonsurae et habitus, parcimonia cibi et potus, labor fere continuus, et ordinatissimus per omnia vivendi modus? Caeterum de virtute ipsa pietatis, quam haec species exterior promittit, quam prope nihil in me meique similibus valeat inveniri, pudor mihi esset confiteri, si non omnibus essemus manifesti. Quae est enim virtus pietatis, nisi charitas non ficta, humilitas vera, patientia longanimis, obedientia non segnis? In his virtutibus earumque similibus, quantum vobis liceat gloriari, vestro, fratres, relinquimus judicio; de me siquidem ingenue confiteor, quia nomina quidem earum scio, saporem adhuc ignoro. Merito itaque pudorem mihi pariter et timorem incutit habitus quem gero religionis, cui fere nullum suffragatur testimonium virtutis. Numquid enim tuto mihi possum usurpare monachi nomen et honorem, cujus non habeo meritum et virtutem; cum, sicut ante nos dictum est, simulata sanctitas, duplicata sit iniquitas (AUG. in psal. LXIII); et lupus sub ovina pelle deprehensus graviore sit sententia percellendus? Propterea vos quoque, fratres, ut tuto gloriari possitis, in hac, qua corpora vestra decorata sunt, specie pietatis, ponite corda vestra in virtute ejus; ut species in corporibus, virtus in cordibus, probatos vos exhibeant tam angelis quam hominibus, sitque, sicut scriptum est: Omnes qui viderint eos, cognoscent illos quia isti sunt semen cui benedixit Dominus (Isa. LXI, 9).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Brothers, I must altogether fear—whether you too should, you yourselves must judge—that this saying which was prophesied by the Apostle concerning the last times applies especially to us; where, describing the wickedness of the men who were then to come, such as can now clearly be read in the life and conduct of men, he concluded his long catalogue of evils thus: "Having," he says, "the appearance of godliness, but denying the power thereof" (II Tim. III, 5). For what has so much the appearance of godliness as this which we put forward—the humility of the tonsure and habit, the sparingness of food and drink, the almost continuous labor, and the altogether well-ordered manner of life? But as for the very power of godliness which this outward appearance promises, how little it is to be found in me and those like me—it would shame me to confess, were we not already manifest to all. For what is the power of godliness, but unfeigned charity, true humility, long-suffering patience, ready obedience? How far you may boast in these and similar virtues, brothers, I leave to your own judgment; as for myself, I confess frankly that I know the names of these virtues, but I do not yet know their taste. Rightly, then, the habit of religion which I wear strikes me with shame and fear alike, since it is supported by almost no testimony of virtue. For can I safely assume the name and honor of monk, when I do not have the merit and virtue of one? As it has been said before us, "feigned holiness is doubled iniquity" (AUG. in psal. LXIII); and a wolf caught under sheep's clothing is to be struck with a graver sentence. Therefore you too, brothers, so that you may boast safely in this outward appearance of godliness with which your bodies are adorned, place your hearts in its power; so that the appearance in your bodies and the power in your hearts may show you approved both to angels and to men, and so that it may be as it is written: "All that see them shall know them, that these are the seed which the Lord hath blessed" (Isa. LXI, 9).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Haec est, fratres, christianae fidei pietas vera, hoc est habere mysterium fidei in conscientia pura. Ut enim mysterium fidei, quod hodie nobis mystica commendaverunt Magorum munera, fideliter et digne conservaremus immaculatum in conscientia pura, hodie itidem Christus baptizatus, non sibi sed nobis, Aspersit, sicut Apostolus ait, corda a conscientia mala, et abluit corpora aqua munda (Hebr. X. 22). Quam felix, o fratres, anima illa, quae sic lota in salutem, mox e vestigio secuta est Salvatorem, ut deinceps adhaerens ei cum Apostolis, illam meruit audire vocem: Qui lotus est, non indiget nisi ut pedes lavet, sed est mundus totus! (Joan. XIII, 10.) Caeterum qui baptizatur a mortuo, et iterum tangit eum, quid proficit lavatio illius? (Eccli. XXXIV, 30.) Ego postquam Baptismo lotus fui, non unum mortuum, sed tot mortuos quot opera mortis, tetigi; et, juxta Petrum apostolum, contigit mihi illud veri proverbii, Canis reversus ad vomitum suum, et sus lota in volutabro luti (II Petr. II, 4). Quid igitur faciam? quibus ulterius aquis sordes tantas diluam? Audio quia sicut una fides, sic unum Baptisma est, nec secundo Baptismati locus est, quoniam quicunque baptizamur, in morte Christi baptizamur; qui sicut semel mortuus est, sic et semel baptizatus est, ut et nobis unici modum et formam Baptismatis praescriberet. Diffiderem forsitan ulterius posse mundari, nisi quia desperantem reducit in spem, inter alias Scripturae consolationes, etiam fidele consilium Elisei, etiamsi totus instar Naaman Syri lepra sim perfusus, ac veterno incurabili possessus. Vade, inquit, et lavare septies in Jordane, et mundaberis. Si dixisset, Lavare ter, mundaberis, continuo intellexissem trinam mersionem qua inundantur baptizati, diceremque totum illud miraculum gratiam prophetare Baptismatis, ut jam tunc Jordanis de virtute Dominici Baptismi coepisset ad salutem gentium operari. Nunc autem cum signanter dicat, lavare septies in Jordane, quid sibi vult septenarius iste, aut quis est Jordanis ille? Jordanis, ut aiunt, interpretatur Descensus eorum. Quorum? Illorum utique qui humiliantur ad poenitentiam, qui nimirum quanto profundius descendunt per gradus humilitatis, tanto se penitius mergunt et plenius abluunt spiritualis alveo Jordanis.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. This, brothers, is the true godliness of the Christian faith; this is to hold the mystery of faith in a pure conscience. For in order that we might faithfully and worthily keep undefiled in a pure conscience the mystery of faith which the mystical gifts of the Magi commended to us today, Christ, baptized today, not for himself but for us, as the Apostle says, "sprinkled our hearts from an evil conscience, and washed our bodies with clean water" (Hebr. X. 22). How happy, O brothers, is that soul which, thus washed unto salvation, straightway followed the Savior in his very footsteps, so that thereafter, clinging to him with the apostles, it deserved to hear that voice: "He that is washed needeth not but to wash his feet, but is clean wholly!" (Joan. XIII, 10.). But he who is washed after touching a dead body, and touches it again, what does his washing profit him? (Eccli. XXXIV, 30.) I, after I was washed in Baptism, have touched not one dead body, but as many dead bodies as there are works of death; and, according to the apostle Peter, that true proverb has befallen me: "The dog returned to his vomit," and "the sow washed, to her wallowing in the mire" (II Petr. II, 4). What, then, shall I do? With what further waters shall I wash away such great filth? I hear that, just as there is one faith, so there is one Baptism, and there is no place for a second Baptism, since whoever of us are baptized, are baptized into the death of Christ; who, just as he died once, so was baptized once, that he might prescribe for us too the manner and form of a single Baptism. I might perhaps despair of being able to be cleansed any further, were it not that, among the other consolations of Scripture, the faithful counsel of Elisha brings back the despairing soul to hope—even if I were, like Naaman the Syrian, entirely covered with leprosy, and possessed by an incurable lethargy. "Go," he said, "and wash seven times in the Jordan, and you shall be made clean." If he had said, "Wash three times, and you shall be made clean," I would at once have understood the threefold immersion by which the baptized are overwhelmed, and I would say that that whole miracle prophesied the grace of Baptism, so that the Jordan even then began, by the power of the Lord's future Baptism, to work for the salvation of the nations. But now, since he expressly says, "wash seven times in the Jordan," what does this number seven mean, or what is that Jordan? Jordan, as they say, is interpreted "Their Descent." Whose descent? Surely of those who are humbled unto repentance, who indeed, the more deeply they descend by the steps of humility, the more inwardly do they immerse themselves and the more fully do they wash in the channel of the spiritual Jordan.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Ad meipsum, o Deus, conturbata est anima mea, memor peccatorum suorum; propterea memor ero tui de terra Jordanis, quomodo scilicet in descensu humiliationis mundaveris Naaman leprosum. Descendit, inquit, et lavit septies in Jordane, juxta sermonem viri Dei, et mundatus est. Descende et tu, o anima mea, de curru superbiae in salubres aquas Jordanis, qui de fonte domus David, toto jam profluit orbe in ablutionem peccatoris et menstruatae. Haec est nimirum humilitas poenitendi, quae, de domo pariter et exemplo profluens Christi, toto jam praedicatur orbe, totiusque purgat crimina mundi. O vos, Naaman Syri: non enim unus, sed innumeri: o, inquam, divites, sed leprosi; superbi, sed aerumnosi; quare tam vehementer abhorretis lavari his medicinalibus aquis? cur vobis ita viluit noster iste Jordanis prae fluviis Damasci? Dicitis enim, si forte quaerentibus aliquando consilium salutis imitanda praedicetur humilitas et paupertas Christi: Nunquid non meliores sunt fluvii Damasci omnibus aquis Israel, ut laver in eis, et munder? (IV Reg. V, 10, 14, 12.) Nunquid non est melius, et ad purgationem peccatorum efficacius, quotidie benefacere de affluentia mundi, quam semel omnia relinquendo pauperem fieri? Sed enim audi, Naaman. Fluvium Damascenum absorbebit Leviathan, et non mirabitur; nam de Jordane si habeat fiduciam quod influat in os ejus (Job XL, 18), spes eum frustrabitur. Neque enim grande reputat quantiscunque, praeter humilitatem christianam, virtutibus affluas: cum etiam pauperes Christi devorare se posse confidat, sed nihil in eis inimicus proficiat. Damascus secundum nomen suum, Civitas sanguinis est, et aquae ejus sanguine mistae sunt; quia opera etiam bona carnalium et saecularium, vix a quocunque peccato pura sunt. Et quomodo id quod infectum est sanguine, sanguinem mundabit? qua ratione lepram, id quod leprosum est curabit? At Jordanis noster ipse quidem purum profluit, nec te calumniari poterunt superbi, si totus in eo mersus fueris, ac velut consepultus humilitati Christi.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Within myself, O God, my soul is troubled, mindful of its sins; therefore I will remember you from the land of the Jordan—namely, how, in the descent of humiliation, you cleansed Naaman the leper. He went down, it says, and washed seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of the man of God, and was cleansed. Go down, you too, O my soul, from the chariot of pride into the healthful waters of the Jordan, which, flowing from the fountain of the house of David, now pours forth through the whole world for the washing of the sinner and of her who is unclean. This indeed is the humility of repentance, which, flowing alike from the household and the example of Christ, is now preached throughout the whole world, and purges the crimes of the whole world. O you Naamans of Syria—for there is not one, but countless many: O, I say, rich, yet leprous; proud, yet wretched—why do you so vehemently shrink from being washed in these healing waters? Why has our Jordan grown so cheap in your eyes compared to the rivers of Damascus? For you say, if perchance to those seeking the counsel of salvation the humility and poverty of Christ is preached as something to be imitated: "Are not the rivers of Damascus better than all the waters of Israel, that I may wash in them, and be made clean?" (IV Reg. V, 10, 14, 12.). Is it not better, and more effective for the cleansing of sins, to do good daily out of the abundance of the world, than, by forsaking all at once, to become poor? But hear this, Naaman. Leviathan will swallow up the river of Damascus, and not marvel at it; for if he should have confidence that the Jordan will flow into his mouth (Job XL, 18), his hope will be disappointed. For he does not reckon it a great thing, however much you may abound in virtues apart from Christian humility, since he is confident that he can devour even the poor of Christ—but in them the enemy makes no progress. Damascus, according to its name, is the "City of Blood," and its waters are mingled with blood; for even the good works of carnal and worldly men are scarcely pure from any sin whatsoever. And how shall that which is stained with blood cleanse blood? By what reasoning shall that which is itself leprous cure leprosy? But our Jordan flows pure indeed, nor will the proud be able to slander you, if you have been wholly immersed in it, and as it were buried together with the humility of Christ.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Audi saltem, o Naaman, domesticos tuos, humiles amicos, fideles consiliarios. Naaman recedebat indignans adversum virum Dei, quem consuluerat; at illi, Pater, inquiunt, etsi rem grandem dixisset tibi propheta, certe facere debueras. Fidele prorsus verbum, rationis et sapientiae plenum; quippe suggestio est rationalium hominis sensuum, quos sibi Deus testes retinuit adversus hominem ipsum. Pater, inquiunt, etsi rem grandem dixisset tibi Propheta, certe facere debueras. Non credere namque Prophetae, Dei est injuria: non tentare omnia pro salute, odium est sui ipsius et invidia. Quid enim grande esse potest in praecepto, ubi salus est in promisso? Quanto magis non debet videri grande vel difficile, discere ab Jesu quia mitis est et humilis corde, cum in eo pariter inveniatur et requies animae, et praesens medela spiritualis leprae, pignusque salutis aeternae? Tandem vix aegreque obtinetur a superbo peccatore ut descendat in Jordanem et lavet; si tamen septies lavat, totumque se plenius et saepius mergat, non moratur effectus salutis fidem prophetico facere sermoni. Sed, proh dolor! quanta est hujus nostri miseria temporis! quia non solum divites, sed etiam pauperes leprosi, ita inveniuntur delicati, ut vix usque ad talos salubribus intingi patiantur aquis: aut si semel laverint, mox sibi plenissime videantur mundati.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Listen at least, O Naaman, to your own household, your humble friends, your faithful counselors. Naaman was going away indignant against the man of God whom he had consulted; but they said, "Father, even if the prophet had told you a great thing, surely you ought to have done it." A thoroughly faithful word, full of reason and wisdom; indeed it is the suggestion of a man's rational senses, which God has kept for himself as witnesses against the man himself. "Father," they say, "even if the Prophet had told you a great thing, surely you ought to have done it." For not to believe the Prophet is an injury to God; not to attempt everything for one's salvation is hatred and envy toward oneself. For what great thing can there be in a command, where salvation lies in the promise? How much less ought it to seem a great or difficult thing to learn from Jesus, because he is meek and humble of heart, since in him is found alike both rest for the soul, and a present remedy for spiritual leprosy, and the pledge of eternal salvation? At last, it is only with difficulty and reluctance that a proud sinner is brought to go down into the Jordan and wash; yet if he washes seven times, and plunges himself more fully and more often, the effect of salvation does not delay in proving the prophetic word true. But, alas, how great is the misery of this our present time! For not only the rich, but even the poor who are leprous, are found so delicate that they scarcely allow themselves to be dipped up to the ankles in these healthful waters; or if they wash once, they straightway seem to themselves most fully cleansed.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 7. Et Elisaeus non ita sentit, sed signanter exprimit, Septies lavare, et mundaberis. Sciebat nimirum humilitatem Christi, quae nobis imitanda est, si perfecte volumus mundari, septemplicis esse virtutis. Prima virtus, quod, cum dives esset, pauper factus est. Secunda, quod paupertati extremitatem adjiciens, in praesepi positus est. Tertia, quod Matri subditus. Quarta, quod servi manibus hodie inclinavit caput. Quinta, quod discipulum furem tulit et proditorem. Sexta, quod sic fuit mansuetus ante iniquum judicem. Septima, quod crucifixoribus tam clemens intercessor fuit apud Patrem. His vestigiis, licet satis a longe, gigantem sequeris, si paupertatem diligis, si inter pauperes extremitatem eligis, si monasterii subditus es disciplinae, si minorem tibi pateris praeesse, si falsos fratres aequanimiter tuleris, si mansuetudine vincas cum judicaris, si charitatem rependas illis a quibus injuste pateris. Haec humilitas plane sine injuria unici Baptismi rebaptizat: quia mortem Christi non iterat, sed mortificationem et sepulturam criminum instaurat; et quod in illo Baptismo gestum est specie, hic rursus impletur veritate. Haec siquidem humilitas coelos aperit, spiritum adoptionis restituit: Pater agnoscit filium, quippe in innocentia et puritate pueri regenerati reformatum. Unde bene de Naaman Scriptura meminit quia restituta est caro ejus, sicut caro pueri parvuli (IV Reg. V, 13, 10 et 14): significans ut arbitror, quia eorum, qui sic se abluunt, non solum corda recuperant innocentiam parvulorum; sed etiam corpora secundum quemdam modum puerilem sibi vindicant puritatem mortificatione membrorum. Sic enim de quodam sanctorum legitur, quia in membris defuncti, septennis quodammodo pueri gratia videbatur (De S. Martino dictum apud Sulpicium). Ecce, fratres, qui primi gratiam Baptismatis tantis voluptatum sordibus amisimus, ecce verum Jordanem, descensum scilicet humilium, ubi die rebaptizari licet, invenimus. Hoc tantum est, ut non parcamus nobis de die in diem descendere profundius, et plenius mergi, Christoque penitus consepeliri. Ipsi gratias agamus, cujus humilitas et formam Baptismi hodie dedicavit credentibus, et gratiam non disparem reservavit poenitentibus. Ipsi gloria per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 7. And Elisha thinks no differently, but expressly states: 'Wash seven times, and you shall be clean.' For he knew that the humility of Christ, which we must imitate if we wish to be perfectly cleansed, is of a sevenfold virtue. The first virtue: that, though he was rich, he became poor. The second: that, adding the extremity of poverty, he was laid in a manger. The third: that he was subject to his Mother. The fourth: that today he bowed his head to the hands of a servant. The fifth: that he bore a disciple who was a thief and a betrayer. The sixth: that he was so meek before an unjust judge. The seventh: that he was so merciful an intercessor with the Father for those who crucified him. In these footprints, though at quite a distance, you follow the giant, if you love poverty, if among the poor you choose the lowest place, if you are subject to the discipline of the monastery, if you allow one lesser than yourself to be set over you, if you bear false brothers with equanimity, if you conquer by meekness when you are judged, if you repay with charity those at whose hands you suffer unjustly. This humility plainly rebaptizes without injury to the one Baptism, because it does not repeat the death of Christ, but renews the mortification and burial of sins; and what was accomplished in that Baptism as a figure is here fulfilled again in reality. Indeed, this humility opens the heavens, restores the spirit of adoption: the Father recognizes the son, inasmuch as he is reshaped into the innocence and purity of a regenerated child. Hence Scripture rightly records of Naaman that his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child (IV Reg. V, 13, 10 et 14): signifying, as I judge, that the hearts of those who wash themselves in this way not only recover the innocence of little children, but their bodies too, in a certain childlike manner, claim for themselves a purity through the mortification of the members. For thus it is read of a certain one of the saints, that in the limbs of the deceased there seemed to appear, as it were, the grace of a seven-year-old child. (Said of St. Martin, in Sulpicius.) Behold, brothers, we who lost the grace of the first Baptism through such great filth of pleasures—behold, we have found the true Jordan, namely the descent of the humble, where it is permitted to be rebaptized daily. This alone is needed: that we not spare ourselves from descending more deeply day by day, and being more fully submerged, and being wholly buried together with Christ. Let us give thanks to him, whose humility today both consecrated the form of Baptism for believers, and reserved a grace not unlike it for penitents. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric, pleading with Jeremiah that he is a child, praises John the Baptist, who prophesied before he could speak and made his parents prophets. Grace flowed principally into Mary, from her into John and from John into his parents. John stood nearer to Christ than any other mortal and prepared a perfect people for the Lord. Guerric urges the brothers to bring forth fruits worthy of repentance and seeks John's intercession. The sermon appears under the heading for the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: IN NATIVITATE S. JOANNIS BAPTISTAE.

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De laudibus sancti.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the praises of the saint.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Ah! Domine Deus, ecce nescio loqui, quia puer ego sum (Jerem. I, 6). Fratres, si Jeremias, sicut ex lectione audistis hesterna, ne praedicationis susciperet officium, verecundius quam justius minorem causabatur aetatem, quanto rectius ego sensum causarer minorem? Si sanctum ex utero, et quem manifeste divina mittebat electio, aetas deterrebat infirmior, mihi quae frons esse potest ad loquendum, cui nec ad sanctitatem suffragatur conscientia. nec ad sermonis facultatem suppetit scientia? Illi erat timori pueritia sua, mihi non erit puerilitas mea? Verumtamen tu, puer propheta Altissimi, de quo sermonem hodie nostri debet locus officii, puerilitatem nostram non pateris excusatam haberi, quin saltem gestiamus more puerorum de te quoquomodo balbutire; qui etiam in materia leviori, plena necdum didicimus verba formare. Tuum erit, o vox Verbi, vox sapientiae, tibi devotae solvere vinculum linguae, qui necdum loquens, usum loquendi muto potuisti patri reformare. Nec sine fenore magno rediit intercepta facultas loquendi, cui simul accessit gratia prophetandi, ut videlicet uterque parens aliquid sibi gauderet praerogatum de praerogativa filii.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "Ah, Lord God, behold, I know not how to speak, for I am a child" (Jerem. I, 6). Brethren, if Jeremiah, as you heard from yesterday's reading, pleaded his younger age—more out of modesty than out of right—so as not to take up the office of preaching, how much more rightly might I plead my lesser understanding? If a man holy from the womb, and one whom the divine election was manifestly sending, was deterred by his tender age, what boldness can there be for me to speak, for whom conscience lends no support toward holiness, nor knowledge supplies ability of speech? If his boyhood was a source of fear to him, shall not my childishness be one for me? Yet you, O boy-prophet of the Most High, of whom our office today must speak, do not allow our childishness to excuse us from being at least eager, in the manner of children, to stammer something about you however we can—we who, even in lighter matters, have not yet learned to form complete words. It will be yours, O voice of the Word, voice of Wisdom, to loose the bond of the tongue devoted to you—you who, before you could yet speak, were able to restore to your mute father the use of speech. Nor did the recovered faculty of speech return without great profit, since along with it came also the grace of prophesying, so that each parent might rejoice in having received something as a prerogative from the prerogative of the son.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Qui enim propheta, et plus quam propheta futurus erat, imo ante prophetare quam profari, prius Deum quam se ipsum sentire coeperat, parentes quoque suos prophetas faciebat; et in eos qui in se transfuderant carnis substantiam, spiritus sui et gratiae superabundantiam refundebat. Nam et Elisabeth, postquam exsultavit in gaudio infans in utero ejus, tunc et ipsa prophetavit repleta Spiritu sancto; quia necdum loquens filius, matri tamen occultam Domini praesentiam exsultatione manifesta revelavit. Salutabat Salvatorem motu, quo poterat, et in occursum Domini praecursor impiger erumpere gestiebat. Plane incomparabilis gratia, inaestimabilis divinae virtutis potentia. Vox Mariae dum auribus Elisabeth insonat, ad cor Joannis penetrat, qui abstrusus intra materna latebat viscera, spiritum ejus animat, gaudioque salutari vegetat: et cui virtus naturae vix adhuc totam infuderat animam, virtus vocis Mariae pleniorem infudit prophetiam, adeo ut etiam de plenitudine filii copiose videatur in matrem refundi. Vere gratia plena Maria: manifeste Deus totius gratiae in ea erat, de cujus munificentia tam copiose, tam magnifice, principaliter in Matrem, de Matre in Joannem, de Joanne in parentes gratiae largitas profluebat. Flumina prorsus de ventre Mariae fluebant aquae vivae, et fons vitae et gratiae oriebatur de medio paradisi ad irriganda ligna paradisi.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. For he who was to be a prophet, and more than a prophet—indeed, who began to perceive God before he perceived himself, and to prophesy before he could speak—made his own parents prophets as well; and upon those who had transfused into him the substance of their flesh, he poured back the overflow of his spirit and grace. For Elizabeth too, after the infant leapt for joy in her womb, then herself prophesied, filled with the Holy Spirit; because the son, not yet able to speak, nevertheless revealed to his mother by manifest exultation the hidden presence of the Lord. He greeted the Savior by the movement he was able to make, and, as forerunner, longed eagerly to burst forth to meet the Lord. Truly incomparable grace, inestimable power of divine virtue! While the voice of Mary sounded in the ears of Elizabeth, it penetrated to the heart of John, who lay hidden within his mother's womb; it animated his spirit and quickened him with saving joy. And to him, into whom the power of nature had scarcely yet infused a complete soul, the power of Mary's voice infused a fuller prophecy, so much so that from the fullness of the son there seems to have overflowed abundantly even into the mother. Truly "full of grace" is Mary: manifestly the God of all grace was in her, from whose munificence the bounty of grace flowed so abundantly, so magnificently—principally into the Mother, from the Mother into John, from John into the parents. Truly rivers of living water flowed from the womb of Mary, and the fountain of life and grace arose from the midst of paradise to water the trees of paradise.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Proxima erat fonti cedrus ista nobilis, Joannem loquor, consobrinum et amicum sponsi, praecursorem, Baptistam, et martyrem Domini: ideoque nimirum uberius irrigata in tantum excrevit, ut inter natos mulierum nihil illa sublimius posset inveniri. Omnino Salvatori proximus erat, qui non solum copula sanguinis conjunctus, aut amicitia intimus erat, sed etiam gloria annuntiationis, novitate nativitatis, sanctitate pene originali, praedicatione consimili, auctoritate baptizandi, virtute patiendi, ante mortales omnes ei propius accedebat. Denique si alia cessarent omnia, si cuncta de eo silerent prophetarum praeconia; solius gratia nominis ejus (9), quod vocatum est ab angelo, priusquam in utero conciperetur, satis abundeque singularem in eo futuram Dei gratiam testabatur. Dignum quippe erat ut gratiam Dei, quam gratia plena profudit, plenus gratia praedicaret, et gratia non mediocri emineret, qui gratiae tempus a tempore legis velut medius limes disterminaret. Usque ad Joannem enim Lex et Prophetae prophetaverunt (Luc. XVI, 16); qui videlicet primus ostendit praesentem, quem Lex et Prophetia promiserant venturum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Nearest to the fountain was this noble cedar—I speak of John, cousin and friend of the Bridegroom, forerunner, Baptist, and martyr of the Lord: and therefore, watered more abundantly, he grew so great that among those born of women none more exalted could be found. He was altogether nearest to the Savior—he who was joined not only by the bond of blood or intimate in friendship, but who also approached nearer to him than all other mortals, in the glory of the annunciation, the novelty of his birth, a holiness almost original, a preaching very similar, authority to baptize, and courage in suffering. In short, if all else were silent, if the proclamations of the prophets said nothing of him; the grace of his name alone (9)—which was given by an angel before he was conceived in the womb—would sufficiently and abundantly testify to the singular grace of God that was to be in him. For it was fitting that he who was full of grace should preach the grace of God which she who was full of grace poured forth, and that he who was to mark the dividing line, as it were, between the time of grace and the time of the law, should himself stand out with no small grace. For "the Law and the Prophets prophesied until John" (Luc. XVI, 16); he indeed was the first to show as present the one whom the Law and Prophecy had promised as coming.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Merito igitur nativitas hujus pueri multos gaudere tunc fecit, hodieque facit, qui in senectute parentum natus, mundo senescenti gratiam praedicaturus erat renascendi. Merito nativitatem istam, quam mirabiliter operatur gratia, miraturque natura, solemniter veneratur Ecclesia: praesertim cum singularis illius nativitatis, cujus gratia naturam reparavit, per hanc pignora fidelia sibi videat esse praemissa. Non ingratam se probat Ecclesia, non immemorem: fideliter agnoscit qua devotione, qua gratiarum actione suscipere debeat Praecursorem, per quem ipsum agnovit Salvatorem. Mihi plane novo nascitur gaudio lucerna mundi, cujus indicio lucem veram agnovi lucentem in tenebris, sed non comprehensam a tenebris. Mihi prorsus ineffabili nascitur gaudio, cum quo tot et tanta mundo nascuntur bona; qui videlicet Ecclesiam primus catechizat, per poenitentiam initiat, per baptismum praeparat, praeparatam Christo consignat et copulat; et quam ad vivendum temperanter informat, etiam ad moriendum fortiter propria morte confirmat, atque in his omnibus plebem perfectam Domino parat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Rightly, then, did the birth of this boy cause many to rejoice at that time, and it causes rejoicing today as well—he who, born in the old age of his parents, was to preach to an aging world the grace of being born again. Rightly does the Church solemnly venerate this birth, which grace wrought so wondrously and nature marveled at: especially since she sees in it faithful pledges sent before her of that singular nativity whose grace repaired nature. The Church proves herself neither ungrateful nor forgetful: she faithfully recognizes with what devotion, with what thanksgiving, she ought to receive the Forerunner, through whom she came to know the Savior himself. For me indeed the lamp of the world is born with new joy, by whose sign I have recognized the true light shining in the darkness, yet not overcome by the darkness. For me indeed he is born with ineffable joy, with whom so many and such great goods are born to the world—he who first catechizes the Church, initiates her through penance, prepares her through baptism, and, once prepared, consigns and joins her to Christ; and who forms her to live temperately, and also, by his own death, confirms her to die bravely, and in all these things prepares a perfect people for the Lord.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. O fratres, quorum propositum est (utinam et ita desiderium) ad perfectionem festinare; quam cito christianam assequeretur perfectionem, qui huic magistro animum accommodaret docibilem: cujus etiam prima elementa justitiae modum supergressa sunt perfectionis humanae; cujus rudimenta primaevae aetatis gravitatem sapientiae vicere senilis! Qui enim, antequam natus, sanctus fuit, quid mirum si in processu conversationis plus quam sanctus fuit? Mirari possumus, imitari non possumus sanctitatem tuam, sanctorum sanctissime: omnino necesse est ut, qui de publicanis et peccatoribus plebem perfectam Domino parare festinas, humanius eis loquaris quam vivas; et modum perfectionis non secundum vitae formulam tuae, sed secundum virtutem mediocritatis temperes humanae. Facite, inquit, dignos fructus poenitentiae (Matth. III, 8). Nos quidem, o fratres, gloriamur perfectius loqui, quam vivere: Joannes autem sublimius vivens quam possint homines vel intelligere, loquitur tamen eis prout possunt audire. Facite, inquit, fructus dignos poenitentiae Humanum, inquit, dico, propter infirmitatem carnis vestrae (Rom. VI, 19) Si nondum esse potest in vobis omnium plenitudo bonorum, sit saltem vera omnium poenitudo malorum. Si nondum facere praevaletis perfectae fructus justitiae, sit interim haec vestra perfectio, ut faciatis dignos fructus poenitentiae.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. O brothers, whose purpose it is (would that the desire were likewise!) to hasten toward perfection: how quickly would that man attain Christian perfection who made his mind teachable to this master—whose very first elements of righteousness surpassed the measure of human perfection; whose rudiments, in his earliest age, outdid the gravity of old men's wisdom! For he who was holy before he was born—what wonder if, in the course of his life, he was more than holy? We can marvel at your holiness, O holiest of the holy ones, but we cannot imitate it. It is altogether necessary that you, who hasten to prepare for the Lord a perfect people out of publicans and sinners, speak to them more mildly than you live, and temper the measure of perfection not according to the pattern of your own life, but according to the capacity of human mediocrity. 'Bring forth,' he says, 'fruits worthy of repentance' (Matth. III, 8). We indeed, O brothers, boast of speaking more perfectly than we live; but John, living more sublimely than men can even understand, nevertheless speaks to them as they are able to hear. 'Bring forth,' he says, 'fruits worthy of repentance. I speak in human terms,' he says, 'because of the weakness of your flesh' (Rom. VI, 19). If the fullness of all good things cannot yet be in you, let there at least be true repentance for all evil things. If you cannot yet manage to produce the fruits of perfect righteousness, let this be your perfection for the present: that you bring forth fruits worthy of repentance.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Si recordari volumus, fratres, lectionis hesternae, ad dignos fructus poenitentiae pertinet quod Jeremiae, aut certe Joanni sub typo Jeremiae dictum est, Ut evellas, et destruas, et disperdas, et dissipes: ad fructus justitiae, ut aedifices et plantes (Jerem. I, 10, et XVIII, 7). Beatus qui manus hujus exstirpatoris adjuverit (nam ipse Dei adjutor est), qui videlicet cooperans verbo et gratiae Dei, in hoc studium et operam dederit ut evellat et disperdat de affectionibus et moribus suis omnem plantationem quam non plantavit Pater coelestis, destruat et dissipet omnem aedificationem Babylonicae superbiae et confusionis; ut postmodum melius aedificet et plantet, fiatque sicut scriptum est, Lateres ceciderunt, sed quadris lapidibus aedificabimus. Sycomoros succiderunt, sed cedros immutabimus (Isa. IX, 10). Ascendat abies pro saliuncula, et myrtus pro urtica (Id. LV, 13): omnis scilicet pulchritudo et gratia virtutum, pro situ et horrore vitiorum. Quis, putas, est ille tam perfectus in nobis, ut saltem hoc initium perfectionis habeat, qui scilicet ita digne perfecteque poenitens sit, ac tota severitate damnet mala sua quae fecit, prioribus usquequaque renuntians vitiis, ut omne germen maledictionis radicitus evellat et disperdat de agro cordis, ita ut de radice pessima, nullus amplius germinet fructus amaritudinis; quique semel ita destruat ac dissipet omnem altitudinem extollentem se adversus humilitatem Christi, ut iterum non reaedificet quae destruxit? Quam felix hodie esset Ecclesia sanctorum, quanta pace et gratia florerent congregationes beatorum pauperum, si fructus istos quos facere debuerat, rudium poenitentia, vel eorum qui perfecti et sancti videri volunt, afferret justitia! Denique, qui nec justitiam sanctorum, nec exactam habemus poenitentiam peccatorum, redimamus vel ex parte aliqua teporem nostrum devota veneratione sanctorum: praecipue beati Joannis, cujus tam magnifice sanctitas effloruit supra modum aliorum, ut crederetur Sanctus sanctorum. Magnificentiam gloriae sanctitatis ejus loquamur ac meditemur, fratres mei, ut propitium faciat peccatis nostris eum, cujus singulariter amicus esse meruit, Filium Dei, qui cum Patre et Spiritu sancto vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. If we wish to recall, brothers, yesterday's reading, it belongs to worthy fruits of repentance what was said to Jeremiah—or indeed to John under the type of Jeremiah—'that you may root out, and pull down, and destroy, and throw down'; and to the fruits of righteousness belongs, 'that you may build and plant' (Jerem. I, 10, et XVIII, 7). Blessed is he who helps the hands of this uprooter (for he himself is God's helper)—namely, one who, cooperating with the word and grace of God, devotes study and effort to this: that he may root out and cast away from his affections and habits every planting which the heavenly Father did not plant, and may destroy and throw down every edifice of Babylonian pride and confusion; so that afterward he may build and plant the better, and it may come to pass as it is written: 'The bricks have fallen, but we will build with squared stones; the sycamores have been cut down, but we will change them for cedars' (Isa. IX, 10). 'Let the fir tree rise up in place of the brier, and the myrtle in place of the nettle' (Id. LV, 13)—that is, let all the beauty and grace of the virtues rise up in place of the squalor and horror of the vices. Who, do you suppose, is so perfect among us that he has even this beginning of perfection—namely, one who repents so worthily and so perfectly, and with total severity condemns the evils he has done, utterly renouncing his former vices, that he roots out and casts away, down to the root, every seed of cursing from the field of his heart, so that from that most evil root no fruit of bitterness may ever sprout again; and who, having once destroyed and thrown down every height that exalts itself against the humility of Christ, does not build up again what he has destroyed? How happy would the Church of the saints be today, with what peace and grace would the congregations of the blessed poor flourish, if the repentance of the untaught, or the righteousness of those who wish to appear perfect and holy, bore those fruits which it ought to have produced In short, since we have neither the righteousness of the saints nor the exact repentance of sinners, let us redeem our lukewarmness, at least in some part, by devout veneration of the saints—especially of blessed John, whose holiness blossomed so magnificently beyond the measure of others that he was believed to be the Holy One of the holy ones. Let us speak of and meditate upon the magnificence of the glory of his holiness, my brothers, so that he may render favorable toward our sins the one whose singular friend he merited to be—the Son of God, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns through all the ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: (9) Joannes enim gratia Dei interpretatur.

passages.label: English
passages.text: (9) For John is interpreted as "the grace of God."

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric reads the saying that from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence. Repentance is the force by which sinners seize what was not granted to nature, and the brothers must wrestle without relenting, as Jacob wrestled with the angel. Christ, weakened even to death by love, cannot resist such force. Guerric calls the brothers to magnanimity and constancy under the example of John. The sermon appears under the heading for the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO II.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON II.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De vi necessaria ad rapiendum regnum coelorum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the force necessary to seize the kingdom of heaven.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. A diebus Joannis Baptistae regnum coelorum vim patitur, et violenti diripiunt illud (Matth. XI, 12). Merito igitur laeta nobis est ejus nativitas, cujus tam fausta sunt tempora, ut regnum Dei, jam exinde nobis expositum sit ad diripiendum, quibus utique justitia non sufficiebat ad promerendum. Merito multi in nativitate ejus gaudent, sicut promittebat angelus; sub quo tanta felicitate mutatus est temporum status, ut regnum Dei quod ante nulla innocentium obtinebat justitia, nunc poenitentium invadat et possideat violentia. Quid enim aliud debuit dici poenitentia peccatorum, nisi violentia in regnum coelorum? An non violentia est, rapere virtute quod non erat concessum naturae; ut qui natura erant filii irae et gehennae, labore improbo qui omnia vincit, intrudant se in haereditatem sanctorum et consortium gloriae? An non plane violentus Deo strenuus ille luctator patriarcha Jacob, qui, ut scriptum est, contra Deum fortis fuit et invaluit, qui cum eo luctatus usque mane, constanter et obnixe tenebat rogantem dimitti, Non dimittam te, inquiens, nisi benedixeris mihi? Dico quia cum Deo luctatus est: Deus siquidem erat in angelo, cum quo luctatus est. Alioquin nec angelus diceret, Cur quaeris nomen meum, quod est mirabile? nec Jacob diceret, Vidi Dominum facie ad faciem (Gen. XXXII, 26, 29, 30): sed neque Dominus de Jacob diceret per Osee prophetam, in Bethel locutus est nobiscum (Osee XII, 4). Bona igitur violentia, quae benedictionem extorsit: felix lucta, qua Deus homini succubuit, victusque victorem gratia benedictionis et honore sanctioris nominis muneravit! Quid enim, si tetigit nervum femoris ejus, et emarcuit, ac de caetero claudicavit? Facilis jactura corporis damnumque consolabile, quod tanto compensatum est munere: praesertim illi qui potuit dicere, Super salutem et omnem pulchritudinem dilexi sapientiam (Sap. VII, 10). Utinam marcescat in me non solum nervus femoris, sed virtus totius corporis; dummodo vel unam merear benedictionem angeli. Utinam non solo claudicem cum Jacob, sed et moriar cum Paulo, ut gratiam et nomen Israelis obtineam munere perpetuo. Jacob quidem femur gerit marcidum, Paulus vero, corpus emortuum: quia mortificationem membrorum, quam coepit propheticae religionis initium, ad integrum consummavit Evangelium. Jacob claudicans, quia ex parte quae mundi sunt cogitans, alterum pedem a terra suspensum portat. Paulus cogitans solum quae Dei sunt, sive in corpore, sive extra corpus, nescit, Deus scit (II Cor. XII, 3), totus tamen in spiritu liber ad coelum volat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent bear it away" (Matth. XI, 12). Rightly, then, is his birth joyful for us, since its times are so blessed that the kingdom of God is thenceforth set before us to be seized by force—by us, indeed, for whom righteousness alone would not have sufficed to merit it. Rightly do many rejoice at his nativity, as the angel promised; for under him the state of the times was changed to such happiness that the kingdom of God, which before no righteousness of the innocent could obtain, is now invaded and possessed by the violence of the penitent. For what else ought the repentance of sinners to be called, but violence against the kingdom of heaven? Is it not violence, to seize by force what was not granted to nature; so that those who were by nature children of wrath and of hell, by relentless labor that conquers all things, thrust themselves into the inheritance of the saints and the fellowship of glory? Was not that strenuous wrestler, the patriarch Jacob, plainly violent toward God, who, as it is written, was strong against God and prevailed, who, wrestling with him until morning, held fast, steadfastly and insistently, to him who asked to be let go, saying, "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me"? I say that he wrestled with God: for God indeed was in the angel with whom he wrestled. Otherwise the angel would not have said, "Why dost thou ask my name, which is wonderful?" nor would Jacob have said, "I have seen the Lord face to face" (Gen. XXXII, 26, 29, 30): nor would the Lord have said of Jacob through the prophet Hosea, "In Bethel he spoke with us" (Osee XII, 4). Good, then, was the violence that extorted a blessing: happy the struggle, in which God yielded to man, and, being conquered, rewarded the victor with the grace of a blessing and the honor of a holier name! For what matter is it, if he touched the sinew of his thigh, and it withered, and he limped thereafter? Easy is the loss of the body, and consolable the damage, which was compensated by so great a gift: especially for him who could say, "Above health and all beauty have I loved wisdom" (Sap. VII, 10). Would that not only the sinew of my thigh might wither in me, but the strength of my whole body, provided only I might merit even one blessing of the angel. Would that I might not only limp with Jacob, but also die with Paul, that I might obtain the grace and name of Israel by an everlasting gift. Jacob indeed bears a withered thigh, but Paul a body as it were dead: because the mortification of the members, which the beginning of prophetic religion first undertook, the Gospel brought to full consummation. Jacob limps, because, thinking in part on the things that are of the world, he carries one foot suspended from the earth. Paul, thinking only on the things that are of God, whether in the body or out of the body, he knows not, God knows (II Cor. XII, 3), yet wholly free in spirit flies to heaven.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Vobis itaque dicimus, fratres, qui aggressi estis coelum rapere, qui congressi estis luctari cum angelo qui viam custodit ligni vitae: vobis, inquam, dicimus omnino necesse esse ut constanter et irremisse luctemini; non dico usque ad enervationem femoris, unde generatio propagatur carnis, sed etiam usque ad mortificationem corporis. Hoc tamen ipsum nec sic labor noster poterit assequi, nisi tactu et beneficio divinae virtutis, cum vestram videlicet constantiam invincibilem sibi probaverit. Sic enim scriptum est: Cumque videret quod eum superare non posset, tetigit nervum femoris ejus, et statim emarcuit! (Gen. XXXII, 25). An non tibi cum angelo, imo cum Deo ipso luctari videris, quando quotidie praeproperis tuis resistit votis? Lavaris velut aquis nivis, ut mundus sis corde et corpore, et ipse sordibus intingit te. Dicis, Sapiens efficiar (Eccle. VII, 24), et ipse longius recedit a te. Clamas ad eum, nec exaudit te: vis accedere ad eum, et repellit te. Decernis rem, et in contrarium tibi cedit, et per omnia fere in duritia manus suae adversatur tibi. O dissimulatrix clementia, quae duritiam te simulas; quanta pietate pugnas adversus eos pro quibus pugnas! Licet enim haec celes in corde tuo, scio tamen quia diligis diligentes te, et immensa multitudo dulcedinis tuae, quam abscondis timentibus te. Noli igitur desperare, constanter age, felix anima, quae cum Deo luctari coepisti: amat utique vim abs te pati, desiderat a te superari. Nam et cum iratus est, manumque ad feriendum extendit, quaerit, ut ipse confitetur, virum similem Moysi, qui resistat sibi; et si non invenerit, conqueritur et dicit: Non est qui consurgat, et teneat me (Isai. LXIV, 7). Nam si implacabilis sit ejus ira, inflexibilisque sententia, flebit et dicet Jeremias qui resistere tentaverat: Fortior fuisti, et invaluisti (Jerem. XX, 7).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. To you, then, we speak, brothers, who have set out to seize heaven, who have come to grapple with the angel who guards the way of the tree of life: to you, I say, we declare that it is altogether necessary that you wrestle steadfastly and without relenting; I do not say to the withering of the thigh, whence the generation of flesh is propagated, but even to the mortification of the body. Yet even this our labor will not be able to attain, unless by the touch and favor of divine power, when he has proved your constancy invincible to himself. For thus it is written: "And when he saw that he could not overcome him, he touched the sinew of his thigh, and immediately it withered" (Gen. XXXII, 25). Do you not seem to yourself to wrestle with the angel, nay with God himself, when daily he resists your hasty desires? You wash yourself as it were with the waters of snow, that you may be clean in heart and body, and he dips you in filth. You say, "I shall become wise" (Eccle. VII, 24), and he withdraws further from you. You cry out to him, and he does not hear you: you wish to approach him, and he repels you. You determine upon a thing, and it turns out contrary to you, and in almost everything, by the hardness of his hand, he opposes you. O dissembling mercy, that feigns hardness; with how great pity do you fight against those for whom you fight! For although you conceal these things in your heart, I know nevertheless that you love those who love you, and the immense abundance of your sweetness, which you hide for those who fear you. Do not despair, then; act steadfastly, happy soul, who have begun to wrestle with God: he indeed loves to suffer violence from you, he desires to be overcome by you. For even when he is angry, and stretches out his hand to strike, he seeks, as he himself confesses, a man like Moses, who may resist him; and if he does not find one, he complains and says: "There is none that ariseth, and taketh hold of me" (Isai. LXIV, 7). For if his anger were implacable, and his sentence inflexible, Jeremiah, who had attempted to resist, will weep and say: "Thou wast stronger than I, and didst prevail" (Jerem. XX, 7).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Sed absit, fratres, qui placita ei postulatis, absit ut fortis adversum vos sit, qui pro vobis infirmari usque ad mortem voluit! Tot vulneribus confossus est, toto corpore crucifixus est; unde, quaeso, virtus ei esse potest ad resistendum illi charitati, quae veluti victum et captum per omnia genera infirmitatum usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis perduxit? Jam non fortis ut mors, sed fortior quam mors dilectio: cum virtute dilectionis infirmata sit usque ad mortem Dei fortitudo; cujus tamen infirmitas fortior inventa est omni fortissimo; cujus mors probata est esse mors tua, o mors. Virtute igitur dilectionis armatus sis, quicunque es ille pius invasor, qui rapere contendis regnum coelorum: et securus esto, quia facile vinces regem ipsum coelorum. Si qua enim videtur tibi adversari difficultate, aut duritia; ne sis pusillanimis, sed intellige qua mente id faciat. Nempe ut contrarietate ipse tibi acuat animum, sicut solet esse natura magnanimorum ac fortium; ut vires exercitet, constantiam probet, multiplicet victorias, augeatque coronas.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. But far be it, brothers—you who ask of him what is pleasing—far be it that he should be strong against you, he who was willing to be weakened even unto death for you! He was pierced with so many wounds, he was crucified in his whole body; whence, I ask, can he have strength to resist that love which led him, as though conquered and captured, through every kind of weakness even unto death—death, moreover, of the cross? Now love is not strong as death, but stronger than death: since by the strength of love the strength of God was weakened even unto death; yet his weakness was found stronger than every strongest thing; whose death has proved to be your death, O death. Be armed, therefore, with the strength of love, whoever you are, you devout invader who strive to seize the kingdom of heaven: and be assured that you will easily conquer the King of heaven himself. For if some difficulty or hardness seems to oppose you, do not be faint of heart, but understand with what mind he does this. Surely it is so that by this opposition he may himself sharpen your spirit, as is the nature of the magnanimous and strong; so that he may exercise your strength, test your constancy, multiply your victories, and increase your crowns.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Quamobrem accingimini, filii Israel, et estote filii fortitudinis: non enim opus est nisi magnanimitate et constantia, quae nullis possit terreri adversis. Infirmus dicat, Fortis sum: et prae gaudio spei se nesciat infirmum, cui tam facile jam jamque capiendum est coelum. Plane coelum violenter rapit, qui imbecillitati suae vim facit, aut aetati. Imo, ut magis proprie loquar, plane vim facit propriae perditioni, qui intonante tuba mandati, nescit parcere sibi. Homo enim in laboribus, ut Scriptura ait, laborat sibi, et vim facit perditioni suae (Prov. XVI, sec. LXX). Accingimini, inquam, viri virtutis, et sequimini ducem ac magistrum felicis hujus militiae; Joannem Baptistam loquor, a diebus cujus coelum esse coepit expugnabile. Iste siquidem est, qui velut alter David princeps factus latronum, piorumque ductor praedonum, et victoriosum illum exercitum publicanorum et peccatorum per illam laudabilem ac religiosam violentiam post se induxit in regnum coelorum. Quis enim scelestus aut profanus tubam ejus audivit, Poenitentiam agite, appropinquavit enim regnum coelorum (Matth. III, 2); et non se continuo praeparavit ad bellum? Sequimini, inquam, ducem istum, cujus vexilla proprio rutilant sanguine, cujus hodie virtutes ac triumphos debita decantastis veneratione. Ipse, nisi fallor, quos post se traxerit exemplo, juvabit merito, commendabitque suffragio, cum inter natos mulierum nullus sit acceptior regi summo Jesu Christo Domino nostro, qui vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Wherefore gird yourselves, sons of Israel, and be sons of fortitude: for nothing is needed but magnanimity and constancy, which can be terrified by no adversities. Let the weak man say, I am strong; and for the joy of hope let him not know himself weak, for whom heaven is now so easily, at any moment, to be seized. He plainly seizes heaven by violence who does violence to his own weakness, or to his age. Indeed, to speak more properly, he plainly does violence to his own ruin who, when the trumpet of the command is sounding, does not know how to spare himself. For man, as Scripture says, labors for himself in his labors, and does violence to his own ruin (Prov. XVI, sec. LXX). Gird yourselves, I say, men of valor, and follow the leader and master of this happy warfare—I speak of John the Baptist, from whose days heaven began to be stormable. For he it is who, like another David made prince of robbers, and leader of devout plunderers, led after him into the kingdom of heaven that victorious army of publicans and sinners through that praiseworthy and religious violence. For what wicked or profane man heard his trumpet, 'Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand' (Matth. III, 2), and did not immediately prepare himself for war? Follow, I say, this leader, whose banners gleam red with his own blood, whose virtues and triumphs you have today sung with due veneration. He himself, unless I am mistaken, will aid by his merit and commend by his intercession those whom he has drawn after him by example, since among those born of women none is more acceptable to the highest King, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

passages.text: The edition prints non solo rather than the expected non solum (not only).
