Nativity of Saint John the Baptist
sermons.occasion_detail: Nativity of Saint John the Baptist

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric takes up Christ's praise that no one born of women is greater than John the Baptist, and sets it beside the praise God gave Noah, Moses and David. John's greatness lay in humility: thought to be the greatest of all, he declared himself unworthy to take off Christ's sandals, and so Christ glorified him. Guerric warns that the proud imitate the devil by envy and detraction, while John lessened himself so that another might appear. The sermon appears under the heading for the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO III.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON III.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Iterum de laudibus Sancti.

passages.label: English
passages.text: Again, on the praises of the Saint.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Inter natos mulierum non surrexit major Joanne Baptista (Matth. XI, 11). Salomon ait: Laudent te labia proximi tui (Prov. XXVII, 2). Sed quam felicius et gloriosius, cum laudant quempiam labia Dei sui! Deus quippe nec falli potest, nec adulari. Deus neminem facile laudat, quem laude posse inflari videat, vel quem ex fine debere reprobari praevideat. Homini quidem recte dicitur, ne laudet hominem in vita sua; cujus sicut scire non potest intima, si nec praescire novissima; cum de seipso quoque confiteri habeat: Nihil mihi conscius sum, sed non in hoc justificatus sum (I Cor. IV, 4). Sunt enim justi et sapientes, et opera eorum in manu Dei sunt et tamen nemo scit utrum sit dignus amore an odio, sed omnia in futurum servantur incerta (Eccle. IX, 1, 2). Felix igitur, qui testimonio ipsius Judicis dignum se amore scire meruerit; nisi quod testimonium justitiae praesentis, mutabilitati humanae suspicionem ac metum non adimit de futuris. Indubitabile tamen eximiae virtutis et magnae perfectionis est indicium, quoties hominem adhuc corruptioni subditum, suae suffragio laudis illud irrefragabile Dei dignatur judicium. Magnum profecto justitiae praeconium quod summa justitia dicit ad Noe: Te vidi justum coram me (Gen. VII, 1). Magni quidem insigne meriti, quod Abrahae testificatur Deus, propter ipsum implendas esse promissiones, quae ad ipsum factae sunt (Gen. XVII, et XXII, 17, 18). Quantae autem illud est gloriae, quod de beato Job Dominus gloriatur adversus invidum: Numquid considerasti servum meum Job, quod non sit ei similis in terra: homo simplex et rectus, et timens Deum, ac recedens a malo? (Job. I, 8.) Quantae etiam illud erat gratiae, quod pro Moyse aemulabatur et confundebat aemulos ejus? Si quis, inquit, fuerit inter vos propheta Domini, in visione apparebo ei, vel per somnium loquar ad illum. At non talis servus meus Moyses, qui in omni domo mea fidelissimus est. Ore enim ad os loquor ei, et palam, non per aenigmata videt Deum. Quare ergo non timuistis detrahere servo meo Moysi? (Num. XII, 6-8.) Quis vero in omnibus sicut David, de quo gratulatur Dominus, quia invenit virum secundum cor suum? (III Reg. XI, 4.)

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Among those born of women there has not arisen a greater than John the Baptist (Matth. XI, 11). Solomon says: Let the lips of your neighbor praise you (Prov. XXVII, 2). But how much more blessed and glorious it is when the lips of his God praise someone! For God can neither be deceived nor flattered. God does not easily praise anyone whom he sees could be puffed up by praise, or whom he foresees must in the end be rejected. To a man indeed it is rightly said that he should not praise a man in his lifetime; for just as he cannot know his inmost parts, so he cannot foreknow his final end; since he must also confess of himself: I know nothing against myself, yet I am not thereby justified (I Cor. IV, 4). For there are just and wise men, and their works are in the hand of God, and yet no one knows whether he is worthy of love or of hatred, but all things are kept uncertain for the future (Eccle. IX, 1, 2). Happy, therefore, is he who by the testimony of the Judge himself has deserved to know himself worthy of love; except that the testimony of present righteousness does not remove from human mutability the suspicion and fear concerning things to come. Nevertheless it is an undoubted sign of surpassing virtue and great perfection whenever that unshakable judgment of God deigns to support with its praise a man still subject to corruption. Great indeed is the proclamation of righteousness when supreme Righteousness says to Noah: I have seen you just before me (Gen. VII, 1). Great indeed is the mark of merit when God testifies concerning Abraham, that for his sake the promises made to him would be fulfilled (Gen. XVII, et XXII, 17, 18). But how great is that glory, when the Lord boasts of blessed Job against the envious one: Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth: a simple and upright man, and fearing God, and avoiding evil? (Job. I, 8.) How great also was that grace, that he was jealous on Moses' behalf and confounded his rivals? If there be, he says, a prophet of the Lord among you, I will appear to him in a vision, or speak to him in a dream. But not so my servant Moses, who is most faithful in all my house. For I speak to him mouth to mouth, and openly, not in riddles does he see God. Why then did you not fear to speak against my servant Moses? (Num. XII, 6-8.) But who among all men was like David, of whom the Lord rejoices, because he found a man after his own heart? (III Reg. XI, 4.)

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Verumtamen quantumlibet magni fuerint, sive isti, sive alii; nec inter istos, nec inter alios natos mulierum, teste Nato Virginis, surrexit major Joanne Baptista. Nam etsi stella differat a stella in claritate, et in choro sanctorum siderum, quae ante exortum veri Solis illustrarunt noctem hujus saeculi, quadam effulserunt claritate mirabili; nullum tamen in omnibus majus aut splendidius lucifero isto, lucerna scilicet ardenti et lucenti, quam Pater Christo suo paravit: lucifero, inquam, praelucanae lucis, qui praecursor Solis diem instantem mortalibus nuntiavit; dormientibus in tenebris et umbra mortis clamitans et dicens: Poenitentiam agite; appropinquavit enim regnum coelorum (Matth. III, 2). Ac si diceret: Nox praecessit, dies autem appropinquavit: abjicite opera tenebrarum (Rom. XIII, 12). Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis, et illuminabit te Christus (Ephes. V, 14).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Nevertheless, however great these men were, whether these or others; neither among these nor among others born of women, by the testimony of the Son born of the Virgin, has there arisen a greater than John the Baptist. For although star differs from star in brightness, and in the choir of holy stars which before the rising of the true Sun illumined the night of this age, shining with a certain wondrous brightness; yet none among them all was greater or more splendid than this day-star, that is, the lamp burning and shining, which the Father prepared for his Christ: the day-star, I say, of the light before dawn, who as forerunner of the Sun announced to mortals the day now at hand; crying out and saying to those sleeping in darkness and the shadow of death: Repent; for the kingdom of heaven is at hand (Matth. III, 2). As if he said: The night has passed, but the day has drawn near: cast off the works of darkness (Rom. XIII, 12). Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you (Ephes. V, 14).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Non est autem negligenter praetereundum, sed etiam atque etiam considerandum, quam sublimis meriti, quam excellentis gratiae et virtutis, oculus ille quem nil fallit, eum perviderit, qui post tanta praecedentium praeconia, hanc de illo sententiam tulit: quod inter natos mulierum, nullus illo major surrexit; nec nisi de ordine Angelorum, vel qui pervenisset ad aequalitatem Angelorum, aliquem ei praeferendum judicavit. Nec semel quidem, aut perfunctorie vel breviter laudem ejus attigit, sed quotiescunque se offerebat occasio sermonis, laudibus ejus delectabatur immorari: quod satis probat historia Evangelii. Propterea Marcus quoque, Lucas et Joannes initia librorum praeconiis ejus dedicaverunt: ut videlicet auctoritas tanti nominis prima fronte praelati, totum deinceps commendabilius redderet Evangelium; et lucerna in ipso ingressu ac vestibulo ardens et lucens perduceret ad lucem, quae lucebat in tenebris, sed a tenebris nequibat comprehendi. Matthaeus enim, quia eum nativitas Domini in initiis occupatum tenuit, mox ut puerum nutriendum Nazareth commendavit, ad Praecursorem et Baptistam ejus stylum convertit, arbitrans imperfectum fore quidquid de Sponso diceret, si de individuo amico Sponsi reticeret. Haec namque cura non minima fuit, non solum Evangelistis narrantibus, sed etiam Prophetis et Angelis praenuntiantibus, ut lucerna Christi, testis Domini talis induceretur, cujus splendore et auctoritate inimici facile confunderentur, et ex cujus magnitudine incomparabilis Altissimi magnitudo manifeste monstraretur. Cum enim maximus inter natos mulierum Natum Virginis testabatur tam longe magnitudinem suam vincere, ut indignum se confiteretur ejus calceamenta portare: quid aliud dabatur intelligi, nisi quia ille erat magnus Dominus, cujus magnitudinis non est finis (Psal. CXLIV, 3); et de quo dicitur: Quoniam quis in nubibus aequabitur Domino, similis erit Deo in filiis Dei? (Psal. LXXXVIII, 7.) Et haec utique illa magnitudo Joannis fuit, qua inter magnos tam magnus excrevit, quia videlicet virtutes suas magnas et innumeras, quibus nulli mortalium secundus fuit, maxima omnium virtutum humilitate cumulavit sibi; cum putaretur summus omnium, ultro ac devotissime praeferens humillimum omnium et in tantum praeferens, ut calceamentis ejus detrahendis se testaretur indignum (Luc. III, 16).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. But this must not be passed over carelessly; rather it must be weighed again and again, how sublime the merit, how excellent the grace and virtue, which that eye that nothing deceives beheld in him of whom, after such great praises of those who went before, he pronounced this sentence: that among those born of women none greater than he has arisen; nor did he judge anyone fit to be set above him, except one from the order of Angels, or one who had attained equality with the Angels. Nor did he touch on his praise only once, or in passing, or briefly; but as often as an occasion for speaking presented itself, he delighted to linger over his praises — as the history of the Gospel sufficiently proves. For this reason Mark also, and Luke, and John dedicated the openings of their books to his praises: so that the authority of so great a name, set forth at the very front, might thereafter render the whole Gospel more commendable; and the lamp, burning and shining right at the entrance and in the vestibule, might lead on to the light which was shining in the darkness, but which the darkness could not grasp. For Matthew, since the nativity of the Lord kept him occupied at the outset, as soon as he had committed the child to Nazareth to be raised, turned his pen to the Forerunner and Baptist of the Lord, judging that whatever he said about the Bridegroom would be incomplete if he kept silent about the Bridegroom's inseparable friend. For this concern was no small one, not only for the Evangelists in their narrating, but also for the Prophets and the Angels in their foretelling: that the lamp of Christ, such a witness of the Lord, should be set forth, by whose splendor and authority enemies might easily be confounded, and from whose greatness the incomparable greatness of the Most High might be plainly displayed. For when the greatest among those born of women testified that the Born of the Virgin so far surpassed his own greatness that he confessed himself unworthy to carry his sandals, what else was one given to understand, except that he was that great Lord, of whose greatness there is no end (Psal. CXLIV, 3); and of whom it is said: For who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? who shall be like to God among the sons of God? (Psal. LXXXVIII, 7.). And this indeed was that greatness of John, by which he grew so great among the great: namely, that he crowned his great and countless virtues — in which he was second to no mortal — with the greatest of all virtues, humility; so that, though he was thought the highest of all, he freely and most devoutly set before himself the lowliest of all, and preferred him so greatly that he testified himself take off his sandals (Luc. III, 16).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Mirentur igitur alii, quod a Prophetis praenuntiatus; quod ab archangelo promissus, et eodem quo Christus; cum tamen Christus in cubiculo, Joannes in oraculo; quod de tam sanctis ac nobilibus parentibus; quod de senibus et sterilibus, contra debitum naturae, dono gratiae; quod ante sanctus quam natus; ante propheta, quam prophetaret; quod plus quam propheta, quia angelus angelicum officium vitamque gerens in terris, in carne praeter carnem vivens; et licet innocentissimus, poenitentiae tamen formam plus exemplo quam verbo tradens; quod in spiritu et virtute Eliae praecurrens adventum Redemptoris, et viam ei parans in eremo; quod corda patrum ad filios, et filiorum ad patres convertit; quod Filium baptizare, Patrem audire, Spiritum sanctum videre meruit; quod denique usque ad mortem pro veritate certavit: ut etiam ad inferos Christum praecurreret; ante passionem Christi, martyr Christi fuit. Mirentur, inquam, haec alii, si tamen est qui digne possit mirari: nobis, fratres, non solum miranda, sed et imitanda proponitur virtus humilitatis ejus, qua major se credi, cum potuit, noluit; imo credentes ne errarent, quantum valuit compescuit. Fidelis enim amicus Sponsi, magis amator Domini sui, quam sui; se minui, ut ille cresceret optabat, et de minoratione sui gloriam illius augere satagebat (Joan. III, 29, 30), ante Apostolum opere et veritate dicens illud apostolicum: Non nosmetipsos praedicamus, sed Dominum Jesum Christum (II Cor. IV, 5). Ideo nimirum magna est gloria ejus in salutari tuo, in Jesu tuo, Domine, cujus justitiae et bonitatis est diligentes se diligere, est glorificantes se glorificare. Magna prorsus gloria ejus in Jesu, magna a Jesu: qui et apud se glorificavit eum consortio gloriae suae, et apud homines testimonio vocis suae. Persuasum sibi habebat Joannes illud fidele Sapientis consilium: Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur: non enim qui se ipsum commendat, ille probatus est, sed quem Deus commendat (II Cor. X, 17, 18). Maluit itaque in Domino sane, quam in seipso vane gloriari; quia et maluit veraciter a Domino, quam fallaciter a seipso commendari. Ideo probatus est Deo et hominibus; et gloria ejus veritas apud homines, felicitas apud Deum: qui si seipsum glorificasset, gloria sua nihil esset.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Let others, then, marvel that he was foretold by the Prophets; that he was promised by an archangel, and by the same archangel as Christ, though Christ was announced in a chamber, John in the sanctuary; that he was born of such holy and noble parents; that he was born of parents old and barren, against the due course of nature, by the gift of grace; that he was holy before he was born; a prophet before he prophesied; that he was more than a prophet, because he was an angel, carrying on an angelic office and life on earth, living in the flesh beyond the flesh; and although most innocent, yet delivering the pattern of penance more by example than by word; that, going before the coming of the Redeemer in the spirit and power of Elijah, he prepared his way in the wilderness; that he turned the hearts of the fathers to the children, and of the children to the fathers; that he merited to baptize the Son, to hear the Father, to see the Holy Spirit; and finally, that he strove even unto death for the truth, so that he went before Christ even into the underworld — a martyr of Christ before the passion of Christ. Let others, I say, marvel at these things, if indeed there is anyone who can worthily marvel at them: to us, brothers, there is set forth not only to be marveled at, but also to be imitated, the virtue of his humility, by which — though he could have let himself be believed greater — he was unwilling; indeed, he restrained, as far as he was able, those who so believed, lest they err. For as the faithful friend of the Bridegroom, loving his Lord more than himself, he desired to be made small that the Bridegroom might grow great, and he strove, by his own diminishment, to increase the Bridegroom's glory (Joan. III, 29, 30), saying by deed and in truth, before the Apostle, that apostolic word: We preach not ourselves, but the Lord Jesus Christ (II Cor. IV, 5). Therefore, no wonder, great is his glory in your salvation, in your Jesus, O Lord, whose justice and goodness it is to love those who love him, to glorify those who glorify him. Great indeed is his glory in Jesus, great from Jesus: who glorified him both with himself, by the fellowship of his own glory, and before men, by the testimony of his own voice. John had taken to heart that faithful counsel of the Wise One: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord; for it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom God commends (II Cor. X, 17, 18). He therefore preferred to glory soundly in the Lord, rather than vainly in himself; for he preferred also to be commended truly by the Lord, rather than falsely by himself. Therefore he was approved by God and by men; and his glory is truth before men, happiness before God — for if he had glorified himself, his glory would have been nothing.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. O filii hominum, usquequo gravi corde? utquid diligitis vanitatem, et quaeritis mendacium? (Psal. IV, 3.) Utquid vanam et mendacem gloriam diligitis, et gloriam quae a Deo solo est, non vultis? Sed quomodo quaeritis? Utinam agendo fortia, non loquendo sublimia! utinam saltem vera loquendo, licet vane, et non mentiendo plane! utinam denique mentiendo tantum de vobis, non etiam detrahendo de aliis! Hoc jam non est gloriam accipere vel quaerere, sed magis furari et rapere. Quaerere siquidem gloriam, non sua, sed contraria via; non illa scilicet cui debetur gloria, sed contumelia, id est, non virtutis titulo, sed mendacii et detractionis latrocinio: quid aliud est hoc, nisi rapere, vel furari nequiter, quod concupieris turpiter? Certe si gloriam ab homine non quaereres, sed oblatam acciperes, jam ex hoc secundum veritatem non ambulares. Nunc autem quid, cum non solum accipis si offertur, sed et quaeris cum non offertur? quid denique, cum alium velut trucidas venenosa et insidiosa lingua, ut gloriam ejus tibi rapias; ut de malo ejus tu melior, de contemptu ejus tu gloriosior appareas? Sit ergo illud, gloriam scilicet accipere vel quaerere ab homine, insipientium vanitas: quid istud, nisi saevientium crudelitas? Sit certe illud, ut mitius loquar, tentatio humana: quid istud, nisi imitatio diabolica? Plane imitantur diabolum qui sunt ex parte illius, id est, omnes superbi. Ipse est enim rex super omnes filios superbiae.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. O sons of men, how long will you be dull of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek after a lie? (Psal. IV, 3.) Why do you love vain and lying glory, and refuse the glory that comes from God alone? But how do you seek it? Would that it were by doing brave deeds, not by speaking lofty words! Would that it were at least by speaking the truth, even if vainly, and not by plainly lying! Would that, finally, it were only by lying about yourselves, and not also by detracting from others! This is no longer to receive or seek glory, but rather to steal and to plunder. For to seek glory by a way not its own but contrary to it — that is, not by the way to which glory is properly due, but by disgrace; not, that is, by the title of virtue, but by the robbery of lying and detraction — what else is this but wickedly to seize or steal what you have shamefully coveted? Certainly, if you did not seek glory from man but accepted it when offered, even in this you would not be walking according to truth. But what of it, when you not only accept it if offered, but seek it when it is not offered? What, finally, when you all but murder another with a venomous and treacherous tongue, so as to snatch his glory for yourself — so that from his disgrace you may appear better, from his contempt more glorious? Let it be, then, that to receive or seek glory from man is the vanity of fools: but what is this other thing, if not the cruelty of the savage? Let the former, to speak more gently, be a human temptation: but what is this latter, if not an imitation of the devil? Plainly those who belong to his party — that is, all the proud — imitate the devil. For he is king over all the children of pride.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Quomodo, inquis, imitantur? Diabolus quia superbivit, meliori se, id est, Deo invidit: quia invidit, detraxit. Sic filii superbiae ejus, mox ut infecti sunt vitio ejus, id est amore propriae excellentiae, invident alienae. Ut coeperint invidere, incipient, si possunt, detrahere, ut scilicet accrescat eis quod derogaverint aliis. Quanto salubrius imitarentur humilitatem Joannis, qui detrahebat sibi, ut adderet alii: qui contendebat minor credi quam credebatur, ut alius inciperet apparere quod non putabatur? Denique si non placet humilitas ex sui honestate et aequitate, placeat saltem ex utilitate: quia nulla via rectior, aut facilior ad gloriam divinam; sed nec ad gratiam humanam ulla pulchrior aut justior, et saepe nulla compendiosior: Quanto, inquit, magnus es, humilia te in omnibus, et invenies gratiam coram Deo et hominibus (Eccle. III, 20, et Philipp. II, 3). Haec beatum Joannem glorificavit apud Deum et homines, sicut est dies haec, quae de nativitate ejus gloriosa consolationem praestat mundo, gaudium coelo, gloriam Deo: cui honor et gloria in saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. How, you ask, do they imitate him? The devil, because he was proud, envied one better than himself, that is, God; and because he envied, he detracted. So the children of his pride, as soon as they are infected with his vice — that is, the love of their own excellence — envy another's excellence. Once they have begun to envy, they will begin, if they can, to detract, so that what they have taken away from others may grow to their own credit. How much more wholesomely would they imitate the humility of John, who detracted from himself in order to add to another; who strove to be thought less than he was thought to be, so that another might begin to appear what he was not thought to be! Finally, if humility does not please by reason of its own honesty and fairness, let it at least please by reason of its usefulness: for there is no path straighter or easier to divine glory; nor is there any way more beautiful or more just — and often none shorter — to human favor either. As it is said: However great you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find favor before God and men (Eccle. III, 20, et Philipp. II, 3). This is what glorified blessed John before God and men, as this day does, which by his glorious nativity grants consolation to the world, joy to heaven, and glory to God — to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric reads Christ's questions to the crowds about John: no reed shaken by the wind, no man in soft garments, but a prophet. John's firmness before Herod, his contempt of bodily comfort and his prophetic grace are set against those who seek ease. Those who cannot match John's rough clothing and food should at least not be reeds in the wind. The sermon appears under the heading for the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO IV.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON IV.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De fortitudine et mortificatione.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On fortitude and mortification.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Coepit Jesus dicere ad turbas de Joanne: Quid existis videre in deserto? (Matth. XI, 7.) Ecce illud quod sponsa de sponso gloriatur in Cantico amoris sui, Ego dilecto meo, et dilectus meus mihi (Cantic. II, 16): Joannes Jesu, et Jesus Joanni. Joannes Jesum praedicat, Joannem Jesus commendat. Par pari redditur, et tam amica quam justa vicissitudine charitas in invicem provocatur, aut remuneratur. Ego enim, inquit Jesus, diligentes me diligo, et glorificantes me glorificabo (Prov. VIII, 17). Habet pietas promissionem vitae quae nunc est, et futurae; et Dominus dilectum sibi quem glorificaturus est in futuro redditione praemii, etiam nunc incipit glorificare redditione [Al. exhibitione] praeconii, testemque suum etiam apud homines proprii sublimat honore testimonii. Quid existis, inquit, videre in deserto? Vos hominem miramini commorantem in deserto: sed per istum pinguescent speciosa deserti, et florebit solitudo, cum ubique novi cultores eremi de Joannis succrescent exemplo. Tunc erit desertum quasi deliciae paradisi, et solitudo quasi hortus Domini. Tunc gloria Libani dabitur ei, decor Carmeli et Saron (Isai. XXXV, 2). Sed quid, inquam, existis videre in deserto? arundinem vento agitatam? (Matth. XI, 7.) Et si moretur in desertis, non est tamen arundo deserti, sed cedrus paradisi, columna coeli, gloria generis humani, miraculum mundi, virtute et merito ultra mensuram hominum, conditione citra naturam angelorum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Jesus began to say to the crowds concerning John: What did you go out into the desert to see? (Matth. XI, 7.) Behold that which the bride boasts of concerning the bridegroom in the Song of her love: I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine (Cantic. II, 16): John is Jesus', and Jesus is John's. John preaches Jesus, Jesus commends John. Like is repaid with like, and charity, by so friendly as well as just a reciprocity, is either provoked or rewarded in turn. For Jesus says, I love those who love me, and I will glorify those who glorify me (Prov. VIII, 17). Godliness has the promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come; and the one dear to him, whom the Lord will glorify in the future by the giving of a reward, he even now begins to glorify by the giving [Other reading: showing] of a proclamation, and he exalts his own witness, even among men, by the honor of his testimony. What, he says, did you go out to see in the desert? You marvel at a man dwelling in the desert: but through him the fair places of the desert shall grow fat, and the solitude shall flourish, when everywhere new cultivators of the wilderness shall spring up after John's example. Then the desert shall be as the delights of paradise, and the solitude as the garden of the Lord. Then the glory of Lebanon shall be given to it, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon (Isai. XXXV, 2). But what, I say, did you go out to see in the desert? A reed shaken by the wind? (Matth. XI, 7.) And though he dwells in the deserts, yet he is not a reed of the desert, but a cedar of paradise, a pillar of heaven, the glory of the human race, the wonder of the world, beyond the measure of men in virtue and merit, yet short of the nature of angels in his condition.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Non est arundo vento agitata, sed palma fortior omni procella, quam nullus turbo quatiat: aut certe cypressus in monte Sion aeternae plantata, altius scilicet quam ut ventorum rabiem timeat. Non est obnoxius tempestatibus hujus aeris, quia superior est cunctis cupiditatibus mundi. In coelo radicem fixit, quo nullus spiritus procellarum aspirat, unde minas et bella ventorum, et cuncta in saeculo adversantia securus irrideat. Irascatur Herodes, insidietur Herodias, de interioribus eorum ebulliat tempestas, ac nequam spiritus procellarum, qui in abyssis cordium eorum cubat, omnes vires suas et argumenta malitiae commoveat: nihil illum terrebit, nihil a sententia movebit, quominus libere nuptias eorum incestas arguat. Quomodo enim flecterent adversa, quem mollire non potuerunt prospera? Flaverunt siquidem aliquando et molles, atque blandientes venti, aurae scilicet favoris popularis: sed nec illis a rectitudine sua potuit inclinari. Vos misistis ad Joannem et testimonium perhibuit veritati. Miserunt enim Judaei sacerdotes et levitas, ut interrogarent eum, Tu quis es? Et confessus est, et non negavit: Quia non sum ego Christus (Joan. I, 19, 20): cum tamen ei flaret favor popularis, et blandiretur existimatio communis, non ut Christum praedicaret se esse, sed ut credentibus tantum non contradiceret. Sed et alias cum discipuli ejus dicerent ei, Rabbi, cui tu testimonium perhibuisti, ecce hic baptizat, et omnes veniunt ad eum: numquid hoc vento potuit agitari, aut de sua desertione, et alterius frequentia et gloria, ad dolorem vel invidiam moveri? Imo constantia immobili ventum repellens et frangens, respondit: Ipsi vos mihi testimonium perhibetis, quia dixerim, Non sum ego Christus, sed quia missus sum ante illum (Joan. III, 26, 28).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. He is not a reed shaken by the wind, but a palm stronger than any storm, which no whirlwind can shake: or rather a cypress planted on the eternal Mount Sion, that is, planted too high to fear the raging of the winds. He is not subject to the storms of this air, because he is above all the lusts of the world. He has fixed his root in heaven, where no spirit of storms breathes, whence he may securely mock the threats and wars of the winds, and all things in the world that are opposed to him. Let Herod rage, let Herodias lay snares, let the storm boil up from their inward parts, and let the wicked spirit of the tempests, which lies in the depths of their hearts, stir up all his powers and the devices of his malice: nothing will terrify him, nothing will move him from his resolve to freely rebuke their incestuous marriage. For how could adversities bend him whom prosperity could not soften? For once gentle and flattering winds also blew—namely the breezes of popular favor: but not even by these could he be bent from his uprightness. You sent to John, and he bore witness to the truth. For the Jews sent priests and Levites to ask him, Who are you? And he confessed, and did not deny: I am not the Christ (Joan. I, 19, 20): although the favor of the people was blowing upon him, and common opinion was flattering him, not that he should preach himself to be the Christ, but that he should merely not contradict those who believed it. But also at another time, when his disciples said to him, Rabbi, he to whom you bore witness, behold, he baptizes, and all come to him: could he be shaken by this wind, or be moved to sorrow or envy at his own forsaking and another's increase and glory? Rather, with unshaken constancy repelling and breaking the wind, he answered: You yourselves bear me witness that I said, I am not the Christ, but that I am sent before him (Joan. III, 26, 28).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Sed quid existis videre? hominem mollibus vestitum? Laudaverat eum de constantia animi, et nunc laudat de contemptu corporis sui, ac postremo de superexcellentia gratiae prophetalis, atque dignitate angelici officii et nominis. His etenim duobus gradibus ad spiritualia ac divina nititur humilitas humana; si videlicet adversus irruentium tentationum ventos immobilis persistat, et desiderio spiritualium bonorum corpus affligat. Sicut enim in initiis, ut vincamus tentationes, corpus est castigandum, ne regnet in eo peccatum: sic etiam victis tentationibus in eodem tamen est persistendum, non solum metu recidendi, sed etiam desiderio proficiendi; ut scilicet de mortificatione carnis spiritus vegetior fiat, et quanto levius ac subtilius vinculum gestat, tanto ad spiritualia liberior assurgat. Joannes qui antequam exiret de ventre, sanctificatus erat, cui illud dicere competebat: Ab infantia mea mecum crevit sanctitas, et de utero matris meae egressa est mecum (Job XXXI, 18); quem nullus tentationis ventus agitare poterat: nec mollibus tamen vestiebatur, nec suavibus vescebatur; sciens utique, quia sicut peccatoribus, ut sancti fiant, sic sanctis, ut sanctiores fiant, necessaria est severior vivendi disciplina. Nunc autem Deo gratias, qui dedit nobis, si tamen dedit, sine pugna victoriam, sine poenitentia veniam, sine opere justitiam, sanctimoniam sine labore, deliciis carnalibus simul et spiritualibus affluere. Induimur, si non purpura et bysso, certe mollioribus et calidioribus quam sint purpura et byssus; et epulamur quotidie splendide: et nihilominus distenti et ructantes crapulam, dormiemus cum Lazaro quondam paupere in sinu Abrahae, vel potius in sinu Christi cum Joanne? Plane si ita est, melius nobiscum actum est, quam cum illis, qui tantis emere laboribus quod nos delicati gratuito possidemus. Plane si ita est, ridenda est magis quam praedicanda vita Joannis: et omnem nationem filiorum Dei, qui dura et arcta via secuti sunt Unicum Patris, reprobare magis expedit, quam imitari.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. But what did you go out to see? A man clothed in soft garments? He had praised him for steadfastness of soul, and now he praises him for contempt of his own body, and finally for the surpassing excellence of his prophetic grace, and the dignity of his angelic office and name. For by these two steps human humility strains toward spiritual and divine things: namely, if it stands unmoved against the winds of assailing temptations, and afflicts the body out of desire for spiritual goods. For just as at the beginning, in order to conquer temptations, the body must be chastised, lest sin reign in it, so also, once temptations have been conquered, one must nevertheless persist in the same discipline, not only from fear of falling back but also from desire of advancing—so that, by the mortification of the flesh, the spirit may become more vigorous, and the lighter and finer the bond it bears, the freer it may rise toward spiritual things. John, who was sanctified before he came forth from the womb, to whom it was fitting to say, 'From my infancy holiness grew up with me, and it went forth with me from my mother's womb' (Job XXXI, 18); whom no wind of temptation could stir—yet he was not clothed in soft garments, nor did he feed on delicacies; knowing well that, just as for sinners in order to become holy, so also for the holy in order to become holier, a stricter discipline of life is necessary. But now, thanks be to God, who has given to us—if indeed he has given it—victory without struggle, pardon without penance, righteousness without labor, holiness without toil, so that we may abound in carnal and spiritual delights at once! We are clothed, if not in purple and fine linen, certainly in garments softer and warmer than purple and fine linen; and we feast splendidly every day; and nevertheless, bloated and belching from our surfeit, shall we sleep with Lazarus, once a poor man, in the bosom of Abraham—or rather, in the bosom of Christ with John? Clearly, if this is so, it has gone better for us than for those who had to purchase with such great labors what we, in our softness, possess as a free gift. Clearly, if this is so, the life of John is more to be laughed at than preached, and it is more fitting to reject than to imitate the whole nation of the sons of God who followed the Only-begotten of the Father along a hard and narrow way.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Verisimilius autem videtur quod non ita est; sed magis sicut Veritas dicit, quia per multas tribulationes oportet nos intrare in regnum Dei (Act. XIV, 21): et sicut discipulus Veritatis perhibet, quia vidua in deliciis vivens mortua est (I Tim. V, 5, 6). Ideo Dominus cum de asperitate vestis laudasset amicum in omni domo sua fidelissimum, Ecce, inquit, qui mollibus vestiuntur, in domibus regum sunt (Matth. XI, 8): volens nimirum intelligi, quia qui sectantur delicias carnis, regno hujus saeculi militant, non regno Dei. Heu! quam terribilem sententiam coelitus audivi contra mollitiem illius magnae et purpuratae meretricis! Quantum, inquit, glorificavit se et in deliciis fuit, tantum date illi tormentum et luctum (Apoc. XVIII, 7). Utinam tamen his deliciis, tantum mollitie vestium, et suavitate epularum contenta esset tenuitudo delicatorum, nec alias spinas vitiorum germinaret in eis rhamnus voluptatum, ut hoc esset omne peccatum eorum, deliciari, non luxuriari! Ipsi viderint, si ita exstinctus est in eis ingenitus ille pestifer ignis, ut tot fomentis circumpositis nequeat reaccendi; praesertim ventis ex adverso flantibus, id est, verbis et risibus lascivis tentantibus. Soleo tamen audire quia saepe vivit etiam in moriente, viget in sene: suscitatur et exsurgit etiam sine fomite, furit nullo irritante. Ipsi ergo viderint sibi. Nihil enim mihi de aliorum conscientiis judicare, cum sciam multos in omni copia et gloria mundi temperanter et pudice vixisse: et e diverso nonnullos in habitu asperiore et victu parciore nequiter egisse. Sed et scio regem Israel sub purpura sua cilicio ad carnem fuisse indutum (IV Reg. VI, 30); et panem solum nonnunquam regibus appositum: cum hodie delicatissima quaeque ac mollia tegat pulla vestis poenitentium, vel magis poenitentiam profitentium; et fastidiis eorum non satis sint opes mundi, non satisfaciant artes et tormenta coquorum. Verum quia in hujusmodi causis facile quisque sibi invenit patrocinium; alius, infirmitatis, alius, societatis cui morem gerit; alius, honoris quem gerit: esto, vivant ut volunt, comedant ut volunt; tantum ne excedat ulterius hoc malum, ad id scilicet, quod qui perpetrare volunt, confiteri nolunt, quia tueri non possunt; et incipiant notari proverbio mulieris nequam, quae comedit, et tergens os suum dicit: Non sum operata malum (Prov. XXX, 20). Nam et de magna illa Babylone, de cujus medio delicati poenitentes isti videbantur exisse, audeam dicere: Quantum vult purpurata sit, quantum vult delicata sit; tantum meretrix non sit, nec divaricet pedes suos omni transeunti.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. But it seems more likely that this is not so; rather, as the Truth says, that we must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations (Act. XIV, 21), and as the disciple of the Truth testifies, that the widow who lives in delights is dead (I Tim. V, 5, 6). Therefore, when the Lord had praised his friend—most faithful in all his house—for the roughness of his garment, he said, 'Behold, those who are clothed in soft garments are in the houses of kings' (Matth. XI, 8): wishing it to be understood, no doubt, that those who pursue the delights of the flesh serve the kingdom of this world, not the kingdom of God. Alas! What a terrible sentence I have heard from heaven against the softness of that great harlot clothed in purple! 'As much,' it says, 'as she glorified herself and lived in delights, so much torment and mourning give to her' (Apoc. XVIII, 7). Would that the frailty of the delicate were content with these delights alone—the softness of garments and the sweetness of feasts—and that the bramble of pleasures did not also germinate other thorns of vice in them, so that this alone might be their whole sin: to take delight, not to indulge in lust! Let them see to it themselves, whether that inborn pestilent fire is so extinguished in them that it cannot be rekindled though so much kindling is heaped around it—especially when winds blow against it from the other side, that is, when lascivious words and laughter tempt it. Yet I am accustomed to hear that it often lives even in the dying man, and thrives in the old man; it is stirred up and rises even without kindling, it rages though nothing incites it. Let them, then, see to it themselves. For it is nothing to me to judge the consciences of others, since I know that many have lived temperately and chastely amid all the abundance and glory of the world, while, on the other hand, some have acted wickedly under a rougher habit and a more frugal diet. But I also know that the king of Israel wore, under his purple, a hairshirt next to his flesh (IV Reg. VI, 30), and that sometimes bread alone was set before kings—whereas today the dark garment of penitents, or rather of those who merely profess penitence, covers the most delicate and soft of things, and the riches of the world are not enough to satisfy their fastidiousness, nor do the arts and torments of cooks suffice. But since in such matters everyone easily finds himself an excuse—one, the excuse of infirmity; another, of the company whose custom he follows; another, of the rank he bears—so be it: let them live as they wish, let them eat as they wish; only let this evil go no further, namely, to the point where those who wish to commit it are unwilling to confess it, because they cannot defend it, and begin to be marked by the proverb of the wicked woman, who eats, and wiping her mouth says, 'I have done no evil' (Prov. XXX, 20). For indeed, concerning that great Babylon, out of whose midst these delicate penitents seem to have come forth, I would dare to say: Let her be clothed in purple as much as she wishes, let her be as delicate as she wishes; only let her not be a harlot, nor spread her legs for every passerby.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Tu ergo si non potes imitari Joannem in asperitate vestitus, vel parcimonia victus: vel in hoc imitari contende, ut non sis arundo vento agitata; et, ut Sapiens ait, Non te ventiles in omnem ventum, et non eas in omnem viam. Sic enim peccator probatur in duplici lingua. Sed esto firmus, inquit, in via Domini (Eccli. V, 11, 12), ne te projiciat ventus a facie terrae seu loci, cui professus es; seu regni, cui praeparandus es. Solet repente ventus vehemens irruere a regione deserti, et concutere quatuor angulos domus filiorum Job (Job I, 19), et fit ruina ejus magna, si tamen super arenam fundata sit, non supra petram; si arundinea sit, non lapidea: imo si is qui aedificat eam, et inhabitat, arundo sit; foris per hypocrisim nitidus, jactantia vel promissione cassa sonorus; intus veritate vacuus. In secreto hujus arundinis Behemoth dormire amat, quae et in locis humentibus (Job XL, 10, 16), ubi nulla fluxarum rerum penuria, sed ad luxum superfluunt omnia, saepius et uberius crescit atque luxuriat (Isai. XXXVI, 7). Huic arundini si quis innitatur, manum ejus perforabit: quia si quis in adjutorium operis eum asciverit, vel alicujus ei muneris functionem imposuerit, sperantem in se gravi scandalo vulnerabit. Patientia tamen Domini hujusmodi arundinem etiam quassatam non conterit, sed sustinet, ut in melius convertatur (Isa. XXIV, 20). Nonnunquam etiam increpat feras arundinis (Psal. LXVII, 31), quae cum principe suo in secreto ejus dormiunt: nonnunquam justi tanquam scintillae aeris candentis in arundineto discurrunt (Sap. III, 7), qui tanquam carbones desolatorii, quidquid in eo steriliter silvescit incendunt, novisque fructibus purum praeparant locum. Hoc agebat Joannes, vox clamantis in deserto, non arundo, sed scintilla in arundineto: cujus sermo, ut scriptum est, sermo scintillae ad commovendum cor (Sap. II, 2) pigrum et stolidum, ut pararet viam Domino. Hoc etiam nunc in nobis agat eadem vox, cooperante Verbo ipso, cujus erat vox, Jesu Christo Domino nostro, qui vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. You, then, if you cannot imitate John in roughness of clothing or frugality of food, strive at least to imitate him in this: that you not be a reed shaken by the wind; and, as the Wise man says, "Do not winnow yourself to every wind, and do not go in every way." For in this way a sinner is proved to have a double tongue. But "be firm," he says, "in the way of the Lord" (Eccli. V, 11, 12), lest the wind cast you down from the face of the land or place to which you have professed yourself, or of the kingdom for which you are to be made ready. A violent wind is accustomed to rush in suddenly from the region of the desert and strike the four corners of the house of the sons of Job (Job I, 19), and its ruin is great — if, that is, it was founded upon sand and not upon rock; if it was made of reed and not of stone; or rather, if the one who builds it and dwells in it is himself a reed — outwardly sleek through hypocrisy, resounding with boasting or with empty promise, but within empty of truth. In the hiding-place of such a reed Behemoth loves to sleep, a reed that also in moist places (Job XL, 10, 16) — where there is no lack of transient things, but all things overflow unto luxury — grows and flourishes more often and more abundantly (Isai. XXXVI, 7). If anyone leans upon this reed, it will pierce his hand: for if anyone takes him on to help in some work, or lays upon him the carrying out of some office, he will wound with grievous scandal the one who trusted in him. Yet the patience of the Lord does not crush even a reed of this kind when it is bruised, but sustains it, that it may be turned to something better (Isa. XXIV, 20). Sometimes, too, he rebukes the beasts of the reed (Psal. LXVII, 31), who sleep with their prince in its hiding-place: and sometimes the just run to and fro in the reed-bed like sparks of glowing bronze (Sap. III, 7), who, like desolating coals, burn up whatever grows there wild and barren, and make ready a clean place for new fruits. This is what John did, the voice of one crying in the desert — not a reed, but a spark within the reed-bed: whose speech, as it is written, was "the speech of a spark" (Sap. II, 2) to stir the sluggish and foolish heart, that he might prepare the way of the Lord. May that same voice now also work this in us, with the cooperation of the Word himself, whose voice it was — Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric distinguishes sorrow over adversity from sorrow over sin. Consolation, confession and penance lead into his account of purification through love, suffering and the judgment to come. The sermon appears in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: IN QUADRAGESIMA.

passages.label: English
passages.text: FOR LENT.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De tribulatione et consolatione.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On Tribulation and Consolation.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Benedictus Deus, Pater misericordiarum et Deus totius consolationis, qui consolatur nos in omni tribulatione nostra (II Cor. 1, 3, 4). Multae tribulationes justorum, et de omnibus his liberabit eos Dominus (Psal. XXXIII, 20). Duplex autem genus tribulationum patimur, quia non solum duplici natura subsistimus, carne scilicet ac spiritu, sed et duplici qualitate vivimus; partim scilicet carnaliter, partim spiritualiter. In mundo eramus toti carnales; in coelo erimus toti spirituales: nunc autem ex parte carnales, ex parte spirituales. Prout autem proficimus in spiritu, aut magis efficimur spirituales et minus carnales, aut magis remanemus carnales et minus spirituales. Propterea duplex modo consurgit tribulatio; quia, quod in nobis carnale est, contristat adversitas; quod spirituale, iniquitas. Si nihil in nobis esset carnale, nulla nos contristaret, imo nulla esset adversitas: si nihil spirituale, non nos nostra contristaret, sed magis delectaret iniquitas, sicut de quibusdam dicitur: Laetantur cum male fecerint, et exsultant in rebus pessimis (Prov. II, 14). Illa ergo nostra de adversitate tristitia, carnalis et secundum saeculum est: haec autem de iniquitate, spiritualis et secundum Deum. Illa mortem operatur, si desit consolatio: haec salutem operatur, si non desit consolatio. Multum tamen interest in adversitate exteriori, cujusmodi sit consolatio tristium; quia consolationi divitum comminatio divina vae intentat aeternum (Luc. VI, 24). Quia nimirum plerumque qui humiliari poterant ex adversitate, gravius superbiunt de prosperitate, proditque ex adipe iniquitas eorum: imo et audacter provocant Deum, cum ipse dederit omnia in manibus eorum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Blessed be God, the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our tribulation (II Cor. 1, 3, 4). Many are the tribulations of the just, and out of all these the Lord will deliver them (Psal. XXXIII, 20). Now we suffer a twofold kind of tribulation, because we not only subsist in a twofold nature—namely flesh and spirit—but also live by a twofold quality; that is, partly carnally, partly spiritually. In the world we were wholly carnal; in heaven we shall be wholly spiritual: but now we are partly carnal, partly spiritual. But insofar as we advance in the spirit, either we become more spiritual and less carnal, or we remain more carnal and less spiritual. Therefore a twofold tribulation now arises; because adversity grieves what is carnal in us, while iniquity grieves what is spiritual. If there were nothing carnal in us, no adversity would grieve us—indeed, there would be no adversity at all; if there were nothing spiritual, our own iniquity would not grieve us, but would rather delight us, as is said of certain men: 'They are glad when they have done evil, and rejoice in most wicked things' (Prov. II, 14). That sorrow of ours, then, which comes from adversity, is carnal and according to the world; but this sorrow, which comes from iniquity, is spiritual and according to God. The former works death, if consolation is lacking; the latter works salvation, if consolation is not lacking. Yet in outward adversity it matters greatly what kind of consolation the sorrowful have; for upon the consolation of the rich the divine threat holds out eternal woe (Luc. VI, 24). For indeed it often happens that those who could have been humbled by adversity grow more gravely proud through prosperity, and their iniquity comes forth from their fatness: nay, they even boldly provoke God, though he himself has given all things into their hands.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Nos autem et cum abundat illa consolatio temporalis, oportet esse gratiores et humiliores: et cum deficit, de aeterna redemptione certiores et laetiores. Cum tamen suppetit sive salus corporum, sive tranquillitas temporum aut copia rerum; ea moderatione utenda ac dispensanda est, ut sit non occasio peccati, sed adjutorium virtutis, ac potius de bonis bona faciamus quam de bonis mali fiamus. Illa namque consolatione, qua se diffundit voluptas, vel extollit vanitas, renuat consolari anima mea (Hebr. XII, 5); magisque eligat cum Moyse et viris Israeliticis affligi, quam temporalis peccati habere jucunditatem. Sive autem consolemur exterius, sive tribulemur, benedictus Deus, qui consolationem internam et aeternam dedit in cordibus nostris, id est, gaudium spei, quae suadet nos etiam gloriari in tribulationibus nostris, pollicens, quia si compatimur, et conregnabimus (II Tim. II, 12). Illam sane tribulationem, quam interius de iniquitate nostra patimur, tanto molestiorem portamus, quanto periculosiorem experimur; quia nimirum quotidie de vita periclitamur, ut veraciter confiteamur: Nisi quia Dominus adjuvit me, paulo minus habitasset in inferno anima mea. Gratias tibi, Domine Jesu, quia si gravia sunt pericula, facilia sunt remedia; quia, si dicebam, Motus est pes meus; misericordia tua, Domine, adjuvabat me (Psal. XCIII, 17, 18). Et quod semel in Petro figurasti corporaliter (Matth. XIV, 29-31), in filiis Petri quotidie adimples spiritualiter. Jussisti nos venire ad te super aquas, id est, hoc mare magnum et spatiosum manibus: ecce virtute tua ambulamus, sed pondere nostro gravamur, et plerumque irruente spiritu procellarum impellimur, ut etiam mergi incipiamus, id est, pene jam jamque tentatori consentiamus. Sed, si celeriter confiteamur pedem motum, id est, titubasse animum, et fideliter invocemus auxilium, tu misericorditer porrigis manum, firmasque et dirigis gressum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. But we, when that temporal consolation abounds, ought to be the more grateful and the more humble; and when it fails, the more certain and the more joyful concerning the eternal redemption. Yet when there is at hand either health of body, or tranquility of the times, or abundance of goods, it must be used and administered with such moderation, that it may be not an occasion of sin but a help to virtue, and that we may rather make good things out of goods than become evil men because of goods. For let my soul refuse to be consoled by that consolation in which pleasure spreads itself abroad, or vanity exalts itself (Hebr. XII, 5); and let it rather choose to be afflicted with Moses and the men of Israel, than to have the temporal delight of sin. But whether we be consoled outwardly or be afflicted, blessed be God, who has given an inward and eternal consolation in our hearts, that is, the joy of hope, which persuades us even to glory in our tribulations, promising that if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him (II Tim. II, 12). That tribulation indeed, which we suffer inwardly from our own iniquity, we bear it as all the more troublesome, the more dangerous we find it to be; for indeed daily we are in peril of our life, so that we may truly confess: 'Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul had almost dwelt in hell.' Thanks be to thee, Lord Jesus, for though the dangers are grievous, the remedies are easy; for, 'if I said: My foot is moved; thy mercy, O Lord, assisted me' (Psal. XCIII, 17, 18). And that which thou didst once figure bodily in Peter (Matth. XIV, 29-31), thou dost daily fulfill spiritually in the sons of Peter. Thou hast bidden us come to thee upon the waters, that is, upon this great and wide sea: behold, by thy power we walk, but we are weighed down by our own weight, and often, when the spirit of storms rushes in, we are driven on so that we even begin to sink—that is, we are almost on the very point of consenting to the tempter. But if we quickly confess that our foot is moved, that is, that our soul has wavered, and faithfully call upon thy help, thou dost mercifully stretch forth thy hand, and dost steady and direct our step.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Super hoc quotidie justus decantat: Impulsus sum, ut caderem, sed non cecidi, quia Dominus suscepit me (Psal. CXVII, 13). Sed, cum ceciderit non collidetur, quia Dominus supponit manum suam (Psal. XXXVI, 24): id est, cum peccaverit, non condemnabitur, quia advocatum habet Jesum, eo quod etsi septies in die cadit, septies resurgit. Non delectatur jacere ubi cadit, et in luto volutari; sed ocius exsurgens excutit se de pulvere, et sordes diluit satisfactione. Per hoc namque justus fit, quod semper in initio sermonis accusator est sui (Prov. XVIII, 17), memor consilii divini, quo dictum est ei: Dic iniquitates tuas, ut justificeris (Isai. XLIII, sec. LXX). Ita fit ut, dum seipsum judicat, et Deum de se vindicat, illum quem judicem metuebat justum, reus advocatum habeat. Justus enim Dominus, et justitias dilexit (Psal. X, 8); nec potest injustas causas suscipere aut tueri, qui, cum acceperit tempus, etiam justitias judicabit. Et tamen qui judicem se minatur futurum superbe de justitia praesumentium, advocatum se pollicetur humiliter peccata confitentium; quoniam apud illum, in cujus conspectu non justificabitur omnis homo, nullatenus causam testificari nostram melius possumus, quam si nosmetipsos accusantes et punientes, justitiam ipsius in nos transferamus, et partes judicis adversus reos exsequamur.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Concerning this the just man daily sings: 'I was thrust, that I might fall, but I did not fall, because the Lord upheld me' (Psal. CXVII, 13). 'But when he shall fall, he shall not be bruised, because the Lord puts his hand under him' (Psal. XXXVI, 24): that is, when he has sinned, he will not be condemned, because he has Jesus as his advocate, for although he falls seven times a day, he rises seven times. He does not delight to lie where he falls, and to wallow in the mire; but rising up quickly, he shakes the dust from himself, and washes away his filth by satisfaction. For by this a man becomes just, because at the very outset of his speech he is always his own accuser (Prov. XVIII, 17), remembering the divine counsel by which it was said to him: 'Declare thy iniquities, that thou mayest be justified' (Isai. XLIII, sec. LXX). Thus it comes about that, while he judges himself and vindicates God's justice against himself, the guilty man has as his advocate him whom, as judge, he feared to be just. For 'the Lord is just, and he has loved justice' (Psal. X, 8); nor can he who, when he shall have received the appointed time, will judge even deeds of justice, take up or defend unjust causes. And yet he who threatens that he will be a judge to those who presume proudly upon their own justice, promises that he will be an advocate to those who humbly confess their sins; since before him, in whose sight no man shall be justified, we can in no way better bear witness to our cause than if, accusing and punishing ourselves, we transfer his justice onto ourselves, and carry out the part of a judge against the guilty.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Sed etsi in aliquo veniali vel per ignorantiam fallimur, vel per infirmitatem vincimur, ut Jebusaeum nostrum nequaquam exterminare praevaleamus, sed semper sub oculis nostris in terra nobiscum habitare patiamur; in hac quoque imperfectione nostra consolatur nos sermo propheticus, qui nos in se transfigurans ait: In ipsis fuimus semper et salvabimur (Isai. LXIV, 5). Imperfectum meum, inquit corpus Christi, viderunt misericordes oculi tui, et in libro tuo omnes scribentur (Psal. CXXXVIII, 16); id est, scripti invenientur tam perfecti quam imperfecti. Pollicetur siquidem Dominus se perfecturum imperfectionem nostram, loquens per Joelem prophetam: Et mundabo, inquit, sanguinem eorum quem non mundaverunt (Joel III, 21). Hinc Isaias, cum praemisisset de perfectione futurae coelestis Jerusalem: Et erit, omnis qui relictus fuerit in Sion, et residuus in Jerusalem, sanctus vocabitur omnis qui scriptus est in vita in Jerusalem: quod in infirmis nonnisi purgatione divina perficienda sit sanctitas illa, subjunxit, dicens: Si abluerit Dominus sordem filiarum Sion, et sanguinem laverit de medio Jerusalem. Consolatur quidem me lavatio quae promittitur; sed terret modus qui subditur: Spiritu, inquit, judicii, et spiritu ardoris (Isai. III, 4). Ignis enim opus cujusque probabit. Si cujus opus arserit, detrimentum patietur: ipse autem salvus fiet merito fundamenti; sic tamen quasi per ignem (I Cor. III, 13, 15).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. But even if in some venial matter we are deceived through ignorance, or overcome through weakness, so that we are by no means able to exterminate our Jebusite, but always allow him to dwell with us in the land before our eyes; in this imperfection of ours too the prophetic word consoles us, which, transfiguring us into itself, says: "In these we have always been, and we shall be saved" (Isai. LXIV, 5). "My imperfection," says the body of Christ, "your merciful eyes have seen, and in your book all shall be written" (Psal. CXXXVIII, 16); that is, both the perfect and the imperfect will be found written there. For the Lord promises that he will perfect our imperfection, speaking through the prophet Joel: "And I will cleanse," he says, "their blood which they have not cleansed" (Joel III, 21). Hence Isaiah, having first said concerning the perfection of the future heavenly Jerusalem: "And it shall come to pass, that everyone who is left in Sion, and remains in Jerusalem, shall be called holy, everyone who is written among the living in Jerusalem" — because in the weak that holiness cannot be perfected except by divine purification, he added, saying: "If the Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Sion, and shall wash the blood from the midst of Jerusalem." The washing that is promised indeed consoles me; but the manner that is added terrifies me: "By the spirit," he says, "of judgment, and the spirit of burning" (Isai. III, 4). For fire will test the work of each one. If anyone's work shall burn, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved on account of the foundation, yet so as by fire (I Cor. III, 13, 15).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Quanto melius nunc arderemus delectabili amore, quam tunc illo poenali ardore? quanto suavius nunc igne amoris purgaremur, ut mundanum in nobis non relinqueretur quod mundi incendio obnoxium inveniretur, sed, sicut tribus pueris ventus roris fieret nobis fornax Babylonis? (Dan. III, 49, 50.) Alioquin, si tepide et negligenter viventes, ligna, fenum, stipulam nobis coacervamus, et tantam ignium materiam hinc nobiscum portamus; cum examen illius purgatorii tales intraverimus, quis poterit de nobis habitare cum igne devorante? aut quis habitabit ex nobis cum ardoribus sempiternis, quando omne etiam vestimentum mistum sanguine erit in combustionem et cibus ignis? (Isai. IX, 5.) Scio quidem quia, si satis arderem igne charitatis, de me quoque diceretur: Dimittuntur ei peccata multa, quoniam dilexit multum (Luc. VII, 47). Nunc autem, si purgari non mereor igne dilectionis, utinam vel purgarer alicujus igne passionis, fieretque mihi quod propheta imprecatur sibi: Ingrediatur putredo in ossibus meis, et subter me scateat, ut requiescam in die tribulationis (Habac. III, 16). Utinam qui coepit, ipse me conterat; solvat manum suam, et succidat me: et haec mihi sit consolatio, ut affligens me dolore non parcat. Verumtamen nosti, Domine, infirmitatem figmenti mei. Quae est enim fortitudo mea, ut sustineam? aut quis finis meus, ut patienter agam? Nec fortitudo lapidum fortitudo mea, nec caro mea aenea est (Job VI, 9-12). Hoc primum quidem peto, Domine, ne in furore tuo arguas me, neque in ira tua corripias me (Psal. VI, 2). Sed, quoniam audio abs te: Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo (Apoc. III, 19); et: Beatus homo qui corripitur a Domino (Job V, 17): corripe me, Domine, in misericordia, et non in furore tuo, ne forte ad nihilum redigas me (Jerem. X, 24), et dicatur de me: Detraxisti eum ab emundatione (Psal. LXXXVIII, 45). Intuere infirmitatem meam, et secundum illam manum tuam moderare, ne vehementia verberis frangat patientiam cordis; sed magis tribulatio patientiam operetur, patientia probationem, probatio spem. Sed vae mihi, si quotidie uror, et non emundor, ut et de me dici contingat: Multo labore sudatum est, et non exivit de anima rubigo ejus, neque per ignem. Immunditia tua exsecrabilis, quia mundare te volui, et non es mundata a sordibus tuis; sed nec mundaberis prius, donec quiescere faciam indignationem meam in te (Ezech. XXIV, 12, 13).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. How much better would it be for us to burn now with delightful love, than then with that punishing fire? How much more sweetly would we be purged now by the fire of love, so that nothing worldly would be left in us found liable to the world's burning, but, as for the three youths, the furnace of Babylon would become for us a wind of dew? (Dan. III, 49, 50.) Otherwise, if living tepidly and negligently we heap up for ourselves wood, hay, and straw, and carry with us from here so much material for fires; when we enter that purgatorial trial being such as this, who among us will be able to dwell with the devouring fire? Or who of us will dwell with the everlasting burnings, when every garment too, mingled with blood, shall be for burning and food for the fire? (Isai. IX, 5.) I know indeed that, if I burned sufficiently with the fire of charity, it would also be said of me: "Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much" (Luc. VII, 47). But now, if I do not merit to be purged by the fire of love, would that I might at least be purged by the fire of some suffering, and that there might happen to me what the prophet calls down upon himself: "Let rottenness enter into my bones, and swarm beneath me, that I may rest in the day of tribulation" (Habac. III, 16). Would that he who has begun would himself crush me; would that he would loosen his hand and cut me off; and let this be my consolation, that in afflicting me with sorrow he would not spare me. Yet you know, Lord, the weakness of my frame. For what is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my end, that I should act patiently? Neither is my strength the strength of stones, nor is my flesh of bronze (Job VI, 9-12). This first indeed I ask, Lord: rebuke me not in your fury, neither chastise me in your wrath (Psal. VI, 2). But since I hear from you: "Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise" (Apoc. III, 19); and: "Blessed is the man whom the Lord corrects" (Job V, 17): correct me, Lord, in mercy, and not in your fury, lest perhaps you reduce me to nothing (Jerem. X, 24), and it be said of me: "You have cut him off from cleansing" (Psal. LXXXVIII, 45). Look upon my weakness, and moderate your hand according to it, lest the violence of the blow break the patience of my heart; but rather let tribulation work patience, patience proof, and proof hope. But woe to me, if I am burned daily and am not cleansed, so that it should happen to be said of me too: "Much labor has been expended, and its rust has not gone out of the soul, not even by fire. Your filthiness is execrable, because I wished to cleanse you, and you have not been cleansed from your filth; nor shall you be cleansed, until I have caused my indignation to rest upon you" (Ezech. XXIV, 12, 13).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Quam vereor ne id cadat in nos, qui districtione vitae, velut quodam purgatorio igne, quotidie coquimur, et nunquam ab iniquitate nostra, sicut oportet, mundamur! et forsitan non mundabimur, donec sedeat Judex ipse quasi ignis conflans et emundans argentum, et purgabit filios Levi (Malach. III, 2, 3). Verumtamen, quantulumcunque proficiat nunc iste ignis, malo tamen interim mihi hunc adhiberi, quam ad illum penitus differri. Nam, si ad invicem comparentur, iste quidem medicina est misericordis, ille ultio irati. Ita sentiebat, qui dicebat: Domine, ne in furore tuo arguas me, neque in ira tua corripias me (Psal. VI, 2). Scio quidem quia tunc etiam, cum conturbata fuerit anima mea, Domine, in ira misericordiae memor eris. Scio quia etiam in luctu et poenis consolarer me spe meliori: et inimicae potestati, cui emendandus ad tempus traditus essem, verbis prophetae responderem, dicens: Ne laeteris, inimica mea, super me, quia cecidi: consurgam, cum sedero in tenebris; Dominus lux mea est. Iram Domini portabo, quia peccavi ei, donec judicet causam meam. Educet me in lucem, videbo justitiam ejus: et aspiciet me inimica mea, et operietur confusione (Mich. VII, 8-10). Et dicam in illa die: Confitebor tibi, Domine, quoniam iratus es mihi: conversus est furor tuus, et consolatus es me (Isai. XII, 1). Verumtamen cur timebo in die mala? Cur non magis in die bona bonis fruor, et diem malam praecaveo? Nonne ecce nunc tempus acceptabile, ecce nunc dies salutis? Cur non audiam modo consilium Sapientis: Quodcunque potest manus tua instanter operare: quia non est consilium, nec ratio, nec sapientia apud inferos quo tu properas (Eccle. IX, 10); et illud Apostoli: Dum tempus habemus, operemur bonum ad omnes? (Galat. VI, 10.) Coeperamus quidem a consolationibus, sed ad terrores devenimus; quia tunc nimirum consolatio utilis erit, si terrori mista fuerit; tunc ingrediemur in veritate tua (Hebr. IV, 3), Domine, si ita laetatur cor nostrum, ut timeat nomen tuum. Alioquin, si omnino vos securos faceremus, diceretur et de nobis: Popule meus, qui beatum te dicunt, ipsi te decipiunt, et vestigia gressuum tuorum dissipant (Isai. III, 12). Tunc autem vere beati erimus, si miseriam nostram recte agnoscamus et pie doleamus: tunc securi in morte erimus, si semper pavidi suspectique vivamus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. How I fear that this may fall upon us, who are daily cooked, as it were by a kind of purgatorial fire, through the strictness of our life, and yet are never cleansed from our iniquity as we ought to be! And perhaps we shall not be cleansed until the Judge himself sits like a refiner's fire, purifying silver, and shall purge the sons of Levi (Malach. III, 2, 3). Nevertheless, however little this fire now profits, I would rather in the meantime have this fire applied to me than be put off entirely until that other one. For if the two be compared with one another, this one is the medicine of a merciful God, that one the vengeance of an angry God. So thought he who said: Lord, rebuke me not in thy fury, nor chastise me in thy wrath (Psal. VI, 2). Indeed I know that even then, when my soul shall be troubled, Lord, in wrath thou wilt remember mercy. I know that even in mourning and punishments I would console myself with better hope, and to the hostile power, to which I would be handed over for a time to be corrected, I would answer in the words of the prophet, saying: Rejoice not, my enemy, over me, because I have fallen; I shall rise again when I sit in darkness; the Lord is my light. I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he judge my cause. He will bring me forth into the light, I shall see his justice; and my enemy shall look upon me, and shall be covered with confusion (Mich. VII, 8-10). And I will say in that day: I will give thanks to thee, O Lord, for thou wast angry with me: thy wrath is turned away, and thou hast comforted me (Isai. XII, 1). But why should I fear in the evil day? Why should I not rather enjoy good things in the good day, and take precaution against the evil day? Is it not now the acceptable time, is it not now the day of salvation? Why should I not now heed the counsel of the Wise Man: Whatsoever thy hand is able to do, do it earnestly: for neither counsel, nor reason, nor wisdom shall be in hell, whither thou art hastening (Eccle. IX, 10); and that saying of the Apostle: While we have time, let us do good to all men (Galat. VI, 10.). We began indeed with consolations, but we have come round to terrors; because surely consolation will be profitable only if it be mingled with terror; then shall we enter into thy truth (Hebr. IV, 3), O Lord, if our heart so rejoices that it fears thy name. Otherwise, if we were to make you altogether secure, it would be said of us too: O my people, they that call thee blessed, the same deceive thee, and destroy the way of thy steps (Isai. III, 12). But then shall we truly be blessed, if we rightly acknowledge our wretchedness and devoutly grieve over it; then shall we be secure in death, if we live always fearful and watchful.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The quoted spirit of judgment and burning comes from Isaiah 4:4; the edition prints Isai. III, 4.
