passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: The father in the parable of the prodigal son receives the penitent before his confession is complete. Guerric considers the abundance of mercy, union with God and the humility that sustains the virtues. The 1879 edition places the sermon on a Saturday in Lent without specifying the week. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO II.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON II.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SABBATO HEBDOMADAE QUADRAGESIMAE. De parabola filii prodigi. (Luc. XV, 11-32.)

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON SATURDAY OF THE WEEK OF LENT. On the parable of the prodigal son. (Luc. XV, 11-32.)

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. O Felix humilitas poenitentium! o beata spes confitentium! quam potens es apud omnipotentem, quam facile vincis invincibilem, quam cito tremendum judicem convertis in piissimum patrem! Prodigus iste filius, cujus hodie in magnam aedificationem nostram audivimus peregrinationem aerumnosam, poenitentiam lacrymosam, susceptionem gloriosam: prodigus, inquam, iste tam graviter reus, nondum confessus erat, sed tantum confiteri deliberaverat; nondum satisfecerat, sed tantum ad satisfaciendum animum inclinaverat: et de solo fere proposito conceptae humilitatis veniam statim obtinuit, quae tanto tempore tantis expetitur votis, imploratur lacrymis, ambitur obsequiis. Latronem in cruce sola confessio absolvit; istum, sola voluntas confitendi. Dixi, inquit, Confitebor adversum me injustitiam meam Domino: et tu remisisti impietatem peccati mei (Psal. XXXI, 5): ubique misericordia praevenit. Praevenerat voluntatem confessionis, ipsam inspirando: praevenit et vocem confessionis, quod confitendum erat indulgendo. Cum adhuc, inquit, longe esset, vidit illum pater ipsius, et misericordia motus est; et accurrens cecidit super collum ejus, et osculatus est eum. Quantum haec verba sonare videntur, tardius videbatur patri filio veniam dedisse, quam illi accepisse. Sic festinabat absolvere reum a tormento conscientiae suae, quasi plus cruciaret misericordem compassio miseri, quam ipsum miserum passio sui. Neque hoc dicimus quo in natura incommutabili humanos ponamus affectus, sed ut in amorem illius summae bonitatis affectus noster dulcescat; dum ipsam plus nos amare, quam ipsi nos amemus, ex similitudine discimus humana.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. O happy humility of penitents! O blessed hope of those who confess! How powerful you are before the Almighty, how easily you conquer the unconquerable, how swiftly you turn the dreadful Judge into the most loving Father! That prodigal son, whose grievous wandering, tearful repentance, and glorious welcome we heard today to our great edification: that prodigal, I say, so gravely guilty, had not yet confessed, but had only resolved to confess; he had not yet made satisfaction, but had only inclined his mind toward making satisfaction—and from the mere purpose of a humility now conceived, he at once obtained the pardon which is sought for so long with such great prayers, implored with tears, and courted with services. The thief on the cross was absolved by confession alone; this man, by the mere will to confess. "I said," he says, "I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord: and thou hast forgiven the wickedness of my sin" (Psal. XXXI, 5): everywhere mercy goes before. It had gone before the will to confess, by inspiring it itself; it went before the voice of confession too, by pardoning what was to be confessed. "When he was yet a great way off," it says, "his father saw him, and was moved with compassion; and running to him, fell on his neck, and kissed him." As far as these words seem to suggest, it seemed the father was slower to give pardon to the son than the son was to receive it! So he hastened to absolve the guilty one from the torment of his conscience, as though the compassion of the merciful one tormented him more than the suffering of his own wretchedness tormented the wretched one himself. We do not say this so as to place human feelings within the unchangeable nature of God, but so that our affection may grow sweet toward the love of that highest goodness, while from this human likeness we learn that he loves us more than we love ourselves.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Vide autem quomodo ubi abundavit delictum, superabundet gratia. Reus vix poterat sperare veniam; Judex, imo non jam judex, sed advocatus, accumulat gratiam. Cito, inquit, proferte stolam primam, et induite illum, et date annulum in manu ejus, et calceamenta in pedes; et adducite vitulum saginatum, et occidite, et manducemus et epulemur: quia hic filius meus mortuus erat, et revixit. Verum ut haec omnia praetereamus, scilicet stolam primam, id est sanctificationem spiritus, qua baptizatus induitur, et poenitens reinduitur; annulum fidei, quo subarrhatur; calceamenta, quibus ad calcanda serpentum venena munitur, vel ad evangelizandum praeparatur; vitulum saginatum, qui ei in altari immolatur; festiva illa gaudia, quae, pro recepto indicta filio, toto celebrantur coelo: ut haec, inquam, omnia taceamus, et doctioribus tractanda servemus; amplexus ille et osculum paternae pietatis, quid non habet gratiae et dulcedinis? quid non felicissimi gaudii? quid non sanctissimae voluptatis? Cecidit inquit, super collum ejus, et osculatus est eum. Cum sic super eum affectabat, quid agebat amplectens et osculans, nisi illum sibi vel se ipsum illi insinuabat, se illi inspirabat, ut, adhaerendo sibi unus, secum fieret spiritus, sicut adhaerendo meretricibus unum cum eis corpus fuerat affectus? Parum erat illi summae misericordiae viscera suae miserationis non claudere miseris; in ipsa sua eos viscera trahit, suisque inserit membris. Non poterat nos sibi arctius astringere, non poterat non magis intimos habere, quam ut incorporaret sibi, et, sicut charitate, sic virtute ineffabili, non solum assumpto corpori, sed etiam ipsi conniteretur spiritui. Quod si tanta est gratia poenitentium, quae erit gloria regnantium? si ista sunt solatia miserorum, quae erunt gaudia beatorum? et qui hoc praerogat in via, quid servat in patria? Utique quod in cor hominis non ascendit; ut ei similes simus, et sit Deus omnia in omnibus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. But see how, where sin abounded, grace abounds the more. The guilty one could scarcely hope for pardon; the Judge—no, no longer a judge, but an advocate—heaps up grace. "Quickly," he says, "bring forth the first robe, and clothe him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet; and bring the fatted calf, and kill it, and let us eat and feast: for this my son was dead, and is come to life again." But to pass over all these things—namely, the first robe, that is, the sanctification of the spirit with which the baptized is clothed and the penitent reclothed; the ring of faith, by which he is betrothed; the shoes, with which he is armed to tread upon the venom of serpents, or prepared to preach the Gospel; the fatted calf, which is sacrificed for him upon the altar; those festive joys which, proclaimed for the recovered son, are celebrated throughout all heaven—to pass over all these, I say, and leave them for more learned men to treat: that embrace and kiss of fatherly love—what grace and sweetness does it not contain? What most blessed joy? What most holy delight does it not hold? "He fell," it says, "on his neck, and kissed him." When he showed such feeling toward him, what was he doing in embracing and kissing him, but insinuating him to himself, or himself to him, breathing himself into him, so that, by clinging to him, the two might become one spirit together, just as, by clinging to harlots, he had been made one body with them? It was too little for that highest mercy not to close the inward depths of its compassion to the wretched; it draws them into its very depths, and grafts them into its own members. It could not bind us more closely to itself or hold us in greater intimacy than by incorporating us into itself and, by ineffable power as by charity, uniting us not only to the body it had assumed but also to its very spirit. But if such is the grace of penitents, what will be the glory of those who reign? If these are the comforts of the wretched, what will be the joys of the blessed? And he who gives this in advance on the way, what does he keep in store in the homeland? Surely that which has not entered into the heart of man: that we may be like him, and God may be all in all.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Jam vero tu, beate peccator (sed licet non ideo beatus quia peccator, sed quia poenitens de peccato), quid tibi, rogo, animi erat inter amplexus patris et oscula, cum prope desperatum refovebat, cum cor mundum tibi innovans, laetitiam salutaris sui tibi refundebat? Et quomodo, inquit, sermo explicabit quod mens non capit? Inenarrabiles gemitus, et inexplicabiles sunt affectus, quos de incomprehensibili velut impraegnatus parturit animus. Angustum est eis cor humanum: unde et scissum effundit se ipsum; et ardorem quem concipit, sed non capit, quibus potest modis, lacrymis, gemitibus, suspiriis, evaporat ac digerit. Norunt haec melius, qui gustaverunt saepius et uberius. Nunc quoque, inquam, cum dimissus post illos amplexus et oscula, te et te ipsum recogitas, cum causam tuam qualis fuerit, qualiterve ab eo judicata sit retractas, et illinc abundantiam delicti tui, hinc superabundantiam gratiae pensas: quid tibi, obsecro, parit cogitatio tua? Quidni, inquit, intolerabilis in meditatione mea exardescat ignis, illinc dolore et pudore, hinc gaudio et amore? Non me hominem putarem, sed lapidem, si ita duri cordis existerem, ut me ipsum non dolerem vel erubescerem, vel ita nequam et ingrati, ut non totus in gaudium vel amorem illius Patris liquefierem.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Now you, blessed sinner (though not blessed because a sinner, but because repentant of sin), what, I ask, was in your heart amid the embraces and kisses of the Father, when he revived you who were nearly in despair, when, renewing a clean heart in you, he poured back into you the joy of his salvation? And how, he says, shall speech unfold what the mind cannot grasp? Unspeakable are the groans, and inexplicable the feelings, which the soul brings forth in labor, as if made pregnant by something incomprehensible. The human heart is too narrow for them; hence, being torn, it pours itself forth, and the fervor it conceives but cannot contain, it releases and works off by whatever means it can—tears, groans, sighs. Those who have tasted this more often and more abundantly know it better. Now too, I say, when, released after those embraces and kisses, you reconsider yourself and yourself again, when you turn over in your mind what your case was, and how it was judged by him, and weigh on the one hand the abundance of your sin, on the other the overabundance of grace: what, I ask, does your reflection bring forth in you? Why, he says, would not an intolerable fire blaze up in my meditation, on the one side from grief and shame, on the other from joy and love? I would not think myself a man but a stone, if I were so hard of heart as not to grieve or blush for myself, or so wicked and ungrateful as not to melt entirely into joy and love of that Father.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Custodi igitur, o felix peccator, custodi sollicite ac vigilanter hunc spiritum tuum, hunc justissimum humilitatis ac pietatis affectum; quo semper ita de te sentias in humilitate, de Domino in bonitate. Nihil illo majus in donis Spiritus sancti, nihil pretiosius in thesauris Dei, nihil sanctius inter omnia charismata, nihil salubrius inter omnia sacramenta. Custodi, inquam, si vis ipse custodiri, humilitatem illius sensus et vocis, qua Patri confiteris, et dicis: Pater, jam non sum dignus vocari filius tuus; fac me sicut unum de mercenariis tuis. Nihil ita Patrem promeretur, sicut hujus vocis affectus; nec melius te filium facies dignum, quam si semper confitearis indignum. Haec humilitas non solum peccatores justificat, sed etiam justos consummat, justitiamque eis accumulat, si videlicet se servos fateantur inutiles, etiam cum quae praecepta sunt, fecerint omnia. Peccatum tuum coram te sit semper, et, juxta consilium Sapientis, etiam de propitiato peccato noli esse absque metu (Eccli. V, 5). Incerta et occulta sunt judicia Dei; non temere praesumendum est de illis, cum nil inde certius teneamus, quam quod in conspectu Dei non justificabitur omnis vivens, nisi in quantum se judicat peccatorem. Alioquin quasi pannus menstruatae universae justitiae nostrae (Isai. XLIV, 6). Blande te misericordia suscepit, pie refovit; time judicium, ne gratia, quae data est humili, auferatur superbienti. Elegisti abjectus esse in domo patris tui; contentus eras fieri quasi unus ex mercenariis; sta in sententia, ut, etiamsi promotus es, adhuc ad majora proveharis. Extremum locum semper occupa, aut certe desidera; servitutem tibi mercenarii, non libertatem filii tibi vindica. Devotione quidem filii Patrem cole, conscius quid ipse de te meruerit; sed humilitate et labore mercenarii contentus esto, conscius quid ipse merueris. Nunquam tibi displiceat humilitas, per quam placere coepisti, et sine qua displicere incipies, quantiscunque pollere virtutibus, quantumcunque patri officiosus deservire videaris. Humilitas siquidem omnium virtutum est maxima, cum tamen virtutem se esse nesciat. Ipsa fere omnium radix, et seminarium, et fomes, et incentivum, et ipsa cumulus et fastigium, custodia et disciplina. Ab ipsa incipiunt, per ipsam proficiunt, in ipsa consummantur, per ipsam conservantur. Cumque omnibus ut virtutes sint tribuat, si qua earum defuerit, vel minus perfecta fuerit, ipsa alterius defectu proficiens, dispendium illius de se compensat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Keep, then, O happy sinner, keep carefully and watchfully this spirit of yours, this most just affection of humility and devotion; by which you should always feel thus about yourself—in humility—and about the Lord—in goodness. Nothing is greater than this among the gifts of the Holy Spirit, nothing more precious among the treasures of God, nothing holier among all the charisms, nothing more wholesome among all the sacraments. Keep, I say, if you wish yourself to be kept, the humility of that feeling and of that voice by which you confess to the Father and say: "Father, I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants." Nothing so wins the Father's favor as the affection of this voice; nor will you make yourself more worthy to be a son than if you always confess yourself unworthy. This humility not only justifies sinners, but also perfects the just, and increases righteousness for them, namely if they confess themselves unprofitable servants even when they have done all that was commanded. Let your sin always be before you, and, according to the counsel of the Wise Man, even concerning sin that has been forgiven, do not be without fear (Eccli. V, 5). The judgments of God are uncertain and hidden; one must not presume rashly about them, since we hold nothing more certain from this than that in the sight of God no living person will be justified, except insofar as he judges himself a sinner. Otherwise, all our righteousness is like a menstrual cloth (Isai. XLIV, 6). Mercy has received you gently, has tenderly nursed you back; fear judgment, lest the grace that was given to the humble be taken away from the one who grows proud. You chose to be an outcast in your father's house; you were content to become as one of the hired servants; stand firm in that resolve, so that even if you are promoted, you may still be advanced to greater things. Always occupy the lowest place, or at least desire it; claim for yourself the servitude of a hired servant, not the freedom of a son. Indeed, worship the Father with the devotion of a son, being conscious of what he himself has deserved from you; but be content with the humility and labor of a hired servant, conscious of what you yourself have merited. Never let humility displease you, through which you began to be pleasing, and without which you will begin to be displeasing, however great the virtues you may possess, however dutifully you may seem to serve the Father. For humility is indeed the greatest of all virtues, even though it does not know itself to be a virtue. It is almost the root, and seedbed, and kindling, and spark of all virtues, and it is itself their crown and summit, their guard and discipline. From it they begin, through it they advance, in it they are perfected, through it they are preserved. And although it grants to all of them that they be virtues, if any of them should be lacking, or less than perfect, humility itself, profiting by the defect of another, compensates by itself for that one's loss.

sermons.occasion_detail: Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: For Mary's birthday Guerric takes the words "Like the vine I brought forth the sweetness of fragrance." As the vine's flower gives its scent without losing its bloom, the Virgin brought forth the Savior without losing her virginity. Christ is the sweetness that draws, the honorableness that sanctifies and the honor that glorifies, and Guerric asks the brothers for a chastity that flowers in gaze, speech and dress. The sermon appears under the heading for the Nativity of Blessed Mary in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: IN NATIVITATE B. MARIAE

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON THE NATIVITY OF BLESSED MARY

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Comparatio partus Virginis cum vite quae incorrupta dat odorem suum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: A comparison of the Virgin's childbearing with a vine that, uncorrupted, gives its fragrance.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Ego quasi vitis fructificavi suavitatem odoris (Eccli. XXIV, 23). Natalem beatissimae Virginis matris celebramus, de qua Vita omnium accepit natalem. Nata est hodie Virgo, de qua Salus omnium voluit nasci, ut natis ad mortem, daret ad vitam posse renasci. Nata est hodie Mater nova, quae primae matris maledictionem dissolvit; ut per istam benedictionem haereditate possideant, qui per illam sub praejudicio maledicti aeterni fuerant nati. Prorsus nova mater, quae novitatem attulit filiis inveteratis, vitiumque sanavit tam ingenitae, quam superadditae vetustatis. Prorsus nova mater, quae tam novo miraculo parit, ut pariat, et virgo sit; ipsumque pariat, qui omnia matremque ipsam inter omnia creavit. Mirabilis quidem novitas fecundae virginitatis, sed longe mirabilior novitas editae prolis. Nulli enim incredibile jam erit Virginem permansisse quae peperit, qui Deum agnoverit esse qui natus fuit. Nullatenus siquidem cum injuria maternae nasceretur integritatis, qui etiam corrupta redintegrare consuevit: nec veritas assumpti corporis potentiae praejudicavit Creatoris, quominus servaret sibi, quod pluribus dedit creaturis. Multas nempe creaturas invenies nasci sine corruptione gignentium, et quadam voce sua Creatori super inviolabili partu suo perhibere testimonium.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "I, like the vine, have brought forth the sweetness of fragrance" (Eccli. XXIV, 23). We celebrate the birthday of the most blessed Virgin Mother, from whom the Life of all received his birth. Today was born the Virgin from whom the Salvation of all willed to be born, so that to those born unto death he might give the power to be reborn unto life. Today was born the new Mother who dissolved the curse of the first mother, so that through this blessing those might possess as an inheritance who, through that first mother, had been born under the judgment of the eternal curse. Truly a new mother, who brought newness to aged children, and healed the fault both of inherited and of added old age. Truly a new mother, who gives birth by so new a miracle that she both gives birth and remains a virgin; and brings forth him who created all things, and the mother herself among all things. Marvelous indeed is the novelty of fruitful virginity, but far more marvelous is the novelty of the offspring brought forth. For to no one will it now be incredible that she who bore remained a virgin, once he has acknowledged that he who was born is God. For in no way would he be born to the injury of his mother's integrity, he who was accustomed even to restore wholeness to corrupted things; nor did the truth of the body he assumed prejudice the power of the Creator, so that he could not keep for himself what he gave to many creatures. For indeed you will find many creatures born without the corruption of those who bear them, and bearing witness, as it were, by their own voice to the Creator concerning their inviolate birth.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Sed loquatur Mater ipsa, quae sui conscia est mysterii, et nos edoceat quomodo vel quid ipsa genuerit. Loquatur autem non novae assertionis argumento, sed antiquo prophetiae oraculo; quia, ut ait Petrus apostolus, etiam miraculis firmior testis est propheticus sermo (II Petr. I, 19). Quid enim minus patet calumniae, aut suspicionem admittit falsitatis, quam testimonium divinitus de nondum natis prolatum? Longe igitur antequam nasceretur Maria, vocem ipsius assumebat Spiritus, qui in ea futurus erat, et tam divinitatem Filii, quam integritatem Matris, opus videlicet suum, contra blasphemias impiorum defendebat, et si persona ipsius, in modo communem intellectum sequimur, quod nunc audistis dicebat: Ego quasi vitis fructificavi suavitatem odoris (Eccli. XXIV, 23). Quod enim personae Sapientiae, id est ipsius Filii, tribuit haec verba contextus lectionis, sicut ipsi scitis, qui regulas nostis Scripturarum, nihil huic praejudicat intellectui, quominus, sicut alia multa, possint aptari personae quoque Virginis matris. Sed neque illud ignoratis quod satis superque suppetant alia testimonia, familiarius ac manifestius huic negotio servientia: sed non erit fraudanda exspectatio vestra de his quae lectio proposuit hodierna.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. But let the Mother herself speak, who is conscious of her own mystery, and let her teach us how, or what, she herself brought forth. Let her speak, however, not by the argument of some new assertion, but by the ancient oracle of prophecy; for, as the apostle Peter says, even more firm than miracles is the prophetic word as witness (II Petr. I, 19). For what is less open to calumny, or admits less suspicion of falsehood, than a testimony uttered by God concerning those not yet born? Long, then, before Mary was born, the Spirit who was to be in her took up her voice, and defended both the divinity of the Son and the integrity of the Mother—his own work—against the blasphemies of the impious; and, speaking in her person, if we follow the common understanding of the manner, he was saying what you have just heard: "I, like the vine, have brought forth the sweetness of fragrance" (Eccli. XXIV, 23). For the fact that the context of the reading attributes these words to the person of Wisdom, that is, to the Son himself, as you yourselves know, who know the rules of Scripture, in no way prejudices this understanding, so that, like many other things, they may also be fitted to the person of the Virgin Mother. But you are also not unaware that there are more than enough other testimonies, more closely and manifestly serving this matter; yet your expectation shall not be cheated as regards what today's reading has set before us.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Respondeat ergo Maria blasphemis tam pro se, quam pro Filio; cunctasque haereses solo interimat verbo, et dicat: Ego quasi vitis fructificavi suavitatem odoris. Ac si aperte dicat: Partus quidem meus non habet exemplum in sexu mulierum, sed habet similitudinem in naturis rerum. Quaeris quomodo virginitas genuit Salvatorem? Sicut flos vitis odorem. Si corruptum inveneris florem, pro eo quod dedit odorem, violatum crede pudorem, quia edidit Salvatorem. Quid potes calumniari in proprietate similitudinis? Quid enim aliud est virginitas, quam flos inviolati corporis? Quid aliud est filius virginitatis, quam suavitas odoris? Tu tamen cave ne bono moriaris odore. Bonus enim aliis odor vitae in vitam, his qui scilicet salvi fiunt: aliis odor mortis in mortem, his scilicet qui pereunt, nimirum tanquam odor vineae florentis animalibus venenatis. Sane suavitate hujus odoris refocillabatur spiritus patriarchae senis, qui filium tangens, et fragrantiam Christi sentiens, de memoria abundantiae suavitatis illius eructabat, dicens: Ecce odor filii mei, sicut odor agri pleni, cui benedixit Dominus (Gen. XXVII, 27). Suavitatem hujus odoris odoratus est Deus Pater, et delectatus repropitiatus est humano generi, cum Filius offerret semetipsum oblationem et hostiam Deo in odorem suavitatis. Hoc suavi odore trahimur, cum per conversionem currimus ad ipsum: hoc trahuntur adolescentulae, cum per devotionem currunt post ipsum. Quanquam alius sit odor ille qui de fama praedicationis percipitur, alius odor iste qui de vestimentis vel unguentis, vel de ipso fortassis corpore ejus quodammodo crassior aspergitur. Qui utique non est aliud quam virtus quae de illo exit, quae pigros excitat, et fervorem amoris innovat, ut ad currendam viam mandatorum exsultare faciat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Let Mary, then, answer the blasphemers both on her own behalf and on behalf of her Son, and let her destroy every heresy with a single word, saying: "I, like the vine, have brought forth the sweetness of fragrance." As if she were saying openly: My childbearing indeed has no example among the sex of women, but it has a likeness among the natures of things. You ask how virginity brought forth the Savior? As the flower of the vine brings forth fragrance. If you find the flower corrupted because it gave forth fragrance, then believe that modesty was violated because it brought forth the Savior. What fault can you find with the fitness of the comparison? For what else is virginity but the flower of an inviolate body? What else is the son of virginity but the sweetness of fragrance? Yet take care that you do not die by a good fragrance. For to some it is a good fragrance of life unto life—namely, to those who are saved; to others it is an odor of death unto death—namely, to those who perish—just as the fragrance of a flowering vineyard is to venomous animals. Indeed, by the sweetness of this fragrance was the spirit of the aged patriarch refreshed, who, touching his son and perceiving the fragrance of Christ, breathed out from the memory of that abundant sweetness, saying: "Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a plentiful field, which the Lord hath blessed" (Gen. XXVII, 27). The sweetness of this fragrance God the Father smelled, and, being delighted, became favorable again to the human race, when the Son offered himself as an offering and a sacrifice to God in an odor of sweetness. By this sweet fragrance we are drawn, when through conversion we run toward him; by this the young maidens are drawn, when through devotion they run after him. Although the fragrance that is perceived from the report of his preaching is one thing, and that fragrance, in a way more tangible, which is shed from his garments or ointments, or perhaps from his very body, is another. Yet this is nothing other than the power that goes forth from him, which rouses the slothful and renews the fervor of love, so that it makes them exult in running the way of the commandments.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Quia ergo tam odoriferum fructum edidit, glorietur Maria et dicat: Ego quasi vitis fructificavi suavitatem odoris. Pulchre quasi vitis: nam botrus Cypri dilectus suus illi (Cantic. I, 13), de quo non solum torcular passionis rubens mustum expressit pretiosi sanguinis, quo calix praeclarus inebriat; sed et quotidie devotio sancta sibi vinum exprimit, quod laetificat cor hominis, et inebriat voluptate gaudii et amoris. Verum non prius inebriat gustus saporis, quam trahat suavitas odoris; nec laetificat gaudium visionis, nisi prius alliciat pietas opinionis: quia nisi crediderimus non intelligemus, nec gustabimus quoniam suavis est Dominus (Psal. XXXIII, 9). Fides siquidem est quae odoratur, experientia quae gustat et fruitur. Ideo fortassis Maria Jesum suum describens per virtutes ipsius et efficientias, primo suavitatem odoris eum nominat; quia videlicet hoc initio Jesus in nobis habet subsistere, si redolentia sanctae opinionis suae ad se nos trahat. Quis sit autem fructus unde iste odor prodit, et quo nos trahat, aperit cum subdit: Et flores mei fructus honoris et honestatis (Eccli. XXIV, 23). Prorsus iste est Jesus suavitas odoris invitans, honestas sanctificans, honor glorificans. Suavitas odoris, qua velut ad viam adducimur: honestas, per quam deducimur: honor, ad quem perducimur. Pulchre autem honestas dicitur, quasi honoris status. Neque enim honor ille summae dignitatis et gloriae statum tunc in nobis habere posset, nisi nunc honestas vitae et morum sedem ei praepararet. Nullus tunc, sicut nunc, passim cernitur honoratus sine honestate, sicut nec ullus honestus sine honore. Est ergo Jesus primo suavitas odoris his quos vocat: deinde, honestas his quos justificat: demum, honor illis quos magnificat. Nam quos praedestinavit, hos et vocavit: et quos vocavit, hos et justificavit: quos autem justificavit, illos et magnificavit (Rom. VIII, 30).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Since, then, she brought forth so fragrant a fruit, let Mary glory and say: I, like a vine, have borne the sweetness of fragrance. Beautifully does she say "like a vine": for her Beloved is to her a cluster of henna (Cantic. I, 13), from which not only did the winepress of the passion squeeze forth the reddening must of precious blood, by which the splendid cup inebriates; but also daily holy devotion presses out for itself a wine which gladdens the heart of man, and inebriates with the delight of joy and love. Yet the taste of flavor does not inebriate before the sweetness of fragrance draws us; nor does the joy of vision gladden unless the devotion of belief first entices us: for unless we have believed we shall not understand, nor shall we taste that the Lord is sweet (Psal. XXXIII, 9). Faith indeed is what smells the fragrance; experience is what tastes and enjoys it. Perhaps for this reason Mary, in describing her Jesus by his virtues and effects, first names him the sweetness of fragrance; because indeed this is the beginning by which Jesus must take root in us, if the fragrance of his holy reputation draws us to himself. But what the fruit is from which this fragrance proceeds, and whither it draws us, she reveals when she adds: And my flowers are the fruit of honor and honorableness (Eccli. XXIV, 23). This indeed is Jesus: the sweetness of fragrance inviting, the honorableness sanctifying, the honor glorifying. The sweetness of fragrance, by which we are drawn, as it were, onto the way; the honorableness, through which we are led along; the honor, to which we are brought. And "honorableness" is beautifully so named, as though it were the settled state (status) of honor. For that honor of highest dignity and glory could not then have its state in us, unless now the honorableness of life and conduct prepares a seat for it. No one then is seen honored without honorableness, as many are everywhere now, just as no one will be honorable without honor. Jesus, therefore, is first the sweetness of fragrance to those whom he calls; then, honorableness to those whom he justifies; finally, honor to those whom he magnifies. For whom he predestined, these he also called; and whom he called, these he also justified; and whom he justified, these he also magnified (Rom. VIII, 30).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Talis est igitur Dilectus meus, ait Maria: et iste est filius meus, o filiae Jerusalem. Iste est benedictus fructus ventris mei, hunc fructificaverunt flores mei. Non ait. Flos; sed, flores: quia cum virgo sancta est, flos virginitatis in ea multiformis est. In Maria tamen gratia singulari prae omnibus multipliciter floruit, quae tota pulchra intus et foris, tota vernabat quadam florulentia et venustate pudoris. Nam et in te quoque si castimonia perfecta sit, non solum reflorebit caro tua, sed et super te totum efflorebit sanctificatio quaedam divina. Non erit aspectus petulans, aut vagus, sed pudicitia floridus: non sermo lascivus aut ineptus, sed verecundia gratus, aut sapientia conditus. Non prurient aures libidine audiendi nova vel turpia, nec palatum desiderio sumendi dulcia. Non erit incessus inordinatus, sed modestus: non ipse habitus non dicam meretricius, sed neque superstitiosus, imo religiosus; totusque hominis tui status sanctimoniae gratia florulentus, ut recte sponso dicere possis, cum eum ad secretum tuum invitaveris, Lectulus noster floridus (Cantic. I, 15). Quinimo ipse totus eris quidam flos pulcherrimus, qualibus sponsa languorem amoris sui fulciri ac recreari desiderat, cum ait: Fulcite me floribus, stipate me malis, quia amore langueo (Cantic. II, 5). Hujusmodi justus, etiam cum senuerit in terra radix ejus, et in pulvere emortuus fuerit truncus illius, ad odorem aquae vivae in resurrectione, id est in refloritione justorum, germinabit sicut lilium: et florebit in aeternum ante Dominum, florem de flore, natum virginem, virginis filium, Sponsum et coronam virginum; florem, inquam, quo coronanda est non solum integritas virginum, sed et castitas continentium: ipsi gloria per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Such, then, is my Beloved, says Mary: and this is my son, O daughters of Jerusalem. This is the blessed fruit of my womb, which my flowers have borne as fruit. She does not say "flower," but "flowers": because, since she is a holy virgin, the flower of virginity in her is manifold. Yet in Mary, by singular grace above all others, it flowered in manifold ways, for she, wholly beautiful within and without, blossomed entirely with a certain flowering and loveliness of modesty. For in you too, if chastity be perfect, not only will your flesh reflower, but also upon you a certain divine sanctification will flower forth entirely. Your gaze will not be wanton or wandering, but blooming with modesty; your speech not lascivious or foolish, but gracious with reserve, or seasoned with wisdom. Your ears will not itch with lust to hear new or shameful things, nor your palate with desire to taste sweet things. Your walk will not be disorderly, but modest; your very dress will be not, I will not say meretricious, but not even superstitious, but rather religious; and the whole condition of your person will be flowering with the grace of holiness, so that you may rightly say to the Bridegroom, when you have invited him into your secret chamber: Our bed is flowery (Cantic. I, 15). Indeed, you yourself will be wholly a most beautiful flower, of the kind with which the Bride desires the languor of her love to be propped up and refreshed, when she says: Prop me up with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love (Cantic. II, 5). Such a just one, even when his root has grown old in the earth, and his trunk has died away into dust, will sprout like a lily at the scent of living water in the resurrection, that is, in the reflowering of the just: and he will flourish forever before the Lord — a flower born of a flower, a virgin born, the son of a virgin, the Bridegroom and crown of virgins; a flower, I say, by which is to be crowned not only the integrity of virgins, but also the chastity of the continent: to him be glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Returning to the feast's reading from a year before, Guerric takes Mary's words "I am the mother of fair love." Christ has a bodily, a moral and a divine form, and Christians love him now in the beauty of his life and teaching. Mary labors to form her Son in all the adopted children, and fair love must rule over base, natural and worldly loves. The sermon appears under the heading for the Nativity of Blessed Mary in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO II.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON II.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De pulchritudine sanctae dilectionis.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the beauty of holy love.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Ego mater pulchrae dilectionis, et timoris, et agnitionis, et sanctae spei (Eccli. XXIV, 24). Meminisse potestis cum praeterito anno loqueremur de principio lectionis hodiernae, non inconvenienter, ut arbitror, beatae Dei Genitrici nos illud assignasse, salvo tamen intellectu illo, quo tota lectio Filio ejusdem proprie competit, id est, Dei sapientiae. Multo autem manifestius in eo quod modo de eadem lectione proposuimus, ejusdem Virginis se demonstrat vox et persona, si tamen advertamus, in eo quod ait, Ego mater pulchrae dilectionis, etc., quam pulchre et commode Filium his virtutum nominibus describat. Notus erat Matri Filius, nec minus utique quam illi qui dicebat: Etsi cognovimus Christum secundum carnem, sed nunc jam non novimus (II Cor. V, 16). Primo novit eum secundum formam carnis, in qua ipsa eum genuit: sed longe hoc a cognitione illius formae, in qua Pater eum genuit. In illa visus est aliquando, et non erat ei species neque decor (Isa. LIII, 2): in ista splendor est gloriae et candor lucis aeternae (Sap. VII, 26), apud quem non est transmutatio, nec vicissitudinis obumbratio (Jac. I, 17). Visio illius formae incredulis auxit peccatum; visio istius justis servatur in praemium. Igitur inter formam carnis et formam Verbi, quasi medius de ista ad illam gradus est, quaedam alia forma Christi, spiritualis quidem, sed quam in carne palam exhibuit; forma scilicet vitae quam in corpore gessit ad informationem eorum qui erant credituri. Si enim secundum exemplar vitae et morum, quod in eo monstratum est, formatus fuerit in nobis Christus; tunc demum idonei erimus videre non formam solum, quae formata est propter nos, sed etiam illam quae formavit nos.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "I am the mother of fair love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope" (Eccli. XXIV, 24). You may remember that last year, when we were speaking about the beginning of today's reading, we assigned it, not unfittingly I think, to the Blessed Mother of God—while still preserving that understanding by which the whole reading properly belongs to her Son, that is, to the Wisdom of God. But much more clearly, in what we have now proposed from this same reading, the voice and person of this same Virgin shows itself—if indeed we notice how beautifully and fittingly, in saying, "I am the mother of fair love," etc., she describes her Son by these names of virtues. The Son was known to the Mother, and indeed no less than to him who said: "Though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer" (II Cor. V, 16). First she knew him according to the form of flesh, in which she herself bore him; but this is far removed from the knowledge of that form in which the Father begot him. In the former he was once seen, and "he had no beauty nor comeliness" (Isa. LIII, 2); in the latter he is "the brightness of glory and the whiteness of eternal light" (Sap. VII, 26), with whom there is "no change, nor shadow of alteration" (Jac. I, 17). The sight of that first form increased the sin of unbelievers; the sight of this second form is kept as a reward for the just. Therefore, between the form of flesh and the form of the Word, as a kind of middle step from the one to the other, there is a certain other form of Christ—spiritual indeed, but one which he openly displayed in the flesh: namely, the form of life which he led in the body for the instruction of those who were to believe. For if Christ shall have been formed in us according to the pattern of life and conduct which was shown in him, then at last we shall be fit to see not only the form which was formed for our sake, but also that form which formed us.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Est utique in Christo alia forma corporalis, alia moralis, alia intellectualis. In corporali frater est; in morali magister est; in intellectuali Deus noster est. Corporalem suscepit, ut impleret sacramentum: moralem exhibuit, ut praeberet exemplum: intellectualem seu divinam revelabit ad praemium. Quanquam etiam corporalem tunc cernere, in quam angeli concupiscunt prospicere, non minima sit portio gloriae. Beatus autem qui nunc amator factus est formae hujus, quae in exemplum est proposita: nam qui scrutator est illius quae in praemium est reposita, opprimetur a gloria (Prov. XXV, 27). Hujus formae mirator et amator factus erat, qui dicebat: Speciosus forma prae filiis hominum (Psal. XLIV, 3). Vis scire quia non formam corporis, sed cordis, non pulchritudinem membrorum, sed morum praedicabat? audi sequentia: Specie tua, inquit, et pulchritudine tua, intende, prospere procede, et regna. Adhuc fortassis dubium est, nisi addat: Propter veritatem, inquit, et mansuetudinem et justitiam (Psal. XLIV, 5). Prorsus haec est species tua et pulchritudo tua, qua regnum acquisivisti, pulcherrime regum; veritas utique sermonum, mansuetudo morum, justitia judiciorum. Hac pulchritudine facile illexisti et subjecisti tibi etiam corda inimicorum, quippe totus concupiscentia et desiderium. Mirabilis triumphus gratiae, omnino novum ac pulcherrimum genus victoriae, hostem non perdere ad mortem fortitudine, sed convertere ad amorem pulchritudine. Ecce mundus totus post eum abiit concupiscens speciem decoris ejus, non quia faciem ejus viderit, sed quia tam multa amabilia de mansuetudine, veritate et justitia ejus audivit. Ex Sion species decoris ejus, quia de Sion exivit lex, et verbum Domini de Jerusalem (Mich. IV, 2): unde scilicet Evangelium ad nos missum est, in quo quaedam pulchrior Christi facies ostensa est; forma scilicet vitae et doctrinae, quam et tradidit verbo, et in se expressit exemplo.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. There is indeed in Christ one form that is bodily, another moral, another intellectual. In the bodily form he is our brother; in the moral form he is our teacher; in the intellectual form he is our God. He took on the bodily form in order to fulfill the sacrament; he displayed the moral form in order to provide an example; he will reveal the intellectual or divine form as a reward. Although even to behold the bodily form then, into which the angels desire to look, is no small portion of glory. But blessed is he who has now become a lover of this form which has been set forth as an example; for he who is a searcher into that form which is reserved as a reward "shall be overwhelmed by its glory" (Prov. XXV, 27). A marveler and lover of this form was he who said: "Thou art beautiful in form above the sons of men" (Psal. XLIV, 3). Do you wish to know that he was praising not the form of the body but of the heart, not the beauty of the limbs but of conduct? Listen to what follows: "With thy comeliness," he says, "and thy beauty, set out, proceed prosperously, and reign." Perhaps this is still doubtful, unless he adds: "Because of truth," he says, "and meekness, and justice" (Psal. XLIV, 5). This indeed is your comeliness and your beauty, by which you acquired your kingdom, O most beautiful of kings: truth of speech, meekness of conduct, justice of judgments. By this beauty you easily enticed and subjected to yourself even the hearts of your enemies, being wholly desire and longing. A wondrous triumph of grace, altogether a new and most beautiful kind of victory—not to destroy the enemy unto death by strength, but to convert him to love by beauty. Behold, the whole world has gone after him, desiring the beauty of his comeliness, not because it saw his face, but because it heard so many lovable things about his meekness, truth, and justice. "Out of Sion is the loveliness of his beauty", because "out of Sion went forth the law, and the word of the Lord out of Jerusalem" (Mich. IV, 2)—whence, namely, the Gospel was sent to us, in which a certain more beautiful face of Christ was shown: namely, the form of life and doctrine, which he both delivered in word and expressed in himself by example.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. In hac forma nosse Christum, interim pietas est Christianorum; cum nosse in forma carnis, scandalum fuerit Judaeorum: nam nosse in forma divinitatis felicitas est, et gaudium angelorum. Ideo et Paulus sciens quia caro non prodest quidquam, sine spiritu videlicet qui vivificat, nosse jam Christum secundum carnem repudiat (II Cor. V, 16): nimirum ut spiritui vivificanti studiosius totus intendat. Hoc ipsum et Maria sapere videtur, quae dilectum uteri sui, dilectum votorum suorum insinuare cupiens affectibus omnium, describit eum non secundum carnem, sed secundum spiritum: quasi diceret et ipsa: Etsi cognovi Christum secundum carnem, sed nunc jam non novi. Cupit namque et ipsa formare Unigenitum suum in omnibus filiis adoptionis, qui etsi geniti sunt verbo veritatis, nihilominus tamen parturit eos quotidie desiderio et cura pietatis, donec occurrant in virum perfectum, in mensuram plenitudinis aetatis Filii sui, quem semel parturivit et peperit; imo, ut Isaias ait, Antequam parturiret peperit (Isai. LXVI, 7): quia peperit sine dolore, nec experta est difficultatem et molestiam parturitionis, cum pareret gaudii fructum aeterni.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. To know Christ in this form is, for the time being, the piety of Christians; whereas to know him in the form of flesh was the stumbling-block of the Jews; for to know him in the form of divinity is the happiness and joy of angels. Therefore Paul also, knowing that the flesh profits nothing without the spirit which gives life, refuses now to know Christ according to the flesh (II Cor. V, 16)—surely so that he might more earnestly direct his whole attention to the life-giving spirit. This same wisdom Mary too seems to show, who, desiring to instill into the affections of all the beloved of her womb, the beloved of her prayers, describes him not according to the flesh but according to the spirit—as if she too were saying: "Though I have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now I know him so no longer." For she too desires to form her Only-begotten in all the sons of adoption, who, although they have been begotten by the word of truth, nevertheless she labors to bring them forth daily by the desire and care of piety, until they attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the fulness of the age of her Son, whom once she labored with and brought forth—or rather, as Isaiah says, "Before she was in labor, she brought forth" (Isai. LXVI, 7); because she brought forth without pain, nor did she experience the difficulty and distress of labor, since she was bringing forth the fruit of eternal joy.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Hunc igitur commendans nobis sic ait: Ego mater pulchrae dilectionis, et timoris, et agnitionis, et sanctae spei (Eccli. XXIV, 24). Ergone est iste Filius tuus, o Virgo virginum? ergone talis est dilectus tuus, o pulcherrima mulierum? Plane talis est dilectus meus, et ipse est Filius meus, o filiae Jerusalem. Dilectus meus est pulchra dilectio in se ipso: dilectus meus est pulchra dilectio, timor, et spes, et agnitio in illo qui natus est ex ipso. Ipse enim est non solum quem diligimus, timemus, agnoscimus, et in quem speramus; sed haec etiam omnia in nobis operatur, atque his virtutibus, veluti quibusdam membris et partibus, in nobis perficitur atque formatur. Tunc enim perfecte, pro modulo hujus vitae, Christus in te formatus est, tunc veritas ipsius in te expressa est, si veritatem quae ipse est agnovisti, et agnitam glorificasti, timore videlicet et spe; et ne spes confundat, charitas diffusa sit in corde. Si huic sensui judicas incongruum, quod alius sit istarum ordo virtutum vel perfectuum, et alius ordo positionis nominum: non enim ait: Ego mater agnitionis, et timoris, et spei, et dilectionis; sed ait: Ego mater pulchrae dilectionis, et timoris, et agnitionis, et sanctae spei: fortassis et in hoc ordine ipso quem ponit, inveniri poterit aliquid congruentiae et rationis. Sicut enim de agnitione timor nascitur, quem, ne in desperationem concidat, spes adjuncta consolatur, ipsique spei, ne confundat, dilectio suffragatur: ita versa vice dilectio castum parit timorem, timorque cum dilectione illuminat agnitionem, secundum illud Sapientis, Qui timetis Dominum, diligite illum, et illuminabuntur corda vestra (Eccli. II, 10). Quanto autem verius illuminato corde Deus agnoscitur, tanto fiducialius in eum speratur. Unde est illud: Sperent in te omnes qui noverunt nomen tuum, Domine (Psal. IX, 11). Spes vero sancta est, sicut Joannes de spe videndi Deum loquens ait: Omnis qui habet hanc spem in illum sanctificat se ipsum, sicut et ille sanctus est (I Joan. III, 3).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Commending him to us, therefore, she speaks thus: I am the mother of fair love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope (Eccli. XXIV, 24). Is this, then, your Son, O Virgin of virgins? Is this, then, your beloved, O most beautiful of women? Truly such is my beloved, and he is my Son, O daughters of Jerusalem. My beloved is fair love in himself: my beloved is fair love, fear, and hope, and knowledge in him who was born of him. For he is not only the one whom we love, fear, acknowledge, and in whom we hope; but he also works all these things in us, and by these virtues, as by certain members and parts, is perfected and formed in us. For then, perfectly—so far as this life allows—is Christ formed in you, then is his truth expressed in you, if you have acknowledged the truth which he himself is, and having acknowledged it, have glorified it, namely with fear and hope; and lest hope confound, let charity be poured out in the heart. If you judge it inconsistent with this meaning that the order of these virtues or perfections should be one thing, and the order of the naming of them another—for she does not say: I am the mother of knowledge, and of fear, and of hope, and of love; but she says: I am the mother of fair love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope—perhaps even in this very order which she sets forth, something of fittingness and reason may be found. For just as fear is born of knowledge, which, lest it fall into despair, is consoled by hope joined to it, and hope itself, lest it confound, is supported by love: so, conversely, love brings forth chaste fear, and fear together with love illumines knowledge, according to that word of the Wise Man: You who fear the Lord, love him, and your hearts shall be enlightened (Eccli. II, 10). But the more truly God is known by an enlightened heart, the more confidently is he hoped for. Hence that word: Let all who know your name, O Lord, hope in you (Psal. IX, 11). And holy is that hope, as John says, speaking of the hope of seeing God: Every one that has this hope in him sanctifies himself, even as he is holy (I Joan. III, 3).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Pulchre autem et proprie dicta est pulchra dilectio, cum charitas Deus sit, ac per hoc summa pulchritudo; sitque virtus ista fere tota pulchritudo Ecclesiae, quam ipse Sponsus ejus in Cantico amoris invenitur tantum ac toties in ea mirari et extollere. Prorsus dilectio pulchra, quae de corde puro est, et conscientia bona, et fide non ficta. Ubi enim cor purum est, nulla est ruga; ubi conscientia bona, nulla est macula: ubi fides non ficta, non est aliquid ejusmodi quod oculis Sponsi displiceat, quominus sibi Ecclesiam nunc gratiosam, tunc gloriosam exhibeat. Distinguenda etiam erat hoc nomine dilectio sanctorum ab amore hominum, sive turpi, qui nec nominandus est inter fideles; sive naturali, quo amantur parentes; sive saeculari, quo se invicem amant propter saeculi necessitates vel cupiditates. Procul ergo, procul; imo nusquam prorsus sub oculis Dei amor turpitudinis: seorsum autem interim cedat amor necessitudinis, solusque regnet amor internae et aeternae pulchritudinis, quo solum Deum, vel propter Deum amant vere pulchri. Tu vero, bone Jesu, pulchritudo Sanctorum, speciosus forma, non modo prae filiis hominum, sed et prae virtutibus coelorum; specie tua et pulchritudine tua, intende, prospere procede, et regna: tamque late regnet pulchra dilectio tua, ut turpem de finibus rerum perturbet et eliminet, saecularem ad se convertat et inclinet, naturalem sub se regat et ordinet; ut illa pulchra et vera dilectione te diligat mundus, qua dilexisti mundum, Salvator mundi, qui vivis et regnas Deus, per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Beautifully and fittingly is it called fair love, since charity is God, and by this is the highest beauty; and this virtue is almost the whole beauty of the Church, which her very Bridegroom in the Song of love is found so greatly and so often to admire and extol in her. Truly it is fair love, which comes from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. For where the heart is pure, there is no wrinkle; where the conscience is good, there is no stain; where faith is unfeigned, there is nothing of the sort that could displease the eyes of the Bridegroom, so as to prevent him from presenting the Church to himself now as gracious, and then as glorious. It was also necessary that the love of the saints be distinguished by this name from the love of men—whether the base love, which must not even be named among the faithful; or the natural love, by which parents are loved; or the worldly love, by which people love one another on account of the necessities or desires of this world. Far, then, far away—nay, altogether absent from the eyes of God—be the love of baseness: let the love of natural ties withdraw aside for the time being, and let the love of inward and eternal beauty alone reign, by which the truly beautiful love God alone, or love others for God's sake. But you, good Jesus, beauty of the Saints, fair in form not only above the sons of men, but even above the virtues of the heavens; with your beauty and your comeliness, set out, proceed prosperously, and reign; and may your fair love reign so widely that it may disturb and banish base love from the bounds of all things, turn worldly love toward itself and incline it, and rule and order natural love beneath itself; so that the world may love you with that fair and true love with which you loved the world, O Savior of the world, who live and reign, God, through all ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric's first Nativity sermon contemplates the eternal Word as a vulnerable child. Four numbered paragraphs move from the renewal brought by Christ's birth to humility, confidence in mercy, and the gentleness that should shape Christian conduct. This reading uses the 1879 Patrologia Latina edition; the approximate 1138–1157 composition range is distinct from that publication date. The Nativity heading does not specify a Christmas Mass. Two editorial notes explain inaccurate Scripture locators printed in the edition without changing the sermon.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: DE NATIVITATE DOMINI.

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Qualia nos doceat Deus puer.

passages.label: English
passages.text: What God as a child teaches us.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Puer natus est nobis (Isai. ix, 6). Puer antiquus dierum. Puer forma corporis et aetate; antiquus dierum, incomprehensibili Verbi aeternitate. Quanquam et in ipsa sua dierum antiquitate et si puer non sit, novus tamen semper sit; imo non tam novus sit, quam ipsa novitas in se semper manens et innovans omnia, a quo quaeque res prout recedit, inveteratur; prout reaccedit, renovatur. Et novo quodam modo unde antiquus, inde novus: quoniam quidem aeternitas ipsius sine initio nascendi, sine defectu veterascendi, ipsa est et antiqua novitas, et nova antiquitas ipsius. Alia tamen est novitas hujus temporalis nativitatis, quia puer natus est nobis innovandis, qui ab aeterno Deus natus est angelis beatificandis. Illa quidem nativitas amplioris gloriae, sed ista profusioris misericordiae. Ista siquidem propter me, qui misericordia indigebam, quoniam miseria circumdatus eram, et miseria quam expiare non poteram. Ostende nobis misericordiam tuam (Psal. lxxxiv, 8), qui nondum idonei sumus videre gloriam tuam: appareat benignitas et humanitas Salvatoris nostri Dei, ut per hanc digni efficiamur et idonei, quibus appareat majestas et divinitas Creatoris nostri Dei. Ostende nobis, Domine, misericordiam tuam, nostra indutam miseria, et novo miserendi genere de ipsa miseria miserorum operantem remedia. Ad hoc siquidem ars misericordiae beatitudinem Dei, et miseriam hominis in unitate Mediatoris temperavit; ut operante sacramento unitatis, per virtutem resurrectionis beatitudo miseriam absorbeat, mortemque vita deglutiat; et totus homo glorificatus in divinae consortium naturae transeat. Usque adeo autem universitas [sic] infirmitates carnis, quibus ob culpam humana subjacet natura, absque culpa videlicet, dignatio suscepit divina; ut nec infantiae recusaret injurias, nec alia, quam communis habet conditio, sortiri vellet exordia: excepto sane, quod per Spiritum sanctum immaculatus nascens de immaculata, vitia nostrae originis emundabat, atque secundae nativitatis nobis sacramenta dedicabat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. A child is born to us (Isaiah ix, 6). A child, the Ancient of Days. A child in bodily form and age; the Ancient of Days in the incomprehensible eternity of the Word. Yet even in that ancientness of his days, although he is not a child, he is always new; indeed, he is not so much new as newness itself, always abiding in itself and making all things new. Every thing grows old as it withdraws from him, and is renewed as it draws near again. And in a certain new way, the very reason he is ancient is the reason he is new: for his eternity, without a beginning through birth or a decline through growing old, is itself both his ancient newness and his new ancientness. Yet the newness of this birth in time is different: he who from eternity was born as God to give the angels blessedness has been born as a child to make us new. That birth indeed has greater glory, but this one has more abundant mercy. This birth is for me, who needed mercy because I was surrounded by misery, and by misery which I could not expiate. Show us your mercy (Psalm lxxxiv, 8), for we are not yet fit to see your glory. Let the kindness and humanity of God our Saviour appear, so that through this we may become worthy and fit for the majesty and divinity of God our Creator to appear to us. Show us, Lord, your mercy, clothed in our misery and, by a new manner of showing mercy, working remedies from the very misery of the miserable. For this purpose the art of mercy has blended God's blessedness and man's misery in the unity of the Mediator, so that, as the sacrament of unity works, blessedness may through the power of the resurrection swallow up misery and life devour death, and the whole man, glorified, may pass into fellowship with the divine nature. Indeed, the divine condescension took upon itself, without sin, all the infirmities of the flesh to which human nature is subject because of sin, to such an extent that it did not refuse the hardships of infancy, nor did it wish to have a beginning different from that of our common condition; except, of course, that, born immaculate of the immaculate Virgin through the Holy Spirit, he cleansed the faults of our origin and consecrated for us the sacraments of a second birth.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Itaque parvulus natus est nobis (Isa. ix, 6), et Deus majestatis exinaniens semetipsum, non solum terreno mortalium corpori, sed etiam infirmae ac pusillae infantium se configuravit aetati. O beata infantia, cujus infirmum et stultum fortius et sapientius est omnibus hominibus; quia nimirum Dei virtus, et Dei sapientia sua in nostris, divina operatur in humanis! Hujus siquidem infantis infirmitas principem mundi triumphat, fortem armatum ligat, crudelem tyrannum captivat, et captivitatem nostram absolvit et liberat. Hujus infantis muta, ut videtur, et elinguis simplicitas linguas infantium facit disertas; linguis hominum loqui facit et angelorum, linguas dividens igneas: inscius iste, ut videtur, ipse est qui docet hominem scientiam et angelum, tanquam vere Deus scientiarum, Sapientia Dei, et Verbum. O sacra et dulcis infantia, quae veram humanis innocentiam refudisti, per quam omnis aetas in beatam redeat infantiam; tibique conformis fiat, non pusillitate membrorum, sed humilitate sensus, et pietate morum. Prorsus vos filii Adae, qui nimis grandes estis in oculis vestris, et in giganteam enormitatem per superbiam excrevistis; nisi conversi fueritis, et effecti sicut parvulus iste, non intrabitis in regnum coelorum (Matth. xviii, 4). Ego sum ostium (Joan. x, 9) regni, ait parvulus iste: nisi incurvetur altitudo virorum, non eos admittet humilitatis janua. Ideo nimirum conquassabit capita in terra multorum (Psal. cxi, 6); et qui elati accedunt, repulsi capite illiso cadent retrorsum. Quid enim? adhuc tu superbis, terra et cinis, postquam Deus factus est humilis? adhuc magnus es in oculis tuis, postquam Deus parvulus factus est sub oculis tuis? Ille semetipsum exinanivit ut pene videretur esse nihil, sine quo factum est nihil: et tu in immensum inflaris et extolleris, existimans te aliquid esse, cum vere sis nihil! ipse te seducis (Galat. vi, 3), clamat tibi Apostolus; cum, etsi aliquid esses, si magnum aliquid esses, tanto magis humiliari te oporteret. Quanto, inquit Sapiens, magnus es, humilia te in omnibus: et invenies gratiam coram Deo (Eccli. iii, 20), qui superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam (Jacobi iv, 6 et I Petr. v, 5); qui et ipse, ut tibi fieret exemplum, cum esset maximus omnium, factus est humillimus omnium et minimus. Parum erat ei, ut fieret minor angelis conditione mortalis naturae, nisi et hominibus minor fieret aetate imbecillis infantiae. Videat igitur pius et humilis, et glorietur, videat impius et superbus, et confundatur. Videat, inquam, Deum immensum, parvulum factum, et infantulum adorandum, stupendum mysterium, redemptionem piorum, gloriam humilium, judicium impiorum, ruinam superborum. O venerandum ac tremendum mysterium! Quam sanctum et terribile est nomen tuum, fons misericordiarum, et abyssus judiciorum! Quis de hoc fonte bibit, et non amavit? quis hanc abyssum consideravit, et non expavit? Qui non amavit, nequam et impius est: sicut qui non expavit, vecors et insensatus est. Nihil tamen est cur judicium expavescas, si non adversus misericordiam insolescas. Et ipse, siquidem mallet amari, quam serviliter timeri: magisque probat quod liber ac voluntarius offert affectus filiorum, quam quod coactitius extorquet metus servulorum. Ideo et nunc cum primo se manifestavit mortalibus, puerum se maluit exhibere, magisque amabilis quam terribilis apparere: ut, quia salvare veniebat, et non judicare; praeferret interim unde provocaret amorem, differret unde incutere posset timorem.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Thus a little child is born to us (Isaiah ix, 6), and the God of majesty, emptying himself, conformed himself not only to the earthly body of mortals, but also to the weak and tiny age of infants. O blessed infancy, whose weakness and foolishness are stronger and wiser than all men, because God's power and God's wisdom work what is their own in what is ours, divine things in human things! For this infant's weakness triumphs over the prince of the world, binds the strong armed man, takes the cruel tyrant captive, and releases and frees our captivity. This infant's simplicity, seemingly mute and without speech, makes the tongues of infants eloquent; dividing fiery tongues, it makes them speak with the tongues of men and angels. This seemingly unknowing child is himself the one who teaches knowledge to man and angel, as truly the God of knowledge, the Wisdom of God, and the Word. O holy and sweet infancy, which has poured true innocence back into mankind, through which every age may return to blessed infancy and be conformed to you, not in smallness of limbs, but in humility of mind and holiness of conduct. Truly, you children of Adam, who are too great in your own eyes and have grown through pride to a monstrous gigantic size: unless you are converted and become like this little child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew xviii, 4). I am the door (John x, 9) of the kingdom, says this little child: unless the tall stature of men bends low, the gate of humility will not admit them. For this reason he will crush the heads of many upon the earth (Psalm cxi, 6); and those who approach with heads raised will be repulsed, their heads struck, and fall backwards. What then? Do you still boast, dust and ashes, after God has become humble? Are you still great in your own eyes, after God has become little before your eyes? He emptied himself so as almost to seem nothing, he without whom nothing was made; and you swell and exalt yourself beyond measure, thinking yourself something when you truly are nothing! You deceive yourself (Galatians vi, 3), the Apostle cries to you; whereas, even if you were something, even something great, you ought all the more to humble yourself. The greater you are, says the Wise Man, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God (Ecclesiasticus iii, 20), who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James iv, 6 and I Peter v, 5). He himself, to become your example, though greatest of all, became humblest and least of all. It was not enough for him to become less than the angels through the condition of mortal nature, unless he also became less than men through the age of helpless infancy. Let the devout and humble see and rejoice; let the impious and proud see and be confounded. Let them see, I say, the immeasurable God made little, an infant to be adored: an astounding mystery, the redemption of the devout, the glory of the humble, the judgment of the impious, the downfall of the proud. O mystery worthy of reverence and trembling! How holy and terrible is your name, fountain of mercies and abyss of judgments! Who has drunk from this fountain and not loved? Who has contemplated this abyss and not trembled? Whoever has not loved is wicked and impious; just as whoever has not trembled is senseless and foolish. Yet there is no reason to dread judgment if you do not rise insolently against mercy. He himself would rather be loved than feared as a slave fears; and he approves more highly what the free and willing affection of children offers than what the forced terror of servants wrings out. Therefore, when he first manifested himself to mortals, he chose to show himself as a child and to appear lovable rather than terrible: since he was coming to save and not to judge, he would for the time display what would awaken love, and defer what could strike fear.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Cum fiducia igitur accedamus ad thronum gratiae ejus, qui nec cogitare sine tremore poteramus de throno gloriae ejus. Nihil hic terroris, nihil severitatis quam metuas; sed omnimoda benignitas atque mansuetudo, de qua praesumas. Et si potestas et terror apud ipsum est, totum tamen interim dissimulat, donec poenitenti parcat, confitentem recipiat. Ne sit tibi scrupulo, quod graviter deliquisti: nescit puer laesus irasci; aut, si irascitur, facile potest placari. Vere nihil placabilius animo hujus pueri, qui in hoc ipsum pacem tuam satisfactionemque praevenit, priorque legatos de pace mittit: ut qui reus es, velis reconciliari. Tantummodo velis, et vere perfecteque velis: non modo veniam indulgebit, sed et gratiam cumulabit: quinimo lucrum non mediocre deputans, ovem recuperasse perditam, diem festum aget cum angelis. Congruebat ergo cum divina mansuetudine aetas innocentis ac facilis infantiae, satisque convenienter et commode salutem peccatorum ab hac exorditus est aetate; ut quos reatus propriae terrebat conscientiae, spes consolaretur non difficilis indulgentiae.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of his grace, we who could not even think of the throne of his glory without trembling. Here there is no terror, no severity for you to fear, but every kind of goodness and gentleness in which to place your trust. Even if power and terror are with him, for the time he conceals it all, until he spares the penitent and receives the one who confesses. Do not let the fact that you have sinned grievously trouble you: a child who has been hurt does not know how to be angry; or, if he is angry, he is easily appeased. Truly nothing is more ready to be appeased than the heart of this child, who anticipates your peace-making and satisfaction for this very purpose, and sends envoys of peace first, so that you, the guilty one, may be willing to be reconciled. Only be willing, truly and fully willing: he will not merely grant pardon, but heap grace upon you; indeed, reckoning the recovery of the lost sheep no small gain, he will celebrate a feast with the angels. The innocent and yielding age of infancy therefore accorded with divine gentleness, and it was fitting and advantageous that he began the salvation of sinners at this age, so that those whom the guilt of their own conscience terrified might be comforted by the hope of pardon readily obtained.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. O puer dulcissime, Jesu bone, quam magna est multitudo dulcedinis tuae, quam abscondisti timentibus te, et perficies sperantibus in te, qui tantam exhibuisti necdum scientibus te! Prorsus dulcedo incomparabilis, et pietas ineffabilis; ut Deum qui creavit me, videam puerum creatum propter me: Deusque majestatis et gloriae non solum similis mihi fiat corporis veritate, sed etiam miserabilis, et velut humanae indigens opis appareat aetatis infirmitate. Vere tu puer Deus, salutare vultus mei, et Deus meus, cum totus sis dulcedo, et desiderium, dulciorem tamen te mihi facit teneritudo membrorum. Haec nimirum te capabilem facit sensibus et affectibus parvulorum, qui nondum sunt te solidum idonei capere cibum. Dulce interim, dulce prorsus et sapidum, cogitare puerum Deum: quin etiam efficax et operatorium ad medendum, ac dulcorandum, si quis in nobis est, rancorem animorum, sermonum amaritudinem, morum austeritatem. Neque enim crediderim, ubi sensus et memoria fuerit hujus divinae dulcedinis, locum irae vel tristitiae inveniri: sed omnis indignatio, et amaritudo cum omni malitia tolletur a nobis. Ita fiet ut quasi modo geniti infantes, modo genitum infantem Dominum digne laudemus, et in consonantia morum et vocum, ex ore infantium et lactentium perficiatur laus infantis, et lactentis Domini Jesu Christi, cui cum Patre et Spiritu sancto laus et jubilatio, per aeterna saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. O sweetest child, good Jesus, how great is the abundance of your sweetness, which you have hidden for those who fear you and will bring to fulfilment for those who hope in you, you who have shown so much to those who do not yet know you! Truly, incomparable sweetness and ineffable loving-kindness: that I should see God who created me as a child created for me; and that the God of majesty and glory should not only become like me in the reality of his body, but even appear pitiable and as if needing human assistance through the weakness of his age. Truly, you, the child who is God, the salvation of my countenance and my God, although you are wholly sweetness and desire, the tenderness of your limbs makes you sweeter still to me. For this makes you comprehensible to the senses and affections of little children, who are not yet fit to receive you as solid food. Meanwhile it is sweet, altogether sweet and savoury, to contemplate God as a child; indeed it is effective and powerful to heal and sweeten whatever rancour of spirit, bitterness of speech, or harshness of conduct is in us. For I could not believe that where there is a sense and remembrance of this divine sweetness, room could be found for anger or sadness; rather, all indignation and bitterness, with all malice, will be taken away from us. Thus, like newborn infants, we shall worthily praise the infant Lord newly born, and in the harmony of our conduct and our voices, from the mouths of infants and nursing children shall be perfected the praise of the infant and nursing Lord Jesus Christ, to whom with the Father and the Holy Spirit be praise and jubilation, through the eternal ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition prints Matth. xviii, 4. The sentence beginning nisi conversi fueritis corresponds to Matthew 18:3; verse 4 continues the teaching on becoming humble like a child. The historical locator remains unchanged in the sermon.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition prints Psal. cxi, 6. The quotation conquassabit capita in terra multorum corresponds to Psalm 109:6 in Vulgate numbering (Psalm 110:6 in common modern numbering). The apparent reference error is retained and explained rather than silently corrected.

sermons.title: Nativity Sermon I: What God as a Child Teaches Us
