passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: This second Nativity sermon belongs to Guerric of Igny's medieval collection of sermons for the liturgical year, here read from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. Its individual date is unknown; the collection is associated approximately with his abbacy in 1138–1157. Taking Isaiah's "a child is born to us, a son is given to us", Guerric reads the gift as the barren Church's joy and the rejected Synagogue's loss: the dowry of the old covenant passes to the new Bride. He then counts what is given with the Son, and asks for right faith, a pure conscience and ready devotion to receive it. The heading names the Nativity without a particular Christmas Mass.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO II.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON II.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Quale donum, contemnente synagoga, suscepit Ecclesia.

passages.label: English
passages.text: What Gift the Church Received When the Synagogue Spurned It

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Puer natus est nobis, et filius datus est nobis (Isai. IX, 6). Inde probatur quod natus est nobis, quia scilicet datus est nobis. Illis enim recte dicitur natus, quibus videtur datus. Et omnibus quidem gratia nativitatis hujus oblata est, sed non ab omnibus suscepta est. Non enim omnium est fides. In propria venit, et sui eum non receperunt (Joan. I, 11). Inutiliter autem natus esset nisi et datus esset: frustraque factus esset filius hominis, si non recepissent eum filii hominum, quibus daret potestatem filios Dei fieri. Vae igitur, Judaea incredula, ingrata et impia: ablatum est a te regnum Dei, et datum est genti facienti fructus ejus. Ejectus Jesus est de Synagoga, sed susceptus est ab Ecclesia. Ejectus est de contradictionibus Judaeorum, constitutus est in caput Gentium. Ecce populus, quem non cognovit, servivit illi, auditu auris obedivit ei; cum de vobis filiis alienis, filiis sceleratis et parricidis, sit pii patris illa querela terribilis: Filios enutrivi et exaltavi, ipsi autem spreverunt me (Isai. I, 2). Sed, qui spernit, nunquid non et ipse spernetur? Quia repulistis verbum Dei, inquiunt apostoli, et indignos vos judicastis vitae aeternae, ecce convertimur ad gentes (Act. XIII, 46). O felix gentilitas! ecce affertur tibi Jesus: curre obviis manibus, extende manus, expande sinus, devotionem tuam probet tam actus quam effectus; filium qui tibi offertur, suscipe fide, amplexare affectu; semperque inter ubera tua commoretur. Et ecce videor mihi audire vocem exsultationis et confessionis de cunctis partibus orbis; a finibus terrae laudes audio, gloriam justi. Est autem sonus ut multitudinis, ut sonus castrorum Dei, vox una laudantium et dicentium: Puer natus est nobis, et filius datus est nobis (Isa. IX, 6). Ipsa est, ni fallor, Ecclesia laetabunda, et laudans, toto orbe terrarum; pro eo quod sibi natum, sibi datum amplexatur filium, quem oblatum, sed ablatum merito videt perfidiae Judaeorum. Lauda, sterilis, quae non pariebas, decanta laudem et jubila, quae non parturiebas: quia per hunc filium qui datus est tibi, multi erunt filii desertae, magis quam ejus, quae vinculo legis Deo maritata (Isa. LIV, 1), ei videbatur adhaerere. Tunc mirabitur et dilatabitur cor tuum (Isa. LX, 5). Tunc dices in corde tuo: Quis genuit mihi istos? Ego sterilis et non pariens, transmigrata et captiva: et istos quis enutrivit? Ego destituta et sola, et isti ubi hic erant? (Isa. XLIX, 21.) O mater incorrupta, virgo fecunda, filius, qui datus est tibi, hos tibi dedit. Est enim Filius Altissimi, cui Pater istos adoptavit, ut sint omnes conformes imaginis ejus, et sit ipse primogenitus in multis fratribus. Dilata, inquit, itaque locum tentorii tui ab ortu ad occasum, et a mari ad mare, quia ad dexteram et ad laevam penetrabis, et semen tuum gentes haereditabit (Isa. LIV, 2, 3). Iste namque unigenitus Mariae, primogenitus est omni creaturae, cui dicitur a Patre: Postula a me, et dabo tibi gentes haereditatem tuam, et possessionem tuam terminos terrae (Psal. II, 8).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. A child is born to us, and a son is given to us (Isai. IX, 6). From this it is proved that he was born to us, namely because he was given to us. For he is rightly said to be born to those to whom he appears to be given. And indeed the grace of this birth was offered to all, but it was not received by all. For not all have faith. He came into his own, and his own did not receive him (Joan. I, 11). But he would have been born in vain unless he had also been given; and the Son of man would have been made in vain, if the sons of men had not received him, to whom he might give the power to become sons of God. Woe, then, unbelieving Judea, ungrateful and impious: the kingdom of God has been taken away from you, and given to a nation that produces its fruits. Jesus was cast out of the Synagogue, but received by the Church. He was cast out amid the contradictions of the Jews; he was set up as the head of the Gentiles. Behold, a people whom he did not know served him; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed him; while concerning you, strange children, wicked and parricidal children, there stands that terrible complaint of the loving Father: 'I have nourished and raised up children, but they have despised me' (Isai. I, 2). But he who despises—shall he not also himself be despised? Because you have rejected the word of God, say the apostles, and have judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles (Act. XIII, 46). O happy Gentile people! Behold, Jesus is brought to you: run to meet him with open hands, stretch forth your hands, open wide your bosom; let both deed and effect prove your devotion; the son who is offered to you, receive with faith, embrace with affection; and let him abide always between your breasts. And behold, I seem to hear a voice of exultation and confession from all parts of the world; from the ends of the earth I hear praises, the glory of the just one. And the sound is as of a multitude, as the sound of the camps of God, one voice of those praising and saying: 'A child is born to us, and a son is given to us' (Isa. IX, 6). This is, unless I am mistaken, the Church, rejoicing and praising throughout the whole world; because she embraces as born to her, given to her, the son whom she sees offered to the faithlessness of the Jews, but deservedly taken away from it. Praise, O barren one who did not bear; sing out praise and shout for joy, you who did not travail: because through this son who is given to you, there will be more children of the deserted one than of her who, bound by the law in marriage to God (Isa. LIV, 1), seemed to cling to him. Then your heart shall marvel and be enlarged (Isa. LX, 5). Then you will say in your heart: Who has borne these for me? I was barren and not bearing, exiled and captive: and who has reared these? I was destitute and alone, and where were these? (Isa. XLIX, 21.) O undefiled mother, fruitful virgin, the son who was given to you has given these to you. For he is the Son of the Most High, for whom the Father has adopted these, that all might be conformed to his image, and that he himself might be the firstborn among many brethren. Enlarge, he says, therefore, the place of your tent from the rising to the setting, and from sea to sea, for you shall spread abroad to the right hand and to the left, and your seed shall possess the nations as an inheritance (Isa. LIV, 2, 3). For this only-begotten of Mary is the firstborn of all creation, to whom it is said by the Father: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession (Psal. II, 8).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Sicut autem, suscepto Dei Filio, Ecclesia sterilis peperit plurimos, et roborata est: ita ipso ejecto, aemula ejus Synagoga, quae multos filios habebat, infirmata est. Ideo enim hodie Ecclesia gratulabunda de dato sibi filio gratiarum actione et voce laudis replet coelos: illa muta sedet in tenebris, aut certe ejulatu fatigat inferos. Misera et caeca, cur non advertit quam manifeste Deus ejus ad nos transierit; quam evidenter ipsa repudiata, solumque retinente libellum repudii, litteram dico legis, quae adulteria ipsius, coarguit, universam dotem ipsius ad novam Sponsam nuptam transtulerit? Ecce in manibus nostris tabulae matrimonii, in duobus Testamentis; ecce sacramenta unctionum, dignitas regum, ordo sacerdotum, ministeria levitarum, cultus templi et vasorum, sacrificiorum veritas, omnis denique ipsorum gloria, translata ab ipsis, collata est nobis, quia causa et veritas omnium, Filius datus est nobis. Ipse calicem legis, quae in manu est Mediatoris, ex hoc Judaeo in hunc Christianum inclinavit. Et omne quod in ea merum ac verum fuit, eliquatum nobis transfudit: faex sola, quae non est exinanita, apud Judaeos remansit; ipsam bibunt, ipsa pars calicis eorum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. But just as, having received the Son of God, the barren Church has borne very many children and has been strengthened, so, with him cast out, her rival the Synagogue, who had many children, has been weakened. For this reason, today the rejoicing Church fills the heavens with thanksgiving and the voice of praise for the son given to her; that other one sits mute in darkness, or indeed wearies the depths below with wailing. Wretched and blind one, why does she not notice how plainly her God has passed over to us; how evidently, having repudiated her and left her only the bill of divorce—I mean the letter of the law, which convicts her of her adulteries—he has transferred her whole dowry to the new Bride, now wedded? Behold, in our hands are the marriage-tablets, in the two Testaments; behold the sacraments of anointings, the dignity of kings, the order of priests, the ministries of Levites, the service of the temple and its vessels, the truth of the sacrifices, and in short, all their glory, taken away from them, has been bestowed upon us, because the cause and the truth of all these things, the Son, has been given to us. He himself has tilted the cup of the law—the law which is in the hand of the Mediator—away from this Jew and toward this Christian. And all that was unmixed and true in the law, he has strained out and poured over to us: only the dregs, which were not emptied, remained among the Jews; that is what they drink, that is their portion of the cup.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Sed quid verbis moror? Numquid enim potest enarrari, quae et quanta sunt data nobis, cum iste Filius datus est nobis? Nonne omne datum optimum, et omne donum perfectum ab ipso, et cum ipso, pariter ad nos descendit? nonne universas opes coeli, omnes thesauros Dei, secum nobis advexit? qui licet adhuc in ipso contineantur absconditi, multa tamen jam et magna, et quasi donativum pugnaturis erogavit; sed nihil omnia ad ea quae victoribus reservavit. Quis enumeret tot munera charismatum, tot genera virtutum, nostrorum scilicet varietatem armorum, subsidia Sacramentorum, fercula Scripturarum, gradus et ordines ministrorum; in omni aetate, sexu, et conditione, natione et lingua, tot martyrum trophaea, confessorum insignia, virginum coronas? si miraris, inquit Ecclesia, unde repente mihi pauperculae haec multitudo divitiarum, et magnitudo gloriae: inde nimirum, quia Filius Dei datus est nobis, Deus gratiae, Dominus virtutum, et Rex gloriae. Imo magis mirum esset, si non sequerentur Dominum bona sua, cum etiam ipse sit omnia bona. Inquirentes, inquit, Dominum, non minuentur omni bono (Psal. XXXIII, 11); quanto magis suscipientes? Si enim miraris ista nobis per Filium data, ego (ut plus mireris) adjiciam omnia omnino nobis cum illo esse donata. Cum enim Filium, per quem et in quo omnia subsistunt, Pater nobis donavit, quomodo non omnia nobis cum illo donavit? (Rom. VIII, 32.) Omnia nostra sunt, ait Apostolus, quia noster est auctor omnium Dominus; ut, etsi videamur tanquam nihil habentes, inveniamur tamen omnia possidentes. Vides igitur quantum, et quale datum sit Filius; quamque probabile sit quod de Sapientia, quae ipse est, legitur: Venerunt mihi omnia bona cum illa, et innumerabilis honestas per manus illius (Sap. VII, 11). Quare autem hoc ita inculco, fratres mei? Quare, nisi ut discatis gloriari, quia filius datus est nobis; et quidquid mundus potest dare, aut promittere vobis, non modo vile et indignum ad illum, sed etiam detrimentum propter illum deputetis? Non quomodo mundus dat, dat ille vobis: tantum grati estote, quia datus est vobis, et satagite ut amplius et perfectius detur vobis. Qui enim semel datus est mundo in forma carnis, et certis diebus aut horis datur fidelibus in specie panis, scilicet in esu Sacramenti sui, saepius et incertis horis datur devotis, in gustu spiritus sui. Primum, ad redemptionem; secundum, ad sanctificationem; tertium etiam ad consolationem. Primum exigit ut fides sit recta; secundum, ut conscientia pura; tertium, ut devotio prompta. Haec mentem elevat, ut gratiae occurrat; cor aperit, ut excipiat; affectum dilatat, ut plurimum ipsius capiat. Non solum autem istam, sed et omnem gratiam abundare faciat in vobis, Deus omnis gratiae, Filius, qui datus est vobis, qui est Deus benedictus in saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. But why do I linger over words? For can it be told, how many and how great are the things given to us, when this Son was given to us? Does not every best gift and every perfect gift come down to us from him, and with him equally? Did he not bring with him to us all the riches of heaven, all the treasures of God? For although these still remain hidden, contained within him, yet already he has paid out many and great things, as it were a donative to those about to fight; but all these are nothing compared to what he has reserved for the victors. Who could count so many gifts of graces, so many kinds of virtues—that is, the variety of our weapons, the aids of the Sacraments, the courses of the Scriptures, the ranks and orders of ministers; in every age, sex, and condition, nation and tongue, so many trophies of martyrs, insignia of confessors, crowns of virgins? If you wonder, says the Church, whence suddenly came to me, poor little one, this multitude of riches and this greatness of glory: it is, of course, because the Son of God was given to us, the God of grace, the Lord of powers, and the King of glory. Indeed it would be far more wonderful if his own goods did not follow the Lord, since he himself is all good things. Those who seek the Lord, it says, shall not be diminished in any good thing (Psal. XXXIII, 11); how much more those who receive him? For if you wonder at these things given to us through the Son, I will add (that you may wonder the more) that absolutely all things have been given to us together with him. For when the Father gave us the Son, through whom and in whom all things subsist, how did he not give us all things together with him? (Rom. VIII, 32.) All things are ours, says the Apostle, because the Lord, the author of all things, is ours; so that, although we seem as having nothing, yet we are found possessing all things. You see, then, how great and of what kind a gift the Son is; and how fitting it is that what is read of Wisdom, which he himself is, applies here: All good things came to me together with her, and innumerable riches through her hands (Sap. VII, 11). Why, then, do I press this point so insistently, my brothers? Why, except that you may learn to glory in this, that the Son has been given to us; and that whatever the world can give or promise you, you should reckon not only as vile and unworthy compared to him, but even as a loss on account of him. He does not give to you as the world gives: only be grateful, because he has been given to you, and strive that he may be given to you more fully and more perfectly. For he who was given once to the world in the form of flesh, and is given to the faithful on fixed days or hours under the appearance of bread—that is, in the eating of his Sacrament—is given more often, and at uncertain hours, to the devout, in the tasting of his Spirit. The first was for redemption; the second, for sanctification; the third, also for consolation. The first requires right faith; the second, a pure conscience; the third, ready devotion. This last lifts up the mind, that it may go out to meet grace; opens the heart, that it may receive it; enlarges the affection, that it may grasp as much of it as possible. May God of all grace, the Son who has been given to you, who is God blessed forever and ever, cause not only this grace but every grace to abound in you. Amen.

sermons.title: Nativity Sermon II: The Gift the Church Received When the Synagogue Spurned It

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: This third Nativity sermon belongs to Guerric of Igny's medieval collection of sermons for the liturgical year, here read from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. Its individual date is unknown; the collection is associated approximately with his abbacy in 1138–1157. The child is born for us, not for himself or the angels, and his birth annuls the ancient condemnation of ours. Guerric dwells on God poured out in the manger, the scandal of hidden strength, and Solomon's judgment between the two mothers. Every soul that does the Lord's will is called to be a mother of Christ in others. The heading names the Nativity without a particular Christmas Mass.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO III.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON III.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De admirabili Dei cum homine commercio.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the Wonderful Exchange Between God and Man

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Puer natus nobis (Isa. IX, 6). Nobis prorsus; non enim sibi, non angelis. Sibi, inquam, natus non est, ut scilicet hac nativitate esse, aut melius esse inciperet, qui antequam temporaliter nasceretur, aeternaliter erat, et perfecta beatitudo sibi erat, quia de Deo perfecto perfectus Deus natus erat. Angelis natus non est; quia nec angelus ille qui in veritate stabat, reparatione indigebat; nec illius qui ceciderat, casus reparabilis erat. Ideo nusquam angelos apprehendit, sed semen apprehendit Abrahae (Hebr. II, 16); et qui Deus natus erat sibi, puer natus est nobis: se quodammodo relinquens, et angelos transiliens, ut ad nos usque deveniens unus fieret e nobis; et exinanitus a semetipso, minoratur ab angelis, ut aequalis fieret nobis. Qui igitur natus aeternaliter sibi et angelis erat beatitudo, natus temporaliter nobis, factus est nobis redemptio; quia nos solos laborare videbat antiquo nostrae nativitatis praejudicio. Quam felix, quam amabilis nativitas tua, puer Jesu, quae nativitatem omnium emendat, conditionem reformat, praejudicium solvit, chirographum damnatae naturae rescindit: ut si quem piget damnabiliter esse natum, possit felicissime renasci! Quotquot autem receperunt eum, dedisti eis potestatem filios Dei fieri (Joan. I, 12). Gratias agimus gratuitae atque gratiosae nativitati tuae, Deus filii hominis, per quem accessum habemus in gratiam istam in qua stamus, et gloriamur in spe gloriae filiorum Dei (Rom. V, 2). Prorsus admirabile commercium, ut sumens carnem, largiaris deitatem! commercium, inquam, charitate, non cupiditate contractum; indulgentiae quidem tuae gloriosum, sed indigentiae meae omnino lucrosum. Vere tu puer misericors, quem sola misericordia puerum fecit: licet pariter misericordia et veritas in te obviaverunt sibi (Psal. LXXXIV, 11). Vere, inquam, tu misericors puer, natus es nobis, non tibi: lucra nostra, non augmenta tua nascens de nobis quaesisti, quia ad hoc solum nasci dignatus es, ut nos minoratione tui proveheres, humiliatione glorificares. Tu exinanitus nos replesti: tu enim omnem tuae plenitudinem divinitatis in hominem transfudisti. Transfudisti, sed non confudisti. Transfusum tamen Deum in hominem non dicerem, si ad mensuram datum huic homini spiritum audirem: si de omni sua plenitudine penes Deum aliquid recedisset, quod non in hominem, cui unitus est, effudisset.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "A child is born to us" (Isa. IX, 6). To us indeed; for he was not born for himself, nor for the angels. He was not born, I say, for himself, as though by this birth he should begin to exist, or begin to exist better—he who, before he was born in time, existed eternally, and was perfect blessedness to himself, because he who was born was perfect God from perfect God. Nor was he born for the angels; for neither did that angel who stood firm in truth need restoration, nor was the fall of the one who had fallen reparable. Therefore he nowhere took hold of angels, but took hold of the seed of Abraham (Hebr. II, 16); and he who was born God for himself was born a child for us: in a certain manner leaving himself behind, and passing over the angels, so that, coming all the way to us, he might become one of us; and having emptied himself of himself, he was made lower than the angels, that he might become equal to us. He, therefore, who born eternally was blessedness to himself and to the angels, born in time for us, was made redemption for us; because he saw that we alone were laboring under the ancient condemnation attached to our birth. How happy, how lovable is your birth, child Jesus, which amends the birth of all, reforms their condition, annuls the sentence, cancels the bond of condemned nature: so that if anyone is grieved to have been born under condemnation, he may be reborn most happily! "But as many as received him, to them you gave power to become sons of God" (Joan. I, 12). We give thanks to your free and gracious birth, God, Son of man, through whom we have access into this grace in which we stand, and we glory in the hope of the glory of the sons of God (Rom. V, 2). Truly a wonderful exchange, that taking on flesh you should bestow deity! An exchange, I say, contracted by charity, not by greed; glorious indeed for your generosity, but wholly profitable for my need. Truly you are a merciful child, whom mercy alone made a child: although in you mercy and truth have met together equally (Psal. LXXXIV, 11). Truly, I say, you, merciful child, were born for us, not for yourself: being born of us, you sought our gain, not any increase for yourself, because you deigned to be born for this alone, that by your diminishment you might advance us, by your humiliation you might glorify us. You, emptied, filled us: for you poured out the whole fullness of your divinity into man. You poured it out, but you did not confound it. Yet I would not say that God was poured into man, if I heard that the Spirit was given to this man by measure: as if something had remained with God from his whole fullness which he had not poured out into the man to whom he was united.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Merito igitur oleum effusum nomen (Cantic. I, 2) Dei hominis, vel certe unguentum exinanitum; cum ita funditus Dei in hominem effusus sit, ut eum semetipsum exinanisse (Phil. II, 7) confiteatur fides Apostoli. Quamquam sic utique se exinanivit, ut in se ipso nihil prorsus minuerit, aut mutaverit; nec alia esse potuit naturae immutabilis exinanitio, quam naturae nostrae, quae terra inanis et vacua est, assumptio. Magna prorsus exinanitio ista in oculis videntium, ut splendor gloriae et figura paternae substantiae, nonnisi formam praeferat servilem, et in ipsa non habens speciem neque decorem. Quasi enim parum exinanitus esset, si homo solum fieret, etiam humanae carnis gloriam ita funditus in se vacuavit, sapientiam infatuavit, infirmavit virtutem, minuit magnitudinem; ut et in nativitate minimum, et in passione se exhiberet novissimum virorum: unde nec reputaverunt eum. Vis autem videre Deum exinanitum a semetipso? vide jacentem in praesepio. Ecce Deus noster (Isa. XXV, 9), Isaias ait, qui de tam longinquo vidit, et cognovit praesepe Domini sui, imo Deum in praesepi. Ecce, inquit, Deus noster. Ubi, quaeso? In praesepio, inquit. Infantulum quidem ibi invenio. Hunccine tu dicis illum esse, qui dicit, Coelum et terram ego impleo (Jerem. XXIII, 24): imo cujus majestati angusta est omnis coeli latitudo? Pannis involutum video. Hunccine tu dicis illum esse, qui gloriam et decorem induit lucis inaccessibilis, amictus incircumscripto lumine sicut vestimento? Vagientem audio. Hiccine est qui in coelis tonat, sub cujus vocis tonitruo potestates angelicae submittunt alas suas? Sic est, inquit alius propheta satisfaciens pro Isaia, omnino sic est: Hic est Deus noster, sed exinanitus est, ut te repleat, et a se quodammodo deficere voluit, ut te reficiat. Conclamat omnis chorus prophetarum uno spiritu, eademque sententia, etsi aliqui voce diversa, sic est: Hic est Deus noster, et non aestimabitur alius praeter eum (Baruch. III, 36); neque enim est alius praeter eum. Sed scio, inquit David, scio, quia non credet signo huic, sed contradicet generatio prava et adultera Judaeorum; enarrate vos, apostoli, in progenie altera Gentium. Quid? Quoniam hic quem Judaeus jacentem in praesepi nec respicit, pendentem in cruce despicit; cum miro modo nascitur, non videt; cum mira operatur, invidet; cum dira patitur, irridet: Hic, inquam, hic est Deus noster in aeternum et in saeculum saeculi, ipse reget nos in saecula (Psal. XLVII, 15).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Rightly, then, is the name of God-made-man called "oil poured out" (Cantic. I, 2), or indeed "ointment emptied out"; since God is so utterly poured out into man that the faith of the Apostle confesses that he "emptied himself" (Phil. II, 7). Although he indeed so emptied himself that he diminished or changed nothing at all in himself; nor could the emptying of an unchangeable nature be anything other than the assumption of our nature, which is earth empty and void. Truly this is a great emptying in the eyes of those who behold it, that the splendor of glory and the figure of the Father's substance should show forth nothing but the form of a servant, and in it have neither comeliness nor beauty. For as though it were too little an emptying to become man only, he so utterly emptied in himself even the glory of human flesh, made foolish wisdom, weakened power, diminished greatness; that both in his birth he showed himself the least, and in his passion the last of men: wherefore they did not even esteem him. Do you wish to see God emptied of himself? See him lying in the manger. "Behold our God" (Isa. XXV, 9), says Isaiah, who from so far off saw and recognized the manger of his Lord, indeed God in the manger. "Behold," he says, "our God." Where, I ask? "In the manger," he says. I find there indeed a little infant. Do you say that this is he who says, "I fill heaven and earth" (Jerem. XXIII, 24); indeed, for whose majesty the whole breadth of heaven is too narrow? I see him wrapped in swaddling cloths. Do you say that this is he who is clothed with glory and beauty of inaccessible light, wrapped in unbounded light as with a garment? I hear him crying. Is this he who thunders in the heavens, under the thunder of whose voice the angelic powers lower their wings? "So it is," says another prophet, answering for Isaiah, "entirely so it is: This is our God, but he has emptied himself, that he might fill you, and he willed in a certain manner to fail from himself, that he might restore you." The whole choir of the prophets cries out together with one spirit and the same judgment, though with different voices: "So it is: This is our God, and none other shall be accounted beside him" (Baruch. III, 36); for indeed there is no other besides him. "But I know," says David, "I know that this perverse and adulterous generation of the Jews will not believe this sign, but will contradict it; you, apostles, declare it among another people, the Gentiles." What? That he whom the Jew does not even look upon lying in the manger, and despises hanging on the cross; when he is born in a wondrous manner, the Jew does not see it; when he performs wondrous works, he envies; when he suffers dreadful things, he mocks: This, I say, this is our God forever and world without end; he himself shall rule us forever (Psal. XLVII, 15).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Et ecce jam praedicantibus apostolis, testificantibus prophetis, etsi vellus siccatum est, sed areae latitudo infusa est (Judic. VI, 39, 40): etsi cucurbita aruit, Ninive salvata est (Jonae III et IV); et amissio Judaeorum, divitiae facta est mundi, et salus gentium. Adorant omnes reges terrae parvulum qui natus est nobis, omnes gentes serviunt ei: quia si qui sunt qui non serviant, vel non sint servituri, quasi non sint, sic sunt coram eo (Isa. XL, 17); gens etiam et regnum, quod non servierit ei, peribit. Jam tamen videmus et gaudemus impletum, quod per Isaiam fuerat a Patre promissum: Viri sublimes ad te transibunt, tui erunt, post te ambulabunt, te adorabunt, teque deprecabuntur. Et merito, inquit, quia in te tantum est Deus, et non est absque te Deus. Vere tu es Deus absconditus, Deus Israel Salvator (Isa. XLV, 14, 15). Si unquam manifestius, si expressius potuit dici Jesus Deus, nunquam credat Judaeus: aut certe si derogat haec esse dicta de Jesu, ostendat alium in quo sit Deus, et qui sit Deus, nec praeter eum Deus; quando quidem nec personarum Trinitatem fatetur, ut assignare possit Deum, in quo sit Deus, ita ut alius Deus praeter eum non sit. Sed te, perfide, scandalizat, quod ad pietatem aedificare debuerat; quod scilicet Deus absconditus, et homo oculis adhibitus est, tanquam lutum ex sputo, quod ad videndum Deum caecum illuminaret. Hoc, inquam, scandalo tibi est, quod in infirmitate carnis abscondita est fortitudo Dei; et in infirmitate crucis abscondita est fortitudo hominis Dei; quod inglorius inter viros aspectus ejus, et forma ejus inter filios hominum: unde nec reputasti eum, sed putasti quasi leprosum, et percussum a Deo, et humiliatum; cum Deus posuerit in eo iniquitates omnium nostrum (Isa. LIII, 4, 5). Nam et tuam quoque suscepisset, si tu eam vel ad extremum deponere voluisses. At tu, miser, non deponis, sed apponis iniquitatem super iniquitatem; super sanguinem prophetarum, sanguinem Filii Dei et Apostolorum. Impone igitur, quandoquidem ita vis, impone jugum iniquitatum tuarum, tibi et filiis tuis: mihi enim regnum Christi portare magis decet, ut meas ipse portet iniquitates. Tu porta colligationes impietatis, fasciculos deprimentes: ego portem fasciculum myrrhae, quem Maria mihi colligavit, pannisque involutum in praesepi reposuit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. And behold, now that the apostles are preaching and the prophets bearing witness, even though the fleece was dried up, yet the breadth of the threshing floor was soaked (Judic. VI, 39, 40); even though the gourd withered, Nineveh was saved (Jonae III et IV); and the loss of the Jews has become the riches of the world, and the salvation of the Gentiles. All the kings of the earth adore the little child who is born for us, all nations serve him; for if there are any who do not serve him, or who will not serve him, they are before him as though they were not (Isa. XL, 17); indeed, the nation and the kingdom that does not serve him shall perish. Now, however, we see and rejoice that what was promised by the Father through Isaiah has been fulfilled: 'Lofty men shall pass over to you, they shall be yours, they shall walk after you, they shall worship you, and shall make supplication to you.' And rightly so, he says, because God is in you alone, and there is no God apart from you. Truly you are the hidden God, the God of Israel, the Savior (Isa. XLV, 14, 15). If Jesus could ever have been called God more plainly, more expressly — let the Jew never believe it. Or indeed, if he denies that these things were said of Jesus, let him show another in whom God dwells, and who is God, and besides whom there is no other God — since he does not even confess the Trinity of Persons, so that he might be able to point out some God in whom God is, such that there is no other God besides him. But you, faithless one, are scandalized by what ought to have built up your piety: namely, that God was hidden, and the man was applied to the eyes like the clay made from spittle, to enlighten the blind so that he might see God. This, I say, is a scandal to you: that in the weakness of the flesh the strength of God was hidden; and in the weakness of the cross was hidden the strength of the God-man; that his appearance was without glory among men, and his form among the sons of men — hence you did not esteem him, but thought him as it were a leper, struck by God, and humbled; whereas God had placed upon him the iniquities of us all (Isa. LIII, 4, 5). For he would have taken up your iniquity too, if you had only been willing at last to lay it down. But you, wretched man, do not lay it down, but heap iniquity upon iniquity — upon the blood of the prophets, the blood of the Son of God, and of the Apostles. Impose, then, since you so wish, impose the yoke of your iniquities upon yourself and upon your children: for it is more fitting for me to bear the kingdom of Christ, so that he himself may bear my iniquities. You carry the bundles of impiety bound together, weights that press down; I will carry the bundle of myrrh, which Mary bound up for me, and wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in the manger.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Vos igitur, fratres mei, qui cognovistis praesepe Domini vestri, Dominumque in praesepi, quem Israel non cognovit: vos, inquam, quibus Salvator ideo non viluit, quia misericors esse voluit; sed eo vobis tenerior in affectu, quo minor est in aspectu: cantate, et exsultate et psallite, Puer natus est nobis, filius datus est nobis. De Judaeis quidem est natus, sed nobis est natus; quia illis ablatus, nobis est datus. Cantate Domino canticum novum, quia mirabilia fecit. Notum fecit Dominus salutare suum (Psal. XCVII, 1-3): adeo ut et asinus de Gentibus cognoscat in praesepi Dominum suum, fenum sibi factum, quia omnis caro fenum (Isa. XL, 6). In conspectu namque Gentium revelavit justitiam suam (Psal. XCVII, 2): quam Judaeus ignorat, velum adhuc habens super faciem suam. Velum habet, quia zelum tenet: unde nec velum videt, sed invidet quod puer natus est nobis, filius datus est nobis. Nec invidet, quod cupiat habere sibi, sed quod cupiat perire et mihi et sibi. Mallet aemula et mala meretrix infantem necari, quam vivum mihi dari. Sed judicium nostri Salomonis, cujus sermo penetrabilior omni gladio ancipiti, scrutans corda et renes in invenienda matre non erravit: Date, inquit, Ecclesiae infantem vivum: haec est enim mater ejus (III Reg. III, 26, 27). Quicunque enim fecerit voluntatem ejus, ipse mater, et frater, et soror ejus est (Matth. XI, 50). O Domine Salomon, tu matrem dicis, ego ancillam profiteor. Ancilla Christi sum: fiat mihi secundum verbum tuum (Luc. I, 38). Et quidem matrem amore et sollicitudine me praestabo, quantum potero; sed conditionis meae semper memor ero.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. You therefore, my brothers, who have known the manger of your Lord, and the Lord in the manger, whom Israel did not know: you, I say, to whom the Savior has not thereby become worthless, because he wished to be merciful; but is all the dearer to your affection, the less he is in outward appearance — sing, and exult, and make music: 'A child is born to us, a son is given to us.' He was indeed born of the Jews, but he was born for us; because, taken away from them, he was given to us. Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done wonderful things. The Lord has made known his salvation (Psal. XCVII, 1-3): so much so that even the ass from among the Gentiles recognizes in the manger his Lord, who has been made hay for him, since all flesh is hay (Isa. XL, 6). For in the sight of the Gentiles he has revealed his righteousness (Psal. XCVII, 2), which the Jew does not know, still having a veil over his face. He has a veil, because he clings to jealousy; hence he does not even see the veil, but envies that a child is born to us, a son is given to us. Nor does he envy in the sense of wishing to have him for himself, but in that he wishes him to perish both for me and for himself. The rival and wicked harlot would rather the infant be killed than be given alive to me. But the judgment of our Solomon, whose word is sharper than any two-edged sword, searching hearts and inmost parts, did not err in finding the mother: 'Give,' he said, 'the living child to the Church, for she is his mother' (III Reg. III, 26, 27). For whoever does his will, he is his brother, and sister, and mother (Matth. XI, 50). O Lord Solomon, you call me mother; I profess myself a handmaid. I am the handmaid of Christ: be it done to me according to your word (Luc. I, 38). And indeed I will show myself a mother in love and care, as far as I am able; but I will always remain mindful of my condition.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. O fratres, hoc nomen matris non est singulare praelatis, quamvis specialis eis incumbat cura maternae sollicitudinis et pietatis: commune est et vobis, qui facitis voluntatem Domini. Utique et vos matres estis pueri qui datus est in vobis, et in vobis, ex quo videlicet a timore Domini concepistis, et parturistis spiritum salutis. Vigila igitur, o mater sancta, vigila super curam recens nati, donec formetur in te Christus, qui natus est tibi: quia quo tenerior est, eo facilius potest perire tibi, qui nunquam perit sibi. Spiritus siquidem qui in te est, si tibi exstinctus fuerit, redit ad Deum qui dedit illum. Vigila, inquam, super curam recens nati, memor quoniam aemula tua dormiens oppressit filium, qui datus erat ei. Quae est enim illa, nisi carnalis anima, quae spiritum exstinguit negligentia et inertia. Hujusmodi homines, cum religionis amiserint fervorem, ipsius tamen sibi arrogant gloriam et nomen. Inde contentiones carnalium adversus spirituales, etiam in capitulis, ubi verus Salomon invisibiliter judex praesidet. Filius meus, inquiunt carnales, vivit, et tuus mortuus est: ego spiritum Dei habeo, tu non habes; in me vivit amor Dei, in te mortuus est: dum scilicet aemulantur sibi religionis auctoritatem, cujus spirituales habent veritatem; ut subducta eis auctoritate, consuetudines inducant pro sui sensus libidine. Et revera quidem mater vult aemulae dari vivum et integrum infantem, non invidens ei gloriam, dummodo habeat et virtutem, sed illa, Nec mihi, inquit, nec tibi sit, sed dividatur (III Reg. III, 26); quia nimirum sanctitatis sibi cupit retinere honorem, et aliis relinquere laborem. Sed non errat qui judicat, etsi aliquandiu dissimulat. Gladius Salomonis matrem invenit, cui adjudicat indivisum, sicut affectum charitatis, sic effectum potestatis; sicut fervorem operandi, sic favorem imperandi. Vos itaque, fratres, in quibus fides per dilectionem operans nata est de Spiritu sancto, custodite eam, pascite, nutrite, tanquam parvulum Jesum, donec formetur in vobis puer qui natus est nobis; qui non solum nascendo, sed vivendo et moriendo, formam cui conformemur tradidit nobis: memor quippe semper, quod non nisi nobis natus fuit, nec nisi nobis vivere voluit, nec mori nisi pro nobis, qui pro se non habuit; ut et nos per ipsum renasceremur, secundum ipsum viveremus; in ipso moreremur, qui vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. O brothers, this name of mother is not reserved to prelates alone, although a special care of maternal solicitude and devotion falls upon them: it is common also to you, who do the will of the Lord. Indeed you too are mothers of the child who is given in you, and in you, from the moment, that is, when you conceived from the fear of the Lord and brought forth the spirit of salvation. Watch, therefore, O holy mother, watch over the care of the newly born, until Christ, who was born for you, be formed in you: for the more tender he is, the more easily he can perish for you, though he never perishes for himself. For the Spirit who is in you, if he be extinguished in you, returns to God who gave him. Watch, I say, over the care of the newly born, remembering that your rival, while sleeping, overlay the son who had been given to her. For who is that rival but the carnal soul, which extinguishes the spirit through negligence and sloth? Such men, when they have lost the fervor of religion, nonetheless claim for themselves its glory and name. Hence arise contentions of carnal men against spiritual men, even in chapters, where the true Solomon invisibly presides as judge. 'My son,' say the carnal, 'lives, and yours is dead: I have the Spirit of God, you do not; in me the love of God lives, in you it is dead'—while, that is, they jealously claim for themselves the authority of religion, of which the spiritual possess the truth; so that, authority having been wrested from them, they may introduce customs according to the lust of their own judgment. And indeed the true mother wishes the living and whole infant to be given to her rival, not envying her the glory, provided she also have the virtue; but that other says, 'Let it be neither mine nor yours, but let it be divided' (III Reg. III, 26); because, of course, she desires to keep for herself the honor of holiness, and leave to others the labor. But he who judges does not err, even though for a while he dissembles. The sword of Solomon finds out the mother, to whom he awards the child undivided, both the affection of charity and the effect of power; both the fervor of working and the favor of commanding. You therefore, brothers, in whom faith working through love has been born of the Holy Spirit, guard it, feed it, nourish it, as the little Jesus, until the child who is born to us be formed in you; who delivered to us not only by being born, but by living and dying, a form to which we should be conformed: ever mindful that he was born for us alone, and willed to live for us alone, and to die for none but us—he who had no need to die for himself—so that through him we might be reborn, according to him we might live, and in him we might die, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

sermons.title: Nativity Sermon III: On the Wonderful Exchange Between God and Man

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: This fourth Nativity sermon belongs to Guerric of Igny's medieval collection of sermons for the liturgical year, here read from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. Its individual date is unknown; the collection is associated approximately with his abbacy in 1138–1157. Beginning from Paul's fullness of time, Guerric reads it as an abundance of grace, the fulfillment of prophecy and the mature age of faith. Salvation is bought at a trifling price, yet the present age meets it with complaint and ingratitude. He closes with thanks for the Word made hay in the manger for beasts as well as men. An editorial note explains an inaccurate printed locator. The heading names the Nativity without a particular Christmas Mass.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO IV.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON IV.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De plenitudine temporis a Christo allata.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the Fullness of Time Brought by Christ

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Ecce jam plenitudo temporis (Galat. IV, 4). Plenitudo ista temporis apud Paulum accipitur, seu propter abundantiam gratiae, seu propter adimpletionem praecedentis prophetiae, seu propter pleniorem aetatem fidei adultae. De singulis videamus. Omnium plenitudo bonorum Christus Dominus est: quippe qui omnibus thesauris sapientiae et scientiae Dei, totiusque gratiae plenus est; imo in quo omnis plenitudo divinitatis habitat corporaliter (Coloss. II, 9). Viderunt apostoli plenum gratiae et veritatis, et de plenitudine ejus omnes acceperunt: adeo ut novissimus eorum et abortivus Paulus, vas electionis, de plenitudine quam acceperat, disseminaret ubique plenitudinem gratiae et veritatis, clamans et dicens: Ecce jam venit plenitudo temporis (Galat. IV, 4). Cum enim plenus omnibus bonis natus esset temporaliter auctor temporis, quidni plenitudinem attulisset temporis? Cum coeli rorarent desuper, et nubes pluerent Justum, Salvatorem terra germinaret, tanta supernae benedictionis ubertas quidni fecunditatem terris omnibus praestaret? Benedixisti, Domine, terram tuam, dedisti benignitatem, et terra nostra dedit fructum suum (Psal. LXXXIV, 2, 13); videlicet de uno grano frumenti, quod germinavit alvus Virginis, ubique terrarum pullulante copiosa messe fidelium. Nolo enim hanc plenitudinem temporis requiras in copia bonorum temporalium, sed aeternorum; non in proventu agrorum, sed coelorum. Si coeli rorant desuper, et nubes pluunt Justum; si terra germinat Salvatorem, et justitia oritur simul; si denique oritur in diebus Domini non solum justitia, sed et abundantia pacis: feliciora tempora ne quaesieris, quando et regnum Dei nihil aliud est quam justitia, et pax, et gaudium in Spiritu sancto (Rom. XIV, 17), quod de illis procedit. Nam et nostrorum temporum ille status judicatur optimus, atque pulcherrimus, cum et justitia moribus imponit disciplinam, et abundantia cum pace quietem vitae praestat et laetitiam. Denique misericordia Domini plena est terra (Psal. CXVIII, 64): benedixit Dominus coronae anni benignitatis suae, et campi ejus repleti sunt ubertate (Psal. LXIV, 12) totius gratiae spiritualis. Et quis, nisi ingratus, plenitudinem neget esse temporis? Quae unquam aurea aetas simile aliquid habuit hujus plenitudini temporis, quando panis angelorum, omnem habens saporem suavitatis et omne delectamentum, apponitur etiam jumentis; et non solum homines, sed et jumenta, cibo pascuntur coelesti? Homines enim et jumenta salvabis, Domine, quemadmodum multiplicasti misericordiam tuam, Deus (Psal. XXXV, 7, 8). Infinite multiplex haec tua, Deus, misericordia, ut qui panis angelorum, non solum hominum dites ac beatifices mensas, sed etiam fenum factus, jumentorum repleas praesepia. Confiteris, o Domine sapientia misericors, quia sapientibus et insipientibus debitor es, ut qui utrosque fecisti, utrisque necessariam alimoniam procures; et tam homines quam jumenta, tam spirituales quam animales, suo quemque gradu et ordine salves. Confiteantur igitur Domino misericordiae ejus, et mirabilia ejus filiis hominum (Psal. CVI, 15): quia misit Verbum suum carnem factum, medicinam et escam omnium; ut etiam incapaces Verbi, sanentur tamen et satientur carne Verbi. Edant itaque pauperes et saturentur, et confiteantur venisse beatam temporis plenitudinem; quando et in praesepibus suis paratum sine sudore vultus sui panem inveniunt coelestem. Numquid ergo mugiet bos, cum ante praesepe sic plenum steterit? (Job VI, 5.) Mugiat, sed prae gaudio spiritus in jubilo cordis; quia praesepe Domini sui, imo Dominum in praesepi suo cognovit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Behold, now is the fullness of time (Galat. IV, 4). This "fullness of time" is taken by Paul in reference either to the abundance of grace, or to the fulfillment of earlier prophecy, or to the fuller age of mature faith. Let us look at each in turn. Christ the Lord is the fullness of all good things: for he is full of all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God, and of all grace; indeed, in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily (Coloss. II, 9). The apostles saw him full of grace and truth, and from his fullness all received: so much so that the last of them and the one born as it were out of due time, Paul, the chosen vessel, from the fullness he had received, scattered everywhere the fullness of grace and truth, crying out and saying: Behold, now the fullness of time has come (Galat. IV, 4). For since the author of time, full of all good things, was born in time, why should he not have brought the fullness of time? When the heavens dropped dew from above, and the clouds rained down the Just One, and the earth brought forth the Savior as its growth, why should such abundance of heavenly blessing not bring fruitfulness to all the earth? You have blessed, O Lord, your land; you have given your bounty, and our land has yielded its fruit (Psal. LXXXIV, 2, 13); namely, from the one grain of wheat which sprouted from the Virgin's womb, a plentiful harvest of the faithful has sprung up throughout all the earth. For I do not want you to seek this fullness of time in an abundance of temporal goods, but of eternal ones; not in the yield of fields, but of heavens. If the heavens drop dew from above, and the clouds rain down the Just One; if the earth brings forth the Savior as its sprout, and righteousness arises at the same time; and if, finally, in the days of the Lord there arises not only righteousness but also abundance of peace: do not seek for happier times, since the kingdom of God is nothing other than righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom. XIV, 17), which proceeds from these things. For indeed that condition of our times is judged best and most beautiful, when righteousness imposes discipline on morals, and abundance together with peace provides quiet of life and gladness. In short, the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord (Psal. CXVIII, 64): the Lord has blessed the crown of the year with his bounty, and his fields are filled with the abundance (Psal. LXIV, 12) of all spiritual grace. And who, unless he is ungrateful, would deny that this is the fullness of time? What golden age ever possessed anything like this fullness of time, when the bread of angels, having every taste of sweetness and every delight, is set before even the beasts of burden; and not only men, but even beasts of burden, are fed with heavenly food? For you will save men and beasts, O Lord; O how you have multiplied your mercy, O God (Psal. XXXV, 7, 8). Infinitely manifold is this your mercy, O God, that you who are the bread of angels not only enrich and make blessed the tables of men, but, having become hay, fill the mangers of beasts of burden. You confess, O Lord, merciful Wisdom, that you are debtor both to the wise and to the foolish, since, having made both, you provide necessary nourishment for both; and you save men as well as beasts, the spiritual as well as the animal, each in its own degree and order. Let his mercies therefore give praise to the Lord, and his wonders to the children of men (Psal. CVI, 15): for he sent his Word made flesh, the medicine and food of all; so that even those incapable of the Word might nevertheless be healed and satisfied by the flesh of the Word. Let the poor therefore eat and be filled, and confess that the blessed fullness of time has come; since even in their mangers they find heavenly bread prepared without the sweat of their brow. Will the ox then bellow, when he has stood before a manger so full? (Job VI, 5.) Let him bellow—but let it be for the joy of spirit, in the jubilation of the heart; because he has recognized the manger of his Lord, indeed, the Lord himself in his manger.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Libet autem adhuc manifestius videre, Christus veniens e coelis quantam plenitudinem temporis advexerit, quam facili et exiguo pretio omne pretiosum comparari posse decreverit. Duobus minutis, seu calice aquae frigidae, aut certe sola bona voluntate, jam a diebus ejus emitur regnum coelorum, quanquam etiam nunc vix inveniat emptorem in tanta multitudine divitum. Proh pudor! etiam nos ipsi, qui jam emere coepimus, jam tabulas emptionis conscripsimus, jam pignus haereditatis accepimus; etiam nos, inquam, toties a pacto resilimus, ac pene complaciti poenitemus, querimur, murmuramus, quasi in negotio simus circumventi; quasi magnum sit illud prope nihil, quod exigitur a nobis. Bene de nobis prophetavit Scriptura: Malum est; malum est, dicit omnis emptor, et cum recesserit, gloriabitur (Prov. XX, 14). An non merito poterit gloriari, qui immensum illud et aeternum pondus gloriae, hoc levi et momentaneo tribulationis suae comparaverit, qui sic pro nihilo salvus factus fuerit? At nunc quotidianas hinc inde querelas et molesta murmura audias: Malum hoc, malum illud; grave hoc, importabile illud; quis tanta ac talia ferat? Ita nemo fere est qui digne pro merito sui rem aestimans dicat: Non sunt condignae passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam quae revelabitur in nobis (Rom. VIII, 18), nisi tunc demum cum coeperit revelari. Tunc plane gloriabitur, qui modo detrahit, ac de pretio se gravari gemit; cum scilicet de foro, id est, de mundo hoc, ubi contractus celebratur hujus commercii, recesserit et in domum aeternitatis suae, secum ferens rem tantam tantillo emptam, redierit. Homo plane secundum cor Dei erat ille, homo simplex sine querela, qui ab hac arte, imo inertia et infidelitate emptorum alienus erat; Davidem dico, qui dicebat: Quoniam non cognovi litteraturam, Domine, memorabor justitiae tuae solius (Psal. LXX, 15, 16). Justitiae meae nullatenus memorabor, ut labores meos exaggerem, merita magnificem; potius memorabor justitiae tuae solius, qui gratis obligasti te mihi promissorem. In veritate tua exaudi me, in justitia tua, et non intres in judicium cum servo tuo (Psal. CXLII, 1, 2): qui, si voluero me justificare, os meum condemnabit me. Per hoc enim, inquit, introibo in potentias Domini (Psal. LXX, 16); quia scilicet justitias meas non statuam: per hoc potentem me faciet, et nunc in praelio, et tunc in regno; quia semper infirmitates meas confitebor. Cum enim infirmor, tunc potens sum (II Cor. XII, 10). Sicut ergo prudenter apud Deum causam agit, qui justitiae suae immemor totum misericordiae committit; sic prudenter emit, qui omnem fictionem, atque avaritiam negotiationis scire renuit; qui inventa illa pretiosa margarita, non solum omnia sua, sed et seipsum ultro ac desideranter inpendit. At nos tepidi, ficti, ingrati, indevoti, voluptatum amatores magis quam Dei, vix ab illa voce infidelis et nequissimi murmuris, Malum est, malum est (Prov. XX, 14), valemus compesci; etiam postquam gustavimus, et vidimus, sicut de muliere forti scriptum est, quoniam bona est negotiatio nostra.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. But I wish to see still more clearly how great a fullness of time Christ brought when he came from the heavens, and with how easy and small a price he determined that everything precious could be purchased. With two mites, or a cup of cold water, or indeed with good will alone, the kingdom of heaven has been bought ever since his days — though even now it scarcely finds a buyer amid so great a multitude of the rich. For shame! Even we ourselves, who have already begun to buy, who have already drawn up the tablets of purchase, who have already received the pledge of inheritance — even we, I say, so often draw back from the bargain, and, having almost agreed, repent, complain, murmur, as though we had been cheated in the transaction; as though that were a great thing — that next-to-nothing which is required of us. Scripture prophesied well concerning us: "It is bad, it is bad," says every buyer, and when he has gone away, he will boast (Prov. XX, 14). And will he not rightly be able to boast, who has purchased that immense and eternal weight of glory with this light and momentary tribulation of his, who has thus been saved for next to nothing? But now you may hear on every side daily complaints and troublesome murmurs: "This is bad, that is bad; this is heavy, that is unbearable; who can bear such great and such things?" Thus there is scarcely anyone who, rightly valuing the matter according to its worth, says: "The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us" (Rom. VIII, 18) — except only then, when it has begun to be revealed. Then clearly he will boast, who now disparages it and groans that he is burdened by the price; that is, when he has departed from the marketplace — that is, from this world, where the contract of this trade is transacted — and has returned to the house of his eternity, carrying with him so great a thing bought for so small a price. That man was truly a man after God's own heart, a simple man without complaint, who was a stranger to this art — or rather, to this sluggishness and faithlessness of buyers; I mean David, who said: "Because I have not known letters, O Lord, I will be mindful of your justice alone" (Psal. LXX, 15, 16). "I will by no means be mindful of my own justice, so as to exaggerate my labors or magnify my merits; rather I will be mindful of your justice alone, who freely bound yourself to me as one who promises." "Hear me in your truth, in your justice, and do not enter into judgment with your servant" (Psal. CXLII, 1, 2): for if I wished to justify myself, my own mouth would condemn me. "For by this," he says, "I will enter into the powers of the Lord" (Psal. LXX, 16); that is, because I will not establish my own righteousness: by this he will make me powerful, both now in the battle and then in the kingdom; because I will always confess my weaknesses. "For when I am weak, then I am powerful" (II Cor. XII, 10). Just as, therefore, he pleads his case wisely before God who, forgetful of his own righteousness, commits everything to mercy, so he buys wisely who refuses to know any pretense or greed in the trading; who, having found that precious pearl, spends not only all that he has, but also himself, freely and eagerly. But we, lukewarm, false, ungrateful, undevout, lovers of pleasures more than of God, can scarcely restrain ourselves from that voice of faithless and most wicked murmuring, "It is bad, it is bad" (Prov. XX, 14) — even after we have tasted and seen, as it is written of the valiant woman, that our trading is good.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Adhuc ferebat me quidam implacabilis zelus adversus ingratitudinem et infidelitatem hujus temporis nostri; sed revocat me, de qua sermonem institui, sancta ac beata plenitudo temporis Christi, qua etiam hodie plenius pascendi estis. Conjunctim tamen currunt, pariterque feruntur haec duo tempora tam diversa, tamque adversa, tempus scilicet gratiae, et tempus malitiae; cum tamen nonnisi unum tempus inveniatur utriusque. Si enim modo non esset tempus gratiae, non diceret Apostolus: Ecce nunc tempus acceptabile, ecce nunc dies salutis (II Cor. VI, 2). Et iterum, si modo non esset tempus malitiae, non diceret idem apostolus: Redimentes tempus, quoniam dies mali sunt (Ephes. V, 16). Confligunt igitur in tempore uno gratia et ingratitudo, velut in stadio uno. Jam olim siquidem sapientia pugnat adversus malitiam, propter quod et nunc in hujus mundi descendit aream. Pugnat, inquam, nolens vinci a malo, sed volens vincere in bono malum. Abundabat iniquitas, et licet humana congelata esset, divina tamen non frigescebat charitas. Magnus ille ardor charitatis, et revera, sicut scriptum est, aquis multis inexstinguibilis (Cantic. VIII, 7); quod cum extremum jam judicium postularet multitudo peccatorum, Deus tamen Filium suum misit, non ut judicaret mundum, sed ut salvaretur per ipsum (Joan. III, 17). Cum igitur jam pene consummata mundi malitia finem indicaret temporis, Redemptoris adventus novam et inopinatam plenitudinem temporis rebus infudit humanis. Cum enim mundus consenuisset, atque prope interitum esset temporis aetate, subito ad adventum Conditoris sui, nova et insperata renovatus est virtutis juventute, fideique quodam juvenili calore. Fides siquidem, cujus primaevum tempus, velut quaedam pueritia, fuit in Patriarchis, qui exorti sunt primo mane Ecclesiae nascentis; adolescentia vero in Prophetis; ad plenitudinem demum juvenilis excrevit roboris in Apostolis, quando et calorem suae virtutis mundo spectabilem praebuit in tam praeclaris, atque fortissimis innumerabilium martyrum triumphis. Hanc adultam ac plenam aetatem fidei vocat Apostolus plenitudinem temporis, quando scilicet hi qui sub paedagogo legis erant, nihilque a servo differebant, dum erant parvuli, jam adulti libertatem filiorum receperunt per Unigenitum Patris (Galat. VI, 1-9). Qui nimirum, ut nulla plenitudo suo deesset tempori, plenus tam gratia quam veritate venit, quatenus et per gratiam impleri faceret legis mandata, et per veritatem impleret ipse promissa; adeo ut quidquid etiam universis retro saeculis mystice gestum aut dictum fuit, totum verius ac plenius impletum sit in hac plenitudine temporis. Nam et hic ipse dies tot sacramenta, tot oracula, quasi recapitulata in brevi hodie exhibuit, ut de eo vere dici possit: Consummatus in brevi, explevit tempora multa (Sap. IV, 13).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. A certain relentless zeal against the ingratitude and unfaithfulness of our present time was still carrying me along; but the holy and blessed fullness of the time of Christ, on which I began this sermon, and with which you are to be fed more fully even today, calls me back. Yet these two times, so different and so opposed to each other—namely, the time of grace and the time of malice—run together and are carried along jointly, even though there is found to be but one single time for both. For if the present were not the time of grace, the Apostle would not say: 'Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation' (II Cor. VI, 2). And again, if the present were not the time of malice, the same Apostle would not say: 'Redeeming the time, because the days are evil' (Ephes. V, 16). Grace and ingratitude, therefore, clash together in one single time, as if in one single arena. For wisdom has long since been fighting against malice, and for this reason it has now also come down into the arena of this world. It fights, I say, unwilling to be conquered by evil, but willing to conquer evil with good. Iniquity was abounding, and although human charity had grown cold, divine charity nevertheless did not grow cold. That great ardor of charity is indeed, as it is written, unquenchable by many waters (Cantic. VIII, 7); for though the multitude of sins now demanded the final judgment, yet God sent his Son, not to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him (Joan. III, 17). Therefore, when the malice of the world, now almost complete, was signaling the end of time, the coming of the Redeemer poured out upon human affairs a new and unexpected fullness of time. For when the world had grown old, and was near destruction through the age of time, suddenly, at the coming of its Founder, it was renewed with a new and unhoped-for youthfulness of virtue, and with a certain youthful warmth of faith. For faith, whose earliest age—a kind of childhood, as it were—was in the Patriarchs, who arose in the first morning of the Church then being born; whose adolescence was in the Prophets; at last grew up into the fullness of youthful strength in the Apostles, when it also displayed to the world the warmth of its vigor, made visible in the splendid and most valiant triumphs of countless martyrs. This mature and full age of faith the Apostle calls the fullness of time—namely, when those who were under the schoolmaster of the law, and who, while they were children, differed in nothing from a slave, now grown up, received the freedom of sons through the Only-begotten of the Father (Galat. VI, 1-9). He indeed, so that no fullness might be lacking to his own time, came full both of grace and of truth, so that through grace he might cause the commands of the law to be fulfilled, and through truth he himself might fulfill the promises; to such a degree that whatever had been done or said mystically throughout all the ages gone before was fulfilled more truly and more fully in this fullness of time. For even this very day has displayed, as it were recapitulated in brief, so many mysteries, so many oracles, that of it may truly be said: 'Being perfected in a short time, he fulfilled many years' (Sap. IV, 13).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Cum ergo tot modis constet quia venit beata plenitudo temporis, recte querelas insipientium Salomon compescuit, dicens: Ne dicas, Quid, putas, causae est quod meliora fuere tempora priora quam nunc sunt? Stulta est, inquit, hujusmodi interrogatio (Eccle. VII, 11), cum manifeste felicissima tempora fecerit hominibus gratia Dei; ingratitudo autem hominum pessima fecerit ea sibi. O tempus acceptabile, cui tam beatum, tam auspicatum initium dedit dies iste, quo natus conditor aeternus temporis, aeternitatem mortalibus nuntiavit! O vere dies salutis dies iste, quo nata salus mundi se ipsam poculum salutare miscuit aegrotis! O fratres, de die isto loquebatur, ni fallor, Sapiens filio suo: Non defrauderis a die bono. Et exponens quid sit non defraudari: Particula, inquit, boni doni non te praetereat (Eccli. XIV, 14). Diem quippe bonum pro eo dicit, quia datum est hodie donum bonum, prorsus datum optimum, donumque perfectum, descendens a Patre luminum; quod quale sit nemo scit, nisi qui accepit. At vos, fratres, spiritum qui ex Deo est accepistis, ut sciatis quae a Deo donata sunt vobis, qui ex sententia cordium cantatis: Filius datus est nobis (Isai. IX, 6). Filius iste, panis est filiorum, qui de seipso hodie beatum ac solemne universae familiae Patris exhibet epulum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Since, then, it is established in so many ways that the blessed fullness of time has come, Solomon rightly checked the complaints of fools, saying: 'Do not say, What do you suppose is the reason that former times were better than now are?' 'Such a question,' he says, 'is foolish' (Eccle. VII, 11), since plainly the grace of God has made the times most happy for mankind, but the ingratitude of men has made those same times most wretched for themselves. O acceptable time, to which this day gave so blessed, so auspicious a beginning—the day on which the eternal Founder of time was born and announced eternity to mortals! O truly this day is the day of salvation, on which the salvation of the world, being born, mixed itself as a saving cup for the sick! O brothers, it was of this day, unless I am mistaken, that the Wise Man spoke to his son: 'Do not defraud yourself of a good day.' And explaining what it means not to be defrauded, he says: 'Let not the portion of a good gift pass you by' (Eccli. XIV, 14). He calls it a good day precisely because today a good gift was given—indeed the very best gift given, and a perfect gift, descending from the Father of lights—a gift of such a kind that no one knows it except the one who has received it. But you, brothers, have received the Spirit who is from God, that you may know the things that have been given to you by God, you who sing from the conviction of your hearts: 'A Son is given to us' (Isai. IX, 6). This Son is the bread of sons, who today, from himself, provides a blessed and solemn banquet for the whole family of the Father.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Gratias tibi, Pater misericordiarum, qui panem nostrum quotidianum das nobis hodie, tantaque largitate aperuisti manum tuam ad implendum omne animal benedictione, ut ipsa etiam benedictione plenum inveniatur eorum praesepe. Quam miserum, quam brutum ac stolidum, imo quam sibi nequam et invidum illud animal, quod sese isto die bono defraudat, ut eum particula doni boni praetereat, ut scilicet expers gratiae coelestis, quae ei proposita est, fiat, diemque totius refectionis et gaudii tristi ac jejuno corde praetereat; quasi necdum venerit copiosissima plenitudo temporis, nec praesepia simplicium et humilium panis impleverit coelestis! Hujusmodi hominem sibi nequam et invidum, Deo ingratum et injuriosum, notat Sapientia, cum ait: Oculus malus ad mala opera, et non saturabitur pane, indigens et in tristitia erit super mensam suam. Ideo, inquit, non saturabitur bonis anima ipsius, quia oculus ejus ad mala, nec revertetur oculus ejus, ut videat bona, ut cum pietate et fide consideret quae ei apposita sunt in magna divitis mensa. Nequam est enim, inquit, oculus lividi, avertens faciem suam et despiciens animam suam (Eccli. XIV, 10, 8). Procul dubio, fratres, si faciem non avertimus a consideratione illius qui jacet in praesepi, ipso intuitu possumus felicissime pasci, dicemusque: Dominus pascit me, et nihil mihi deerit; in loco pascuae, ibi me collocavit (Psal. XXII, 1, 2). Tunc plane sciemus quia venit desideratissima plenitudo temporis, in quo misit Deus Filium suum, per quem tanta jam replemur plenitudine bonorum: ipsi benedictio et gratiarum actio, et nunc, et per infinita saecula saeculorum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Thanks be to you, Father of mercies, who give us our daily bread today, and who with such great generosity have opened your hand to fill every living creature with blessing, that even their manger is found full of that same blessing. How wretched, how brutish and foolish—indeed how wicked and grudging toward itself—is that creature which cheats itself on this good day, so that the portion of the good gift passes it by; so that, lacking the heavenly grace set before it, it lets the day of all refreshment and joy pass by with a sad and fasting heart, as though the most abundant fullness of time had not yet come, and the heavenly bread had not filled the mangers of the simple and the humble! Wisdom marks out such a man, wicked and grudging toward himself, ungrateful and offensive toward God, when it says: 'An evil eye is bent toward evil deeds, and he shall not be satisfied with bread; he shall be needy and sorrowful at his own table.' 'Therefore,' it says, 'his soul shall not be filled with good things, because his eye is bent toward evil things, nor will his eye turn back to see good things,' so that he might with devotion and faith consider what has been set before him at the great table of the rich host. 'For wicked,' it says, 'is the eye of the envious man, turning away his face and despising his own soul' (Eccli. XIV, 10, 8). Without doubt, brothers, if we do not turn our face away from gazing on him who lies in the manger, by that very gaze we can be most happily fed, and we shall say: 'The Lord feeds me, and I shall want nothing; in a place of pasture, there he has set me' (Psal. XXII, 1, 2). Then we shall clearly know that the most longed-for fullness of time has come, in which God sent his Son, through whom we are now filled with so great a fullness of good things: to him be blessing and thanksgiving, both now and through the endless ages of ages.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition prints the reference as Galat. VI, 1-9; the passage on the heir under tutors and the fullness of time is Galatians 4:1-9. The printed reference is kept.

sermons.title: Nativity Sermon IV: On the Fullness of Time Brought by Christ
