passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: This fifth Nativity sermon belongs to Guerric of Igny's medieval collection of sermons for the liturgical year, here read from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. Its individual date is unknown; the collection is associated approximately with his abbacy in 1138–1157. The brothers came to hear the Word of God, but at Bethlehem they may also see it. Guerric draws lessons from the infant Word's silence, poverty and humility, and from the shepherds' simple faith. He ends at the altar, where the same body lies hidden under humble forms as the infant was wrapped in cloths. The heading names the Nativity without a particular Christmas Mass.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO V.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON V.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De mira Dei providentia in nativitate Christi.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On God's Wonderful Providence in the Birth of Christ

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Convenistis, fratres, ad audiendum verbum Dei. Deus autem aliquid melius providit nobis, ut non solum audire, sed etiam videre datum nobis hodie sit Verbum Dei, si modo transeamus usque Bethlehem, et videamus hoc verbum quod fecit Dominus, et ostendit nobis (Luc. II, 15). Noverat hominum sensus invisibilium incapaces, coelestium indocibiles, ad fidem quoque difficiles, nisi res ipsa de qua fides suadetur, visibiliter ipsis sensibus convincendis ingeratur. Nam etsi fides est ex auditu, multo tamen proclivius ac promptius ex visu: sicut illius exemplo docemur, cui dicitur, Quia vidisti me, credidisti (Joan. XX, 29); qui scilicet dum audiebas incredulus fuisti. Quia enim difficilius audita, quam visa creduntur, ideo merito fides illorum qui non viderunt, a Domino beata praedicatur; quippe qui plus detulerint auctoritati sermonis, quam experientiae proprii sensus, aut rationis. Deus tamen per omnia volens satisfacere tarditati nostrae, Verbum suum quod prius fecerat audibile, hodie fecit nobis etiam visibile, imo et tractabile; ut et quidam ex nobis potuerint dicere: Quod fuit ab initio, quod audivimus, quod vidimus oculis nostris, quod perspeximus, et manus nostrae tractaverunt de Verbo vitae (Joan. I, 1). Fuit ab initio illius, quae sine initio est, aeternitatis; audivimus promissum ab initio temporis; vidimus et contrectavimus exhibitum in fine temporis. Alias autem invenies quod non solum visibile et tractabile, sed etiam gustabile et odorabile nobis Verbum Dei factum sit, quippe quod per omnes vias sensuum, aditum sibi ad animam quaesierit, quatenus sicut per sensus mors intraverat, sic per eosdem rediret et vita. Quod ergo Verbum caro factum est (Joan. I, 14), nobis qui toti sumus caro, factum est; ut qui antea Verbum Dei tantum poteramus audire, jam carnem factum et videre possimus et gustare, omnesque sensus in testimonium auditus convocare; quatenus omnes nostri sensus consensu uno, et voce una confiteantur, Sicut audivimus, sic vidimus (Psal. XLVII, 9). Incomparabiliter tamen amplius tunc concessum est visui, quam unquam fuerat auditui, cum modo videatur Verbum, quod Deus est, et antea magnum haberetur audire verbum quodcunque ex Deo. Et verbum quidem quod ex Deo est, vidi aliquando, fratres, cum taedio audiri; sed Verbum quod Deus est, nunquid poterit nisi cum gaudio videri? In me primum sententiam feram: quia Verbum, quod Deus est, cum se hodie mihi videndum praebeat in eo quod sum, si me non laetificat, impius sum; si non aedificat, reprobus sum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. You have come together, brothers, to hear the word of God. But God has provided something better for us, so that today it is given to us not only to hear but also to see the Word of God — if only we go over as far as Bethlehem, and see this word which the Lord has made, and shown to us (Luc. II, 15). He knew that the senses of men are incapable of invisible things, unteachable in heavenly things, and also slow to believe, unless the very thing of which faith is being persuaded is impressed visibly upon the senses themselves so as to convince them. For although faith is from hearing, yet it comes much more readily and easily from sight: as we are taught by the example of him to whom it was said, "Because you have seen me, you have believed" (Joan. XX, 29) — that is, you who, while you were only hearing, were unbelieving. For since things heard are believed with more difficulty than things seen, therefore the faith of those who have not seen is rightly proclaimed blessed by the Lord; since they gave more credit to the authority of the word than to the experience of their own sense or reason. Yet God, wishing in every way to satisfy our slowness, has today made for us even visible — indeed even touchable — his Word, which before he had made only audible; so that some of us have even been able to say: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life" (Joan. I, 1). He was from the beginning of that eternity which has no beginning; we heard him promised from the beginning of time; we saw and touched him shown forth at the end of time. Elsewhere, too, you will find that the Word of God was made for us not only visible and touchable, but even tastable and smellable, since through every avenue of the senses it sought an entrance to the soul, so that just as death had entered through the senses, so also life might return through the same senses. Therefore that "the Word was made flesh" (Joan. I, 14) was done for us, who are wholly flesh; so that we, who before could only hear the Word of God, might now both see and taste it made flesh, and might summon all our senses as witness to our hearing; so that all our senses, with one consent and one voice, might confess, "As we have heard, so have we seen" (Psal. XLVII, 9). Yet incomparably more was then granted to sight than had ever been granted to hearing, since now the Word which is God is seen, whereas before it was reckoned a great thing merely to hear any word whatsoever from God. And indeed, brothers, I have sometimes seen a word which is from God heard with weariness; but can the Word which is God possibly be seen except with joy? Let me pass judgment first upon myself: since the Word, which is God, offers itself today to be seen by me in that which I am — if it does not make me glad, I am impious; if it does not build me up, I am reprobate.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Si quis ergo, fratres, acediosus invenitur inter nos, nolo diutius ut fatigentur aures ejus sermone nostro contemptibili; transeat usque Bethlehem, et illud in quod desiderant Angeli prospicere, prospiciat ibi, Verbum scilicet Dei, quod Dominus ostendit nobis; imaginetur animo, Sermo Dei vivus et efficax qualis ibi jaceat [ al. qualiter ibi taceat] in praesepi. Si tantum pietas oculum illuminet intuentis, quid tam delectabiliter potest videri, tam salubriter cogitari? Quid aeque mores aedificat, spem roborat, charitatem inflammat? Omnino fidelis sermo, et omni acceptione dignus, omnipotens Sermo tuus, Domine; qui tam alto silentio a regalibus Patris sedibus animalium illapsus praesepibus (Sap. XVIII, 15), melius interim suo nobis silentio sermocinatur. Qui habet aures audiendi, audiat quid nobis hoc pium et mysticum aeterni Verbi loquatur silentium; quoniam, nisi me fallit auditus, inter alia quae loquitur, loquitur pacem in plebem sanctorum, quibus reverentia ipsius et exemplum religiosum imposuit silentium, et rectissime quidem imposuit. Quid enim tanto pondere, tantaque auctoritate disciplinam commendat silentii, quid tanto terrore compescit inquietum malum linguarum procellasque verborum, sicut Sermo Dei silens in medio hominum? Non est sermo in lingua mea, confiteri videtur omnipotens Sermo, dum Matri subditus est; et nos qua dementia dicemus, Linguam nostram magnificabimus, labia nostra a nobis sunt; quis noster Dominus est? (Psal. XI, 5.) Liberet mihi, si liceret, obmutescere et humiliari, et silere etiam a bonis, ut attentius et diligentius aurem possem adhibere vocibus arcanis, sacrisque sensibus hujus divini silentii, et vel tanto tempore sub silentio discere in schola Verbi, quanto Verbum ipsum sub disciplina siluit Matris.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. If then, brothers, anyone among us is found weighed down with listlessness, I do not wish his ears to be wearied any longer by our contemptible discourse; let him go over to Bethlehem, and there look upon that into which the angels desire to look, namely the Word of God, which the Lord has shown us; let him picture in his mind how the living and effective Word of God lies there [alternate reading: how it keeps silence there] in the manger. If only piety would illumine the eye of the one beholding, what could be seen so delightfully, thought upon so wholesomely? What equally builds up conduct, strengthens hope, inflames love? Altogether faithful is the saying, and worthy of all acceptance — your almighty Word, O Lord; who, gliding down in so deep a silence from the Father's royal throne into the mangers of animals (Sap. XVIII, 15), meanwhile speaks to us the better by his very silence. Let him who has ears to hear, hear what this pious and mystical silence of the eternal Word speaks to us; for, unless my hearing deceives me, among the other things it speaks, it speaks peace to the people of the saints, upon whom reverence for it and its devout example have imposed silence — and most rightly has it imposed it. For what commends the discipline of silence with such weight and such authority, what restrains with such terror the restless evil of tongues and the storms of words, as the Word of God, silent in the midst of men? "There is no word in my tongue" — the almighty Word seems to confess this, while he is subject to his Mother; and with what madness shall we say, "We will magnify our tongue, our lips are our own; who is our Lord?" (Psal. XI, 5.). It would please me, if it were permitted, to become mute and be humbled, and to keep silence even from good things, so that I might the more attentively and diligently apply my ear to the secret voices and the sacred meanings of this divine silence, and might learn in silence in the school of the Word for at least as long a time as the Word himself kept silence under the discipline of his Mother.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. O fratres, si pie ac diligenter intendamus huic Verbo quod Dominus fecit hodie, et ostendit nobis, quanta, quamque facile possemus ab ipso perdoceri? Verbum siquidem breviatum est, ita tamen ut in eo consummatum sit omne verbum quod ad salutem est, quia nimirum verbum consummans et abbrevians in aequitate ipsum est. Et haec consummatio abbreviata inundavit justitiam (Isa. X, 23), sicut promissum meministis per Isaiam; quia de sua plenitudine in participes suos redundavit justitiam, ut abundet justitia ipsorum, plus quam et Pharisaeorum et Scribarum; licet illi per tam multiplices se exercitent justificationes legis, isti autem brevi ac simplici contenti sint verbo fidei. Sed quid mirum si omnia verba sua nobis Verbum Dei breviavit, quando et se ipsum breviari, et quodammodo minui voluit, adeo ut de incomprehensibili immensitate sui ad augustias uteri quodammodo se contraxerit, et, continens mundum, in praesepi se passum sit contineri? In coelo Verbum istud horribili altitudine sua virtutes angelicas stupefacit: in praesepi simplices et hebetes pascit: ibi subtilissimis Angelorum intellectibus inscrutabile, hic etiam obtusis hominum sensibus palpabile. Quia enim Deus non poterat loqui nobis quasi spiritualibus, sed quasi carnalibus, Verbum ejus factum est caro, ut non solum audire, sed et videre posset omnis caro quod os Domini locutum est. Et quia in sapientia sua non cognovit mundus sapientiam Dei, dignatione ineffabili eadem Sapientia Dei se stultitiam fecit, ut quamlibet idiotis vel hebetibus se discibilem praeberet, et per stultitiam praedicationis salvos faceret credentes. Confiteor tibi, Pater, Domine coeli et terrae, quia sapientiam tuam abscondisti a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revelasti eam parvulis. Ita, Pater, sic fuit placitum ante te (Matth. XI, 25, 26), ut parvulis daretur parvulus qui natus est nobis, quandoquidem altitudo superborum nimis abhorret ab hujus humilitate parvuli, et quod altum est apud homines, abominabile est apud Deum, qui, cum veraciter altus sit, parvulus factus est pro nobis. Cum solis nimirum parvulis concordat iste parvulus, in solis requiescit humilibus et quietis. Sicut igitur parvuli gloriantes de eo, cantant, Parvulus natus est nobis (Isa. IX, 6), sic et ipse gloriatur de eis: Ecce ego, inquiens, et pueri mei, quos mihi donavit Dominus (Id. V, 18). Ut enim parvulo Filio suo Pater sodales daret de coaetaneis suis, statim primo omnium ab innocentia parvulorum coepit gloria martyrii; hoc significante Spiritu sancto, quia nonnisi talium esset regnum coelorum (Matth. XIX, 14).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. O brothers, if we attend to this Word which the Lord has made today, and shown to us, piously and diligently, how much—and how easily—might we be thoroughly taught by it? For indeed the Word has been shortened, yet in such a way that in it every word that pertains to salvation is fulfilled, because it is indeed the word that completes and cuts short in equity. And this shortened completion has overflowed with righteousness (Isa. X, 23), as you recall was promised through Isaiah; for from his own fullness he has poured forth righteousness upon those who share in him, so that their righteousness abounds more than that of the Pharisees and Scribes—though those exercise themselves through so many manifold justifications of the law, while these are content with the brief and simple word of faith. But what wonder is it if the Word of God has shortened all his words for us, when he himself willed to be shortened, and in a certain manner diminished, so much so that from the incomprehensible immensity of himself he contracted himself, as it were, to the narrow confines of a womb, and he who contains the world suffered himself to be contained in a manger? In heaven this Word, by its awesome height, strikes the angelic powers with astonishment; in the manger it feeds the simple and the dull: there inscrutable even to the most subtle intellects of the Angels, here even palpable to the dull senses of men. For since God could not speak to us as to spiritual beings, but as to carnal ones, his Word was made flesh, so that all flesh might not only hear, but also see, what the mouth of the Lord has spoken. And because the world, in its own wisdom, did not know the wisdom of God, by ineffable condescension this same Wisdom of God made itself foolishness, so that it might offer itself as teachable even to the unlearned and the dull, and through the foolishness of preaching might save those who believe. I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden your wisdom from the wise and prudent, and have revealed it to little ones. Thus, Father, so it was pleasing before you (Matth. XI, 25, 26), that the little one who was born for us should be given to little ones, since the haughtiness of the proud shrinks utterly from the humility of this little one, and what is high among men is abominable before God, who, though he is truly high, was made a little one for us. For this little one agrees indeed only with little ones; he rests only in the humble and the quiet. Therefore, just as little ones, glorying in him, sing, 'A little one is born to us' (Isa. IX, 6), so also he himself glories in them, saying, 'Behold, I and my children, whom the Lord has given me' (Id. V, 18). For in order that the Father might give companions to his little Son from among his own contemporaries, the glory of martyrdom began first of all from the innocence of little children; the Holy Spirit signifying by this that the kingdom of heaven belongs only to such as these (Matth. XIX, 14).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Si tales effici volumus, fratres, iterum atque iterum transeamus usque Bethlehem, et diligentius intueamur hoc Verbum quod caro factum est per Deum immensum, qui parvulus factus est, ut in hoc visibili et breviato Verbo discamus sapientiam Dei, quae tota humilitas facta est. In hanc quippe virtutem illa omnimoda virtus se interim totam contulit. Nihil aliud illa summa Sapientia interim scire voluit, nisi illam scilicet humilitatem, cujus se postmodum magistrum voluit profiteri. Et iste quidem, quod nimirum in suggillationem mei ipsius loquor, iste, inquam, digne et juste magister docendae humilitatis effectus est; qui, licet eam sibi non ignoraret et originalem a Matre, et naturalem a Patre, nihilominus tamen ab ipso Matris utero didicit eam ex his quae passus est. In diversorio viatorum natus est, ut hospites et peregrinos super terram, ipsius exemplo edocti, nos esse confiteremur. Ibi quoque novissimum eligens locum, in praesepio positus est, ut et nos illud Davidicum: Elegi abjectus esse in domo Dei, magis quam habitare in tabernaculis peccatorum (Psal. LXXXIII, 11), opere disceremus. Pannis involutus est, ut habentes tantum quibus tegamur, his contenti simus; per omnia paupertate materna contentus, Matrique per omnia subditus, ut totius religionis forma jam in ejus nativitate nata videretur. Beata sane simplicium fides pastorum, quae, cum invenisset infantem pannis involutum, nequaquam in illis scandalizata est ad incredulitatem, ut minora de eo sentiret, sed aedificata potius ad pietatem, ut tantae dignationi gratior fieret! Quanto namque se pro ipsis profundius humiliatam ac funditus exinanitam illa exhibuit majestas, tanto facilius et plenius, si digne de eis sentire volumus, totos eorum affectus sibi illius rapuit et vindicavit charitas.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. If we wish to become such as these, brothers, let us again and again go over to Bethlehem, and look more diligently upon this Word made flesh through the immense God, who became a little one, so that in this visible and shortened Word we may learn the wisdom of God, which has become wholly humility. For indeed that all-encompassing power has for the time being wholly given itself over to this one virtue. For the time being that highest Wisdom willed to know nothing else but that very humility, of which it afterward willed to profess itself the teacher. And he indeed—which I say to my own reproach—he, I say, became worthily and justly the teacher appointed to teach humility; who, although he was not ignorant of it, having it as original from his Mother and natural from his Father, nevertheless learned it even from his Mother's womb, from the things which he suffered. He was born in a wayfarers' inn, so that, taught by his example, we might confess ourselves to be guests and pilgrims upon the earth. There also, choosing the lowest place, he was laid in a manger, so that we too might learn by deed that word of David: 'I have chosen to be an outcast in the house of God, rather than to dwell in the tabernacles of sinners' (Psal. LXXXIII, 11). He was wrapped in swaddling clothes, so that we, having only enough to cover us, might be content with that; content in all things with his Mother's poverty, and subject to his Mother in all things, so that the whole pattern of religion might be seen to be already born in his very birth. Blessed indeed was the simple faith of the shepherds, which, when it found the infant wrapped in swaddling clothes, was by no means scandalized by them into unbelief, so as to think less of him, but was rather built up into piety, so as to become more pleasing to so great a condescension! For the more deeply that majesty showed itself humbled and utterly emptied out for their sake, the more easily and fully—if we wish to think worthily of them—did his love seize and claim for itself the whole of their affections.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Fratres, et vos invenietis hodie infantem pannis involutum, et positum in praesepio altaris; videte vilitas tegminis ne offendat aut turbet obtutum vestrae fidei, veritatem reverendi corporis sub aliis rerum formis intuentis. Sicut enim mater Maria quibusdam assumentis pannorum involvit infantem, sic mater gratia dispensatoriis speciebus rerum ejusdem sacri corporis nobis obtegit veritatem; sic etiam mater sapientia aenigmatibus et figuris arcanam divini Verbi contegit majestatem; quatenus et ibi simplicitas fidei, et hic exercitium studii, meritum sibi cumulet ad salutem. Nam ego, fratres, cum vobis veritatem, quae Christus est, verbis meis enuntio, quid aliud quam Christum pannis satis vilibus involvo? Beatus tamen, cui nec in pannis istis Christus est vilior, sicut nec merces pretiosae prudenti vilescunt propter veteres quibus amiciuntur sacculos. Christus plane est, quem vobis tradere cupio, qualibuscunque sermonibus nostris, ut, juxta sermonem Petri apostoli, sanctificetis eum in cordibus vestris (I Petr. III, 15.) Suscipite in mansuetudine insitum verbum, quod potest salvare animas vestras (Jacobi I, 21). Et verbum Christi abundanter habitet in vobis, amor scilicet et memoria Verbi incarnati, quatenus tam feliciter quam fideliter decantetis: Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis (Joan. I, 14). Tota igitur pietate cogitemus Christum in pannis, quibus Mater eum operuit, ut aeterna felicitate videamus gloriam et decorem quem ei Pater induit, gloriam quasi Unigeniti a Patre, cum quo et cum Spiritu sancto honor et gloria, per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Brothers, you too will find today an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes, and laid in the manger of the altar; see that the cheapness of the covering does not offend or disturb the gaze of your faith, which beholds the truth of that venerable body under other forms of things. For just as Mother Mary wrapped the infant in some scraps of cloth, so Mother Grace covers for us the truth of that same sacred body with outward forms of things appointed for the dispensation; and so too Mother Wisdom covers the hidden majesty of the divine Word with enigmas and figures; so that in the one case the simplicity of faith, and in the other the exercise of study, may each heap up its own merit unto salvation. For I, brothers, when with my words I announce to you the truth which is Christ, what else am I doing but wrapping Christ in rather cheap swaddling-cloths? Yet blessed is he to whom Christ is not thereby made cheaper, even in such cloths — just as precious wares do not become worthless in the eyes of a prudent man because of the old sacks in which they are wrapped. It is truly Christ whom I desire to hand over to you, by whatever kind of words of ours, so that, according to the saying of the apostle Peter, you may sanctify him in your hearts (I Petr. III, 15.). Receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls (Jacobi I, 21). And let the word of Christ dwell abundantly in you — that is, the love and remembrance of the incarnate Word — so that you may sing, as happily as faithfully: The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us (Joan. I, 14). Let us therefore, with all devotion, think upon Christ in the swaddling-clothes with which his Mother covered him, so that in eternal blessedness we may see the glory and beauty with which the Father has clothed him — the glory as it were of the Only-Begotten from the Father — with whom, and with the Holy Spirit, be honor and glory, through all ages of ages. Amen.

sermons.title: Nativity Sermon V: On God's Wonderful Providence in the Birth of Christ

sermons.author: Guerric of Igny
metadata: Guerric of Igny, Sermones per annum, Dominica in ramis palmarum, sermo I, Quomodo Christus omnia homini factus, in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier frères, 1879), cols. 127–130.
Internet Archive, 2011; PIMS, University of Toronto; University of Toronto funding.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric of Igny’s first Palm Sunday sermon presents Christ’s service as the remedy for human pride. Christ is imagined addressing the disobedient servant, offering to bear his burdens, feed him and redeem him; the meditation then turns to the Passion and a prayer for grace to imitate humility, patience and obedience in the common life. The collection belongs approximately to Guerric’s abbacy in 1138–1157, but no individual delivery date is established. This reading follows the 1879 Patrologia Latina edition. The source explicitly names Palm Sunday. Historical polemic is retained and identified in an editorial note.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: DOMINICA IN RAMIS PALMARUM.

passages.label: English
passages.text: PALM SUNDAY

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Quomodo Christus omnia homini factus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: How Christ Became All Things for Man

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Hoc sentite in vobis, quod et in Christo Jesu, qui, cum in forma Dei esset (Philipp. ii, 5, 6), etc. Audiat servus nequam et fugitivus, hominem dico, qui, cum esset in natura et conditione servili et necessitate serviendi, servire detrectans, arripere sibi conatus est libertatem et aequalitatem Domini sui. Christus cum in forma Dei esset, non rapina, sed natura aequalis, quia coomnipotens, coaeternus et consubstantialis, exinaniens semetipsum, non solum formam servi accepit, in similitudinem hominum factus; sed etiam ministerium servi implevit, humilians semetipsum, et obediens factus Patri usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis (Ibid. 8). Sed parum tibi videatur quod, cum esset Filius et coaequalis, tanquam servus servivit Patri, si non et servo suo plus quam servus servivit. Factus quidem erat homo, ut serviret Creatori. Et quid justius quam ut servias illi a quo creatus es, sine quo nec esse potes? et quid beatius aut sublimius quam servire illi cui servire regnare est? Non serviam, inquit homo Creatori. Ego igitur serviam tibi, inquit Creator, homini. Tu recumbe; ego ministrabo, ego tibi pedes lavabo. Tu quiesce; ego languores tuos feram, infirmitates portabo. Utere me, ut libet, in omni necessitate tua, non modo ut servo tuo, sed etiam ut jumento tuo, ut peculio tuo. Si fatigatus aut oneratus es, ego te et onus tuum feram, ut legem meam primus impleam. Alter, inquit, alterius onera portate, et sic adimplebitis legem Christi (Galat. vi, 2). Si esuris, aut sitis, et ad manum forte nihil melius habes, nec alter tibi vitulus aeque saginatus praesto est, ecce ego paratus immolari, ut carnes meas comedas, et sanguinem bibas. Nec verearis ex morte servi damna servitii ejus pati; etiam comestus et bibitus, manebo tibi integer et vivus, serviamque ut prius. Si in captivitatem ductus aut venumdatus es, ecce vende me, teque pretio mei, vel me ipso pretio redime. Vile quidem mancipium videor; sed etsi noctu et clanculo distrahar quasi res furtiva, etsi ab avarissimis Judaeorum sacerdotibus emar; attamen saltem triginta argenteos appretiari potero; hoc pretio mei poterit emi sepultura peregrinorum, me pretio vita sepultorum. Si infirmaris, et mori times, ego moriar pro te, ut de sanguine meo tibi conficias medicamenta vitae.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Have this mind in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God (Philipp. ii, 5, 6), etc. Let the wicked runaway servant hear this—I mean man, who, although by nature and condition a servant and under the necessity of serving, refused to serve and tried to seize for himself the freedom and equality of his Lord. Christ, being in the form of God, equal by nature rather than by robbery, because he is equally almighty, coeternal and consubstantial, emptied himself. He not only took the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, but also fulfilled a servant’s ministry, humbling himself and becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross (Ibid. 8). Yet think it little that, although the Son and coequal, he served the Father as a servant, unless he also served his own servant more than a servant would. Man had indeed been made to serve the Creator. What could be more just than to serve him by whom you were created, without whom you cannot even exist? And what could be happier or more exalted than to serve him whom to serve is to reign? “I will not serve,” man says to the Creator. “Then I will serve you,” the Creator says to man. “Recline at table; I will minister to you, I will wash your feet. Rest; I will bear your ailments and carry your infirmities. Use me as you please in every need, not only as your servant but also as your beast of burden, as your property. If you are tired or burdened, I will carry you and your burden, so that I may be the first to fulfil my own law. Bear one another’s burdens, he says, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ (Galat. vi, 2). If you are hungry or thirsty and happen to have nothing better at hand, and no other calf as well fattened for you is at hand, here I am, ready to be sacrificed, so that you may eat my flesh and drink my blood. Do not fear that the servant’s death will cost you his service: even when eaten and drunk, I shall remain whole and alive for you, and I shall serve as before. If you have been taken captive or sold, sell me, and redeem yourself with my price, or with myself as the price. I seem a worthless slave; yet even if I am sold by night and in secret as stolen property, even if I am bought by the most avaricious priests of the Jews, I can still be valued at least at thirty pieces of silver. With this price paid for me a burial place for strangers can be bought; with me as the price, life for the buried. If you are sick and afraid to die, I shall die for you, so that from my blood you may prepare medicines of life for yourself.”

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Euge, serve bone et fidelis, servisti revera, servisti in omni fide et veritate, servisti in omni patientia et longanimitate. Non tepide, qui exsultasti ut gigas ad currendam viam (Psal. xxiii, 6) obedientiae non ficte, qui etiam animam post tot et tantos labores superimpendisti; non murmurose, qui, innocens flagellatus, nec os aperuisti. Scriptum est, et justum est: Servus sciens voluntatem domini sui, et non faciens digna, plagis vapulabit multis (Luc. xii, 47, 48). Sed iste servus, obsecro, quid non dignum fecit? quid debuit facere et non fecit? Bene omnia fecit, clamant qui facta ejus observabant, et surdos fecit audire et mutos loqui (Marc. vii, 37). Omnia fecit digna, et quomodo sic omnia passus est indigna? Dorsum posuit ad flagella, plagis vapulavit non paucis nec parvis; indicio sunt sanguinis rivuli qui de tot partibus profluunt corporis. Contumelia et tormento interrogatus fuit, veluti servus aut latro subditus quaestioni, qua confessio extorqueatur criminis. O detestabilem superbiam hominis servire contemnentis, quae alio exemplo non poterat humiliari, nisi servitute et tali servitute Domini sui! et utinam vel sic possit! utinam vel nunc habeat et referat gratiam tantae humilitati ac bonitati! Sed, ut mihi videtur, adhuc audio eumdem Dominum apud Isaiam conquerentem de ingratitudine nequam servi, ubi scilicet ait: Non te servire feci in oblatione, nec laborem tibi praebui in thure. Verum tamen me servire fecisti in peccatis tuis, laborem praebuisti mihi in iniquitatibus tuis (Isai. xliii, 23, 24). Et quem laborem? Usque ad defatigationem, esuriem et sitim; sed usque ad sudorem, sudorem autem sanguinis decurrentis in terram (Luc. xxii, 44); sed usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis: ne omnia modo replicem, quod alapis caesus, sputis illitus, coronatus spinis, confixus clavis, lancea perforatus, aceto et felle potatus. Hoc torcular, inquit, calcavi solus, et de gentibus non est vir mecum (Isai. lxiii, 3). Vos ergo, qui statis tota die otiosi, attendite et videte si est labor sicut labor meus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Well done, good and faithful servant! You have truly served; you have served with all faithfulness and truth, with all patience and forbearance. Not lukewarmly, for you rejoiced like a giant to run the course (Psal. xxiii, 6) of obedience; not insincerely, for after so many and such great labours you spent your very life besides; not with murmuring, for, though innocent and scourged, you did not even open your mouth. It is written, and it is just: “The servant who knows his lord’s will and does not act worthily will be beaten with many blows” (Luc. xii, 47, 48). But this servant, I ask you, what did he do that was unworthy? What ought he to have done that he did not do? “He has done all things well,” cry those who observed his deeds, “and has made the deaf hear and the mute speak” (Marc. vii, 37). He did everything worthily; how, then, did he suffer all these unworthy things? He offered his back to the scourges; he was beaten with blows neither few nor small, as the streams of blood flowing from so many parts of his body bear witness. He was questioned with insult and torture, like a slave or robber subjected to torment to wring out a confession of crime. O detestable pride of man, who disdains to serve! No other example could humble it except the service, and such service, of his own Lord. If only even this could do so! If only even now he would feel and show gratitude for such humility and goodness! Yet I seem still to hear the same Lord complaining in Isaiah about the wicked servant’s ingratitude, where he says: “I did not make you serve me with offerings, nor impose labour on you with incense. Yet you have made me serve with your sins; you have imposed labour on me with your iniquities” (Isai. xliii, 23, 24). And what labour? To the point of exhaustion, hunger and thirst; even to sweat, sweat of blood running down to the ground (Luc. xxii, 44); even to death, death on a cross. I need not now recount everything: how he was struck with blows, smeared with spittle, crowned with thorns, fastened with nails, pierced with a lance, given vinegar and gall to drink. “This winepress,” he says, “I have trodden alone, and of the nations there is no man with me” (Isai. lxiii, 3). You, then, who stand idle all day, attend and see whether there is any labour like my labour.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Utique valde laborasti, Domine mi, in serviendo mihi; justum profecto et aequum esset ut saltem de caetero tu quiesceres, tuusque tibi servus vel ordine vicis suae, quia ad ipsum ventum est, serviret. Quam magno, Domine mi, inutile tibi meum redemisti servitium, qui nec ministeriis indiges Angelorum! Quam suavi et benigna arte pietatis recuperasti tibi et subdidisti contumacem servum, vincens in bono malum, humilitate confundens superbum, beneficiis obruens ingratum! Sic nimirum, sic sapientia vincit malitiam; sic carbones ignis congessisti super caput contumacis, quibus accenderetur ad poenitentiam. Vicisti ergo, Domine, vicisti rebellem: ecce do manus in vincula tua, jugoque tuo suppono cervicem. Dignare tantum ut tibi serviam, patere ut tibi laborem. Accipe me servum sempiternum, licet inutilem, nisi nunc quoque mecum sit et mecum laboret gratia tua, semper et praeveniens et subsequens. Praeveniat nos, prior ostendens humilitatis et patientiae exempla, subsequatur nos, adjuvans ut imitemur ostensa. Quam felices nos, o fratres mei, si super hoc audiamus consilium Apostoli: Hoc sentite, inquit, in vobis quod et in Christo Jesu (Philipp. ii, 5) praecessisse cognoscitis! hoc est, nullus extollatur supra se, sed magis humilietur infra se; qui major est, aliis serviat; si quis laeditur, prior satisfaciat; in commune usque ad mortem quisque obediat. His vestigiis, fratres, sequemur Christum in forma Dei, in qua vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. You have indeed laboured greatly, my Lord, in serving me. Surely it would be just and right that at least from now on you should rest, and that your servant should serve you, if only because his turn has now come. At what a price, my Lord, you have redeemed my service, useless to you who do not even need the ministries of angels! With what a gentle and kindly art of loving mercy you have won back and subjected your stubborn servant, overcoming evil with good, confounding the proud by humility, overwhelming the ungrateful with benefits! In this way, truly, wisdom conquers malice; in this way you have heaped coals of fire upon the stubborn man’s head, to kindle him to repentance. You have conquered, then, Lord; you have conquered the rebel. Here I offer my hands for your bonds and bow my neck beneath your yoke. Only deign to let me serve you; allow me to labour for you. Receive me as your servant for ever, though a useless one, unless even now your grace is with me and labours with me, always both going before and following after. May it go before us, first showing examples of humility and patience; may it follow us, helping us to imitate what has been shown. How happy we shall be, my brothers, if in this we heed the Apostle’s counsel: “Have this mind in you,” he says, “which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philipp. ii, 5), as you know it was in him before you. That is, let no one exalt himself above himself, but rather humble himself beneath himself; let the greater serve the others; if anyone is injured, let him be the first to make amends; let each obey in the common life unto death. In these footsteps, brothers, we shall follow Christ in the form of God, in which he lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The passage about the Jewish priests preserves the sermon’s historical anti-Jewish polemic. It is source rhetoric, not an editorial endorsement. The sacrifice, flesh, blood and continuing life imagery is retained in the translation.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition cites Psalm 23:6 for the running giant. The image is in Psalm 18:6 in historical Vulgate numbering (Psalm 19 in modern numbering). The following Luke 12:47–48 reference is also retained; the saying about many blows occurs in verse 47.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The sermon has three numbered sections; the final prayer continues within the third.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: “Going before and following after” describes grace that initiates and assists our imitation of Christ. Guerric asks the injured person—not the person causing injury—to be first to make amends.

sermons.title: Palm Sunday Sermon I: Christ Becomes All Things for Us

sermons.author: Guerric of Igny
metadata: Guerric of Igny (collection attribution), Sermones per annum, SERMO II., De crucis scientia et virtute., in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier frères, 1879), cols. 130-134.
Internet Archive, 2011; PIMS, University of Toronto; University of Toronto funding.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric preaches Christ crucified in the days of the Passion. He presents the cross as hidden strength that overcame the devil, and Christ's ascent of the cross as free, triumphant and fruitful for the redeemed. He warns those who bear the sign of the cross falsely and urges the brothers to crucify their vices through the fear of God and to persevere on the cross until evening. His argument includes polemic against Jews. The sermon appears under the Palm Sunday heading in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO II.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON II.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De crucis scientia et virtute.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the knowledge and power of the cross.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Paulus, doctor noster in fide et veritate, si hodie veniret ad nos, puto quia non judicaret se aliquid scire inter nos, nisi Jesum Christum, et hunc crucifixum (I Cor. II, 2). In his siquidem diebus in quibus anniversaria dominicae passionis et crucis memoria solemniter celebratur, nihil, ut arbitror, convenientius praedicatur, quam Jesus Christus, et hic crucifixus. Nam et aliis quibuslibet diebus quid unquam potest praedicari fidelius? quid audiri salubrius? quid cogitari fructuosius? Quid enim tam pium fidelium affectibus, tam medicinale moribus; quid sic interficit peccata, crucifigit vitia, virtutes nutrit et roborat, sicut crucifixi memoria? Loquatur ergo Paulus inter perfectos sapientiam in mysterio absconditam; mihi, cujus imperfectum vident etiam oculi hominum, loquatur Christum crucifixum, his quidem qui pereunt stultitiam, mihi autem et his qui salvi fiunt, plane Dei virtutem Deique sapientiam; mihi prorsus altissimam atque nobilissimam philosophiam, per quam infatuatam irrideo tam mundi quam carnis sapientiam. Quam perfectum me putarem, quam provectum in sapientia, si Crucifixi vel idoneus invenirer auditor, qui factus est nobis a Deo non solum sapientia, sed et justitia, et sanctificatio, et redemptio! (Id. I, 30.) Omnino si Christo confixus es cruci, sapiens es, justus es, sanctus es, liber es. An non sapiens, qui, cum Christo exaltatus a terra, sapit et quaerit quae sursum sunt? an non justus, in quo destructum est corpus peccati, ut ultra non serviat peccato? an non sanctus, qui semetipsum exhibuit hostiam vivam, sanctam, placentem Deo? an non vere liber, quem Filius liberavit, qui de libertate conscientiae illam liberam vocem Filii sibi assumere confidit: Venit princeps mundi hujus, et in me non habet quidquam? (Joan. XIV, 30.) Vere apud Crucifixum misericordia, et copiosa apud eum redemptio, qui sic redimit Israel ex omnibus iniquitatibus ejus, ut principis hujus mundi calumnias liber evadere mereatur.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Paul, our teacher in faith and truth, if he came to us today, I think he would judge that he knew nothing among us except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (I Cor. II, 2). Indeed, in these days in which the yearly memory of the Lord's passion and cross is solemnly celebrated, nothing, I think, is more fittingly preached than Jesus Christ, and him crucified. For on any other days as well, what can ever be preached more faithfully? What heard more wholesomely? What thought upon more fruitfully? For what is so pious for the affections of the faithful, so medicinal for morals; what so kills sins, crucifies vices, nourishes and strengthens virtues, as the memory of the Crucified One? Let Paul, then, speak wisdom hidden in mystery among the perfect; to me, whose imperfection even the eyes of men can see, let him speak of Christ crucified — to those indeed who perish, foolishness, but to me and to those who are being saved, plainly the power of God and the wisdom of God; to me indeed the loftiest and most noble philosophy, by which, having made foolish the wisdom of both world and flesh, I laugh it to scorn. How perfect I would think myself, how advanced in wisdom, if I were found a fit hearer of the Crucified, who was made for us by God not only wisdom, but also righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption! (Id. I, 30.) Altogether, if you have been nailed with Christ to the cross, you are wise, you are righteous, you are holy, you are free. Is he not wise who, lifted up from the earth with Christ, savors and seeks the things that are above? Is he not righteous in whom the body of sin has been destroyed, so that he no longer serves sin? Is he not holy who has presented himself a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God? Is he not truly free whom the Son has set free, who from the freedom of conscience dares to take up for himself that free utterance of the Son: The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me? (Joan. XIV, 30.) Truly with the Crucified is mercy, and with him abundant redemption, who so redeems Israel from all his iniquities that he deserves to escape free from the slanders of the prince of this world.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Sciat tamen, sciat quicunque est ille beatus et verus Israel, non esse hoc suae meritum perfectionis, sed divinae gratiam redemptionis; non scilicet quia peccatum non fecerit, nec inventus sit dolus in ore ejus, sed quia ille cujus haec laus propria est, Christus scilicet, purgavit peccata illius, qui per sanguinem crucis suae purgationem peccatorum faciens, ibi maxime triumphavit principatus et potestates, ubi abscondita erat fortitudo ejus. Erat abscondita, sed non perdita; quia crucifixus ex infirmitate, vivebat ex virtute Dei. Erat occulta, sed non erat otiosa; quia crucifixus veterem hominem in omnibus electis crucifigebat. Crucifigebat mundum Paulo, et Paulum mundo (Galat. VI, 14). Crucifigebat denique tyrannum hujus mundi, omnesque suae antiquae ministros tyrannidis. Hamum plane sub esca recondebat, qui sub infirmitate fortitudinem abscondebat. Ac perinde ille homicida ab initio sitiens humanum sanguinem, dum irruit in infirmitatem, incidit in virtutem: morsus dum momordit, confixus dum Crucifixum appetivit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Yet let him know, let whoever is that blessed and true Israel know, that this is not the merit of his own perfection, but the grace of divine redemption; not indeed because he has committed no sin, nor has guile been found in his mouth, but because he to whom this praise properly belongs, namely Christ, has purged his sins — he who, by making purgation of sins through the blood of his cross, triumphed over principalities and powers precisely there where his strength was hidden. It was hidden, but not lost; for, crucified out of weakness, he lived by the power of God. It was concealed, but not idle; for the Crucified One was crucifying the old man in all the elect. He was crucifying the world to Paul, and Paul to the world (Galat. VI, 14). He was crucifying, in short, the tyrant of this world, and all the ministers of his ancient tyranny. He was plainly hiding the hook beneath the bait, he who was hiding strength beneath weakness. And accordingly that murderer from the beginning, thirsting for human blood, while he rushed upon weakness, fell into power: biting, he was bitten; and while he sought to seize the Crucified, he was himself pierced.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Gratias cruci et clavis tuis, Domine Jesu: video perforatas fauces illius draconis, ut transeant liberati, qui etiam fuerant absorpti. Et qui fiduciam habebat quod influeret Jordanis in os ejus (Job. XL, 18), fluvium, quem absorbuerat, se non minima ex parte perdidisse frendens irascitur. De illis quippe faucibus nobis isti venerunt qui hodie nobiscum nobilem ac magnificum crucis decantant triumphum. Plane de ore leonis liberati sunt, imo de ventre inferi regressi sunt. Irascatur ergo, fremat et tabescat de cujus dentibus praeda erepta est: nam Christus gratulabitur quod non gratis crucifixus est. Lugeat infernus et mors; ille morsus, ista mortua: nam coeli laetantur, et exsultat Ecclesia, quod Christus infernum spoliat, mortemque triumphat. In conversione nempe istorum triumphum suae renovavit passionis, crucisque miracula suscitavit. In istis crux refloruit, hunc fructum pretiosum nunc etiam arbor vitae tulit. Quomodo namque maneret sterilis, quae non modo rigata, sed etiam vivifica facta est sanguine Salvatoris? jam non poenitebit eum quod in palmam ascendit, cum tantum tamque pretiosum de ea fructum collegerit. Hunc quippe fructum inter alios praevidebat, cum voluntarius ad crucem properabat. Dixi, inquit, ascendam in palmam, et apprehendam fructus ejus (Cantic. VII, 8). Paucis absolvit quod voluntate passus sit, quod passione exaltatus sit, quod non sine fructu nostro passus sit. In dicto siquidem proponentis, arbitrii libertas; in ascensu, triumphi sublimitas; in apprehensione fructuum, redemptionis monstratur utilitas. Vos, insensati Judaei, clamabatis quidem, Ascende, calve; ascende, calve (IV Reg. II, 23); sed ordinationi ejus liberrimae, qui sponte decreverat ascendere, non potuit furor vester nisi servire. Ascendit crucem voluntate, triumphavit in ea potestate, fructum ex ea collegit pietate. Uno igitur opere et Judaeum irrisit, et diabolum peremit, atque christianum redemit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Thanks be to your cross and your nails, Lord Jesus: I see the jaws of that dragon pierced through, so that they who had even been swallowed up might pass through, now set free. And he who had confidence that the Jordan would flow into his mouth (Job. XL, 18) now, gnashing his teeth, is enraged that he has lost no small part of the river he had swallowed. For from those jaws came to us these who today with us sing the noble and magnificent triumph of the cross. Plainly they have been freed from the mouth of the lion, indeed they have returned from the belly of hell. Let him then be enraged, let him gnash and waste away, from whose teeth the prey has been snatched away: for Christ will rejoice that he was not crucified in vain. Let hell and death mourn; the one bitten, the other dead: for the heavens rejoice, and the Church exults, that Christ despoils hell and triumphs over death. In the conversion of these, indeed, he has renewed the triumph of his passion, and raised up again the miracles of the cross. In these the cross has flowered again; this precious fruit the tree of life has borne even now. For how could it remain barren, which has been not only watered, but even made life-giving by the blood of the Savior? Now he will not regret that he climbed up into the palm tree, since he has gathered from it so great and so precious a fruit. For indeed he foresaw this fruit among others when, of his own will, he hastened to the cross. I said, he says, I will climb up into the palm tree, and I will take hold of its fruits (Cantic. VII, 8). In a few words he sums up that he suffered willingly, that he was exalted by his passion, that he did not suffer without fruit for us. For in the saying of one proposing, the freedom of will is shown; in the climbing, the sublimity of triumph; in the taking hold of the fruits, the usefulness of redemption is displayed. You, senseless Jews, cried out indeed, Go up, you baldhead; go up, you baldhead (IV Reg. II, 23); but your rage could do nothing but serve the most free ordinance of him who of his own accord had decreed to go up. He climbed the cross by his will, he triumphed on it by his power, he gathered fruit from it by his loving-kindness. By one and the same work, then, he mocked the Jew, destroyed the devil, and redeemed the Christian.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Dicant igitur qui redempti sunt a Domino, quos redemit de manu inimici, et de regionibus congregavit eos (Psal. CVI, 2); dicant, inquam, voce et mente magistri sui: Mihi autem absit gloriari, nisi in cruce Domini nostri Jesu Cristi (Galat. VI, 14)! in qua sapientia Dei nequam infatuavit consilium, justitia destruxit eum qui habebat mortis imperium, misericordia liberavit captivum. Merito prorsus, o sapiens gloriator, gloriaberis in cruce Domini tui, cujus liberatus es triumpho, vivificatus mysterio, justificatus exemplo, munitus signo. Sic enim justae rationis consequentia postulare videtur, ut exemplum Crucifixi ad justificationem suam imprimant moribus, qui signum crucis ad munimen sui imprimunt frontibus, et illius vivant lege, cujus armantur fide. Alioquin fallaciter miles characterem regis gestat, cujus praescriptum non observat; nec recte se tuetur illius signo, cujus non paret imperio. Vide autem quanta perversitas et abusio sit, ut inimici crucis Christi tueri se velint signo crucis Christi: dum securi sunt, luxuriantes contra pietatem crucis; cum in periculo deprehensi sunt, volentes esse defensi virtute crucis. Plane inimici crucis Christi sunt, amici ventris sui; quorum deus venter est, quorum idolum nummus est. Sciat tamen, sciat quicunque nunc fallaciter sibi Crucifixi signum usurpat; nequaquam se illo tueri poterit in illa necessitate suprema, quando jam non arbitrio hominum, sed judicio et ministerio Angelorum signabitur Thau super frontes virorum gementium et dolentium, ut discernantur salvandi a multitudine perditorum (Ezech. IX, 4-7).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Let those therefore say who have been redeemed by the Lord, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy, and gathered out of the regions (Psal. CVI, 2); let them say, I say, with the voice and mind of their teacher: But far be it from me to glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (Galat. VI, 14)! In which the wisdom of God made foolish the counsel of the wicked one, justice destroyed him who had the empire of death, mercy freed the captive. Most deservedly indeed, O wise boaster, will you glory in the cross of your Lord, by whose triumph you were set free, by whose mystery you were given life, by whose example you were justified, by whose sign you were fortified. For thus the sequence of right reason seems to require: that those who imprint the sign of the cross on their foreheads for their protection should also imprint the example of the Crucified on their character for their justification, and should live by the law of him by whose faith they are armed. Otherwise a soldier falsely bears the mark of a king whose decree he does not observe; nor does he rightly protect himself by the sign of him whose command he does not obey. But see what great perversity and abuse it is, that enemies of the cross of Christ should wish to protect themselves by the sign of the cross of Christ: while they are secure, living wantonly against the piety of the cross; when they are caught in danger, wishing to be defended by the power of the cross. Plainly they are enemies of the cross of Christ, friends of their own belly; whose god is the belly, whose idol is money. Let him know, however, let whoever now falsely usurps to himself the sign of the Crucified know this: he will by no means be able to protect himself by it in that supreme necessity, when no longer at the discretion of men, but by the judgment and ministry of Angels, the Thau will be marked upon the foreheads of men who groan and grieve, so that those to be saved may be distinguished from the multitude of the lost (Ezech. IX, 4-7).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Sed et Paulus, dux ille strenuus militiae christianae, fidelis signifer, qui stigmata Crucifixi in corpore suo portabat, nunc quoque in hac verorum ac falsorum militum confusione, signo utique notabili istos ab illis discern[e]bat, cum dicebat: Qui autem sunt Christi, carnem crucifixerunt cum vitiis et concupiscentiis (Galat. V, 24). Cauta prorsus et circumspecta definitio, ac velut formam referens de ipsius veritatis exemplari impresso. Nimirum quod impressum retinet vita, signantius exprimit lingua. Qui ergo Christo confixus erat cruci, de propriae conscientiae exemplari formam istam protulit: Qui Christi sunt, carnem crucifixerunt cum vitiis et concupiscentiis. Noverat vir multae scientiae et experientiae, multos esse aut fore qui crucifigerent concupiscentias carnis, et sinerent regnare vitia cordis; multos e contrario qui, fiducia pacati cordis, negligerent mortificationem corporis. Sed sicut nonnunquam divina justitia spiritum sibi non subditum, contumeliis carnis licet afflictae flagellat, sic plerumque corpus incrassatum recalcitrat, et nova bella spiritui jam quieto resuscitat. Eapropter vult Apostolus ut, crucifixis tam vitiis interioribus quam concupiscentiis exterioribus, mundemus nos ab omni inquinamento carnis et spiritus, perficientes sanctimoniam in timore Dei (II Cor. VII, 1). Timor nempe Dei, velut quidam clavi in altum defixi, cruci nos configit, et velut affixus justitiae continere nos facit, ut non exhibeamus membra nostra arma iniquitatis, sed justitiae; et, licet sit, non tamen regnet peccatum in nostro mortali corpore. Sane quod timor Dei comparetur configentibus clavis, sententia est David, qui ait: Confige, quasi a clavis, timore tuo carnes meas; a judiciis enim tuis timui (Psal. CXVIII, 120). Si ergo nondum praevales ut vitia exstinguas, in hoc vult te esse sollicitum Apostolus, ut crucifigas. Non ait: Qui Christi sunt, exstinxerunt vitia, quae virtus paucorum est; sed, crucifixerunt, sine quo salus nulla est, sicut, praeter crucem Christi, nulla redemptio est. Ideo namque Redemptor ad operandam et informandam salutem nostram hunc passionis modum elegit, ut redemptionis sacramentum, justificationis fieret exemplum; ut quomodo videlicet ipse similitudinem carnis peccati crucifixit, de peccato damnans peccatum, sic nos, imo multo magis nos, carnem peccatricem cruciemus, crucifigentes, etsi nondum exstinguentes in ea peccatum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. But Paul too, that vigorous leader of the Christian army, that faithful standard-bearer, who bore the marks of the Crucified in his own body, now also, in this confusion of true and false soldiers, distinguished the one from the other by a quite notable sign, when he said: But those who are Christ's have crucified the flesh with its vices and desires (Galat. V, 24). A truly cautious and circumspect definition, and one that, as it were, reproduces the form impressed from the very model of truth itself. For indeed, what life retains as impressed, the tongue expresses the more pointedly. He, then, who had been fastened with Christ to the cross, brought forth this form from the model of his own conscience: Those who are Christ's have crucified the flesh with its vices and desires. This man of great knowledge and experience knew that there are, or will be, many who crucify the desires of the flesh and yet allow the vices of the heart to reign; and many others, on the contrary, who, trusting in a heart at peace, neglect the mortification of the body. But just as divine justice sometimes scourges a spirit not subject to itself with the reproaches of the flesh, even though the flesh be already afflicted, so too the body, once fattened, often grows restive, and stirs up new wars against a spirit already at rest. For this reason the Apostle wishes that, with both the inner vices and the outer desires crucified, we should cleanse ourselves from all defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God (II Cor. VII, 1). For indeed the fear of God, like certain nails driven deep, fastens us to the cross, as though fixed to righteousness, makes us hold ourselves in check, so that we do not present our members as weapons of iniquity, but of righteousness; and, though sin be present, it does not reign in our mortal body. Indeed, that the fear of God should be compared to nails that fasten us is the saying of David, who says: Pierce my flesh, as with nails, with your fear; for I have feared your judgments (Psal. CXVIII, 120). If, then, you are not yet able to extinguish your vices, the Apostle wishes you to be anxious about this at least: that you crucify them. He does not say: Those who are Christ's have extinguished their vices — which is the virtue of few — but, have crucified them, without which there is no salvation, just as, apart from the cross of Christ, there is no redemption. For this is why the Redeemer chose this manner of suffering for working out and shaping our salvation: that the sacrament of redemption might become the pattern of justification; so that, just as he himself crucified the likeness of sinful flesh, for sin condemning sin, so we — indeed, all the more we — should torment our sinful flesh, crucifying it, even if we do not yet extinguish sin within it.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Hic recordari potes quia Moyses ad placandam iram Domini crucifixit principes Israelitarum (Num. XXV, 4-9); Josue autem, qui et Jesus, quinque reges Amorrhaeorum (Josue X, 26). Si enim iram Domini, quam meruimus, placare volumus, necesse est ut per continentiam nos cruciemus. Jesus autem noster, qui nos in terram promissionis introducturus est, vitia quinque sensuum in nobis crucifiget, imo et exstinguet; si tamen, sicut est justum, pendeamus in patibulis usque ad vesperum. Hujus enim perseverantiae in cruce Salvator de se ipso tibi curavit exemplum praebere, nolens consummari nisi in cruce, aut deponi de cruce ante vesperum tam diei ipsius quam vitae suae. Balaam dicebat, Moriatur anima mea morte justorum (Num. XXIII, 10); tu vero dic, Moriatur anima mea morte Domini mei Jesu Christi, et fiant novissima mea illius similia; ut videlicet in voluntaria cruce poenitentiae pendere merear usque ad terminum vitae. Quanta fiducia de cruce Filii, in manus Patris spiritum commendabis! imo quanta clementia Pater suscipiet quem Filius commendabit (8)! Filius namque qui causam animae tuae semel in cruce suscepit agendam, nunquam eam agere desinit, apud Patrem semper interpellans. Vade securus, vade gratulabundus, ubi judex tuus est advocatus tuus; tantummodo signum crucis, mortificationem Jesu, quam circumfers in corpore tuo, secum deferat spiritus tuus. Dominus autem gloriae, qui pro vobis, fratres, passus, in vobis est glorificatus, dignetur vos habere socios passionis et gloriae, et gloriantes in cruce glorificet in ea claritate quam habuit apud Patrem ante initium saeculorum, et habiturus est per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Here you may recall that Moses, to appease the wrath of the Lord, crucified the princes of the Israelites (Num. XXV, 4-9); and Joshua—who is also called Jesus—crucified the five kings of the Amorites (Josue X, 26). For if we wish to appease the wrath of the Lord, which we have deserved, it is necessary that we crucify ourselves through self-restraint. But our Jesus, who is to lead us into the land of promise, will crucify in us the vices of the five senses—indeed, will even extinguish them—provided only that, as is right, we hang upon the gibbets until evening. For of this perseverance on the cross the Savior took care to offer you an example in his own person, unwilling to be consummated except on the cross, or to be taken down from the cross before the evening both of that very day and of his life. Balaam said, 'Let my soul die the death of the righteous' (Num. XXIII, 10); but you should say, 'Let my soul die the death of my Lord Jesus Christ, and let my last end be like his'—that is, that I may merit to hang upon the voluntary cross of penance even to the end of life. With what confidence, from the cross of the Son, will you commend your spirit into the hands of the Father! Indeed, with what tenderness will the Father receive him whom the Son commends! (8) For the Son, who once on the cross undertook to plead the cause of your soul, never ceases to plead it, interceding always before the Father. Go in security, go rejoicing, where your judge is your advocate; only let your spirit carry with it the sign of the cross, the mortification of Jesus, which you bear about in your body. And may the Lord of glory, who suffered for you, brothers, and was glorified in you, deign to count you companions of his passion and his glory, and, as you glory in the cross, glorify you in that splendor which he had with the Father before the beginning of the ages, and which he will have through all ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: (8) Vide similia sup. serm. 1 de Adventu, circ. fin., item apud S. Bernard., serm. 3 pasch., n. 3 et 8.

passages.label: English
passages.text: (8) See similar passages above in Sermon 1 for Advent, near the end; likewise in St. Bernard, Sermon 3 for Easter, nn. 3 and 8.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric sets the procession and the Passion side by side: Christ honored as king and Christ condemned as a thief. He hears the Son's cry of abandonment and answers it with the future glory that the procession prefigured. Christ's meekness when honored and his zeal in cleansing the temple form a pattern for those in authority; his unchanged mind amid changed fortunes is set before the brothers. His argument includes polemic against Christ's Jewish opponents. The sermon appears under the Palm Sunday heading in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.
