passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De duplici specie qua Christus proponitur spectandus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the twofold appearance under which Christ is set before us to be beheld.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Desiderium animae nostrae, speciosum forma prae filiis hominum, hodierna dies alia et alia specie repraesentat filiis hominum: utraque quidem specie spectabilem, in utraque desiderabilem et amabilem, quia in utraque salvatorem hominum; licet in una sublimem, in altera humilem; in ista gloriosum, in illa aerumnosum; in ista venerabilem, in illa miserabilem: si tamen dici decet miserabilis, qui miseriam suscepit dignatione miserationis, ut de miseria sua misericordiam praestaret miseris; non ut qui sibi beatitudo est, misericordiam a miseris flagitaret. Ubi ergo miserandus videri voluit, ibi et amplius venerandus fuit. Sed sustinui, inquit, qui simul contristaretur, et non fuit; qui consolaretur, et non inveni (Psal. LXVIII, 21). Ita qui miseratione omnium miser ultro fieri voluit, apud nullum fere miserationem invenit. Sed ubi, inquies, spectatur hodie sublimis et gloriosus, ubi humilis et aerumnosus? Vide processionem; audi passionem. In his evidenter agnoscere poteris quod Isaias ait: Sicut obstupuerunt super eum multi, sic inglorius erit inter viros vultus ejus, et forma ejus inter filios hominum (Isai. LII, 14). Obstupuerunt multi de gloria quasi victoris triumphantis, cum Jerusalem ingrederetur; sed nihilominus paulo post vultus ejus inglorius et despectus, cum pateretur. Cum intrasset Jerosolymam, ait Matthaeus, commota est universa civitas, dicens: Quis est hic? (Matth. XXI, 10). Cum pateretur, confusio faciem ejus operuit, ut vere confiteatur: Exaltatus, humiliatus sum et confusus (Psal. LXXXVII, 16). Sane quod hic se confusum dicit, intelligendum est secundum hoc quod alibi dicit de facie corporis: Operuit confusio faciem meam (Psal. LXVIII, 8); quia non pepercerunt in faciem meam spuere, velare, percutere et illudere. Nam facies mentis quae semper et immobiliter habitabat cum vultu Dei, nec turbari poterat nec confundi. Dominus Deus, inquit, auxiliator meus; ideo non sum confusus; ideo posui faciem meam ut petram durissimam, et scio quoniam non confundar (Isai. L, 7). In te enim, Domine, speravi, non confundar in aeternum (Psal. XXX, 2). Confundantur potius illi, et non confundar ego; paveant, et non paveam ego (Jerem. XVII, 18).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. The desire of our soul, beautiful in form beyond the sons of men, today's feast presents to the sons of men under one appearance and another: in each appearance indeed worthy of beholding, in each desirable and lovable, because in each he is the Savior of men; although in one sublime, in the other humble; in this one glorious, in that one full of hardship; in this one venerable, in that one pitiable—if indeed it is fitting to call pitiable him who took on wretchedness by the condescension of his compassion, so that out of his own misery he might show mercy to the wretched; not as one who, being blessedness itself, should beg for mercy from the wretched. Therefore where he wished to appear pitiable, there he was all the more to be venerated. But I waited, he says, for one who would grieve with me, and there was none; for one who would console me, and I found none (Psal. LXVIII, 21). Thus he who willingly chose to become wretched out of compassion for all found compassion from almost no one. But where, you will ask, is he beheld today as sublime and glorious, and where as humble and full of hardship? Look at the procession; listen to the Passion. In these you will be able clearly to recognize what Isaiah says: As many were astonished at him, so his countenance shall be without glory among men, and his appearance among the sons of men (Isai. LII, 14). Many were astonished at the glory, as of a triumphant victor, when he entered Jerusalem; but nonetheless, a little afterward his countenance was without glory and despised, when he suffered. When he had entered Jerusalem, says Matthew, the whole city was stirred, saying: Who is this? (Matth. XXI, 10). When he suffered, confusion covered his face, so that he might truly confess: I was exalted, I have been humbled and confounded (Psal. LXXXVII, 16). Indeed, when he here says he was confounded, it must be understood according to what he says elsewhere about the face of his body: Confusion has covered my face (Psal. LXVIII, 8); because they did not spare to spit upon my face, to cover it, to strike it, and to mock it. For the face of his mind, which dwelt always and unchangeably with the countenance of God, could neither be disturbed nor confounded. The Lord God, he says, is my helper; therefore I am not confounded; therefore I have set my face like the hardest rock, and I know that I shall not be confounded (Isai. L, 7). For in thee, O Lord, have I hoped; let me never be confounded (Psal. XXX, 2). Let them rather be confounded, and let me not be confounded; let them fear, and let me not fear (Jerem. XVII, 18).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Si igitur, ut dicere coeperam, hodierna processio simul et passio considerentur, ibi plane videtur Jesus sublimis et gloriosus, hic humilis et aerumnosus. In processione namque cogitatur in honore regis; in passione spectatur in poena latronis. Ibi circumdant eum gloria et honor; hic non est ei species neque decor. Ibi gaudium hominum et gloria plebis; hic opprobrium hominum et abjectio plebis. Ibi acclamatur ei: Hosanna filio David, benedictus qui venit rex Israel (Matth. XXI, 9); hic inclamatur, reus mortis (Id. XXVI, 66); subsannaturque quod se fecerit regem Israel. Ibi cum ramis palmarum ei occurritur; hic alapis palmarum in faciem caeditur, et arundine percutitur caput. Ibi praeconiis sublimatur; hic saturatur opprobriis. Ibi certatim ei via sternitur vestimentis alienis; hic exuitur propriis. Ibi tanquam rex justus et salvator suscipitur in Jerusalem; hic tanquam reus et seductor damnatus ejicitur de Jerusalem. Ibi sedet in asino stipatus obsequiis; hic pendet in ligno crucis caesus flagellis, confossus plagis, et desertus a suis. Ecce plus quam Job hic, cui tam repente, tam vehementer omnia semel in contrarium Deus vertit. Sufferentiam Job audistis, finem Domini vidistis (Jacobi V, 11), ait Jacobus apostolus. Ac si diceret: Sufferentia Job fuit usque ad reditum substantiae; sufferentia Domini usque ad exitum vitae. Job quidem patienter damna sustinuit, sed mox in terra sua duplicia suscepit; Christus ut erat repletus miseriis, et inebriatus amaritudinibus, e mundo migravit. Itaque plus quam Job hic, qui de summa, ut putabatur, repente semelque dejectus felicitate, in extrema atque gravissima finem sortitus est calamitate. Et haec, inquit, passus sum absque iniquitate manus meae, cum haberem mundas ad Deum preces (Job XVI, 18), etiam pro crucifixoribus, ut eis ignosceret.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. If, then, as I began to say, today's procession and Passion are considered together, there Jesus is plainly seen as sublime and glorious, here as humble and full of hardship. For in the procession he is regarded with the honor of a king; in the Passion he is beheld with the punishment of a thief. There glory and honor surround him; here there is in him no comeliness nor beauty. There is the joy of men and the glory of the people; here the reproach of men and the outcast of the people. There he is acclaimed: Hosanna to the son of David, blessed is he who comes, the king of Israel (Matth. XXI, 9); here it is cried out against him that he is guilty of death (Id. XXVI, 66); and he is mocked for having made himself king of Israel. There he is met with branches of palms; here he is struck in the face with blows of the palm of the hand, and his head is beaten with a reed. There he is exalted with acclamations; here he is filled with reproaches. There the way is strewn before him eagerly with others' garments; here he is stripped of his own. There he is received into Jerusalem as a just king and savior; here he is cast out of Jerusalem as a condemned criminal and deceiver. There he sits upon an ass surrounded by homage; here he hangs on the wood of the cross, scourged with lashes, pierced through with wounds, and abandoned by his own. Behold, here is one greater than Job, for whom God so suddenly, so violently, turned all things at once into their opposite. You have heard of the patience of Job, you have seen the end of the Lord (Jacobi V, 11), says the apostle James. As if he said: The patience of Job lasted until the return of his possessions; the patience of the Lord lasted until the end of his life. Job indeed patiently bore his losses, but soon received double in his own land; Christ, filled as he was with miseries and made drunk with bitterness, departed from the world. Therefore here is one greater than Job, who, cast down suddenly and once for all, as it seemed, from the summit of happiness, met his end in the utmost and gravest calamity. And these things, he says, I have suffered without iniquity of my hand, since I had pure prayers to offer to God (Job XVI, 18), even on behalf of those who crucified me, that he might forgive them.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. An non igitur recte videbitur velut turbatus tanta tamque subita rerum mutatione Filius Patrem interpellare illa voce lacrymabili: Deus, Deus meus, utquid dereliquisti me? (Matth. XXVII, 46). Certe manus tuae fecerunt me! in voluntate tua deduxisti me, et paulo ante cum gloria suscepisti me; et sic repente praecipitas me? Elevans allisisti me, quasi super ventum ponens me, et elidens valde. Exaltatus, humiliatus sum et confusus; et eo confusus amplius, quo tunc exaltatus sublimius, et nunc humiliatus profundius; quantoque tunc altius elevatus, tanto nunc gravius allisus. Justum quidem est, o Pater, ut qui se exaltat humilietur, et elatio indigni digna dejectione puniatur; sed nunquid similiter justum erat ut, quem tu exaltaveras, ita confusibiliter humiliaretur, et gloriam quam humilitas meruerat, tanta sequeretur contumelia? Nunquid mihi, Pater, iratus fuisti, quod vel ad horam hic me passus sum honorari; et illud etiam perexiguum quod susceperam de bonis hujus mundi, exsolvendum erat ante mortem in poenis et contumeliis, ne postea mihi posset objici: Fili, suscepisti bona in vita tua? (Luc. XVI, 25). At qui tuus erat honor, o Pater, honor erat Filii; quia qui non honorificat Filium, non honorificat Patrem qui misit illum. Ecce exprobrant inimici tui, Domine, exprobrant commutationem Christi tui; ecce gloriantur in contumelia mea et tormento, qui paulo ante cruciabantur gloria et honore meo. Nunquid non respondebo exprobrantibus mihi verbum, ut sciant aliquando qua dispensatione commutaveris Christum tuum, quo consilio sic exaltaveris mox humiliandum, vel humiliaveris exaltatum?

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Will it not, then, rightly seem that the Son, as though troubled by so great and so sudden a change of circumstances, cries out to the Father with that tearful voice: "God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matth. XXVII, 46). Surely your hands made me! By your will you led me, and but a little while ago you received me with glory; and do you now so suddenly cast me down? Lifting me up, you have dashed me down, setting me as it were upon the wind, and shattering me exceedingly. Exalted, I have been humbled and confounded; and the more confounded, the more sublimely I was then exalted, and the more deeply I am now humbled; and the higher I was then lifted up, the more grievously am I now dashed down. It is indeed just, O Father, that whoever exalts himself should be humbled, and that the pride of the unworthy should be punished with a fitting downfall; but was it likewise just that he whom you had exalted should be so shamefully humbled, and that such great contempt should follow the glory which humility had merited? Were you, Father, angry with me, because I allowed myself to be honored here even for an hour; and was even that very small portion which I had received of the goods of this world to be paid back before death in sufferings and insults, lest afterward it might be objected to me: "Son, you received good things in your life" (Luc. XVI, 25)? But the honor that was yours, O Father, was the honor of the Son; for he who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him. Behold, your enemies, Lord, reproach—they reproach the changed state of your Christ; behold, they glory in my contempt and torment, who but a little while ago were tormented by my glory and honor. Shall I not then answer those who reproach me with a word, that they may know at last by what dispensation you have changed your Christ, by what counsel you have thus exalted one soon to be humbled, or humbled one who was exalted?

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Respondebis, o Domine Jesu, respondebis exprobrantibus tibi verbum, et verbum asperum, quando scilicet respondebit eis in facie arrogantia eorum, et arguet eos malitia eorum, videntes in quem transfixerunt. Cum enim videbunt Filium hominis venientem in nubibus cum potestate magna et majestate (Matth. XXIV, 30), tunc scient quod modo nolunt credere, quia illius posterioris gloriae, prior hodiernae processionis gloria, mysterium fuerit et figura; sicut passionis contumelia, meritum et causa. Tunc intelligent quia Christus nunc honoratus, nunc ludibrio habitus, his qui pereunt positus est in offensionem et ruinam, sicut his qui salvi fiunt, in resurrectionem et doctrinam; quia quod sacramentum est redemptionis, simul est etiam documentum aedificationis. Sic enim postulabant merita superborum, ut eorum superbiae et honor Christi fieret scandalum, et mors praecipitium; atque invidiam juste pereuntium gloria triumphantis excitaret, morientis poena damnaret. Caeterum his qui salvi fiunt, id est nobis, omnino erat necessarium ut Christus, transiens viam hujus mundi, sequentibus se viam sterneret, sicut per adversa, sic etiam per prospera; atque prius exaltatus, post humiliatus, suo traderet exemplo qualiter modestia servaretur in honore, patientia teneretur in contumelia vel dolore. Ipse siquidem honorari potuit, inflari non potuit; voluit despici, sed nescivit aut pusillanimitate dejici, aut ira morderi. Sicut enim alias cum vellent eum rapere et facere regem, ipse refugiens, et in solitudinem ad orandum aufugiens (Joan. VI, 15), docuit exemplo quod dixit et verbo, ne scilicet velimus in sublime tolli; sic modo quadam alia dispensatione sese ad horam honorari patiens, et nihilominus solitam, quia inolitam, mansuetudinem in honore retinens, formam dabat his qui in potestate sunt constituti. Qui tamen ut discerent ea discretione per humilitatem esse mansueti, ut, cum res postularet, per zelum essent erecti, Dominus statim in templum regressus, flagello facto de funiculis vindicat injurias Patris, magisque eligit furorem sacerdotum in necem suam provocare, quam templi profanationem dissimulare (Matth. XXI, 12, 13).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. You will answer, O Lord Jesus, you will answer those who reproach you with a word—and a harsh word—namely, when their own arrogance shall answer them to their face, and their own malice shall accuse them, as they see him whom they pierced. For when they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds with great power and majesty (Matth. XXIV, 30), then they will know what they now refuse to believe: that the earlier glory of today's procession was the mystery and figure of that later glory, just as the contempt of the Passion was its merit and cause. Then they will understand that Christ, now honored, now held up to mockery, has been set, for those who perish, as a stumbling block and a ruin, just as for those who are being saved he has been set for resurrection and instruction; because that which is a sacrament of redemption is at the same time also a lesson for edification. For thus the deserts of the proud demanded: that for their pride even the honor of Christ should become a scandal, and his death a stumbling-block to ruin; and that the glory of the triumphant one should arouse the envy of those who are justly perishing, while the punishment of the dying one should condemn that envy. But for those who are being saved, that is, for us, it was altogether necessary that Christ, passing along the way of this world, should pave the way for those who follow him, as much through adversity as through prosperity; and that, first exalted and afterward humbled, he should hand down by his own example how modesty is to be kept in honor, and patience held fast in contempt or sorrow. For he indeed could be honored, but could not be puffed up; he chose to be despised, but did not know how to be cast down by faintheartedness, or stung by anger. For just as on another occasion, when they wished to seize him and make him king, he fled, withdrawing into solitude to pray (Joan. VI, 15), teaching by example what he had also said in word—namely, that we should not desire to be raised to the heights—so now, by a certain other dispensation, allowing himself to be honored for an hour, and nevertheless retaining in that honor his accustomed meekness (accustomed, because ingrained), he gave a pattern to those who are set in positions of power. Yet, that they might learn to be meek through humility with such discretion that, when the matter demanded it, they should be roused through zeal, the Lord, returning at once into the temple, with a whip made of cords avenges the injuries done to his Father, and chooses rather to provoke the fury of the priests to his own death than to overlook the profanation of the temple (Matth. XXI, 12, 13).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Ut igitur, fratres, inoffenso pede tam per prospera, quam per adversa sequamur ducem nostrum, in processione consideremus eum in honore positum, in passione contumeliis et doloribus subditum; nunquam tamen in tanta mutatione rerum mente mutatum, etsi vultum immutaverit coram Abimelech, id est regno [al. rege] Judaeorum, quam commutationem Christi caecitas exprobrat perfidorum. De immutabili mentis illius statu dicit Scriptura: Homo sanctus in sapientia permanet sicut sol; nam stultus ut luna mutatur (Eccli. XXVII, 12). De mutatione faciei illius dicit alia Scriptura: Sapientia hominis lucet in vultu ejus, et potentissimus faciem illius immutabit (Eccle. VIII, 1). Prorsus in vultu tuo, Domine Jesu, qualitercunque videatur immutatus, sive gloriosus sive inglorius appareat, lucet sapientia, de vultu tuo candor lucis aeternae radiat; utinam super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine, effulgeat! Vultus tuus sicut in tristibus, sic in laetis sibi modestus, serenus, ac totus arcano lumine cordis floridus; justis hilaris et jucundus, poenitentibus clemens et pius. Intendite, fratres, in vultum serenissimi Regis. In hilaritate vultus regis vita, dicit Scriptura, et clementia ejus quasi imber serotinus (Prov. XVI, 15). Aspexit in Protoplastum, et mox animatus spiravit in vitam (Gen. I, 27); respexit Petrum, et mox compunctus respiravit ad veniam. Mox enim ut Dominus respexit Petrum, Petrus de clementia piissimi vultus suscepit imbrem serotinum, lacrymas post peccatum (Luc. XXII, 61, 62). Lux vultus tui, o lumen aeternum, teste Job, non cadit in terram (Job. XXV, 3). Quae enim communicatio luci ad tenebras (II Cor. VI, 14)? Animae potius fidelium radios illius excipiant, aspiretque bene consciis laetitiam, sauciis medicinam. Plane vultus triumphantis Jesu, qualis spectandus est in processione, laetitia et jubilus; vultus morientis, qualis cogitandus est in passione, medela et salus. Qui timent te, videbunt me, inquit, et laetabuntur (Psal. CXVIII, 74); qui dolent se, videbunt me, et sanabuntur, sicut aspicientes in serpentem ligno suspensum post venena serpentium. Te igitur, gaudium et salus omnium, seu videant sedentem in asino, seu pendentem in ligno, vota benedicant omnium; ut, cum viderint regnantem in throno, laudent in saecula saeculorum, cui laus et honor per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Therefore, brothers, so that we may follow our leader with unstumbling foot both through prosperity and through adversity, let us consider him in the procession set in honor, and in the passion subjected to insults and sorrows; yet never changed in mind amid so great a change of circumstances, even though he changed his countenance before Abimelech, that is, before the kingdom [or, in another reading, the king] of the Jews—a change in Christ which the blindness of the faithless throws back at him as a reproach. Concerning the unchangeable state of his mind, Scripture says: The holy man abides in wisdom like the sun; but the fool is changed like the moon (Eccli. XXVII, 12). Concerning the change of his countenance, another Scripture says: The wisdom of a man shines in his face, and the most powerful will change his countenance (Eccle. VIII, 1). Indeed, in your countenance, Lord Jesus, however it may seem changed, whether it appears glorious or inglorious, wisdom shines; from your countenance the brightness of eternal light radiates. Would that the light of your countenance might shine upon us, Lord! Your countenance, whether in sorrow or in joy, is modest in itself, serene, and altogether flourishing with the hidden light of the heart; to the just, cheerful and pleasant; to the penitent, merciful and kind. Attend, brothers, to the countenance of the most serene King. In the cheerfulness of the king's countenance is life, says Scripture, and his clemency is like the late rain (Prov. XVI, 15). He looked upon the first-formed man, and at once the man, given life, breathed into life (Gen. I, 27); he looked back upon Peter, and at once, struck with compunction, Peter breathed again unto pardon. For as soon as the Lord looked back upon Peter, Peter received from the clemency of that most merciful countenance the late rain, tears after sin (Luc. XXII, 61, 62). The light of your countenance, O eternal light, as Job bears witness, does not fall to the ground (Job. XXV, 3). For what fellowship has light with darkness (II Cor. VI, 14)? Rather let the souls of the faithful receive its rays, and let it breathe joy upon those of good conscience, and healing upon the wounded. Clearly the countenance of Jesus triumphant, such as is to be beheld in the procession, is joy and jubilation; the countenance of the dying one, such as is to be contemplated in the passion, is remedy and salvation. Those who fear you, he says, will see me and will rejoice (Psal. CXVIII, 74); those who grieve over themselves will see me and will be healed, just as those who looked upon the serpent raised up on wood were healed after the poison of serpents. You, therefore, joy and salvation of all—whether they see you seated upon the ass, or hanging upon the wood—let the prayers of all bless you; so that when they shall see you reigning upon the throne, they may praise you forever and ever, to whom be praise and honor through all ages of ages. Amen.

Psalm 12:1–2 (printed locator; quotation from Psalm 112:1–2, historical numbering)

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric hears the children's Hosanna as praise prompted by the Holy Spirit. The poverty of the king riding on an ass is the sign by which the humble recognize Christ, and he warns against a lukewarm response to grace. He contrasts the Church that received Christ with the Synagogue that rejected him, then invites the brothers to nest like doves in the clefts of the rock by meditating on Christ's wounds. His argument includes polemic against the Synagogue. The sermon appears under the Palm Sunday heading in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO IV.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON IV.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Qualiter Christus benedicendus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: How Christ Is to Be Blessed.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Hosanna filio David (Matth. XXI, 9). Vox exsultationis et salutis, vox gaudii et pietatis, vox fidei et amoris, adgratulans adventui Redemptoris, atque prophetico protestans gaudio desideratae laetitiam redemptionis. Hosanna filio David, ait haec familia David; salus est illi qui factus est ex semine David, ut salvet eos qui sunt ex fide David. Laudate, laudate, pueri, Dominum, laudate nomen Domini (Psal. XII, 1, 2); dicite: Sit nomen Domini benedictum (Job. I, 21), sit benedictus, qui venit in nomine Domini. Ex ore istorum perfecisti, o Pater, laudem Filii tui, ut incorrupto simplicis innocentiae testimonio destruas inimicum et ultorem (Psal. VIII, 3), pharisaeum et pontificem; non ultorem divinae legis, ut mentita est iniquitas sibi, sed invidiae propriae et furoris. Sed convertetur dolor ejus in caput ejus, et in verticem ipsius iniquitas ejus descendet (Psal. VII, 17). Deus laudem meam ne tacueris, ait Filius Patri; quia os peccatoris et os dolosi super me apertum est (Psal. CVIII, 2). Nihil potest negare Pater Filio; non tacuit laudem Filii vox paterna saepius audita de coelo, non tacuerunt creaturae, in tot signis et prodigiis confitentes eum auctorem naturae. Angeli testati sunt, daemones confessi sunt, ordo propheticus voce consona sibi invicem respondentes cecinerunt. Sed ista demum perfecta laus est, quam aetas illa non tacet, quae nescit adulari, et quod Spiritus suggerit, dissimulare non potest. Quid enim manifestius quam quod illa aetas a semetipsa, tam nova, tam insolita nec dicebat nec faciebat; sed Spiritus sanctus more suo per ora simplicium loquens, testimonium Filio perhibebat?

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Hosanna to the Son of David (Matth. XXI, 9). A voice of exultation and salvation, a voice of joy and devotion, a voice of faith and love, rejoicing at the coming of the Redeemer, and with prophetic gladness proclaiming the joy of the long-desired redemption. Hosanna to the Son of David, says this household of David; salvation belongs to him who was made of the seed of David, that he might save those who are of the faith of David. Praise, praise, O children, the Lord; praise the name of the Lord (Psal. XII, 1, 2); say: Blessed be the name of the Lord (Job. I, 21); blessed be he who comes in the name of the Lord. Out of the mouths of these, O Father, you have perfected the praise of your Son, that by the incorrupt testimony of simple innocence you might destroy the enemy and the avenger (Psal. VIII, 3) — the Pharisee and the high priest; not an avenger of the divine law, as iniquity falsely claims of itself, but an avenger of his own envy and fury. But his sorrow shall be turned back upon his own head, and his iniquity shall come down upon his own crown (Psal. VII, 17). O God, do not be silent concerning my praise, says the Son to the Father; for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful has been opened against me (Psal. CVIII, 2). The Father can deny nothing to the Son; the Father's voice, heard many times from heaven, did not keep silent the praise of the Son; the creatures did not keep silent, confessing him, in so many signs and wonders, to be the author of nature. The angels bore witness, the demons confessed, the order of the prophets sang in harmonious voice, answering one another. But this, after all, is the perfect praise, which that age does not keep silent — an age that does not know how to flatter, and cannot hide what the Spirit suggests. For what could be plainer than that that age, of itself, neither said nor did things so new, so unheard of; but the Holy Spirit, speaking in his own manner through the mouths of the simple, was bearing witness to the Son?

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Plane Spiritus sanctus conscius operum Christi, quid ille scilicet Christi pareret adventus, quid gaudii, quid salutis humano generi passio parturiret illius, praesaga in cordibus innocentium gaudia suscitabat, atque ad prophetandam mundo redemptionis laetitiam, simplicium sibi ministeria sensuum assumebat. Istos nempe Spiritus alloquebatur, vocans ea quae non sunt, tanquam ea quae sunt, cum per prophetam suum dicebat quae hodie per ipsum facta sunt, mandabat tunc, et nunc creata sunt. Exsulta, inquit, satis, filia Sion; jubila, filia Jerusalem: ecce Rex tuus veniet tibi justus et Salvator, ipse pauper et ascendens super asinum (Zach. IX, 9 et Matth. XXI, 5). Jam, inquit, exsulta satis, quae hactenus in tristitia fuisti; jam te satia, si tamen satiari potes, gaudio ineffabili, quod sic desiderium satiat ut amplius et felicius esurire faciat. Repleatur gaudio os tuum, et lingua tua exsultatione; cui si nec os nec lingua possunt sufficere, supereffundat jubilus quod non capit affectus. Jubila, inquit, filia Jerusalem. Beatus enim populus qui scit jubilationem (Psal. LXXXVIII, 16). Plane beatus populus qui scit et intelligit hodie sibi ineffabiliter gaudendum, quando ei Salvator advenit promissus et exspectatus ab initio saeculorum. Beatus populus qui tota alacritate devotionis hodie ei occurrit, corde simul et voce acclamans ei: Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini (Matth. XXI, 9). In hoc siquidem benedictus est a Patre Filius, ut qui benedixerit ei, benedictionibus repleatur, non una scilicet, sed pluribus; quia nimirum benedictio quam Domino quia feneratur, cum multiplici fenore redit in caput ejus. Vae genti peccatrici, semini nequam, filiis sceleratis! ad quos spectat illa Domini querela terribilis: Non feneravi, nec feneravit mihi quisquam; omnes maledicunt mihi, dicit Dominus (Jerem. XV, 10, 11). Judaicus populus hic erat, qui in ratione dati et accepti communicare contempsit Domino, nolens benedicere Benedictum Dei Patris, ut benediceretur ab eo; sed Samaritanum, daemoniacum vocans, insanis atque blasphemis Deum insectabatur maledictis (Joan. VIII, 48, 52, 53). Maledicent illi, inquit, et tu benedices (Psal. CVIII, 28); nam ab eis benedictio quam noluerunt, elongabitur ad gentes. Benedicite, gentes, Deum nostrum, quoniam qui prior feneravit vobis, praeveniens vos in benedictionibus dulcedinis, fenerantibus sibi multiplices restituet usuras in benedictionibus beatitudinis.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Clearly the Holy Spirit, aware of the works of Christ — of what the coming of Christ would bring forth, what joy, what salvation his passion would bring forth for the human race — was stirring up prophetic joys in the hearts of the innocent, and was taking to himself the service of simple senses in order to prophesy to the world the gladness of redemption. Indeed the Spirit was speaking to these, calling the things that are not as though they were, when through his prophet he spoke of what is today being accomplished through him; he commanded it then, and now it has been brought into being. Rejoice greatly, he says, O daughter of Sion; shout for joy, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, your King shall come to you, just and a Savior, himself poor and riding upon an ass (Zach. IX, 9 et Matth. XXI, 5). Now, he says, rejoice greatly, you who until now have been in sorrow; now sate yourself — if indeed you can be sated — with ineffable joy, which so satisfies desire that it makes it hunger more abundantly and more happily. Let your mouth be filled with joy, and your tongue with exultation; and if neither mouth nor tongue can suffice for this, let the shout of joy overflow with what feeling cannot contain. Shout for joy, he says, O daughter of Jerusalem. For blessed is the people that knows jubilation (Psal. LXXXVIII, 16). Truly blessed is the people that knows and understands that today it must rejoice ineffably, since the Savior has come to it, promised and awaited from the beginning of the ages. Blessed is the people that today, with the whole eagerness of devotion, goes out to meet him, acclaiming him with heart and voice together: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord (Matth. XXI, 9). For in this the Son is blessed by the Father, so that whoever blesses him may be filled with blessings — not one only, but many; because indeed the blessing that is lent to the Lord returns upon the lender's own head with manifold interest. Woe to the sinful nation, the wicked seed, the children of wickedness! It is to them that the Lord's terrible complaint applies: I have not lent, nor has anyone lent to me; all curse me, says the Lord (Jerem. XV, 10, 11). This was the Jewish people, who scorned to share with the Lord in the account of giving and receiving, refusing to bless the Blessed One of God the Father, so that they might be blessed by him; but instead, calling him a Samaritan and possessed by a demon, they pursued God with mad and blasphemous curses (Joan. VIII, 48, 52, 53). They will curse, he says, but you will bless (Psal. CVIII, 28); for from them the blessing which they refused will be carried far off to the nations. Bless, O nations, our God, for he who first lent to you, going before you in blessings of sweetness, will restore to those who lend to him manifold interest in blessings of beatitude.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Ego tamen vereor, fratres mei, ne forte haec tempora teporis et infidelitatis tangat illa querela Domini: Non feneravi, nec feneravit mihi quisquam (Jerem. XV, 10); quia videlicet gratia offertur, nec suscipitur; promittitur merces operi, et vix aliquis spe illius operatur. Dominus siquidem fenerat, cum talenta servis partiens, scientiam verbi vel gratiam cujuslibet muneris ad lucrum praerogat: Domino autem fenerat jucundus homo qui miseretur et commodat, dicente Scriptura: Feneratur Domino, qui misericordiam facit proximo (Prov. XIX, 17). Imo Domino feneratur quicunque spe divinae retributionis aliquid operatur, ut dicere possit: Scio cui credidi (II Tim. I, 12), scio qui dixit: Si quid erogaveris, cum rediero reddam tibi (Luc. X, 35). Nos autem aut nihil aut ita timide gelideque feneramus ei, quasi debitor infidelis sit, aut non habeat unde reddere possit. Magnae prorsus fidei illa plebs Hebraea, quae, cum eum pauperem sedentem super asellum, et ipsum non suum, cerneret, omni tamen securitate ac devotione fenerabat ei, non solum vestimenta sua in via sternens, sed et se totam, quantum poterat, honori ejus impendens. Sed nimirum intelligebat super egenum et pauperem; quippe cui propheta signum dederat intelligendi Salvatorem, ipsam qua superbis viluit, paupertatem. Ipse, inquit, pauper, et ascendens super asinum (Zach. IX, 9). Hoc, inquit, signo poteris venientem agnoscere Regem tuum, cujus regnum non est de hoc mundo, quia scilicet, ad debellandam superbiam quae regnat in mundo, paupertatem seu humilitatem evangelizabit sicut verbo sic etiam exemplo.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Yet I fear, my brothers, lest perhaps these times of lukewarmness and unbelief be touched by that complaint of the Lord: "I have not lent, nor has anyone lent to me" (Jerem. XV, 10); because, that is, grace is offered and not received, a reward is promised for the work, and scarcely anyone works in hope of it. For the Lord lends when, distributing talents to his servants, he grants beforehand knowledge of the word or the grace of any gift, for profit; but a man who is kind, who shows mercy and lends, lends to the Lord, as Scripture says: "He who shows mercy to his neighbor lends to the Lord" (Prov. XIX, 17). Indeed, whoever does anything in hope of divine repayment lends to the Lord, so that he can say: "I know whom I have believed" (II Tim. I, 12), "I know him who said: If you spend anything, when I return I will repay you" (Luc. X, 35). But we either lend nothing to him, or lend so timidly and coldly, as if he were an unfaithful debtor, or had nothing with which to repay. Truly great was the faith of that Hebrew people, who, although they saw him sitting poor upon a young ass, and not even his own, nevertheless lent to him with complete confidence and devotion, not only spreading their garments in the way, but spending their whole selves, as much as they could, in his honor. For they understood, no doubt, concerning the needy and the poor one; since the prophet had given them a sign by which to recognize the Savior—namely, that very poverty for which the proud held him cheap. "He himself," it says, "poor, and riding upon an ass" (Zach. IX, 9). By this sign, it says, you will be able to recognize your King as he comes, whose kingdom is not of this world, because, to overthrow the pride that reigns in the world, he would preach poverty or humility as much by example as by word.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Beata itaque filia Sion, quae humilitatem tanquam armaturam coelestem, tanquam insigne regium didicit venerari. Misera mater ejus infidelis illa Sion, quae cum humilem vidit, fastidivit, cum honoratum vidit, invidit. Beata, inquam, Ecclesia primitivorum, quae tam fideliter agnovit, tamque gratanter suscepit venientem in nomine Domini; infelix Synagoga perfidorum, quae, venturum in suo nomine parata suscipere, illius qui Patris gloriam quaerebat cruciabatur honore. Increpa, inquiunt, discipulos tuos; quasi scilicet aut illorum simplicitas posset adulari, aut ipsius puritas vanis posset laudibus delectari. Dico, inquit, vobis, quia si hi tacuerint, lapides clamabunt (Luc. XIX, 39, 40); quia Deus laudem meam non tacebit. Prorsus ita est: si tacuerint, lapides clamabunt; quia tempore passionis isti tacuerunt, sed lapides clamaverunt, dum in testimonium et laudem morientis, petrae scissae sunt, et monumenta aperta sunt (Matth. XXVII, 51, 52). Prorsus ita est, quia modo tacente Synagoga, juxta illud: Nocte tacere feci matrem tuam (Ose. IV, 5), clamat vivis ex lapidibus Gentium Ecclesia, clamant plane lapides, de quibus suscitavit filios Abrahae qui potens est. Laudate, inquit propheta, habitatores petrae, de vertice montium clamabunt (Isai. XLII, 11). Ecce hodie in foraminibus petrae, in cavernis maceriae vox columbae resonat, clamantis et dicentis: Hosanna filio David; benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini (Matth. XXI, 9).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Blessed, then, is the daughter of Sion, who has learned to venerate humility as a heavenly armor, as a royal insignia. Wretched is her unbelieving mother, that Sion, who, when she saw him humble, disdained him, and when she saw him honored, envied him. Blessed, I say, is the Church of the firstborn, which so faithfully recognized and so gratefully received him who came in the name of the Lord; unhappy is the Synagogue of the faithless, which, prepared to receive one coming in his own name, was tormented by the honor paid to him who sought the glory of the Father. "Rebuke," they say, "your disciples"—as though either their simplicity could flatter, or his purity could be delighted by empty praises. "I tell you," he says, "that if these are silent, the stones will cry out" (Luc. XIX, 39, 40); because God will not be silent about my praise. And indeed it is so: if they are silent, the stones will cry out; for at the time of the Passion these men were silent, but the stones cried out, when, in testimony and praise of the dying one, the rocks were split and the tombs were opened (Matth. XXVII, 51, 52). And indeed it is so, because now, while the Synagogue is silent—according to that word: "I have made your mother be silent at night" (Ose. IV, 5)—the Church of the Gentiles cries out from living stones; truly the stones cry out, from which he who is able raised up sons of Abraham. "Praise," says the prophet, "you inhabitants of the rock, they will cry out from the top of the mountains" (Isai. XLII, 11). Behold, today in the clefts of the rock, in the hollows of the wall, the voice of the dove resounds, crying out and saying: "Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord" (Matth. XXI, 9).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Benedictus qui, ut nidificare possem in foraminibus petrae, manus, pedes et latus perforari sibi tulit, et se mihi totum aperuit, ut ingrediar in locum tabernaculi admirabilis, et protegar in abscondito tabernaculi sui. Opportunum quidem petra refugium erinaciis, sed et habitatio grata columbis, cujus foramina tot vulneribus toto fere corpore patentia, et veniam offerunt reis, et gratiam conferunt justis. Imo vero tuta habitatio, fratres mei, turrisque fortitudinis a facie inimici, pia ac sedula meditatione Christi Domini vulneribus immorari, fideque et amore Crucifixi, animam ab aestu carnis, a turbine saeculi, ab impetu diaboli contutari. Super omnem gloriam mundi protectio hujus tabernaculi, videlicet in umbraculum diei ab aestu, in securitatem et absconsionem a turbine et a pluvia, ut per diem sol non urat te prosperitate, nec turbo moveat in tempestate. Ingredere igitur in petram, o homo, abscondere in fossa humo (Isai. II, 10), pone tibi latibulum in Crucifixo. Ipse petra, ipse humus, quia Deus et homo; ipse petra forata, humus fossa, quia foderunt manus meas, inquit, et pedes meos (Psal. XXI, 17). Abscondere, inquit, in fossa humo a facie timoris Domini (Isai. II, 10): hoc est, ab ipso fuge ad ipsum, a judice ad redemptorem, a tribunali ad crucem, a justo ad misericordem; ab eo qui percutiet terram virga oris sui, ad eum qui inebriat terram stillicidiis cruoris sui; ab eo qui spiritu labiorum suorum interficiet impium, ad eum qui sanguine vulnerum suorum vivificat exstinctum. Quinimo non ad ipsum tantum, sed in ipsum fuge, in foramina petrae ingredere, in fossa humo abscondere, in ipsis manibus foratis, in fosso latere te ipsum reconde. Vulnus enim in latere Christi, quid nisi ostium in latere Arcae salvandis a facie diluvii? Illud tamen figura, istud autem veritas, ubi non modo servatur vita mortalis, sed recuperatur immortalis. Ideo quippe latus suum pius et misericors aperuit, ut cruor te vulneris vivificet, calor corporis refocillet, spiritus cordis quasi patenti et libero meatu aspiret. Ibi tuto latebis, donec traneat iniquitas; ibi nequaquam algebis, eo quod in visceribus Christi non frigescat charitas; ibi deliciis afflues, ibi gaudiis superefflues; vel tunc demum cum a vita capitis tua et omnium membrorum corporis ejus absorpta fuerit mortalitas.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Blessed is he who, so that I might build a nest in the clefts of the rock, allowed his hands, feet, and side to be pierced, and opened himself wholly to me, that I might enter into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, and be sheltered in the hidden place of his tabernacle. The rock is indeed a fitting refuge for hedgehogs, but it is also a pleasing dwelling for doves, and its openings—laid open by so many wounds over almost the whole body—both offer pardon to the guilty and bestow grace upon the just. Indeed, my brothers, it is a safe dwelling, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy, to dwell with pious and diligent meditation upon the wounds of the Lord Christ, and by faith and love of the Crucified, to keep the soul safe from the heat of the flesh, from the whirlwind of the world, from the assault of the devil. Above all the glory of the world is the protection of this tabernacle, namely, a shelter by day from the heat, a security and hiding place from whirlwind and rain, so that the sun of prosperity may not burn you by day, nor the whirlwind disturb you in time of storm. Enter, therefore, into the rock, O man; hide yourself in the dug earth (Isai. II, 10); make for yourself a hiding place in the Crucified One. He himself is the rock, he himself the earth, because he is God and man; he himself is the pierced rock, the dug earth, for he says, "they have dug through my hands and my feet" (Psal. XXI, 17). "Hide yourself," he says, "in the dug earth from before the fear of the Lord" (Isai. II, 10): that is, flee from him to him, from the judge to the redeemer, from the tribunal to the cross, from the just one to the merciful one; from him who shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, to him who makes the earth drunk with the drippings of his blood; from him who shall slay the wicked with the breath of his lips, to him who gives life to the dead by the blood of his wounds. Nay, flee not only to him, but into him; enter into the clefts of the rock, hide yourself in the dug earth; conceal yourself in his very pierced hands, in his opened side. For what is the wound in the side of Christ but the door in the side of the Ark for those to be saved from the face of the flood? That, however, was a figure, but this is the truth, where not only is mortal life preserved, but immortal life is recovered. For this reason indeed the pious and merciful one opened his side, so that the blood of the wound might give you life, the warmth of the body might refresh you, and the breath of the heart might breathe upon you, as it were, through an open and free passage. There you will lie hidden in safety until iniquity passes away; there you will never grow cold, because love does not grow cold in the heart of Christ; there you will abound in delights, there you will overflow with joys—or rather, then at last, when your mortality, and that of all the members of his body, shall have been swallowed up by the life of the Head.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Merito itaque columba Christi, formosa Christi, cui ipsius vulnera tam tuta quam grata ad nidificandum paravere foramina, laudes ipsius utique hodie laetabunda decantat, ac de passionis memoria vel imitatione, de vulnerum meditatione, tanquam de foraminibus petrae vox suavis in auribus sponsi resonat. Caeterum vobis, fratres mei, qui tanto interius nidificastis in foraminibus petrae, quanto secretius vivitis in Christo, et vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo (Coloss. III, 3); vobis incumbit omnino ut quorum est conversatio quietior et tutior, sit etiam devotio dulcior; praesertim hodie, cum et recursus temporis et repraesentatio operis velut interesse nos facit illi gaudio solemni quo susceptus est in Jerusalem. Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini; ipsi benedictio, regnum et imperium, qui est super omnia Deus benedictus in saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Rightly, then, does the dove of Christ, the fair one of Christ—for whom his very wounds have prepared clefts as safe as they are pleasant for nesting—today joyfully sing forth his praises; and from the memory or imitation of the passion, from meditation on the wounds, as it were from the clefts of the rock, a sweet voice resounds in the ears of the Bridegroom. But as for you, my brothers, who have nested the more inwardly in the clefts of the rock the more secretly you live in Christ, and whose life is hidden with Christ in God (Coloss. III, 3): it falls upon you entirely that, since your way of life is quieter and safer, your devotion should also be sweeter—especially today, when both the return of the season and the re-enactment of the deed make us, as it were, present at that solemn joy with which he was received into Jerusalem. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; to him be blessing, kingdom, and dominion, who is over all things, God blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The quoted call to praise the name of the Lord comes from Psalm 112:1–2 in Vulgate numbering (113:1–2 in modern numbering); the edition prints Psal. XII, 1, 2.

sermons.title: Palm Sunday Sermon IV

Internet Archive, 2011; PIMS, University of Toronto; University of Toronto funding.

Hebrews 6:5 (printed locator; quotation includes 6:4, see note)
Psalm 101:5 (historical numbering; printed punctuation retained, see note)

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric of Igny presents the Father's gift of the Son for redemption and of the Holy Spirit for adoption as signs of divine generosity. He contrasts that generosity with human ingratitude, urging his hearers to hope for others' repentance while avoiding both despair about others and presumption about themselves. Fear made chaste by love guards spiritual joy. The Spirit's outpouring at Pentecost becomes an invitation to thirst for God's gifts; Guerric then warns against spiritual loss of appetite, slander and the passions that conflict with sharing Christ's table. The individual sermon is undated; its collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157 and is read here from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The historical heading names the feast of Pentecost, and Guerric recalls the Spirit given to the Apostles on this day.
