passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De Dei charitate et hominum ingratitudine.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On God's Charity and Human Ingratitude

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Ineffabilis Deus, ineffabilis misericordia ejus. Secundum nomen ejus, ita et opus ejus. Plane ineffabilis divinae circa nos dignatio charitatis. Parum erat Patri, tradidisse Filium, ut redimeret servum; nisi daret et Spiritum sanctum, quo servum adoptaret in Filium. Dedit filium in pretium redemptionis; dedit Spiritum in privilegium adoptationis: se denique totum servat haereditatem adoptatis. O Deum, si fas est dici, prodigum sui, prae desiderio hominis! An non prodigum, qui non solum sua, sed et se ipsum impendit, ut hominem recuperaret, non tam sibi, quam homini ipsi? an non prodigum, qui, sicut proprio Filio suo non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum (Rom. viii, 32), sic nec Spiritui sancto pepercit, ut ita loquar, sed nova et mira largitate super omnem carnem effudit illum? Multum quidem effusus sui prodigus ille filius, qui tam patrimonium, quam se ipsum donavit meretricibus; sed multo effusior pater in recuperationem perditi filii, quam ille in perditionem sui (Luc. v); si tamen ulla debet esse comparatio gratiae et pecuniae, spiritus et carnis, Dei et hominis: Vide enim quanta largitate toto orbe gratia Spiritus effusa sit, non solum justis confirmandis, sed et peccatoribus justificandis: quomodo ubique gentium, Spiritu creante novum genus hominum, renovata sit facies terrae: imo quanta quotidie mutatio fiat per dexteram Excelsi, ut repente perditissimi hominum publicani et meretrices, justos quam plurimos praecedant in regno Dei, et novissimi fiant primi. Prorsus non sicut delictum, ita et donum: quia ubi abundavit delictum, ibi superabundans gratia (Rom. v, 15, 20): non solum donat delicta, sed etiam virtutum accumulat merita; et sublimius restituit lapsos redemptio, quam constituerat prima creatio. Sane in his omnibus quanto mirabilior Dei gratia praedicatur, tanto damnabilior hominis duritia convincitur, si gratiam vel oblatam recuset, vel acceptam non servet. Cui enim non offertur? super quem non effulget lumen illius? quis se abscondit a calore ejus? Neque enim reliquit se Deus sine testimonio apud conscientias hominum, illustrans eos splendore veritatis, et fovens calore bonitatis; cum et lux vera illuminet omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum (Joan. i, 9), et Deus faciat oriri solem suum super bonos et malos, et pluat super justos et injustos (Matth. v, 45). Sed vae illis qui rebelles sunt lumini, et resistunt Spiritui sancto, nec acquiescunt veritati quam intelligunt; et sicut lutum ex calore solis, ita ex bonitate et beneficiis Dei duriores fiunt, audacter etiam provocantes eum, cum ipse dederit omnia in manibus eorum!

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. God is beyond all telling; his mercy is beyond all telling. As is his name, so also is his work. Beyond all telling indeed is the condescension of divine charity towards us. It was too little for the Father to have handed over the Son to redeem the servant, unless he also gave the Holy Spirit, through whom he might adopt the servant as a son. He gave the Son as the price of redemption; he gave the Spirit as the privilege of adoption; finally, he keeps his whole self as the inheritance of those adopted. O God, prodigal of himself, if one may say so, in his longing for man! Is he not prodigal, who spends not only what is his but his very self, to recover man, not so much for himself as for man's own sake? Is he not prodigal, who, just as he did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all (Rom. viii, 32), likewise did not spare the Holy Spirit, so to speak, but poured him out upon all flesh with a new and wondrous generosity? That prodigal son indeed poured himself out lavishly, giving both his patrimony and himself to harlots; but the father was far more lavish in recovering his lost son than the son had been in losing himself (Luc. v), if indeed grace and money, spirit and flesh, God and man ought to be compared at all. For see how generously the grace of the Spirit has been poured out throughout the world, not only to strengthen the just but also to justify sinners; how everywhere among the nations the face of the earth has been renewed, as the Spirit creates a new race of men; indeed, how great a change is wrought daily by the right hand of the Most High, so that suddenly the most abandoned of men, publicans and harlots, go before very many of the just into the kingdom of God, and the last become first. Truly, the gift is not like the trespass, for where the trespass abounded, grace is superabundant (Rom. v, 15, 20): it not only forgives trespasses but heaps up the merits of virtues; and redemption restores the fallen to a higher state than the first creation had established. In all this, surely, the more wondrous God's grace is proclaimed to be, the more deserving of condemnation man's hardness is proved to be, if he either refuses grace when offered or fails to keep it once received. For to whom is it not offered? Upon whom does its light not shine? Who hides himself from its warmth? For God has not left himself without witness in men's consciences, enlightening them with the splendour of truth and warming them with the heat of goodness, since the true light enlightens every man coming into this world (Joan. i, 9), and God makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust (Matth. v, 45). But woe to those who rebel against the light and resist the Holy Spirit, who will not assent to the truth they understand; and who, like clay under the sun's heat, grow harder through God's goodness and benefits, even boldly provoking him, although he himself has put all things into their hands!

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Verum quid ad nos de his qui foris sunt? Ad vos potius nobis est sermo, qui spiritum adoptionis filiorum accepistis, habentes eumdem spiritum in signum adoptionis et pignus haereditatis; qui velut quidam character insignis, vasa misericordiae a vasis irae discernit. Quanquam de salute nostra, vel magis de spe salutis, ea nobis modestia gaudendum sit, ut quod in illis dolemus, adhuc de nobis pro nostra mutabilitate timeamus. Sicut enim de illis desperare impium, ita de nobis praesumere est temerarium, cum tam de nobis quam de illis, qualiscunque sit scientia praesentium, nulla possit esse praescientia futurorum; nec levis sit injuria summae potestati, penes quam est arbitrium vitae et mortis, si vel de illis tam crudeliter, vel de nobis tam audacter praejudicetur ejus judiciis. Denique de massa eorum sumus assumpti, et qui paulo ante eramus, sicut et illi, natura et vita filii irae, repente facti sumus filii gratiae. Nos ergo simus illis exemplum spei ad poenitentiam; ipsi nobis, timoris ad perseverantiam. In nobis se misericordia commendat, ut ametur; in illis se judicium exserit ut timeatur. Misericordiam et judicium cantabo tibi, Domine (Psal. c, 1): pro ista gratias agens, pro illo preces fundens, pro ista gratus et laetus, pro illo timoratus et cautus: de utroque eruditus exsultabo tibi cum tremore, quia tunc ingrediar in veritate tua, si ita laetetur cor meum ut timeat nomen tuum. Neque enim timor iste, quem amor castum facit, gaudium tollit, sed custodit; non destruit, sed instruit; non inamaricat, sed condit: ut tanto sit durabilius, quanto modestius; tanto verius, quanto severius; tanto dulcius, quanto sanctius. O castum et fidele gaudium! quam fidelis est illa de te sententia Sapientis: Non est census super salutem corporis, et non est oblectatio super gaudium cordis! (Eccli. xxx, 16) Hoc utique gaudio non est gaudere impiis, quorum fatuos risus et frivola gaudia Sapiens detestatur et increpat. Risum, inquit, reputavi errorem, et gaudio dixi: Quid frustra deciperis? (Eccle. ii, 2) Risus dolore miscebitur, et extrema gaudii luctus occupat (Prov. xiv, 13).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. But what have we to do with those who are outside? Our discourse is addressed rather to you, who have received the spirit of adoption as sons, possessing that same spirit as the sign of adoption and pledge of the inheritance; like a distinctive seal, he distinguishes vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath. Yet we must rejoice in our salvation, or rather in the hope of salvation, with such restraint that, because of our own changeableness, we still fear for ourselves what we lament in them. For just as it is impious to despair of them, so it is rash to presume concerning ourselves, since, whatever knowledge there may be of present things, there can be no foreknowledge of things to come, either concerning ourselves or concerning them; nor is it a slight affront to the supreme power, in whose hands lies the determination of life and death, if his judgments are prejudged so cruelly concerning them or so boldly concerning ourselves. After all, we have been taken from their same mass, and we who a little while ago, like them, were children of wrath by nature and manner of life have suddenly become children of grace. Let us therefore be for them an example of hope leading to repentance; let them be for us an example of fear leading to perseverance. In us mercy commends itself, that it may be loved; in them judgment shows itself, that it may be feared. I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, O Lord (Psal. c, 1): giving thanks for the one, pouring out prayers concerning the other; grateful and glad for the one, fearful and watchful concerning the other. Instructed by both, I will exult before you with trembling, for I shall walk in your truth when my heart rejoices in such a way as to fear your name. For this fear, which love makes chaste, does not take joy away but guards it; does not destroy it but builds it up; does not embitter it but seasons it, so that it is the more lasting for being more restrained, the truer for being more serious, the sweeter for being holier. O chaste and faithful joy! How true is the Wise Man's saying about you: There is no wealth above bodily health, and no delight above joy of heart! (Eccli. xxx, 16) It is not for the impious to rejoice with this joy: the Wise Man detests and rebukes their foolish laughter and frivolous joys. Laughter, he says, I reckoned an error, and to joy I said: Why are you vainly deceived? (Eccle. ii, 2) Laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy (Prov. xiv, 13).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. O bone Jesu, quam dissimile est illud gaudium tuum, quo interim consolaris renuntiantes illi falso et fallaci gaudio! quam melior est misericordia tua super vitas! quam melior est dies una in atriis tuis super millia! quanto beatiores facis pauperes tuos ipsa paupertate tua, quam mundus facere possit sua quantalibet affluentia, ubi quidquid affluit, defluit, sibique inhaerentem pereffluere facit! Aliis affluebat deliciis illa pauper familia Christi, quam fluminis impetus inundabat laetificans civitatem Dei; cum scilicet hodierna die Spiritus, tanquam torrens, replevit totam domum ubi erant sedentes (Act. ii, 2.) Apostoli. Exhibebat quippe divina Veritas, quod per prophetam promiserat: Ecce ego declino in vos, ut flumen pacis, et ut torrens inundans gloriae gentium (Isai. lxvi, 12. Quantum illis affluebat, quibus tantus influebat! quantumque de illis profluebat, de quorum ventre fluebant flumina aquae vivae! Nec solum de corde benevolentia charitatis, sed etiam ex ore vehementia profluebat torrentis eloquii, cui non poterant resistere et contradicere omnes eorum adversarii: sicut de Stephano dicitur, quia non poterant resistere sapientiae et Spiritui qui loquebatur (Act. vi, 10).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. O good Jesus, how different is that joy of yours, with which you meanwhile console those who renounce that false and deceitful joy! How much better is your mercy than lives! How much better is one day in your courts than thousands! How much happier you make your poor through your very poverty than the world could make them with any abundance of its own, where whatever flows in flows away, and makes whoever clings to it flow away with it! That poor household of Christ abounded in other delights, flooded by the rushing river that gladdens the city of God, when on this very day the Spirit, like a torrent, filled the whole house where the Apostles were sitting (Act. ii, 2.). For divine Truth was fulfilling what he had promised through the prophet: Behold, I turn towards you as a river of peace, and as an overflowing torrent of the glory of the nations (Isai. lxvi, 12. How abundantly he flowed upon them, into whom so great a One flowed! And how much flowed forth from those out of whose innermost being flowed rivers of living water! Not only did the benevolence of charity flow from their hearts, but from their mouths also flowed the force of a torrent of speech, which none of their adversaries could resist or contradict, as it is said of Stephen that they could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit who spoke (Act. vi, 10).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Ad hujusmodi gaudia vos interim, fratres, consolator vester invitat. Hoc torrente voluptatis suae sitibundas amantium mentes potare desiderat. Si quis, inquit, sitit, veniat et bibat (Joan. vii, 37). O affluens liberalitas Dei! o indeficiens largitas divinae bonitatis! Spiritum, cujus hodie primitias dedit Apostolis, offert universis. Thesaurum suum, fontem aquae vivae aperit tam hominibus quam jumentis; tanquam et ipse omnibus sapientibus et insipientibus debitor sit. Omnes, inquit, sitientes, venite ad aquas (Isai. lv, 1). Ecce personas non accipit, conditiones non discernit, merita non requirit: tantum sitire quis noverit, venire velit. Gratia quippe non admittit fastidientes; sed sicut esurientes implet bonis, sic divites dimittit inanes. O fastidium tinea cordium, rubigo mentium languor pessimus animarum, quod abominari facis bonum Dei verbum, contemnere coeleste donum, fastidire manna propter ollas carnium! Quae enim lues tam pestifera, quis morbus tam lethalis, qui sic faciat hominem immemorem suae salutis, ridentem ac male securum appropinquare usque ad portas mortis? Sed unde, rogo tam late lues ista Christi ovilia infecit, greges invasit, ut quam pluribus de grege Domini videatur etiam locus horroris et vastae solitudinis, locus pascuae ubi sunt collocati, et in pascuis uberrimis, in herbis virentibus misere pereant fastidio languidi? An non, quaeso gustaverunt donum coeleste, et participes facti sunt Spiritus sancti; gustaverunt nihilominus bonum Dei verbum, et virtutes saeculi venturi? (Hebr. vi, 5.) Si enim non gustaverunt bonum Dei verbum, unde toties eructavit cor eorum verbum bonum, cum scilicet de memoria abundantiae suavitatis ejus eructabant labia eorum hymnum? Nunc autem divinis intersunt laudibus, et dormitant; aut otiosa vel etiam perniciosa mente pertractant: sedent ad librum, et oscitant: verbum exhortationis audiunt, et ipso auditu laborant: de pascuis mutantur in pascua, et tam ista fastidiunt quam illa: jugiter versantur inter fercula vitae, et moriuntur fame. Unde ergo post illam felicem experientiam, gustumque suavem supernae dulcedinis, tanta haec oblivio, et incuria boni, languorque mentium subintravit? Sola relicta est eis vox illa plangentis, si tamen plangere velint: Percussus sum ut fenum, et aruit cor meum, quia oblitus sum comedere panem meum (Psal. ci, 5. Currebant utique bene: quis eos fascinavit retrorsum converti? Spiritu coeperunt: quomodo nunc carne consummantur? Voluptuose vescebantur: quomodo nunc intereunt in viis?

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Meanwhile, brothers, your Comforter invites you to joys of this kind. With this torrent of his delight he longs to give drink to the thirsty minds of those who love him. If anyone thirsts, he says, let him come and drink (Joan. vii, 37). O overflowing generosity of God! O unfailing bounty of divine goodness! The Spirit whose firstfruits he gave to the Apostles today he offers to everyone. He opens his treasury, the fountain of living water, to men and beasts alike, as though he too were debtor to all, wise and unwise. All you who thirst, he says, come to the waters (Isai. lv, 1). See, he shows no partiality, distinguishes no ranks, requires no merits: let a man only know how to thirst and be willing to come. For grace does not admit those who have lost their appetite; but as it fills the hungry with good things, so it sends the rich away empty. O loss of appetite, moth of hearts, rust of minds, most grievous sickness of souls, you who make them loathe the good word of God, despise the heavenly gift, and tire of manna for the sake of the flesh pots! For what plague is so deadly, what sickness so lethal, as to make a man so forgetful of his salvation that he approaches the very gates of death laughing and falsely secure? But how, I ask, has this plague infected Christ's sheepfolds so widely and invaded his flocks, that to so many of the Lord's flock even the pasture where they have been placed seems a place of horror and vast solitude, and in the richest pastures, amid green grass, they miserably perish, sick with loss of appetite? Have they not, I ask, tasted the heavenly gift and become sharers in the Holy Spirit; have they not also tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come? (Hebr. vi, 5.) For if they have not tasted the good word of God, how did their hearts so often pour forth a good word, when their lips poured forth a hymn from the remembrance of his abundant sweetness? But now they attend the divine praises and doze; or turn over idle or even harmful thoughts in their minds. They sit at their books and yawn; they hear a word of exhortation and find even listening a burden; they move from pasture to pasture and tire of the one as much as the other; they are continually surrounded by dishes of life, and die of hunger. How then, after that happy experience and sweet taste of heavenly sweetness, have such forgetfulness, such neglect of the good and such sickness of mind crept in? All that remains to them is that cry of lament, if indeed they are willing to lament: I have been struck down like grass, and my heart has withered, because I have forgotten to eat my bread (Psal. ci, 5. They were indeed running well: who has bewitched them into turning back? They began in the Spirit: how are they now being brought to completion in the flesh? They used to feed in delight: how are they now perishing on the roads?

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Videant, quaeso, ipsi, ne forte inimicus homo, qui super bonum semen patrisfamilias lolium suum superseminare consuevit, post illam suavem escam Christi, felle suo fauces eorum tinxerit, ac per hoc non modo desiderium, sed et memoriam prioris gustus aboleverit. Enimvero statim denuntiat Apostolus his qui ejusmodi sunt: Non potestis calicem Domini bibere, et calicem daemoniorum. Non potestis mensae Domini participes esse, et mensae daemoniorum (I Cor. x, 20, 21). An non tibi videtur non modo potatus sed et inebriatus calice daemoniorum, qui libidinis, irae, impatientiae, aut similium raptatur furore passionum? Ego, ut loquar de his quae jam magis in usu quam in crimine sunt, puto quod et ille mensae daemoniorum particeps sit, et pascens eos pascatur ab eis, cujus os abundat malitia, lingua concinnat dolos, sedens adversus fratrem suum loquitur et adversus filium matris suae ponit scandalum: qui etiamsi non detrahit, detrahentem libenter audit; qui scurrilitate stultiloquii cachinnantes dissolvit. Videat ergo qui ejusmodi est, an dignum sit ut, volutatus velut in cruore immolatio et sordibus daemonum, mox admittatur ad mensam Christi et Angelorum. Absit autem, fratres mei, ut, haec dicens, innocentiam vestram, qua plurimum delector, inscribam sceleri; sed haec dico ut salvi sitis, et aliorum exemplo cautiores facti, manusque lavantes in sanguine peccatoris, gratiam Spiritus sancti quam alii negligentia perdunt, vos omni vigilantia servare curetis; ad laudem et gloriam ipsius largitoris Jesu Christi Domini nostri, qui vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Let them themselves consider, I beg, whether perhaps the enemy, who is accustomed to sow his tares over the householder's good seed, has, after that sweet food of Christ, stained their throats with his gall, and thereby blotted out not only the desire but even the memory of their former taste. Indeed, the Apostle at once warns those who are like this: You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons (I Cor. x, 20, 21). Does he not seem to you to have drunk from the cup of demons and even to be drunk with it, who is swept away by the fury of lust, anger, impatience or similar passions? To speak of things which are now more often treated as customary than as sinful, I think that he too shares in the table of demons, feeding them and being fed by them, whose mouth abounds in malice, whose tongue contrives deceit, who sits and speaks against his brother and sets a stumbling block against his mother's son; who, even if he does not slander, gladly listens to a slanderer; who with the buffoonery of foolish talk makes his hearers dissolve in loud laughter. Let such a man consider, then, whether it is fitting that, after wallowing as though in sacrificial blood and the filth of demons, he should at once be admitted to the table of Christ and the Angels. But far be it from me, my brothers, in saying this to charge with wickedness your innocence, in which I take very great delight. I say these things so that you may be saved and, made more watchful by the example of others and washing your hands in the blood of the sinner, may take care with all vigilance to preserve the grace of the Holy Spirit which others lose through negligence, to the praise and glory of its giver himself, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The sermon contains five numbered sections. The titles follow the printed edition.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition cites Luke 5 for the prodigal son; the narrative is in Luke 15. The printed reference is retained.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition leaves the parenthesis after Isaiah 66:12 unclosed. The quotation is complete; the words that follow begin Guerric’s comment.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The Latin prints cruore immolatio, an irregular blood-and-sacrifice phrase. “Sacrificial blood” conveys its meaning in this warning about the table of demons; the uncertain Latin wording is retained.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The Hebrews quotation includes Hebrews 6:4 as well as the printed 6:5. The edition also cites 1 Corinthians 10:20–21 and leaves the parenthesis after Psalm 101:5 unclosed. The final image of washing hands in a sinner’s blood is Guerric’s biblical language.

sermons.title: Pentecost Sermon I: God's Charity and Human Ingratitude

sermons.author: Guerric of Igny
metadata: Guerric of Igny (collection attribution), Sermones per annum, SERMO II., De linguarum mysterio et dono lacrymarum., in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier frères, 1879), cols. 160-164.
Internet Archive, 2011; PIMS, University of Toronto; University of Toronto funding.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric reads the fiery tongues of the apostles at Pentecost. He wishes for a tongue to praise God, or at least one to heal the wounds of those who confess, and calls blessed those who draw grace from licking the sores of sinners. He asks for the unutterable groanings of the Spirit in place of the manual labor his office excuses, and urges the brothers to seek the gift of tears, through which the Spirit consoles those who mourn. The sermon appears under the Pentecost heading in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO II.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON II.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De linguarum mysterio et dono lacrymarum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the mystery of tongues and the gift of tears.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Loquebantur variis linguis Apostoli magnalia Dei (Act. II, 11.). Nimirum ex abundantia cordis linguae loquebantur in eis. Exsultationes Dei in gutture eorum, quia charitas Dei diffusa erat in cordibus eorum. O Domine Deus meus, et ego utique similiter laudarem, si similiter potatus essem. Quia vero arida est anima mea, ideo est et torpida lingua. Sed sicut adipe et pinguedine repleatur anima mea, et labiis exsultationis laudabit os meum (Psal. LXII, 6). Eructabunt labia mea hymnum; sed cum docueris me justificationes tuas: id est cum dederis gustare quam suavis es, ut discam te diligere toto corde, tota anima, tota virtute. Bonus es tu, et in bonitate tua doce me justificationes tuas (Psal. CXVIII, 12). Bonitas siquidem tua, unctio tua est, qua doces eos de quibus praedictum est: Erunt omnes docibiles Dei (Joan. VI, 45). Beatus homo quem tu erudieris, Domine, et de lege tua docueris eum (Psal. XCIII, 12). Lex Domini immaculata convertens animas (Psal. XVIII, 8), charitas est: lex utique ignea, quae est in dextera ejus, quae cum digito Dei scribitur super latitudinem cordis, et ipsum cor amoris incendio, et eos ignito fervere facit eloquio. De excelso, inquit, misit ignem in ossibus meis, et erudivit me (Thren. I, 13). O quanta facilitate et celeritate, quanta copia et facultate, ignis ille quem Dominus Jesus misit in terram, non solum erudivit imperitos, sed etiam expedivit impeditos! Prorsus igneae linguae, quas ex se dispertivit ignis iste, quae sic ignescere fecerunt non solum mentes, sed et linguas Apostolorum, ut etiam nunc pius auditor ad sermones ignescat eorum. Prorsus ignea lingua Petri, ignea lingua Pauli, in quorum verbis nunc quoque vivit ignis perpetuus, qui et super corda nostra scintillat, si accedamus, si aurum vel animum ab eorum sermonibus non avertamus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "The Apostles spoke in various tongues the great works of God" (Act. II, 11.). Surely it was out of the abundance of the heart that their tongues spoke in them. The exultations of God were in their throat, because the charity of God had been poured out in their hearts. O Lord my God, I too would indeed praise you in like manner, if I had been given to drink in like manner. But because my soul is parched, my tongue too is sluggish. But as my soul shall be filled with marrow and fatness, my mouth shall praise you with lips of exultation (Psal. LXII, 6). My lips shall pour forth a hymn; but only when you have taught me your justifications — that is, when you have given me to taste how sweet you are, so that I may learn to love you with my whole heart, my whole soul, my whole strength. You are good, and in your goodness teach me your justifications (Psal. CXVIII, 12). For your goodness is your anointing, by which you teach those of whom it was foretold: "They shall all be taught of God" (Joan. VI, 45). Blessed is the man whom you, O Lord, shall instruct, and whom you shall teach out of your law (Psal. XCIII, 12). The law of the Lord, unspotted, converting souls (Psal. XVIII, 8), is charity — indeed, a fiery law, which is in his right hand, which is written with the finger of God upon the breadth of the heart, and sets the heart itself ablaze with the fire of love, and makes them burn with fiery speech. "From on high," he says, "he sent fire into my bones, and taught me" (Thren. I, 13). O with what ease and swiftness, with what abundance and power, did that fire which the Lord Jesus sent upon the earth not only instruct the untaught, but also set free the hindered! Truly fiery were the tongues which this fire distributed from itself, which so set ablaze not only the minds but also the tongues of the Apostles, that even now the devout hearer catches fire at their sermons. Truly fiery is the tongue of Peter, fiery the tongue of Paul, in whose words even now a perpetual fire lives, which also sparks upon our hearts, if we draw near, if we do not turn our ear or our mind away from their sermons.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Si meruissem aliquam accipere de linguis hujusmodi, dicerem utique et ego, Dominus dedit mihi linguam mercedem meam, et in ipsa laudabo eum (Eccli. LI, 30); sicut de illis scriptum est, Loquebantur variis linguis Apostoli magnalia Dei. Dicerem et illud: Dominus dedit mihi linguam eruditam ut sciam sustentare eum qui lapsus est, verbo (Isai. L, 4). Apostoli et eorum similes linguis sibi datis magnalia Dei praedicant, tyrannos verberant, daemonia flagellant, terram compluunt, coelos aperiunt; quia linguae eorum claves coeli factae sunt, quippe quibus de ipsis coelis linguae missae sunt. Mihi autem utinam vel lingua canis data sit, qua possim primum quidem propria, deinde et aliena ulcera lingere, si qui forte sunt qui ad hoc ipsum sibi me dignentur admittere. Beati quidem, quibus amor et dilectio divinae laudis cor replet gaudio et os jubilo. Sed et illos utique beatos dixerim, qui, cum de vulneribus animarum virus ablingunt et purulentiam, trahunt in se, quo anima eorum saginetur, spiritum et gratiam. Esuriunt siquidem et sitiunt justitiam, et famem patiuntur ut canes: ideoque nihil fastidiunt quod in corpus suum possint trajicere; neminem peccatorem abominantur, quem ad justitiam possint convertere. Quod Deus mundavit, tu ne immundum dixeris (Act. XI, 9), dictum est Principi Apostolorum, et in ipso aliis: et ob hoc mactat et manducat omne genus reptilium et volatilium, et ait, Quae prius tangere nolebat anima mea, nunc prae angustia impatientis desiderii cibi mei sunt (Job. VI, 7). Quinimo mirum in modum quanto quisque peccator ante conversionem amarior, tanto postmodum conversio ejus dulcior; quantoque desperatior, tanto gratior nobis ejus salus: quia et salvantis gratiam plus miramur, qui ovem perditam reportans in humeris, gaudium facit Angelis super uno peccatore poenitentiam agente, quam super nonaginta novem justis (Luc. XV, 7).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. If I had merited to receive any of such tongues, I too would certainly say: "The Lord has given me a tongue as my reward, and with it I will praise him" (Eccli. LI, 30); just as it is written of them, "The Apostles spoke in various tongues the great works of God." I would also say this: "The Lord has given me a learned tongue, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who has fallen" (Isai. L, 4). The Apostles, and those like them, with the tongues given them, preach the great works of God, scourge tyrants, flog demons, rain down upon the earth, open the heavens; for their tongues have become the keys of heaven, since it was indeed from heaven itself that tongues were sent to them. But as for me — would that at least the tongue of a dog were given to me, with which I might lick, first my own wounds, and then those of others, if perhaps there are any who would deign to admit me to this very task on their behalf. Blessed indeed are those whose heart the love and affection of divine praise fills with joy, and whose mouth with jubilation. But I would also surely call blessed those who, in licking away the venom and pus from the wounds of souls, draw into themselves the spirit and grace by which their own soul is fattened. For they hunger and thirst after justice, and suffer hunger like dogs; and therefore they disdain nothing that they can take into their own body; they abominate no sinner whom they might be able to convert to justice. "What God has cleansed, do not call unclean" (Act. XI, 9), was said to the Prince of the Apostles, and in him to others; and for this reason he slaughters and eats every kind of creeping thing and bird, and says: "The things my soul formerly refused to touch are now, through the anguish of impatient desire, my food" (Job. VI, 7). Indeed, in a wondrous way, the more bitter any sinner was before his conversion, the sweeter afterward is his conversion; and the more he was despaired of, the more welcome to us is his salvation — because we marvel all the more at the grace of him who saves, who, carrying the lost sheep back on his shoulders, causes more joy to the Angels over one sinner doing penance, than over ninety-nine just men (Luc. XV, 7).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Dicant igitur alii quibus datum est: Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua Domine (Psal. CXVIII, 103)! anima autem mea esuriens et famem patiens ut canis, etiam amarum sumet pro dulci, et abominabile pro desiderabili. Delectentur alii lambere mella Scripturarum; ego vero delectabor ulcera lingere peccatorum, mei scilicet mihique similium. Foedum quidem ulcus peccati, visuque horribile; sed tamen ipsum lingere, cujus sit saporis et gratiae, non sapit, non capit, nisi qui salutem periclitantium esurit, et famem patitur ut canis: de qualibus dictum est, Lingua canum tuorum ex inimicis (Psal. CXVIII, 24). Sed vae miseris qui tanto studio pereunt, tantoque desiderio mortem sibi consciscunt, ut vulnera sua tegant, curamque canum refugiant, et asperitatem linguae medicinalis arbitrentur morsum odii lethalis! Oderunt corripientem in porta, et perfecte loquentem abominati sunt (Amos. V, 10). Perfecte loquentem dico, non tam de perfectione disserentem, quam perfecta dilectione corripientem. Sed dicam, Perfecta dilectione, an perfecto odio? Imo utrumque, et perfecta dilectione, et perfecto odio: quia perfectum odium nihil aliud est, quam perfecta dilectio; et una est utriusque perfectio, quam Apostolus determinat, dicens, Odientes malum, adhaerentes autem bono (Rom. XII, 9).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Let others, then, to whom it has been given, say: "How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord!" (Psal. CXVIII, 103). But my soul, hungering and suffering famine like a dog, will take even the bitter for sweet, and the abominable for the desirable. Let others delight to lick the honey of the Scriptures; I, however, will delight to lick the sores of sinners—namely, my own, and those of men like me. Foul indeed is the sore of sin, and horrible to see; yet what savor and grace there is in licking it, no one tastes, no one grasps, except him who hungers for the salvation of those in peril, and suffers famine like a dog: of such it is said, "The tongue of your dogs shall be red from the enemies" (Psal. CXVIII, 24). But woe to the wretched who perish with such zeal, and bring death upon themselves with such desire, that they cover their wounds and flee the care of dogs, judging the roughness of the healing tongue to be the bite of deadly hatred! "They hated him that reproved in the gate, and abhorred him that spoke perfectly" (Amos. V, 10). I say 'spoke perfectly'—not so much one discoursing about perfection, as one reproving with perfect love. But shall I say 'with perfect love,' or 'with perfect hatred'? Rather both: with perfect love and with perfect hatred; for perfect hatred is nothing other than perfect love, and the perfection of both is one, which the Apostle defines, saying, "Hating that which is evil, cleaving to that which is good" (Rom. XII, 9).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text:
4. Sed revertar ad id unde digressus eram. Optabam mihi linguam qua laudarem Deum, vel certe linguam qua confitentium ulcera curarem: in altero quidem mihi quaerens divinae devotionis fructum; in altero, fraternae salutis lucrum: vobis quoque in altero dulcis, in altero fieri desiderans utilis. Nam et de saecularium arte et officio poetarum, ita sumptum est apud quemdam eorum: 
Aut prodesse volunt, aut delectare poetae.
Omne tulit punctum qui miscuit utile dulci.
(HORAT., Art. poet.)
 Optabam, inquam, mihi gratiam oris, qua Deo et vobis officiosus deservirem; ut aliquatenus compensarem verbo, quod minus prosum exemplo. Quanquam satis suspecta mihi sit haec consolatio, si dicam et non faciam; si suppetant suffragia linguae, cum desint merita vitae; imo magis fortasse timendum sit, ne peccanti dicat Deus, Quare tu enarras justitias meas, et assumis testamentum meum per os tuum? (Psal. XLIX, 16). Sed quid agam? Si locutus fuero, non quiescet dolor meus; et si tacuero, non recedet a me (Job. XVI, 7). Pavor est utrobique molestus, et coarctor e duobus; quia locutionem et officii locus exigit, et vita contradicit. Sed recordor verbi quod apud Sapientem inveni: Anima laborantis laborat sibi, quia compulit eum os suum (Prov. XVI, 26). Loquar igitur, non prout locus expetit, sed prout sensus suppetit, imo prout Dominus dederit, in cujus manu sumus et nos, et sermones nostri. Loquar, inquam, et me ipsum lingua obligabo propria, ut vel prae confusione aliquando laborare compellar: et si corpus a labore manuum excusaverit, certe anima laborantis laboret sibi, ut dicat cum David, Laboravi in gemitu meo (Psal. VI, 7). O si mihi dentur illi gemitus inenarrabiles, quibus Spiritus postulat pro sanctis, ut laborem in eis! Procul dubio labor hujusmodi gemituum satis digne pensaret mihi quotidianum laborem manuum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. But I will return to the point from which I digressed. I was wishing for myself a tongue with which to praise God, or at least a tongue with which to heal the sores of those who confess: seeking in the one case for myself the fruit of divine devotion, in the other the gain of my brothers' salvation; desiring to become, for you also, sweet in the one case, useful in the other. For concerning the art and office of the secular poets, this is taken from one of them: 'Poets wish either to profit or to please. He has carried every point who has mixed the useful with the sweet.' (Horace, Art of Poetry). I was wishing, I say, for the grace of speech, by which I might dutifully serve both God and you, so that I might in some measure make up by word for my being of less use by example. Though this consolation is quite suspect to me, if I should speak and not do; if the tongue's resources should be at hand while the merits of life are lacking—indeed it is rather to be feared that God might say to the sinner, "Why do you declare my justices, and take my covenant into your mouth?" (Psal. XLIX, 16). But what shall I do? "If I speak, my sorrow will not rest; and if I am silent, it will not depart from me" (Job. XVI, 7). The dread is troublesome on both sides, and I am constrained between the two; for the place of duty demands speech, and my life contradicts it. But I recall a saying I found in the Wise Man: "The soul of him who labors, labors for himself, because his own mouth has compelled him" (Prov. XVI, 26). I will speak, then, not as the occasion demands, but as understanding supplies—rather, as the Lord shall grant, in whose hand are both we ourselves and our words. I will speak, I say, and I will bind myself by my own tongue, so that I may at least be compelled by shame to labor at some point: and if the body be excused from the labor of the hands, let the soul of him who labors certainly labor for itself, that it may say with David, "I have labored in my groaning" (Psal. VI, 7). O, if only those unutterable groanings might be given to me, with which the Spirit intercedes for the saints, that I might labor in them! Without doubt, labor of such groanings would quite worthily make up for my daily labor of hands.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Sed et vos ipsi, fratres, si aemulari meliora charismata didicistis, optate gemitus hujusmodi a Spiritu vobis infundi. Nescio si sit in donis Spiritus aliud convenientius aut commodius his qui sunt infirmitate et miseria circumdati: nescio si Spiritui sancto qui in columba apparuit, alia vox familiarior gemitu, aut gratior sit. Hoc autem scio, quia in nullo opere tanta tamque parata nobis suppetat materia, sicut in gemitu et planctu nostri: nisi miseriam suam nostra dissimulet superbia, aut sensus obduretur stupore vel amentia. Hoc autem primum circa infirmos, quorum curam suscipit, operatur medicina sancti Spiritus, qui est illuminatio nostra et salus nostra, ut videlicet se ipsum phreneticus sentiat et sciat, et conversus ad cor dicat Domino cum propheta: Postquam convertisti me, egi poenitentiam; et postquam ostendisti mihi, percussi femur meum (Jerem. XXXI, 19). Nisi enim quis apponat scientiam, non apponet dolorem: nisi doluerit, non meretur consolationem. Beati enim qui lugent, quoniam ipsi consolabuntur (Matth. V, 5). Puto quia nec in Apostolis hodie locum invenisset Paracleti consolatio, nisi quia lugebant se desolatos, quia non poterant non lugere filii sponsi, cum sponsus ablatus esset ab eis. Inde erat quod eis dicebat: Nisi ego abiero, Paracletus non veniet ad vos (Joan. XVI, 7). Nisi desolati fueritis praesentia mea corporali, non vos consolabitur visitatio spiritualis. Date, inquit, siceram moerentibus, et vinum his qui amaro animo sunt, non scilicet illis qui ebrii sunt gaudio et luxu saeculi. Quae enim participatio justitiae cum iniquitate? nunquid bibere possunt calicem Domini, et calicem daemoniorum? Bibant, inquit, potius pauperes Apostoli, et obliviscantur egestatis suae (Prov. XXXI, 6, 7), ut dicant: Sicut egentes multos autem, locupletantes (II Cor. VI. 10). Bibant moerentes de absentia sponsi, et dolorum non recordentur amplius, sed dicant: Etsi cognovimus Christum secundum carnem, sed nunc jam non novimus (Id. V, 16). Nam et te ipsum, si pio affectu Psalmistae dicere potueris, Ego sum pauper et dolens (Psal. LXVIII, 30), sic ditabit, sic, laetificabit sobria ebrietas hujus praeclari calicis, ut, etsi pauper sis, paupertas animum non urat; et si dolebas quia peccasti, jam peccati reatus conscientiam non mordeat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. But you yourselves also, brothers, if you have learned to be zealous for the better gifts, desire that such groanings be poured into you by the Spirit. I do not know whether there is among the gifts of the Spirit anything more fitting or more suitable for those who are surrounded by weakness and misery; I do not know whether to the Holy Spirit, who appeared in the form of a dove, any voice is more familiar or more pleasing than a groan. But this I know: that in no work is there so great and so ready a store of material for us as in groaning and lamenting over ourselves—unless our pride disguises our own misery, or our perception is hardened by stupor or madness. Now this is the first thing that the medicine of the Holy Spirit, who is our illumination and our salvation, works upon the sick whose care it undertakes: that the one who is deranged should feel and know himself to be so, and, turning to his heart, say to the Lord with the prophet: 'After you converted me, I did penance; and after you showed me, I struck my thigh' (Jerem. XXXI, 19). For unless one adds knowledge, he will not add sorrow; unless he has grieved, he does not merit consolation. For blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matth. V, 5). I think that the consolation of the Paraclete would not have found a place among the Apostles today, had they not been mourning themselves as desolate—for the sons of the bridegroom could not but mourn when the bridegroom had been taken from them. Hence it was that he said to them: 'Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you' (Joan. XVI, 7). Unless you have been left desolate of my bodily presence, a spiritual visitation will not console you. 'Give,' he says, 'strong drink to those that mourn, and wine to those who are of bitter mind'—not, that is, to those who are drunk with the joy and excess of this world. For what fellowship has justice with iniquity? Can they drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of devils? Let the poor Apostles rather drink,' he says, 'and forget their poverty' (Prov. XXXI, 6, 7), so that they may say: 'As needy, yet enriching many' (II Cor. VI. 10). Let those who mourn over the absence of the bridegroom drink, and let them remember their sorrows no more, but say: 'And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer' (Id. V, 16). For you yourself too, if with the pious feeling of the Psalmist you can say, 'I am poor and sorrowful' (Psal. LXVIII, 30), the sober inebriation of this glorious cup will so enrich you, will so gladden you, that although you are poor, poverty will not burn your soul; and if you were sorrowful because you had sinned, the guilt of sin will no longer gnaw at your conscience.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Vide autem, si non et ipse Spiritus sanctus in judicium venit in hunc mundum, ut qui dolent non doleant, et qui rident, aeterno et inconsolabili se luctui tradant. Melius est igitur ire ad domum luctus quam ad domum convivii (Eccli. VII, 3). Et revera sapiens, etsi aliquando consolationem meretur, ut dolorum non recordetur amplius, eorum scilicet de quibus consolationem accipit, semper tamen, ut locum paret consolationibus novis, novas exquirit de se ipso causas doloris; non statim blandiens sibi, quasi jam per omnia justus sit; sed eo subtilior, quo jam illuminari coepit; eo districtior, quo justificari coepit, fit accusator et judex sui. Ei ergo qui ejusmodi est, crebro, nisi fallor, Spiritus consolator advenit, quoniam et adventum jam ipse suum antevenit; adveniens scilicet ut consolationem tribuat, sed anteveniens, ut lugere doceat. Luctus siquidem pius atque religiosus, in doctrina Spiritus et ordine primus, et utilitate invenitur praecipuus; quippe cum sit summa sapientia sanctorum, custodia justorum, sobrietas modestorum, prima incipientium virtus, proficientium stimulus, perfectorum cumulus, pereuntium salus, periclitantium portus, promissionem denique habens consolationum quae nunc sunt, et gaudiorum quae futura sunt; ad quae nos perducat qui vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. But consider whether the Holy Spirit himself does not come into this world for judgment, so that those who grieve may grieve no more, and those who laugh may give themselves over to eternal and inconsolable mourning. It is better, therefore, to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting (Eccli. VII, 3). And indeed the wise man, even though he sometimes merits consolation so that he no longer remembers those sorrows for which he receives comfort, nevertheless always seeks out new causes of sorrow from himself, so as to make room for new consolations; not at once flattering himself as though he were already righteous in every respect, but becoming his own accuser and judge—the more discerning, the more he has begun to be enlightened; the more strict, the more he has begun to be justified. To one, then, who is of this kind, the comforting Spirit, unless I am mistaken, comes often, since he himself anticipates his own coming—coming, that is, to grant consolation, but anticipating it in order to teach mourning. For pious and devout mourning is found, in the teaching of the Spirit, to be first in order and chief in usefulness; since it is the highest wisdom of the saints, the guardianship of the just, the sobriety of the modest, the first virtue of beginners, the spur of those advancing, the crown of the perfect, the salvation of those perishing, the harbor of those in peril—having, finally, the promise both of the consolations that now are, and of the joys that are to come; to which may he bring us who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition prints aurum (gold), where aurem (ear) is expected alongside animum (mind).

sermons.occasion: In natali Apostolorum Petri et Pauli

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric reads Zechariah's vision of two olive trees beside the golden lampstand as Peter and Paul, sons of the oil of splendor who stand before the Lord. Christ is the lampstand, golden by substance, while believers are gilded by grace. Guerric reminds the brothers, who share one property and one house, to keep the fervor of their first profession, and reads the oil of splendor as the Holy Spirit, who anoints and enlightens. The sermon appears under the heading for the Apostles Peter and Paul in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: IN NATALI APOSTOLORUM PETRI ET PAULI

passages.label: English
passages.text: ON THE BIRTHDAY (FEAST) OF THE APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De duabus olivis ad dexteram candelabri.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the two olive trees at the right hand of the lampstand.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Et respondi, inquit Zacharias, et dixi ad angelum qui loquebatur in me: Quid sunt duae olivae istae ad dexteram candelabri et ad sinistram ejus? Isti sunt, inquit, duo filii olei splendoris, qui assistunt Dominatori universae terrae (Zach. IV, 4, 11, 14). De candelabro quod viderat totum aureum, et septem lucernas ejus super illud intellexerat Propheta, sed nec nobis dubitare jam licet, cum in lumine ejus videamus lumen. Hoc lumen cum alia demonstret, seipsum ignorari non patitur, sed testimonium perhibens de seipso loquitur: Ego sum lux mundi (Joan. VIII, 12). Lux ex divinitate, candelabrum ex humanitate. Et ipsum totum aureum, non auratum; quia sive divinitas, sive sapientia, sive charitas auro significetur, haec omnia Christus non per participationem, sed per substantiam. Nos cum simus natura plumbei, vel magis lutei, gratia et participatione ipsius, non aurum vel aurei, sed ut multum aurati. Septem lucernae super ipsum, septem spiritus, septem oculi Domini, qui discurrunt in universam terram. De his ergo Propheta certus, de duabus olivis quidnam sint percunctatur, auditque ab angelo qui in eo loquebatur: Isti sunt duo filii olei splendoris, qui assistunt Dominatori universae terrae (Zach. IV, 14). Interpretentur alii ut volunt aut possunt, unusquisque pro sensu suo: sive Enoch et Eliam, qui apud Deum in secreto vivunt; sive Moysen et Eliam, qui cum eo in monte visi sunt; sive duos ordines praedicatorum, veteris scilicet ac novi Testamenti: ut qui Veteris, ad sinistram sint propter promissa temporalia; qui Novi, ad dexteram, propter aeterna: ego quidquid a regula fidei non discrepat, aut a contextu lectionis non nimie dissonat, suscipio, veneror, amplector.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "And I answered," says Zechariah, "and I said to the angel who spoke in me: What are these two olive trees at the right hand of the lampstand, and at the left thereof? These," he says, "are the two sons of the oil of splendor, who stand before the Ruler of the whole earth" (Zach. IV, 4, 11, 14). The Prophet had understood the lampstand which he had seen, all of gold, and its seven lamps upon it; but we are no longer permitted to doubt, since in his light we see light. This light, though it shows other things, does not allow itself to go unknown, but bears witness of itself and says: "I am the light of the world" (Joan. VIII, 12). Light from his divinity, lampstand from his humanity. And it itself is wholly gold, not gilded; because whether divinity, or wisdom, or charity is signified by gold, Christ is all these, not by participation, but by substance. We, since by nature we are leaden, or rather of clay, by grace and participation in him are not gold or golden, but at most gilded. The seven lamps upon him are the seven spirits, the seven eyes of the Lord, which run through the whole earth. Concerning these, then, the Prophet, being certain, inquires what the two olive trees might be, and hears from the angel who was speaking in him: "These are the two sons of the oil of splendor, who stand before the Ruler of the whole earth" (Zach. IV, 14). Let others interpret as they will or can, each according to his own understanding: whether Enoch and Elijah, who live with God in secret; or Moses and Elijah, who were seen with him on the mountain; or the two orders of preachers, namely of the Old and the New Testament—so that those of the Old are on the left on account of temporal promises, and those of the New are on the right on account of eternal ones: I accept, venerate, and embrace whatever does not disagree with the rule of faith, nor conflict excessively with the context of the reading.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Puto tamen, sine praejudicio melioris intellectus, Petrum et Paulum non absurde posse intelligi: imo absurdum videri, qui hodie aliud interpretari velit, cum hodie nihil aliud cantet aut tractet Ecclesia ubique terrarum, quam praeconia Patrum doctorumque suorum. Nam etsi aliis possit aptari, puto quia istis specialius congruit, seu illud quod tanquam duae olivae circa candelabrum a Propheta videntur, seu quod duo filii esse olei splendoris ab angelo memorantur. Et alterum quidem altero exponitur, visio scilicet prophetica interpretatione angelica: ut inde intelligantur olivae, quia filii olei splendoris; inde circa candelabrum, quia Domino assistunt. Quia enim ex oleo Spiritus sancti sunt regenerati, hodieque florent et fructificant sicut oliva fructifera in domo Domini, etiam oleastro gentili, qui in ipsos insertus est, impertientes pinguedinis suae succum ac dulcedinis, gratias illis agat sterilis dudum et amara gentilitas; et si non ab ipsis, tamen per ipsos est, quod nunc tam copioso, tam pretioso fructu per orbem abundat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. I think, however, without prejudice to a better understanding, that Peter and Paul can not unreasonably be understood here; indeed it would seem unreasonable for anyone today to wish to interpret it otherwise, since today the Church throughout the whole world sings or treats of nothing else than the praises of her Fathers and teachers. For even though it could be fitted to others, I think that it applies more specially to these two, whether as regards what is seen by the Prophet as two olive trees around the lampstand, or what is called by the angel the two sons of the oil of splendor. And indeed the one is explained by the other—the prophetic vision, that is, by the angelic interpretation—so that from it we understand them to be olive trees because they are sons of the oil of splendor, and around the lampstand, because they stand before the Lord. For since they were regenerated from the oil of the Holy Spirit, and today they flourish and bear fruit like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord, even the wild olive of the Gentiles, which has been grafted into them, receiving from them the sap of their richness and sweetness—let the Gentile world, once barren and bitter, give thanks to them; and even if it is not from them, yet it is through them that there now abounds throughout the world so abundant, so precious a fruit.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Vobis tamen, fratres, quibus sicut substantia et domus una, ita cor unum et anima una: vobis, inquam, specialius in ipsis censeo gloriandum, qui sicut novella olivarum de eorum radice traduxistis non solum fidei succum, sed et formam vitae atque ordinis exemplum. Quod si novella olivarum vos, utique et filii olei vos, filii uncti, qui est Christus Dei; diceturque et de vobis, cum hodie ad altare accedetis: Filii tui sicut novellae olivarum, in circuitu mensae tuae (Psal. CXXVII, 3). O novella olivarum nobilium! o generosum germen tam pinguium, tamque feracium arborum! semper, obsecro, recordare de qua pullulaveris stirpe, de qua succreveris radice, ne unquam sterilitas operum, aut amaritudo morum te degenerem arguat, aut, quod absit, inutilem ignibus addicat. Cave, quaeso, notam infelicium temporum, de quibus meministi prophetatum: Mentietur opus olivae, et arva non afferent cibum (Habac. III, 17). Duo tamen praecipue tibi existimo cavenda: ne aut per teporem fias sicut oliva projiciens florem suum, sicut legis in Propheta, ut videlicet fructum quem in initiis novitii fervoris promittebas non facias; aut cum feceris, ne per superbiam perdas, et dicat tibi Jeremias: Olivam uberem, pulchram, fructiferam, speciosam vocavit Dominus nomen tuum: sed heu! ad vocem loquelae grandis exarsit ignis in ea, et combusta sunt omnia fruteta ejus (Jerem. XI, 16). Confidimus autem de vobis meliora, dilectissimi, tametsi ita loquamur. Confidimus quia oleum splendoris, vel magis olei splendor, cujus estis filii, sicut et patres nostri Apostoli, unctione sua docebit vos de omnibus: nec solum deterget torporem, quia oleum est; sed et discutiet errorem, quia splendor est.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Yet to you, brothers, for whom, just as there is one property and one house, so there is one heart and one soul: to you, I say, I judge it belongs more especially to glory in them, you who, like young shoots of the olive, have derived from their root not only the sap of faith, but also the pattern of life and the example of your order. But if you are young shoots of the olive trees, then surely you too are sons of the oil, sons of the Anointed, who is the Christ of God; and it shall be said of you also, when today you approach the altar: "Your children are like young olive plants round about your table" (Psal. CXXVII, 3). O noble young shoots of olive trees! O generous offspring of trees so rich and so fruitful! Always, I beg you, remember from what stock you have sprung, from what root you have grown, lest ever the barrenness of works, or the bitterness of conduct, convict you of degeneracy, or—God forbid—condemn you as useless to the fires. Beware, I beg, of the mark of unhappy times, of which you remember it was prophesied: "The labor of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no food" (Habac. III, 17). Yet I think there are two things especially you must guard against: either that through lukewarmness you become like an olive tree casting off its flower, as you read in the Prophet—that is, that you fail to produce the fruit which in the beginnings of your novice fervor you promised; or, having produced it, that through pride you lose it, and Jeremiah say to you: "The Lord called your name a fruitful olive tree, fair, fruitful, beautiful: but alas! at the voice of a great utterance fire has blazed up in it, and its branches are all burned" (Jerem. XI, 16). We trust, however, better things of you, most beloved, even though we speak thus. We trust that the oil of splendor—or rather, the splendor of the oil—whose sons you are, as were our fathers the Apostles, will by its anointing teach you all things: not only will it wipe away sluggishness, because it is oil, but it will also dispel error, because it is splendor.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Scio posse intelligi olei splendoris, id est, quod de splendore Filio procedit, vel quod splendorem illuminationis diffundit: sed puto quia non inconvenienter etiam per intransitionem accipi potest oleum, quod splendor est. Utrumque siquidem Spiritus est in natura sui, et unctio scilicet spiritualis, et splendor invisibilis: utrumque in nobis operatur munere sui. Ungit affectus ex eo quod oleum est: illuminat intellectus ex eo quod splendor est. Qui tamen non ex alio atque alio, sed ex uno ipso et oleum, et splendor est; quia nonnisi unum ipsum est. Ungit affectus, quia charitas est: illuminat intellectus, quia veritas est. Ungit affectus, cum devotionem donat: illuminat intellectus, cum mysteria revelat. Cum bonitatem docet, ut simus simplices sicut columbae, ungit affectus: cum scientiam docet, ut simus prudentes sicut serpentes, illuminat intellectus. Illuminat, ut habeamus in nobis salem: ungit, ut habeamus inter nos pacem. In hoc igitur te nobis probabis filium olei splendoris, si suavem et unctum per benevolentiam, discretum et maturum per sapientiam te nobis exhibueris; ut suavitas veritate sit condita, et aequitate charitas ordinata. Puto autem quod hanc germinam virtutem sui, vel affectum muneris sui, propter quam splendor voluit dici, etiam in illo igne Spiritus sanctus significaverit, in quo ipse invisibilis invisibiliter Apostolis apparuit. Qui enim splendor fuit in aspectu oculorum, oleum, nisi fallor, fuit in sensu corporum: ut veluti in quodam lavacro olei viderentur sibi baptizati, cum super eos effunderetur ignis iste coelestis. Verumtamen qualiscunque fuerit in eis corporaliter sensus illius ignis (parum enim interest qualis sentiatur, sed qualiter operetur), illud, ut opinor, et probabilius dicitur, et religiosius creditur, quod idem ignis qui inflammavit et illuminavit corda, refrigeravit corpora: ut per charitatem mentes arderent, et per castitatem membra frigerent, et utrumque congrueret singulis, sive illud Jeremiae, De excelso misit ignem in ossibus meis (Thren. I, 13); sive illud Psalmistae, Caro mea immutata est propter oleum (Psal. CVIII, 24). Nisi forte aliquid de lege membrorum contra legem mentis relinquere voluit Spiritus, ut virtus in infirmitate perficeretur.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. I know that 'oil of splendor' can be understood as meaning that which proceeds from Splendor, the Son, or that which pours forth the splendor of illumination. But I think that, not unfittingly, it can also be taken appositionally, as 'oil, which is splendor.' For indeed the Spirit is both of these in his very nature—spiritual anointing, and invisible splendor—and he works both of these in us by the gift of himself. He anoints the affections insofar as he is oil; he illuminates the intellect insofar as he is splendor. Yet he is not oil from one source and splendor from another, but from one and the same self he is both oil and splendor, because he is nothing other than one and the same. He anoints the affections, because he is charity; he illuminates the intellect, because he is truth. He anoints the affections when he grants devotion; he illuminates the intellect when he reveals mysteries. When he teaches goodness, that we may be simple as doves, he anoints the affections; when he teaches knowledge, that we may be prudent as serpents, he illuminates the intellect. He illuminates, that we may have salt within us; he anoints, that we may have peace among ourselves. In this, then, you will prove yourself to us a son of the oil of splendor, if you show yourself to us sweet and anointed through benevolence, and discreet and mature through wisdom; so that sweetness may be seasoned with truth, and charity ordered by equity. I think, moreover, that the Holy Spirit signified this twofold power of his—or this affective working of his gift—on account of which he wished to be called splendor, even in that fire in which he, invisible, appeared invisibly to the Apostles. For what was splendor to the sight of their eyes was, unless I am mistaken, oil to the sense of their bodies: so that they seemed to themselves baptized as in a kind of bath of oil, when that heavenly fire was poured out upon them. Yet whatever the bodily sensation of that fire may have been in them (for it matters little how it was felt, but how it worked), this, I think, is both the more probable and the more devout belief: that the same fire which kindled and illumined their hearts also cooled their bodies, so that through charity their minds burned, and through chastity their members grew cool; and each saying fit the case—whether that of Jeremiah, 'He sent fire from on high into my bones' (Thren. I, 13), or that of the Psalmist, 'My flesh is changed because of oil' (Psal. CVIII, 24). Unless perhaps the Spirit wished to leave something of the law of the members at war with the law of the mind, so that power might be perfected in weakness.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Sed prosequamur quod proposuimus. Isti sunt, inquit, duo filii olei splendoris, qui assistunt Dominatori universae terrae (Zach. IV, 14). Ecce habes bonitatem in oleo, scientiam in splendore: accipe disciplinam in eo quod ait, qui assistunt Dominatori universae terrae; ut agnoscas eos vere discipulos illius fuisse cui cantamus, Bonitatem et disciplinam et scientiam doce me (Psal. CXVIII, 66). Haec est namque perfectio disciplinae, tam in mente, quam in corpore; ut proponentes Dominum in conspectu nostro semper, semper et ubique majestati aeternae, quae nos inspicit et judicat sine intermissione, cum metu et reverentia assistamus, pervigili fide ac jugi devotione. Sicut oculi, inquit, servorum in manibus dominorum suorum, ita oculi nostri ad Dominum Deum nostrum (Psal. CXXII, 2), intentissime et indeclinabiliter observantes nutus ejus, quid velit, quid jubeat, ut quam celerrime devotio nostra obediat. Sic Moyses invisibilem tanquam videns sustinebat, nec unquam imminentis metum judicis dissimulare poterat. Sic Elias et alii Prophetae qui dicebant: Vivit Dominus, in cujus conspectu sto (IV Reg. V, 16). Inde nimirum et gratiam, et nomen assecuti sunt Videntium; quoniam quae semper intuebantur per fidem non fictam, merebantur saepius intueri per speciem, licet factam. Haec fides vigil, non ficta, non dissimulatrix, ipsa est, ut arbitror, quae sola vel maxime facili compendio ad perfectionem perducit; quae gravitatem disciplinae, sobrietatemque modestiae, tam interiori quam exteriori nostro tribuit, et velut in disciplina famulantium Domino semper assistere facit. Hac virtute meruerunt Apostoli dici filii olei splendoris: ut sicut Domino astiterunt in terris contemplando per fidem, ita nunc ei assistant in coelis contemplando per speciem; Regemque in decore suo videant oculi eorum, cujus timorem hic meditabatur cor eorum. Hac via, fratres, sequimini Patres fidei vestrae, et auctores Ordinis, quatenus eorum provocati exemplis et adjuti suffragiis, quo ipsi hodie praecesserunt, pervenire valeatis, adjuvante Domino nostro Jesu Christo, qui vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. But let us continue what we have proposed. 'These,' he says, 'are the two sons of the oil of splendor, who stand before the Lord of all the earth' (Zach. IV, 14). Behold, you have goodness in the oil, knowledge in the splendor: receive discipline in what he says, 'who stand before the Lord of all the earth'; that you may recognize that they were truly disciples of him to whom we sing, 'Teach me goodness, and discipline, and knowledge' (Psal. CXVIII, 66). For this is the perfection of discipline, both in mind and in body: that, setting the Lord ever before our sight, we should always and everywhere stand before the eternal majesty—which beholds and judges us without ceasing—with fear and reverence, with ever-watchful faith and unfailing devotion. 'As the eyes of servants are on the hands of their masters, so are our eyes toward the Lord our God' (Psal. CXXII, 2), watching most intently and unswervingly for his least sign—what he wills, what he commands—so that our devotion may obey as swiftly as possible. Thus Moses endured, as one who saw him who is invisible, and could never put out of mind the fear of the Judge who was at hand. Thus Elijah and the other Prophets, who said: 'The Lord lives, in whose sight I stand' (IV Reg. V, 16). From this, surely, they obtained both the grace and the name of 'Seers'; because that which they always beheld through unfeigned faith, they often merited to behold through a vision—though a created one. This watchful faith, not feigned, not dissembling, is itself, I think, that which alone, or at least most readily and by the easiest path, leads to perfection; which bestows the gravity of discipline and the sobriety of modesty on both our inward and our outward self, and causes us, as it were in the discipline of servants, to stand always before the Lord. By this virtue the Apostles deserved to be called sons of the oil of splendor: so that just as they stood before the Lord on earth, contemplating through faith, so now they stand before him in heaven, contemplating through vision; and their eyes behold the King in his beauty, whose fear their heart meditated here below. By this way, brothers, follow the Fathers of your faith and the founders of your Order, so that, roused by their examples and helped by their intercessions, you may be able to arrive where they themselves have gone before this day, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.
