sermons.occasion: In natali Apostolorum Petri et Pauli

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric reads the bride's two breasts in the Song of Songs as Peter and Paul, who nourish the Church with the milk of doctrine. The heavenly Church grieved that its little sister had no breasts until the Spirit filled the apostles at Pentecost. Paul fed others with his words and was fed by their works; Peter received the revelation of the Son and the keys of heaven. The sermon appears under the heading for the Apostles Peter and Paul in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO II.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON II.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Quomodo fidelium animos alant apostoli.

passages.label: English
passages.text: How the apostles nourish the souls of the faithful.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Duo ubera tua sicut duo hinnuli capreae gemelli, qui pascuntur in liliis, donec aspiret dies, et inclinentur umbrae (Cant. IV, 5, 6). Videte, fratres, ne degeneretis. Ut taceam de nobilitate patris vestri, nobilis est mater quae vos genuit, generosa sunt ubera quibus lactati estis. Mater vestra est sponsa cui haec dicuntur, cujus ubera voce sponsi laudantur. Quae nimirum duo ubera Ecclesiae Petrum et Paulum esse, non solum interpretatur nobis dies ista, in qua potamur ab uberibus consolationis eorum satis jucunde et abunde; sed etiam evidentia operis ipsorum approbant argumenta ac monumenta doctrinae. Quibus enim aliis uberibus nutriti sunt filii Ecclesiae, sive ex praeputio, sive ex circumcisione? Istos utique ego reor esse, de quibus olim parvulae et pauperculae consolatio divina promittebat Ecclesiae: Reges nutritii tui erunt (Isai. XLIX, 23), et mammilla regum lactaberis (Isa. LX, 16). Nisi enim tam generoso lacte nutrita esset, nunquam ad hoc virtutis ac gloriae culmen excrevisset. Ad ubera parvulos Petrus invitabat, quibus dicebat: Sicut modo geniti infantes, lac concupiscite (I Petr. II, 2). Ubera Paulus praebuerat quibus dicebat: Lac vobis potum dedi (I Cor. III, 2); et illud; Factus sum in medio vestri sicut nutrix sedens et nutriens filios suos (I Thess. II, 7). Quam plenus autem lacte redundaverit spirituali, pulchre significatum est unda illius lactis visibilis, quod de corpore ipsius fertur exisse loco sanguinis, cum decollatus hodierna die pro illis, quibus dabat mammillam, dedit et animam. Plane nihil in eo sanguineum, sed totum lacteum; qui nihil carnale, nihil suum cogitabat, sed tantum quod aliis utile erat. Nec tam habebat ubera, quam ipse totus uber erat; qui ita misericordia uberi affluebat, ut non modo spiritum suum desideraret totum filiis immulgere, sed et corpus impendere.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a roe, which feed among the lilies, until the day break and the shadows retire (Cant. IV, 5, 6). Take care, brothers, that you do not degenerate. To say nothing of the nobility of your father, noble is the mother who bore you, and generous are the breasts at which you were nursed. Your mother is the bride to whom these words are spoken, whose breasts are praised by the voice of the bridegroom. That these two breasts of the Church are, without doubt, Peter and Paul, is interpreted for us not only by this present day, on which we drink from the breasts of their consolation most pleasantly and abundantly, but also the clear evidence of their work and the monuments of their teaching confirm it. For by what other breasts have the children of the Church been nourished, whether from the uncircumcised or from the circumcision? These, surely, I judge to be they of whom long ago the divine consolation promised to the little and poor Church: Kings shall be your nursing fathers (Isai. XLIX, 23), and you shall be suckled with the breast of kings (Isa. LX, 16). For unless she had been nourished with milk so generous, she would never have grown to this summit of virtue and glory. Peter invited little children to the breasts, to whom he said: As newborn babes, desire the milk (I Petr. II, 2). Paul had offered breasts to those to whom he said: I gave you milk to drink (I Cor. III, 2); and also this: I became in the midst of you as a nurse sitting and nourishing her children (I Thess. II, 7). How full he overflowed with spiritual milk is beautifully signified by that wave of visible milk which is reported to have flowed from his body in place of blood, when, beheaded on this very day for those to whom he gave the breast, he gave also his soul. Clearly nothing bloody was in him, but all was milky; for he thought nothing carnal, nothing of his own, but only what was useful to others. Nor did he so much have breasts, as he himself was wholly a breast; for he so abounded in overflowing mercy that he desired not only to pour out his whole spirit for his children, but also to spend his very body.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Antequam haec duo ubera, Petrum et Paulum, accepisset primitiva Ecclesia sanctorum in terris, conquerebatur et dicebat Ecclesia beatorum spirituum in coelis: Soror nostra parva est, et ubera non habet (Cantic. VIII, 8). Cum enim Christus rediens in coelum reliquisset pusillum gregem discipulorum, ac nondum misisset Spiritum suum, quo erant fetanda viscera, et implenda ubera sanctorum: erat, ut opinor, illa Ecclesia in coelis sollicita pro filiolis sponsi, sive jam natis, sive nascituris, cui videlicet committerentur alendi; eo quod Ecclesiam istam viderent parvam numero, virtute et auctoritate, et sine uberibus doctrinae. Nam et ipse Sponsus in diebus carnis suae genuerat aliquos verbo veritatis, et quandiu fuerat cum eis, lactaverat eos uberibus aedificationis et consolationis. Et ipse siquidem Sponsus habet ubera meliora vino (Cant. I, 1), id est, doctrina legali, vel gaudio saeculari. Habet, inquam, Sponsus ubera, ne ullum de omnibus officiis et nominibus pietatis eum praetereat: ut qui pater est creatione naturae, vel regeneratione gratiae, seu etiam auctoritate disciplinae, sit etiam mater affectu clementiae, sit et nutrix sedulitate officii curae. Erant igitur parvuli, quos alebat initium aliquod creaturae ejus, sed nonnisi initium: multumque supererat curae et laboris, donec adducerentur ad perfectum, et formaretur Christus in eis. Cum autem et ipse reliquisset eos; superni spiritus, etsi laeti de reditu Unigeniti, de nova tamen adoptionis progenie solliciti, quodammodo affectu suo videbantur apud eum conqueri: Quis illos nutriet? Lactasti eos, sed ante tempus ablactasti. Non enutristi juvenes, nec ad incrementum perduxisti virgines: quis illos nutriet? Soror nostra parva est, et ubera non habet. Dixisti Petro: Pasce agnos meos (Joan. XXI, 15, 16): sed nec ipse adhuc sufficientiam lactis in uberibus habet. Cito pietas ejus aresceret, qui plus adhuc cuti suae quam animabus parvulorum timet. Facile relinqueret agnos in tentatione, qui Pastorem tam suum quam illorum negavit in interrogatione. Ecce autem repente Spiritu misso de coelo, tanquam lacte de propriis Christi uberibus effuso, Petrus impletus est lacte plurimo: nec multo post de Saulo fit Paulus, praedicator de persecutore, mater de tortore, nutrix de carnifice; ut plane intelligeres totum ejus sanguinem mutatum in lactis dulcedinem, saevitiam in pietatem.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Before the primitive Church of the saints on earth had received these two breasts, Peter and Paul, the Church of the blessed spirits in heaven was complaining and saying: Our sister is little, and has no breasts (Cantic. VIII, 8). For when Christ, returning to heaven, had left behind a tiny flock of disciples, and had not yet sent his Spirit, by which the wombs of the saints were to conceive and their breasts to be filled, that Church in heaven was, I suppose, anxious for the little children of the bridegroom, whether already born or yet to be born, to whom they were to be entrusted for nourishing—because they saw this Church to be small in number, in power and in authority, and without the breasts of doctrine. For the Bridegroom himself, in the days of his flesh, had begotten some by the word of truth, and as long as he was with them had suckled them with the breasts of edification and consolation. For indeed the Bridegroom himself has breasts better than wine (Cant. I, 1), that is, better than the teaching of the law, or than worldly joy. The Bridegroom has breasts, I say, lest any of all the offices and titles of piety should pass him by: so that he who is father by the creation of nature, or by the regeneration of grace, or even by the authority of discipline, might also be mother by the affection of his clemency, and nurse by the diligence of his caring office. There were, then, little children, whom he was nourishing, a kind of beginning of his creation, but only a beginning: and much of care and labor still remained, until they should be brought to perfection, and Christ be formed in them. But when he too had left them, the spirits above, though rejoicing at the return of the Only-begotten, yet anxious about the new offspring of adoption, seemed in a way, by their own affection, to complain before him: Who will nourish them? You have nursed them, but you have weaned them before their time. You have not nourished the young men, nor brought virgins to full growth: who will nourish them? Our sister is little, and has no breasts. You said to Peter: Feed my lambs (Joan. XXI, 15, 16); but even he does not yet have sufficiency of milk in his breasts. Quickly would his devotion wither, who still fears more for his own skin than for the souls of the little ones. Easily would he abandon the lambs in temptation, who denied the Shepherd, both his own and theirs, under questioning. But behold, suddenly, the Spirit having been sent from heaven, as if milk had been poured out from Christ's own breasts, Peter was filled with abundant milk: and not long after, Saul became Paul—a preacher from a persecutor, a mother from a torturer, a nurse from an executioner; so that you might clearly understand that all his blood had been changed into the sweetness of milk, and his savagery into tenderness.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. His igitur uberibus geminis pectori suo affixis gloriatur Ecclesia, non modo matrem se esse fecundam, sed et civitatem munitam. Ego, inquit, murus, et ubera mea turris (Cantic. VIII, 10). Mille clypei pendent jam de turribus istis, omnis armatura fortium. Ipse quoque sponsus de eisdem uberibus in laudem sponsae in carmine amoris, mystico sermone sic ait: Duo ubera tua sicut duo hinnuli capreae gemelli (Cant. IV, 5). Capream hoc loco accipimus Ecclesiam; acutam visu ad penetranda mysteria Christi, agilem saltu ad transilienda spinosa hujus saeculi, potentem ad exsuperanda venena serpentis antiqui. Cujus duo gemelli non inconvenienter, ut arbitror, intelliguntur hi duo Apostoli; germani fide, consimiles devotione, pares merito et virtute, unanimes charitate, conjuncti in ipsa etiam passione et morte. Quomodo enim in vita sua dilexerunt se, ita et in morte non sunt separati. Quia vero desideria summorum pascuntur in profectibus minorum, donec scilicet aspirante gratia tollant se ad contemplandum sublimia, bene de his hinnulis subditur: Qui pascuntur in liliis, donec aspiret dies, et inclinentur umbrae (Cant. II, 16, 17). Animalia cum declinant aestum diei, captant umbrosa pascua convallium, ubi et liliorum solet esse proventus uberior, donec spirante tepescentis aura vesperi, egrediantur ad aperta camporum, vel ardua montium. Sic et hinnuli nostri quandiu non aspirat eis ad contemplandum clementior aura diei aeterni, pascuntur in liliis convallium; id est, delectantur in virtutibus humilium, aut etiam occupantur in actionibus eorum. Cum autem aspirat dies ille mentibus eorum, egrediuntur et saliunt ad uberiora et feliciora pascua montium aeternorum. Per me, inquit Pastor et ostium, si quis introierit salvabitur, et ingredietur Ecclesiam, et egredietur saepius contemplando, semel migrando ad coelestem patriam; et pascua inveniet, et hic, et ibi. Hic, inter lilia agri; ibi, inter ligna paradisi: hic, in floribus; ibi, in fructibus: hic, in virtutibus sanctorum; ibi, in gaudiis Angelorum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. With these two breasts, then, fastened to her bosom, the Church glories not only that she is a fruitful mother, but also a fortified city. 'I,' she says, 'am a wall, and my breasts are a tower' (Cantic. VIII, 10). A thousand shields now hang from these towers, the whole armory of the mighty. The Bridegroom himself, too, speaking of these same breasts in praise of the Bride, in the song of love, says in mystical language: 'Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a roe' (Cant. IV, 5). By 'roe' here we understand the Church: sharp of sight to penetrate the mysteries of Christ, nimble in leaping to spring over the thorns of this world, strong to overcome the poisons of the ancient serpent. Her two twin fawns, I think, are not unfittingly understood to be these two Apostles: brothers in faith, alike in devotion, equal in merit and virtue, of one mind in charity, joined even in their very passion and death. For as they loved one another in life, so in death they were not separated. Now because the desires of the highest are fed on the progress of the lesser, until, that is, with grace breathing upon them they lift themselves up to contemplate things sublime, it is rightly added of these fawns: 'Who feed among the lilies till the day break, and the shadows retire' (Cant. II, 16, 17). Animals, when they avoid the heat of the day, seek out the shaded pastures of the valleys, where too the growth of lilies is usually more abundant, until, as the cooling breeze of evening breathes, they go out to the open fields or the steep mountains. So too our fawns, so long as the gentler breeze of the eternal day does not breathe upon them for contemplation, feed among the lilies of the valleys; that is, they delight in the virtues of the humble, or are even occupied in their actions. But when that day breathes upon their minds, they go out and leap to the richer and happier pastures of the eternal mountains. 'By me,' says the Shepherd and the door, 'if any man enter in, he shall be saved'; and he shall enter the Church, and shall go out—often by contemplating, once by passing over to the heavenly homeland—and he shall find pastures, both here and there. Here, among the lilies of the field; there, among the trees of paradise: here, in flowers; there, in fruits: here, in the virtues of the saints; there, in the joys of the Angels.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Prorsus in loco pascuae ibi me Dominus collocavit, cum ecclesiae sanctorum associavit, cujus venter sicut acervus tritici vallatus liliis (Cant. VII, 2), ut pascat simul et tritici gustu, et liliorum aspectu. Quid enim acervus tritici, nisi copia divini sermonis in tot libris undique congestis? Quid lilia, nisi justi qui germinant sicut lilium, et florent immarcessibiliter ante Dominum; quorum tantus candor in sanctimonia corporis et cordis puritate, tanta fragrantia in opinione, tanta medicinalis virtus in opere et sermone? Non mediocre pabulum istud fideli animae, videre circa se tot lilia tanta venustate et gratia florentia, ubi omnium virtutum ex eis, licet diversarum ex diversis, capere possit exempla. Iste fundatior humilitate, ille amplior charitate. Alius robustior ad patientiam, alius velocior ad obedientiam. Iste frugalitate parcior, ille labore utilior: iste devotior in oratione, ille in lectione studiosior: iste in administratione prudentior, ille in quiete sanctior. Sed licet aliquam insignius florentem in unoquoque gratiam mireris, non una tamen, sed multae virtutes in singulis, sicut flores in liliis. Quot enim justi, tot lilia: quot virtutes eorum, tot flores liliorum. Qui igitur haec videns gaudet in illis, aut etiam proficit ex illis, quid, nisi pascitur in liliis?

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Indeed, it was there, in that place of pasture, that the Lord set me, when he joined me to the church of the saints, whose belly is like a heap of wheat set about with lilies (Cant. VII, 2), so that it may feed at once by the taste of the wheat and the sight of the lilies. For what is the heap of wheat but the abundance of the divine word, gathered together from so many books on every side? And what are the lilies but the just, who spring up like the lily and flower unfadingly before the Lord; whose whiteness is so great in the holiness of body and purity of heart, whose fragrance so great in reputation, whose healing power so great in deed and word? It is no small pasture for a faithful soul to see around it so many lilies flowering with such beauty and grace, where it may gather examples of all the virtues from them, though these be diverse virtues from diverse persons. This one is more firmly grounded in humility, that one more abundant in charity. One is stronger for patience, another swifter for obedience. This one is more sparing in frugality, that one more useful in labor; this one more devout in prayer, that one more studious in reading; this one more prudent in administration, that one more holy in quiet. But although in each you may admire some one grace flowering more conspicuously, yet there is not one virtue alone, but many, in each, as there are many flowers in lilies. For as many as the just, so many the lilies; as many as their virtues, so many the flowers of the lilies. He, then, who, seeing these things, rejoices in them, or even profits by them—what is he doing, but feeding among the lilies?

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Pascebat Paulus: sed nihilominus in illis quos pascebat. Pascebat eos sermonibus, pascebatur eorum operibus. Ventrem quidem suum, imo et alienum pascebat manibus propriis (Act. XX, 34; I Cor. IV, 12; I Thess. II, 9, et II Thess. III, 8): mentem vero non tam suis pascebat bonis quam alienis, qui non quaerebat quod sibi utile, sed quod aliis. Nunc vivimus, inquit, si vos statis in Domino (I Thess. III, 8). Quae enim gloria mea, aut gaudium, aut corona? Nonne vos ante Deum? (I Thess. II, 19; Philipp. IV, 1.) Ideo saepius ei spirabat dies aeterni luminis, atque afflabat eum lenior aura Spiritus sancti, cujus vi rapiebatur ad interna pascua, aliquando paradisi, aliquando tertii coeli, sive in corpore, sive extra corpus, nescio, inquit, Deus scit (II Cor. XII, 3). Dignum quippe erat, ut qui fideliter pascebat, fideliter pasceretur: et qui foris gaudebat in bonis dominicae familiae, in gaudium Domini sui juberetur intrare, atque repleretur in bonis domus Dei, non solum istius visibilis, pro qua sudabat, sed etiam illius invisibilis, ad quam spirabat, unde et dies ei aspirabat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Paul fed others, but nonetheless was himself fed in those whom he fed. He fed them with his words, and was fed by their works. His own belly indeed—nay, even that of others—he fed with his own hands (Act. XX, 34; I Cor. IV, 12; I Thess. II, 9, et II Thess. III, 8); but his mind he fed not so much with his own goods as with those of others, for he sought not what was profitable to himself, but what was profitable to others. 'Now we live,' he says, 'if you stand fast in the Lord' (I Thess. III, 8). 'For what is my glory, or my joy, or my crown? Are you not it, before God?' (I Thess. II, 19; Philipp. IV, 1.). Therefore the day of eternal light breathed upon him the more often, and the gentler breeze of the Holy Spirit blew upon him, by whose power he was caught up to the inward pastures, now of paradise, now of the third heaven—'whether in the body, or out of the body, I know not,' he says, 'God knows' (II Cor. XII, 3). It was indeed fitting that he who fed others faithfully should himself be faithfully fed, and that he who outwardly rejoiced in the goods of the Lord's household should be bidden to enter into the joy of his Lord, and be filled with the good things of the house of God—not only of that visible house, for which he toiled, but also of that invisible one, toward which he breathed, whence also the day breathed upon him.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Nec minora de beato Petro sentienda puto, cum maxima sit gloria Pauli, illius coaequari meritis, quem judicium Veritatis potestate et primatu praetulit universis. Cum enim Pater qui est in coelis veritatem Unigeniti Petro revelabat (Matth. XVI, 2-6), quid aliud quam dies ei aeternus aspirabat, et dies diei verbum eructabat? Cui autem magis pervium fuisse coelum credendum est, quam ipsi Janitori, cujus lingua clavis coeli facta est? Qui potestatem habebat claudere coelum nubibus, et aperire portas ejus, quomodo ipse non saepius intrasse credetur? Esuriit aliquando Petrus, et coelum ei apertum est, cum adhuc in terra consisteret; tantaque ei inde ciborum copia missa est, ut adhuc multa supersint, licet plurima mactaverit, et manducaverit, immunda et virulenta animalia in sancta et florulenta convertens lilia (Act. X, 10-16): ut videlicet deliciose pasceretur in liliis, donec aspirante die, gloriose in ipsis pasceretur coelis. Sed ecce dum commendamus vobis duo haec ubera sponsae, hora jam praeteriit, qua de ipsis uberibus lac vobis cupiebamus immulgere: quanquam et aliis diebus hoc ipsum facere possimus et soleamus. De uberibus siquidem Apostolorum lac vobis trahimus, quoties de verbis eorum ad aedificationem vestram tractamus. Nunc igitur pro tempore satis sit admonere, si tamen moneri indigetis, ut sicut ubera ista diligitis, ita lac eorum semper concupiscatis; ut in eo crescatis in salutem, donec formatum in vobis exhibeatis Salvatorem Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum, qui vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. I think we should judge no less highly of blessed Peter, since it is Paul's greatest glory to be made equal in merits to him whom the judgment of Truth preferred above all others in power and primacy. For when the Father who is in heaven revealed to Peter the truth concerning the Only-Begotten (Matth. XVI, 2-6), what else was this but that the eternal day breathed upon him, and day uttered speech unto day? And to whom must heaven be believed to have been more open than to that very Doorkeeper, whose tongue was made the key of heaven? He who had the power to shut heaven with clouds, and to open its gates — how shall he not be believed to have entered it the more often himself? Once Peter hungered, and heaven was opened to him while he still stood on earth; and so great an abundance of food was sent to him from there, that much still remained over, although he had already slaughtered and eaten many unclean and venomous creatures, turning them into holy and flowering lilies (Act. X, 10-16): so that, to be sure, he might be fed delightfully among lilies, until, when the day breaks,, he might be fed gloriously in the very heavens themselves. But behold, while we commend to you these two breasts of the Bride, the hour has already passed in which we desired to draw out for you the milk from those very breasts — although on other days we are able, and are accustomed, to do this very thing. For indeed we draw milk for you from the breasts of the Apostles, as often as we treat of their words for your edification. For now, then, let it suffice for the time to admonish you, if indeed you need admonishing, that just as you love these breasts, so you may always long for their milk; that in it you may grow unto salvation, until you show forth, formed in you, the Saviour Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The Father's revelation to Peter is Matthew 16:17. The edition prints Matth. xvi, 2-6.

sermons.occasion: In natali Apostolorum Petri et Pauli

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Pressed by the brothers, Guerric finishes the verse he began the day before: "Until the day breathe, and the shadows be inclined." He distinguishes shadows that chill and darken the soul from those that cool and enlighten it, and holds that even the clearest vision of this life is a bright shadow in a mirror. He invites the laboring brothers to rest in the shade of Christ, and warns against the heavy shade of worldly cares in which Leviathan sleeps. The sermon appears under the heading for the Apostles Peter and Paul in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO III.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON III.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De eo quod scriptum est: « Donec aspiret dies, et inclinentur umbrae. » (Cant. II, 17).

passages.label: English
passages.text: On what is written: "Until the day breathe, and the shadows be inclined." (Cant. II, 17).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Erratis, fratres, in me; sed amore magis, ut arbitror, aut humilitate, quam temeritate. Putatis me Scripturarum scientiam habere, qui vix unquam attigi vel primum limen scientiae. Displicet enim vobis, ut mihi videtur, quod capitulum Scripturae, de quo heri sum locutus, non sum ad finem usque persecutus: quasi illa mihi sit facultas, ut valeam Scripturas explanare, aut etiam explanationes aliorum digne et congrue ad memoriam revocare. Sed neque hoc mihi solet propositum esse, ut Scripturam, unde sermonem ordior, exponam; sed ut de ipsa, et secundum ipsam sermonem debitum suo diei persolvam. Huc accedit quod magister noster (10) ille interpres Spiritus sancti, de toto illo carmine nuptiali loqui instituit, spemque nobis dedit ex eis quae jam edidit, quia si pervenerit ad locum de quo quaeritis, donec aspiret dies, et inclinentur umbrae, umbras ipsas ponat in lucem intelligentiae: quod dictum est vel erit in tenebris, nobis dicet in lumine. Vos tamen dicitis, et recte dicitis, quia vetera novis supervenientibus projicietis; quantoque magis incondita seu rancida fuerint vetera nostra, tanto nova illius sapidiora erunt et gratiora. Nam et ipse Jesus servat vivum bonum usque ad extremum, sciens utique quomodo nostro sit fastidio medendum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. You are mistaken about me, brothers; but out of love, I think, or out of humility, rather than out of rashness. You suppose me to have knowledge of the Scriptures—I who have scarcely ever touched even the first threshold of knowledge. For it displeases you, as it seems to me, that I did not pursue to its end the chapter of Scripture of which I spoke yesterday: as though I had the capacity to explain the Scriptures, or even to recall to memory, worthily and fittingly, the explanations of others. But it has never been my custom to set out to expound the Scripture from which I begin my sermon; rather, my aim is to pay to each day the sermon owed to it, drawn from and in accordance with that Scripture. To this is added the fact that our master (10), that interpreter of the Holy Spirit, has undertaken to speak on that whole nuptial song, and has given us hope, from what he has already set forth, that if he should come to the passage you are asking about—"until the day breathe, and the shadows be inclined"—he will set those very shadows into the light of understanding: what has been said, or will be said, in darkness, he will tell us in the light. Yet you say, and you say rightly, that you will cast aside the old things when the new ones come; and the more unrefined or stale our old things have been, the more savory and pleasing the new ones from him will be. For Jesus himself keeps the living good even to the last, knowing well how our distaste is to be remedied.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Quia igitur cogitis me (nam impatientes dilationis vos video), nec spes incerta futuri praesenti satisfacit desiderio; ecce vobis morem gero, finemque versiculi, de quo heri loquebamur, suo, prout potero, reddam principio. Illud enim quaerere videmini, quid sit aspirante die spirituali umbras inclinari; cum magis consequens videretur, ut non crescere, sed minui tunc et deficere, dicerentur. Nam si sequamur proprietatem verbi, hoc est umbris crescere, quod inclinari: cum umbrarum ea natura sit, ut quanto inclinantur, tanto procumbant longiores; quantoque surgunt, tanto stent minores. Unde et poeta vesperum significans ait: Majoresque cadunt altis de montibus umbrae. (VIRG. Buc. eclog. 1.) Sed sciendum, quia cum haec proprietas umbrarum sit corporalium, longe alia est spiritualium, de quibus non dubitamus hic loqui Spiritum sanctum. Nam sicut corporalibus umbris inclinari est crescere, sic spiritualibus hoc est inclinari, quod deponi, minui, vel deficere. Umbrae autem spirituales sunt umbrosi spiritus et tetri, seu daemonum, seu hominum: umbrae sunt tenebrae errorum: umbrae sunt obscurae significationes veterum sacramentorum. Et umbrae quidem significationum jam inclinatae sunt ad occasum et finem: umbrae autem errorum de die in diem inclinantur ad diminutionem: umbrae vero tenebrosorum spirituum tandem inclinabuntur in infernum et mortem. Primum quidem factum est, cum dies aeternus aspiravit, apparens in carne: secundum quotidie fit, cum magis ac magis aspirat illustrans veritate: tertium novissime fiet, cum aspirabit rutilans in majestate.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Since, then, you compel me (for your impatience at delay is plain to me), and an uncertain hope of the future does not satisfy a present desire; behold, I will indulge you, and will render, as best I can, the end of the little verse we were discussing yesterday, together with its own beginning. For you seem to be asking what it means for the shadows to be inclined when the spiritual day breathes forth; whereas it would seem more fitting to say that then they are not increasing but diminishing and failing. For if we follow the proper sense of the word, for shadows "to be inclined" is the same as "to grow": since it is the nature of shadows that the more they are inclined, the longer they stretch out; and the more they rise, the shorter they stand. Whence the poet, signifying evening, says: "And longer shadows fall from the high mountains." But it must be understood that, while this is the property of bodily shadows, the case is far different with spiritual shadows, of which we do not doubt the Holy Spirit is speaking here. For just as for bodily shadows to be inclined is to grow, so for spiritual shadows to be inclined is to be laid down, diminished, or to fail. Now the spiritual shadows are the shadowy and gloomy spirits, whether of demons or of men: shadows are the darknesses of errors: shadows are the obscure significations of the old sacraments. And indeed the shadows of significations have already been inclined toward their setting and their end: but the shadows of errors are inclined, day by day, toward diminishment: while the shadows of the dark spirits will at last be inclined into hell and death. The first indeed came to pass when the eternal Day breathed forth, appearing in the flesh: the second happens daily, as he breathes forth more and more, enlightening with truth: the third will happen at the very last, when he will breathe forth glowing in majesty.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Videre autem mihi videor et alias umbras intra nos, quae velut in quodam speculo de rebus aliis nascuntur in sensu nostro, et obumbrant nobis, vel obumbrant nos. Obumbrant nos quae refrigidant et obscurant nos: obumbrant nobis quae refrigerant et illuminant nos. Istae quidem noxiae et graves, illae delectabiles et salubres, istae namque de inferioribus sunt et mundanis; illae, de superioribus et divinis. Anima nempe humana in quodam medio condita et posita est, ut sub ipsa esset mundus, supra ipsam Deus. Supra ipsam, a quo et ad quem et propter quem facta est: sub ipsa, quod propter ipsam factum est. Nam sicut propter animam corpus, sic propter corpus domus ejus, id est, mundus. Cum igitur incurvatur ad corporalia vel mundana, ascendunt in eam umbrae de inferioribus: cum erigitur ad divina, inclinantur super eam umbrae de superioribus. Illius enim rei quam cogitat, umbram sibi format. Quanquam de divinis satis dubia umbra est, quantumcunque cogitationis evacuatur acies: aut certe non umbra ipsius rei, sed aliud pro illa est, nisi cum aspirat dies ille. Nam tunc quoque non videtur, ut arbitror, nisi umbra, quae etsi luminosa, etsi gloriosa est, tamen umbra est; sicut cum in facie speculi tersa et lucida, splendidissimae rei splendens imago resultat. Caeterum videre faciem veritatis ipsius, vel veritatem faciei ejus, sicut nunquam erit hujus corporis: ita nec modo est hujus temporis, nec aliquando erit, donec corpus dissolvet mortalitas, aut absolvet immortalitas, et tempus absorbebit aeternitas, et spiritum qui nunc gravatur corpore et mutatur tempore, sublevabit ad se, et firmabit in se immortalis et immutabilis divinitas.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. But it seems to me that I can see other shadows within us as well, which, as it were in a kind of mirror, arise in our senses from other things, and either cast shade for us, or overshadow us. Those overshadow us which chill and darken us: those cast shade for us which cool and illuminate us. The former indeed are harmful and heavy, the latter delightful and wholesome; for the former come from lower, worldly things, the latter from higher, divine things. For the human soul has been established and placed in a kind of middle position, so that the world should be beneath it, and God above it. Above it is he from whom, and to whom, and for whose sake it was made; beneath it is what was made for its sake. For just as the body exists for the sake of the soul, so the soul's house—that is, the world—exists for the sake of the body. When, therefore, the soul bends down toward bodily or worldly things, shadows from the lower things rise up into it; but when it is lifted up toward divine things, shadows from the higher things are inclined over it. For of whatever thing it thinks upon, it forms for itself a shadow. Although, concerning divine things, the shadow is quite uncertain, however much the keenness of thought is emptied out: or rather, it is not the shadow of the thing itself, but something else in its place, except when that day breathes forth. For then too, I think, nothing is seen except a shadow—which, even though luminous, even though glorious, is nevertheless a shadow; just as when, on the face of a mirror polished and bright, the shining image of a most splendid thing is reflected back. But to see the face of truth itself, or the truth of its face, will never belong to this body—just as it is not now the lot of this present time, nor ever will be, until mortality dissolves the body, or immortality releases it, and eternity swallows up time, and the immortal and unchangeable divinity lifts up to itself, and establishes firmly in itself, the spirit which is now weighed down by the body and changed by time.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Initium hujus gratiae, et perfectionem illius gloriae Paulus satis proprie distinguebat, cum dicebat: Videmus nunc per speculum in aenigmate; tunc autem facie ad faciem (I Cor. XIII, 12). Ut autem et hoc ipsum sit, scilicet ut videamus per speculum et in aenigmate, opus est non solum ut facies speculi nostri ab omni phantasmate et umbra corporalium tersa sit: sed etiam ut ille sublimis, habitans lucem inaccessibilem, dignetur ad nos inclinari, et vel per umbram suae imaginis manifestari. Quantumcunque enim contendamus a visibilibus ad invisibilia, nihil nostra apprehendet humilitas, nisi condescendat illa majestas. Moyses ascendit in montem, et Dominus inclinavit coelos et descendit (Exod. XIX, 20). Et alius: Exsurge inquit in occursum meum, et vide (Psal. LVIII, 6). Ideo nec umbra videtur, nisi inclinetur; nec inclinari dicitur, nisi aspirante die: quia neque per speculum et in aenigmate possumus Deum videre, nisi inclinante se majestate, et aspirante favore gratiae. Sane hoc ipsum quod umbra vocatur comparatione manifestae veritatis, ineffabilis plerumque gloriae est et splendoris, in illis scilicet quorum est perlucidum speculum mentis. Cujus felicis experientiae Paulus sibi conscius, de se sibique similibus loquebatur: Nos vero omnes gloriam Domini speculantes, in eamdem imaginem transformamur a claritate in claritatem, tanquam a Domini Spiritu (II Cor. III, 18). Sic enim in promissione dictum est: Implebit splendoribus animam tuam (Isai. XVIII, 11.). Ut autem claritates istas umbras esse noveris, audi David: Dies mei, inquit, sicut umbra declinaverunt. Transibat quidem et ipse David de claritate in claritatem, tanquam de die in diem, Sed heu! tam breves et obscuros dies, tam longas et laboriosas noctes habet hiems ista, ut et propheta laborans in gemitu suo, lavansque per singulas noctes lectum lacrymis, merito plangat: Dies mei sicut umbra declinaverunt! (Psal. CI, 12.) Prorsus melior est dies una in atriis tuis super millia (Psal. LXXXIII, 11) dierum meorum; quia dies mei sicut umbra quamvis lucida: dies illa una, lux vera et mera, sicut sine umbra, sic sine vespera; cum dies meos faciat plurimos et brevissimos assidua longarum noctium interpolatio.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Paul distinguished quite properly the beginning of this grace and the perfection of that glory, when he said: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face" (I Cor. XIII, 12). But in order for this very thing to come about—namely, that we see through a glass and in a dark manner—it is necessary not only that the face of our mirror be wiped clean of every phantasm and shadow of corporeal things, but also that he who is exalted on high, dwelling in inaccessible light, deign to incline himself toward us, and be made manifest to us at least through the shadow of his image. For however much we strive to pass from the visible to the invisible, our lowliness will apprehend nothing unless that majesty condescends. Moses went up into the mountain, and the Lord bowed down the heavens and came down (Exod. XIX, 20). And another says: "Arise to meet me, and behold" (Psal. LVIII, 6). Therefore the shadow is not seen unless it is inclined; nor is it said to incline except when the day breathes forth: because we cannot see God through a glass and in a dark manner unless majesty inclines itself and the favor of grace breathes upon us. Indeed, this very thing which is called a shadow, in comparison with manifest truth, is for the most part of ineffable glory and splendor—namely, in those whose mirror of the mind is perfectly clear. Conscious of this happy experience, Paul spoke of himself and those like him: "But we all, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord" (II Cor. III, 18). For thus it was said in the promise: "He will fill your soul with splendors" (Isai. XVIII, 11.). But that you may know that these very splendors are shadows, listen to David: "My days," he says, "have declined like a shadow." David too was indeed passing from glory to glory, as it were from day to day. But alas! this winter has days so short and dark, and nights so long and laborious, that the prophet himself, laboring in his groaning and washing his bed every night with tears, justly laments: "My days have declined like a shadow!" (Psal. CI, 12.). Truly "better is one day in your courts" (Psal. LXXXIII, 11) than a thousand of my days; because my days are like a shadow, however bright; but that one day is true and pure light—as it is without shadow, so it is without evening—whereas my days are made very many and very brief by the constant interruption of long nights.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Caeterum, si quaeratur cur umbrae pluraliter dictae sint, cum res ipsa, cujus umbrae sunt, una sit: ideo nimirum, quia nunc minus, nunc amplius nobis Altissimi virtus obumbrat; nunc obscurius, nunc manifestius veritas sese nobis innotescens adumbrat: et sicut non aequaliter semper spirat, ita nec similiter semper nobis imagines format. Hoc et Apostolus innuit, qui transire se confitetur a claritate in claritatem (II Cor. III, 18), a minore scilicet in majorem: et propheta, qui non splendore sed splendoribus implendam promittit fidelem animam (Isai. LVIII, 11). Sic Jacobus Deum memorat patrem luminum (Jacobi I, 17), cum lumen, cujus pater est, et unum sit et unicum. Quanquam sic possit intelligi pater luminum, quomodo pater misericordiarum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Furthermore, if it be asked why the shadows are spoken of in the plural, when the thing itself, of which they are shadows, is one: it is doubtless because now the power of the Most High overshadows us less, now more; now the truth, making itself known to us, casts its shadow more obscurely, now more manifestly: and just as he does not always breathe upon us equally, so neither does he always form images for us in like manner. The Apostle hints at this too, confessing that he passes "from glory to glory" (II Cor. III, 18), that is, from a lesser to a greater glory; and the prophet, who promises that the faithful soul will be filled not with a splendor but with splendors (Isai. LVIII, 11). Thus James calls God "the Father of lights" (Jacobi I, 17), though the light of which he is Father is one and unique. Although it can be understood that he is called "Father of lights" in the same way he is called "Father of mercies."

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Jam vero vos fratres, qui laboratis portantes pondus diei et aestus, vel secundum Isaiam, in spiritu vestro duro meditamini per diem aestus (Isa. XXVII, 8), ad umbras istas placet invitare quas ille dies serenus aspirans rorem misericordiae cupit aestuantibus inclinare. Audite ipsum diem, ad umbrarum refrigeria clementer vos invitantem: Venite ad me, omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos (Matth. XI, 28). Servus enim sub sole laborans, ut ait Job, desiderat umbram (Job VII, 2), in qua scilicet a labore recreetur ad laborem, vel per horam dimidiam, qua silentium fit in coelo: quam cum obtinuerit indulgentia Prioris sui, gloriatur et dicit, Sub umbra illius, quem desiderabam, sedi. In qua nimirum umbra, quia non sola sessio est ad quietem, sed etiam refectio ad satietatem, congrue subdit: Et fructus ejus dulcis gutturi meo (Cantic. II, 3). Sic enim dictum est per prophetam: Convertentur sedentes in umbra ejus, vivent tritico et germinabunt sicut vitis (Osee XIV, 8). Servus seu mercenarius, quem saepius haec umbra recreaverit, longanimiter praestolabitur finem operis sui. Sic enim habes: Servus desiderat umbram, et mercenarius praestolatur finem operis sui (Job VII, 2). In umbra quidem non finis, sed pausatio. Finis enim erit operis remuneratio, cum evacuatis omnibus umbris, videbimus eum sicuti est: cui modo dicimus, In umbra tua vivemus inter gentes (Thren. IV, 20); inter angelos nempe, non in umbra, sed in luce manifesta.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Now, brothers, you who labor, bearing the burden of the day and the heat, or who, according to Isaiah, meditate in your hard spirit through the day of heat (Isa. XXVII, 8), it is fitting to invite you to these shadows which that serene day, breathing forth the dew of mercy, desires to incline toward those who burn with heat. Hear the Day himself, mercifully inviting you to the refreshments of the shadows: "Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you" (Matth. XI, 28). For the servant laboring under the sun, as Job says, desires the shadow (Job VII, 2), namely, that in it he may be refreshed from labor for labor, or at least for the half hour in which silence is made in heaven; and when he has obtained this by the indulgence of his Prior, he glories and says, "Under the shadow of him whom I desired, I sat." And because in this shadow there is not only sitting for rest, but also feasting to satisfaction, he fittingly adds: "And his fruit was sweet to my throat" (Cantic. II, 3). For so it is said through the prophet: "They that dwell under his shadow shall be turned, they shall live by the wheat and shall blossom as the vine" (Osee XIV, 8). The servant or hireling, whom this shadow has often refreshed, will patiently await the end of his work. For thus you have it: "The servant desires the shadow, and the hireling awaits the end of his work" (Job VII, 2). In the shadow, indeed, there is not the end, but a pause. For the end will be the reward of the work, when, all shadows having been emptied away, we shall see him as he is—to whom we now say, "Under your shadow we shall live among the nations" (Thren. IV, 20)—that is, among the angels, not in shadow, but in manifest light.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 7. Hoc autem notandum, quod cum umbrae illae de superioribus inclinantur supra nos, umbrae istae de inferioribus inclinantur infra nos. Cum enim divinis propinquamus, mundana superamus: et quatenus vel ad umbram lucis accedimus, eatenus mortis umbram evadimus. Lux enim et vita in coelo, mors in inferno: umbra autem mortis in hoc terreno et tenebroso loco. Cum igitur spiritus altius nos elevat inter terram et coelum, non tangimur umbra terrenorum: et licet nondum plena luce fruamur coelorum, tamen umbris illuminamur montium aeternorum, vel certe montis illius umbrosi et condensi, de quo venit Sanctus sanctorum. Mox tamen pondere nostro in regionem umbrae mortis revolvimur, ubi et diutissime sedere cogimur, donec visitatione orientis ex alto consolemur. Cogimur, inquam, et utinam cogamur, et non delectemur! utinam quod patimur, necessitatis tantum sit, non etiam voluntatis aut voluptatis! Sed heu! tam facile, tam libenter projicimus nos, et obdormiscimus sub gravi umbra juniperi spinosae et infructuosae arboris, tam negligentes et securi torpescimus et immorimur curis et desideriis hujus mundi! Propterea Leviathan, qui sub umbra dormit, cubile sibi, nisi praecaveamus, ponit in nobis; quia videlicet amicas sibi umbras hujus saeculi invenit in sensibus et affectibus nostris. Istae siquidem umbrae, teste Job, protegunt umbra ejus (Job. XL, 20, 17); quia nimirum curae et desideria saecularia, quae sunt in nobis, umbram nobis abscondunt imminentis damnationis, ut eam non praevideamus, donec in ipsam impingamus. Aspira, o dies dierum, obumbra supra caput nostrum in die belli, inclina super nos umbras salutis et refrigerii, et inclinentur subtus nos umbrae torporis et taedii, imo caecitatis et mortis. Et licet contingant nos umbrae de cogitatione terrenorum, non nos contegant tenebrae, id est, umbrae crassiores de amore eorum; sed semper respiremus in luminosum amorem tuum, o Pater luminum, qui vivis et regnas per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 7. Now this must be noted: that while those shadows from the higher things incline over us, these shadows from the lower things incline beneath us. For when we draw near to things divine, we rise above worldly things; and to the extent that we approach even the shadow of the light, to that extent we escape the shadow of death. For light and life are in heaven, death is in hell; but the shadow of death is in this earthly and darksome place. When, therefore, the spirit lifts us higher, between earth and heaven, we are not touched by the shadow of earthly things; and although we do not yet enjoy the full light of the heavens, nevertheless we are illumined by the shadows of the eternal mountains — or at least of that shadowy and dense mountain from which the Holy One of holy ones came. Yet soon, by our own weight, we are rolled back down into the region of the shadow of death, where we are forced to sit for a very long time, until we are consoled by the visitation of the Dayspring from on high. We are forced, I say — and would that we were only forced, and did not take delight in it! Would that what we suffer were a matter of necessity alone, and not also of will or of pleasure! But alas, how easily, how willingly we fling ourselves down and fall asleep under the heavy shadow of the juniper, a thorny and fruitless tree; so negligent and so unconcerned do we grow sluggish and lose ourselves in the cares and desires of this world! Therefore Leviathan, who sleeps beneath the shadow, makes his lair in us, unless we take care — because, indeed, he finds shadows of this age that are friendly to him in our senses and affections. For these shadows, as Job testifies, protect his shadow (Job. XL, 20, 17); because, truly, the worldly cares and desires that are in us hide from us the shadow of the damnation that hangs over us, so that we do not foresee it until we strike against it. Breathe upon us, O Day of days; overshadow our heads in the day of battle; incline over us the shadows of salvation and refreshment, and let the shadows of torpor and weariness — nay, of blindness and death — be inclined beneath us. And though the shadows that come from the thought of earthly things may touch us, let not the darkness — that is, the thicker shadows that come from the love of them — cover us over; but let us always breathe toward your luminous love, O Father of lights, who live and reign through all ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric of Igny reads the Purification's ceremony of lights through Simeon receiving Christ in the temple. Mary's obedience prompts a call to humility, bodily chastity and purity of heart; carrying a candle should express devotion and good deeds. Simeon cherishes the Word in flesh like light in wax, and Guerric invites his hearers to become lamps themselves. He develops the image through faith, charitable works, speech that builds up others, prayer and a sincere intention before God. The sermon closes by contrasting divine examination with the enduring light promised beyond death. The individual sermon is undated; its collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157 and is read here from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The source names the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, traditionally known as Candlemas.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Sint lumbi vestri praecincti, et lucernae ardentes in manibus vestris (Luc. xxii, 35). Sint lumbi nostri praecincti, ut Purificationem Mariae aemulemur; sint lucernae ardentes in manibus, ut gaudium Simeonis, lumen in manibus portantis, etiam visibili signo in nobis repraesentemus. Simus videlicet casti corpore, et mundi corde; et Purificationem Mariae expressimus: simus ardentes devotione, et lucentes opere; et cum Simeone Christum portamus in manibus. Maria tamen non tam purificata fuit, quam mysterium Purificationis commendavit, implendo legalem, significando spiritualem. Quid enim in ea purificandum esse potuit, quae virgo concepit, virgo peperit, virgoque permansit, imo quae ipso conceptu plane purificata fuit, si quid forte minus ante puritatis habuisset [alias habuit)? Quid, inquam, mundandum habuit conceptus ille, qui solus potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine (Job. xiv, 4), qui fontem quo immundus purificetur edidit, fontem domus David, qui hodieque patet indefesseque scatet in ablutionem peccatoris, et menstruatae? (Zach.. xiii, 1.) Suscepit tamen Mater totius puritatis, purgationis legitimae speciem, ut simul et obedientissimae humilitatis virtutem, et evangelicae purificationis insinuaret veritatem. Ubi nunc ille, qui tam fallaciter quam contumaciter praesumens de sanctitate, detrectat purgatoria poenitentium remedia subire? Esto quod sanctus sit; nunquid sicut sanctarum Sanctissima, quae Sanctum sanctorum peperit, Maria? Utinam, fratres mei, utinam nos illam haberemus humilitatem in peccatis nostris quam vere habuerunt sancti in virtutibus suis. Sed omittimus nunc istud, ut quod coepimus prosequamur. Ac primo quidem de illa spirituali Purificatione, quam Maria, offerens pro se et pro Filio par turturum aut duos pullos columbarum, nobis commendavit, prosequeremur, nisi quod patres nostri, sicut vobis notissimum est, omnia ad liquidum prosecuti sunt; et quomodo turtur ad castitatem carnis, columba ad simplicitatem mentis pertineat, diligenter discurrerunt; nec illud quidem praetereuntes, quid sit sacrificium de uno turture vel pullo columbino, quid holocaustum de altero. Hoc unum tamen adjicimus, quod quanto notiora nobis sunt mysteria, tanto districtius et justius eorum a nobis exiguntur opera; quia scienti bonum et non facienti, peccatum est illi (Jac. iv, 17); et servus sciens voluntatem domini sui, et non faciens digna, plagis vapulabit multis (Luc. xii, 47).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands (Luc. xxii, 35). Let our loins be girded, so that we may imitate Mary's Purification; let lamps be burning in our hands, so that by a visible sign we too may represent the joy of Simeon carrying the light in his hands. Let us be chaste in body and clean in heart, and we have expressed Mary's Purification; let us burn with devotion and shine in our deeds, and with Simeon we carry Christ in our hands. Yet Mary did not so much undergo purification as commend the mystery of Purification, by fulfilling the legal purification and signifying the spiritual one. For what could there have been in her needing purification, when she conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and remained a virgin; indeed, when in the very act of conceiving she was fully purified, if perhaps she had previously possessed any lesser degree of purity [variant: possessed)? What, I ask, did that conceived child have that needed cleansing, he who alone can make clean one conceived of unclean seed (Job. xiv, 4), who brought forth the fountain by which the unclean may be purified, the fountain of the house of David, which even today stands open and flows unceasingly for the washing of the sinner and the menstruating woman? (Zach.. xiii, 1.) Nevertheless, the Mother of all purity accepted the outward form of purification prescribed by the law, to convey both the virtue of most obedient humility and the reality of evangelical purification. Where now is the man who, presuming on his holiness as deceitfully as obstinately, refuses to undergo the cleansing remedies of penitents? Granted that he is holy: is he as holy as Mary, the Holiest of holy women, who bore the Holy of holies? Would that, my brothers, would that we had in our sins the humility that the saints truly had in their virtues! But we leave this aside now, to continue what we began. First, indeed, we would pursue that spiritual Purification which Mary commended to us by offering for herself and her Son a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, were it not that our fathers, as you well know, have treated everything with complete clarity. They have carefully explained how the turtledove pertains to chastity of the flesh and the dove to simplicity of mind, without passing over what is meant by the sacrifice of one turtledove or young pigeon and the whole burnt offering of the other. Yet we add this one point: the better known the mysteries are to us, the more strictly and justly are the deeds they require demanded of us; for to him who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin (Jac. iv, 17); and the servant who knows his master's will and does not act worthily will be beaten with many blows (Luc. xii, 47).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Relinquentes igitur quod tractatum est sufficienter, illud potius tractemus, si placet, quid haec pulcherrima Ecclesiae consuetudo luminarium hodie gestandorum, aut factum repraesentet, aut faciendum demonstret. Quanquam ne id puto quidem vobis incognitum, etiamsi nunquam sit auditum. Quis enim hodie, cereum ardentem gestans in manibus, non statim illius senis recordetur, qui, hodie Jesum accipiens in ulnas suas, Verbum in carne tanquam lumen in cera, ipsum esse lumen ad illuminationem gentium perhibebat? Erat profecto et ipse lucerna ardens et lucens, testimonium perhibens de lumine, qui ad hoc ipsum in Spiritu quo plenus erat, venit in templum, ut, suscipiens misericordiam tuam, Deus, in medio templi tui praedicaret ipsam esse misericordiam, et lumen populi tui. Vere tu, senex serene, lumen portabas non modo manibus, sed et sensibus; qui sic eras illuminatus, ut, cum tanto ante futuram illuminationem gentium tam clare videres, etiam nunc inter tenebras Judaicae infidelitatis, hodierna claritas fidei nostrae tibi coruscaret. Laetare jam, senior juste, vide jam quod praevidebas: discussae sunt mundi tenebrae, ambulant gentes in lumine tuo; plena est omnis terra gloria luminis illius quod occultum in sinu fovebas, imo quo sensus tuos refovebas. O fomes amoris, ipse amor suavis et dulcis ad refocillandam animam! Prorsus suavis et dulcis, etiam cum crucias et affligis; cruciatus feliciter delectans, sicut ignis salubriter refrigerans. Ignis iste, fratres, si in sinu absconditus fuerit, vestimenta non comburit; imo illum ignem exstinguit, qui, in sinu celatus, non modo vestimentum adurit, sed et quod vestitum est, depascit, id est, corpus et animam pariter, consumit. Deus, inquit, noster ignis consumens est (Deut. iv, 24), sed ignem consumentem; nam animam refovet, demulcet mentem, spiritum recreat, reparatque pereuntem. Hujus ignis vim Simeon non ignorabat, qui in sinu suo eum portare gaudebat, pectusque senile fotu illius calefaciebat. Quanto salubrius et suavius ignis iste senem nostrum calefecit, quam regem David Abisag Sunamitis? (III Reg. i, 17) nisi forte Abisag hic ignis idem fuit, sapientia scilicet, cujus amplexu non solum recalescunt frigidi, sed etiam reviviscunt mortui.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. Leaving aside, then, what has been sufficiently treated, let us consider instead, if you please, what past event this most beautiful custom of the Church, carrying lights today, represents, or what action it shows us we should perform. Yet I do not think even this is unknown to you, though you may never have heard it explained. For who today, carrying a burning candle in his hands, would not immediately remember that old man who today took Jesus in his arms, the Word in flesh like light in wax, and testified that he was the light to enlighten the nations? He himself, indeed, was also a burning and shining lamp, bearing witness to the light. In the Spirit who filled him he came into the temple for this very purpose: receiving your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple, to proclaim it to be the mercy and light of your people. Truly, serene old man, you carried the light in your understanding as well as in your hands. You were so enlightened that, while seeing so clearly so far in advance the future enlightenment of the nations, even then, amid the darkness of Jewish unbelief, the present brightness of our faith flashed before you. Rejoice now, righteous elder; see now what you foresaw: the world's darkness has been scattered, the nations walk in your light; the whole earth is full of the glory of that light which you cherished hidden in your bosom, or rather, by which you warmed your understanding. O kindling of love, love itself, pleasant and sweet for reviving the soul! Truly pleasant and sweet, even when you torment and afflict: a torment that brings happy delight, like a fire that gives wholesome coolness. This fire, brothers, if it is hidden in the bosom, does not burn the garments; rather, it extinguishes that fire which, concealed in the bosom, not only scorches the garment but devours what is clothed, that is, consumes body and soul together. Our God, it says, is a consuming fire (Deut. iv, 24), but one that consumes the consuming fire; for it warms the soul, soothes the mind, refreshes the spirit, and restores the one who is perishing. Simeon knew the power of this fire: he rejoiced to carry it in his bosom and warmed his aged breast with its heat. How much more wholesomely and pleasantly this fire warmed our old man than Abishag the Shunammite warmed King David! (III Reg. i, 17) Unless perhaps Abishag was this very same fire, namely wisdom, in whose embrace not only do the cold grow warm again, but even the dead return to life.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Amplectere igitur, o beate senex, sapientiam Dei, et recalescant atque recanescant quasi de novo sensus tui; astringe uberibus tuis misericordiam Dei, et erit senectus tua in misericordia uberi. Inter ubera, inquit, mea commorabitur (Cantic. i, 12), etiam cum reddam illum Matri suae, manebit apud me. Et cum inter materna ubera continebitur, nihilominus inter ubera mea commorabitur, et ubera quoque mea inebriabit misericordia uberi; etsi non quantum ubera Matris. Illa quippe sicut singulariter mater est summae misericordiae, sic excellenter habet ubera uberis misericordiae. Gratulor et gratificor tibi, gratia plena, quae misericordiam genuisti quam suscepi; cereum praeparasti, quem accepi. Tu ceram ministrasti suscepto lumini, Virgo virginum Virgini; dum incorrupta mater incorruptibile Verbum, incorrupta carne vestisti. Eia, fratres mei, ecce ardet cereus in manibus Simeonis, accendite et vos cereos vestros de illius mutuatione luminis, lucernas dico quas Dominus jubet esse in manibus vestris (Luc. xii, 35). Accedite ad eum, et illuminamini, ut non tam lucernas feratis quam ipsi lucernae sitis, lucentes intus et foris, vobis et proximis. Sit ergo lucerna in corde, sit in manu, sit in ore. Lucerna in corde luceat vobis: lucerna in manu vel ore luceat proximis Lucerna in corde, est pietas fidei; lucerna in manu, exemplum operis; lucerna in ore, sermo aedificationis. Non solum autem coram hominibus lucere nos necesse est per operationem et sermonem, sed et coram angelis, per orationem, coram Deo per intentionem. Lucerna nostra coram angelis est pura devotio, cum in conspectu angelorum psallimus sapienter vel oramus ardenter; lucerna coram Deo, simplex intentio, ut ei soli placeamus, cui nos probavimus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Embrace, then, blessed old man, the wisdom of God, and let your faculties grow warm and gray again, as though anew; clasp God's mercy to your breasts, and your old age will abound in mercy. Between my breasts, he says, he will dwell (Cantic. i, 12); even when I give him back to his Mother, he will remain with me. And when he is held between his Mother's breasts, he will nevertheless dwell between my breasts, and will also fill my breasts to overflowing with abundant mercy, though not as much as his Mother's breasts. For just as she is uniquely the mother of supreme mercy, so her breasts possess abundant mercy in an outstanding way. I rejoice with you and give you thanks, full of grace, who bore the mercy I have received; you prepared the candle I have taken. You supplied wax for the light that was received, O Virgin of virgins, for the Virgin, when as an uncorrupted mother you clothed the incorruptible Word in uncorrupted flesh. Come, my brothers: see, the candle burns in Simeon's hands. Light your own candles too by borrowing from his light, I mean the lamps the Lord commands to be in your hands (Luc. xii, 35). Come to him and be enlightened, so that you may not so much carry lamps as be lamps yourselves, shining within and without, for yourselves and your neighbors. Let there be a lamp, then, in the heart, in the hand, and in the mouth. Let the lamp in the heart shine for you; let the lamp in the hand or mouth shine for your neighbors. The lamp in the heart is the devotion of faith; the lamp in the hand, the example of deeds; the lamp in the mouth, speech that builds up. We must shine not only before men through deeds and speech, but also before angels through prayer, and before God through intention. Our lamp before angels is pure devotion, when in the sight of angels we sing psalms with understanding or pray fervently; the lamp before God is a single intention, to please him alone, to whom we have approved ourselves.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Et ne putemur, in his quae dicimus, sensus nostri somnia secuti fuisse; probemus nos potius in omnibus adhaesisse testimoniis Scripturae. Quod enim fides lucerna sit, testatur Salomon loquens de muliere forti, Non exstinguetur in nocte lucerna ejus (Prov. xxxi, 18); quod utique intelligimus, Non deficiet in tentatione fides ejus. Nam et de charitate, quae nihil aliud est quam fides operans per dilectionem, apud eumdem legimus Salomonem: Lampades ejus, lampades ignis atque flammarum. Aquae multae non poterunt exstinguere charitatem, nec flumina obruent illam (Cantic. viii, 6, 7). Quod opus bonum lucerna sit, lux ipsa veritatis indicat, cum ait, Sint lumbi vestri praecincti, et lucernae ardentes in manibus vestris (Luc. xii, 35): et, Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant opera vestra bona (Matth. v, 16). Quod sermo aedificationis lucerna sit, David dicit: Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, et lumen semitis meis (Psal. cxviii, 105). Et Petrus apostolus de sermone prophetico, cui benefacitis, inquit, intendentes, tanquam lucernae lucenti in obscuro loco (II Petr. i, 19). Declaratio quoque sermonum Dei illuminat, et intellectum dat parvulis (Psal. cxviii, 130), sive cum sermones evangelici declarant umbram legis, sive cum ipsi sermones tam Evangelii quam legis declarantur expositionibus dilucidis, qui non intelligentibus parvulis videbantur obscuri; et in lumine dicimus quod dictum erat nobis in tenebris. Ideo Philippus in figura cujuslibet ecclesiastici doctoris dictus est os lampadis, eo quod de ore ipsius ad illuminationem audientium coruscaret ignitum eloquium Domini. Sermonem autem Dei intelligo, fratres mei, quidquid spiritus ejus dignatione sua loquitur in vobis; omnem utique sermonem qui bonus est ad aedificationem fidei, in provocationem charitatis. Si quis ergo vestrum loquitur, quasi sermones Dei (I Petr. iv, 11); ut etiam in privatis colloquiis omnis sermo malus non procedat de ore vestro, sed si quis est ad aedificationem fidei, ut gratiam det audienti; ut qui audierit, dicat gratias agens tibi, Benedictus sermo oris tui, quia lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, et lumen semitis meis (Psal. cxviii, 105). De oratione autem quod et ipsa lucerna sit, maxime si divinitus sit illuminata, ex eo colligimus quod Salomon ait: Lucerna Domini spiraculum hominis, quae investigat omnia secreta ventris (Prov xx, 27). Lumen namque quod nobis orantibus vel psallentibus desuper aperitur, spiraculum vitae est, in quod suaviter respiramus. Hujus lucernae videtur Job recordari, cum in moerore tentationis recolens cum suspirio laetitiam praeteritae consolationis, ait: Quis mihi tribuat ut sim juxta menses pristinos, secundum dies quibus Deus custodiebat me, quando splendebat lucerna ejus super caput meum, et ad lumen ejus ambulabam in tenebris? (Job, xxix, 2, 3.) Caeterum quod lucerna haec dicitur investigare omnia secreta ventris, id est mentis; non illud esse putandum est, quod Dominus comminatur se scrutaturum in lucernis (Sophon. i, 12): cum istud gratiae sit illuminantis, illud judicii exquirentis. Nam et aliter investigat secreta ventris potio medici; aliter gladius carnificis. Jam vero de intentione, quod et ipsa dicatur lucerna, nemo est qui ambigat, si tamen evangelicum illud intelligat: Lucerna corporis tui est oculus tuus (Matth. vi, 22, et Luc. xi, 34).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. And lest we be thought, in what we say, to have followed the dreams of our own understanding, let us show instead that in everything we have kept to the testimonies of Scripture. For Solomon testifies that faith is a lamp when he says of the valiant woman, Her lamp will not be extinguished in the night (Prov. xxxi, 18); which we understand to mean, Her faith will not fail in temptation. Concerning charity too, which is nothing other than faith working through love, we read in the same Solomon: Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame. Many waters will not be able to extinguish charity, nor will rivers overwhelm it (Cantic. viii, 6, 7). That a good deed is a lamp is shown by the light of truth itself when it says, Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands (Luc. xii, 35); and, Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds (Matth. v, 16). That speech which builds up is a lamp, David declares: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths (Psal. cxviii, 105). And the Apostle Peter says of the prophetic word, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place (II Petr. i, 19). The unfolding of God's words also gives light and understanding to little ones (Psal. cxviii, 130), whether the words of the Gospel make plain the shadow of the law, or the words of both Gospel and law themselves are made plain by clear explanations, having seemed obscure to little ones who did not understand; and we speak in the light what was said to us in darkness. Thus Philip, as a figure of every teacher in the Church, was called the mouth of a lamp, because the Lord's fiery utterance flashed from his mouth to enlighten his hearers. By God's word, my brothers, I mean whatever his Spirit graciously speaks in you: every word, indeed, that is good for building up faith and stirring up charity. If any of you speaks, let him speak as the words of God (I Petr. iv, 11), so that even in private conversations no evil word may proceed from your mouth, but only such as serves to build up faith and give grace to the hearer; so that whoever hears may thank you and say, Blessed is the word of your mouth, for your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths (Psal. cxviii, 105). That prayer too is a lamp, especially when divinely illuminated, we gather from Solomon's saying: The breath of man is the Lord's lamp, which searches all the hidden places of the belly (Prov xx, 27). For the light opened to us from above as we pray or sing psalms is the breath of life, into which we breathe with delight. Job seems to remember this lamp when, in the sorrow of trial, recalling with a sigh the joy of past consolation, he says: Who will grant me to be as in former months, in the days when God guarded me, when his lamp shone above my head and by its light I walked in darkness? (Job, xxix, 2, 3.) Yet when this lamp is said to search all the hidden places of the belly, that is, of the mind, we must not suppose it to be the same as the Lord's threat to search with lamps (Sophon. i, 12): this belongs to illuminating grace, that to searching judgment. For a physician's medicine searches the hidden places of the belly in one way, an executioner's sword in another. As for intention, no one doubts that it too is called a lamp, provided he understands the Gospel saying: The lamp of your body is your eye (Matth. vi, 22, et Luc. xi, 34).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Ut igitur tot lucernas vobis, fratres, illuminetis, accedite ad fontem luminis, et illuminamini, Jesum dico, qui lucet in manibus Simeonis, ut scilicet fidem illuminet, opus illustret, sermonem homini subministret, orationem inflammet, intentionem purget; ut sive opere, sive sermone vel oratione quaeratis placere coram eo in lumine viventium, qui scrutari habet Jerusalem in lucernis suis (Sophon. i, 12), et examinare etiam lumen nostrum. His omnibus accensis, o fili lucis, jam non ambulabis in tenebris, nec timenda tibi erit sententia maledicti, Qui maledixerit patri, vel matri, exstinguetur lucerna ejus in tenebris (Prov. xx, 20), id est, deficiet consolatio hujus lucis, irruentibus undique hinc exterioribus, inde interioribus tenebris. Tibi enim, cui tot interius ardent lucernae, cum exstincta fuerit lucerna hujus vitae, orietur lux inexstinguibilis vitae, et quasi fulgor meridianus consurget tibi ad vesperum: et cum te consumptum putaveris, orieris ut lucifer, et tenebrae tuae erunt sicut meridies (Job. xi, 17, et Isai. lviii, 10). Non tamen erit tibi sol amplius ad lucendum per diem, aut splendor lunae illuminabit te; sed Dominus erit tibi in lucem sempiternam; quia Agnus lucerna est novae Jerusalem cui benedictio et claritas in saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Therefore, brothers, to light so many lamps for yourselves, come to the fountain of light and be enlightened: I mean Jesus, who shines in Simeon's hands, so that he may enlighten faith, make deeds radiant, supply man with speech, inflame prayer, and purify intention. Thus, whether by deed, speech, or prayer, you may seek to please him in the light of the living, before him who is to search Jerusalem with his lamps (Sophon. i, 12) and examine even our light. With all these kindled, O child of light, you will no longer walk in darkness, nor will you have to fear the sentence of the curse: Whoever curses father or mother, his lamp will be extinguished in darkness (Prov. xx, 20); that is, the consolation of this light will fail, as darkness rushes in from every side, outward darkness on one side and inward darkness on the other. For you, within whom so many lamps burn, when the lamp of this life is extinguished, the inextinguishable light of life will arise, and at evening a brightness like noonday will rise for you. When you think yourself consumed, you will rise like the morning star, and your darkness will be as midday (Job. xi, 17, et Isai. lviii, 10). Yet the sun will no longer serve to give you light by day, nor will the brightness of the moon illuminate you; rather, the Lord will be your everlasting light, for the Lamb is the lamp of the new Jerusalem, to whom be blessing and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The source numbers the sections 1, 2, 4, 4, 5; the repeated 4 is retained.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition includes an alternative Latin form after habuisset: [alias habuit). The English translates alias as “variant” and retains the mismatched brackets. Guerric’s conditional wording about Mary’s purity, and his distinction between Mary and the child conceived, are retained. The language about the menstruating woman comes from the sermon’s biblical quotation.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The opening quotation about lamps is printed with Luke 22:35, but comes from Luke 12:35. The reference to Abishag warming David is printed as III Regum 1:17; the episode is in modern 1 Kings 1:1–4. Both source references are retained.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The divine fire consumes the destructive fire while renewing the person. “Grow warm and gray again” preserves Guerric’s wordplay about age and warmth. He applies “Virgin” to Christ as well as to Mary, and develops the imagery of breasts, wax and light. His explanation of Philip as “mouth of a lamp” is his own interpretation. The contrast between a physician’s medicine and an executioner’s sword belongs to the sermon.
