passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Simeon and Anna receive Christ with longing, joy and praise. Guerric describes the encounter as an anointing of the heart, then reads the four figures in the temple as examples of prayer, devotion, humility and charity. The sermon appears in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO II.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON II.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Quanto sit affectu occurrendum Jesu advenienti.

passages.label: English
passages.text: With What Love We Should Go Out to Meet the Coming Jesus

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Sicut ad diem nativitatis, id est adventus Dominici, pertinuit illa gratiarum actio et vox laudis, Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini; et ad diem apparitionis, id est, nostrae illuminationis, illud quod sequitur: Deus Dominus et illuxit nobis, sic etiam quod subsequitur, Constituite diem solemnem in confrequentationibus [Vulg. in condensis] usque ad cornu altaris; non absurde, ut arbitror, pertinere dicetur ad hunc diem, nobis utique celebrem, frequentia solemni, diem scilicet Dominicae Praesentationis, quando a Matre solemniter ad altare praesentatus est Patri. Nam et in eo quod adjungitur, Deus meus es tu, et confitebor tibi; Deus meus es tu, et exaltabo te; confitebor tibi quoniam exaudisti me, et factus es mihi in salutem (Psal. CXVII, 26-28), quid tam convenienter accipimus quam fidem et confessionem Simeonis et Annae, quae et ipsa hora superveniens confitebatur Domino, et loquebatur de illo omnibus qui exspectabant consolationem Israel. (Luc. II, 38)? Bene ergo citharista noster monebat laetari Jerusalem et conventum facere in die tam solemni: Constituite, inquiens, diem solemnem in confrequentationibus usque ad cornu altaris (Psal. CXVII, 27). Non mediocris aut parum solemnis illa frequentia fuit, cum inde venit Jesus et Maria cum turba parentum inducentium puerum, ut facerent secundum consuetudinem legis pro eo (Luc. II, 27); inde occurrit Simeon et Anna cum turba exspectantium consolationem Israel, quibus testificati sunt de eo.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Just as that thanksgiving and voice of praise, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord," belonged to the day of the Nativity, that is, of the Lord's Advent; and just as what follows, "The Lord is God, and he has shone upon us," belonged to the day of the Appearing, that is, of our illumination; so too, I think, it may not unfittingly be said that what comes next, "Appoint a solemn day in the gatherings [Vulg. amid the thick boughs] even to the horn of the altar," belongs to this day — a day certainly made festive for us by a solemn gathering — namely, the day of the Lord's Presentation, when he was solemnly presented by his Mother to the Father at the altar. For in what follows, "You are my God, and I will give thanks to you; you are my God, and I will exalt you; I will give thanks to you, for you have heard me, and you have become my salvation" (Psal. CXVII, 26-28), what do we more fittingly understand than the faith and confession of Simeon and Anna, who, coming in at that very hour, gave thanks to the Lord and spoke of him to all who were awaiting the consolation of Israel (Luc. II, 38)? Well, then, did our harpist urge Jerusalem to rejoice and to hold assembly on so solemn a day, saying: "Appoint a solemn day in the gatherings, even to the horn of the altar" (Psal. CXVII, 27). That gathering was no mean or unimpressive one, when from one side came Jesus and Mary with the crowd of relatives bringing in the child, that they might do for him according to the custom of the law (Luc. II, 27); and from the other side Simeon and Anna came to meet them with the crowd of those awaiting the consolation of Israel, to whom they bore witness concerning him.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Non crediderim ego de hac solemnitate quae tam pium, tam laetum conventum habuit, illam fuisse prophetae querelam lacrymabilem, Viae Sion lugent, quia non est qui veniat ad solemnitatem (Thren. I, 4): nisi forte arguat paucos venisse de tanto populo qui erat in omni Judaea et Jerusalem. Ad comparationem siquidem tantae multitudinis pauci venerunt, et de ipsis paucis paucissimi, ut arbitror, eum receperunt, cum praesentem viderent diu exspectatum, sicut voce Patris par Malachiam fuerat repromissum: Ecce, inquit, veniet ad templum suum sanctum Dominator quem vos quaeritis, et Angelus testamenti quem vos vultis (Malach. III, 1). O Judaei, adest, ecce, Dominator quem vos quaeritis? cur offerentem se vobis non recipitis? Quaeritis et non quaeritis. Sed si quaeritis; quaerite: convertimini et venite (Isai. XXI, 12). Quaeritis qui redimat de manu hominum, non quaeritis qui redimat de manu daemonum. Quaeritis qui eruat de servitute Romanorum, non quaeritis qui eruat de captivitate vitiorum. Si vere utique liberatorem quaeritis, quaerite liberatorem animarum vestrarum, qui salvum faciat populum suum a peccatis eorum. Si quaeritis sublimem, quaerite prius humilem, quoniam, ut ait Daniel: Humillimum hominem constituet Deus super omne regnum (Dan. IV, 14). Si quaeritis dominatorem potentiae, quaerite prius doctorem justitiae, quia justitia firmabitur thronus ejus (Prov. XXV, 5), et justitia et judicium praeparatio sedis ejus (Psal. LXXXVIII, 15). Quia enim perfecte non quaeritis, ideo nec praesentem invenitis, sicut de vobis ipse praedixit: Quaerent me mali, et non invenient me, quia oderunt me (Joan. VII, 34-36). Quaerent absentem, nec invenient etiam praesentem, quia oderunt lucem mala eorum opera arguentem, cum sapientia non nisi per dilectionem possit quaeri, nedum inveniri. Simeon namque, quia pio et fideli quaerebat desiderio, quaesitum invenit, et inventum agnovit sine alterius indicio, sine humano scilicet testimonio. Nam Spiritus est qui testificatur quoniam Christus est veritas (I Joan. V, 6); virtus utique quae de ipso procedit, unctio docens de omnibus, quae de illo, singulariter secundum nomen suum uncto, multipliciter profluit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. I would not believe that of this solemnity, which had so devout and so joyful a gathering, there held true that tearful complaint of the prophet: "The ways of Sion mourn, because there is none that comes to the solemnity" (Thren. I, 4) — unless perhaps it be charging that few came, out of so great a people as was then in all Judea and Jerusalem. For in comparison with so great a multitude, few came; and of those few, I think, very few indeed received him, though they saw present before them him who had long been awaited, just as had been promised by the voice of the Father through Malachi: "Behold," he says, "the Ruler whom you seek shall come to his holy temple, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire" (Malach. III, 1). O Jews, behold — is the Ruler whom you seek present here? Why do you not receive him who offers himself to you? You seek, and you do not seek. But if you seek, then seek: turn and come (Isai. XXI, 12). You seek one who may redeem you from the hand of men; you do not seek one who may redeem you from the hand of demons. You seek one who may rescue you from servitude to the Romans; you do not seek one who may rescue you from captivity to vices. If indeed you truly seek a liberator, seek the liberator of your souls, who will save his people from their sins. If you seek one who is exalted, seek first one who is humble, since, as Daniel says: "God will set the most humble of men over every kingdom" (Dan. IV, 14). If you seek a ruler of power, seek first a teacher of justice, for "his throne shall be established by justice" (Prov. XXV, 5), and "justice and judgment are the preparation of his seat" (Psal. LXXXVIII, 15). For because you do not seek perfectly, therefore you do not find him even when he is present, just as he himself foretold concerning you: "The wicked will seek me, and will not find me, because they have hated me" (Joan. VII, 34-36). They will seek him absent, and will not find him even when present, because they hated the light that exposes their evil works, since wisdom cannot be sought — much less found — except through love. For Simeon, because he sought with pious and faithful desire, found what he sought, and recognized what he had found without any other indication, that is, without human testimony. For it is the Spirit who testifies that Christ is the truth (I Joan. V, 6) — namely, the power that proceeds from him, the anointing that teaches concerning all things, which flows forth in many ways from him who, uniquely according to his own name, is the Anointed One.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Quid autem putamus, fratres mei, unctus iste, qui ungit etiam quos non tangit, quomodo candidum et sanctum pectus senis nostri perunxerit, cum suscipiens eum in ulnas suas, astringeret eum uberibus suis, et gestiret includere, si posset, in intimis cordis sui? Quid, inquam, putamus ille suavis et mitis, qualem insinuabat seipsum castissimo sinui pii senis, qualis illabebatur medullis, quam delectabilem et salubrem, imo quam omnino ineffabilem se implicabat ossibus, inspirabat sensibus? Prorsus liquescebat unctus in unctionem, quasi ad ignem resolutus ad amplectentis amorem; ut nimirum doceret unctio quod dicit lectio, sed non discit nisi dilectio. Quomodo enim legis? Unguentum, inquit, exinanitum [Vulg. effusum] nomen tuum (Cantic. I, 2). Hoc siquidem unguentum exinanitur, cum a quadam duritia sui resolvitur, non ut pereffluat substantia illius, sed ut fluant aromata illius, ut quasi nihil habens solidi sentiri possit, teneri non possit. Aut certe magis anima senis liquescebat in amplexu hujus uncti, vel unguenti, ut diceret: Anima mea liquefacta est, ut dilectus meus infusus est mihi. Infusio itaque unctionis, testimonium est uncti. Haec seni testabatur de puero, Simeoni de Christo, tanquam spiritus veritatis et charitatis, veritate docens, charitate ungens et accendens, et omnia interiora gelidi senis ponens, quasi cum unguenta bulliunt. Motus bullientium unguentorum, aestus desideriorum: sonus eorum, jubilus affectuum pariter dicentium (si tamen aliquid exprimere valentium), Deus meus es tu, et confitebor tibi; Deus meus es tu, et exaltabo te (Isa. XXV, 1). Lumen ad revelationem gentium, et gloriam plebis tuae Israel (Luc. II, 32), annuntians te. Confitebor, inquam, tibi, quoniam exaudisti me, quotidie cum lacrymis dicentem, Quando consolaberis me? (Psal. CXVIII, 82.) Exaudisti me, et nunc demum Simeonem, id est, exauditum fecisti me; quia factus es mihi in salutem (Psal. CXVII, 28). Jesus mihi factus ex semine David secundum carnem, qui David et omnia fecisti secundum deitatem, omnibus quidem generaliter factus es in Salvatorem; sed mihi specialiter factus es in salutem, pectus morbidum perungens, vitalemque resuscitans calorem, animam refocillans, et oculos illuminans. Defecerat enim anima mea in salutare tuum, o Domine, Pater Domini mei Jesu Christi, defecerunt oculi mei in eloquium tuum, dicentes: Quando consolaberis me? (Psal. CXVIII, 82.) Factus eram sicut uter in pruina, frigidus corpore, aridus corde, spiritu marcidus, et totus desiderio languidus. Sed quia in verbum tuae promissionis supersperavi, non visurum scilicet me mortem, nisi viderem Christum tuum, quod speravi jam video, quod desideravi teneo, quod concupivi complector. Video Deum Salvatorem meum in carne mea, et salva facta est anima mea. Viderunt oculi mei salutare Dei, et illuminati sunt interiores oculi mei, qui languebant prae inopia. Omnino ad tactum hujus pueri, hujus hominis novi, renovata est ut aquilae juventus mea, sicut paulo ante mihi loquens pollicebar. Introibo ad altare Dei, ubi Maria Jesum offert Patri, ad Deum qui laetificat senectutem meam, imo renovabit juventutem meam (Psal. XLII, 4).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. But what do we think, my brothers, as to how this Anointed One—who anoints even those he does not touch—anointed the white and holy breast of our old man, when, taking him up into his arms, he pressed him to his breast and longed, if he could, to enclose him in the innermost depths of his heart? What, I say, do we think—how sweet and gentle he was, in the way he insinuated himself into the most chaste bosom of the devout old man, how he glided into his inmost marrow, how delightful and health-giving—nay, how utterly ineffable—was the way he entwined himself in his bones and breathed himself into his senses? Truly the Anointed was melting into anointing, as though dissolved by fire into the love of the one embracing him; so that the anointing itself might teach what the reading tells, but which only love can learn. For how do you read? 'Your name,' it says, 'is an ointment emptied out [Vulg. poured out]' (Cantic. I, 2). This ointment indeed is emptied out when it is dissolved from a certain hardness of itself, not so that its substance flows entirely away, but so that its fragrant spices may flow forth, so that, having as it were nothing solid, it may be perceptible but not graspable. Or rather, the old man's soul was melting in the embrace of this Anointed One, or of this ointment, so that he might say: 'My soul has melted, as my beloved has been poured into me.' The pouring-in of the anointing, then, is the testimony of the Anointed One. This it testified to the old man concerning the child, to Simeon concerning Christ, as the Spirit of truth and of love, teaching by truth, anointing and kindling by love, and setting all the inward parts of the chilled old man aglow, as it were, when ointments come to a boil. The stirring of boiling ointments is the ardor of desires; their sound is the jubilation of affections speaking together (if indeed anything can be expressed), 'You are my God, and I will give thanks to you; you are my God, and I will exalt you' (Isa. XXV, 1). 'A light for the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel' (Luc. II, 32), announcing you. I will give thanks to you, I say, because you have heard me, day after day saying with tears, 'When will you console me?' (Psal. CXVIII, 82.). You have heard me, and now at last you have made Simeon—that is, you have made me—one who is heard; because you have become my salvation (Psal. CXVII, 28). Jesus, made for me of the seed of David according to the flesh, you who made David and all things according to your Godhead, have become Savior of all generally; but to me specially you have become salvation, anointing my sick breast, reviving my vital warmth, refreshing my soul, and enlightening my eyes. For my soul had fainted for your salvation, O Lord, Father of my Lord Jesus Christ, my eyes had failed for your word, saying, 'When will you console me?' (Psal. CXVIII, 82.). I had become like a wineskin in the frost, cold in body, dry in heart, withered in spirit, and altogether languishing with desire. But because I had hoped beyond hope in the word of your promise, namely that I should not see death unless I had seen your Christ, what I hoped for I now see, what I desired I now hold, what I longed for I now embrace. I see God my Savior in my flesh, and my soul has been saved. My eyes have seen the salvation of God, and my inward eyes, which were failing for want, have been enlightened. Altogether, at the touch of this child, this new man, my youth has been renewed like the eagle's, just as a little while ago I was promising myself, speaking to myself. 'I will go in to the altar of God, where Mary offers Jesus to the Father, to God who gives joy to my old age—nay, who will renew my youth' (Psal. XLII, 4).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Nec minore fortassis gaudio exsultabat cor Annae in Domino; quae, ut arbitror tanto majoris fuit meriti, quanto altioris propositi et sanctioris desiderii, quam illa Anna mater Samuelis; cum illa cogitaret quae mundi sunt, quomodo placeret viro; haec quomodo Deo. illa de thoro viri quaereret sobolem; haec de sinu Patris peteret Salvatorem. Haec igitur, quodam presagio gratiae excellentis quae in vita ejus effloruit, qua etiam gratiam Redemptoris agnoscere et praedicare meruit, gratiae nomen accepit; exemplar verae viduitatis, speculum sanctitatis, et vivum in emortuo corpore simulacrum totius virtutis. Haec finem Legis et initium Evangelii sentiens propinquare, ritus Judaicos christiana jam coeperat pietate mutare, jejuniis potius et orationibus serviens nocte ac die, quam cibis et potibus et variis baptismatibus, justitiis carnis, non animae. Inde erat quod benedictione filiorum, quae in Lege magni habebatur, contempta, nomen melius a filiis et filiabus elegerat, et jam per annos octoginta quatuor, lignum esse aridum lignoque insidere arido, tanquam turtur amissa semel conjuge, gaudebat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Nor was the heart of Anna perhaps exulting in the Lord with any less joy; who, I think, was of so much the greater merit as she was of a higher purpose and a holier desire than that other Anna, the mother of Samuel; since that Anna thought on the things of the world, how she might please her husband, but this one thought how she might please God; that Anna sought offspring from her husband's bed, but this one sought the Savior from the bosom of the Father. This woman, therefore, by a kind of presaging of the excellent grace which flowered in her life—by which she also deserved to recognize and proclaim the grace of the Redeemer—received the name of grace; an example of true widowhood, a mirror of holiness, and a living image, in a body already as good as dead, of every virtue. Sensing that the end of the Law and the beginning of the Gospel were drawing near, she had already, with Christian devotion, begun to exchange the Jewish rites, serving night and day rather in fastings and prayers than in foods and drinks and various washings—righteousnesses of the flesh, not of the soul. Hence it was that, despising the blessing of children, which was held in great esteem under the Law, she had chosen a better name than sons and daughters, and now, for eighty-four years, rejoiced to be a dry stick and to sit upon a dry stick, like a turtledove that has lost its mate once for all.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Ecce habes par turturum, senem justum, et viduam anum, utrumque castum, utrumque desiderio Redemptoris gemebundum; qui utique semetipsos hostiam vivam, sanctam, Deo placentem, Domino et pro Domino obtulerunt. Par turturum sane dico, non conjugum, sed conjunctorum, non copula matrimonii, sed sacratioris mysterii; pares nimirum fide, aequales castitate, similes devotione, consortes praedicatione gratiae, ambos provectae aetatis, ambos perfectae sanctitatis, qui etiam ante Evangelium, evangelicae puritatis ac pietatis in utroque sexu primitias dedicaverunt. Hi duo vario decore virtutem adornaverunt thalamum tuum, Sion, ad suscipiendum Christum Regem; non parietes templi tui, sed penetralia cordis sui secreta cubiculi, ubi adorare Patrem in spiritu et veritate jubemur (Joan. IV, 23), ubi et suscipitur qui in manufactis se nequaquam habitare testatur (Act. VII, 48). In istis itaque suscepit Christum fidelis Sion, in istis gaudens et laetabunda occurrit Deo suo. Alias vix habet ubi reclinet caput suum, et secundum Isaiam, Aporiatus est, et non est qui occurrat (Isa. LXIX, 16). Sufficit tamen istorum occursus ad omnem solemnitatem et laetitiam, eo quod consummatio abbreviata inundet justitiam, et consummata atque abundans justitia paucorum facile compenset infidelitatem multorum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Behold, you have a pair of turtledoves: the righteous old man, and the aged widow, both chaste, both groaning with desire for the Redeemer; who indeed offered themselves as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, to the Lord and for the Lord. I call them, indeed, a pair of turtledoves — not of spouses, but of those joined together; not by the bond of matrimony, but by a more sacred mystery; equal, surely, in faith, equal in chastity, alike in devotion, companions in the preaching of grace, both of advanced age, both of perfect holiness, who, even before the Gospel, dedicated in both sexes the firstfruits of evangelical purity and piety. These two, with varied beauty, adorned your bridal chamber, O Zion, with virtue, for the receiving of Christ the King — not the walls of your temple, but the inner recesses of their hearts, the secret chamber, where we are bidden to worship the Father in spirit and in truth (Joan. IV, 23), where also he is received who testifies that he dwells in no way in things made by hands (Act. VII, 48). In these, then, faithful Zion received Christ; in these, rejoicing and glad, she went out to meet her God. Apart from these, he scarcely has anywhere to lay his head, and, according to Isaiah, 'He was dismayed, and there was none to meet him' (Isa. LXIX, 16). Yet the meeting of these two suffices for all solemnity and gladness, because a shortened consummation overflows with righteousness, and the consummated and abundant righteousness of a few easily compensates for the unfaithfulness of many.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 7. Mihi omnino celebris est iste conventus, mihi solemnis ista processio, omnique festiva gaudio, ubi hinc advenit puer et puerpera, Jesus et Maria; inde occurrit senex et vidua, Simeon et Anna; hinc Dominus et Domina, inde servus et ancilla; hinc Mediator et Mediatrix, inde tam fideles tamque devoti ipsorum testes et ministri. In hoc denique conventu misericordia et veritas obviaverunt sibi, misericordia scilicet redemptionis in Jesu, veritas confessionis in senibus. In hoc occursu, justitia et pax osculatae sunt; dum justitia piorum senum, et pax reconciliantis mundum invicem in osculo affectuum et gaudio Spiritus consociatae sunt. Recte ergo quod hac nocte cantavimus, ad laetitiam hujus diei pertinere credimus, salvo duntaxat alio profundiore intellectu: Laetare, Jerusalem; et diem festum agite, omnes qui diligitis eam (Isai. LXVI, 10). Ac si diceretur: Laetata est Nazareth de annuntiatione, Bethlehem de nativitate: laetare et tu, Jerusalem, de purificatione, quoniam qui in Nazareth conceptus, et in Bethlehem natus est, in Jerusalem est susceptus et praedicatus. Et diem, inquit, festum agite, sive conventum facite, omnes qui diligitis eam, scilicet Jerusalem, id est, Festiva devotione convenite in templum, ad suscipiendum Redemptorem, omnes qui exspectatis redemptionem Israel.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 7. To me this gathering is altogether festive, to me this procession is solemn and full of festive joy, where on this side comes the child and the woman who bore him, Jesus and Mary; on that side comes to meet them the old man and the widow, Simeon and Anna; here the Lord and the Lady, there the servant and the handmaid; here the Mediator and the Mediatrix, there such faithful and devoted witnesses and ministers of them. In this gathering, finally, mercy and truth have met one another — namely, the mercy of redemption in Jesus, the truth of confession in the elders. In this meeting, righteousness and peace have kissed, while the righteousness of the devout elders and the peace of him who reconciles the world have been joined together in the kiss of affections and the joy of the Spirit. Rightly, then, do we believe that what we sang this night pertains to the joy of this day — without prejudice to another, deeper interpretation: 'Rejoice, Jerusalem, and keep festival, all you who love her' (Isai. LXVI, 10). As if it were said: Nazareth rejoiced at the annunciation, Bethlehem at the nativity; rejoice also, you, Jerusalem, at the purification, since he who was conceived in Nazareth and born in Bethlehem is received and proclaimed in Jerusalem. 'And keep festival,' it says, or 'make assembly, all you who love her' — namely, Jerusalem — that is: Gather with festive devotion into the temple, to receive the Redeemer, all you who await the redemption of Israel.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 7. Jam vero, fratres, si moraliter, sicut mos vester est, aedificari vestra quaerit Sanctitas, quatuor illas illustres in hac processione consideret personas; quarum vita, non solum ecclesias illustrat, sed et coelos adornat: Jesum loquor et Mariam, Simeonem et Annam. Et, ut ab inferioribus ad superiora progrediatur sermo, in Anna, quae jejuniis et obsecrationibus serviebat nocte ac die, jejunium nobis commendatur et oratio; in Simeone, qui tanto Jesum amplectitur gaudio, pietas et devotio; in Maria, quae cum nihil deberet legi, in hac scilicet parte purificationis legem nihilominus implevit, humilitas et obedientia; in Domino autem Jesu, qui factus ex muliere, factus est etiam sub lege, ut eos qui sub lege erant redimeret, charitas et misericordia. Nam castitatis sanctimonia, cujus laus, ut comperi, vestram semper puritatem delectat, in omnibus effulsit communiter, licet satis dissimiliter; cum in senibus fuerit labore continentiae; in puella, munere gratiae; in puero, jure et proprietate naturae, non pueritiae recens natae, sed puritatis innatae. In ipso non solum hujus virtutis, sed etiam omnium origo et perfectio; ab ipso singularum distributio; per ipsum earum conservatio; apud ipsum remuneratio. Apud ipsum igitur ambiamus, tam virginis Mariae, quam Simeonis et Annae meritis suffragantibus, ut quod minus habemus virtutis largiatur, quod largitus fuerit tueatur; ut depositum ipsius, per tutelam ipsius integrum ei reconsignantes, remunerationem consequamur ipsius, qui vivit et regnat per omnia saecula seculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 7. Now indeed, brothers, if your Holiness seeks to be built up morally, as is your custom, let it consider those four illustrious persons in this procession, whose life not only illumines churches but also adorns the heavens: I mean Jesus and Mary, Simeon and Anna. And, that the sermon may proceed from lower things to higher, in Anna, who served night and day in fastings and prayers, fasting and prayer are commended to us; in Simeon, who embraces Jesus with such great joy, piety and devotion; in Mary, who, though she owed nothing to the Law, nevertheless in this matter of the purification fulfilled the Law all the same, humility and obedience; and in the Lord Jesus, who, made of a woman, was also made under the Law, that he might redeem those who were under the Law, charity and mercy. For the holiness of chastity — the praise of which, as I have learned, always delights your own purity — shone forth in all of them alike, though in quite dissimilar ways: in the elders it was through the labor of continence; in the maiden, through the gift of grace; in the child, by the right and property of nature — not of a childhood recently born, but of purity that is innate. In him is the origin and perfection not only of this virtue but of all virtues; from him comes the distribution of each; through him their preservation; with him their reward. Let us therefore petition him, with the merits of the Virgin Mary, and of Simeon and Anna, interceding for us, that he may grant what virtue we lack, and may guard what he has granted; so that, handing back to him intact, under his own protection, his deposit entrusted to us, we may obtain his reward — who lives and reigns through all the ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Simeon carries the child who is the Ancient of Days. Guerric considers the virtues of old age, the reception of the Word in hearing and prayer, and the fear of God that accompanies justice. The sermon appears in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO III.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON III.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Quomodo Simeon imitandus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: How Simeon Is to Be Imitated

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Senex puerum portabat, senex plenus dierum, puerum antiquum dierum. Longitudine dierum adimpleverat Deus senem istum, ut ostenderet ei salutare suum in vultu nostro; sed adhuc aliorum longitudine dierum adimpleturus erat, ut ostenderet ei salutare suum in vultu suo. Plenus ergo dierum temporalium portabat antiquum dierum antiquorum, atque spei aeternae pignus fidelissimum tenebat in sinu repositum; quod videlicet dies suos super dies regis adjiceret; puer ille, juventutemque ejus renovaret ut aquilae. Quanquam senem quoque istum, sicut Abraham, cum dicitur plenus dierum, libentius accipiam plenum virtutum quam temporum: cum tempora statum nullum habeant, suoque accessu decedentia, hominem potius exhauriant quam adimpleant. Sed neque magnum est, imo magis malum est, multis vixisse diebus, si non senueris virtutibus; cum puer centum annorum moriturus sit, et peccator centum annorum maledicendus (Isai. LXV, 20). Ideo, Si annis multis vixerit homo, ut ait Salomon, et in omnibus laetatus fuerit, meminisse debet tenebrosi temporis et dierum multorum, qui cum venerint, vanitatis arguentur praeterita (Eccle. XI, 8). Caeterum e contrario, Senectus venerabilis est, non diuturna, neque numero annorum computata. Cani sunt enim sensus hominis, et aetas senectutis vita immaculata (Sap. IV, 8, 9). Si hac utique senectute Simeon non consenuisset, nunquam coronam senum, sapientiam Dei Christum portare meruisset. Sic namque scriptum est: Corona dignitatis senectus, quae in viis justitiae reperitur (Prov. XVI, 31). Et quae est illa senectus, quae est in viis justitiae reperitur, quae reperienti in coronam aptatur, nisi sapientia Dei Christus? ipse namque merito justorum operum tribuit canos sensus sapientiae, quam postmodum formabit justis in coronam gloriae. Sanctus itaque senex Simeon, ut sanctius senesceret adhuc, senectutem sapientium, sive sapientiam senum factam puerum, in viis justitiae, cum scilicet in spiritu venit in templum, reperit, et comperit in veritate; quia senectus erat in lactente, sapientia in infante, virtus in infirmitate, Verbum in carne. O infantia, o senectus! quam bene vobis pariter convenit in hujus pueri sensibus et moribus; quo utique nihil innocentius, sed nihil sapientius, nihil jucundius, sed nihil maturius, nihil mitius, sed nihil justius!

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. An old man was carrying a boy—an old man full of days, carrying the Boy who was ancient of days. God had fulfilled this old man with length of days, that He might show him His salvation in our face; but He was still going to fulfill him with the length of other days, that He might show him His salvation in His own face. Full, then, of temporal days, he was carrying the Ancient of ancient days, and he held, laid up in his bosom, the most faithful pledge of eternal hope: namely, that that Boy would add His days above the days of the king, and renew his youth like the eagle's. Although, when it is said of this old man too, as of Abraham, that he was "full of days," I would rather understand it as full of virtues than of time; since times have no permanence, but by their very passing rather drain a man than fill him up. Nor indeed is it a great thing—rather it is a worse thing—to have lived many days, if you have not grown old in virtues; since the boy of a hundred years shall die, and the sinner of a hundred years shall be accursed (Isai. LXV, 20). Therefore, "If a man has lived many years," as Solomon says, "and has rejoiced in them all, he ought to remember the dark time and the many days, which when they come, the past will be proved vain" (Eccle. XI, 8). But on the other hand, "Venerable old age is not that of long duration, nor counted by the number of years. For the understanding of a man is gray hairs, and a spotless life is the age of old age" (Sap. IV, 8, 9). If Simeon had not grown old with this very old age, he would never have deserved to carry the crown of old men, the Wisdom of God, Christ. For thus it is written: "Old age is a crown of dignity, when it is found in the ways of justice" (Prov. XVI, 31). And what is that old age which is found in the ways of justice, which fits the one who finds it as a crown, except the Wisdom of God, Christ? For He Himself, in reward for the deeds of the just, bestows the gray hairs of wisdom, which afterward He will fashion for the just into a crown of glory. And so holy old Simeon, that he might grow old yet more holily, found and truly discovered, in the ways of justice—that is, when he came in the Spirit into the temple—the old age of the wise, or the wisdom of old men become a child; because old age was in the nursing infant, wisdom in the babe, strength in weakness, the Word in flesh. O infancy, O old age! how well you agree together in the senses and manners of this Boy, than whom indeed nothing is more innocent, yet nothing more wise; nothing more delightful, yet nothing more mature; nothing more gentle, yet nothing more just!

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Vobis, o filii hominum, vobis jam tunc ipso suo silentio loquebatur Dei Sermo, ut videlicet malitia sitis parvuli, sensibus autem perfecti. Alii siquidem ex vobis columba seducta non habens cor, simplicitatem non salientes prudentia, relinquuntur fatui; alii sapientes sunt ut faciant mala, bene autem facere nesciunt, et, prudentiam non dulcorantes bonitate, efficiuntur acerbi. Prorsus congruum et gratum utrisque temperamentum atque condimentum puer iste antiquus dierum, in pueritia praeferens ingenitam sibi innocentiam, et de antiquitate dierum referens primogenitam omnium sapientiam. Si quis se imperfectum sensibus, aut inconditum intelligit moribus, veniat in templum cum Simeone, et puerum quem mater affert Maria, accipiat in manibus, id est Verbum Dei quod mater offert Ecclesia, complectatur affectibus Ipsum utique repositum in sinu sensus aedificabit, mores dulcorabit, totum statum mentis et ordinem vitae grata et salubri suavitate temperabit. Non solum autem mater Ecclesia in audiendo, sed multo magis mater gratia in orando, puerum tibi dabit amplectendum, si modo frequens et devotus orator venias in templum, ut dicas quotidie Deo: Adorabo ad templum sanctum tuum in timore tuo (Psal. V, 8). Quem enim Ecclesia praedicans offert auribus, gratia illuminans infert cordibus, eo utique praesentiorem et suaviorem, quo nudam veritatem puris tradidit sensibus. Veritatem quippe, quae est Christus, Maria vestitam carne, Ecclesia vestitam sermone, gratia nudam tradit amplectendam Spiritus infusione: quanquam hoc ipsum diverso modo fiat, pro captu scilicet suscipientis animae, sive pro arbitratu dispensantis misericordiae. Licet enim ipsam summae veritatis faciem non facile videamus, magnusque habeatur, cui vel per speculum et in aenigmate eam intueri datur: quiddam tamen ipsius, cum Spiritus nobis illabitur, veluti nudum sentimus, sensusque noster in amorem ipsius veluti ad nudum confricatur. Tunc prorsus ex sententia dicere possumus, et cantare laetabundi: Suscepimus, Deus, misericordiam tuam, in medio templi tui (Psal. XLVII, 10). Beatus qui ut dignius et crebrius eam suscipiat, congruum ei locum in cordis penetralibus parat. Beata Sion illa, quae thalamum suum diligenter ac decenter adornat, ut cum digno ac placito Christum regem honore suscipiat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. To you, O sons of men, even then by His very silence the Word of God was speaking, namely, that you should be children in malice, but mature in understanding. For some of you, like a dove that has been deceived, having no heart, not tempering simplicity with prudence, are left foolish; others are wise to do evil, but know not how to do good, and, not sweetening prudence with goodness, become harsh. A thoroughly fitting and pleasing blend and seasoning for both is this Boy who is ancient of days, who in His childhood displays the innocence native to Him, and from the antiquity of His days brings forth the wisdom that is firstborn of all things. If anyone perceives himself imperfect in understanding, or unformed in manners, let him come into the temple with Simeon, and let him receive into his hands the Boy whom His mother Mary brings—that is, the Word of God which the Church, His mother, offers—and let him embrace Him in his affections. He, once laid up in the bosom of the mind, will build up the understanding, sweeten the manners, and temper the whole condition of the soul and order of life with a pleasing and wholesome sweetness. But not only will Mother Church give you the Boy to embrace in hearing, but much more will Mother Grace give Him to you in prayer, if only you come as a frequent and devout worshiper into the temple, so as to say daily to God: "I will worship toward thy holy temple in fear of thee" (Psal. V, 8). For the One whom the Church, preaching, offers to the ears, grace, illuminating, brings into the hearts—all the more present and sweet, the more it has delivered the naked truth to pure senses. For the Truth, which is Christ, Mary delivers clothed in flesh, the Church delivers clothed in speech, but grace delivers Him naked to be embraced, by the infusion of the Spirit: although this itself happens in different ways, according to the capacity of the soul that receives, or according to the judgment of the mercy that dispenses it. For although we do not easily see the very face of the highest Truth, and he is accounted great to whom it is given even to behold it through a mirror and in an enigma; yet something of it, when the Spirit flows into us, we feel as it were bare, and our spiritual sense is, as it were, rubbed bare so as to love Him. Then indeed we can say with full conviction, and sing joyfully: "We have received thy mercy, O God, in the midst of thy temple" (Psal. XLVII, 10). Blessed is he who, that he may receive it more worthily and more often, prepares a fitting place for it in the inner chambers of his heart. Blessed is that Sion which diligently and fittingly adorns her bridal chamber, that she may receive Christ the King with due and pleasing honor.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. O sancta Sion, anima speculans aeterna, considera quae sit illa majestas suscipienda; cogita qua cura ac diligentia te illi praeparare locum oporteat. Si quis dixerit: Et ad haec quis idoneus? quis esse potest magnificentiae et gloriae tanti Regis congruus ornatus? Frustra, inquit David, paupertatem quispiam causetur: In pace factus est locus ejus (Psal. LXXV, 3); et: Justitia et judicium praeparatio sedis ejus (Psal. LXXXVIII, 15). Simeon utique quia hujusmodi palliis thalamum adornavit, ideo Christum cum multa suscipere gratia dignus fuit. Vis videre quia in pace invenerat locum Domino, quia sedem praeparaverat ei in justitia et judicio? Homo, inquit, erat in Jerusalem, cui nomen Simeon; et homo iste justus et timoratus (Luc. II, 25). In pace erat domus Simeonis, qui habitabat in Jerusalem, id est, in visione et amore pacis; de qua scilicet Jerusalem audierat David promittentem: Non commovebitur in aeternum qui habitat in Jerusalem (Psal. CXXIV, 1, 2). Et, ut noveris quia pacis habitator et amator erat, pacemque imperturbabilem illius stabilis et aeternae Jerusalem prae omnibus requirebat; cum pacem dei et hominum Jesum, qui pacem super pacem dare veniebat, sinu recepit, haec prima vox de pectore senis jamdudum pacem meditantis erupit: Nunc dimittis servum tuum, Domine, secundum verbum tuum, in pace (Luc. II, 29). Postquam viderunt oculi mei salutare tuum, qui est pax nostra faciens utraque unum, non solum Judaeum et Gentilem, sed etiam Deum et hominem, et in homine spiritum et carnem: jam hoc solum superest desideriis servi tui, ut in pace in idipsum dormiam et requiescam (Psal. IV, 9); et pax Dei quae exsuperat omnem sensum, me totum in illius summae et simplicis unitatis absorbeat consensum. Venit pax quam sustinui: requiescat in pace qui pacem quaesivit, et quae pacis sunt sectari semper studuit. Sic quippe Isaias ait: Veniat pax, requiescat in cubili suo, quia ambulavit in directione sua (Isai. LVII, 2). In pace utique Simeon straverat cubile suum, qui omnibus aliis curis ejectis solum in corde meditabatur Jesum, ubi et reclinavit susceptum. In directione quoque sua ambulaverat, qui justus et timoratus erat, exspectans consolationem Israel, adventanti quotidie desideriis occurrebat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. O holy Zion, soul that gazes on things eternal, consider what majesty it is you must receive; think with what care and diligence you must prepare a place for him. If someone should say: "And who is fit for this? What adornment can be worthy of the magnificence and glory of so great a King?" — in vain, says David, would anyone plead poverty as an excuse: "His place is made in peace" (Psal. LXXV, 3); and: "Justice and judgment are the preparation of his throne" (Psal. LXXXVIII, 15). Simeon indeed, because he adorned his chamber with coverings of this kind, was therefore worthy to receive Christ with great grace. Do you wish to see that he had found a place for the Lord in peace, that he had prepared a seat for him in justice and judgment? "There was," it says, "a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon; and this man was just and God-fearing" (Luc. II, 25). Simeon's house was in peace, for he dwelt in Jerusalem, that is, in the vision and love of peace; concerning which Jerusalem he had heard David promising: "He who dwells in Jerusalem shall never be moved" (Psal. CXXIV, 1, 2). And, that you may know he was a dweller in and lover of peace, and sought above all things the unshakeable peace of that stable and eternal Jerusalem: when he received into his bosom Jesus, the peace of God and of men, who came to give peace upon peace, this first word burst forth from the breast of the old man who had long been meditating on peace: "Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant, according to your word, in peace" (Luc. II, 29). After my eyes have seen your salvation, who is our peace, making both one — not only Jew and Gentile, but also God and man, and in man spirit and flesh — now this alone remains for the desires of your servant, that "in peace I may sleep and rest in the very same" (Psal. IV, 9); and that the peace of God which surpasses all understanding may absorb me wholly into agreement with that highest and simple unity. The peace I have awaited has come: let him rest in peace who sought peace, and who always strove to pursue what belongs to peace. For thus indeed Isaiah says: "Let peace come, let him rest in his bed, because he walked in his straight way" (Isai. LVII, 2). Simeon indeed had made his bed in peace, since, casting out all other cares, he meditated on Jesus alone in his heart, and there also he laid him down once received. He had likewise walked in his straight way, he who was just and God-fearing, awaiting the consolation of Israel, meeting its coming each day with his desires.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. In eo igitur quod justus dicitur et timoratus, justitiam et judicium intellige, quo sedes Dei praeparatur. Et justitia quidem suo nomine demonstratur: judicium vero timoris nomine, vel timor nomine judicii ideo recte accipi posse putatur, quia scilicet timor non solum nascitur de futuri consideratione judicii, sed etiam operatur nunc in nobis quamdam illius formam et exsecutionem judicii. Qui enim prohibemur judicare ante tempus de proximis (I Cor. IV, 5), jubemur de nobis ut, dum nosmetipsos dijudicamus, a Domino non judicemur (I Cor. XI, 31, 32). Porro timor iste sanctior est, cum justitiam sequitur, quam cum praecedit: quia qui praecedens ad justitiam initiat, sequens eadem consummat et conservat; dum scilicet de justitia praesumere non sinit, sed omnia opera sua hominem vereri facit, ut post judicium sui adhuc de subtiliore judicio suspectus sit, dicatque sibi: Qui judicat me Dominus est (I Cor. IV, 4), qui cum acceperit tempus, etiam justitias judicabit. Qui sine timore isto est, non poterit justificari (Eccli. I, 28), ut Scriptura testatur; quia quantumcunque se justis exercitet operibus, alieni comedunt robur ejus, dum suam volens justitiam constituere, justitiae Dei non est subjectus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. In the fact, then, that he is called just and God-fearing, understand justice and judgment, by which the seat of God is prepared. Justice indeed is shown by its own name; but judgment, it is thought, may rightly be understood under the name of fear, or fear under the name of judgment, because fear not only arises from the consideration of the judgment to come, but also now works in us a certain form and execution of that judgment. For we who are forbidden to judge our neighbors before the time (I Cor. IV, 5) are commanded, as regards ourselves, that while we judge ourselves we may not be judged by the Lord (I Cor. XI, 31, 32). Moreover, this fear is holier when it follows justice than when it precedes it: for the fear that precedes initiates one into justice, while the fear that follows completes and preserves it — namely, by not allowing a man to presume upon his justice, but making him regard all his own works with fear, so that even after judging himself he remains apprehensive of a more searching judgment, and says to himself: "He who judges me is the Lord" (I Cor. IV, 4), who, when he has taken the appointed time, will judge even acts of justice. He who is without this fear cannot be justified (Eccli. I, 28), as Scripture testifies; for however much he exercises himself in just works, strangers devour his strength, since, wishing to establish his own justice, he is not subject to the justice of God.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Vigilanter itaque Evangelium perfectam commendans Simeonis justitiam, non ait: Timoratus et justus, ne timorem, qui est initium justitiae, intelligeremus: sed ait, justus et timoratus, ut timorem, qui justitiae per omnes gradus comes individuus ipsam promovet et tuetur, ipsius exemplo disceremus. Nam neque illud putaverim otiosum, quod non timentem dixit, sed timoratum: non novum, non horarium, aut perfunctorium volens intelligi timorem illum; sed qui utique versus esset in habitum, qui altius hominis imbibisset affectum, possideret sensum, modestia et gravitate sermonem ornaret et vultum, circumspectione moderaretur actum, totum denique interioris et exterioris hominis componeret statum. Neque enim vanis animum consolationibus resolvebat, qui consolationem Israel exspectabat. Quod et ipsum ad suae cumulum adjecerat justitiae, ut sollicitus non pro sua tantum, sed etiam pro populi consolatione, longa suspensus maneret exspectatione.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Watchfully, then, the Gospel, commending Simeon's perfect justice, does not say "fearing and just," lest we should understand thereby the fear that is the beginning of justice; but says "just and fearing," so that by his example we might learn of that fear which, as an inseparable companion of justice through all its degrees, advances and guards it. Nor would I think it without purpose that it said not "fearing" but "God-fearing": not wishing that fear to be understood as something new, momentary, or superficial; but one that had truly become a settled habit, that had penetrated more deeply into the man's affections, possessed his mind, adorned his speech and countenance with modesty and gravity, moderated his action with circumspection, and finally composed the whole state of the inner and outer man. For he who awaited the consolation of Israel did not relax his mind with vain consolations. And this very thing he had added to the sum of his justice: that, anxious not only for his own consolation but also for that of the people, he remained in suspense through a long expectation.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Denique, ut manifestius audias quam pretioso ac vero nitore virtutum, non fuco colorum adornaverat thalamum suum illa Sion, id est Simeon, Spiritus sanctus, inquit, erat in eo. Quid huic ornatui Sion illa terrena comparare poterat, in omni illa multifaria thalami, id est templi sui, ambitione et gloria? Si faciem templi coronis ornasset aureis, quid aurum nisi lutum etiam sine comparatione virtutis? Puto quia nec Salomon in omni gloria sua ornatus est sicut Simeon: cum ille sapientiam, qua florebat, in senectute perdiderit, iste susceperit. Te tamen, o infidelis Sion, thalamus tuus arguit, quod cum satis tibi Praedictum esset: Ecce veniet ad templum suum Dominator quem vos quaeritis (Malach. III, 1); adorna thalamum tuum, Sion, induere vestimentis gloriae tuae, civitas Sancti (Isai. LII, 1): tu tamen nihil prorsus ad quotidianum cultum templi in adventu ipsius addidisti, non vela, non coronas, non lucernas plures, aut victimas, non alios psalmos, aut cantica; omnino inhonoratum, insalutatum remittis, qui te salvare venerat. Ideo utique tuus iste thalamus, domus gloriae tuae deserta tibi relinquetur; imo non relinquetur lapis super lapidem, qui non destruatur. Tibi enim, Domine, templum augustius, amplius et perfectius, scilicet Ecclesiam magnam a solis ortu usque ad occasum fides aedificabit gentium, et secundum nomen tuum, Deus, ita et laus tua in fines terrae; unde etiam hodie laudes audivimus, gloriam justi, voces scilicet laudantium et dicentium: Suscepimus, Deus, misericordiam tuam in medio templi tui (Psal. XLVII, 11, 10), id est, in communione sancti populi tui. O fratres, suscepistis misericordiam Dei et vos, imo abundantius vos: videte ne in vacuum susceperitis, ne gratiam ingratitudine vacuetis. Gaudeat ergo vestra devotio: quem Simeon hodie portavit in sinu suo, vos omni die glorificate et portate in corpore vestro Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum, cui honor et gloria in saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Finally, that you may hear more clearly with how precious and true a splendor of virtues—not with the paint of colors—that Sion, that is, Simeon, had adorned his bridal chamber, the Gospel says: The Holy Spirit was in him. What could that earthly Sion compare to this adornment, in all the manifold pomp and glory of her bridal chamber, that is, of her temple? If she had crowned the face of her temple with golden crowns, what is gold but mud, even without comparison to virtue? I think that not even Solomon in all his glory was adorned as Simeon was: since Solomon lost in old age the wisdom in which he had flourished, while Simeon received it. Yet your own bridal chamber convicts you, O unfaithful Sion, since it had been foretold to you plainly enough: "Behold, the Lord whom you seek shall come to his temple" (Malach. III, 1); "Adorn your bridal chamber, O Sion; put on the garments of your glory, O city of the Holy One" (Isai. LII, 1): yet you added absolutely nothing to the daily service of the temple at his coming—no veils, no crowns, no additional lamps or victims, no other psalms or songs; you sent away wholly unhonored and unsaluted the one who had come to save you. Therefore that very bridal chamber of yours, the house of your glory, will be left deserted to you; indeed, not one stone upon another will be left that will not be thrown down. For you, O Lord, a more august, more ample, and more perfect temple—namely, the great Church—the faith of the nations will build, from the rising of the sun to its setting, and according to your name, O God, so also your praise unto the ends of the earth; whence also today we have heard praises, the glory of the just one, namely, the voices of those praising and saying: "We have received, O God, your mercy in the midst of your temple" (Psal. XLVII, 11, 10), that is, in the communion of your holy people. O brothers, you too have received the mercy of God, indeed more abundantly; see that you have not received it in vain, lest you empty grace through ingratitude. Let your devotion therefore rejoice: him whom Simeon today carried in his bosom, do you every day glorify and carry in your body—Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Mary's purification introduces an account of contrition, bodily penance, works of mercy and faith, and patience in tribulation. Guerric closes by asking how faithfulness and mercy govern the use of goods shared with the poor. The sermon appears in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO IV.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON IV.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De quatuor purificationis nostrae generibus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On the Four Kinds of Our Purification

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Postquam impleti sunt dies purgationis Mariae (Luc. II, 21). Scriptura redemptionis nostrae narrans mysteria, sic refert quae pro nobis historialiter sunt gesta, ut significet quae moraliter a nobis sunt gerenda. Cum enim hodie beatae Purificatio Mariae recensetur, manifeste de nostra ipsorum purificatione admonemur. Quem vero tanti non moveat auctoritas exempli, cum videamus scilicet, quia illa sanctarum sanctissima, quae nihil purgandum habuit, purgationis tamen legalis implere mandatum non renuit? O mater immaculata, mater intacta, nonne tuae tibi conscia es puritatis; quia scilicet integritatem tuam nec conceptus, nec partus violavit, sed sacravit? Quare ergo, tanquam muliebre aliquid in concipiendo vel pariendo sis passa, sic mundationis quae muliebri provisa est infirmitati, quaeris remedia? Sic, inquit, decet nos implere omnem justitiam (Matth. III, 15), ut quae summae mater electa sum justitiae, speculum quoque sim totius et exemplar justitiae. Novi ego superbiam filiorum Evae, quae promptior est ad excusandum, quam ad expurgandum commissa. Necessarium arbitror, ut vitiis originis antiquae statim in initiis omnia novae generationis occurrant exempla. Mater praevaricationis peccavit et excusavit procaciter: mater redemptionis non peccet, et satisfaciat humiliter; ut filii hominum qui de matre vetustatis traducunt necessitatem peccandi, de matre saltem novitatis trahant humilitatem purgandi.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "After the days of Mary's purification were fulfilled" (Luc. II, 21). Scripture, in narrating the mysteries of our redemption, relates the things that were historically done for us in such a way as to signify what must morally be done by us. For when today the Purification of the Blessed Mary is commemorated, we are plainly admonished concerning our own purification. For who would not be moved by the authority of so great an example, seeing that she, the holiest of holy women, who had nothing needing to be purged, nevertheless did not refuse to fulfill the mandate of the legal purification? O immaculate Mother, O inviolate Mother, are you not conscious of your own purity—since neither conception nor childbirth violated your integrity, but rather consecrated it? Why then do you seek the remedies of that cleansing which was provided for feminine infirmity, as though you had suffered something womanly in conceiving or giving birth? "Thus," she says, "it becomes us to fulfill all justice" (Matth. III, 15), so that I, who have been chosen as the mother of the highest Justice, may also be the mirror and exemplar of all justice. I know the pride of the children of Eve, which is readier to make excuses than to purge away what has been committed. I judge it necessary that, right from the beginning, all the examples of the new generation should at once confront the vices of the ancient origin. The mother of transgression sinned and insolently made excuses: let the mother of redemption not sin, and let her humbly make satisfaction; so that the sons of men, who inherit from the mother of the old order the necessity of sinning, may at least draw from the mother of the new order the humility of being purged.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. O filii hominum, tempus purgationis advenit, quando Mater summae puritatis, de cujus purgatione dies festus est nobis, pariter et fontem edidit, et exemplum dedit nobis quod debeamus purgari. Satius est, o fratres, et suavius fonte purgari quam igne. Prorsus qui fonte non fuerint modo purgati, igne habent purgari, si tamen purgari meruerint: quando scilicet Judex ipse, quasi ignis conflans, sedebit conflans et emundans argentum, et purgabit filios Levi (Malach. III, 4, 5). Nunc Christus aqua diluens; tunc ignis consumens. Modo fons patens in ablutionem peccatoris et menstruatae; tunc flamma saeviens et ignis vorans usque ad medullas animae. De ardore siquidem irati fontis ille purgatorius ignis exardescet in conspectu ejus, et inflammabit in circuitu inimicos ejus. Ascendit, inquit, fumus in ira ejus, et ignis a facie ejus exarsit (Psal. XVII, 19). Inde cadent super eos carbones poenaliter purgatorii, quibus modo non adhibentur carbones salubriter desolatorii: qualem illum fuisse reor carbonem sublatum de altari, qui prophetae labia purgavit (Isai. VI, 5-7). An vero et illi carbones hujusmodi queant intelligi, de quibus cuidam dicitur: Ecce dati sunt tibi carbones, et sedebis super eos; hi erunt tibi in adjutorium: vobis relinquo dijudicandum. Illud autem non dubius assero, quia ignis ille, quem Dominus Jesus misit in terram (Luc. XII, 49), si vehementer (sicut est voluntas mittentis) in nobis arserit, ignis ille purgatorius qui in judicio purgabit filios Levi, non ligna, non fenum, non stipulam consumenda reperiet in nobis. Uterque quidem ignis purgatorius, sed satis differenti modo. Iste siquidem purificat ungendo, ille urendo. Hic refrigerium roris, ibi spiritus judicii et spiritus ardoris, quo abluet Dominus sordes filiarum Sion, et sanguinem Jerusalem lavabit de medio ejus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. O sons of men, the time of purification has come, when the Mother of the highest purity—whose purification is for us a feast day—has both brought forth the fountain and given us the example that we ought to be purified. It is better, brothers, and sweeter, to be purified by the fountain than by fire. Indeed, those who are not purified now by the fountain will have to be purified by fire, if indeed they are found worthy to be purified at all: namely when the Judge himself, like a refining fire, shall sit refining and cleansing silver, and shall purge the sons of Levi (Malach. III, 4, 5). Now Christ washes with water; then he will consume with fire. Now the fountain stands open for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman; then the raging flame and the devouring fire will reach to the very marrow of the soul. For indeed, from the heat of his wrathful fountain that purgatorial fire will blaze forth in his sight, and will inflame his enemies round about. "Smoke went up," he says, "in his wrath, and fire was kindled from his face" (Psal. XVII, 19). From it the coals of punitive purgation shall fall upon those to whom the healthfully desolating coals are not now applied—such a coal, I think, as that one taken from the altar, which purged the lips of the prophet (Isai. VI, 5-7). Or indeed, might those coals also be understood to be of this kind, of which it is said to a certain one: "Behold, coals have been given to you, and you shall sit upon them; these shall be for your help"—I leave it to you to judge. But this I assert without doubt: that the fire which the Lord Jesus sent upon the earth (Luc. XII, 49), if it burns fiercely in us (as is the will of the one who sends it), that purgatorial fire which in judgment will purge the sons of Levi will find in us no wood, no hay, no stubble to be consumed. Both fires are indeed purgatorial, but in a quite different manner. For the one purifies by anointing, the other by burning. In the one there is the refreshment of dew; in the other, the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning, by which the Lord will wash away the filth of the daughters of Sion, and shall wash the blood of Jerusalem from the midst of her.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Est quidem et in hoc ipso multa Domini clementia erga filias Sion: sed longe clementius et mitius purificata est illa, quam beatam praedicant filiae Sion, cui scilicet dictum est: Spiritus sanctus superveniet in te, et virtus Altissimi obumbrabit tibi. Haec nempe supernae virtutis obumbratio, vera fuit purificatio Mariae; non ista, quae quadam mystica dispensatione tantum specie tenus hodie celebrata est. Haec plane fuit tota ac vera sanctificatio Matris et Filii, sicut et angelus exposuit ei. Ideo, inquit, et quod nascetur ex te Sanctum, vocabitur Filius Dei (Luc. I, 35). Antea namque purificanda erat natura mortalis, ut Deum conciperet, non posteaquam concepisset: cum concepisse Sanctum sanctorum summa sanctificatio sit, et ea quae Mater ipsius sanctitatis effecta sit, nihil sanctius esse possit. Cum ergo filiae Sion quae mollius et dissolutius vivunt, et ardorem forsitan experiuntur carnis, merito purificandae sint spiritu judicii et spiritu ardoris; Virgo perpetua ac singularis, quae sola Spiritus obumbratione Deum concepit, solo purificata est spiritu gratiae et refrigerio roris. Omnium sane purgationum, quibus conditio reparatur mortalis, haec beatae purificatio Virginis mitissima atque felicissima fuit: nam illa filiarum Sion quae purgatorio fiet igne judicii, sicut novissima, sic et severissima omnium erit. Nec ista itaque potest esse nobis nisi admirationi, nec illa nisi formidini: quippe qui nec ad istam possimus aspirare, et in illam, si sapimus, semper formidamus incidere. Omnino si sapimus, semper clamabimus, plus emendatione morum, quam strepitu verborum: Domine, ne in furore tuo arguas me, neque in ira tua corripias me (Psal. VI, 2).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. There is indeed in this very thing much clemency of the Lord toward the daughters of Sion: but far more clement and gentle was the purification of her whom the daughters of Sion proclaim blessed, to whom it was said: "The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you." This overshadowing of supernal power was truly the purification of Mary—not that one which, by a certain mystical dispensation, was today celebrated only in outward appearance. That overshadowing was plainly the whole and true sanctification of both Mother and Son, as the angel also explained to her. "Therefore," he says, "that which shall be born of you, holy, shall be called the Son of God" (Luc. I, 35). For mortal nature had to be purified beforehand, so that it might conceive God—not afterward, once it had conceived; since to have conceived the Holy of Holies is the highest sanctification, and nothing can be holier than she who was made the Mother of that very holiness. Therefore, since the daughters of Sion, who live more softly and dissolutely, and perhaps experience the burning of the flesh, are rightly to be purified by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning; the perpetual and singular Virgin, who alone conceived God by the overshadowing of the Spirit, was purified by the spirit of grace alone and by the refreshment of dew. Of all the purifications by which mortal condition is restored, this purification of the Blessed Virgin was the gentlest and most blessed; for that purification of the daughters of Sion, which will be accomplished by the purgatorial fire of judgment, will be, as the last of all, so also the severest of all. Neither, therefore, can the one be anything to us but a matter for admiration, nor the other anything but a matter for dread: since we can neither aspire to that former one, and, if we are wise, we must always fear falling into that latter one. Altogether, if we are wise, we shall always cry out—more by the amendment of our conduct than by the noise of words—"Lord, rebuke me not in your fury, nor chastise me in your wrath" (Psal. VI, 2).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Necessarie igitur nobis et misericorditer inter utrumque genus purgationis, illud summum ad quod non attingimus, et illud ultimum quod metuimus, alia purgationum genera pietas providit divina, sicut tempus et locum poenitentiae, sic plurima salutis indulgens remedia. Quae licet multa ac varia sint, sub quatuor tamen generibus videntur omnia fere posse comprehendi; ne scilicet indigesta multitudine rerum memoriam confundamus auditoris. Haec igitur quatuor esse arbitror quibus opportune et commode his diebus purgationis nostrae purgari possumus: scilicet contritionem cordis, afflictionem corporis, opera pietatis et fidei, patientiam tribulationis. Ad hunc siquidem modum quatuor invenies, quibus mundum generaliter purificat Christus, purgationem peccatorum faciens: aquam scilicet et sanguinem, spiritum et ignem. Hic est, inquit Joannes, qui venit per aquam et sanguinem. Hic est qui baptizat in Spiritu sancto et igni (I Joan. V, 6, 8). Aqua baptizavit, pedesque discipulorum lavit, dedicans baptismum quoque lacrymarum, quae de contritione profluunt cordis. Sanguinem fudit; ut et nos mortificatione corporis participantes ejus passioni, lavemus stolas nostras in sanguine Agni. Spiritum dedit; ut charitas Dei ac proximi diffusa in cordibus nostris per Spiritum, multitudinem in nobis operiat peccatorum. Quae, si minus perfecta est, ut tot et tanta non sufficiat operire, admovet ignem conflator ille, qui purgat filios Levi; et quidquid residuum est rubiginis, ignis excoquit, seu praesentis, seu futurae tribulationis, ut tandem decantare possint: Transivimus per ignem et aquam, et eduxisti nos in refrigerium (Psal. LXV, 12). Sic nempe et mundus iste prius baptizatus aqua diluvii, postea purgatus igne judicii, in novum transibit statum incorruptionis.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Necessarily, then, and mercifully, between these two kinds of purgation—the highest, which we do not attain, and the last, which we fear—divine kindness has provided for us other kinds of purgation, granting, as it grants a time and place for penance, many remedies of salvation as well. Though these are many and varied, they can nevertheless almost all be comprehended under four kinds, lest we confuse the hearer's memory with an undigested multitude of things. These, then, I judge to be the four by which we can be fittingly and conveniently purified in these days of our purification: namely, contrition of heart, affliction of the body, works of piety and faith, and patience in tribulation. In this manner you will find four things by which Christ generally purifies the world, effecting a purgation of sins: namely, water and blood, spirit and fire. 'This is he,' says John, 'who came by water and blood. This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit and in fire' (I Joan. V, 6, 8). He baptized with water, and washed the feet of the disciples, consecrating also the baptism of tears, which flow from contrition of heart. He shed blood, that we too, sharing in his passion through mortification of the body, might wash our robes in the blood of the Lamb. He gave the Spirit, that the love of God and of neighbor, poured into our hearts through the Spirit, might cover a multitude of sins in us. If this love is too imperfect to suffice to cover so many and so great sins, that refiner applies the fire, who purges the sons of Levi; and whatever rust remains, the fire—whether of present or future tribulation—smelts away, so that at last they may be able to sing: 'We have passed through fire and water, and you have brought us out into a place of refreshment' (Psal. LXV, 12). Thus, indeed, this world too, first baptized with the water of the flood, and afterward purged by the fire of judgment, will pass into a new state of incorruption.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Denique, ut teneris atque delicatis geramus aliquatenus morem, si lacrymas non habent, si labores horrent, si nesciunt ferre tribulationem: nunquid et illud excusabunt, quod Salomon commendat: Per misericordiam, inquiens, et fidem purgantur peccata? (Prov. XV, 27; XVI, 6.) Quid misericordia suavius? quid fide jucundius? Haec oleum est membris, illa lumen oculis. Haec ungit affectus, illa sensus illuminat, dirigitque gressus: ut ad lumen ejus ambules in tenebris, ut invisibilia contempleris, et futuram tuam beatitudinem jam animo praesumptam mediteris. Bene autem dicitur, per misericordiam et fidem purgari peccata: quia misericordia de proprio impendens, redimit debita; fides autem etiam gratis sine operibus indulgentiam impetrat. De misericordia nempe dicit propheta: Iniquitates tuas redime misericordiis pauperum (Dan. IV, 24); et Dominus prophetarum: Date eleemosynam, et omnia munda sunt vobis (Luc. XI, 41). De fide autem ait Apostolus: Fide mundans corda eorum (Act. XV, 9); et Dominus apostolorum: Vade, inquit, fides tua te salvum fecit (Marc. X, 52). Quanquam in hac Salomonis sententia, possit intelligi non fides qua credimus, sed qua credibiles nos exhibemus, dum fidem Deo et hominibus servamus; ut quod hic dicitur: Per misericordiam et fidem purgantur peccata (Prov. XV, 27), et paulo post: Misericordia et veritate redimitur iniquitas (Prov. XVI, 6), eadem sit in diversitate verborum repetita sententia. Recte igitur misericordia et veritas seu fides sociata sunt: cum in omnibus viis nostris nisi misericordia et veritas obvient sibi, plus augeri quam purgari peccata sit verendum. Ut enim de aliis actionibus interim taceam, et de misericordiis pauperum loquar, quas abundantius nunc fieri temporis hujus postulat necessitas: quid in ipsis etiam, quibus peccata purganda sunt, peccati committitur, si misericordia fide, vel fides misericordia destituatur?

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Finally, that we may to some extent make allowance for the tender and delicate—if they have no tears, if they shrink from labors, if they do not know how to bear tribulation—will they also excuse themselves from what Solomon commends, saying: 'By mercy and faith sins are purged'? (Prov. XV, 27; XVI, 6.). What is sweeter than mercy? What more delightful than faith? The one is oil for the limbs, the other light for the eyes. The one anoints the affections, the other illumines the senses and directs the steps, so that by its light you may walk in darkness, that you may contemplate invisible things, and meditate upon your future blessedness already anticipated in the soul. And it is well said that sins are purged by mercy and faith: because mercy, spending from one's own goods, redeems debts, while faith, even freely, without works, obtains pardon. Of mercy indeed the prophet says: 'Redeem your iniquities by mercies shown to the poor' (Dan. IV, 24); and the Lord of the prophets: 'Give alms, and all things are clean to you' (Luc. XI, 41). Of faith the Apostle says: 'cleansing their hearts by faith' (Act. XV, 9); and the Lord of the apostles says: 'Go, your faith has made you whole' (Marc. X, 52). Although in this saying of Solomon one might understand not the faith by which we believe, but that by which we show ourselves trustworthy, in that we keep faith with God and with men; so that what is said here, 'By mercy and faith sins are purged' (Prov. XV, 27), and a little afterward, 'By mercy and truth iniquity is redeemed' (Prov. XVI, 6), is the same statement repeated in different words. Rightly, then, are mercy and truth, or faith, joined together: since unless mercy and truth meet one another in all our ways, it is to be feared that sins are increased rather than purged. For, to say nothing for now of other actions, and to speak of mercies shown to the poor, which the necessity of this present time demands be done more abundantly: what sin is committed even in those very acts by which sins are to be purged, if mercy is deprived of faith, or faith of mercy?

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Audiant ergo quibus dispensatio credita est; audiant quibus credita non est: isti scilicet, ne sic velint esse fideles, ut misericordiam deserant; illi, ne sic velint esse misericordes, ut fidem laedant. Sunt enim aliqui qui plus volunt esse fideles quam oportet; et sunt aliqui qui plus volunt esse misericordes quam eis liceat. Qui ergo contra fidem indebitam usurpant misericordiam, audiant Salomonem dicentem: Multi homines misericordes vocantur; fidelem autem virum quis inveniet? (Proverb. XX, 6.) Qui autem velut propter fidem negligunt debitam misericordiam, audiant plus quam Salomonem dicentem: Quod superest date eleemosynam (Luc. XI, 41); ut saltem abundantia vestra aliorum suppleat inopiam. Multum prorsus pepercit infirmae et pusillae nostrae fidei, qui bona communia non ex aequo fratribus partiri, sed ex eo quod superest propriae necessitati, jussit eleemosynam eis impertiri. Ut enim taceamus de jure naturae, quae quidquid parens omnium terra generat, omnibus commune terrigenis adjudicat: illis saltem quibus indifferens est germanitas adoptionis, et communis sors haereditatis quomodo communis non erit usus panis quem Pater administrat coelestis? Esto tamen, sit istud jus ordinatae charitatis, quod moderatio Evangelii suas cuique necessitates primum excepit: quis ille est qui recte metiatur necessitates proprias qui inter necessarium et superfluum aequo judicio discernat? Attendamus nobis, fratres, ne de mortibus pauperum fratrum nostrorum incipiamus judicari, si superflue retinemus aut insumimus nobis unde vita eorum valeat sustentari. Et quoniam hodierna purificatio purissimae ac pauperrimae Virginis de nostra nos purificatione loqui commonuit, in hoc maxime nostram constare puritatem noverimus, si quidquid superfluum est nobis amputemus: ut non solum sanctitate castitatis, sed etiam simplicitate paupertatis aliquatenus aemulemur pauperem matrem pauperis Christi, cui regnum et imperium, et nunc et per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Let them hear, then, to whom the stewardship has been entrusted; and let them hear to whom it has not been entrusted: those without the stewardship, lest they wish to be so faithful that they abandon mercy; those entrusted with it, lest they wish to be so merciful that they injure faith. For there are some who wish to be more faithful than they ought, and there are some who wish to be more merciful than is lawful for them. Those, therefore, who contrary to faith, arrogate to themselves an undue mercy, let them hear Solomon saying: "Many men are called merciful; but who shall find a faithful man?" (Proverb. XX, 6.) But those who, as it were for the sake of faith, neglect due mercy, let them hear one greater than Solomon saying: "That which remains over, give as alms" (Luc. XI, 41), that at least your abundance may supply the want of others. He has indeed greatly spared our weak and feeble faith, who did not command that common goods be divided equally among the brethren, but that alms be given to them out of what remains over and above one's own necessity. For to say nothing of the law of nature, which assigns whatever the earth, the parent of all, brings forth, as common to all her children—for those at least to whom the brotherhood of adoption is undivided, and the lot of inheritance common, how shall the use of the bread which the heavenly Father dispenses not also be common? Yet granted that this is the right of ordered charity, that the moderation of the Gospel has first reserved to each his own necessities: who is he that rightly measures his own necessities, who with fair judgment distinguishes between the necessary and the superfluous? Let us take heed, brothers, lest we begin to be judged for the deaths of our poor brothers, if we superfluously keep back or spend upon ourselves that by which their life might be sustained. And since today's purification of the most pure and most poor Virgin has reminded us to speak of our own purification, let us know that our purity consists chiefly in this: that we cut away whatever is superfluous to us; so that not only in holiness of chastity, but also in simplicity of poverty, we may in some measure imitate the poor mother of the poor Christ, to whom belong kingdom and dominion, both now and for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Cleansing the bridal chamber of the soul begins with expelling vices and cultivating virtues. The sermon then turns to Mary and Simeon in the temple and to reverence for the Eucharist. The 1879 edition includes it under Guerric, but its footnote records Horstius's doubt about that attribution and its earlier printing among Bernard's works. The individual sermon is undated.
