passages.text: SERMO V (2).

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON V (2).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De mundanda et adornanda Christo anima.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On Cleansing and Adorning the Soul for Christ

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. « Adorna thalamum tuum, Sion, et suscipe regem Christum, quem virgo concepit, virgo peperit, virgo post partum quem genuit adoravit (3). » Ad nos, fratres, ad nos loquitur Spiritus sanctus, qui sumus Sion, qui sumus speculantes, qui die ac nocte levamus oculos nostros ad Dominum Deum nostrum, donec misereatur nostri. Adornemus igitur thalamum nostrum, et suscipiamus regem Christum. Ecce, fratres, Christus in propria veniens, et a suis repulsus, non habet ubi caput reclinet. Prae foribus nostris inter materna brachia vagiens, per Spiritum sanctum quaerit hospitium, dicens: « Adorna thalamum tuum, Sion. » Emundemus igitur thalamum nostrum, prius expellendo quae oculos Christi intrando offendere possunt; et sic demum adornemus ea inferendo quibus delectatur et gaudet. Quae sunt, ait forsitan aliquis vestrum, quae oculos Christi offendere possunt? Cui dicimus: Nihil ita oculos ejus offendit, sicut superbia, quae angelum de coelo, et hominem expulit de paradiso: quae est initium omnis peccati: quam hortatur nos Spiritus sanctus vitare, dicens: Quid superbis, terra et cinis? (Eccli. X, 9); et alibi: Omnis caro fenum; exsiccatum est fenum, et flos ejus decidit (Isai. XL, 6, 7; Eccli. XIV, 18). Videamus nunc quid superbia fecit. Angelum de coelo, et hominem expulit de paradiso. Merito haec oculos Christi offendit quae pulcherrimum opus ejus in coelo et in paradiso foedavit; quae fecit de angelo diabolum, et de homine nuper creato justo perfidum. Quae sicut est peccatorum primum et maximum, sic est omnium regina et mater vitiorum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "Adorn your bridal chamber, Sion, and welcome Christ the king, whom a virgin conceived, a virgin bore, and after bearing him a virgin adored him (3)." It is to us, brothers, to us that the Holy Spirit speaks, we who are Sion, we who are watchmen, who day and night lift up our eyes to the Lord our God until he have mercy on us. Let us, then, adorn our bridal chamber and welcome Christ the king. Behold, brothers, Christ coming into his own, and rejected by his own, has nowhere to lay his head. Crying before our doors amid his mother's arms, he seeks lodging through the Holy Spirit, saying: "Adorn your bridal chamber, Sion." Let us therefore cleanse our bridal chamber, first by expelling whatever might offend the eyes of Christ upon his entering; and only then let us adorn it by bringing in those things in which he delights and rejoices. What things, someone among you may perhaps ask, can offend the eyes of Christ? To him we say: Nothing offends his eyes so much as pride, which cast an angel out of heaven and man out of paradise; which is the beginning of all sin; which the Holy Spirit urges us to avoid, saying: Why are you proud, earth and ashes? (Eccli. X, 9); and elsewhere: All flesh is grass; the grass withers and its flower falls (Isai. XL, 6, 7; Eccli. XIV, 18). Let us now see what pride has done. It cast an angel out of heaven and man out of paradise. Rightly does this offend the eyes of Christ, which defiled his most beautiful work in heaven and in paradise; which made of an angel a devil, and of man, newly created righteous, a faithless man. As it is the first and greatest of sins, so it is the queen and mother of all vices.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Videndum est igitur et sollicite considerandum, ut eam mens nostra cum tota prole sua excludat, ut thalamus noster emundatus et ornatus Christum regem qui foris [al. fores] pulsat, suscipiat. Cum tota, inquam, prole sua, septem scilicet principalibus vitiis. Quae sunt haec? Inanis gloria, invidia, ira, tristitia, avaritia, ventris ingluvies, luxuria. Hae sunt filiae superbiae, quae matrem suam sequuntur: quae hospitium quodcunque intraverint, fetidum reddunt. Sed quae nobis cum istis communio? Quis consensus templo Dei cum idolis? Nulla nobis (Deo agimus gratias) cum eis societas, quas, exuentes veterem hominem cum actibus suis, gladio verae confessionis et poenitentiae enecavimus. Nihil igitur in nobis ultra possit superbia, quae de archangelo diabolum, et de primo homine fecit impium et Creatori suo rebellem. Nihil habeat in nobis vana gloria, qui a die conversionis nostrae, in cruce Domini nostri Jesu Christi coepimus gloriari cum Apostolo dicentes: Mihi autem absit gloriari, nisi in cruce Domini nostri Jesu Christi, per quem mihi mundus crucifixus est, et ego mundo! (Galat. VI, 14). Gloria itaque nostra sit crux Christi quam portamus, et testimonium conscientiae per crucem Christi purgatae, de qua Apostolus ait: Gloria nostra haec est, testimonium conscientiae nostrae (II Cor. I, 12). In qua conscientia gloriari, de donis Dei est Deo gratias agere. Ad quod nos hortatur Apostolus, dicens: Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur (I Cor. I, 31; Jer. IX, 24; II Cor. X, 17): id est, in Domino de puritate conscientiae suae glorietur. Non enim qui se ipsum commendat, etc. Caeterum qui in se gloriatur, et qui sibi placet, stulto homini placet. Qui in alio homine gloriatur, aut laudem in mente ab ore alterius exspectat, mercedem operum recipit, ac oleo peccatoris ungit caput suum, auditque prophetam sibi dicentem: Maledictus homo qui ponit spem suam in homine (Jerem. XVII, 6). Et in die judicii cum dixerint: Domine, Domine, aperi nobis, ait: Amen dico vobis, nescio vos (Matth. XXV, 11, 12). Haec vana gloria filia est superbiae; quae in quocunque fuerit, inobedientem facit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. We must therefore watch and carefully consider that our mind exclude pride together with its whole offspring, so that our chamber, cleansed and adorned, may welcome Christ the king who knocks outside [or: at the doors]. With its whole offspring, I say, namely the seven principal vices. What are these? Vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony of the belly, lust. These are the daughters of pride, who follow their mother: whatever lodging they enter, they make foul. But what fellowship have we with these? What agreement has the temple of God with idols? We have no partnership with them (thanks be to God), for, stripping off the old man with his deeds, we have slain them with the sword of true confession and penance. Let pride, then, have no further power in us — pride which made of an archangel a devil, and of the first man a wicked man rebellious against his Creator. Let vainglory have nothing in us, we who from the day of our conversion have begun to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, saying with the Apostle: But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world! (Galat. VI, 14). Let our glory, then, be the cross of Christ which we bear, and the testimony of a conscience purged through the cross of Christ, of which the Apostle says: Our glory is this, the testimony of our conscience (II Cor. I, 12). To glory in such a conscience is to give thanks to God for God's gifts. To this the Apostle exhorts us, saying: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord (I Cor. I, 31; Jer. IX, 24; II Cor. X, 17): that is, let him glory in the Lord concerning the purity of his conscience. For it is not he who commends himself, etc. But he who glories in himself, and who pleases himself, pleases a foolish man. He who glories in another man, or expects praise in his mind from another's mouth, receives the reward of his works, and anoints his own head with the oil of the sinner, and hears the prophet saying to him: Cursed is the man who puts his hope in man (Jerem. XVII, 6). And on the day of judgment, when they shall say: Lord, Lord, open to us, he says: Amen I say to you, I know you not (Matth. XXV, 11, 12). This vainglory is a daughter of pride; whoever harbors it, it makes disobedient.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Rursum, post conversionem, nihil ultra in nobis habeat invidia, per quam mors intravit in orbem terrarum. Diabolus enim invidit homini ascensum unde corruerat, et propter hoc tentavit, et in anima occidit. Haec est illa, quae non magnos, sed parvos semper torquet (Sap. II, 24, 25), dicente sancto Job: Parvulum occidit invidia (Job V, 2). In eo enim quod aliquis alicui invidet, minorem se ostendit ei cui invidet. Sic diabolus invidit primo homini, sic Esau Jacob, et Cain Abel. Haec invidia parvulum occidit; quia nisi inferior esset, de bono alterius non doleret. Hac peste nullus moritur, nisi qui terrena haec appetit, quae tota non veniunt pluribus. Unde si qua desiderat, illi invidet qui penitus ea accepit, vel illi partem habendo quantitatem ei restringit. Hunc parvulum occidit invidia, quia dum non potest adipisci quod alii invidet, in odium, invidiae filiam, cadit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Again, after conversion, let envy have no further place in us, through which death entered into the world. For the devil envied man the ascent from which he himself had fallen, and for this reason tempted him, and slew him in the soul. This is that vice which torments not the great, but always the small (Sap. II, 24, 25), as holy Job says: Envy slays the little one (Job V, 2). For in that someone envies another, he shows himself lesser than the one he envies. Thus the devil envied the first man, thus Esau envied Jacob, and Cain envied Abel. This envy slays the little one; because unless he were inferior, he would not grieve over another's good. No one dies of this plague except one who craves these earthly things, which do not come whole to many. Hence if anyone desires such things, he envies the one who has received them entirely, or the one who, by having a part, restricts their quantity for him. Envy slays this little one, because, since he cannot obtain what he envies in another, he falls into hatred, the daughter of envy.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Rursum, fratres, post conversionem nostram ira non habeat in nobis locum, quia, ut ait Dominus in Evangelio, gradatim ducit ad gehennae puteum, dicens: Qui irascitur fratri suo, reus erit judicio. Qui dixerit, Racha, hoc est, vocem indignationis per iram emiserit, reus erit concilio, in quo tractatur qua poena sit mulctandus. Qui dixerit, Fatue, hoc est, tale quid fecerit aut verbo aut verbere, ut inter fratres despiciatur, reus erit gehennae ignis (Matth. v, 22), nisi resipuerit. Haec est ira, quae stultorum oculos exstinguit, sapientium oculos nonnunquam turbat, dicente Psalmista: Turbatus est prae ira oculus meus (Psal. vi, 8). Et de ira stulti Job ait: Virum stultum interficit iracundia (Job. v, 2). Ecce duas iras videmus; quarum altera nonnunquam turbat oculum, altera semper exstinguit. Altera venit ex impatientia; altera, ex zelo rectitudinis. Altera venit ex vitio; altera, ex virtute. De altera quae venit ex virtute Psalmista ait: Irascimini, et nolite peccare (Psal. iv, 5; Ephes. iv, 26). Quasi dicat: Crudeles estote in vitium, mites in fratrem, considerantes vosmetipsos, ne et vos tentemini. De altera, quae venit ex vitio, ait Apostolus: Sol non occidat super iracundiam vestram (Ephes. iv, 26): id est, Christus, qui est sol justitiae, mentem vestram irascentem non deserat, qui cum ira nunquam habitat. Ira, quae venit ex zelo rectitudinis, debemus irasci prius nostris erratibus; et post, erratibus proximorum: quae melior est risu, quia per tristitiam vultus corrigitur proximus (Eccle. vii, 4). Quae debet tamen subesse rationi, ne sit immoderata, sed in ultione peccati tempus et modum consideret. Haec sapientes interdum turbat: ira per vitium stultos occidit, dum in rixas et in contumeliam linguam relaxat.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Again, brothers, after our conversion let anger have no place in us, because, as the Lord says in the Gospel, it leads step by step down to the pit of hell, saying: Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment. Whoever says, Raca—that is, utters a cry of indignation through anger—shall be liable to the council, in which it is determined with what penalty he is to be punished. Whoever says, Fool—that is, does something, either by word or by blow, such that his brother is held in contempt among the brothers—shall be liable to the fire of hell (Matth. v, 22), unless he comes to his senses. This is the anger that puts out the eyes of fools, and sometimes troubles the eyes of the wise, as the Psalmist says: My eye is troubled because of anger (Psal. vi, 8). And of the fool's anger Job says: Anger kills the foolish man (Job. v, 2). Behold, we see two angers; of which the one sometimes troubles the eye, the other always puts it out. The one comes from impatience; the other, from zeal for righteousness. The one comes from vice; the other, from virtue. Of the one that comes from virtue the Psalmist says: Be angry, and do not sin (Psal. iv, 5; Ephes. iv, 26). As if he were saying: Be fierce against vice, gentle toward your brother, considering yourselves, lest you too be tempted. Of the other, which comes from vice, the Apostle says: Let not the sun go down upon your anger (Ephes. iv, 26): that is, let Christ, who is the sun of righteousness, not abandon your angry mind, for he never dwells together with anger. As for the anger that comes from zeal for righteousness, we ought to be angry first at our own faults, and afterward at the faults of our neighbors; and this is better than laughter, because through the sadness of the countenance the neighbor is corrected (Eccle. vii, 4). Yet it must remain subject to reason, lest it be immoderate, but should consider the time and measure in punishing sin. This anger sometimes troubles the wise; but anger through vice kills fools, as it lets the tongue loose into quarrels and insult.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Rursum, fratres, post conversionem nostram muniendus est thalamus cordis nostri, ne tristitia rediens introeat: illam dico quae mortem operatur, quae de amissione rerum temporalium venit. Haec est illa quae pravas cogitationes generat, murmurosum monachum reddit, quae fastidium parit, et tenentem aratrum Dei cum uxore Loth retro respicere compellit. Sine dolore namque non potest amittere, quod cum inordinato amore possedit. Hanc itaque tristitiam quae mortem operatur excludamus: et intromittamus eam quae venit de memoria peccatorum, et de peregrinatione nostra, dicamusque cum Psalmista: Heu mihi, quia incolatus meus prolongatus est! habitavi cum habitantibus Cedar, multum incola fuit anima mea (Psal. cxix, 5, 6). Haec est tristitia, quae vitam operatur, de qua ait Apostolus: Quasi tristes, semper autem gaudentes (II Cor. vi, 10). Haec est illa de qua Dominus ad discipulos dicit: Tristitia vestra vertetur in gaudium (Joan. xvi, 20). Altera parit mortem, parit animi rancorem.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Again, brothers, after our conversion the bedchamber of our heart must be fortified, lest sadness return and enter in: I mean that sadness which works death, which comes from the loss of temporal things. This is the sadness that breeds wicked thoughts, makes the monk a grumbler, gives rise to disgust, and compels the one holding the plow of God to look back, like the wife of Lot. For one cannot lose without sorrow what one possessed with disordered love. Let us therefore shut out this sadness which works death, and let us admit that sadness which comes from the memory of our sins and from our condition as pilgrims, and let us say with the Psalmist: Woe is me, for my sojourning is prolonged! I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar, my soul has been long a sojourner (Psal. cxix, 5, 6). This is the sadness that works life, of which the Apostle says: As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (II Cor. vi, 10). This is that of which the Lord says to his disciples: Your sorrow shall be turned into joy (Joan. xvi, 20). The other sadness brings forth death, brings forth rancor of soul.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Rursum, fratres, post conversionem muniamus thalamum nostrum, ne avaritia, quae est radix omnium malorum, rediens introeat, nosque ab unius Dei cultura abstrahat, idolorum cultores faciat. De qua inter caetera sic ait Apostolus ad discipulos suos: Mortificate membra vestra quae sunt super terram: fornicationem, immunditiam, libidinem, concupiscentiam malam, et avaritiam, quae est idolorum servitus (Coloss. iii, 5). Ecce avaritiam idololatriae comparat, et merito: quia sicut uni Deo idololatra nititur auferre gloriam, ne solus habeat nomen Deitatis; ita avarus in Dei res se extendit, ut solus usurpet quae Deus omnipotens in usum plurimorum fecit. Utraque Deo inimica, quia negat Deo quae sunt ejus. Est et avaritia non solum amor congregandae pecuniae aut conservandae, sed ambitio praelationis, cum nititur homo homini praeesse. Haec, ut verum dicam, etiam pauperes (qui semel pro Christo reliquerunt sua) in tantum vexat, ut contra jus et fas, et propositum suum, non tantum velint, sed etiam studeant fratribus et conservis praeesse. Quod si abbas aut prior eorum voto non consenserit, irascuntur, obloquuntur, eosque aut invidos, aut sibi malevolos (qui se non provehunt) clamant. Haec est avaritia quae memoriam mandatorum Dei turbat, dicente Psalmista Domino: Inclina cor meum in testimonia tua, et non in avaritiam (Psal. cxviii, 36): quae proditionis est mater, quae Judam Dei discipulum primum ad mandatorum Dei oblivionem, de oblivione ad proditionem, de proditione traxit ad laqueum.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Again, brothers, after our conversion let us fortify our bedchamber, lest avarice, which is the root of all evils, return and enter in, and draw us away from the worship of the one God, making us worshippers of idols. Concerning this, among other things, the Apostle says thus to his disciples: Put to death your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and avarice, which is the service of idols (Coloss. iii, 5). See how he compares avarice to idolatry, and rightly so: for just as the idolater strives to take glory away from the one God, so that he alone may not bear the name of Deity, so the avaricious man extends himself into the things of God, so that he alone may seize for himself what almighty God made for the use of many. Both are enemies of God, because each denies to God what belongs to him. And avarice is not only the love of gathering or keeping money, but also the ambition for precedence, when a man strives to set himself over another man. This, to speak truly, torments even the poor (who have once left their own goods for Christ's sake) to such a degree that, against right and justice and against their own purpose, they not only desire but even strive to be set over their brothers and fellow-servants. And if the abbot or prior does not consent to their wish, they grow angry, they murmur against him, and cry out that those who do not advance them are either envious or ill-disposed toward them. This is the avarice that disturbs the memory of God's commandments, as the Psalmist says to the Lord: Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to avarice (Psal. cxviii, 36): which is the mother of betrayal, which drew Judas, God's disciple, first to forgetfulness of God's commandments, then from forgetfulness into betrayal, and from betrayal to the noose.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 7. Rursum, fratres, post conversionem nostram muniamus thalamum cordis, ne gula rediens introeat, quae et Adam innocentiae veste, et Esau privavit primogeniti dignitate. Haec est illa pestis quae patres nostros in deserto ingratos beneficiis Dei fecit, quae compulit eos murmurare contra Deum, et dicere: Utinam mortui essemus in Aegypto, quando sedebamus super ollas carnium, et comedebamus allia, cepe, et pepones (Exod. xvi, 3; Num. xi, 5, 6; xiv, 3.) Haec est illa funesta pestis quae eos ad blasphemiam duxit, quasi non esset alia vita post istam, cum dicebant: Comedamus et bibamus; cras enim moriemur (Isa. xxii, 13; II Cor. xv, 32), id est, in futuro. Quasi dicerent: Hoc solum habemus quod comedimus; nihil in futuro post hanc vitam nos habituros speramus. Hanc pestem cum homine perituram pronuntiat Apostolus, dicens: Esca ventri, et venter escis. Deus autem et hunc et hanc destruet (I Cor. vi, 13). Haec pestis tripartita est: quia aut ante horam canonicam, aut aliud quam licet, aut plus quam necesse est facit comedere, et carnis curam in concupiscentiis nititur facere. De qua nascitur inepta laetitia: sicut de populo Israel dicitur: Sedit populus manducare et bibere, et surrexerunt ludere (Exod. XXXII, 6; I Cor. X, 7).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 7. Again, brothers, after our conversion let us fortify the chamber of our heart, lest gluttony, returning, enter in — the vice which deprived Adam of the garment of innocence, and Esau of the dignity of the firstborn. This is that plague which made our fathers in the desert ungrateful for the benefits of God, which drove them to murmur against God and say: "Would that we had died in Egypt, when we sat by the pots of flesh and ate garlic, onions, and melons" (Exod. xvi, 3; Num. xi, 5, 6; xiv, 3.). This is that deadly plague which led them to blasphemy, as though there were no other life after this one, when they said: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die" (Isa. xxii, 13; II Cor. xv, 32) — that is, in the life to come. As if they said: We have only what we eat; we hope to have nothing in the future after this life. The Apostle declares that this plague will perish along with man, saying: "Food for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both the one and the other" (I Cor. vi, 13). This plague is threefold: for it makes a man eat either before the canonical hour, or something other than is permitted, or more than is necessary, and it strives to make provision for the flesh in its lusts. From it is born foolish merriment, just as it is said of the people of Israel: "The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play" (Exod. XXXII, 6; I Cor. X, 7).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 8. Rursum, fratres, post conversionem nostram muniamus thalamum cordis nostri, ne luxuria rediens introitum inveniat: quae pestilentia rediens est pejor quam ante fuerat. Nunquam enim sola redit; sed sicut Dominus ait in Evangelio: Assumit septem spiritus nequiores se, et ingressi habitant ibi: et fiunt novissima hominis illius pejora prioribus (Matth. XII, 45). Haec est pestis illa quae corpus Christi dimembrat, quae de membris Christi facit membra diaboli. Nam qui adhaeret alicui personae causa libidinis explendae, unum corpus fit cum illa persona, et fit membrum diaboli: cujus et illa membrum est per conjunctionem malorum operum. Haec est illa pestis quae ignem infernalem in corpus humanum accendit, ut vegetum sit et robustum ad libidinem explendam: et quae igni illi inexstinguibili materiam semper apponit, et vires ministrat, ut de suo semper habeat unde sine fine ardeat. De his duobus ignibus luxuriae et gehennae habemus auctoritatem Scripturae. De igne luxuriae ait: Omnes adulterantes quasi clibanus succensus a coquente (Osee VII, 4). De igne gehennae ait: Pones eos ut clibanum ignis in tempore vultus tui, hoc est, judicii, ut intus ardeant (sicut clibanus accensus) in conscientia. Dominus in ira sua conturbabit eos (Psal. XX, 10), dicens: Discedite a me, operarii iniquitatis (Luc. XIII, 27; Psal. VI, 9; Matth. VII, 23). Et devorabit eos ignis extremus infernalis, quem accenderunt propter luxuriae foeda opera. Sit ergo, fratres, summa cura et summum studium his qui in talibus sunt, de talibus evadere et fugere.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 8. Again, brothers, after our conversion let us fortify the chamber of our heart, lest lust, returning, find an entrance — a plague which, returning, is worse than it was before. For it never returns alone; but, as the Lord says in the Gospel: "It takes with it seven spirits more wicked than itself, and they enter in and dwell there; and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first" (Matth. XII, 45). This is that plague which dismembers the body of Christ, which turns members of Christ into members of the devil. For whoever clings to another person for the sake of satisfying lust becomes one body with that person, and becomes a member of the devil — of whom that other person is likewise a member, through the joining together of their evil deeds. This is that plague which kindles the infernal fire within the human body, so that it may be lively and vigorous for the satisfying of lust; and which continually supplies fuel to that unquenchable fire, and furnishes it strength, so that it may always have from its own store that by which it burns without end. Concerning these two fires, that of lust and that of hell, we have the authority of Scripture. Of the fire of lust it says: "They are all adulterers, like an oven heated by the baker" (Osee VII, 4). Of the fire of hell it says: "Thou shalt make them as an oven of fire in the time of thy anger" (that is, of judgment), that they may burn within (as in a heated oven) in their conscience. "The Lord in his wrath shall trouble them" (Psal. XX, 10), saying: "Depart from me, you workers of iniquity" (Luc. XIII, 27; Psal. VI, 9; Matth. VII, 23). And the fire of hell at the last shall devour them, which they kindled on account of the foul works of lust. Let it be, therefore, brothers, the greatest care and the greatest zeal of those who are caught in such things, to escape and flee from such things.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 9. Nobis vero qui per gratiam Dei evasimus, et veterem exuimus hominem, qui sumus Sion, sit summum studium thalamum nostrum munire et adornare, et Christum regem suscipere, sicut haec scriptura praecipit quam recitavimus: “Adorna thalamum tuum, Sion.” Quid est adornare thalamum tuum? Virtutes congregare, quibus et pavimentum et parietes quasi cortinis, et floribus tota domus adornetur. Primus ornatus thalami nostri, qui sumus Sion, sit timor, qui est initium sapientiae, id est, primus gradus per quem ascenditur ad sapientiam. De quo timore ait Scriptura: Beatus homo qui semper pavidus (Prov. XXVIII, 14). Et Psalmista ait: Servite Domino in timore, et exsultate ei cum tremore (Psal. II, 11): ut timor auferat securitatem noxiam, et exultatio mortiferam tristitiam. Hic timor generat humilitatem, quae est pretiosissimus ornatus thalami Sion, quae magis placuit Christo cum in thalamum virgineum ingrederetur, dicente beata Maria: Quia respexit humilitatem ancillae suae, ecce enim ex hoc beatam me dicent omnes generationes (Luc. I, 48). Haec, inquam, humilitas est ornatus Sion, id est, pauperum Christi, de quibus ipse dicit: Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum coelorum (Matth. V, 3; Luc. VI, 20). Ecce quomodo timor Domini primus gradus ascensionis, et primus ornatus thalami Sion, alios etiam ornatus generat, humilitatem scilicet, et voluntariam paupertatem. Adorna ergo thalamum tuum, Sion, timore Domini.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 9. But as for us, who by the grace of God have escaped and have put off the old man, who are Sion, let it be our greatest zeal to fortify and adorn our chamber, and to receive Christ the King, just as this Scripture which we have recited commands: "Adorn thy chamber, O Sion." What does it mean to adorn your chamber? To gather together virtues, by which the whole house — both floor and walls — may be adorned as though with hangings and flowers. Let the first adornment of our chamber, we who are Sion, be fear, which is the beginning of wisdom, that is, the first step by which one ascends to wisdom. Of this fear Scripture says: "Blessed is the man that is always fearful" (Prov. XXVIII, 14). And the Psalmist says: "Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice unto him with trembling" (Psal. II, 11): so that fear may remove harmful security, and rejoicing remove deadly sorrow. This fear begets humility, which is the most precious adornment of the chamber of Sion, which pleased Christ most when he entered the virginal chamber, as blessed Mary says: "Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid; for behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed" (Luc. I, 48). This humility, I say, is the adornment of Sion, that is, of the poor of Christ, of whom he himself says: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Matth. V, 3; Luc. VI, 20). Behold how the fear of the Lord, the first step of ascent and the first adornment of the chamber of Sion, also begets other adornments, namely humility and voluntary poverty. Adorn, therefore, your chamber, O Sion, with the fear of the Lord.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 10. Secundus ornatus thalami Sion, et secundus gradus ad sapientiam, est pietas, de qua dicit Scriptura: Miserere animae tuae placens Deo (Eccli. XXX, 24); et alibi: Super quem requiescet spiritus meus, nisi super humilem et quietum? (Isa. LXVI, 2.) Haec miseretur in se peccantibus, fraterna onera portat; magis eligit quaelibet temporalia bona perdere, quam cum fratre lite contendere. Quae profecto pietas aliud nihil est nisi Deum colere, et per cultum Dei Deo placere. Haec in nobis generat mansuetudinem, optimum ornatum thalami Sion, quae filios Dei nos facit, dicente Domino: Beati mites, quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur (Matth. V, 4; Psal. XXXVI, 11). Ecce quomodo pietas secundus ornatus thalami Sion et secundus gradus ascensionis, alium ornatum de se generat mansuetudinem, quae filios Dei efficit. Adorna igitur thalamum tuum, Sion, pietate.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 10. The second adornment of the bridal chamber of Zion, and the second step toward wisdom, is piety, of which Scripture says: "Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God" (Eccli. XXX, 24); and elsewhere: "Upon whom shall my spirit rest, but upon the humble and quiet?" (Isa. LXVI, 2.). This piety has mercy on those who sin against it, bears the burdens of brothers; it chooses rather to lose any temporal goods whatsoever than to contend with a brother in a lawsuit. This piety, indeed, is nothing other than to worship God, and through the worship of God to please God. This generates in us meekness, the best adornment of the bridal chamber of Zion, which makes us sons of God, the Lord saying: "Blessed are the meek, for they shall be called sons of God" (Matth. V, 4; Psal. XXXVI, 11). Behold how piety, the second adornment of the bridal chamber of Zion and the second step of ascent, generates from itself another adornment, meekness, which makes us sons of God. Adorn, therefore, your bridal chamber, O Zion, with piety.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 11. Tertius ornatus thalami Sion et tertius gradus ascensionis est scientia, quae homini sui cognitionem praebet, ut scilicet homo, neque minus neque plus quam debet de se praesumat. Quorum alterum, scilicet de se nimium praesumere, in mala facit praecipitem; alterum, scilicet se non cognoscere, facit ad quaelibet bona torpentem. Ad hanc scientiam Spiritus sanctus invitat Ecclesiam in Canticis: Si ignoras te, o pulchra inter mulieres, abi post vestigia gregum tuorum, scilicet haereticorum: et pasce haedos tuos (Cantic. I, 7), hoc est, carnales concupiscentias. Haec scientia praebet nobis fiduciam vincendi omnes tentationes per veram fidem, dicente Domino in Evangelio: Si potes credere, omnia possibilia sunt credenti (Marc. IX, 22), per Dei scilicet gratiam, et liberum arbitrium. Videmus jam quomodo scientia tertius ornatus thalami Sion, et tertius gradus ascensionis, alium ornatum in nobis generat, religiosum videlicet luctum, qui consolationem a Domino in futuro meretur. Haec scientia parat in nobis dolorem et luctum peregrinationis, ut videndo mala exsilii quae patimur, cum luctu desideremus patriam a qua peregrinamur, audiamusque a Domino nobis dici: Beati qui lugent, quoniam ipsi consolabuntur (Matth. V, 6; Isa. LXI, 2).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 11. The third adornment of the bridal chamber of Zion and the third step of ascent is knowledge, which grants a man knowledge of himself, so that a man presumes of himself neither less nor more than he ought. Of these two faults, the one—presuming too much of oneself—makes one headlong into evils; the other—not knowing oneself—makes one sluggish toward whatever is good. To this knowledge the Holy Spirit invites the Church in the Canticle: "If you know not yourself, O fairest among women, go forth after the footsteps of your flocks"—that is, of the heretics—"and feed your kids" (Cantic. I, 7), that is, carnal desires. This knowledge affords us confidence to overcome all temptations through true faith, the Lord saying in the Gospel: "If you can believe, all things are possible to him that believes" (Marc. IX, 22), namely through the grace of God and free will. We see now how knowledge, the third adornment of the bridal chamber of Zion and the third step of ascent, generates in us another adornment, namely religious mourning, which merits consolation from the Lord in the future. This knowledge prepares in us the sorrow and grief of pilgrimage, so that, seeing the evils of exile which we suffer, we may with grief desire the homeland from which we are pilgrims, and may hear it said to us by the Lord: "Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted" (Matth. V, 6; Isa. LXI, 2).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 12. Quartus ornatus thalami Sion, est fortitudo, quae convenit laborantibus pro veris bonis acquirendis. Haec est quae munit thalamum Sion, ut non extollatur prosperis, non frangatur adversis: quae linguam increpantem et blandientem his verbis confundit, dicens: Domine, libera animam meam a labiis iniquis, et a lingua dolosa (Psal. CXIX, 2). Haec est illa quae semper de die in diem robustior, esuriem et sitim justitiae in thalamo Sion accendit, facitque eam audire a Domino: Beati qui esuriunt et sitiunt justitiam, quoniam ipsi saturabuntur. Adorna igitur thalamum tuum, Sion, fortitudine. Quintus ornatus thalami Sion est consilium, quo homo infirmitates suas requirit, suum posse et suum non posse investigat: et ex sua infirmitate alios considerat, aliis parcit et miseretur, sicut et vult Deum sibi misereri; aliis dimittit debita, sicut sibi vult dimitti a Deo: mereturque audire a Domino: Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur (Matth. V. 4, 7). Adorna igitur thalamum tuum, Sion, consilio. Sextus ornatus thalami Sion, est intellectus; qui mentem hominis super haec infirma rapit, omnesque corporeas substantias intellectuali intuitu transiens, non corporeis substantiis figitur, volensque ultra progredi, et propius accedere audit a Domino: Ne appropinques huc (Exod. III, 5): non enim videbit me homo, et vivet (Exod. XXXIII, 20). Hic intellectus convenit iis qui a Deo purgatum oculum habent, de quibus dicitur: Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt (Matth. V, 8). Adorna igitur thalamum tuum, Sion, intellectu.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 12. The fourth adornment of the bridal chamber of Zion is fortitude, which belongs to those laboring to acquire true goods. This is what fortifies the bridal chamber of Zion, so that it is not lifted up by prosperity, nor broken by adversity; which confounds the tongue that rebukes and the tongue that flatters with these words, saying: "Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips, and from a deceitful tongue" (Psal. CXIX, 2). This is that virtue which, growing ever stronger from day to day, kindles in the bridal chamber of Zion a hunger and thirst for justice, and makes it hear from the Lord: "Blessed are they that hunger and thirst after justice, for they shall be filled." Adorn, therefore, your bridal chamber, O Zion, with fortitude. The fifth adornment of the bridal chamber of Zion is counsel, by which a man examines his own weaknesses, searches out what he can and cannot do; and from his own weakness considers others, spares and shows mercy to others, just as he wishes God to show him mercy; forgives others their debts, as he wishes to be forgiven by God; and merits to hear from the Lord: "Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy" (Matth. V. 4, 7). Adorn, therefore, your bridal chamber, O Zion, with counsel. The sixth adornment of the bridal chamber of Zion is understanding, which snatches the mind of man above these weak things, and, passing by intellectual gaze beyond all bodily substances, is not fixed upon bodily substances; and wishing to go further and draw nearer, hears from the Lord: "Come not near hither" (Exod. III, 5): "for man shall not see me, and live" (Exod. XXXIII, 20). This understanding belongs to those who have had their eye purged by God, of whom it is said: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" (Matth. V, 8). Adorn, therefore, your bridal chamber, O Zion, with understanding.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 13. Septimus ornatus thalami Sion, est sapientia, quae convenit iis qui intellectualibus oculis aeterna contemplantur; quorum conversatio in coelis est, qui cupiunt dissolvi, et esse cum Christo: in quorum persona dicebat Apostolus: Mihi vivere Christus est, et mori lucrum. Quasi diceret: Ut Christum magnificem, Christo vivere volo tantum, et Christus est praemium mortis. Et post pauca: Coarctor autem e duobus, desiderium habens dissolvi et esse cum Christo, multo melius: manere autem in carne, necessarium propter vos (Philipp. I, 21, 23, 24). Ecce quid facit vera sapientia, quae omnes rebelles motus corporis ita subjugat, ut nullam ultra pugnam in carne sentiat: pro infirmis fratribus (ut eis Christum nuntiet) exsilium libenter patitur; probra non audit, damna non sentit, auferenti tunicam dimittit pallium, percutienti unam maxillam praebet et alteram, auditque a Domino: Beati pacifici, quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur (Matth. V, 9). Hi ornatus thalami Sion: istis nos adornemus qui sumus Sion, et regem Christum suscipiamus, quem Virgo concepit, Virgo peperit, Virgo post partum quadragesima, hoc est hodierna die, in templo Dei praesentavit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 13. The seventh adornment of the bridal chamber of Zion is wisdom, which belongs to those who with intellectual eyes contemplate eternal things; whose conversation is in heaven, who desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ: in whose person the Apostle said: "To me to live is Christ, and to die is gain." As if he said: "That I may magnify Christ, I wish only to live for Christ, and Christ is the reward of death." And shortly after: "But I am straitened between the two, having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, a thing by far the better: yet to abide in the flesh is necessary for your sake" (Philipp. I, 21, 23, 24). Behold what true wisdom does, which so subjugates all the rebellious movements of the body that it no longer feels any battle in the flesh: for the sake of weak brothers (that it may announce Christ to them) it willingly endures exile; it does not hear reproaches, it does not feel losses, to him that takes away its coat it gives up its cloak also, to him that strikes one cheek it offers the other also, and hears from the Lord: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God" (Matth. V, 9). These are the adornments of the bridal chamber of Zion: with these let us, who are Zion, adorn ourselves, and let us receive Christ the king, whom the Virgin conceived, the Virgin bore, and the Virgin, on the fortieth day after the birth—that is, on this very day—presented in the temple of God.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 14. In lege namque scriptum erat, ut mulier quae suscepto semine peperisset masculum, quadragesimo die purgata templum cum filio intraret, deferens hostias secum pro peccato, agnum anniculum immaculatum. Si autem non haberet agnum, par turturum, sive duos pullos columbae offerret (Levit. XII, 2, 4, 6, 8). Haec omnia beata Virgo non ex necessitate, sed ex humilitate implevit. Abstinuit ab introitu templi quadraginta diebus, non necesse habens purgari, quae sine omni delectatione, salvo virginitatis sigillo, de Spiritu sancto concepit. Obtulit hostiam non pro peccato, sicut aliae mulieres, sed pro humilitate: ostendens etiam in hoc quod Filius Dei Jesus Christus non solvere venerat legem, sed adimplere. Et ecce Simeon grandaevus, qui acceperat responsum non visurum se mortem nisi videret Christum Domini, et eum susciperet quem exspectabat, accepit eum in ulnas suas, hoc est, inter brachia sua amplexatus est; illum qui appendit tribus digitis molem terrae, qui omnia implet, omnia complectitur, inter brachia portat, dicens: Nunc dimittis, servum tuum, Domine, secundum verbum tuum, in pace. Cupio dissolvi, et ejus adventum cum patriarchis et prophetis in inferno exspectare, qui inter te et humanum genus facturus est pacem. Quia viderunt oculi mei salutare tuum, Filium tuum, quem desideravi, de quo responsum a Spiritu sancto accepi. Lumen ad revelationem gentium, et gloriam plebis tuae Israel (Luc. II, 29, 30, 32). De quo ait Isaias: Populus qui ambulabat in tenebris, vidit lucem magnam (Isa. IX, 2): quia, cum plenitudo Gentium intraverit, tunc omnis Israel salvus fiet (Rom. XI, 25, 26).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 14. For it was written in the Law that a woman who, having conceived, had borne a male child, should on the fortieth day, once purified, enter the temple with her son, bringing with her sacrifices for sin, a lamb of one year without blemish. But if she had no lamb, she was to offer a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons (Levit. XII, 2, 4, 6, 8). All these things the Blessed Virgin fulfilled not out of necessity, but out of humility. She abstained from entering the temple for forty days, though she had no need of purification, she who, without any delight, with the seal of her virginity unbroken, had conceived of the Holy Spirit. She offered the sacrifice not for sin, as other women did, but out of humility, showing also by this that the Son of God, Jesus Christ, had not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it. And behold, Simeon, now advanced in years, who had received the answer that he would not see death until he had seen the Christ of the Lord, and had received him whom he awaited, took him into his arms—that is, embraced him between his arms—him who weighs the mass of the earth with three fingers, who fills all things and embraces all things. Simeon carries him in his arms, saying: Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant, according to your word, in peace. I desire to be dissolved, and to await with the patriarchs and prophets in hell his coming, who is to make peace between you and the human race. For my eyes have seen your salvation, your Son, whom I desired, concerning whom I received an answer from the Holy Spirit. A light for the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel (Luc. II, 29, 30, 32). Of whom Isaiah says: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light (Isa. IX, 2): because, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, then all Israel shall be saved (Rom. XI, 25, 26).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 15. Audite, fratres, audite quid offert Maria, quid Simeon suscipit: Unigenitum Dei, Deo Patri consubstantialem et coaeterum, Verbum in principio. Et, ut utilitatem et consolationem nostram audiamus, illum offert Virgo, quem Deus Abrahae promisit, dicens: In semine tuo, hoc est, in Christo, benedicentur omnes gentes (Gen. XXII, 18; XII, 3, et XVIII, 18); et quem David promisit, dicens: De fructu ventris tui ponam super sedem tuam (Psal. CXXXI, 11). Hic est quem Virgo offert, patriarcharum gaudium, desiderium prophetarum, Gentium exspectatio, Judaeorum qui eum receperunt salvatio, ruinae angelorum reparatio. Talis est quem Virgo offert Deo, imo multo major quam lingua, aut hominum, aut angelorum possit dicere. Et cum sit tantus ac talis, qualem aut quantum ipse se novit, non sufficit Virgini ipsum solum offerre; sed hostiam, quam lex praeceperat, pro eo obtulit: ob humilitatis scilicet exemplum, ut nos doceret quomodo et nos eum debeamus offerre. Duos turtures, aut duos pullos columbae pro eo obtulit. Columba, fratres, simplex est animal, felle caret, rostro non laedit, in cavernis petrarum nidificat, alienos pullos nutrit, juxta fluenta manet, ut visa umbra accipitris fugiat, meliora grana eligit, gemitum pro cantu reddit, gregatim volat, alis se defendit, visum recuperat. Et nos, fratres, cum ante altare steterimus, ut Dei Filium Deo offeramus, cum eo et pro eo par turturum, castitatem corporis et animae offeramus: et duos pullos columbarum, pro cantu gementes, compunctionem geminam pro desiderio patriae coelestis, et de consideratione nostrae miseriae habentes. Columba felle caret: et nos ira careamus, quae peccare nos facit. Rostro non laedamus, sed percussi in unam maxillam, alium praebeamus. In cavernis petrarum nidificemus; in fide plagarum Christi refugium habeamus. Alienos pullos nutriamus; de filiis diaboli facientes verbo praedicationis filios Dei. Juxta flumina maneamus: id est, juxta hunc mortalitatis fluxum sedentes, umbram accipitris, hoc est, peccata quae sunt umbra diaboli, malorum ruinas considerantes, ab ejus ungulis fugiamus. Meliora grana eligamus id est, meliores sententias in Scripturis sanctis. Gregatim volemus. unum consensum in bono in congregatione sub pastore habentes. Alis Novi et Veteris Testamenti contra inimicos Dei nos defendamus; vel duobus praeceptis charitatis, Dei videlicet amore et proximi. Visum recuperemus, de bono actionis ad bonum semper intendentes contemplationis.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 15. Hear, brothers, hear what Mary offers, what Simeon receives: the Only-begotten of God, consubstantial and coeternal with God the Father, the Word in the beginning. And, that we may hear of our profit and consolation, the Virgin offers him whom God promised to Abraham, saying: In your seed, that is, in Christ, all nations shall be blessed (Gen. XXII, 18; XII, 3, et XVIII, 18); and whom David promised, saying: Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne (Psal. CXXXI, 11). This is he whom the Virgin offers: the joy of the patriarchs, the desire of the prophets, the expectation of the Gentiles, the salvation of the Jews who received him, the restoration of the ruin of the angels. Such is he whom the Virgin offers to God—indeed far greater than any tongue, whether of men or of angels, can tell. And although he is so great and of such a kind as he alone knows himself to be, it was not enough for the Virgin to offer him alone; but she offered for him the sacrifice which the Law had commanded—namely, as an example of humility, that she might teach us how we too ought to offer him. She offered for him two turtledoves, or two young pigeons. The dove, brothers, is a simple creature; it has no gall, does not wound with its beak, builds its nest in the clefts of the rocks, nourishes the young of others, dwells beside the streams so that, seeing the shadow of the hawk, it may flee; it chooses the better grains, utters a moan instead of a song, flies in flocks, defends itself with its wings, and recovers its sight. And we, brothers, when we stand before the altar to offer the Son of God to God, let us offer with him and for him a pair of turtledoves—the chastity of body and soul; and two young pigeons, groaning instead of singing, having a twofold compunction: one from desire for our heavenly homeland, and one from the consideration of our own misery. The dove has no gall: let us likewise be without anger, which makes us sin. Let us not wound with our beak, but, struck on one cheek, let us offer the other. Let us nest in the clefts of the rocks; let us have our refuge in the faith of the wounds of Christ. Let us nourish the young of others, making, by the word of preaching, sons of God out of the children of the devil. Let us dwell beside the rivers: that is, sitting beside this flow of mortality, considering the shadow of the hawk—that is, sins, which are the shadow of the devil—and the ruin of the wicked, let us flee from his claws. Let us choose the better grains, that is, the better teachings in the Holy Scriptures. Let us fly in flocks, having one accord in good within the congregation under the shepherd. Let us defend ourselves against the enemies of God with the wings of the New and Old Testament; or with the two precepts of charity, namely, the love of God and of neighbor. Let us recover our sight, always directing ourselves from the good of action toward the good of contemplation.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 16. Fratres charissimi, tales oportet nos esse cum corpus Christi consecramus, cum consecratum manducantes sacrificamus, cum vobis idem corpus in salutem corporis et animae porrigimus. Tales etiam vos oportet esse, cum sacrum sacramentum de manibus nostris accipitis, scientes, quod qui corpus Christi indigne accipit, et sanguinem ejus indigne bibit, judicium sibi manducat et bibit (I Cor. XI, 29). Verum, quia raro invenitur talis qui in se haec omnia habeat, diligat illum qui bonum habet, quod in se non habet: et in illo habeat, quod in se non videt. Neque enim credere debemus quod soli sacerdoti supradictae virtutes sint necessariae, quasi solus consecret et sacrificet corpus Christi. Non solus sacrificat, non solus consecrat, sed totus conventus fidelium qui astat, cum illo consecrat, cum illo sacrificat (4). Nec solus ligni faber facit domum, sed alius virgas, alius ligna, alius trabes, etc., comportat. Debent itaque astantes habere de suo, sicut et sacerdos, fidem firmam, orationem puram, devotionem piam. Sciendumque quod sine firma fide nemo astantium esse debet. Caeteras vero virtutes, quas supra diximus, etsi omnes non habent, diligant illum qui habet quod in se non inveniunt, et in illo habeant quod in se nondum vident. Sicut Petrus in Joanne virginitatis habet meritum: sic Joannes in Petro martyrii habet praemium.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 16. Dearest brothers, such as these ought we to be when we consecrate the body of Christ, when, by eating what has been consecrated, we offer sacrifice, when we hold out that same body to you for the salvation of body and soul. Such also ought you to be when you receive the sacred sacrament from our hands, knowing that whoever receives the body of Christ unworthily and drinks his blood unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself (I Cor. XI, 29). But because one is rarely found who has all these things in himself, let him love the one who has the good which he himself does not have, and let him possess in that other what he does not see in himself. For we ought not to believe that the aforesaid virtues are necessary to the priest alone, as though he alone consecrates and sacrifices the body of Christ. He does not sacrifice alone, he does not consecrate alone, but the whole assembly of the faithful who stand present consecrates with him, sacrifices with him (4). Nor does the carpenter alone build the house, but one brings rods, another timber, another beams, and so on. Therefore those standing present ought to have of their own, just as the priest does, firm faith, pure prayer, pious devotion. And it should be known that no one of those standing present ought to be without firm faith. As for the other virtues we have mentioned above, even if not all possess them, let them love the one who has what they themselves do not find in themselves, and let them possess in him what they do not yet see in themselves. Just as Peter has in John the merit of virginity, so John has in Peter the reward of martyrdom.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 17. Sciendum quoque, quod corpori Christi, quem Maria hodie praesentavit in templo, quem Simeon in ulnis suis suscepit, tria debemus: dignitatem, reverentiam et fructum. Dignitatem, ut cum Dei Filium, Deum de Deo, omnipotentem, creatorem omnium, judicem vivorum et mortuorum credamus. Dignitatem, ut credamus nos statim postquam de corpore exierimus, ab eo, sicut a judice, percepturos sicut gessimus, sive bonum, sive malum. Ille namque quem Maria in templo praesentavit, quem Simeon suscepit, quem in manibus consecrantes ante Deum levamus, benedicimus, manducamus, vobis porrigimus manducandum; ille familiaris noster, judex erit noster. Caveamus ergo ab eo separari per judicium post mortem, cui ita sumus familiares in vita. Dicamus itaque ei in corde, cum eum tractamus; dicamus cum eum consecramus: Domine, ad te veniemus post mortem, ante tuum tribunal judicandi astabimus. Qui nobis ita familiaris esse dignaris in vita, quod a nobis tractaris, consecraris, manducaris, noli nobis alienus esse in morte, sed parce nobis in die mala. Confundantur daemones qui nos tunc persequentur, destrue fortitudinem illorum in virtute tua; quia non est qui pugnet pro nobis, nisi tu Deus et familiaris noster. Haec est dignitas quam ei debemus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 17. We should also know that to the body of Christ, which Mary presented today in the temple, which Simeon received into his arms, we owe three things: dignity, reverence, and fruit. Dignity, that we believe him to be the Son of God, God of God, omnipotent, creator of all things, judge of the living and the dead. Dignity, that we believe that immediately after we leave the body, we shall receive from him, as from a judge, according as we have done, whether good or evil. For he whom Mary presented in the temple, whom Simeon received, whom we, consecrating, lift up in our hands before God, whom we bless, whom we eat, whom we hold out to you to be eaten — he who is so familiar to us will be our judge. Let us take care, then, not to be separated from him at the judgment after death, from him with whom we are so intimate in this life. Let us therefore say to him in our heart, when we handle him; let us say when we consecrate him: Lord, we shall come to you after death; we shall stand before your tribunal to be judged. You who deign to be so familiar with us in this life, that you are handled by us, consecrated by us, eaten by us — do not be a stranger to us in death, but spare us on the evil day. Let the demons who will then pursue us be confounded; destroy their strength by your power; for there is no one to fight for us except you, God and our familiar one. This is the dignity we owe him.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 18. Debemus ei et reverentiam, investigare scilicet nosmetipsos: et si invenimus cor pollutum foedis cogitationibus aut mala voluntate, ab ejus contactu, ut ab igne, et nos et alios arceamus. Ignis enim consumens est (Deut. IV, 24.), ad quem indignus non debet accedere, ne interius consumatur, et in reprobum sensum tradatur. Exeat ergo extra castra, sicut Moyses praecepit, qui nocturno pollutus est somno (Deut. XXIII, 10), hoc est, qui per negligentiam istius obscurae vitae (quae tota ut somnus pertransit) pervenit usque ad pollutas cogitationes. Exeat extra castra, hoc est, dum in illo statu est, judicet se indignum societate fidelium communicantium hoc sacro corpore, lavetque vestimenta sua per sanctam confessionem; et post solis occasum, hoc est, post tentationis calorem et ardorem jam mortuum, laetus redeat, et cum aliis fidelibus communicet. Haec est reverentia quam debemus corpori Christi, quem virgo Maria hodierna die in templo praesentavit, quem Simeon laetus inter brachia suscepit.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 18. We also owe him reverence, namely, to search ourselves, and if we find a heart defiled by foul thoughts or evil will, to keep both ourselves and others from contact with him, as from fire. For he is a consuming fire (Deut. IV, 24.), whom an unworthy person ought not approach, lest he be consumed within and be given over to a depraved mind. Let him therefore go outside the camp, as Moses commanded, who has been defiled by nocturnal sleep (Deut. XXIII, 10) — that is, let him who through the negligence of this dark life (which passes away wholly like sleep) has come even to defiled thoughts. Let him go outside the camp, that is, while he is in that state, let him judge himself unworthy of the fellowship of the faithful who partake of this sacred body, and let him wash his garments through holy confession; and after the setting of the sun — that is, after the heat and burning of temptation has now died down — let him return joyfully, and commune with the other faithful. This is the reverence we owe to the body of Christ, whom the Virgin Mary presented in the temple on this day, whom Simeon joyfully received into his arms.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 19. Debemus etiam fructum scire, intelligere scilicet quem fructum accipimus, si eum digne comedimus. Audite, fratres, non me, sed Apostolum dicentem: Calix benedictionis cui benedicimus, nonne communicatio sanguinis Christi est? Calix, id est communicatio calicis, facit nos habere quamdam communionem cum Christo. Et panis, quem frangimus, nonne participatio corporis est Domini? (I Cor. X, 16.) Ac si dicat: Panis, quem frangimus, facit nos unum corpus sub Christo capite: quoniam, sicut unus panis ex multis granis conficitur, qui postea in corpus Christi et per fidem, et per sancta verba, quae Christus suos docuit, convertitur: sic diversi participantes hoc corpore in unitate fidei, spei et charitatis, unum corpus cum Christo sunt, ad Christum statim post mortem venturi, et cum Christo sicut cum capite suo sine fine regnaturi: quem Virgo concepit, Virgo peperit. Virgo in templo hodierna die praesentavit, qui cum Patre et Spiritu sancto, vivit et regnat Deus, per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 19. We ought also to know the fruit, that is, to understand what fruit we receive if we eat him worthily. Hear, brothers, not me, but the Apostle saying: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a communion of the blood of Christ? The cup, that is, the sharing of the cup, makes us have a certain communion with Christ. And the bread, which we break, is it not a participation in the body of the Lord? (I Cor. X, 16.). As if he were saying: The bread which we break makes us one body under Christ as head: for just as one bread is made from many grains, which is afterward converted into the body of Christ both by faith and by the holy words which Christ taught his own, so the various people who partake of this body in the unity of faith, hope, and charity are one body with Christ, destined to come to Christ immediately after death, and to reign without end with Christ as with their head — whom the Virgin conceived, the Virgin bore. The Virgin presented him in the temple on this day — he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, through all the ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: (2) De hoc sermone dubitat Horstius an sit Guerrici: tum quod desideretur in manuscripto Coloniensi, qui ipsius sermones continet. tum quod Guerrici stylus pressior et nervosior videatur. Porro licet hactenus Bernardi operibus insertus sit, minus tanto dignus est auctore.

passages.label: English
passages.text: (2) Horstius doubts whether this sermon is Guerric's: both because it is missing from the Cologne manuscript, which contains his sermons, and because Guerric's style seems more compressed and vigorous. Moreover, although it has hitherto been inserted among the works of Bernard, it is less worthy of so great an author.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: (3) Ita canit Ecclesia in officio hujus diei.

passages.label: English
passages.text: (3) So the Church sings in the Office of this day.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: (4) Solum sacerdotem esse proprium et sufficientem ministrum Eucharistiae consecrandae de fide est, ut patet ex can. 4 conc. Nic. ubi Patres dum diaconos reprehendunt, quod quibusdam in locis administrent Eucharistiam presbyteris, idque de caetero fieri prohibent, hanc ejusce decreti reddunt rationem: Hoc inquiunt, neque regula neque consuetudo tradidit ut qui offerendi sacrificii non habent potestatem, his qui offerunt corpus Christi porrigant. Idem statuit conc. Lateran. sub Innoc. III, et refertur cap. Firmiter extra de sum. Trin. Nam veritate sacramenti explicata, ita subjungit: Et hoc utique sacramentum nemo potest conficere nisi sacerdos, qui rite fuerit ordinatus, secundum claves Ecclesiae, quas concessit apostolis eorumque successoribus Jesus Christus. Ita fere Isambertus, in 3 q. 82, art. 1. Quanquam dici potest, astantes etiam suo modo sacrificium offerre et conficere per sacerdotem et cum sacerdote qui populi mediator et minister est. Unde in canone missae olim ita legebatur: Et omnium circumstantium, qui tibi offerunt hoc sacrificium laudis, quibus verbis haec inserta sunt: Pro quibus tibi offerimus, vel qui tibi offerunt. etc.

passages.label: English
passages.text: (4) That the priest alone is the proper and sufficient minister for consecrating the Eucharist is a matter of faith, as is clear from canon 4 of the Council of Nicaea, where the Fathers, in rebuking the deacons because in certain places they were administering the Eucharist to the presbyters, and forbidding that this be done henceforth, give this reason for the decree: "Neither rule nor custom," they say, "has handed down that those who have no power of offering the sacrifice should give the Body of Christ to those who offer it." The Lateran Council under Innocent III established the same thing, and it is referred to in the chapter "Firmiter" in the Decretals, On the Most High Trinity; for having explained the truth of the sacrament, it adds: "And indeed no one can consecrate this sacrament except a priest who has been duly ordained, according to the keys of the Church which Jesus Christ granted to the apostles and their successors." So, more or less, Isambert, in part 3, question 82, article 1. Although it may be said that those standing by also, in their own way, offer and accomplish the sacrifice through the priest and with the priest, who is the mediator and minister of the people. Whence in the canon of the Mass it used to be read: "And of all those standing round, who offer to Thee this sacrifice of praise," words into which these were inserted: "For whom we offer to Thee," or "who offer to Thee," etc.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: Authorship uncertain. The edition presents this sermon as Guerric's, but its footnote (2) reports that the earlier editor Horstius doubted it: the sermon is missing from a Cologne manuscript of Guerric's sermons, and its style is less terse and vigorous than his. It had also been printed among the works of Bernard of Clairvaux.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition prints alium, where aliam (agreeing with maxillam) is expected. The printed form is kept.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition prints cum, evidently a misprint for eum (him). The printed form is kept.
