passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Simeon's completed purification prompts an examination of negligence and the use of time. Guerric considers purification through prayer, watchful faith and the final vision of God. The sermon appears in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO VI.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON VI.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De perficienda nostri purificatione, ut Domino sisti possimus.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On Perfecting Our Purification So That We May Be Presented to the Lord

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Postquam impleti sunt dies purgationis, tulerunt Jesum in Jerusalem. O quam felix est, de quo dici potest: Impleti sunt dies purgationis ejus: ut jam nihil aliud ei supersit, nisi ut ferant eum in Jerusalem supernam, et sistant eum Domino (Luc. II, 22). Talis nimirum erat Simeon ille noster senex, tam desiderabilis quam plenus desideriis, cujus cum jam olim, ut arbitror, essent impleti dies purgationis, hodie impleti sunt etiam dies exspectationis: ut jam, secundum verbum Domini, nihil aliud ei restaret, postquam vidisset Christum Domini, Christum pacem Dei et hominum, nisi ut dimitteretur in pace, et dormiret in pace in idipsum; hoc est, ut ferrent eum in Jerusalem pacis aeternae, et sisterent eum ad contemplandam pacem quae exsuperat omnem sensum. O Simeon vir desideriorum, impletum est in bonis desiderium tuum. O beate senex, renovata est ut aquilae juventus tua. Introisti jam ad altare Dei illud supernum, aeternum, totum aureum, ad Deum qui laetificat juventutem tuam aeterna visione sui, cujus laetificavit senectutem hodierna visione Christi sui. Ad altare illud invisibile jam ipse praesentatus es Patri; cui ad altare hoc visibile Filium hodie praesentasti. Ibi Filium ipsum, quem hodie tuo sinu gestasti, aeterno jam et indissolubili tibi conseris amplexu.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. "After the days of purification were fulfilled, they carried Jesus up to Jerusalem." O how happy is he of whom it can be said: "The days of his purgation were fulfilled," so that nothing else remains for him but that they carry him up to the heavenly Jerusalem and present him to the Lord (Luc. II, 22). Such, surely, was our Simeon of old, that elder as desirable as he was full of desires, whose days of purgation had, I think, long since been fulfilled; and today his days of expectation also were fulfilled, so that, according to the word of the Lord, nothing else remained for him, once he had seen the Christ of the Lord, the Christ who is the peace of God and of men, but to be dismissed in peace and to sleep in peace in that very peace — that is, that they should carry him into the Jerusalem of eternal peace, and present him to behold the peace which surpasses all understanding. O Simeon, man of desires, your desire has been fulfilled with good things! O blessed elder, your youth has been renewed like the eagle's! You have already come to that heavenly altar, eternal, wholly golden, to God who gladdens your youth with the eternal vision of himself, who gladdened your old age today with the vision of his own Christ. At that invisible altar you yourself have already been presented to the Father, to whom at this visible altar you presented the Son today. There you now embrace in an eternal and indissoluble embrace that very Son whom today you bore in your own arms.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Repletum est igitur in bonis beati senis desiderium, cujus tota erat exspectatio et desiderium, Exspectatio gentium et Desideratus earum. Renovata est ut aquilae juventus ejus, quoniam in senectute bona impleti sunt dies purgationis ejus. Alioquin nequaquam illius capax novitatis esse posset, nisi sedulo vetustatem his diebus expurgasset. Fratres, expurgate vetus fermentum, dum tempus habetis ad expurgandum; ut cum impleti fuerint dies vestrae purgationis, inveniamini et vos capaces illius gaudii, quo plena est jam anima Simeonis. Et quidem dies qui ad purgandum nobis dati sunt, velimus, nolimus, implemus: sed vae nobis si dies implentur, et purgatio minime impletur; ut postea necesse sit illo nos igne repurgari, quo nihil poenalius, nihil acrius, aut vehementius in hac vita excogitari potest. Sed quis ille tam perfectus, tam sanctus, qui cum hinc exierit, nihil illi debeat igni: qui sic ad purum omnem in se scoriam excoxerit peccati, ut gloriari possit castum se habere cor, ut dicere possit: Mundum est cor meum, purus sum a peccato? (Prov. XX, 9.) Pauci quidem sunt electi; sed inter illos paucos paucissimi sunt, ut arbitror, ita perfecti, ut purgationem illam impleverint, de qua Sapiens dicit: De negligentia purga te cum paucis (Eccli. VII, 34). Omnino, si de negligentia nos purgaremus, de paucis essemus. Nunc autem quoniam non modo minima, sed et maxima negligimus, longe a paucis de terra divisi sumus, et de nobis dicit ille, qui paucitatem sanctorum multitudini praefert negligentium: Inter multos erant mecum (Psal. LIV, 19).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. The desire of the blessed old man, therefore, was fulfilled with good things: his whole expectation and desire was the Expectation of the nations and their Desired One. His youth was renewed like the eagle's, because in a good old age the days of his purgation were fulfilled. Otherwise he could by no means have been capable of that newness, had he not diligently purged away his oldness in those days. Brethren, purge out the old leaven while you have time to purge it, so that when the days of your purgation have been fulfilled, you too may be found capable of that joy with which the soul of Simeon is now filled. And indeed the days given us for purging, whether we will or not, we do fulfill; but woe to us if the days are fulfilled and the purgation is by no means fulfilled, so that afterward we must needs be purged again by that fire than which nothing more penal, nothing more bitter or more violent can be conceived in this life. But who is so perfect, so holy, that when he departs from here he owes nothing to that fire — who has so thoroughly burned out every dross of sin in himself that he can boast of having a chaste heart, that he can say: "My heart is clean, I am pure from sin"? (Prov. XX, 9.) Few indeed are the elect; but among those few, fewest of all, I think, are so perfect as to have fulfilled that purgation of which the Wise Man says: "Purge yourself from negligence with the few" (Eccli. VII, 34). Certainly, if we purged ourselves of negligence, we would be among the few. But now, since we neglect not only the smallest things but even the greatest, we are far removed from the few on earth, and of us he says, who prefers the fewness of the saints to the multitude of the negligent: "They were with me among the many" (Psal. LIV, 19).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Et quid hodie tam proprium simul et commune his quos religionis fovet umbra, sicut negligentia? et, ut de meipso loquar, quoties derident hostes Sabbata mea? quoties dormitat anima mea prae taedio, diemque fere totum, ac si tempus revocabile esset, inertia consumo? Et utinam sic dormitaret anima mea, ut apertis et vigilantibus oculis, ipse mihi misero non fingerem somnia vana et illusoria! At nunc in perversum mutata sententia, ego vigilo, et cor meum dormit, somnoque tam gravi, ut vix aliquando valeat expergisci ad tonitruum supernae illius increpationis: Usquequo, piger, dormis? quando consurges e somno tuo? Paululum dormies, paululum dormitabis, paululum conseres manus ut dormias; et veniet tibi quasi viator egestas, et pauperies quasi vir armatus (Prov. VI, 8-11; XXIV, 33, 34). Illud sane miserrimum est, quod hodie non putatur jactura, sed lucrum, si dies qui nobis ad purgationem dati sunt, elabantur nobis dormiendo, praetereant et pereant negligendo. Gentilis, aiunt, cum sederet ad mensam, venissetque in mentem nihil strenuum, aut memorabile se egisse die illo; cum gemitu gravi et dolore mensam repulit, exclamans: « O amici, diem perdidi (5) » Nos hodie dicere videmur, diem lucrifeci, si sine opere totus per inertiam possit elabi. Sic nullus fere est qui tempori pretium ponat, qui cogitet apud se quantum valeat ad comparandam aeternitatem dies una. Putasne est aliquis in nobis, qui quotidianam dierum suorum a semetipso rationem exigat; qui cujusque diei dispendia vel emolumenta diligenter sibi describat: ut si deprehenderit se hodie negligenter egisse, vindicet in seipsum, ac de caetero cautius agat? Beatus ille servus, quem, cum venerit dies extremus, invenerit ita facientem.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. And what today is at once so proper and so common to those whom the shadow of religion shelters, as negligence? And, to speak of myself, how often do enemies mock my Sabbaths? How often does my soul drowse from weariness, and I consume almost the whole day in idleness, as though time could be recalled! And would that my soul drowsed in such a way that, with eyes open and watchful, I did not fashion for myself, wretched man, vain and illusory dreams! But now, in a perverse reversal, I am awake, and my heart sleeps — and sleeps so heavily that it can scarcely ever be roused by the thunder of that heavenly rebuke: "How long will you sleep, O sluggard? When will you rise from your sleep? You will sleep a little, you will slumber a little, you will fold your hands a little to sleep; and your want shall come upon you like a traveler, and your poverty like an armed man" (Prov. VI, 8-11; XXIV, 33, 34). This indeed is most wretched, that today it is not thought a loss but a gain, if the days given us for purgation slip away from us in sleep, and pass by and perish through negligence. The pagan, they say, sitting at table, when it came to his mind that he had done nothing vigorous or memorable that day, pushed back the table with heavy groaning and grief, exclaiming: "O friends, I have lost a day (5)!" We today seem to say, "I have gained a day," if it can slip away entirely through idleness, without any work. Thus there is almost no one who sets a price on time, who considers within himself how much a single day is worth toward securing eternity. Do you think there is anyone among us who demands of himself a daily account of his days, who diligently sets down for himself the losses or gains of each day, so that if he finds he has acted negligently today, he punishes himself for it, and acts more cautiously thereafter? Blessed is that servant whom, when the last day comes, he shall find so doing.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Hoc nempe esset de negligentia cum paucis purgari, si recte et utiliter implerentur dies purgationis, ut aliquando posset accessus ad sancta salubriter obtineri. Alioquin, quandiu manserit quis in sanguine purificationis suae, sancivit aeterna justitia (sicut scriptum est in lege Moysi) ut omne sanctum non tangat, nec ingrediatur sanctuarium, donec impleantur dies purgationis ejus (Levit. XII, 4). Viderint ergo qua fronte ingrediantur sanctuarium, qua conscientia non solum tangant sancta, sed etiam tractent et sumant Sanctum sanctorum; qui scilicet nondum liberati de sanguinibus, nullum tamen suae purificationis studium gerunt. Annon audiunt protestantem et dicentem: Cum extenderitis manus vestras, avertam oculos meos; manus enim vestrae sanguine plenae sunt? (Isai. I, 15.) Quid enim, si mundus sum a sanguine alieno, et conculcari me Dominus videt in sanguine proprio (Ezech. XVI, 6), sicut de Jerusalem loquitur per Ezechielem? Quid, inquam, mihi proderit, si veloces non sunt pedes mei ad effundendum sanguinem proximorum; et veloces sunt affectus mei ad acquiescendum carni et sanguini, de quibus dicit Apostolus: Quia caro et sanguis regnum Dei non possidebunt? (I Cor. XV, 50.) Maledictus, inquit Jeremias, qui prohibet gladium suum a sanguine (Jerem. XLVIII, 10): id est, qui vitia carnis et sanguinis sibi parcit abscindere. Libera me de sanguinibus, Deus, Deus salutis meae (Psal. L, 16), ne cum sanguine purificationis meae sanctuarium ingrediens, aut sancta contingens, reus inveniar corporis et sanguinis tui, indigne manducans et bibens. Verumtamen gratias tibi, Deus, Deus salutis meae, qui in hoc ipsum pretiosum tuum fudisti sanguinem, ut immunditiam nostri purificares sanguinis, tactumque peccatricis sanguinem fluentis, sed salutem desiderantis non abhorreres: sciens nimirum quod nullus potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine, nisi tu, qui solus es; nec sanis, sed male habentibus, melius tamen habere cupientibus, medicus opus est. Tangere itaque Sanctum sanctorum, sicut illis quos delectat in sanguine suo versari, judicium est mortis: sic illis qui desiderant purificari, remedium est salutis, juxta prophetiam Simeonis, Quia hic positus est in ruinam et in resurrectionem multorum (Luc II, 34).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. This indeed would be to be purified from negligence along with the few, if the days of purification were rightly and profitably fulfilled, so that access to holy things might at some point be beneficially obtained. Otherwise, as long as anyone remains in the blood of his purification, eternal justice has decreed (as it is written in the law of Moses) that he shall not touch anything holy, nor enter the sanctuary, until the days of his purification are fulfilled (Levit. XII, 4). Let them consider, then, with what effrontery they enter the sanctuary, with what conscience they not only touch holy things but even handle and consume the Holy of Holies — those, namely, who are not yet freed from blood, and yet make no effort at all toward their own purification. Do they not hear him protesting and saying: 'When you stretch out your hands, I will turn away my eyes; for your hands are full of blood'? (Isai. I, 15.). For what does it profit me if I am clean of another's blood, while the Lord sees me trampled underfoot in my own blood (Ezech. XVI, 6), as he speaks of Jerusalem through Ezekiel? What, I say, will it profit me if my feet are not swift to shed the blood of my neighbors, while my affections are swift to acquiesce to flesh and blood, of which the Apostle says: 'For flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God' (I Cor. XV, 50.)? 'Cursed,' says Jeremiah, 'is he who withholds his sword from blood' (Jerem. XLVIII, 10): that is, he who spares himself from cutting away the vices of flesh and blood. Deliver me from blood, O God, God of my salvation (Psal. L, 16), lest, entering the sanctuary with the blood of my purification, or touching holy things, I be found guilty of your body and blood, eating and drinking unworthily. Yet thanks be to you, God, God of my salvation, who for this very purpose poured out your precious blood, that you might purify the uncleanness of our blood, and did not abhor the touch of a sinful woman flowing with blood, yet desiring salvation: knowing well that no one can make clean what was conceived of unclean seed, except you, who alone can; nor is the physician needed for the healthy, but for those who are ill, yet desire to be better. Thus to touch the Holy of Holies is, for those who delight in wallowing in their own blood, a sentence of death; but for those who desire to be purified, it is a remedy of salvation, according to the prophecy of Simeon: 'For this one is set for the fall and for the resurrection of many' (Luc II, 34).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Fratres, et vos quidem in sanguine fuistis, sed abluti estis, sed purificati estis: nisi quia, sicut justus confitetur: Si loti fueritis velut aquis nivis, sordibus vos statim intingit (Job IX, 30, 31), non solum conditio corrupta, sed etiam voluntas infirma; ut semper novis sordibus opus sit purificatione nova. Illa vero mirabilis et miserabilis est in hominibus sui negligentia, ut, cum nemo sit qui se purificatione non indigere praesumat, vix tamen est aliquis qui tempus ad hoc indultum, quasi purgatissimus sit, non negligat. Fratres, breves dies hominis sunt (ibid., 25), sed tamen valde pretiosi sunt; imo quo breviores, eo pretiosiores; quia dies sunt purificationis, cum statim postmodum futuri sint dies retributionis. Beati qui in diebus istis lavant stolas suas, et candidas eas faciunt in sanguine Agni; ne postea vestimentum eorum, si mistum fuerit sanguine, sit in combustionem et cibus ignis (Isai. IX, 5). Nec solum timor urget supplicii, sed etiam spes invitat praemii, ut omni cura et instantia nostrae modo studeamus purificationi; ut quod hodie figurare voluit in seipso Filius Dei quadam dispensatoria specie, completum quandoque gaudeamus in nobis ipsa rerum veritate. Quid illud? Postquam, inquit, impleti sunt dies purgationis, tulerunt Jesum in Jerusalem, ut sisterent eum Domino (Luc. II, 23). Et nos utique, si tempora purgationis legitime fuerint a nobis impleta, tollent in supernam Jerusalem ministeria angelorum, ut illic assistentes vultui Dei, oblatio ejus simus accepta et immaculata. Ibi demum purificabimur ex toto; sicut a peccato, sic etiam a poena peccati. Ibi nostrae purificationis ipsa erit consummatio, quae et remuneratio; cum scilicet divinus ignis totos nos absumet in holocaustum Domino.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Brothers, you too were indeed in blood, but you have been washed, you have been purified — except that, as the just man confesses: 'If you have been washed as it were with waters of snow, it immediately plunges you into filth' (Job IX, 30, 31), it is not only our corrupted condition but also our weak will that does this, so that there is always need of new purification for new filth. But this is a marvelous and wretched thing in men — this negligence of themselves — that, though there is no one who presumes himself not to need purification, there is scarcely anyone who does not neglect the time granted for this, as though he were already most thoroughly purified. Brothers, the days of man are few (ibid., 25), yet they are very precious; indeed, the shorter they are, the more precious — because they are days of purification, since immediately afterward will come the days of retribution. Blessed are those who in these days wash their robes, and make them white in the blood of the Lamb; lest afterward their garment, if it be mingled with blood, be for burning and fuel for fire (Isai. IX, 5). Not only does the fear of punishment press us, but the hope of reward also invites us, so that we should now strive toward our purification with all care and urgency; so that what the Son of God today willed to prefigure in himself by a certain outward dispensation, we may one day rejoice to see fulfilled in us in the very truth of the reality. What is that? 'After,' it says, 'the days of purification were fulfilled, they brought Jesus to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord' (Luc. II, 23). And we too, surely, if the times of our purification have been rightly fulfilled by us, the ministries of angels will carry us up into the heavenly Jerusalem, so that, standing there before the face of God, we may be his acceptable and unblemished offering. There at last we shall be purified wholly — as from sin, so also from the punishment of sin. There the very consummation of our purification will take place, which will also be our reward; when, that is, the divine fire shall consume us wholly as a holocaust to the Lord.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Porro hunc ipsum beatissimae purificationis inexplicabilem modum nec modo quidem cessat aemulari devotio sanctorum, quantum tamen corruptela corporum, et sollicitudo terrenae inhabitationis permittunt: dum scilicet mente excedentes in illam Jerusalem, verum orationis locum, illic in conspectu Domini quasi turturem et columbam pro seipsis ac de seipsis offerunt; corde videlicet et carne exsultantes in Deum vivum, quia scilicet columba invenit sibi domum, et turtur nidum, altaria tua, Domine virtutum (Psal. LXXXIII, 4). Ego tamen arbitror quod ad meritum non sit inferius, et fortassis ad purgationem efficacius, si illud quod per speculum et in aenigmate raro et raris experiri datur, id est, ut in Jerusalem sistantur Domino, nos per fidem jugiter actitemus: proponentes scilicet Dominum in conspectu nostro semper, et oculos ejus et judicia super nos pervigili fide, irremissoque semper timore cogitantes. Fides ista, fratres, sit in vobis, et eritis de paucis: timor iste sit in vobis, et de negligentia purgabitis vos cum paucis; quia timor iste nihil facile negligit. Denique ab initio hujus pertransibitis, sicut sponsus sponsae pollicetur, euntes de virtute in virtutem, a claritate in claritatem, tanquam a Domini Spiritu (II Cor. III, 18): proficientes de visione quae est per fidem, ad illam quae est per speculum et imaginem, ac postremo, de illa, quae est in imagine speciei, ad eam quae erit in ipsa veritate faciei, seu facie veritatis. Si enim jugiter praesentiam Domini, licet velatam, intendatis per fidem; aliquando etiam revelata facie gloriam ejus speculabimini, licet per speculum et imaginem. Cum autem impletis diebus purgationis venerit quod perfectum est, assistetis Domino in Jerusalem, habitantes cum vultu ejus, ac sine fine contuentes eum facie ad faciem, cui benedictio, et claritas in saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Moreover, the devotion of the saints does not even now cease to imitate this inexpressible manner of most blessed purification, so far as the corruption of our bodies and the anxious care of our earthly dwelling permit: that is, when, rising above in mind into that Jerusalem which is the true place of prayer, they there offer in the sight of the Lord, as it were, a turtledove and a dove for themselves and of themselves; rejoicing, namely, in heart and flesh unto the living God, because indeed the dove has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest, even your altars, O Lord of hosts (Psal. LXXXIII, 4). Yet I reckon that it is no less meritorious, and perhaps more effective for purgation, if that which is granted to be experienced rarely and by the few through a mirror and in a riddle — namely, to be presented to the Lord in Jerusalem — we continually practice through faith: setting the Lord always before our sight, and pondering, with ever-watchful faith and unrelaxing fear, his eyes and his judgments upon us. Let this faith, brothers, be in you, and you will be among the few; let this fear be in you, and you will purify yourselves from negligence along with the few, since this fear neglects nothing easily. Finally, from this beginning you will pass on, as the Bridegroom promises to his bride, going from strength to strength, from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord (II Cor. III, 18): advancing from the vision that comes through faith, to that which comes through a mirror and image, and at last, from that which is in the image of a likeness, to that which will be in the very truth of the face, or the face of truth. For if you continually fix your attention, through faith, upon the presence of the Lord, veiled though it be, you will one day also behold his glory with face unveiled, though still as through a mirror and image. But when, the days of purification being fulfilled, that which is perfect shall come, you will stand before the Lord in Jerusalem, dwelling with his countenance, and gazing upon him face to face without end — to whom be blessing and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: (5) Titus imp., apud Sueton. Iisdem pene verbis queritur Seneca, epist. 1.

passages.label: English
passages.text: (5) The Emperor Titus, in Suetonius. Seneca complains in almost the same words, Epistle 1.

sermons.title: Purification Sermon VI: On Perfecting Our Purification So That We May Be Presented to the Lord

sermons.author: Guerric of Igny
metadata: Guerric of Igny, Sermones per annum, De ressurrectione Domini, sermo I, Pulchre verba Jacob de Joseph applicantur ad resurrectionem Christi, in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier frères, 1879), cols. 141–144.
Internet Archive, 2011; PIMS, University of Toronto; University of Toronto funding.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric of Igny reads the news that Joseph is alive as a figure of the announcement that Jesus has risen. Jacob’s grief and renewed spirit become a pattern for the apostles’ passage from doubt to joy, and for the hearers’ growth in love. The Holy Spirit’s witness, love that seeks Christ’s life rather than its own advantage, and Christ’s flesh as provision for the journey shape the concluding exhortation. The individual sermon is not dated; the collection is associated approximately with Guerric’s abbacy in 1138–1157 and is read here from the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. Its historical heading names the Resurrection of the Lord, and the sermon explicitly celebrates Easter.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: DE RESSURRECTIONE DOMINI.

passages.label: English
passages.text: THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO I.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON I

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: Pulchre verba Jacob de Joseph applicantur ad resurrectionem Christi.

passages.label: English
passages.text: Jacob’s Words about Joseph Are Aptly Applied to Christ’s Resurrection

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Nuntiaverunt Jacob, dicentes: Joseph vivit. Quo audito, revixit spiritus ejus, et ait: Sufficit mihi, si Joseph filius meus vivit. Vadam et videbo eum antequam moriar. (Gen. xlv, 26, 28). Dicetis forsitan, mihi, Bene; sed quid ad rem? quid de Joseph ad gaudium hujus diei, ad gloriam resurrectionis Christi? Pascha est, et tu iterum apponis quadragesimalia? Agnum paschalem esurit anima nostra, cui se per tam longa praeparavit jejunia. Ardens est cor nostrum in nobis de Jesu, Jesum desideramus; sed nondum meremur ipsum videre vel de ipso audire. Jesum, non Joseph esurimus; Salvatorem, non somniatorem; dominatorem coeli, non Aegypti; non qui pavit ventres, sed qui pascit mentes, sed esurientes. In hoc saltem nos adjuvet sermo tuus, ut, quem esurimus, amplius esuriamus. Legimus enim: Beati qui esuriunt, quoniam ipsi saturabuntur. (Matth. v, 6). Cum audimus, magis esurimus. Nam et qui epulas commendat, famem irritat. Si de Jesu audierimus, auditui nostro dabitur gaudium et laetitia, et exsultabunt ossa humiliata. Humiliata sunt ossa nostra quadragesimali afflictione et luctu, magis autem dolore passionis ejus; sed exsultabunt nuntio resurrectionis ejus. Cur ergo tuum Joseph nobis ingeris, cum praeter Jesum, quidquid loquaris non sapiat nobis: praesertim hodie, cum paschalis agnus comeditur, cum Pascha nostrum immolatus est Christus?

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. They brought news to Jacob, saying: Joseph is alive. On hearing this, his spirit revived, and he said: It is enough for me if Joseph my son is alive. I will go and see him before I die. (Gen. xlv, 26, 28). Perhaps you will say to me: Very well; but what has this to do with the matter? What has Joseph to do with the joy of this day, with the glory of Christ’s resurrection? It is Easter, and you are serving Lenten fare again? Our soul hungers for the Paschal Lamb, for whom it has prepared itself through such long fasts. Our heart burns within us for Jesus; we long for Jesus, but we do not yet deserve to see him or hear about him. We hunger for Jesus, not Joseph; for the Saviour, not the dreamer; for the ruler of heaven, not Egypt; for him who feeds minds, and hungry minds at that, rather than him who fed bellies. At least let your sermon help us in this: to hunger still more for him for whom we hunger. For we read: Blessed are those who hunger, for they shall be filled. (Matth. v, 6). As we hear, we hunger more. For one who praises a feast also whets the appetite. If we hear about Jesus, joy and gladness will be granted to our hearing, and the bones brought low will exult. Our bones have been brought low by Lenten affliction and mourning, and still more by grief for his Passion; but they will exult at the news of his resurrection. Why, then, do you thrust your Joseph upon us, when whatever you say apart from Jesus has no savour for us, especially today, when the Paschal Lamb is eaten, when Christ our Passover has been sacrificed?

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 2. Ovum sive nucem apposui vobis, fratres; frangite testam, et invenietis escam. Joseph discutiatur, et Jesus invenietur agnus paschalis, quem esuritis; qui tanto dulcius comeditur, quanto latens abstrusius, et studiosius quaeritur, et difficilius invenitur Dicitis mihi: Quid Joseph ad Christum? quid historia quam proposui ad diem istum? Multum per omnem modum. Historiam recordamini, et ultro sese vobis revelabit pietas mysterii, si modo Jesum interpretem habeatis, qui, hodieque resurgens, de occidente littera loquitur suis in via, et aperit Scripturas. Quis enim in omnibus Patriarchis et Prophetis manifestius aut signantius quam Joseph figuram exprimit Salvatoris? Et, ut breviter summam perstringam, secundum illud: Da occasionem sapienti, et addetur ei sapientia (Prov. ix, 9), si cum fide ac pietate cogitemus interpretationem nominis ejus, deinde quod prae caeteris fratribus pulchra facie et decorus aspectu (Gen. xxxix, 6), quod innocens actu, prudens intellectu, quod venditus a suis, suos a morte redemit, quod prius humiliatus usque ad ergastulum, et sic exaltatus usque ad solium, quod denique pro merito operis sui novo nomine appellatus est inter gentes Salvator mundi (Gen. xli, 45); si haec omnia, inquam, pie ac fideliter cogitemus, nonne incunctanter agnoscimus quam vere sit a Domino dictum: In manibus Prophetarum assimilatus sum? (Ose. xii, 10).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 2. I have served you an egg or a nut, brothers; break the shell, and you will find food. Let Joseph be examined, and Jesus will be found, the Paschal Lamb for whom you hunger. He is eaten all the more sweetly when, hidden more deeply, he is sought more earnestly and found with greater difficulty. You say to me: What has Joseph to do with Christ? What has the story I have set before you to do with this day? Much in every way. Recall the story, and the loving mercy of the mystery will reveal itself to you of its own accord, provided you have Jesus as your interpreter, who, rising even today from the letter that kills, speaks to his own on the road and opens the Scriptures. For who among all the patriarchs and prophets expresses the figure of the Saviour more clearly or distinctly than Joseph? And, to touch briefly on the main points, according to the saying, Give the wise man an opportunity, and wisdom will be added to him (Prov. ix, 9): if we consider with faith and devotion the meaning of his name; then how, beyond his other brothers, he was beautiful in face and comely in appearance (Gen. xxxix, 6); how he was innocent in deed and prudent in understanding; how, sold by his own, he redeemed his own from death; how he was first humbled as far as the prison and then raised as high as the throne; and finally how, in recognition of his work, he was given a new name among the nations, Saviour of the world (Gen. xli, 45)—if, I say, we consider all these things devoutly and faithfully, do we not acknowledge without hesitation how truly the Lord said: Through the hands of the prophets I have been represented in likeness? (Ose. xii, 10).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Jam vero si veniamus ad verba illa quae de historia proposui, puto quia non tam expositione indigebunt, quam admirationem et gaudium movebunt; quod videlicet tam evidenter resurrectio Christi testificata sit a Lege et Prophetis, et historia vetus tam proprie nova sacramenta loquatur, ut, cum prophetia legitur, pene Evangelium mutatis duntaxat nominibus audiri videatur. Nuntiaverunt, inquit, Jacob, dicentes: Joseph vivit. Quid aliud hic intelligere possum, nisi, Nuntiaverunt Apostolis dicentes: Jesus vivit? Jacob namque nihil aliud quam Apostolorum chorum intelligo; nec absurde, ut arbitror: non solum quia de Jacob orti sunt, non solum quia de Jacob Israel facti sunt, cum de lucta activae ad visionem et requiem contemplativae transierunt; sed etiam quia Patres sunt multitudinis credentium, id est verorum Israelitarum, sicut ille carnalium. Sicut ille, sic isti, suum Joseph cum putarent periisse, inconsolabiliter doluerunt; cum audissent vivere, difficulter et tarde crediderunt; cum cognovissent, ineffabiliter gavisi sunt. Nuntiaverunt, inquit, Jacob, dicentes: Joseph vivit. Quo audito Jacob, quasi de gravi somno evigilans, tamen non credebat eis (Gen. xlv, 26). Quasi aliis verbis mihi videtur dictum, quod in Evangelio legitur scriptum: Illa vadens, haud dubium quin Maria Magdalene, nuntiavit his qui cum ea fuerant lugentibus et flentibus; et illi audientes quia viveret et visus esset ab ea, non crediderunt. Post haec ostensus est duobus in via, et illi exeuntes nuntiaverunt caeteris, nec illis crediderunt (Marc. xvi, 10-13). Item apud Lucam. Et regressae a monumento, nuntiaverunt haec omnia illis undecim, et caeteris omnibus; et visa sunt ante illos sicut deliramentum verba ista, et non credebant illis (Luc. xxiv, 9, 11); nimirum quia evigilabant de gravi somno taedii et desperationis. Cum autem, inquit, vidisset Jacob universa quae Joseph miserat ei, revixit spiritus ejus, et ait: Sufficit mihi si Joseph filius meus vivit. Vadam et videbo eum, antequam moriar. (Gen. xlv, 27, 28). Sic utique in Apostolis parum profecerunt verba, donec acceperunt munera. Nam et ipse Jesus cum se eis praesentem exhibuit, non tam persuasit ostensione corporis, quam aspiratione muneris.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Now, if we turn to those words from the story which I set before you, I think they will need explanation less than they will stir wonder and joy. For Christ’s resurrection is so plainly attested by the Law and the Prophets, and the ancient story speaks so aptly of the new mysteries, that when the prophecy is read, it seems almost as though we were hearing the Gospel with only the names changed. They brought news to Jacob, it says, saying: Joseph is alive. What else can I understand here but: They brought news to the apostles, saying: Jesus is alive? By Jacob I understand none other than the company of the apostles, and not unreasonably, I think. This is not only because they descended from Jacob, nor only because from Jacob they became Israel when they passed from the struggle of the active life to the vision and rest of the contemplative life, but also because they are fathers of the multitude of believers, that is, of the true Israelites, just as he was of the Israelites according to the flesh. Like him, when they thought their Joseph had perished, they grieved inconsolably; when they heard he was alive, they believed with difficulty and slowly; when they knew it, they rejoiced beyond words. They brought news to Jacob, it says, saying: Joseph is alive. On hearing this, Jacob, as though waking from a deep sleep, nevertheless did not believe them (Gen. xlv, 26). It seems to me to say in other words what we read written in the Gospel: She went—undoubtedly Mary Magdalene—and brought the news to those who had been with her, mourning and weeping; and when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe. After this he appeared to two on the road, and they went out and brought the news to the others, but they did not believe them either (Marc. xvi, 10-13). Again, in Luke: Returning from the tomb, they told all these things to the eleven and to all the others; and these words seemed to them like nonsense, and they did not believe them (Luc. xxiv, 9, 11). For they were indeed waking from the deep sleep of weariness and despair. But when Jacob saw all that Joseph had sent him, it says, his spirit revived, and he said: It is enough for me if Joseph my son is alive. I will go and see him before I die. (Gen. xlv, 27, 28). So too, words made little headway with the apostles until they received gifts. For when Jesus himself showed himself present to them, he persuaded them less by displaying his body than by breathing his gift upon them.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Scitis quia cum venit ad eos januis clausis, et stetit in medio eorum, illi conturbati et conterriti existimabant se spiritum videre (Luc. xxiv, 37). Cum autem insufflavit in eos, dicens: Accipite Spiritum sanctum (Joan. xx, 22), vel cum coelitus misit eumdem Spiritum, sed aliud donum, haec utique dona, resurrectionis et vitae indubitata testimonia fuerunt et argumenta. Spiritus enim est qui testificatur apud sanctorum corda et per eorum ora, quoniam Christus est veritas, vera resurrectio et vita. Ideo et Apostoli, qui prius dubitabant etiam post intuitum corporis viventis, post gustum spiritus vivificantis, virtute magna reddebant testimonium resurrectionis. Adeo plus est corde Jesum concipere, quam oculis videre, vel auribus de ipso audire; tantoque potentior est operatio Spiritus apud sensus hominis interioris, quam corporalium apud sensus exterioris. Quis enim dubietati relinquatur locus, ubi qui testificatur, et cui testificatur, unus fuerit Spiritus? Si unus Spiritus et unus sensus, parque consensus. Tunc ergo vere, sicut de Jacob legitur, revixit eorum spiritus, qui jam propemodum luctu erat exstinctus, imo desperatione sepultus. Tunc, nisi fallor, quisque eorum dicebat sibi: Sufficit mihi quod Joseph meus vivit; quia vivere mihi Christus est, et mori lucrum. Vadam igitur in Galilaeam, in montem ubi constituit nobis Jesus, et videbo eum, et adorabo antequam moriar, ut postea nunquam moriar; quia omnis qui videt Filium et credit in eum, habet vitam aeternam, ut, etiamsi mortuus fuerit, vivat (Joan. vi, 40, et xi, 26).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. You know that when he came to them with the doors closed and stood in their midst, they were troubled and terrified and thought they were seeing a spirit (Luc. xxiv, 37). But when he breathed upon them, saying: Receive the Holy Spirit (Joan. xx, 22), or when he sent from heaven the same Spirit but a different gift, these gifts were indeed unquestionable testimonies and proofs of resurrection and life. For it is the Spirit who bears witness in the hearts of the saints and through their mouths that Christ is the truth, the true resurrection and life. Thus the apostles, who had doubted even after looking upon his living body, after tasting the life-giving Spirit bore witness to the resurrection with great power. So much greater is it to receive Jesus in the heart than to see him with the eyes or hear about him with the ears; and so much more powerful is the Spirit’s action upon the senses of the inward man than that of bodily things upon the senses of the outward man. For what room can remain for doubt when the one who bears witness and the one to whom witness is borne are one Spirit? If there is one Spirit, there is also one perception and equal agreement. Then truly, as we read of Jacob, their spirit revived, which had already been almost extinguished by grief, indeed buried by despair. Then, unless I am mistaken, each of them said to himself: It is enough for me that my Joseph is alive, for to me to live is Christ and to die is gain. I will therefore go to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus has appointed to meet us, and I will see him and worship before I die, so that thereafter I may never die; for everyone who sees the Son and believes in him has eternal life, so that even if he has died, he may live (Joan. vi, 40, et xi, 26).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Nunc ergo, fratres mei, quid vobis testatur gaudium cordis vestri de amore Christi? Puto equidem (an recte, vos videritis) quoniam si unquam amastis Jesum, seu vivum, seu mortuum, sive redivivum, hodie, cum tam crebro in Ecclesia personant et consonant nuntii Resurrectionis, cor vestrum in vobis gloriatur sibi, et dicit: Nuntiaverunt mihi, dicentes: Jesus Deus meus vivit. Quo audito revixit spiritus meus, qui dormitabat prae taedio, vel languebat tepore, aut nimia deficiebat pusillanimitate. Nam et de morte suscitat criminosos jucunda vox hujus felicis nuntii. Alioquin certe desperandus est et oblivione sepeliendus, quem Jesus, regrediens ab inferis, in intimo reliquit inferni. In hoc sane noveris quod spiritus tuus plene in Christo revixerit. si quod sequitur ex sententia dixerit: Sufficit mihi, si Jesus vivit. O vocem fidelem et plane dignam amicis Jesu! o castissimum affectum, qui sic loquitur: Sufficit mihi si Jesus vivit! Si vivit, vivo, cum de ipso pendeat anima mea, imo ipse sit vita mea, ipse sufficientia mea. Quid enim mihi deesse poterit, si Jesus vivit? Imo desint omnia alia, nihil interest mea, dummodo Jesus vivat. Ipse ergo, si placet ei, desit mihi; sufficit mihi, dummodo vivat ipse vel sibi. Cum sic amor Christi totum absorbuerit affectum hominis, ut, negligens et immemor sui nonnisi Jesum Christum et ea quae sunt Jesu Christi sentiat, tunc demum, ut arbitror, perfecta est in eo charitas. Huic utique qui sic affectus est, non est onerosa paupertas: iste non sentit injurias, ridet opprobria, contemnit damna, mortem lucrum deputat; imo nec mori se putat, cum magis de morte ad vitam transire se sciat, et fidenter dicat; Vadam et videbo eum, antequam moriar.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. Now then, my brothers, what does the joy of your heart testify to you about love for Christ? I think indeed—you must judge whether rightly—that if you have ever loved Jesus, whether living, dead, or restored to life, today, when the messengers of the Resurrection sound out so often and in harmony in the Church, your heart within you takes its delight and says: They brought me news, saying: Jesus my God is alive. On hearing this, my spirit revived, which had been dozing from weariness, languishing in lukewarmness, or failing through excessive faintheartedness. For the joyful voice of this happy news raises even sinners from death. Otherwise, surely, that man must be given up for lost and buried in oblivion whom Jesus, returning from the underworld, has left in its deepest depths. By this you may know for certain that your spirit has fully come to life again in Christ: if it sincerely says what follows, It is enough for me if Jesus is alive. O faithful utterance, entirely worthy of Jesus’ friends! O most chaste love, which speaks in this way: It is enough for me if Jesus is alive! If he lives, I live, since my soul depends upon him; indeed, he himself is my life, he himself all that suffices me. For what could I lack if Jesus is alive? Indeed, let everything else be lacking: it matters nothing to me, provided Jesus lives. Let even he himself, then, be absent from me, if that pleases him; it is enough for me, provided he himself lives, even for himself alone. When love for Christ has so absorbed all a person’s affection that, neglectful and forgetful of self, that person is mindful only of Jesus Christ and the things of Jesus Christ, then at last, I think, charity is perfected in that person. For one so disposed, poverty is no burden; he does not feel injuries, laughs at reproaches, despises losses, and counts death as gain. Indeed, he does not even think he is dying, knowing rather that he is passing from death to life, and confidently saying: I will go and see him before I die.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 6. Nos tamen, fratres mei, licet non simus tantae nobis puritatis conscii, eamus nihilominus, eamus videre Jesum in montem Galilaeae coelestis, ubi constituit nobis. Eundo crescet affectus, et saltem perveniendo perficietur. Eundo, via prius arcta et difficilis dilatatur, et virtus infirmis augetur. Ut enim nec Jacob, nec aliquis de domo Jacob se excusaret a via praeter alia munera, missa sunt pauperi seni sumptus et vehicula, ne quis videlicet aut paupertatem causaretur, aut infirmitatem. Caro Christi est viaticum, spiritus vehiculum. Ipse est cibus, ipse currus Israel et auriga ejus. Cum perveneris, tua sunt optima quaeque, non Aegypti, sed coeli: in optimo loco regni tuus Joseph tibi requiem providit. Qui prius misit Angelos, mulieres, et Apostolos resurrectionis suae testes et nuntios, nunc ipse clamat e coelo: Ecce ego quem mortuum lugebatis hoc triduo, mortuus quidem fui propter vos, sed ecce vivo, et data est mihi omnis potestas in coelo et in terra (Matth. xxviii, 18). Venite ad me, qui laboratis fame: et ego reficiam vos. (Id. xi, 28), Venite, benedicti Patris mei, percipite regnum quod vobis paravi (Id, xxv, 34). Qui vos eo vocat, ipse perducat, ubi cum Patre et Spiritu sancto vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 6. Yet, my brothers, although we are not conscious of such purity in ourselves, let us go nonetheless; let us go to see Jesus on the mountain of heavenly Galilee, where he has appointed to meet us. As we go, love will grow, and at least on arriving it will be perfected. As we go, the road, at first narrow and difficult, grows wider, and strength increases for the weak. For, so that neither Jacob nor anyone of Jacob’s household might excuse himself from the journey, besides the other gifts, provisions and vehicles were sent to the poor old man, so that no one might plead either poverty or weakness. Christ’s flesh is provision for the journey; the spirit is the conveyance. He himself is the food, he himself the chariot of Israel and its driver. When you arrive, all the best things are yours, of heaven rather than Egypt: in the best place in the kingdom your Joseph has provided rest for you. He who first sent angels, women, and apostles as witnesses and messengers of his resurrection now himself cries from heaven: Behold, I whom you mourned as dead these three days was indeed dead for your sake, but behold, I live, and all power in heaven and on earth has been given to me (Matth. xxviii, 18). Come to me, you who labour with hunger, and I will refresh you. (Id. xi, 28), Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom which I have prepared for you (Id, xxv, 34). May he who calls you there himself lead you to where, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition prints the Latin title RESSURRECTIONE. The opening quotation from Genesis belongs to the first paragraph.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The Mark quotation reads “those who had been with her,” rather than the familiar Gospel wording “with him.” The Latin and English follow the sermon. Guerric’s comparison between Jacob and Israel and the Apostles is his own typological interpretation.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition cites John 6:40 and 11:26. Its combined quotation also draws on John 11:25 (“even if he has died”).

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The sermon adapts Christ’s invitations: “you who labour with hunger,” “I will refresh you,” and “the kingdom which I have prepared for you.” The abbreviation Id. refers back to Matthew.

sermons.title: Resurrection Sermon I: Joseph Lives, Jesus Lives

sermons.author: Guerric of Igny
metadata: Guerric of Igny (collection attribution), Sermones per annum, SERMO II., De duplici nostra resurrectione., in J.-P. Migne, Patrologiae cursus completus, Series Latina, vol. 185, pars prior (Paris: Garnier frères, 1879), cols. 144-148.

passages.label: Editorial introduction
passages.text: Guerric reads the blessing on those who share in the first resurrection. Christ is both resurrections: by the sacrament of his rising he works the first, of souls, and by its example he will work the second, of bodies. Death reigned from Adam until Christ, free of sin and of the debt of death, died and rose for us. Guerric calls the poor to buy and eat the paschal bread, and warns those who squander in idle talk the sweetness received in devotion. The sermon appears under the Resurrection heading in the 1879 edition of Patrologia Latina. The collection is associated approximately with Guerric's abbacy in 1138–1157; the individual sermon is undated.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: SERMO II.

passages.label: English
passages.text: SERMON II.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: De duplici nostra resurrectione.

passages.label: English
passages.text: On our twofold resurrection.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 1. Beatus et sanctus qui habet partem in resurrectione prima (Apoc. XX, 5). Ego sum, inquit Jesus, resurrectio et vita (Joan. XI, 25). Ipse utique resurrectio prima, ipse et resurrectio secunda. Resurgens quippe a mortuis primitiæ dormientium Christus, et sacramento suæ resurrectionis operatus est nobis resurrectionem primam, et exemplo ejusdem suæ resurrectionis operabitur nobis secundam. Prima enim est animarum, cum eas sibi conresuscitat in novitatem vitae: secunda erit corporum cum reformabit corpus humilitatis nostrae, configuratum corpori claritatis suae (Philipp. iii, 21). Recte igitur resurrectionem et vitam Christus se profitetur, quandoquidem per ipsum et in ipsum resurgimus, ut secundum ipsum et apud ipsum vivamus: nunc quidem secundum ipsum, in sanctitate et justitia; postmodum apud ipsum, in beatitudine et gloria. Porro sicut resurrectio prima capitis nostri Domini Jesu Christi causa est et argumentum secundae resurrectionis, quae erit totius ipsius corporis, sic unicuique nostrum prima resurrectio animae, qua reviviscit a morte peccati, argumentum est et causa secundae suae resurrectionis, qua corpus liberabitur non modo a corruptione mortis, sed etiam ab omni corruptibilitate mortalitatis. Quod enim haec illius argumentum et causa sit, Apostolus evidenter ostendit, ubi ait: Si spiritus Christi habitat in vobis, qui suscitavit Christum a mortuis vivificabit et mortalia corpora vestra, propter inhabitantem spiritum ejus in vobis (Rom. viii, 11).

passages.label: English
passages.text: 1. Blessed and holy is he who has a part in the first resurrection (Apoc. XX, 5). I am, says Jesus, the resurrection and the life (Joan. XI, 25). He himself is indeed the first resurrection, and he himself the second resurrection. For Christ, rising from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep, has by the sacrament of his own resurrection wrought for us the first resurrection, and by the example of that same resurrection of his will accomplish for us the second. For the first is of souls, when he raises them together with himself into newness of life; the second will be of bodies, when he will refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory (Philipp. iii, 21). Rightly, therefore, does Christ declare himself to be resurrection and life, since it is through him and in him that we rise, that according to him and with him we may live: now indeed according to him, in holiness and justice; afterward with him, in blessedness and glory. Moreover, just as the first resurrection of our Head, the Lord Jesus Christ, is the cause and proof of the second resurrection, which will be that of his whole body, so for each one of us the first resurrection of the soul, by which it revives from the death of sin, is the proof and cause of his second resurrection, by which the body will be freed not only from the corruption of death but also from all corruptibility of mortality. That the one is indeed the proof and cause of the other, the Apostle clearly shows where he says: If the Spirit of Christ dwells in you, he who raised up Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, because of his Spirit dwelling in you (Rom. viii, 11).

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3 Bene igitur dicitur. Beatus et sanctus qui habet partem in prima resurrectione (Apoc. xx, 6). Sanctus videlicet propter primam, quam jam adeptus est per innovationem animae; beatus propter secundam, quam feliciter exspectat in corporis restitutione. Denique unde beatus sit, eadem aperit Scriptura, cum subdit: In his scilicet qui partem habent in prima resurrectione, mors secunda non habet potestatem, etiamsi prima mors visa est ad horam in eis exercuisse dominationem. Regnavit quippe mors ab Adam usque ad Moysen, etiam in eos qui peccaverunt in similitudinem praevaricationis Adae (Rom. v, 14). Sed sicut Christus, sic et christianus resurgens a mortuis, jam non moritur, mors illi ultra non dominabitur (Id. vi, 9). Itaque in beatis illic nec mors secunda potestatem habebit, nec prima potestatem quam ad tempus habuit, retinebit; quoniam mors una Christi utramque nostram triumphavit, ab ista liberans jam captos, ab illa, capiendos; ne videlicet in illam incidamus, nec in ista remaneamus. Quam vera, quam pia simul et magnifica illa morientis comminatio: Ero mors tua, o mors (Osee. xiii, 14)! Quam pulchre et mirifice triumphavit, qui, mortem pro omnibus gustans, tam suam quam omnium omnimodam mortem absorbuit! Prorsus absorpta est mors in victoria. Securus insultet ei quicunque beatus ille est, qui partem habet in resurrectione prima: Ubi est, mors, victoria tua? ubi est, mors, stimulus tuus? Victa es, quae omnia vincebas; sed et arma perdidisti, in quibus confidebas. Ubi enim est stimulus tuus? Stimulus mortis peccatum (I Cor. xv, 55, 56), quod semel pungens humani radicem generis, in totam propaginem immedicabile mortis venenum diffudit, dicente Apostolo quia per unum hominem peccatum, et per peccatum mors, et ita in omnes homines pertransivit (Rom. v, 12). Victrix ergo regnabat mors ab Adam primo etiam usque ad secundum; quoniam sicut originali lege tenebatur universum genus humanum vinculo peccati, sic etiam debito moriendi.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Rightly, then, is it said: Blessed and holy is he who has a part in the first resurrection (Apoc. xx, 6). He is holy, namely, on account of the first resurrection, which he has already attained through the renewal of the soul; he is blessed on account of the second, which he happily awaits in the restoration of the body. Finally, Scripture itself reveals the reason for this blessedness when it adds: namely, that in those who have a part in the first resurrection, the second death has no power, even though the first death seemed for a time to have exercised dominion over them. For death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who sinned after the likeness of Adam's transgression (Rom. v, 14). But just as Christ, so too the Christian, rising from the dead, no longer dies; death will no longer have dominion over him (Id. vi, 9). And so among the blessed there, neither will the second death have power, nor will the first retain the power it held for a time; since the one death of Christ triumphed over both our deaths, freeing from the one those already captive, and from the other those who were to be captured—namely, that we might not fall into that second death, nor remain in this first one. How true, how pious and at the same time how magnificent is that threat of the dying Christ: I will be your death, O death! (Osee. xiii, 14). How beautifully and wonderfully he triumphed, who, tasting death for all, swallowed up death utterly, both his own and that of all! Death is indeed swallowed up in victory. Let whoever is that blessed one who has a part in the first resurrection boldly taunt death: Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? You who conquered all things are conquered; and you have lost also the weapons in which you trusted. For where is your sting? The sting of death is sin (I Cor. xv, 55, 56), which, once piercing the root of the human race, spread an incurable poison of death through the whole lineage, as the Apostle says, that through one man sin, and through sin death, entered, and so passed into all men (Rom. v, 12). Death, then, reigned as victor from the first Adam even to the second, since, just as the whole human race was held bound by the original law in the bond of sin, so also it was held under the debt of dying.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 3. Deo autem gratias, qui dedit nobis victoriam tam peccati quam mortis, utique per Dominum Jesum Christum, qui prorsus a peccato immunis, ac per hoc liber a debito mortis, hanc tamen ultro pro nobis exsolvit moriens, et peccato nos absolvit resurgens. Christus enim, ait Apostolus, mortuus est propter delicta nostra, et resurrexit propter justificationem nostram (Rom. iv, 25) Moriens namque delictorum nostrorum pendit poenam, et resurgens justificationis perpetuae nobis condidit formam et causam, ut, quomodo videlicet Christus resurgens a mortuis jam non moritur, mors illi ultra non dominabitur (Rom. vi, 9), sic christianus conresurgens Christo jam non peccet ad mortem, nec ei peccatum ultra dominetur. Hic est ille beatus et sanctus, qui partem habet in resurrectione prima, in quem nec potestatem habebit mors secunda, sed absorbebitur in victoriam resurrectionis Christi etiam mors prima. Hic est qui non solum agnovit, sed etiam apprehendit virtutem resurrectionis Christi, et societatem passionis illius; configuratus morti ejus, ut occurrat ad resurrectionem ex mortuis. Non errabat Apostolus, qui, ob lucrum illud, omnia quae ei lucra fuerant non solum detrimenta reputabat, sed etiam velut stercora arbitrabatur, tantum ut Christo inveniretur, configuratus sicut morti, sic et resurrectioni ipsius (Philipp. iii, 7-11). Lucrosum omnino commercium, contemnere ea quae te deterunt et polluunt, ut lucrifacias Christum; imo, si opus sit, non solum tua, sed et te ipsum superimpendere, ut cum tanto fenore immortalitatis et gloriae te ipsum merearis recipere! Quis enim ambigat lucrosum esse commercium, seminare corpus mortale, animale, ignobile, ut surgat immortale, spirituale, gloriosum; mori mundo, ut possis dicere, Mihi vivere Christus est, et mori lucrum? (Id. i, 21.) O cupidi, quid immoramini studio lucrandi? cur non discitis artem lucrandi? cur non vilia, imo detrimenta et stercora contemnitis, ut Christum lucrifaciatis? Quare appenditis argentum non in panibus, et laborem vestrum non in saturitate (Isai. lv, 2)? Ut video, vilior est vobis argento vestro panis ille qui de coelo descendit, et dat vitam mundo. Sed non potest scire quanti [ alias quantus. ] sit, qui non vult gustare qualis sit. Utinam avarus vel ipse sibi pretiosior esset pecunia sua, nec amore illius venalem exponeret animam suam, projiceretque in vita sua intima sua (Eccli. x, 10). Prudens ille negotiator dignusque rerum aestimator, Paulum nimirum loquor, qui nec animam suam, id est animalem sensualemque vitam, pretiosiorem fecit se ipso (Act. xx, 24), id est spiritu suo, quo videlicet connexus inhaerebat Christo, paratus animam perdere, ut in vitam aeternam posset eam custodire.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 3. Thanks be to God, who gave us victory over both sin and death, namely through our Lord Jesus Christ, who, being entirely free from sin, and therefore free from the debt of death, nevertheless willingly paid that death for us by dying, and absolved us from sin by rising again. For Christ, says the Apostle, died for our sins, and rose again for our justification (Rom. iv, 25). For by dying he paid the penalty of our sins, and by rising he established for us the pattern and cause of perpetual justification, so that just as Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. vi, 9), so the Christian, rising together with Christ, may no longer sin unto death, nor may sin have dominion over him any longer. This is that blessed and holy one who has a part in the first resurrection, over whom the second death shall have no power, but even the first death shall be swallowed up in the victory of Christ's resurrection. This is he who has not only recognized but also laid hold of the power of Christ's resurrection, and the fellowship of his passion; being conformed to his death, so that he may attain to the resurrection from the dead. The Apostle was not mistaken, who, for the sake of that gain, counted all the things that had been gains to him not only as losses, but even reckoned them as dung, provided only that he might be found in Christ, conformed both to his death and to his resurrection (Philipp. iii, 7-11). It is altogether a profitable exchange to despise the things that wear you down and defile you, so that you may gain Christ; indeed, if need be, to spend not only your goods but even yourself, so that with such great interest of immortality and glory you may deserve to receive yourself back! For who could doubt that it is a profitable exchange, to sow a mortal, natural, ignoble body, that it may rise immortal, spiritual, glorious; to die to the world, so that you may say, For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain? (Id. i, 21.) O you who are greedy, why do you linger in your zeal for gaining? Why do you not learn the art of gaining? Why do you not despise cheap things — indeed losses and dung — so that you may gain Christ? Why do you weigh out your silver for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy (Isai. lv, 2)? As I see it, that bread which came down from heaven and gives life to the world is of less worth to you than your silver. But one who refuses to taste what it is like cannot know how great it is. Would that the miser were at least more precious to himself than his money, and would not, for love of it, offer his own soul up for sale, and cast away his inmost self while yet alive (Eccli. x, 10). That prudent merchant and worthy appraiser of things — I mean, of course, Paul — who did not reckon his own soul, that is, his natural and sensual life, more precious than himself (Act. xx, 24), that is, than his spirit, by which, closely joined, he clung to Christ, ready to lose his soul so that he might keep it unto eternal life.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 4. Quia igitur qui divitias habent, difficile intrant in regnum coelorum; et qui thesaurizant argentum, citius appendunt illud in inanibus, quam in panibus, in azymis dico sinceritatis et veritatis, cum quibus hodie comedendus est Agnus paschalis; vos beati pauperes, filii pauperis Crucifixi, vos inquam, qui non habetis argentum, properate, emite et comedite. Promptius omnino et facilius emunt bonum illud nihil habentes, quam multa possidentes. Cum deest facultas, sufficit ad emendum bona voluntas, qua plerumque sunt ditiores, qui rebus sunt pauperiores. Hos nimirum recte invitat Scriptura: Venite, emite absque argento, et absque ulla commutatione, vinum et lac (Isai. LV, 1). Vides, o felix pauper, solam a te voluntatem bonam exigi, in illa sola rationem tanti constare commercii? Ne recuses ingratus quod tam gratis offertur, imo ne perdas ingrata voluntate, quod jam merueras beata paupertate. Agnosce quanti lucri sit, non habere partem in ruina mundi, ut partem habeas in resurrectione Christi. Intellige quantae felicitatis sit, non inebriari luxu et furore saeculi, ut cum Christo novum bibas vinum in regno Patris sui. Invitat ipse Agnus paschalis amicos ad delicias corporis et sanguinis sui: Comedite, inquiens, amici, bibite, et inebriamini, charissimi (Cantic. V, 1). Cibus iste et potus, vitae est mysterium, immortalitatis medicamentum, causa resurrectionis primae, pignusque secundae, quia divinae plane in nobis initium substantiae. Participes, inquit Apostolus, Christi effecti sumus, si tamen initium substantiae ejus usque ad finem firmum retineamus (Hebr. III, 14). Qui enim post acceptam gratiam ad vomitum suum revertitur, Divitias quas devoravit evomet, et de ventre illius extrahet eas Deus. Vel certe panis ejus in utero illius vertetur in fel aspidum intrinsecus: quia nimirum gratia percepta in poenam conscientiae vertitur, cum sanguis Testamenti, quo sanctificatus quis fuerat, pollutus ducitur, et Spiritui gratiae contumelia irrogatur. Hoc contemptu et nausea divitiae devoratae evomuntur, ita ut de eo qui ejusmodi est, dicatur: Non remansit quidquam de cibo ejus, et propterea nihil permanebit de bonis illius.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 4. Therefore, since those who have riches enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty, and those who hoard up silver sooner weigh it out for empty things than for bread — I mean the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, with which the paschal Lamb is to be eaten today — you blessed poor, children of the poor Crucified One, you, I say, who have no silver, hasten, buy and eat. Those who have nothing buy that good thing far more readily and easily than those who possess much. When means are lacking, good will suffices for the purchase — and those who are poorer in goods are often the richer in that very will. It is indeed such as these whom Scripture rightly invites: Come, buy wine and milk without silver, and without any price (Isai. LV, 1). Do you see, O happy poor man, that only good will is demanded of you, and that the whole worth of so great a transaction consists in that alone? Do not ungratefully refuse what is offered so freely; rather, do not lose, by an ungrateful will, what you had already merited by blessed poverty. Recognize how great a gain it is to have no part in the ruin of the world, so that you may have a part in the resurrection of Christ. Understand how great a happiness it is not to be made drunk with the luxury and fury of this age, so that you may drink new wine with Christ in the kingdom of his Father. The paschal Lamb himself invites his friends to the delights of his body and blood: Eat, he says, O friends, drink, and be inebriated, O dearly beloved (Cantic. V, 1). This food and drink is the mystery of life, the medicine of immortality, the cause of the first resurrection, and the pledge of the second, because it is plainly in us the beginning of divine substance. We have been made partakers, says the Apostle, of Christ, if indeed we hold the beginning of his substance firm unto the end (Hebr. III, 14). For he who, after receiving grace, returns to his own vomit, shall vomit up the riches he had devoured, and God shall draw them out of his belly. Or certainly, within him, his bread shall be turned to the gall of asps in his belly — because indeed the grace received is turned into punishment of conscience, when the blood of the Testament, by which one had been sanctified, is accounted polluted, and insult is done to the Spirit of grace. By this contempt and loathing, the riches that had been devoured are vomited up, so that of such a one it is said: Nothing remained of his food, and therefore nothing of his goods shall remain.

passages.label: Latin original
passages.text: 5. Videat autem ne forte et ipsum terribilis ista perstringat sententia, qui, cum per gratiam devotionis repletus fuerit in bonis domus Dei, nihil prorsus ex illis in memoria retinet, ut memoriam abundantiae suavitatis divinae nobis eructet; non saporem in sermonibus, tanquam gustum in faucibus; non virtutem in moribus, tanquam succum in visceribus; sed dum statim totum per inania vel scurrilia revomit, gratiam sibi in iram convertit. Prorsus in iram, et iram terribilem, si in ipsum cadit quod Scriptura contexuit dicens: Cum satiatus fuerit, arctabitur, et irruet in eum omnis dolor. Utinam impleatur venter ejus, ut immittat in eum iram furoris sui, et pluat super eum bellum suum (Job XX, 15, 21, 23). Justum quippe sentiebat atque consentiebat Propheta ut pluat super peccatores bellum, qui ad pluviam voluntariam, fructum pacis non retulerunt; sitque ignis, sulphur et spiritus procellarum pars calicis eorum, qui calicem Domini indigne biberunt. Terra enim saepe venientem bibens imbrem, et generans herbam opportunam, accipit benedictionem; proferens autem spinas et tribulos, reproba est et maledictio proxima; cujus consummatio in combustionem (Hebr. VI, 7, 8). Confidimus autem de vobis, fratres, meliora et viciniora saluti. Tantum gratiae Dei grati sitis, et sicut in novam creaturam translati estis paschalibus mysteriis, sic in novitate vitae semper ambuletis. Qui ergo participes Christi effecti estis societate fidei, participatione sacramenti, communione Spiritus sancti, initium substantiae ejus non solum usque ad finem firmum retinere, sed etiam sedulo augere nitimini: ut, qui per tot munerum praerogativas partem habere coepistis in resurrectione prima, tanti fiducia pignoris in die agnitionis consignati, jus vobis perpetuum vindicetis in resurrectione secunda, praestante Domino nostro Jesu Christo, resurrectione et vita nostra, qui pro nobis mortuus per triduum, jam vivit et regnat per omnia saecula saeculorum. Amen.

passages.label: English
passages.text: 5. But let him take care lest this terrible sentence strike him as well who, when he has been filled through the grace of devotion with the good things of the house of God, retains nothing at all of them in memory from which to belch forth—no savor in his speech, as a taste lingering in the mouth; no virtue in his conduct, as sap in the inward parts—but who, straightway vomiting back the whole through empty or scurrilous things, turns grace into wrath for himself. Into wrath indeed, and terrible wrath, if upon him falls what Scripture has woven together, saying: 'When he shall be filled, he shall be straitened, and every sorrow shall rush upon him. Would that his belly might be filled, that God may send upon him the wrath of His fury, and rain down His war upon him' (Job XX, 15, 21, 23). For the Prophet rightly judged, and rightly consented, that war should rain down upon sinners who, in return for the willing rain, did not bring forth the fruit of peace; and that fire, brimstone, and a spirit of storms should be the portion of the cup of those who drank the cup of the Lord unworthily. For the earth, which often drinks in the rain that comes upon it, and brings forth herbage fit for use, receives a blessing; but that which brings forth thorns and briers is worthless and near to a curse, whose end is to be burned (Hebr. VI, 7, 8). But we are confident of better things concerning you, brothers, and things nearer to salvation. Only be grateful for the grace of God, and just as you have been transformed into a new creature by the paschal mysteries, so may you always walk in newness of life. You, then, who have been made partakers of Christ through fellowship of faith, participation in the sacrament, and communion of the Holy Spirit, strive not only to hold firm the beginning of his substance even to the end, but also diligently to increase it: so that you, who through so many prerogatives of gifts have begun to have part in the first resurrection, sealed by the assurance of so great a pledge on the day of recognition, may claim for yourselves a perpetual right in the second resurrection, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, our resurrection and our life, having been dead for us for three days, now lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The edition numbers the second section 3, so two sections carry that number. The reading keeps the printed numeral.

passages.label: Editorial note
passages.text: The blessing on those who share in the first resurrection is Revelation 20:6. The edition prints Apoc. XX, 5 here and Apoc. xx, 6 when the verse returns in the second section.
